cases.name: Rebekah and Abraham’s servant
cases.charge: Abraham: making his servant swear to take no wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites. The servant: asking a sign at the well and worshipping when it came to pass. Rebekah: drawing for the camels, saying, I will go, and covering herself with a vail
cases.summary: Abraham, old and blessed in all things, made the eldest servant of his house swear that he would take no wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites, but go to his own country and kindred, for the Most High never condoned marrying into the other nations (Genesis 24:1-4). The servant asked a sign at the well, and before he had done speaking Rebekah came out, gave him drink and drew for all his camels, and he bowed his head and worshipped (Genesis 24:12-27). Her family inquired at her mouth and she said, I will go; when she saw Isaac she covered herself with a vail, and she became his wife, and he loved her (Genesis 24:58-67).
offenseFull: Abraham was old and well stricken in age, and the Lord had blessed him in all things; he made the eldest servant of his house swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, that he would not take a wife for his son of the daughters of the Canaanites among whom he dwelt, but go to his own country and kindred (Genesis 24:1-4). The Most High never condoned marrying into the other nations; the custom was kept from the beginning, long before Moses, and the reason is given in the law itself: they will turn away thy son from following the Most High to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). Solomon is the prime example: he loved women of the other nations, went into their gods, and had to repent; even him did outlandish women cause to sin (Nehemiah 13:26). Take a wife of the seed of your fathers, for Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob all married wives of their own kindred and were blessed in their children (Tobit 4:12). A woman of a strange nation will teach the son the ways of her own father’s people.

The forefathers arranged marriages. The building block of a strong nation is a strong family, and a strong family comes from marriage, not from young men and women left to their own accord. Abraham told the servant that the Lord God of heaven would send his angel before him; he trusted the oath would be fulfilled, because the Most High goes before the errand (Genesis 24:7).

At the well the servant prayed and asked a sign: the damsel who offers to draw for the camels also is the one appointed (Genesis 24:12-14). Before he had done speaking, Rebekah came out, born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother; the marriages stayed within the kindred (Genesis 24:15). She was very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her: undefiled and beautiful, the kind of wife the forefathers had from the beginning (Genesis 24:16). She gave a stranger drink and drew for all his camels; that kind and easily entreated spirit is the pattern for the daughters of Israel (Genesis 24:17-20). Scripture rarely describes the beauty of wives, and Rebekah is known for hospitality and faith.

When the sign came to pass exactly, the servant bowed his head and worshipped the Lord, who had led him in the way to the house of his master’s brethren (Genesis 24:26-27). Her family asked to keep her ten days, and the servant asked them not to hinder him, seeing the Lord had prospered his way; so they called the damsel and inquired at her mouth, and she said, I will go (Genesis 24:55-58). They blessed her to be the mother of thousands of millions, and that her seed should possess the gate of those which hate them: that is prophecy of Israel, which shall possess the gates of its enemies (Genesis 24:59-60).

Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide; that was a custom of the forefathers, showing the Lord was dealing with them long before the law was written at Sinai (Genesis 24:63). Brothers need that time alone with the Lord, meditating in the scriptures and in prayer. When Rebekah saw Isaac she lighted off the camel, and when the servant told her it was his master, she took a vail and covered herself, which is respect (Genesis 24:64-65). The four mothers covered their heads with actual material as a sign of submission. The power a woman has on her head is obedience, and long hair does not do away with the covering, for Rebekah covered herself (1 Corinthians 11:10-15).
judgmentFull: The servant told Isaac all things that he had done, and Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah’s tent, and she became his wife, and he loved her; he was comforted after his mother’s death, for he received a righteous wife like unto his mother (Genesis 24:66-67). She became his wife, and then he loved her: ordained, and then love. There is no love at first sight; what is called that is lust at first sight, and disorder follows when it is the primary mover. Isaac and Rebekah are the type of marriage in which both submit to the scriptures, both are obedient, and both are happy.

Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah to wife. Brothers waiting on a wife, be patient and stay virtuous; Isaac waited forty years, and the Most High had the right sister appointed (Genesis 25:20). Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife because she was barren, as all husbands should do: pray for your wives; and the Lord was entreated of him, and Rebekah conceived (Genesis 25:21). Sisters who are barren, do not nag your husband, but pray, because only the Lord can open your womb.
The covenant narrows again here: it runs through Rebekah’s children, and of her two sons it is Jacob who carries it, for Esau sold his birthright. The covenants in Genesis cannot be broken.

cases.name: Jacob, deceiving Isaac for the blessing
cases.charge: Obeying his mother’s voice, who carried the word of the Lord that the elder shall serve the younger; receiving the blessing prophesied before his birth
cases.summary: Before either child was born the Lord told Rebekah that two nations were in her womb, two manner of people, and that the elder shall serve the younger; it was said unto her, not unto him (Genesis 25:23; Romans 9:12). Esau sold the birthright himself and despised it. When Isaac, whose eyes the Lord let grow dim, sent Esau for venison to bless him, Rebekah moved on the word she carried, took the curse upon herself, and sent Jacob in with the kid skins and his brother’s raiment (Genesis 27:1-17). Isaac blessed him, and when it was known he confirmed it: he shall be blessed (Genesis 27:33). It was not Jacob’s trickery and not his plan; the supplanting was of the Holy Ghost.
offenseFull: The children struggled together within Rebekah, and the Lord told her that two nations were in her womb, two manner of people, one stronger than the other, and the elder shall serve the younger (Genesis 25:22-23). Nations goes back to races: they were twins, but not identical, two different nations, not alike in look, behaviour or thought, down to the voice. The one people stronger than the other is the so-called blacks, Latinos and Native Americans under the line of Jacob. Good is set against evil: the works of the Most High are two and two, one against another, Jacob against Esau (Ecclesiasticus 33:14-15).

The first came out red, all over like an hairy garment; the scriptures describe the man because a nation comes from him, and Esau’s seed is the red, hairy, melanin-lacking people of the world today (Genesis 25:25). Isaac loved Esau for his venison, but Rebekah loved Jacob, because the Lord had told her the prophecy, and only Rebekah knew it (Genesis 25:28). Esau sold his birthright for red pottage and sware it away for a meal; it was not taken, he sold it, and thus Esau despised his birthright (Genesis 25:29-34).

Isaac’s eyes were dim so that he could not see, and the Lord allowed that blindness for a purpose, so that the blessing could pass to Jacob; what looks like evil can be for good, as Joseph’s slavery in Egypt was for good (Genesis 27:1; Genesis 50:20). How is the elder going to serve the younger if the elder gets all of the blessings? Rebekah heard and moved for Jacob because she carried the word from the Lord, and she knew this was the moment. Jacob himself objected that his father would feel him, and he would seem a deceiver and bring a curse upon himself, and his mother took the curse upon herself and told him only to obey her voice (Genesis 27:5-13). She was following God’s instructions from the beginning: this is all predestination, and the Most High moved her to do it.

She made savoury meat such as his father loved, put Esau’s raiment on Jacob so he would smell like the field, and put the skins of the kids of the goats on his hands and the smooth of his neck, because Esau’s hair was goat hair, straight and long, not sheep’s wool (Genesis 27:14-16). Jacob told his father he was Esau his firstborn; asked how he had found the venison so quickly, he said the Lord his God brought it to him; asked again whether he was his very son Esau, he said he was (Genesis 27:19-24). Christians read this and blame Jacob, saying he stole Esau’s blessing and lied; but Esau had already despised and sold his birthright. Isaac was not stupid: hunting venison takes time; he felt him, and he called him near to kiss him, because he wanted to smell him (Genesis 27:21-27).

Jacob is called a supplanter, but the supplanting was of the Holy Ghost: the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, it was said unto her, not unto him, that the elder shall serve the younger (Romans 9:11-13). What Jacob did was due to his mother, and she was being obedient to God.
judgmentFull: The blessing is rulership of the earth: the dew of heaven, the fatness of the earth, plenty of corn and wine; people serving him and nations bowing down to him, not as equals; lordship over his brethren; a curse upon every one that cursed him and a blessing upon every one that blessed him (Genesis 27:28-29). All of Israel has this blessing, but it does not come into fruition until the appointed time.

When Esau came in, Isaac trembled very exceedingly and confirmed it: he had blessed him, and he shall be blessed, and it could not be undone; he had made him Esau’s lord and given him all his brethren for servants, and that is how the elder shall serve the younger (Genesis 27:33, 37). Esau said Jacob had supplanted him these two times, but Jacob supplanted him once; Esau sold the birthright himself and told his father a pity story (Genesis 27:36). Esau’s portion was the fatness of the earth and to live by the sword, and this is the time period now, where Esau has the dominion and rules first; when his rule is done, Jacob comes into power (Genesis 27:39-40).

Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing and purposed in his heart to slay him, the same hatred Cain had for Abel; he said it in his heart, and the words were told to Rebekah, for the Lord was dealing with her (Genesis 27:41-42). She sent Jacob to Laban her brother until Esau’s fury turned away, weary of her life because of the daughters of Heth (Genesis 27:43-46). Isaac blessed Jacob and charged him not to take a wife of the daughters of Canaan, and the blessing of Abraham passed to Jacob and his seed (Genesis 28:1-4). Christians say Jacob was the evil son and Esau the good one; Jacob was the good one, and Esau the profane one, the fornicating one, the one that despised his birthright.

cases.name: Esau
cases.charge: Despising his birthright; marrying the daughters of Heth against the fathers’ law; hating his brother because of the blessing and purposing to kill him
cases.summary: The first came out red, all over like an hairy garment, and his colour was written down because a nation comes out of him; Esau is the return of Cain’s lineage, as Jacob is the return of Seth (Genesis 25:25). A man of the field as Cain was, he sold the birthright for a meal, took Hittite wives to his parents’ grief, and when the blessing went to Jacob he purposed in his heart to slay him (Genesis 25:34; Genesis 26:34-35; Genesis 27:41). His own anger turned away; his children’s did not, and the perpetual hatred remained in his seed (Ezekiel 35:5).
offenseFull: The first came out red, all over like an hairy garment, and they called his name Esau (Genesis 25:25). Esau means wasted away: his melanin was wasted away. Jacob is not described, because he looked like his father and mother and like everybody from the time of Adam; the only colour differential was Esau, so the scribes had to write down his colour. Cain’s line was cursed with a lack of melanin, and in Esau that lineage returns. This is the nativity of the first Caucasian man, Esau, the so-called white man. Jacob’s hand took hold on Esau’s heel, and that is prophecy: Esau is the end of the world and Jacob the beginning of it that followeth (2 Esdras 6:7-9).

Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field, as Cain was a tiller of the ground; Cain was the firstborn and Esau the firstborn, and it is the same spirit (Genesis 25:27; Genesis 4:2). He came from the field faint and asked for that same red pottage, with red meat in it not cooked all the way, and therefore was his name called Edom, red (Genesis 25:29-30). He asked what profit the birthright would do him, sware, and sold it; he was the heir of Abraham’s inheritance and did not care about God’s blessings, and that is what made him profane (Genesis 25:31-34). A man fails of the grace of God when God says something and he refuses to do it (Hebrews 12:15).

At forty he took Judith and Bashemath, daughters of the Hittites, which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah; he went straight against the fathers’ law of marrying within the kindred, and that is the nature of the vessel (Genesis 26:34-35). Later he went to Ishmael and took Mahalath also, answering his father’s grief by doing his own thing (Genesis 28:8-9). That is what made him a fornicator: whoredom falls under fornication, and he married Hittite and Ishmaelite women, when the fathers from the beginning married their own kindred (Hebrews 12:16; Tobit 4:12). His children’s mixing with the Hittites did not make Esau’s line black; God kept that line the way it is.

When the blessing went to Jacob he cried with a great and exceeding bitter cry, and told his father that Jacob had supplanted him these two times, a pity story over a birthright he had sold himself (Genesis 27:34-36). Esau became bitter after that, and thereby many were defiled; he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears (Hebrews 12:15-17). He hated Jacob because of the blessing and said in his heart that when the days of mourning for his father came he would slay his brother: the beginning of the perpetual hatred (Genesis 27:41). Cain killed Abel and was himself killed the same violent way, and that is why Rebekah asked why she should be deprived of them both in one day (Genesis 27:45; Wisdom of Solomon 10:3).
judgmentFull: His portion was the fatness of the earth and the dew of heaven; by his sword he should live, getting the lands by war, the same blessing Cain’s line had in Tubalcain’s weapons; and he should serve his brother (Genesis 27:39-40; Genesis 4:22). He first broke the yoke from off his neck in the days of Jehoram, when Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah (2 Kings 8:20). Because Israel went into sin and was conquered, Esau came out from under dominion and built up his power, and Israel has served him since: the Greeks, the Romans, the Spanish, the French, the Dutch, the Germans. This is the time of his dominion, and when his rule is done, Jacob comes into power.

His own anger turned away, but his children’s did not; the hatred passed to his seed, the perpetual hatred for which the Lord set his face against Mount Seir (Ezekiel 35:5). Edom pursued his brother with the sword, cast off all pity, and kept his wrath for ever (Amos 1:11). Their malice was bred in them and their cogitation would never be changed, for it was a cursed seed from the beginning (Wisdom of Solomon 12:10-11). In the day that the strangers carried Judah away he was as one of them, rejoiced over their destruction, laid hands on their substance and cut off those that escaped, and the Edomites burned the first temple and, as the Romans, destroyed the second (Obadiah 1:11-14; 1 Esdras 4:45).

The Lord loved Jacob and hated Esau, and laid his mountains and his heritage waste; Edom said they would return and build, and they rebuilt and became the superpower in the world, but they shall build and he will throw down, and they shall be called the border of wickedness, the people against whom the Lord hath indignation for ever (Malachi 1:2-4). Esau hated Jacob right back, because God hated him. Though he exalt himself as the eagle, as Greece, Rome, Spain, France, Russia, Britain and America all carry the eagle, and set his nest among the stars, thence the Lord will bring him down; the house of Jacob shall be a fire and the house of Esau stubble, and none shall remain (Obadiah 1:3-4, 18).

The descendants of Esau, the sworn enemies of the descendants of Jacob even to the end of the world, went out from Mount Seir, subjugated Italy, founded Rome and the Roman Empire, and hold the dominion over all Europe, Esau detaining his brother Jacob in captivity until the Messiah, the son of David, appears; and the prophecies against Edom have not yet received their full accomplishment.

cases.name: Isaac
cases.charge: Dwelling in the land the Lord told him of, and not going down into Egypt in the famine, as his father Abraham had obeyed the Lord’s voice
cases.summary: In a famine, when Egypt had food, the Lord told Isaac not to go down into Egypt but to sojourn in the land, and performed to him the oath sworn to Abraham, because Abraham obeyed his voice (Genesis 26:1-5). Isaac did what he was told and dwelt in Gerar (Genesis 26:6). He reaped a hundredfold, and the Philistines envied him because he was a law keeper (Genesis 26:12-14).
offenseFull: There was a famine in the land, and Isaac had a plan: he had to move to where there was food, and in that region Egypt usually had food, so Egypt was his first logical choice (Genesis 26:1). The Most High stepped in and told him not to go down into Egypt, but to dwell in the land which he would tell him of (Genesis 26:2). There had to be some fear in it, for he was not moving to see the sights; he moved because of the famine, and he was told to stay, and he did.

Everything that went to Abraham now passed on to Isaac, from the voice of the Lord to him: seed as the stars of heaven, all these countries, and in his seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed (Genesis 26:3-4). That does not put everybody in the covenant. The seed is Christ, and the children of the prophets and of the covenant are Israel, scattered into every nation; the all nations is Israel, because Israel is in all nations, and through Christ scattered Israel in all the kindreds of the earth receives repentance, being turned every one from his iniquities, and comes back to the Father (Galatians 3:16; Acts 3:25-26; Amos 2:11).

The reason the oath stood is that Abraham obeyed the Lord’s voice and kept his charge, his commandments, his statutes and his laws (Genesis 26:5). The covenant passed from Abraham down to Isaac because his father kept it, and it would not have existed had Abraham not walked perfect. Isaac dwelt in Gerar, where he was told to dwell; he did not go to Egypt; he did what he was told (Genesis 26:6).

Isaac said of Rebekah that she was his sister, fearing that the men of the place would kill him for her, as his father had done before him; and Abimelech looked out at a window and saw Isaac sporting with Rebekah his wife and knew (Genesis 26:7-11). Take the lesson from the sporting: love your wife, play with your wife, keep the flirting and the freshness in the marriage, and give her love, attention and affection all the days; Isaac took full advantage of living joyfully with the wife he loved (Ecclesiastes 9:9).
judgmentFull: Isaac sowed in that land and received in the same year a hundredfold, and the Lord blessed him, and the man waxed great until he became very great; and the Philistines envied him and stopped with earth the wells his father’s servants had digged (Genesis 26:12-15). The Philistines envied Isaac because he was a law keeper. The nations envy the prosperity of Israel; it is not for anything done to them, for the blessing itself is what is hated, and they want Israel’s blessing to be their blessing. Abimelech then told him to go from them, for he was much mightier than they (Genesis 26:16).

Isaac digged again the wells of his father, and the herdmen of Gerar strove for Esek and for Sitnah; he removed and digged Rehoboth, and they strove not, and he said that now the Lord had made room for them, and they would be fruitful in the land (Genesis 26:17-22).

Abimelech came to him from Gerar with Phichol the chief captain of his army, saying they had done him nothing but good, though his people had stopped the wells and sent him away; and Isaac answered plainly, asking why they came to him, seeing they hated him (Genesis 26:26-29). The Philistines hated Isaac, and the Lord had sent him away from them. They knew the Lord was with him because the land was blessed while Isaac was there; when Isaac left, there was no more blessing, and the Lord dried up the land. Isaac was not simple: he separated from the people that hated him rather than assimilating among them, and he dealt with their covenant with open eyes, for words can be smoother than butter while war is in the heart (Psalms 55:21).
He made them a feast, and they sware one to another in the morning, and he sent them away in peace; and that same day his servants told him they had found water (Genesis 26:30-33).

cases.name: Laban and the changed wages
cases.charge: Deceiving his kinsman and hired servant: giving the elder daughter in place of the younger, and changing his wages ten times over twenty years
cases.summary: Laban of the house of Nahor, an idolater as his fathers were, received Jacob as his bone and his flesh, took seven years of service for Rachel and brought him Leah (Genesis 29:14-30). The Lord blessed Laban for Jacob’s sake, yet Laban deceived him, changed his wages ten times, and would have sent him away empty (Genesis 30:27; Genesis 31:7, 42). When Jacob went home Laban pursued him, and God came to him in a dream and told him to speak to Jacob neither good nor bad (Genesis 31:23-29).
offenseFull: Jacob went north out of Canaan and then east to Haran, where the family had remained since Terah stopped there; Laban was of Nahor’s line, and Jacob had come home to dwell among family (Genesis 29:1-5; Genesis 11:26-31). Laban said that Jacob was surely his bone and his flesh, which in the scriptures means, we are family, and because Jacob was his brother he asked what his wages should be (Genesis 29:14-15).

Leah was tender eyed, but Rachel was beautiful and well favoured, and Jacob loved Rachel and served seven years for her, and they seemed to him but a few days for the love he had to her (Genesis 29:16-20). Many have run out of their wits for women and become servants for their sakes: Jacob became a servant fourteen years, because he was deceived and served another seven (1 Esdras 4:18-26). In the evening Laban brought Leah to him, and in the morning it was Leah; Laban answered that it must not be so done in their country, to give the younger before the firstborn, and required seven other years for Rachel (Genesis 29:23-30). Laban did Jacob wrong from the first wife.

Laban had learned by experience that the Lord had blessed him for Jacob’s sake; with Jacob in his household he was increasing (Genesis 30:27). Jacob understood that the Most High was blessing Laban because of him, and he asked when he should provide for his own house also (Genesis 30:29-30). A man looks to provide for his own house.

Jacob asked no gift, only terms: the speckled, spotted and brown cattle from that day would be his hire (Genesis 30:31-32). That refusal is the spirit the forefathers walked in, for the Most High was their provider (Genesis 14:21-23). Jacob set terms that could be checked in the open, so that his righteousness would answer for him in time to come: judge me on my works; my word is my bond. He said it because he knew they were going to have something bad to say about his increase (Genesis 30:33). Laban agreed, then removed that same day the ringstraked and spotted cattle into the hand of his own sons and set three days’ journey between himself and Jacob (Genesis 30:34-36).

Laban’s sons said that Jacob had taken away all that was their father’s, and Laban’s countenance was not toward him as before; Laban had just acknowledged that the Lord blessed him for Jacob’s sake, and now he looked at Jacob sideways because of what his sons said (Genesis 31:1-2). Laban deceived Jacob and changed his wages ten times: when he said the speckled shall be your wages, the cattle bare speckled, and when he said the ringstraked, they bare ringstraked (Genesis 31:7-8). Laban was not right; he was taking from Jacob what he had earned, and that is evil. Jacob served fourteen years for the two daughters and six for the cattle, consumed by drought by day and frost by night, and Laban would have sent him away empty after twenty years (Genesis 31:38-42).

Laban pursued him and asked why he had stolen his gods (Genesis 31:23, 30). That question tells what Laban was: an idolater of the house of Nahor, like his fathers who served other gods; that is why the Most High told Abram to get out from his country and from his kindred, separating him so that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and their children after them, would not be idolaters (Joshua 24:2; Genesis 12:1).
judgmentFull: God came to Laban the Syrian in a dream by night and told him to take heed that he speak not to Jacob either good or bad (Genesis 31:24). That was a warning: threaten Jacob, and I will hurt you; leave him alone. Laban admitted that it was in the power of his hand to do Jacob hurt, but the God of Jacob’s father had spoken to him the night before (Genesis 31:29).

The God of Jacob’s father had been with him, and God suffered Laban not to hurt him (Genesis 31:5-7). God had become a shield for Jacob, so that after all those afflictions Jacob came out victorious over him, and every time Laban changed the wages the Lord blessed Jacob. God saw his affliction and the labour of his hands and rebuked Laban the night before (Genesis 31:42). God sees the affliction of the righteous; when a man knows he is right, he has no need to go after anyone, for God will fight for him.

They made a covenant at the heap and the pillar, that neither would pass over it to the other for harm, and Laban rose early, kissed his sons and his daughters, blessed them and returned to his place (Genesis 31:44-55).

cases.name: Rachel and the stolen teraphim
cases.charge: Stealing her father’s images, worshipping idols in the covenant household, and hiding them under her with a lie when he searched
cases.summary: Rachel stole the images that were her father’s, idols of an idolater’s house; she was beautiful, and she was a thief (Genesis 31:19; Proverbs 31:30). She hid them, sat upon them, and lied to her father when he searched (Genesis 31:34-35). The strange gods stayed in the household until Jacob set his house in order before Bethel (Genesis 35:1-4). The Lord knew the spirit in her; she was not right, and the Lord killed her after she bore Benjamin (Genesis 35:16-19).
offenseFull: Rachel was beautiful, the one Jacob loved, but she had a character: the Lord knew the spirit in the two sisters, and when Leah was hated he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren (Genesis 29:17, 30-31). Favour is deceitful and beauty is vain, but a woman that fears the Lord shall be praised (Proverbs 31:30).

When Laban went to shear his sheep, Rachel had stolen the images that were her father’s (Genesis 31:19). Yes, she was fine, but she was a thief; she might have been a fine thief, but she was a thief. Those images were carved graven images, and they were gods; that which is made with hands is cursed, and so is he that made it (Wisdom of Solomon 14:8). Laban’s own question, why he had stolen his gods, tells what house she came out of: Laban was an idolater of the house of Nahor, whose fathers served other gods (Genesis 31:30; Joshua 24:2).

Jacob answered that with whomsoever Laban found his gods, let him not live, for Jacob knew not that Rachel had stolen them (Genesis 31:32). Jacob did not know his wife was a thief. A man has to know his wife, for a woman can be doing secret evil, and then things happen in the marriage and nobody knows why.

Rachel had taken the images and put them in the camel’s furniture and sat upon them, and told her father she could not rise up before him, for the custom of women was upon her; and he searched and found not the images (Genesis 31:34-35). The custom of women is her menstruation, the sorrow pronounced on the woman, in which the law made her unclean (Genesis 3:16; Leviticus 15:19). Rachel was still worshipping idols; she was not worshipping the God of Israel in the beginning, and she had the spirit of a thief, an idolater and a liar.
judgmentFull: The images stayed in the camp. God told Jacob to go up to Bethel, and Jacob said to his household and to all that were with him to put away the strange gods that were among them, and be clean, and change their garments (Genesis 35:1-2). The strange gods were there because Rachel had stolen her father’s images and hidden them. Jacob knew his wife was dealing with idols, and he was the one who had to set the house in order: to go and deal with the Lord he had to get his house in order first, and he did it immediately.

They gave Jacob all the strange gods and their earrings, and Jacob hid them under the oak by Shechem (Genesis 35:4). Idolatry hidden in the household must be put away before you can stand at Bethel. Rachel was still his wife; he kept her and put the idols away.

From Eve to Rachel the scriptures warn how sin enters through the household, for of the woman came the beginning of sin; sisters, stay in the spirit and guard against the serpent’s beguiling as the mothers were beguiled (Ecclesiasticus 25:24).

Rachel travailed in hard labour and died bearing her second son; and Jacob set a pillar upon her grave in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem (Genesis 35:16-20). God killed Rachel. As pretty as she was, she was not right, and the Lord killed her after she had Benjamin: the Lord gave her two children, Joseph and Benjamin, and then she had to go.

cases.name: Jacob at Peniel
cases.charge: Praying humbly and pleading the covenant before his brother who purposed to slay him; and wrestling until the breaking of the day, saying, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me
cases.summary: Facing Esau, who had purposed to slay him, Jacob was greatly afraid, prayed humbly, pleaded the covenant made to the fathers, and sent his present before him (Genesis 32:3-20). Left alone, he wrestled a man until the breaking of the day; the angel had to put his thigh out of joint to stop him, and with his thigh out of joint Jacob held on and would not let go without a blessing (Genesis 32:24-26). He was named Israel, a prince that has power with God, for he had power over the angel and prevailed (Genesis 32:28; Hosea 12:3-4).
offenseFull: His messengers returned saying that Esau was coming with four hundred men, and Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed (Genesis 32:3-7). His fear was rightful: the last word he had of Esau was that Esau purposed in his heart to slay him once their father’s mourning came. The hatred began at the blessing, and the scriptures show in Ezekiel that it never ended. The violent man imagines mischiefs in his heart and is continually gathered together for war, and that is what Jacob understood was coming toward him (Genesis 27:41-42; Psalms 140:1-2).

Jacob prayed humbly, confessing that he was not worthy of the least of all the mercies, and asked to be delivered from the hand of his brother; he was not too proud to confess his fear to the Most High (Genesis 32:9-11). He pleaded the covenant, that the Lord had said he would make his seed as the sand of the sea. That is the pattern for prayer: plead the promise made to the fathers and ask the Most High to remember his covenant (Genesis 32:12).

He sent droves before him as a present, spaced apart, every servant instructed what to say, to appease Esau with the present that went before him; he moved strategically to soften Esau before they met face to face, and that was scriptural, for a man’s gift makes room for him and brings him before great men (Genesis 32:13-20; Proverbs 18:16).

Jacob was left alone, and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day (Genesis 32:24). That is endurance and strength: a boxing match is twelve rounds, and Jacob fought until daybreak. The man had to touch the hollow of his thigh and put it out of joint, because Jacob would not be beaten (Genesis 32:25). With his thigh out of joint he did not give up; he kept on wrestling, and he would not let the angel go except he blessed him (Genesis 32:26). That is faith with works. Cleave unto the Most High and depart not away, that you may be increased at your last end; fight the good fight of faith and lay hold on eternal life the way Jacob laid hold and would not let go (Ecclesiasticus 2:3; 1 Timothy 6:12).

Jacob was trained by Isaac and Abraham, and Abraham was a warrior who armed three hundred and eighteen trained servants born in his own house and went by night to bring back Lot (Genesis 14:14-16). Imagine his descendants, David running through warriors, and Samson: the forefathers were intellectual and physically powerful men.
judgmentFull: His name should be called no more Jacob, but Israel, for as a prince he had power with God and with men, and had prevailed (Genesis 32:27-28). Israel means a prince that has power with God, and no other man in scripture wrestled an angel. The Lord put his name upon the men of Israel, princes of God, and they prevail through Christ. Jacob was a god on the earth (Psalms 82:6).

The God of Israel is he that gives strength and power to his people; he is the power source. When Israel went astray and served other gods, the name and the power were taken, and the nations called the people by every other name. Returning to the Most High is how the name and the power return, and not by carnal weapons of warfare (Psalms 68:35). Israel is still wrestling, mentally and spiritually, to get its true name back and a true understanding of who it is as a people, and to put away the slave names and the slave mentality.

The one Jacob wrestled was an angel: by his strength he had power with God, he had power over the angel and prevailed, and he wept and made supplication unto him (Hosea 12:3-4). The man would not give his name, but he blessed Jacob there, and Jacob called the place Peniel, for he had seen God face to face and his life was preserved (Genesis 32:29-30). The word God, Elohim, is plural, which clears up the passages where men are said to have seen God and yet no man has seen the Father.

The sun rose upon him and he halted upon his thigh; therefore the children of Israel eat not of the sinew which shrank, which is upon the hollow of the thigh, unto this day (Genesis 32:31-32). God appeared to Jacob again at Bethel and confirmed the name: a nation and a company of nations would be of him, and kings would come out of his loins (Genesis 35:10-11). The nation and company of nations of Abraham’s covenant is Israel.

cases.name: Shechem son of Hamor
cases.charge: Taking Jacob’s daughter Dinah and defiling her, coveting what was not his behind her father’s back; then seeking to marry into the house he had wronged and make the two peoples one
cases.summary: Dinah, Jacob’s only daughter, went out to see the daughters of the land without supervision, and Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, took her, lay with her and defiled her (Genesis 34:1-2). He did it backwards, taking first and loving after, and his father came proposing that the two peoples intermarry and become one, the exact opposite of the law (Genesis 34:3-10). On the third day Simeon and Levi slew Hamor and Shechem with the edge of the sword, a sword given of God to take vengeance of the strangers who defiled the maid (Genesis 34:25-26; Judith 9:2).
offenseFull: Dinah went out to see the daughters of the land without supervision, and Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, took her, lay with her and defiled her (Genesis 34:1-2). The forefathers were not perfect men: they let their daughter walk around, and she was taken by a Hamite, for the Hivite was of Canaan (Genesis 10:15-17). The lesson stands for every generation: keep watch over the daughters and do not give overmuch liberty, for the father wakes for the daughter, lest she be defiled and made a reproach (Ecclesiasticus 7:24; Ecclesiasticus 26:10; Ecclesiasticus 42:9-11). A sister should not be in such places without the presence of a man, and she should keep the modest apparel the scriptures document.

This was stranger rape, a violent act: he forced himself on her (Deuteronomy 22:25-27). Judith remembers it: they loosened the girdle of a maid to defile her and discovered her thigh to her shame, meaning he tore her clothes off, and polluted her virginity to her reproach (Judith 9:2). Under it is a covetous spirit, desiring another person’s body, something that does not belong to you; that is the sickness, and it is the tenth commandment broken (Exodus 20:17).

Dinah was also enticed. She went out on her own, away from her father and her twelve brothers; Shechem saw that she was not walking in the spirit of her fathers and took her, and his soul clave to her, and he loved her and spoke kindly to her, which is the seducing (Genesis 34:3). She was enticed, beguiled, allured away from her protection. To go behind the father’s back and entice the daughter is coveting and is evil, for the daughter is under her father, and if the father utterly refuses to give her, the man pays and still does not get her (Exodus 22:16-17). Jacob, Simeon and Levi took that risk with the surrounding nations rather than let Shechem keep Dinah.

He did it backwards, taking first and loving after; that is the world’s pattern, not righteousness. When Jacob’s sons heard it, the men were grieved and very wroth, because he had wrought folly in Israel in lying with Jacob’s daughter, which ought not to be done; the laws were in place and kept long before they were written in stone at Sinai (Genesis 34:7). Israel should not be mixing with other nations, and on top of that a violent act was committed against one of Israel’s daughters.

Hamor proposed the exact opposite of the law: make marriages with us, give your daughters to us and take our daughters, dwell with us and become one people (Genesis 34:8-10). Assimilation and intermarriage is the offer the nations always make, and it is the offer the law forbids. The sons of Jacob answered deceitfully that they could not give their sister to one uncircumcised, and required every male of the city to be circumcised; Hamor and Shechem persuaded the city by reasoning that the wealth of Jacob’s house would become theirs (Genesis 34:13-24).
judgmentFull: After such a violent act swift judgment was waiting for him, and the marriage offer was his attempt to clean up the act. On the third day, when they were sore, Simeon and Levi took each man his sword, came upon the city boldly and slew all the males, and slew Hamor and Shechem his son with the edge of the sword, and took Dinah out of Shechem’s house (Genesis 34:25-26). Father and son both received it: a violent act deserves a violent judgment, and the law for the man who forces a damsel is death (Deuteronomy 22:25).

Two men do not take a city alone. The sword of Simeon was given of God to take vengeance of the strangers that defiled the maid; the Lord gave their rulers to be slain and orchestrated it, and they were moved with the zeal of the Most High (Judith 9:2-4). The judgment fell not only on the one who did it but on those who consented to it.

Jacob was troubled that they had made him to stink among the inhabitants of the land, being few in number (Genesis 34:30). The brothers answered, should he deal with our sister as with a harlot? There shall be no whore of the daughters of Israel; the daughters of Israel are not to be handled so (Genesis 34:31; Deuteronomy 23:17). After that the record says nothing more of Dinah; she had to live with the stain.

cases.name: Simeon and Levi at Shechem
cases.charge: Answering Shechem and Hamor deceitfully, and in their anger slaying every male of the city while the men were sore; anger that Jacob cursed for being fierce, and wrath for being cruel
cases.summary: When Shechem defiled their sister Dinah, the sons of Jacob answered him and Hamor deceitfully, requiring every male of the city to be circumcised, and on the third day, when the men were sore, Simeon and Levi slew every male (Genesis 34:13-26). Jacob on his deathbed cursed their anger and their wrath and divided them in Jacob and scattered them in Israel (Genesis 49:5-7). Simeon is the so-called Dominican and Levi the so-called Haitian today, brethren on the one island of Hispaniola, divided.
offenseFull: Shechem the son of Hamor took Dinah, Jacob’s only daughter, and defiled her, and her brothers were grieved and very wroth, because he had wrought folly in Israel (Genesis 34:1-7). Hamor proposed the exact opposite of the law, that the two peoples give and take daughters and become one people; assimilation and intermarriage is the offer the nations always make, and it is the offer the law forbids (Genesis 34:8-10).

The sons of Jacob answered deceitfully: they could not give their sister to one uncircumcised, and every male of the city must be circumcised before they would consent; Hamor and Shechem persuaded the whole city, reasoning that the wealth of Jacob’s house would become theirs (Genesis 34:13-24).

On the third day, when they were sore, Simeon and Levi took each man his sword, came upon the city boldly and slew all the males; they slew Hamor and Shechem, took Dinah out, and the sons of Jacob spoiled the city and carried away the substance and the households, because the city had defiled their sister (Genesis 34:25-29). Simeon and Levi did not play.

Two men do not take a city alone. The sword of Simeon was given of God to take vengeance of the strangers that defiled the maid; they were moved with the zeal of the Most High, and he was behind the judgment (Judith 9:2-4).

Jacob was troubled that they had made him to stink among the inhabitants of the land, being few in number, and feared the nations round about would gather against his house (Genesis 34:30). The brothers answered, should he deal with our sister as with a harlot? There shall be no whore of the daughters of Israel (Genesis 34:31; Deuteronomy 23:17).
judgmentFull: Jacob gathered his sons to tell them what should befall them in the last days. The blessings are twofold, speaking to each tribe in its own day and in the last days, and they show who the tribes are today (Genesis 49:1). Simeon and Levi are brethren; instruments of cruelty are in their habitations; his soul was not to come into their secret, nor his honour be united to their assembly, for in their anger they slew a man and in their selfwill they dug down a wall; cursed be their anger, for it was fierce, and their wrath, for it was cruel; he would divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel (Genesis 49:5-7). For in their anger they slew a man refers to Shechem, when their sister was defiled and they slew every male of the city while the men were sore.

Levi had no whole portion but cities scattered throughout all the tribes, and as Judah was scattered to the four corners of the earth so was Levi, for Judah, Benjamin and Levi made up the southern kingdom (Joshua 21:1-8). Simeon’s inheritance lay within the inheritance of Judah (Joshua 19:1-9). Levi is divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel today, with Haitian communities in New York, Chicago, Miami, Europe and through the Americas.

Simeon is the so-called Dominican and Levi the so-called Haitian today. All the tribes of Israel are brethren, but Jacob named these two because in the last days they would dwell together on the same island, Hispaniola, and would not be getting along, so he had to remind them they are brothers. The instruments of cruelty in their habitations are the witchcraft practised on that island, voodoo in Haiti and brujeria in the Dominican Republic, with which they hurt their own brethren. Because of those practices the Most High does not unite them: the division on the island is of the Lord, and the two nations stay divided on one island even though Levi helped free Simeon from slavery, when Levi abolished slavery on the whole island. Simeon and Levi are known for quick tempers; their anger is a curse for the evil they did at Shechem.

The Lord also told the priests of Levi that if they would not hear and give glory to his name he would make them contemptible and base before all the people, because they had not kept his ways but had been partial in the law (Malachi 2:1-9). Levi will continue under it until Levi repents, and all the twelve tribes are under the curse for serving other gods.

When Moses came down from the mount, Levi was the first to come to him and took the sword against their own brethren who sinned, and did not acknowledge father, mother, brother or children; for they observed the Lord’s word and kept his covenant (Exodus 32:26-28; Deuteronomy 33:8-9). The only way Simeon and Levi will unite is with the word of God under the black Messiah: the law, the statutes, the commandments and the high holy days are what will unify the two tribes, and if those two tribes are unified, all twelve can be.

cases.name: Reuben
cases.charge: Going up to his father’s bed and lying with Bilhah, his father’s concubine
cases.summary: Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob, went and lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and Israel heard it (Genesis 35:22). That is fornication not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father’s wife (1 Corinthians 5:1). The judgment followed him: unstable as water, he would not excel, and because he defiled his father’s bed his birthright was given unto the sons of Joseph (Genesis 49:3-4; 1 Chronicles 5:1).
offenseFull: After Rachel died bearing Benjamin and was buried in the way to Ephrath, Israel spread his tent beyond the tower of Edar, and there Reuben lay with Bilhah (Genesis 35:16-22).

The Gentiles here are the other nations: the thing was not done even among them (1 Corinthians 5:1). The law had already forbidden it: a father’s wife is the father’s own nakedness, and that means the stepmother (Leviticus 18:8). The wicked mind reasons that she is not the biological mother, so it is fine to lust after her; the scripture says no, that is wicked. The man who lies with his father’s wife uncovers his father’s nakedness, and under the law both of them were to be put to death (Leviticus 20:11).

Even before the truth, most men know not to touch what belongs to another man: a man who deals with a married woman is watched and not trusted, for if he will do that, he will do anything. That is the covetous spirit of seeing what another man has and wanting it, and that is why the Lord put covetousness over another man’s wife in the ten commandments (Exodus 20:17).
judgmentFull: Jacob gathered his sons to tell them what should befall them in the last days, and he called Reuben his firstborn, his might, the beginning of his strength, the excellency of dignity and the excellency of power; then, unstable as water, he would not excel, because he went up to his father’s bed (Genesis 49:1-4). The firstborn is the father’s posterity, and the excellency of dignity and power belonged to him. This is the case study, the precedent, of a man lying with his father’s wife: the statute broken, and the judgment, which under the law is death, and on Reuben something more.

Because he defiled his father’s bed his birthright was given unto the sons of Joseph, and the genealogy is not to be reckoned after the birthright: although he was born first, he is not recorded as having the birthright (1 Chronicles 5:1). That is why Ephraim is called the firstborn (Jeremiah 31:9). Judah prevailed above his brethren, and of him came the chief ruler, who is Christ, though the birthright was Joseph’s, much as Esau came out first but did not keep the place of the heir (1 Chronicles 5:2).

Reuben remained a son of Israel, and his characteristic shows again: at the pit he would not have Joseph slain, meaning to return him to his father, and in the famine he offered his own two sons as surety for Benjamin (Genesis 37:21-22; Genesis 42:22, 37).

The tribe of Reuben, with Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh, went a-whoring after the gods of the people of the land, which the fringes were given to prevent, and the Most High stirred up the spirit of Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria, who carried them into captivity unto this day (1 Chronicles 5:25-26; Numbers 15:38-39).

The blessings of Jacob are for the last days, and Reuben is the so-called Seminole Indian today: the excellency of power, for the Seminoles were great warriors, and unstable as water, for they were nomads, always moving around, as the scripture said (Genesis 49:1-4). The Seminoles were the last tribe the Europeans were able to take down.

cases.name: Joseph’s brothers
cases.charge: Envying and hating their brother, conspiring to slay him, selling him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, and deceiving their father with the blood of a kid
cases.summary: Joseph was seventeen when he brought his father the evil report of his brethren, as the law of the witness required, and he dreamed that his brethren and his father bowed down to him (Genesis 37:2-11). Moved with envy, his brethren conspired to slay him, sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, and deceived their father with his coat dipped in the blood of a kid (Genesis 37:18-35; Acts 7:9). The dream came true in Egypt, their conscience convicted them, and Joseph forgave them: they thought evil against him, but God meant it unto good (Genesis 42:21; Genesis 50:15-21).
offenseFull: Joseph was seventeen years old when he brought unto his father the evil report of his brethren (Genesis 37:2). That was law, not tale bearing: a witness who hears and does not utter it bears his iniquity, and the law was already around, and Joseph kept it (Leviticus 5:1). Applying that law is what got him sold into Egypt, because his brothers hated him for it. His intent was not to spoil anyone’s pleasure; he was keeping the commandments.

Israel loved Joseph more than all his children and made him a coat of many colours, and his brethren hated him and could not speak peaceably unto him (Genesis 37:3-4). That hatred started because they saw the affinity Jacob had for Joseph. It is real hatred among brothers, and the same spirit is on Israel today, where a brother cannot even receive a shalom in peace.

He dreamed that their sheaves made obeisance to his sheaf, and then that the sun, the moon and the eleven stars bowed to him, and his father interpreted it at once (Genesis 37:5-10). The Lord speaks by the prophets in visions and similitudes, and the vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, as the likeness of a face to a face (Hosea 12:10; Ecclesiasticus 34:3). The same figures mark Israel: the woman clothed with the sun, with a crown of twelve stars, is the daughter of Zion, and the twelve stars are the tribes (Revelation 12:1).

His brethren envied him (Genesis 37:11). Envy means to covet something, and they envied his gifts and his dream. Consuming envy has no fellowship with wisdom; when envy takes over, wisdom leaves (Wisdom of Solomon 6:23). When they saw him afar off, before he even came near, they conspired to slay him and mocked him as the dreamer: that is the same spirit Cain had, and the same spirit Esau had, and whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer (Genesis 37:18-20; 1 John 3:15). As Joseph’s kin conspired to kill him, so Christ’s own brethren did not believe on him, and the chief priests and elders consulted to take him by subtilty and kill him (John 7:5; Matthew 26:3-4).

Reuben delivered him to the pit, meaning to return him to his father; Judah asked what profit there was in slaying their brother and concealing his blood, and they sold him to the Ishmaelites, the people known today as the Arab man, for twenty pieces of silver (Genesis 37:21-28). Their envy for Joseph turned into hatred for their father too, for they cared nothing for what losing the child of his old age would do to him. They dipped the coat in the blood of a kid and let their father believe an evil beast had devoured him, dealing falsely and lying against the law (Genesis 37:31-35; Leviticus 19:11). Envy will have a man do evil: the patriarchs, moved with envy, sold Joseph into Egypt, and envy caused them to persecute the one God appointed to save them (Acts 7:9).
judgmentFull: Jacob could not see the lie because the thing was of the Lord (Genesis 37:33-35). The famine itself was called by the Most High, and he sent a man before them, even Joseph, sold for a servant, whose feet they hurt with fetters, until the time that his word came (Psalms 105:16-19).

The dream came true: in the famine his ten brethren came down to buy corn and bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth (Genesis 42:6). Their conscience was activated: they were verily guilty concerning their brother, for they saw the anguish of his soul when he besought them and would not hear, and they knew this distress had come upon them for what they did to him (Genesis 42:21). Joseph turned himself about from them and wept, for although they did evil to him, he still loved his brothers (Genesis 42:24).

Judah, who had proposed the sale, became surety for Benjamin and offered to abide as a bondman in his place, for he knew his father’s life was bound up in the lad’s life (Genesis 44:30-34). When Joseph made himself known, he told them not to be grieved nor angry with themselves, for God sent him before them to preserve life and save the whole house of Israel by a great deliverance; had he not been in Egypt, they would have died in the famine (Genesis 45:4-8). Joseph kept the law of forgiveness, not until seven times but until seventy times seven: his own brothers sold him into slavery, and he forgave them, and that is the law Israel must keep with one another today (Matthew 18:21-22).

When their father died they feared he would requite them and sent pleading forgiveness; Joseph wept, and told them to fear not, for he was not in the place of God: they thought evil against him, but God meant it unto good, to save much people alive; and he comforted them and nourished them and their little ones (Genesis 50:15-21). Only a spiritual man can understand that: Joseph reflected on all that happened to him and knew it was God’s divine plan, though he may not have understood it while he was in the midst of it (Romans 8:28). Keep that spirit of forgiveness: sometimes people do evil against you, but the Most High means it unto good for you.

cases.name: Er and Onan
cases.charge: Er: wickedness in the sight of the Lord. Onan: refusing to raise up seed to his dead brother, spilling it on the ground
cases.summary: Judah took the daughter of Shuah, a Canaanite, and had Er, Onan and Shelah, and Er his firstborn was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord slew him (Genesis 38:1-7). Onan was told to go in unto his brother’s wife and raise up seed to his brother, and he refused, spilling it on the ground, and the Lord slew him also (Genesis 38:8-10). The sin was refusing to raise up seed to his brother, not the act itself, and what happened here later became law in Israel (Deuteronomy 25:5-10).
offenseFull: Judah lay with a Canaanite woman, which was forbidden; the forefathers were not the most righteous men in the world (Genesis 38:1-5). He took a wife for Er his firstborn, whose name was Tamar, and there is nothing wrong with a father taking a wife for his son; that is a good thing, and marriage is honourable in all (Genesis 38:6; Hebrews 13:4). But children can go to the left and do what is not pleasing to the Lord: people pray and fast and intercede for children and can still get unprofitable ones, and Judah had some.

Judah told Onan to go in unto his brother’s wife, marry her, and raise up seed to his brother (Genesis 38:8). That was lawful; that is how it was done: a brother died leaving no children, and the next brother raised up a child to keep the dead man’s name and land. The Most High puts stock in a name; a good name is better than precious ointment (Ecclesiastes 7:1). Genesis 38 comes before Deuteronomy 25: the law did not start with Moses.

Onan knew the seed would not be his: the child would be called after his dead brother’s name, not his own (Genesis 38:9). When he went in unto his brother’s wife he spilled it on the ground, lest he should give seed to his brother, and the seed he spilled is the seed by which a woman conceives (Leviticus 12:2). He knew he was supposed to raise up his brother’s name so that the heritage might continue, and he got the devil on him; he would not help raise up his own brother’s name.

Do not build a doctrine on the wrong point. The Lord did not slay him for putting seed on the ground; he slew him because he did not raise up seed to his dead brother. He did not love his neighbour as himself; that is the law he broke, and he despised his brother (Leviticus 19:17-18). We must have an unconditional love one for another and for our people, for what is done unto one of the least of Christ’s brethren is done unto him (Matthew 25:35-40).
judgmentFull: Both died at the Lord’s hand: Er for his wickedness, and Onan because the thing which he did displeased the Lord (Genesis 38:7, 10). The muster of Judah keeps the record that Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan, and both died childless (Numbers 26:19).

What happened here later became law: when brethren dwelt together and one died childless, his widow was not to marry a stranger; her husband’s brother took her to wife, and her firstborn succeeded in the name of the dead, that his name be not put out of Israel (Deuteronomy 25:5-6). It stood for the name not being put out because of the land inheritance in Israel. This is no longer the law, so do not try to use it as an excuse toward your brother’s wife.

The man who refused was called before the elders; his brother’s wife loosed his shoe from off his foot and spat in his face, and his house was called in Israel the house of him that hath his shoe loosed, and carried the reproach (Deuteronomy 25:7-10). In Ruth the nearer kinsman could not redeem, lest he mar his own inheritance, and the right passed to Boaz, who performed the kinsman’s part (Ruth 3:10-13; Ruth 4:1-6).

The law also guards the other end: a man who has taken a new wife does not go out to war nor is charged with any business for a year, but is free at home to cheer up his wife, so that he may raise up his own seed unto Israel, and his brother need not raise it up for him (Deuteronomy 24:5). Judah’s house did not end with these deaths: Tamar bore Pharez and Zarah, and Judah’s line went down into Egypt in the end, where Judah died with his brethren (Genesis 38:27-30; Exodus 1:6).

cases.name: Judah and Tamar
cases.charge: Not keeping his promise to give Tamar to Shelah; going in to a woman he took for a harlot by her attire; and ordering her burnt for the child he had begotten
cases.summary: Judah promised Tamar, his twice widowed daughter in law, to Shelah, and did not perform it (Genesis 38:11-14). She put off her widow’s garments, covered herself with a vail, and sat where Judah would pass; he thought her to be a harlot because of the attire and went in to her, and she took his signet, bracelets and staff as a pledge and conceived by him (Genesis 38:14-18). When he heard she was with child by whoredom he ordered her brought forth and burnt, until she produced the pledge and he acknowledged that she had been more righteous than he (Genesis 38:24-26).
offenseFull: Judah went down from his brethren and took the daughter of a Canaanite named Shuah, which was forbidden; the forefathers were not the most righteous men in the world (Genesis 38:1-2).

After Er and Onan died, Judah told Tamar to remain a widow at her father’s house till Shelah his son was grown, lest he die also as his brethren did (Genesis 38:11). Once her husband died she went back to her father’s house, because before she married her father was her head, and he would take care of her as he did before. Shelah was still too young: the key word is until he was grown, the age of a man (Tobit 1:9). Older women were not given to young boys as husbands.

When Shelah was grown and she was not given unto him to wife, she saw that Judah had not kept his promise; he forgot about her (Genesis 38:14). Judah thought her to be an harlot because of the attire; the scriptures show a harlot was always known by her dress, as the woman with the attire of an harlot and subtil of heart (Genesis 38:15; Proverbs 7:10). Judah was not the most righteous man: he asked to lie with her for the price of a kid of the flock, and gave his signet, bracelets and staff as a pledge until he sent it (Genesis 38:16-18). Although the forefather Judah thought Tamar was a harlot and went to lie with her, understanding of God’s laws teaches that we cannot do that: the members of Christ are not to be made the members of an harlot (1 Corinthians 6:15).

When his friend could not find her to receive the pledge, Judah said to let her keep it, lest they be shamed: he knew what he had done was wrong (Genesis 38:20-23). About three months after, when she began to show, he was told his daughter in law had played the harlot and was with child by whoredom, and he ordered her brought forth and burnt (Genesis 38:24). Burning was the law for a harlot. A woman promised in the covenant that plays the harlot and brings an heir by another disobeys the law of the Most High, and her reproach is not blotted out; that is why the judgment was so heavy (Ecclesiasticus 23:22-26).
judgmentFull: When she was brought forth she sent him his own signet, bracelets and staff, saying she was with child by the man whose these were, and Judah acknowledged them: she had been more righteous than he, because he had not given her to Shelah his son (Genesis 38:25-26). The child was his, and he was in the wrong. He knew her again no more, because it was wrong in the first place.

A pregnant girl returned to her father’s house would be made a public example and put to death, as Tamar nearly was; that is why Joseph, a just man, was minded to put Mary away privily, to hide her (Matthew 1:19).

Twins were in her womb: the midwife bound a scarlet thread on the hand of the first, but his brother broke forth first and was called Pharez, which is a breach, and after him came Zarah with the scarlet thread (Genesis 38:27-30). Judah’s sons were five, Er, Onan and Shelah by the Canaanite, and Pharez and Zarah by Tamar, and the line of the kings runs through Pharez (1 Chronicles 2:3-4). Pharez begat Hezron, and from him the line runs down to Boaz, Obed, Jesse and David the king, and in the genealogy of Christ, Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar (Ruth 4:18-22; Matthew 1:3). Judah’s line went down into Egypt in the end, and Judah died there with his brethren (Exodus 1:6).

cases.name: Joseph
cases.charge: Refusing his master’s wife day by day and fleeing from her, naming adultery a great wickedness and sin against God; faithful in servitude and in prison
cases.summary: Sold by his brethren at seventeen and bought by Potiphar, Joseph was faithful in his captivity, and the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for his sake (Genesis 39:1-6). Tempted day by day by his master’s wife, he refused, calling it a great wickedness and sin against God long before Sinai, and when she caught his garment he fled from sin as from the face of a serpent (Genesis 39:7-12). Lied on and put in prison, he kept the laws of God there also, and the Lord was with him and gave him favour, so that he would stand where he could save the whole house of Israel alive (Genesis 39:20-23; Genesis 50:20).
offenseFull: The Lord was with Joseph in his captivity, and his master saw that the Lord made all that he did to prosper; Potiphar made him overseer over his house, and the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake, just as Laban was blessed for Jacob’s sake (Genesis 39:1-6). The Most High deals with his people even in captivity and gives them compassion before them who carried them captive (1 Kings 8:50).

He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much, and that explains Joseph: he was in slavery, and he was faithful to Potiphar, and Potiphar raised him up (Luke 16:10). Just as Joseph was in captivity, we are in captivity, but that does not mean we can steal, lie, or rob; on the jobs out here, deal right, for God is watching each and every one of us. Diligence and slothfulness cannot be turned on and off; what you practise, you become good at.

Joseph was a goodly person and well favoured, a man people looked at as having integrity and good character, and his master’s wife cast her eyes upon him and asked him to lie with her (Genesis 39:6-7). Satan had to come in: it was too good in that house, he had been promoted and the Lord was with him, and now he had to be tested.

He refused: his master had committed all that he had to his hand and kept back nothing from him but her, because she was his wife; how then could he do this great wickedness and sin against God (Genesis 39:8-9). He immediately resisted the devil; he did not have to think, which shows the scripture was always in his mind: an easy decision, no negotiation, no emotional engagement whatsoever. He knew it was wickedness that would destroy his reputation and everything he had worked so hard for, and that he was sinning not against her but against the Lord ultimately. Notice that Joseph was not blaming God that he was in slavery.

Adultery was known as sin from the beginning, long before Sinai: Abraham kept the commandments, statutes and laws, and Abimelech knew that one lying with another man’s wife would have brought guiltiness upon his people (Genesis 26:5, 10). The Egyptians loved beautiful women, as Sarah was in danger in Egypt because of her beauty, and Potiphar’s wife was not bad looking; nobody was watching him, and Joseph still said no (Genesis 12:14). That is where integrity comes from: making the right decisions when nobody is watching.

She spoke to Joseph day by day, trying to wear him down, and he hearkened not; then she caught him by his garment when none of the men of the house were within, and he left his garment in her hand and fled (Genesis 39:10-12). That is the example: flee from sin as from a serpent, for whoever comes too near it will be bitten, and its teeth are as the teeth of a lion, slaying the souls of men (Ecclesiasticus 21:2). He saw sin like a snake and ran like a rabbit, for he knew thirty more seconds of entertaining her would be the bite. Everybody’s demon is not the same, but generally it is sexual demons that get the brothers; take a page out of what our forefather Joseph did.
judgmentFull: She lied and held his garment as evidence, and his master’s wrath was kindled, and he put Joseph into the prison without seeking understanding, for jealousy is the rage of a man (Genesis 39:13-20; Proverbs 6:34-35). Doing what was right, he went back into a lower estate. Joseph understood what his father taught him: whoever comes to serve the Lord must prepare his soul for temptation, take cheerfully whatever is brought upon him, and be patient when he is changed to a low estate (Ecclesiasticus 2:1-4). Jacob was wealthy, and Joseph was taken from all that into poverty and a prison; just as it goes for us, it went for our father Joseph.

But the Lord was with Joseph and showed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison, who committed all the prisoners to his hand, and whatever he did the Lord made it to prosper (Genesis 39:21-23). Wrongly accused and thrown into prison, he continually let his light shine, and he was raised up to authority over all who were in the prison. When a man’s ways please the Lord, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him, and that is what happened with Joseph (Proverbs 16:7). Everywhere Joseph went the favour followed, because the Most High was ordering his steps the whole way.

He asked the butler only to make mention of him to Pharaoh, for he had been stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews and had done nothing to be put into the dungeon; and the butler forgot him (Genesis 40:14-15, 23). He went in at seventeen and came out at thirty, thirteen years in prison and servitude, to stand before Pharaoh and ride in the second chariot (Genesis 41:41-46).

These are not fictional tales; this is the history of our fathers, and we are our fathers. From seventeen Joseph endured slavery, false accusation and thirteen years in the dungeon without blaming God, stayed faithful in the least things, and lived to see that what his brothers meant for evil, God meant unto good, to save much people alive (Genesis 50:20).

cases.judgment: She lied and held his garment as evidence, and his master’s wrath was kindled, and he put Joseph into the prison without seeking understanding, for jealousy is the rage of a man (Genesis 39:13-20; Proverbs 6:34-35). Doing what was right, he went back into a lower estate. Joseph understood what his father taught him: whoever comes to serve the Lord must prepare his soul for temptation, take cheerfully whatever is brought upon him, and be patient when he is changed to a low estate (Ecclesiasticus 2:1-4). Jacob was wealthy, and Joseph was taken from all that into poverty and a prison; just as it goes for us, it went for our father Joseph.

cases.name: Potiphar’s wife
cases.charge: Soliciting her husband’s servant day by day, and lying on him with his garment as false evidence when he refused her and fled
cases.summary: His master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and asked him to lie with her, and she spoke to him day by day, trying to wear him down, and he refused (Genesis 39:7-10). When she caught his garment and he fled, she could not get her way, so she lied, and kept his clothes as false evidence (Genesis 39:11-18). On her word Joseph was put into the prison (Genesis 39:19-20).
offenseFull: His master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and asked him to lie with her (Genesis 39:7). She spoke to him day by day, trying to wear him down, and he hearkened not to lie by her or to be with her (Genesis 39:10). He refused because adultery was known as sin from the beginning, long before Sinai: Abraham kept the commandments, statutes and laws, and the nations themselves knew adultery brought guilt (Genesis 39:9; Genesis 26:5, 10). Do not sit at all with another man’s wife nor drink with her, lest the heart incline to her and desire lead into destruction; both of them will destroy everything (Ecclesiasticus 9:9).

She arranged the empty house, when none of the men of the house were within, caught him by his garment, and he left it in her hand and fled (Genesis 39:11-12). When she saw he had fled, she lied: she called the men of her house and cried that the Hebrew had come in to mock them and to lie with her, and she laid up his garment by her until his lord came home (Genesis 39:13-18). She could not get her way, so she lied, and she kept his clothes as false evidence.

The scriptures warn of that spirit: the woman whose heart is snares and nets and her hands as bands, from whom whoso pleaseth God shall escape; and the strange woman whose lips drop as an honeycomb, but whose end is bitter and whose ways are moveable (Ecclesiastes 7:26; Proverbs 5:3-6). The same mouth that flattered turns and accuses. A backbiting tongue has disquieted many and overthrown the houses of great men; somebody that lies on you can do much destruction, and many more have fallen by the tongue than by the sword, and that is what Potiphar’s wife did to Joseph (Ecclesiasticus 28:14, 18).

This is the same spirit our people met in slavery, and a lot of us were put to death because of it: Emmett Till was put to death for a lying woman, and there are many cases like it. That is how you know this is spiritual Egypt: the same false cry of rape was raised against our people in the time of slavery, and that is how Rosewood was burned down. A lot of brothers have been locked up the same way, when a woman lies on a man who refuses her; do not deal with a woman like that.
judgmentFull: When his master heard the words of his wife, his wrath was kindled and he put Joseph into the prison where the king’s prisoners were bound (Genesis 39:19-20). He did not seek understanding, for jealousy is the rage of a man: he will not spare in the day of vengeance, nor regard any ransom, and that is why no plea could reach Potiphar (Proverbs 6:32-35). Joseph was falsely accused, as Christ was when many bare false witness against him (Mark 14:55-58).

But the Lord was with Joseph, showed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison (Genesis 39:21-23). His feet were hurt with fetters and he was laid in iron, the prison where the king’s prisoners were bound, until the time that his word came, and the king loosed him and made him lord of his house (Psalms 105:18-21).
No sentence on Potiphar’s wife is recorded.

cases.name: Job
cases.charge: Perfect and upright, fearing God and eschewing evil; and in all his loss he sinned not with his lips
cases.summary: Job lived in the land of Uz but was not of that nation, for he was a son of God, as Israel lives in America today and is not Caucasian (Job 1:1). He offered burnt offerings for his children after their birthdays, in case they had sinned (Job 1:4-5). Satan, who needed the Lord’s permission, was given all that Job had and then his flesh, and Job did not sin with his lips (Job 1:12; Job 2:6-10). When he prayed for his friends, the Lord turned his captivity (Job 42:10).
offenseFull: Job was a man of the land of Uz, perfect and upright, one that feared God and eschewed evil, the greatest of all the men of the east (Job 1:1-3). Living in the land of Uz did not make him of that nation, because he was a son of God; so Israel lives in America and in Europe today and is not Caucasian, but the sons of God. Job is a true man, and he is also a representation of the twelve tribes of Israel. Job was not an Edomite. The Hebrew, the Latin Vulgate and the King James all end at Job 42:17; the Greek Septuagint adds a passage out of the Syriac book naming him Jobab among the kings of Edom, and that addition is commentary, not scripture. Esau came out red (Genesis 25:25), but Job said his skin was black upon him: his skin, not his condition (Job 30:30). The law of sacrifice was not given to Esau, yet the Lord sent the three friends to offer at Job’s hand (Numbers 28:1-2; Job 42:8), and Ezekiel ranks Job with Noah and Daniel (Ezekiel 14:14, 20).

Before the trial, when Job prepared his seat in the street he was a judge, one of the judges of the law; he delivered the poor and the fatherless, and broke the jaws of the wicked and took back what the wicked stole: he was not a pushover (Job 29:7-17; Deuteronomy 16:18). His sons feasted in their houses, every one his day, which is their birthdays; the only time birthdays are read of in the scriptures, the heathen kept them, and celebrating birthdays is not a custom of Israel (Job 1:4; Job 8:4). Job knew what his sons were doing, and offered burnt offerings for them (Job 1:5).

When the sons of God came before the Lord, Satan came also among them (Job 1:6). The sons of God are the lineage of Adam, for before we were called Israelites we were called the sons of God; and the angels are also called the sons of God, because God created them. Satan was not kicked out of heaven; he works for God, subject to him, much like us. The Lord asked whether he had considered his servant Job (Job 1:8): every time a man does more good works, the harder Satan comes at him, and Satan always goes to the Lord for permission. Satan said Job feared God only because God had made a hedge about him (Job 1:9-10); a hedge is protection, and the hedge is angels. All that Job had was put in Satan’s power, but not Job himself (Job 1:12), for both good and evil come from the Lord (Isaiah 45:7).

In one day the Sabeans, the fire of God, the Chaldeans and a great wind took first his source of income, his business and his goods, then his family (Job 1:13-19). Just as Job lost his source of income, so did Israel as a people: the fruit of our land and all our labours eaten by a nation we knew not, and our sons and daughters gone into captivity (Deuteronomy 28:33, 41). Job fell down and worshipped and blessed the name of the Lord (Job 1:20-22). Job understood that everything we have comes from the Lord, and he did not ask God why he had done this to him.

The Lord bragged on him, that he still held fast his integrity, and Satan was given his flesh but not his life: he took orders, just as we take orders (Job 2:3-7). The sore boils were his fifth trial, his health, and what Job went through Israel goes through as a nation: no soundness from the sole of the foot to the head, but putrifying sores, like Job had (Isaiah 1:5-6). His wife told him to curse God and die: if Satan cannot get to a man, he comes through his woman, as he went to Eve. Job told her she spoke as one of the foolish women, and asked whether they should receive good at the hand of God and not evil (Job 2:9-10).
judgmentFull: When the Lord answered him, Job confessed that he had uttered what he understood not, and repented in dust and ashes, the custom of our forefathers as a sign of sorrow and repentance (Job 42:2-6). The Lord’s wrath was kindled against the three friends, and the sacrifice for their sin had to be brought to Job, the righteous one in the matter (Job 42:7-9).

The Lord turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends, and gave him twice as much as he had before (Job 42:10-17). The purpose of the trial was to see whether Job would stay faithful or curse the Most High. The same thing happens to us: we endure to the end as Job did, and the Most High will turn the captivity of the Israelites who kept the commandments and repay them far more than double (Revelation 14:12).

James gives Job as the example of suffering affliction and of patience (James 5:11). Job knew that his redeemer lived, and the redeemer is Christ; he understood the regeneration, that Christ would return in the latter days and that Job would be back to see him for himself, with his own eyes and not in another person’s body (Job 19:25-27). As soon as a man gives his life to the Lord, Satan comes before the throne to try him, and that pattern still operates today (Ecclesiasticus 2:1). Job’s life is a template for what each one of us will have to go through.
