cases.name: Job’s three friends
cases.charge: Not speaking of God the thing that is right, as Job had; accusing him of sin he was not in, when the Lord was only trying him
cases.summary: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite came by appointment to mourn with Job and comfort him (Job 2:11). Then they accused Job of being in sin, claiming that was why God was putting him through the boils and the loss of his children, his cattle and everything he had (Job 4-22). The Lord’s wrath was kindled against them, because they had not spoken of him the thing that was right, as Job had; their sacrifice had to be brought to Job, and it was Job’s righteous prayer that spared them (Job 42:7-10).
offenseFull: When Job’s three friends heard of his affliction they came, rent their mantles, and sat with him in silence, for his grief was very great (Job 2:11-13). Friends come to a man’s affliction to give correction, harsh reality and hard truth; not to butter him up knowing he is in the wrong, but to give him straight facts.

Eliphaz answered that Job had strengthened many, and now that it had come upon him, he fainted (Job 4:3-5). That cuts deep: a man can give other people the scriptures and be the strongest person out there, and then fall apart as soon as a trial comes to him. A man can be wise and teach many and yet be unprofitable to himself (Ecclesiasticus 37:19): Eliphaz was telling Job that he was the man who comforted everybody, and now that his own turn had come he was fainting and wanted to give up; we should all be mindful of that. Then he asked who ever perished being innocent (Job 4:7), telling Job that maybe it was something he did, something he needed to examine himself with. Sometimes it is something we did, but a lot of times it is not; it is for us to go through something because we can handle it, and be a shining example to the next person.

Bildad asked whether God perverts judgment and said that if Job’s children had sinned, God had cast them away for their transgression, pointing back to the children celebrating their days (Job 8:3-4). He promised a latter end that would greatly increase if Job were pure and upright, on the false premise that Job was not already upright (Job 8:5-7; Job 1:1). Zophar mocked Job for saying his doctrine was pure, and said God exacted of him less than his iniquity deserved (Job 11:4-6); that is a heavy precept, for the Most High gives us less than we deserve.

At last Eliphaz asked whether Job’s wickedness was not great (Job 22:5), throwing his righteousness back as filthy rags, as if keeping the commandments profits nothing; there is falsehood in that answer, for Christ told us that if we keep the commandments and follow him, we will rule on thrones with him (Matthew 19:27-28). He accused Job of stripping the naked and withholding bread from the hungry (Job 22:6-9), claiming that his suffering proved he was sinning, but the Lord was only trying him. The truth is the opposite: when Job had his riches he dealt righteously, helped people, taught people, and was looked up to like an elder in the city.

Job called them forgers of lies and physicians of no value, because what they told him could not help him, and told them that to hold their tongue would be wisdom (Job 13:4-5). He warned them about speaking wickedly for God and talking deceitfully for him, accepting God’s person to defend their own accusations (Job 13:7-8). He called them miserable comforters (Job 16:2): instead of comforting a sick man they tore him down, with no knowledge that the Most High was letting Satan have his way with Job to see if he would curse God. Elihu’s wrath was kindled against the three because they had found no answer and yet had condemned Job (Job 32:3). Elihu also spoke prophetically about times to come, of the oppressed crying out by reason of the arm of the mighty, as Israel is oppressed today (Job 35:9; Deuteronomy 28:29).
judgmentFull: The Lord told Eliphaz the Temanite that his wrath was kindled against him and his two friends, because they had not spoken of him the thing that was right, as his servant Job had (Job 42:7). Throughout the book the three dealt wrongly with Job, and did not deal righteously as their brother Job did. Job was a perfect man, which is why the Most High held him up as the one who spoke rightly while his friends did not (Job 1:1).

He commanded them to take seven bullocks and seven rams, go to Job and offer a burnt offering for themselves, and Job would pray for them, lest he deal with them after their folly (Job 42:8). The sacrifice for their sin had to be brought to Job, the righteous one in the situation. That is how the priesthood worked from Leviticus on: the sacrifice was brought to the priests, who offered it on the people’s behalf, and if a man did not bring his sacrifice, what he did would not be forgiven.

Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar went and did as the Lord commanded them, and the Lord accepted Job (Job 42:9). It was not the prayer alone that availed but the prayer of a righteous man, for the Most High deals with those that are dealing in righteousness, and it was Job’s righteous prayer that spared his friends (James 5:16). The Lord turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends, and afterward his brethren and acquaintances came and ate bread with him, and his friends returned as well (Job 42:10-11).

cases.name: Pharaoh of the Exodus
cases.charge: Dealing wisely with Israel: institutional slavery, hard bondage, the sons cast into the river, and refusing to let the Lord’s people go through the plagues
cases.summary: A new kingdom arose over Egypt that knew not Joseph and dealt wisely with Israel: institutional slavery, taskmasters, treasure cities Israel built and did not dwell in, and the sons cast into the river (Exodus 1:8-22). Pharaoh said he knew not the Lord, and the Lord hardened his heart to show his power in him, and every plague put a god of Egypt to shame, until the firstborn died and the sea covered his host (Exodus 5:2; Exodus 9:16; Exodus 12:12; Exodus 14:28). What they did to Israel in ancient Egypt is what they did to Israel in America, and that is why this place is spiritually called Egypt (Revelation 11:8).
offenseFull: The children of Israel multiplied in Egypt and waxed exceeding mighty (Exodus 1:5-7); Israel had those babies, the nation did not cast away its children, and we became a nation within a nation. There arose a new king that knew not Joseph (Exodus 1:8): not merely one king but a new kingdom, the eighteenth dynasty, which did not recognize Joseph and did not care what Joseph had done for the previous dynasty. Pharaoh told his people to deal wisely with them (Exodus 1:9-10): that is institutional slavery, setting up institutions to keep Israel down in society, where they cannot own this and cannot do that. They set taskmasters over them, Israel built the treasure cities Pithom and Raamses and did not dwell in them, and the Egyptians made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in mortar and brick and all manner of service in the field (Exodus 1:11-14); the bitter herbs of the Passover represent that bondage. The mural of Israel’s bondage in Egypt was found in the Theban tomb of Rekhmire, governor and vizier at the time of Thutmose III. Those are the curses: build a house and not dwell in it, the stranger above Israel very high and Israel very low, and they that hate us reigning over us (Deuteronomy 28:30, 43-44; Leviticus 26:17).

The same wise dealing works on Israel in America today, through Planned Parenthood and the prison industrial complex. The taskmasters today are the governors, the politicians, the police officers and the agents, with institutional laws like Jim Crow and the black codes to keep Israel low; on the plantation the taskmaster was the overseer in the field, and today the taskmaster is the boss. The White House was built by enslaved people who did not dwell in it (Deuteronomy 28:30). When the midwives would not kill the sons, Pharaoh charged all his people to cast every son into the river (Exodus 1:22).

Moses and Aaron told Pharaoh to let the Lord’s people go to hold a feast in the wilderness, and that feast was the Passover; Pharaoh answered that he knew not the Lord (Exodus 5:1-2). He sent them back to their burdens, took away the straw and kept the tale of bricks: fewer resources, the same production and the same deadline, and the pattern of oppression has not changed (Exodus 5:6-13). The officers of Israel set over their own brethren were beaten (Exodus 5:14), so that the anger of the oppressed lands on their own brother, the supervisor they can see, instead of on the power above him. The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart and tells why: he raised him up to show his power in him (Exodus 9:16; Romans 9:17); and the Lord hardens the hearts of the powers of Babylon now, so that they keep passing laws and pressing against his people, that he may show his power again. Under the hail he said he had sinned this time, as though all the other times were not sin, and when it ceased he sinned yet more (Exodus 9:27, 34).
judgmentFull: Against all the gods of Egypt the Lord executed judgment, and each plague put an Egyptian god to shame (Exodus 12:12). The river turned to blood mocked Sobek, the god of the rivers, who could not defend his own waters; the frogs mocked Heqet, and Pharaoh had to go to the Lord and not to her; the lice and the flies mocked Beelzebub, the lord of flies and uncleanness, and these were no ordinary flies but biting and killing (Wisdom of Solomon 16:9); the murrain mocked Hathor, the goddess of cattle; the boils upon the magicians mocked Sekhmet, the goddess of health and beauty; the darkness showed that the sun god Ra is no god at all; and the death of the firstborn showed that Osiris and Isis control neither life nor death, for unto God the Lord belong the issues from death (Psalms 68:20). The plagues touched Pharaoh, his servants and the Egyptians only, and not Israel in Goshen, because this was the Lord redeeming the Israelites (Exodus 8:22; Exodus 9:26).

At midnight the Lord smote all the firstborn, from Pharaoh’s own son to the firstborn of the captive in the dungeon (Exodus 12:29); the destroyer was Christ, the almighty word of God, who leaped down from heaven as a fierce man of war (Wisdom of Solomon 18:15). The man who had threatened to kill Moses called for him by night to go and serve the Lord, and to bless him also, for the Lord’s anointed and his prophets are not to be touched (Exodus 12:31-32; Psalms 105:15). There was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where there was not one dead, and Israel spoiled the Egyptians and took everything (Exodus 12:30-36). Israel departed from Rameses (Exodus 12:37; Numbers 33:3), which gives the name of the Pharaoh ruling at the Exodus.

The Most High kept one more judgment in store for that wicked nation (Exodus 14:4). He took off their chariot wheels in the sea, and the waters returned and consumed them (Exodus 14:25-28): our salvation was their destruction, for the Red Sea opened for Israel and closed on Egypt in the same hour. He will do the same to the wicked nation that has done the same things to Israel today. The Lord will not suffer his people to dwell in the land of Egypt any longer, but will smite Egypt with plagues as before and destroy all the land thereof (2 Esdras 15:10-12): as before lets you know this is not ancient Egypt, whose land was not destroyed, but spiritual Egypt, and this is the new Exodus.

They set taskmasters over them, Israel built the treasure cities Pithom and Raamses and did not dwell in them, and the Egyptians made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in mortar and brick and all manner of service in the field (Exodus 1:11-14); the bitter herbs of the Passover represent that bondage. The mural of Israel’s bondage in Egypt was found in the Theban tomb of Rekhmire, governor and vizier at the time of Thutmose III. Those are the curses: build a house and not dwell in it, the stranger above Israel very high and Israel very low, and they that hate us reigning over us (Deuteronomy 28:30, 43-44; Leviticus 26:17).
cases.judgment: Against all the gods of Egypt the Lord executed judgment, and each plague put an Egyptian god to shame (Exodus 12:12). The river turned to blood mocked Sobek, the god of the rivers, who could not defend his own waters; the frogs mocked Heqet, and Pharaoh had to go to the Lord and not to her; the lice and the flies mocked Beelzebub, the lord of flies and uncleanness, and these were no ordinary flies but biting and killing (Wisdom of Solomon 16:9); the murrain mocked Hathor, the goddess of cattle; the boils upon the magicians mocked Sekhmet, the goddess of health and beauty; the darkness showed that the sun god Ra is no god at all; and the death of the firstborn showed that Osiris and Isis control neither life nor death, for unto God the Lord belong the issues from death (Psalms 68:20). The plagues touched Pharaoh, his servants and the Egyptians only, and not Israel in Goshen, because this was the Lord redeeming the Israelites (Exodus 8:22; Exodus 9:26).

cases.name: Shiphrah and Puah, the midwives
cases.charge: Fearing God and not doing as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saving the men children alive
cases.summary: Pharaoh commanded the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill every son upon the stools and save the daughters alive (Exodus 1:15-16). They feared God and saved the men children alive, and answered that the daughters of Israel are not as the women of the nations (Exodus 1:17-19). Because they feared God, God dealt well with them and made them houses (Exodus 1:20-21).
offenseFull: The king of Egypt told the Hebrew midwives, one named Shiphrah and the other Puah, that if it were a son upon the stools they should kill him, and if a daughter she should live (Exodus 1:15-16). Pharaoh commanded the male children killed at birth: that is oppression, and America does the same thing. The fruit of the body is killed today through abortion, and the males are taken through the school to prison pipeline: conditions of poverty are created, drugs are brought into the community, and then the brothers are put away for the rest of their lives; that whole system was set up, and that is them dealing wisely. They tried to destroy the poor secretly, because they are trying to stop the prophets from coming on the earth; cursed shall be the fruit of thy body (Deuteronomy 28:18).

The midwives feared God and did not do as the king commanded, but saved the sons alive (Exodus 1:17). The midwives were Israelites, and they operated in faith, for fear and faith go together in terms of the Lord. Having our children murdered is against the laws of God, and that is the reason these sisters did not do it.

Called to account, they answered Pharaoh that the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women, for they are lively and are delivered before the midwives come in unto them (Exodus 1:18-19). They pleaded their case that they were unable to do it the way he instructed, because before they could get to the baby the Hebrew woman had already delivered; they were lying to Pharaoh to save the lives of the sons of Israel. The Israelites are not like the Hamites, the Egyptians: the daughters of Israel are not as the women of the nations.
judgmentFull: Therefore God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied and waxed very mighty (Exodus 1:20); the Most High blessed the women who saved the children of Israel alive. Because they feared God, he made them houses (Exodus 1:21): not only houses in Egypt, but the Lord let it be known that they would have a spiritual house too.

Since Pharaoh could not stop the women bearing sons and could not get the midwives to kill them, he charged all his people to cast every son into the river (Exodus 1:22). The same spirit was in Herod, who, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, slew all the children in Bethlehem two years old and under (Matthew 2:16). Under affliction Israel kept multiplying, and through all that has been done against the womb of our women, from the sterilization of our people since the 1920s to Planned Parenthood in the community, the people still multiply.

cases.name: Moses, and the Egyptian in the sand
cases.charge: Slaying the Egyptian who smote a Hebrew, one of his brethren, and hiding him in the sand
cases.summary: Moses grew up as an Egyptian although he was a Hebrew, nursed in his first years by his own mother, and when he was grown he knew the Israelites were his brethren (Exodus 2:7-11). He saw an Egyptian smiting a Hebrew, an abuse of power with his brother’s life in danger, and slew the Egyptian and hid him in the sand; he did not kill out of hatred (Exodus 2:11-12). The Hebrew who did the wrong threw the killing in his face, Pharaoh sought to slay him, and by faith he forsook Egypt for Midian; the man they refused is the same man God sent to be a ruler and a deliverer (Exodus 2:13-15; Hebrews 11:27; Acts 7:35).
offenseFull: Amram and Jochebed of the house of Levi hid their goodly child, exceeding fair, three months (Exodus 2:1-2; Exodus 6:20; Acts 7:20). Pharaoh’s daughter knew the child was a Hebrew and no Egyptian because the Most High put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel, though both peoples were dark of skin (Exodus 2:5-6; Exodus 11:7). Miriam was crafty, and the child’s own mother was paid wages to nurse him (Exodus 2:7-9). Raised in the palace, he received one of the finest educations in the world, learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and mighty in words and in deeds (Acts 7:22).

When he was full forty years old it came into his heart to visit his brethren, and he looked on their burdens (Exodus 2:11; Acts 7:23). He did not forget where he came from, and did not act as though he were an Egyptian now; he still knew who he came from. The Egyptian smiting the Hebrew was not ordinary work; he was going too far, and Moses saw that his brother’s life was in danger, an abuse of power at the hand of the Egyptian. He looked this way and that way and slew the Egyptian (Exodus 2:12): not his immediate brother, but one of his people, oppressed.

Moses did not kill out of hatred; he was in the spirit of the Lord, fulfilling the will of God. The man who forbears to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and says he knew it not, is known to him that ponders the heart and is rendered according to his works (Proverbs 24:11-12): God will judge the man who sees his brother at the point of death and does not intervene, so Moses was in the right and did nothing wrong. That does not mean a man can go out and slaughter anybody. He did not just marvel at the oppression (Ecclesiastes 5:8); he used his position for his people, unlike many who hold a position of power today and will not risk it for their people, and Moses is the ultimate revolutionary, as Christ is. He supposed his brethren would have understood how that God by his hand would deliver them, but they understood not (Acts 7:25).

The second day two Hebrews strove together: when all have a real enemy, two men in the same conditions of oppression fight each other (Exodus 2:13). He that did the wrong thrust Moses away and asked who made him a prince and a judge, and whether he meant to kill him as he killed the Egyptian (Exodus 2:14; Acts 7:27). When a people is oppressed they take the oppression out on one another and brothers become their own enemies; the same spirit answers correction among Israel today, pointing the finger at the one who corrects, and the people a man tries to help will turn on him that quick. Moses feared, not that he was scared, but that the thing was known (Exodus 2:14).
judgmentFull: When Pharaoh heard this thing he sought to slay Moses (Exodus 2:15): whether he grew up with Moses or not, Pharaoh was an Egyptian, and Moses had killed one of his people. By faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king (Hebrews 11:27): he knew he had done nothing wrong and that the Lord would preserve his life, as Christ told his disciples to flee into the next city when persecuted (Matthew 10:23). Moses gave up his whole upbringing and position: he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter (Hebrews 11:24-26); in Egypt his head was shaved, his beard cut, his dress and customs Egyptian, and he laid all of it down to be an Israelite. Things were not bad for Moses in Egypt; he made things bad for himself by killing the Egyptian, while some of our people had money and high standing and were content with the oppression, as many with money are comfortable in modern day Egypt today.

At the well in Midian he stood up for the seven daughters of the priest against the shepherds, a man of war and not a weak man (Exodus 2:16-17). They told their father an Egyptian had delivered them, taking him for an Egyptian by his dress, his carriage and his skin, for Moses was a very dark-skinned man, the same colour as the Egyptians, who were a dark race of Ham; Israel was always being mistaken for Egyptians (Exodus 2:19; Acts 21:37-39; Genesis 42:7-8). He married Zipporah, a Midianite and not an Israelite, and named his son Gershom, a stranger in a strange land (Exodus 2:21-22).

No sentence upon the killing is recorded. After forty years the angel of the Lord appeared to him in the bush, and the man they had refused, asking who made him a ruler and a judge, is the same man God sent to be a ruler and a deliverer (Acts 7:30-35), as Christ is the stone the builders refused (Psalms 118:22).

cases.name: Moses and the uncircumcised son
cases.charge: Not circumcising his son, the token of the covenant, so that the Lord met him by the way in the inn and sought to kill him
cases.summary: Moses took his wife and his sons and returned toward Egypt with the rod of God in his hand, to tell Pharaoh that Israel was the Lord’s son, his firstborn (Exodus 4:20-23). By the way in the inn the Lord met him and sought to kill him, because Moses had not circumcised his son: he represented God, yet had not kept the seal of the covenant (Exodus 4:24). Zipporah took a sharp stone and circumcised the child, and the Lord let him go (Exodus 4:25-26). This shows the laws did not begin at Sinai, and the covenant still stands.
offenseFull: Circumcision was the token, the sign, the seal of the covenant the Most High made with Abraham, a visible confirmation carried through all the generations (Genesis 17:10-11; Romans 4:11). Every man child was to be circumcised on the eighth day, and the uncircumcised man child, that soul shall be cut off from his people, for he has broken the covenant (Genesis 17:12-14); that is why Moses was worthy of death. This shows the laws did not begin at Sinai.

Moses had married Zipporah, a Midianite and not an Israelite (Exodus 2:21). The Lord allowed him a heathen wife because of his circumstance, for he had to flee from Pharaoh. The law teaches against it because a wife who does not serve the God of Israel raises the children confused, not fully keeping our beliefs, and the house is divided between two gods and two beliefs; that is what is seen here. The Egyptians did not practise circumcision; they were a nation of uncleanness, and the covenant was between the Lord and Israel, who were told not to do after the doings of the land of Egypt where they had dwelt (Leviticus 18:3).

He was to tell Pharaoh that Israel is the Lord’s son, even his firstborn (Exodus 4:22): the firstborn gets the inheritance, and Israel is God’s heir. Israel was not the first nation created but the first the Most High chose, the apple of his eye. If Pharaoh refused to let him go, the Lord would slay Pharaoh’s firstborn (Exodus 4:23), and that is what came to pass.
judgmentFull: On the journey into Egypt they stopped in an inn, and the Lord met him and sought to kill him (Exodus 4:24). In order for the Lord not to kill Moses, his son had to be circumcised. Zipporah took a sharp stone, cut off the foreskin of her son and cast it at his feet, and called him a bloody husband (Exodus 4:25): bloody because of the circumcision she had to perform herself. His wife was not pleased: the words most likely mean that she reproached him and his religion, which required this bloody ceremony, though they may also be read as affection, that she had now espoused him afresh by circumcising her son.

So the Lord let him go (Exodus 4:26). Moses sent her back: Jethro took Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after he had sent her back, and brought her and his sons to Moses in the wilderness at the mount of God when the mission was done (Exodus 18:2-5).

The covenant still stands: a son of Israel is circumcised on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3), and a man that comes to the truth grown must still be circumcised, even at forty, fifty or sixty years, as Abraham himself was circumcised at ninety and nine, and as Paul circumcised Timothy, whose father was a Greek (Genesis 17:24; Acts 16:1-3). Nothing that defiles enters the kingdom (Revelation 21:27). Romans 2 does not do away with circumcision of the flesh: circumcision profits if a man keeps the law; the Jews who grew up circumcised and broke the law made their circumcision uncircumcision, and the uncircumcised of the cast-off northern kingdom who keep the righteousness of the law are counted as circumcised (Romans 2:25-29). Circumcision of the heart is putting away the evil of the doings, as the prophets command Israel to take away the foreskins of the heart (Jeremiah 4:4; Deuteronomy 10:16); the scribes and Pharisees were clean on the outside of the cup but full of iniquity within (Matthew 23:25-28).

cases.name: The magicians of Egypt
cases.charge: Withstanding Moses with their enchantments, copying the signs of the Lord by sorcery, and resisting the truth
cases.summary: The Lord made Moses a god to Pharaoh and Aaron his prophet (Exodus 7:1). When Aaron’s rod became a serpent, the magicians of Egypt, whose names were Jannes and Jambres, did in like manner with their enchantments, and Aaron’s rod swallowed up their rods (Exodus 7:10-12; 2 Timothy 3:8). They could only add to the plagues and never take one away; at the lice they could not, and at the boils they could not stand before Moses, for the boil was upon them (Exodus 8:18-19; Exodus 9:11). With every plague the Most High mocked a god of Egypt.
offenseFull: The Lord made Moses a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron his brother was his prophet: Moses was as God and Aaron was the mouthpiece, because Moses kept saying he was of uncircumcised lips (Exodus 7:1-2). The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart for his glory, that he might lay his hand upon Egypt by great judgments (Exodus 7:3-5).

It was Aaron who cast down the rod before Pharaoh, and it became a serpent; a lot of people to this day say it was Moses with the rod, because they do not read the Bible (Exodus 7:10). Then Pharaoh called the wise men and the sorcerers, and the magicians did in like manner with their enchantments (Exodus 7:11). Their names were Jannes and Jambres, known for withstanding Moses (2 Timothy 3:8). Back then there was real spiritual power; some of them dealt with Satan on a high level.

They could do half the thing and never the whole. They turned the water to blood and could not turn it back clear (Exodus 7:22). They brought up frogs and could not get rid of them, so Pharaoh had to call for Moses to entreat the Lord; he could not call on Heqet, the god of frogs (Exodus 8:7-8). At every plague they tried to show they could do it too, but it was small, nothing on the level and scale of what the Lord was doing through Moses and Aaron. With hatred comes rebellion, and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, as the Lord had said (Exodus 7:22).
judgmentFull: Aaron’s rod swallowed up their rods (Exodus 7:12). Each plague put an Egyptian god to shame: the river turned to blood mocked Sobek, the god of the rivers, who could not defend his own waters; the frogs mocked Heqet; the lice and the swarms of flies mocked Beelzebub, the lord of flies and uncleanness; the murrain mocked Hathor; the boils mocked Sekhmet, the goddess of health and beauty; the hail and fire mocked Nut and Geb, the sky and the earth; and the darkness showed that the sun god Ra is no god at all (Exodus 12:12). Nothing could help the Egyptians; there is no god but the Lord.

At the lice the magicians tried with their enchantments, but their magic was not that strong; they could not, and they told Pharaoh it was the finger of God (Exodus 8:18-19). At the boils they could not stand before Moses, for the boil was upon the magicians themselves and upon all the Egyptians (Exodus 9:11). Many Egyptologists claim this never happened, because to admit it is to admit that the idols they call gods and goddesses were powerless before the God of Israel and do not exist at all.

Jannes and Jambres were defeated when they withstood Moses; they proceeded no further, and their folly was made manifest when Aaron’s serpent ate up theirs (2 Timothy 3:8-9). Whoever resists the truth has the same spirit and will end the same way, for nothing can be done against the truth (2 Corinthians 13:8). The magicians of Egypt are those who call themselves scientists today, the witches of this earth. The pastor who resists the truth that his people are the Israelites is like Jannes and Jambres, and so was the Council of Nicaea, which opposed the word of God. As the Lord brought plagues on Egypt, he will do the same again when Israel is delivered from spiritual Egypt, which is America.

cases.name: Israel at the first Passover
cases.charge: Doing as the Lord commanded Moses and Aaron: the lamb, the blood on the door, the flesh roast with fire, the unleavened bread and bitter herbs
cases.summary: On the Passover night every house of Israel with the blood of the lamb on its doorposts was passed over, while the Lord smote all the firstborn of Egypt and executed judgment against all its gods (Exodus 12:12-13, 29). The lamb without blemish represents Christ, the bitter herbs the bitter bondage of Egypt, and the unleavened bread being without sin. Israel did as the Lord commanded, and the selfsame day he brought them out by their armies (Exodus 12:28, 50-51).
offenseFull: This month was made the beginning of months, the first month of the year: the month Abib, in which Israel came out of Egypt (Exodus 12:1-2; Exodus 13:4). Abib is the name before the exile; afterward it was called Nisan, and it falls between March and April. The new year begins in the springtime, not on the first of January in the dead of winter; that is another lie taught in Babylon.

On the tenth day every man took a lamb for an house, a male of the first year without blemish, kept it up until the fourteenth day, and the whole assembly killed it in the evening (Exodus 12:3-6). The evening of the fourteenth day is the fifteenth, and that is the Passover, for the day begins and ends at even. The feast days and the sacrifices are a shadow of things to come, but the body is of Christ (Colossians 2:16-17). The lamb without blemish and without spot points to Christ, who was sinless, foreordained before the foundation of the world but manifest in these last times for the nation of Israel (1 Peter 1:19-20).

They took a bunch of hyssop, used like a paintbrush, dipped it in the blood in the bason and struck the lintel and the two side posts, and none went out at the door of his house until the morning (Exodus 12:7, 21-23). Putting the blood over the doorpost showed that they believed the Lord; a Hebrew who refused would have been killed along with the Egyptians.

They ate the flesh that night roast with fire, not raw nor boiled, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, and let nothing remain until the morning (Exodus 12:8-10). The bitter herbs represent the captivity, the bitter bondage and all the evil Israel went through in Egypt, when their lives were made bitter in the field; the unleavened bread represents being without sin (Exodus 1:14). They ate it with loins girded, shoes on their feet and staff in hand, in haste, ready to move, because the Lord was about to pass over Egypt and deliver them out of captivity (Exodus 12:11). The children of Israel went away and did as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron (Exodus 12:28).
judgmentFull: The Lord passed through the land that night and smote all the firstborn of man and beast, and against all the gods of Egypt he executed judgment; where he saw the blood, he passed over (Exodus 12:12-13). The destroyer was Christ, the almighty word of God, who leaped down from the royal throne as a fierce man of war in the quiet silence of that night; the dead were too many to bury, and upon the destruction of the firstborn the Egyptians acknowledged this people to be the sons of God (Wisdom of Solomon 18:10-16; John 1:1).

At midnight every firstborn died, from Pharaoh’s on the throne to the captive’s in the dungeon (Exodus 12:29). In this Christ showed that Osiris and Isis, the supposed gods of life and death, control neither life nor death, for unto God the Lord belong the issues from death (Psalms 68:20). Against the children of Israel not a dog moved his tongue (Exodus 11:7).

They went out the selfsame day, at the end of four hundred and thirty years, and spoiled the Egyptians of silver, gold and raiment; they came out with great substance, as the Lord had told Abraham (Exodus 12:35-41; Genesis 15:14). The feast of unleavened bread is kept because in this selfsame day the Most High brought the armies of Israel out of Egypt; he deals with armies, and when he brings Israel out of this place he is bringing out an army again, an exceeding great army, not choir boys (Exodus 12:17; Ezekiel 37:10).

The day is a memorial, a feast to the Lord throughout the generations, by an ordinance for ever (Exodus 12:14). Seven days no leaven is found in the houses, and whoever eats leavened bread is cut off from Israel (Exodus 12:15-20); the old leaven represents malice and evil in the mind and heart (1 Corinthians 5:8). Not a bone of the lamb is broken, as not a bone of Christ was broken on the cross (Exodus 12:46; John 19:36).

It was not done away. Christ kept the Passover, and at the Passover dinner he named the bread his body and the cup his blood of the new testament, shed for the remission of sins (Matthew 26:17-28). The blood on the doorpost represents Christ’s blood and the new covenant, so no one kills a lamb and puts blood on his doorpost today; killing a lamb will not protect anyone from the wrath of God, but believing in Christ and doing what is right will. Christ our passover is sacrificed for us; therefore the feast is still kept, with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, and not spiritualized away (1 Corinthians 5:7-8). As the Lord came into Egypt the first time to deliver Israel, he is coming again in a new Passover, destroying their enemies and delivering the twelve tribes from spiritual Egypt, which is America (Isaiah 19:1, 20).

cases.offense: This month was made the beginning of months, the first month of the year: the month Abib, in which Israel came out of Egypt (Exodus 12:1-2; Exodus 13:4). Abib is the name before the exile; afterward it was called Nisan, and it falls between March and April. The new year begins in the springtime, not on the first of January in the dead of winter; that is another lie taught in Babylon.

cases.name: Amalek
cases.charge: Smiting the hindmost, the feeble and faint and weary, when Israel came out of Egypt; and he feared not God
cases.summary: Amalek, the grandson of Esau and a duke of Edom, was the first nation to come against Israel after Egypt (Exodus 17:8; Genesis 36:12, 16). He did not meet the mighty men in the front; he went to the back to slay the women, the children and the old when Israel was faint and weary, and he feared not God (Deuteronomy 25:17-18). The Lord swore to have war with Amalek from generation to generation, and his latter end is that he perish for ever (Exodus 17:16; Numbers 24:20).
offenseFull: Then came Amalek and fought with Israel in Rephidim (Exodus 17:8). Esau is Edom, the twin brother of Jacob; Timna, concubine to Eliphaz, Esau’s son, bore him Amalek, and Amalek is named among the dukes that came of Eliphaz in the land of Edom, the nobility of Edom (Genesis 36:1, 12, 16). Amalek was the first of the nations: the first nation to war against Israel when they came out of Egypt into the wilderness (Numbers 24:20).

Moses rehearsed the manner of it forty years later: Amalek met Israel by the way and smote the hindmost, all that were feeble behind, when they were faint and weary, and he feared not God (Deuteronomy 25:17-18). The elderly and the old were in the back while the young were in the front, and Esau took the opportunity to attack from the rear, when Israel was tired and worn out. They preyed on the weak and the tired. He did not care about Israel’s God, and he still does not. That same spirit works against the nation’s young and old today.
judgmentFull: When Moses held up his hand Israel prevailed, and when he let it down Amalek prevailed; Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands until the going down of the sun, and Joshua discomfited Amalek with the edge of the sword (Exodus 17:11-13). Moses was about eighty years old holding a rod above his head all day; the fathers were mighty men, stronger than we are today.

The Lord told Moses to write it for a memorial in a book and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, for he would utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven, and he swore to have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Exodus 17:14-16). Deuteronomy 25 is that rehearsal, and Amalek’s latter end is that he perish for ever (Deuteronomy 25:17-19; Numbers 24:20). God does not forget; he marks everything they do.

By the time Moses rehearsed it forty years had passed and the children of Amalek had done nothing themselves; hundreds of years after that the Lord remembered how Amalek laid wait for Israel in the way, and sent Saul by Samuel to smite Amalek and utterly destroy all that they had (1 Samuel 15:2-3). That answers the argument, I never did anything to you: the nations do not get away with what they did to his people, and the judgment carries to the seed. Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High said remember; this is a righteous grudge, for the law against bearing a grudge is toward the children of one’s own people, not toward the enemies the Most High has sworn against (Leviticus 19:18).

Israel were no tyrants: Saul warned the Kenites to depart from among the Amalekites for the kindness they showed Israel coming up out of Egypt, for the Most High discriminates righteously (1 Samuel 15:6). Saul spared Agag, and Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal, measure for measure for what Amalek’s sword had done (1 Samuel 15:9, 33). Saul did not finish Agag’s line, and in Esther’s day Haman the Agagite of that same seed rose against Israel (Esther 3:1). The king calls him a Macedonian, a stranger from the Persian blood, for the Edomites became the Greek Macedonians (Rest of Esther 16:10; 1 Maccabees 1:1).

The war runs from generation to generation, and it is now more spiritual than ever, because the adversary has established the imagination that they are the Jews, and Israel casts down that imagination every day. Today that seed says they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan, claiming the identity of Israel, and the Lord will make them come and worship before Israel’s feet and know that he has loved Israel (Revelation 2:9; Revelation 3:9). The whole world is set up between Jacob and Esau: Esau, the so-called white man, is the end of this world, with Amalek leading; it is not speaking of the Arab man (2 Esdras 6:7-10). The enmity was set from the garden between the serpent’s seed and the woman’s seed; they bruised Christ’s heel, but at the end of the world Jacob bruises the head (Genesis 3:15; Romans 16:20). Until then Israel lives peaceably with all men, lays hands on no one, and does not incite or condone any violence; the day of payback belongs to the return of the Lord (Romans 12:18; Psalms 137:7-9).

cases.name: Moses
cases.charge: Refusing to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter; faithful in all the Lord’s house; very meek, above all the men upon the face of the earth
cases.summary: Things were not bad for Moses in Egypt; he made them bad for himself, and by faith he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing affliction with the people of God over the pleasures of sin for a season (Hebrews 11:24-25). He gave up his whole upbringing and position to be what he was called to be, an Israelite. The Lord spoke with his servant Moses mouth to mouth, for he was faithful in all his house, and the man Moses was very meek, above all the men upon the face of the earth (Numbers 12:3, 7-8).
offenseFull: In ancient Egypt everybody was not badly off. Some of Israel had money and high standing and were comfortable with the oppression, as the celebrities, entertainers and pastors with money are comfortable in modern day Egypt now (Exodus 5:14). Things were not bad for Moses; he made them bad for himself by killing the Egyptian (Exodus 2:11-12). He did not just marvel at the oppression; he used his position for his people. Moses is the ultimate revolutionary, as Christ is.

By faith he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter (Hebrews 11:24-26). In Egypt his head was shaved, his beard cut, his dress and customs Egyptian, and he laid all of it down to be an Israelite. The same claim stands now: the remnant does not want the names of the captivity but the natural heritage of Israel, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of this land. Moses was a very dark-skinned man, the same colour as the Egyptians, and the daughters of the priest of Midian took him for an Egyptian (Exodus 2:19); that is why the hand made leprous as snow and turned again to his natural dark skin was a sign (Exodus 4:6-7).

He was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and mighty in words and in deeds (Acts 7:22). He did not stutter, as is commonly taught; he grew up in Pharaoh’s house speaking the Egyptian language and then spent forty years in Midian, and a language moves on in forty years, so Aaron, who spoke the Hebrew of the people fluently, was given him for a mouth, and he was to Aaron instead of God (Exodus 4:10-16). Forty years he kept his father in law’s flock, doing nothing of significance in a carnal sense, and when he was called he answered, who am I (Exodus 3:11). A man’s goings are of the Lord (Proverbs 20:24): the Lord used a man unknown, so that the destruction of Egypt would be a marvel to remember him by, and he put down the mighty from their seats (Luke 1:52).

He stood in the middle, interceding between the people and God, and asked to be blotted out of the Lord’s book if their sin was not forgiven; that is a real leader, putting himself in the way of harm for his people (Exodus 32:11, 32). The Lord spoke to him face to face, as a man to his friend: there was no mediator between Moses and the Lord, for Moses himself was the mediator between the Lord and the people (Exodus 33:11).
judgmentFull: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman, who was Zipporah, the daughter of the priest of Midian; a place called Midian and a woman called an Ethiopian is no contradiction (Numbers 12:1). They had not spoken against him when he saved them out of Egypt; the murmuring came from somewhere else and they took hold of it. The Lord heard it, came down in the pillar of the cloud, and declared the difference: to a prophet he speaks in a vision and a dream, but with his servant Moses, faithful in all his house, mouth to mouth, and not in dark speeches (Numbers 12:2-8).

Miriam became leprous, white as snow, and Moses cried to the Lord to heal her; she was shut out of the camp seven days, as one whose father had spit in her face, and the people journeyed not until she was brought in again (Numbers 12:10-15). The spit is correction, a father putting his child in her place, and a charge to raise children to respect the elders and the men of the Lord.

The Lord showed him the land, but he could not go over; he died according to the word of the Lord and was buried in a valley in Moab, and no man knows his sepulchre to this day (Deuteronomy 34:1-6). He was a hundred and twenty years old, his eye not dim nor his natural force abated: not weak and sickly, but in full strength, and still he had to go up and die because he could not enter the land (Deuteronomy 34:7).

There arose not a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face (Deuteronomy 34:10). Some say Joshua was the prophet raised up like Moses, and therefore there is no Christ; but the passage that says Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom says in the same breath that there arose not a prophet like Moses. Joshua was a mighty prophet, but he did not fit that word; Christ did (Deuteronomy 34:9; Deuteronomy 18:18).

cases.name: The manna hoarders
cases.charge: Keeping manna overnight against the word of Moses; going out to gather on the sabbath
cases.summary: The whole congregation murmured for the flesh pots of Egypt, and the Lord rained bread from heaven with a daily portion, to prove whether they would walk in his law or not (Exodus 16:2-4). Some left of it until the morning, and it bred worms and stank; some went out on the seventh day to gather and found none, and the Lord asked how long they would refuse to keep his commandments (Exodus 16:20, 27-28). The manna represents Christ, the word on which Israel depends daily, and the sabbath was already binding in the wilderness.
offenseFull: The whole congregation murmured against Moses and Aaron, wishing they had died in Egypt when they sat by the flesh pots and ate bread to the full (Exodus 16:2-3). The Lord commanded Moses to bring the people out, and when things got tough they made it his fault. They wanted to go back to Egypt for dependency on Egypt, not realizing how much greater a thing God had in store for his people. That is Israel today: when deliverance does not come easy, the people turn on the man sent to them instead of trusting the Most High who sent him. Their murmurings were not against Moses and Aaron but against the Lord, for complaining against the leadership the Most High sets is murmuring against the Most High himself (Exodus 16:8).

The Lord rained bread from heaven, a certain rate every day, that he might prove them, whether they would walk in his law or not (Exodus 16:4). They were already keeping the sabbath; the proving was whether they would stay on him daily, seeking him as the source and the supply. They said it is manna, for they knew not what it was, and the word means, what is it; Moses told them it was the bread the Lord had given them, and what they did not yet know was that he was speaking of Christ (Exodus 16:15). Every man gathered according to his eating, an omer for every man, and he that gathered much had nothing over (Exodus 16:16-18): the portion was different for everyone, by appetite, family size and need, because everybody needs a different level of nourishment of the word of God.

Moses said that no man should leave of it until the morning; it was not to be stored. Some did not hearken and left it, and it bred worms and stank (Exodus 16:19-20). If the bread represents the word of God, yesterday’s studies, yesterday’s class, yesterday’s nourishment for the spirit is not enough for the following day; not that it has no value, but it is not enough. On the sixth day they gathered twice as much and baked what they would bake, and what was laid up for the sabbath did not stink nor breed a worm (Exodus 16:22-24). That is why nothing is cooked on the sabbath: everything is prepared on Friday before sundown, and the leftovers are eaten the next day. Still some of the people went out on the seventh day to gather, and found none (Exodus 16:27).
judgmentFull: The hoarded bread bred worms and stank, and Moses was wroth with them (Exodus 16:20). To the sabbath gatherers the Lord asked how long they would refuse to keep his commandments and his laws; he had given them the sabbath and the bread of two days on the sixth day, and every man was to abide in his place on the seventh day (Exodus 16:28-29). The sabbath was already binding in the wilderness. Abiding in his place is about not going out to gather food on the sabbath; the sabbath is still a holy convocation in all the dwellings, and Israel comes together on it (Leviticus 23:3).

The same manna that bred worms on other nights was preserved for the sabbath, and an omer of it was laid up before the Testimony for the generations: that is the power of the Most High (Exodus 16:32-34). Israel ate manna forty years, until they came to the borders of Canaan (Exodus 16:35). The Lord humbled them and fed them with manna that they might know that man does not live by bread only; the manna was to teach that nourishment is dependent on God, daily (Deuteronomy 8:3). Christ was saying the spirit needs daily nourishment to survive the wilderness, and this is a wilderness, a proving ground with grace, as the fathers had forty years of grace to get it right (Matthew 4:4).

Give us this day our daily bread is not about the food that is eaten; the whole prayer pertains to the kingdom, and it is a reminder of the manna and of the spiritual nourishment needed every day (Matthew 6:11). They did all eat the same spiritual meat, and that Rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:1-4). Christ is the true bread from heaven: the fathers ate manna in the wilderness and are dead, and he that comes to him shall never hunger (John 6:31-35, 49). They soon forgot his works and lusted exceedingly in the wilderness for the flesh pots of Egypt, willing to go back into captivity to have their bellies filled (Psalms 106:13-14).

cases.name: Bezaleel and Aholiab
cases.charge: Making all that the Lord commanded, and teaching others to do it
cases.summary: The Lord called Bezaleel of Judah by name and filled him with the spirit of God in wisdom, understanding, knowledge and all manner of workmanship, gave him Aholiab of Dan, and put wisdom in the hearts of all that were wise hearted (Exodus 31:1-6). God sets every member in the body as it pleases him. The two trained their brethren, Israel did according to all that the Lord commanded Moses, and Moses looked upon all the work and blessed them (Exodus 35:34; Exodus 39:42-43).
offenseFull: The Lord called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and filled him with the spirit of God to devise cunning works in gold, silver and brass, in cutting of stones and in carving of timber; with him he gave Aholiab the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, and put wisdom in the hearts of all that were wise hearted, that they might make all that he had commanded (Exodus 31:1-6). Bezaleel most likely never thought that God had given him a gift; in his mind he was just good at something. But God created him for this purpose and brought him to them, and gave him that talent so that the tabernacle, the ark, the mercy seat, the garments and everything the Lord commanded could be made (Exodus 31:7-11).

The Most High still works the same way. Carpenters, plumbers, electricians, builders, painters and cooks come into the congregation, and he sets every one in the body as it pleases him; no one appoints himself over the camp or the kitchen. There are diversities of operations but the same God working all in all, and the body is not one member but many; the nation cannot be all teachers (1 Corinthians 12:6-11, 14, 18). The Lord will send souls in so that the work gets done: a school goes from a fold-up table with a cloth to a built stage because the Lord brought in builders. But no one may sit on another’s talents or sit on his own hands; everything in its time and order, but a gift must be used.

Every one whose heart stirred him up and whose spirit made him willing brought the Lord’s offering, both men and women, and all the women that were wise hearted spun with their hands (Exodus 35:21-26). The people brought much more than enough, until they were told to stop (Exodus 36:5-7). The Lord is watching whether the nation operates with a willing heart or a covetous spirit, and the question for every school is whether it brings more than enough. The Lord put it in Bezaleel’s heart that he might teach, he and Aholiab: the two the Most High dealt with in workmanship trained their brethren, and Israel put its talents together and built (Exodus 35:34). It is the same today: brothers and sisters with different talents use them and teach others in the congregation.
judgmentFull: The children of Israel did according to all that the Lord commanded Moses; they brought every piece to Moses, and he looked upon all the work, and they had done it as the Lord had commanded, and Moses blessed them (Exodus 39:42-43). It is like finishing a building, the painting, sanding and nailing done, and standing back to see the finished work: all praises to the Most High, and the people are blessed.

The breastplate carried twelve stones according to the names of the children of Israel, like the engravings of a signet, and the shoulders of the ephod carried the same for a memorial (Exodus 39:8-14). The Most High had Israel representing: when the priest stepped on the scene you already knew what nationality he was, for nationality is very important to the Lord and he took it very seriously. The bells and pomegranates went upon the hem of the robe round about, and the word keeps saying round about, because the fringes go all throughout the garment and not only at four corners (Exodus 39:24-26). The plate of the holy crown was of pure gold, written like a signet, Holiness to the Lord (Exodus 39:30). This is the black man’s heritage: the forefathers, the priests, wore crowns of real pure gold.

Then a cloud covered the tent of the congregation, and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle; the forefathers were blessed to witness these things firsthand (Exodus 40:34). That spirit of workmanship on Israel is why the tabernacle, and later the house Solomon built for the Lord, outshined anything the world had seen. In the kingdom the sons of strangers shall build up Israel’s walls, but it will be Israel directing how the Lord wants it done (Isaiah 60:10).

Bezaleel most likely never thought that God had given him a gift; in his mind he was just good at something. But God created him for this purpose and brought him to them, and gave him that talent so that the tabernacle, the ark, the mercy seat, the garments and everything the Lord commanded could be made (Exodus 31:7-11).
cases.judgment: The children of Israel did according to all that the Lord commanded Moses; they brought every piece to Moses, and he looked upon all the work, and they had done it as the Lord had commanded, and Moses blessed them (Exodus 39:42-43). It is like finishing a building, the painting, sanding and nailing done, and standing back to see the finished work: all praises to the Most High, and the people are blessed.

cases.name: Aaron and Israel at the golden calf
cases.charge: Asking for gods to go before them when Moses delayed; Aaron making the molten calf and proclaiming a feast to the Lord; the people worshipping it and rising up to play
cases.summary: Not forty days after the voice from the mount, the people asked Aaron for gods to go before them (Exodus 32:1). Aaron the high priest, who had seen the miracles in Egypt, made a molten calf in honour of Apis, the bull god of Egypt, and proclaimed a feast to the Lord (Exodus 32:2-6). The spirit that was in Israel in Egypt was still in Israel when they left. Moses stood in the breach, three thousand fell, and the Lord plagued the people because they made the calf, which Aaron made (Exodus 32:11-14; Exodus 32:28; Exodus 32:35).
offenseFull: When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down out of the mount, they gathered to Aaron and asked him to make them gods to go before them, for they did not know what had become of this Moses (Exodus 32:1). Israel is an impatient people and hates waiting, to this day. Any time deliverance did not come when Israel wanted it, the nation rebelled, and Moses and the leadership got the blame; the same spirit is against the leadership of Israel to this day.

Aaron told them to break off their golden earrings; men and women both wore earrings in the scriptures, and that is not the sin (Exodus 32:2-3). He took the gold they had brought out of Egypt, for Aaron had the skills of a smith, made a molten calf, and they called it the god that brought them up out of Egypt (Exodus 32:4). The calf was made in honour of Apis, the bull god of Egypt: they gave the Egyptian god the credit for the Red Sea, not the God of Israel, and Israel retained that idolatry among themselves. They had come out of Egypt following what Egypt had them following, and as soon as Moses was gone they went right back to the evil the slave masters had them doing (Leviticus 18:2-3).

Aaron saw the miracles in Egypt and was set up as high priest, yet he succumbed to the pressure of the people; that is why the Lord chose Moses to lead, for Moses could not be moved by any means. He knew it was idolatry and did it under the guise of good intentions; he made it out of fear, though as high priest he knew better. He was supposed to be the man who held the people in place and kept them true to the Lord, and through passiveness he caused the people of God to sin. When he built the altar before it and proclaimed a feast to the Lord, he was participating in it (Exodus 32:5).

They rose up early, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play (Exodus 32:6). That was a pagan feast, and the play was fornication: in honour of the new god made of their gold they had orgies (1 Corinthians 10:7-8).

The Lord told Moses that the people had corrupted themselves and turned aside quickly out of the way (Exodus 32:7-8). Not forty days gone, and they had already left his commandments: while he was giving Moses the righteous laws to make Israel his special people, Israel was below worshipping a calf. He called them a stiffnecked people, and that has been Israel’s reputation with the Father from the beginning; without the laws of God we are a carnal, rebellious people (Exodus 32:9). The spirit that was in Israel in Egypt was still in Israel when they left, and it is the same coming into this truth: the evil carried in from the world will corrupt a man and turn him from the Lord if it is not put off (Ecclesiastes 5:1). It is no different with our people today who prefer an image of a white Jesus. They had broken the first two commandments just given at Sinai (Exodus 20:3-5).
judgmentFull: The Lord told Moses to let him alone, that his wrath might consume them, and he would make of Moses a great nation; Moses was of the tribe of Levi, of the seed of Jacob, so the Lord could have started over with him (Exodus 32:10). Moses stood in the middle, interceding, and pleaded the Lord’s own name and his oath to Abraham, Isaac and Israel; and the Lord repented of the evil he thought to do (Exodus 32:11-14). He was never going to break his covenant, for consuming the people would have destroyed all the seed of Jacob except Moses, and his counsel stands as declared from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10).

They were feasting and dancing around the idol, and Joshua’s loyalty at the mount is one of the main reasons the Lord chose him to succeed Moses (Exodus 32:17-18). Moses brake the tables, burnt the calf, ground it to powder and made the children of Israel drink of it (Exodus 32:19-20).

Moses had left Aaron in charge and came back to a camp deep in wickedness (Exodus 32:21). Aaron answered that the people were set on mischief, and that he cast the gold into the fire and there came out this calf (Exodus 32:22-24). A leader cannot blame the congregation, the same excuse Saul gave; the charge has to be carried.

Aaron had made the people naked unto their shame among their enemies (Exodus 32:25). That is the same nakedness of the garden, the shame of sin uncovered: to be naked is to be in the midst of sin, and idolatry makes a people naked, not so much physically as spiritually (Genesis 3; Revelation 16:15). Moses stood in the gate of the camp, the sons of Levi gathered to him, and about three thousand men fell that day: three thousand of us dropped before ever reaching the promised land, because of rebelliousness (Exodus 32:26-28).

Moses went up to make atonement and asked to be blotted out of the Lord’s book if their sin was not forgiven; that is a real leader, putting himself in the way of harm for his people (Exodus 32:30-32). The Lord answered that whoever sinned against him is the one he would blot out of his book, and that in the day he visits he would visit their sin upon them; he was not forgetting what they did (Exodus 32:33-34). And the Lord plagued the people, because they made the calf, which Aaron made (Exodus 32:35).

cases.name: The sons of Levi at the golden calf
cases.charge: Answering, Who is on the Lord’s side? and executing the sentence on their own brethren at the golden calf, observing the Lord’s word and keeping his covenant
cases.summary: When Moses stood in the gate of the camp and asked who was on the Lord’s side, only the sons of Levi gathered to him; they took every man his sword, did according to his word without hesitating, and about three thousand men fell (Exodus 32:26-28). That is the zeal Levi had for the Most High, and the blessing of Moses names it: they observed his word and kept his covenant (Deuteronomy 33:9). For it Levi was consecrated, taken instead of the firstborn, and given the teaching of the law; Levi is the so-called Haitian today.
offenseFull: Moses called every man to put his sword by his side and go in and out from gate to gate throughout the camp, slaying his brother, his companion and his neighbour (Exodus 32:26-27). The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses without hesitating, and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men (Exodus 32:28). The Lord chose those particular ones to die; that spirit would have wrecked the nation down the road, so he moved it out of the congregation. Do not be broken when someone leaves the truth; the Lord moves spiritually.

Levi was the first to come and the one who started the killing: they killed their own brothers and their own children, and they did not care; if you broke the laws of the Most High, Levi killed you. That is why the blessing says he had not seen his father or his mother, nor acknowledged his brethren, nor knew his own children: that is the devotion they had for the covenant (Deuteronomy 33:9). Levi was to be devoted to God and strict in judgment.
judgmentFull: Moses told them to consecrate themselves that day to the Lord, every man upon his son and upon his brother, that he might bestow upon them a blessing (Exodus 32:29). The Most High took the Levites instead of all the firstborn, which were his from the day he smote all the firstborn in the land of Egypt; he does not love everybody (Numbers 3:11-13). Aaron and his sons were appointed to the priest’s office, and the stranger that came nigh was to be put to death: anybody outside the tribe of Levi doing the service of the Lord was a stranger (Numbers 3:10).

The last blessing of Moses sets their office: the Urim and the Thummim with the high priest, to teach Jacob the judgments and Israel the law, and to put incense and whole burnt sacrifice before the Lord (Deuteronomy 33:8-10; Ecclesiasticus 45:16-17). That is why Levi had no land of his own but dwelt among all the tribes, making the sacrifices and teaching the laws to the people; his substance is the tithes that Levi would receive, and the work of his hands the freewill offerings (Deuteronomy 33:11; Deuteronomy 14:27-29).

The covenant of the Lord with Levi was of life and peace, given him for the fear wherewith he feared, and there was a time when the children of Israel could not sin while Levi was around (Malachi 2:4-6). That is why Jeroboam kicked Levi out of the priest’s office, and Levi went to the southern kingdom: Levi was the one pushing the law, and if Levi stayed around, Levi would force the people back to the laws of God (2 Chronicles 11:13-14).

Levi was supposed to make sure all the tribes kept the laws of God, and Levi went to the opposite side; so the Lord sent a curse upon Levi, cursed his blessings and corrupted his seed (Malachi 2:1-3). Levi is not the priest today; Christ is the high priest.

The blessings tell who the tribes are in the last days: Levi is the so-called Haitian today and Simeon the so-called Dominican, brethren on the same island, Hispaniola, and not united (Genesis 49:5-7). The smiting through the loins of them that hated him was seen in the Haitian revolution under Toussaint Louverture, a thirteen-year war, and that they rise not again is ultimately fulfilled when Christ returns (Deuteronomy 33:11). The instruments of cruelty in their habitations are the witchcraft practised on that island, such as voodoo, and because of those practices the Most High does not unite the two nations. Levi is under the curse of the Most High and must repent and come back to the Lord; and the Lord will purify the sons of Levi, that they may offer unto him an offering in righteousness (Malachi 3:3).

cases.name: Nadab and Abihu
cases.charge: Offering strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not, taking upon themselves a service not appointed them
cases.summary: The law of the incense had already been given to their own father: a perpetual sweet incense, and no strange incense on that altar (Exodus 30:7-9). Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, offered strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not, and the same fire that had consumed the offering on the altar went out from the Lord and devoured them (Leviticus 10:1-2; Leviticus 9:24). They were not to be mourned, because they died in the midst of sin (Leviticus 10:6).
offenseFull: Nadab and Abihu took either of them his censer, put fire in it and incense on it, and offered strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not (Leviticus 10:1). They were priests, and one of their offices was to burn incense to the Lord; they had served long enough to know better. Commanded them not means thou shalt not: he had already told them not to do it, and they did it anyway.

The instructions for the incense were already given: Aaron was to burn sweet incense every morning and at even, a perpetual incense before the Lord throughout their generations, and no strange incense was to be offered on it (Exodus 30:7-9). There were instructions on what could be burned and what could not; the strange fire is that Nadab and Abihu put strange incense before the Lord. The incense was also nothing out of the ordinary for priests; the fire was the problem, for the Lord never commanded that fire. Strange fire is an unacceptable sacrifice that has nothing to do with the Lord, like the fruit Cain brought. Whoever burns fire in a way different from what was given to the levitical priesthood, it is strange to God, as when altars are set up to other gods and other belief systems, and he will destroy him.

When the Most High gave instructions through Moses on what to sacrifice and how, it was with specificity; you did it exactly the way he told you. The service had to be exactly as prescribed, and deviation carried death, which is a reason to thank the Lord for Christ. God did not require what they did; they were self-willed and did their own thing, out of pride, thinking they knew better.

They were also not the ones authorized to burn it: the order of burning incense was given to Aaron, and in the tabernacle service a man had to be appointed to his service and could not take a service upon himself. Zacharias shows the pattern through the generations: he executed the priest’s office in the order of his course, and his lot, his appointed job, was to burn incense when he went into the temple of the Lord (Luke 1:8-9). We must not do things out of order that the Lord has not commanded, as many camps today do what is not in thus saith the Lord.
judgmentFull: Fire went out from the Lord and devoured them, and they died before the Lord (Leviticus 10:2). It was instant judgment, judgment in this life; he wasted no time, and their names are recorded so that we know what not to do. It was the same fire that came out from before the Lord and consumed the burnt offering upon the altar (Leviticus 9:24).

Moses told Aaron that this was what the Lord had spoken: he will be sanctified in them that come nigh him, and before all the people he will be glorified; and Aaron held his peace (Leviticus 10:3). Aaron held his peace because if you do not do what the Lord tells you, you become the sacrifice: he must be glorified, sanctified and holy in all things, and what he orders a certain way has to be done that way.

Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, carried them in their coats out of the camp (Leviticus 10:4-5). Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar were not to uncover their heads nor rend their clothes, lest they die; they were not to mourn them, because Nadab and Abihu died in the midst of sin and what they did was abominable to the Most High, though the whole house of Israel would bewail the burning (Leviticus 10:6).

Aaron and his sons were not to drink wine nor strong drink when they went into the tabernacle (Leviticus 10:9). That speaks of when they were doing the Lord’s work: no drinking on the job, for they had to be sober minded to teach the difference between holy and profane and to stand in judgment (Leviticus 10:10-11; Ezekiel 44:21-24).

Moses diligently sought the goat of the sin offering and found it burnt, and was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, because it should have been eaten in the holy place to bear the iniquity of the congregation (Leviticus 10:16-18). Aaron answered that such things had befallen him that day, and asked whether the sin offering eaten that day would have been accepted in the sight of the Lord; and Moses was content (Leviticus 10:19-20). Aaron had just seen his sons drop dead before the altar and was in the mindset of mourning; the law says to eat before the Lord rejoicing and not to eat of the hallowed things in mourning, so it would not have been accepted (Deuteronomy 12:7; Deuteronomy 26:14). Nadab and Abihu died before their father and had no children, so Eleazar and Ithamar executed the priest’s office (1 Chronicles 24:2).

cases.name: The blasphemer in the camp
cases.charge: Blaspheming the name of the Lord, and cursing, while striving with a man of Israel in the camp
cases.summary: The son of an Israelitish woman, whose father was an Egyptian, strove with a man of Israel in the camp and blasphemed the name of the Lord, and cursed: he spoke ill of the Lord (Leviticus 24:10-11). He was put in ward until the mind of the Lord was shown, and the Lord commanded that all the congregation stone him; under Moses, blaspheming the Lord was an immediate death sentence, for the stranger as well as for him born in the land (Leviticus 24:12-16; Leviticus 24:23).
offenseFull: The son of an Israelitish woman, whose father was an Egyptian, went out among the children of Israel, and he and a man of Israel strove together in the camp (Leviticus 24:10). We came out of Egypt, and some of our sisters had children by the Egyptians; his mother was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, a Danite sister (Leviticus 24:11). His father being an Egyptian shows he was conceived while Israel was in captivity in the land of Egypt, dwelling among the Egyptians. There is no such thing as being half Israelite or a fourth Israelite: if your parent is Israel, you are Israel. He was also a heathen child among us, fighting with the children of Israel because he was not of them. The strife in the camp likely arose from a man of Israel correcting him concerning the law.

In the striving he blasphemed the name of the Lord, and cursed (Leviticus 24:11). Blasphemy is the act of expressing contempt, scorn, or profound disrespect toward the divine, in insulting speech, writing, or actions, and it has levels to it. When it says he cursed, it does not mean modern curse words; it means he spoke ill of the Lord. Blaspheming and cursing here are the same thing, insulting the divine: cursing, reproaching and blaspheming are synonymous (2 Maccabees 10:34).

Rabshakeh did the same when he told Judah that no god of the nations had delivered his land and the Lord would not deliver them: Hezekiah called that day a day of trouble, and of rebuke, and blasphemy, and the Lord answered that Assyria had reproached and blasphemed the Holy One of Israel (2 Kings 19:3-4; 2 Kings 19:22). Blasphemy is not only speech; actions can blaspheme God. David by his deed gave great occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, for it would get around that the king God chose killed a man for his wife (2 Samuel 12:14); and our fathers blasphemed him by trespassing against him, polluting his sabbaths and serving other gods (Ezekiel 20:27). His name is blasphemed continually every day around the world, and the false image of Christ is blasphemy (Isaiah 52:5).
judgmentFull: They put him in ward, meaning they locked him up, that the mind of the Lord might be shewed them, to know what to do with him (Leviticus 24:12). The Lord commanded that he be brought forth without the camp, that all that heard him lay their hands upon his head, and that all the congregation stone him (Leviticus 24:13-14).

Whosoever curseth his God shall bear his sin, and he that blasphemeth the name of the Lord shall surely be put to death, as well the stranger as he that is born in the land (Leviticus 24:15-16). Under Moses, blaspheming the Lord was an immediate death sentence, and he stands as an example to Israel: do not do what he did. The children of Israel did as the Lord commanded Moses and stoned him (Leviticus 24:23). The God who gave that sentence is still the same God today; he does not change (Malachi 3:6). It was this law that was laid against Stephen, when men were suborned to say he spoke blasphemous words against Moses and against God (Acts 6:11).

In the same breath came the law of recompense: he that killeth any man shall surely be put to death, breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and one manner of law stood for the stranger as for one of your own country (Leviticus 24:17-22). When Christ came he taught the proper understanding of eye for eye for dealing inside the nation: resist not evil, turn the other cheek, let him have the cloak also, go with him twain (Matthew 5:38-42). As the Son of God he had authority to magnify the law. Inside our nation we must practise forgiveness, patience and longsuffering, for we are dealing with our own people, brothers with a conscience; we are the most forgiving people on the planet, except when it comes to each other, and Christ dealt with that.
