cases.judgment: They put him in ward, meaning they locked him up, that the mind of the Lord might be shewed them, to know what to do with him (Leviticus 24:12). The Lord commanded that he be brought forth without the camp, that all that heard him lay their hands upon his head, and that all the congregation stone him (Leviticus 24:13-14).

cases.name: The complainers at Taberah and the lusters at Kibroth-hattaavah
cases.charge: Complaining against the Lord after the deliverance, and lusting after the food of Egypt behind the mixed multitude, despising the manna
cases.summary: The Most High hates it when his people complain. He had just destroyed Egypt for them, and at the first trial in the wilderness they complained, and the fire of the Lord burnt in the uttermost parts of the camp (Numbers 11:1-3). Then the mixed multitude fell a lusting, and Israel followed behind them and wept for the fish, the cucumbers and the garlic of the house of bondage, despising angels’ food (Numbers 11:4-6). Quails came, and with the quails a very great plague, and the place was called the graves of lust (Numbers 11:31-34).
offenseFull: When the people complained it displeased the Lord, and he heard it, and his anger was kindled (Numbers 11:1). He had just destroyed Egypt for Israel, its land, its infrastructure, its firstborn, and drowned its army in the sea, all to save the people out; then at the first trial or tribulation the people jumped off his bandwagon, and the same is still being done to this day.

Nothing spoken behind closed doors is hidden. Inquisition is made into the counsels of the ungodly by the Lord and his angels, for the ear of jealousy heareth all things; there is no word so secret that shall go for nought, and the mouth that slandereth a brother, a sister, the leadership, or the Lord slayeth the soul (Wisdom of Solomon 1:8-11; 1 Kings 22:20). A problem with the leadership the Most High set up is a problem with the Most High himself.

Then the mixed multitude among them fell a lusting, and the children of Israel also wept again (Numbers 11:4). The mixed multitude were the other nations sprinkled in among Israel, heathens that ran out of Egypt after them; they were not to be among the children of Israel as rulers, and the law tells what they were for, to be the bondmen and bondmaids of Israel (Exodus 12:38; Leviticus 25:44-45). It was not Israel complaining at first; the nations lusted after the food of Egypt, and the children of Israel, gullible and assimilated as always, followed right after them and murmured against their God. The same spirit is on the people now: whatever the other nations want to do, our people want to be part of it.

They remembered the fish they ate in Egypt freely, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions and the garlic (Numbers 11:5). They were not free in Egypt; they worked with rigour, and the slave mind was still there: they were free, but their minds were not. Likewise black people and Hispanics today have freedoms but are not free; they have privileges, not freedoms. It is the same with the entertainments and comforts of this captivity, and some will do the same thing again in the wilderness when the Most High brings the people back out. They had just seen the Lord consume the complainers in the uttermost parts of the camp, and they went back and did the same thing.

What they despised was angels’ food, sent from heaven prepared without their labour; they only had to pick it up (Psalms 78:25). It agreed to every taste, tempering itself to every man’s liking, so that whatever the tongue craved that day the manna tasted like it, the very garlic and onions and melons they wept for; to complain about that provision was pure rebellion against the Lord God of heaven and earth (Wisdom of Solomon 16:20-21). They tempted God in their heart by asking meat for their lust (Psalms 78:18).
judgmentFull: At Taberah the fire of the Lord burnt among them and consumed them in the uttermost parts of the camp; the people cried to Moses, and the Most High quenched the fire because Moses prayed on behalf of the children of Israel (Numbers 11:1-3). It is the same fire the Lord is going to bring upon America.

Moses heard the people weep throughout their families, every man in the door of his tent, and asked why the Lord had laid the burden of all this people upon him, as a nursing father (Numbers 11:10-12). He was carrying grown people who acted like children, and he would rather be killed out of hand than bear so rebellious a people alone (Numbers 11:15). The people Moses bore are the same people today, the so-called Blacks, Hispanics, and Native American Indians, and the rebellion and complaining in these chapters is one of the marks of the people.

Because they had despised the Lord which is among them and wept to go back among the oppressors he had just destroyed, he would give them flesh not one day nor two, but a whole month, until it came out at their nostrils and was loathsome to them (Numbers 11:18-20). Moses asked how it could be done for six hundred thousand footmen, not counting women and children, and the Lord answered by asking whether his hand had waxed short: the One who destroyed Egypt asks whether his hand is short (Numbers 11:21-23).

A wind from the Lord brought quails from the sea, two cubits high upon the face of the earth, and while the flesh was yet between their teeth, the wrath of the Lord was kindled and he smote the people with a very great plague, exactly as he had warned; the place was called Kibroth-hattaavah, the graves of lust, because there they buried the people that lusted (Numbers 11:31-34). He gave them their request, but sent leanness into their soul (Psalms 106:15). The lesson also stands in nature: excess of meat brings sickness, and by surfeiting many have perished; animal protein is good for the body, but it is a matter of moderation, not overindulgence (Ecclesiasticus 37:29-31). We are the same people today; these things were written aforetime for our learning, so we can read them and refuse to do as they did (Romans 15:4).

cases.name: Eldad and Medad
cases.charge: Prophesying in the camp when the spirit of the Lord rested on them, and being defended by Moses against envy
cases.summary: Moses could not bear the people alone, so the Lord took of the spirit that was upon him and put it upon seventy elders, and they prophesied and did not cease (Numbers 11:14-25). Two of the men that were written, Eldad and Medad, remained in the camp, and the spirit rested upon them there, and they prophesied in the camp (Numbers 11:26). Joshua asked Moses to forbid them; Moses corrected the envy and wished that all the Lord’s people were prophets (Numbers 11:28-29).
offenseFull: Moses told the Lord he was not able to bear all this people alone, and the Lord told him to gather seventy men of the elders of Israel to the tabernacle; he would take of the spirit upon Moses and put it upon them, that they bear the burden of the people with him (Numbers 11:14-17). Even Moses reached his limit, and the Lord’s answer was delegation: this great work cannot be done by one man. One spirit on seventy men is one accord: they teach differently, but one body, one Lord, one doctrine.

Leadership works the same way today. The spirit on the head, the willingness to put in work, the humility, the patience, is meant to trickle down to the men below him, and the spirit the lead sisters roll in sets the spirit of the sisters in the congregation; that is why the leaders must be right according to the scriptures, because the Most High takes their spirit and lets it come upon the others. The deacons, the captains and the officers are able to prophesy because of what was taught to them by the bishop; they did not come up with it on their own, and even the mannerism of their teaching was learned from him.

The Lord came down in a cloud, took of the spirit that was upon Moses and gave it unto the seventy elders, and when the spirit rested upon them they prophesied and did not cease: they taught, and they did not stop (Numbers 11:24-25). That spirit was the Holy Spirit that Moses had, and the Lord put it upon the elders of Israel; the Holy Spirit was never given to the nations (Isaiah 63:11).

Eldad and Medad remained in the camp; they were of them that were written but went not out unto the tabernacle, and the spirit rested upon them, and they prophesied within the camp, not around the tabernacle, and kept teaching (Numbers 11:26).
judgmentFull: A young man ran and told Moses, and Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses, asked Moses to forbid them (Numbers 11:27-28). Joshua was carrying a spirit of envy, and Moses corrected it: he asked whether Joshua envied for his sake, and wished that all the Lord’s people were prophets and that the Lord would put his spirit upon them (Numbers 11:29). The Most High wants all his people to be prophets, and the prophets are the Israelites. Joshua thought they were trying to take the shine from Moses, not understanding that the Lord took the same spirit Moses had and put it on these men.

Do not envy the gift on another brother or sister; glean from it. A brother may be a better teacher, a sister a better labourer; go and learn from them rather than rolling in envy, for the Lord would put his spirit upon them all. Christ answered John the same way when John forbade one casting out devils in his name: forbid him not, for he that is not against us is for us (Luke 9:49-50).

Moses went into the camp where those men were, he and the elders of Israel (Numbers 11:30). When the Lord’s people prophesy together, they say the same things in different ways and teach the same doctrine, with order, structure and uniformity and no schisms, and that cannot be done without elders (1 Corinthians 1:10).

Joshua’s word is read a second way as well. He was the servant of Moses, being moulded and trained to be a leader, and he never once tried to overthrow Moses; he was loyal, not vainglorious, and in his mind Moses was the teacher and the leader. Joshua also saw something on those men that Moses did not yet see: a man can carry the spirit of God and still teach the scriptures for vainglory and for preeminence. The men who rise up to draw away disciples are well-known men in high positions, loved by the people, as Korah and two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, rose up before Moses (Numbers 16:1-2; Acts 20:30).

The lesson for a man waiting on his ministry is the same: before he teaches he must learn to be a servant and a disciple, to appreciate holding post, then handing out a flyer, then being a reader, and then he learns to be a better teacher, as Elisha would not leave his master’s side (2 Kings 2:4). Let us wait on our ministering; a novice lifted up with pride falls into the condemnation of the devil (Romans 12:6-7; 1 Timothy 3:6).

cases.name: Aaron and Miriam
cases.charge: Speaking against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman, and claiming equal standing with the man the Lord had set over them: hath he not spoken also by us?
cases.summary: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman he had married, Zipporah the daughter of the priest of Midian, whom the Lord allowed him (Numbers 12:1; Exodus 2:21). The woman was the excuse; the issue was power, whether the Lord had spoken only by Moses (Numbers 12:2). The Lord declared the difference, and Miriam became leprous, white as snow, all the pigment gone from her skin, and was shut out from the camp seven days (Numbers 12:4-15).
offenseFull: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married (Numbers 12:1). This is still Zipporah, the daughter of the priest of Midian, whom Moses married in the forty years he dwelt outside Egypt, and whom the Lord allowed him to marry (Exodus 2:16; Exodus 2:21); a place being called Midian and the woman called an Ethiopian is no contradiction. Zipporah and her family were Midianites, not Israelites, and the law was that Israel not marry outside the nation; on the law Miriam was right, but she did not use wisdom in how she dealt with it, it was not the time for her to speak, and it backfired in her face.

They did not speak against Moses when he was saving them out of Egypt, nor when he set Aaron over the men and Miriam over the women; the murmuring came from somewhere else and they took hold of it (Numbers 12:2). The marriage was not the issue; the issue was whether God was dealing with Moses only. He was dealing with Aaron and Miriam, but with Moses more, and Miriam became covetous for power and wanted the glory Moses had. The Ethiopian woman was the excuse. One who has a problem with leadership finds something in the leadership, so that when he gossips and murmurs about the body he looks like the righteous one; open the curtain and it is about power. And the Lord heard it.

Miriam’s name is said first: she was the one who started the murmuring against the leaders. She was making herself equal to Moses and equal to Aaron, trying to usurp authority over the man (1 Timothy 2:12). God deals with the woman also, but on a different level, and he hates the woman’s making herself equal to her man or putting herself above him. Speaking against the men of the Lord is the Jezebel spirit. The man Moses was very meek, above all the men upon the face of the earth (Numbers 12:3). They that despise government, presumptuous and selfwilled, are not afraid to speak evil of dignities, the same spirit that speaks against the men the Most High sets up (2 Peter 2:10).
judgmentFull: The Lord came down in the pillar of the cloud, called Aaron and Miriam forth, and declared the difference (Numbers 12:4-5): to a prophet he makes himself known in a vision and speaks in a dream, but with his servant Moses, faithful in all his house, he speaks mouth to mouth (Numbers 12:6-8). Moses was a greater spirit; some leaders are greater than others, and that must be accepted. The men of the Lord are set up by the Most High, and every idle word spoken against them will be given account of in the day of judgment (Matthew 12:36).

The anger of the Lord was kindled, the cloud departed from off the tabernacle, and Miriam became leprous, white as snow (Numbers 12:9-10). All the pigment left her skin, and that shows Miriam was a black woman. She came to look like a white woman, like an Edomite. Aaron pleaded that she not be as one dead, whose flesh is half consumed when he comes out of his mother’s womb (Numbers 12:12): as a baby born with no pigment in the skin, so Miriam looked when the Lord took the pigment out of her skin, and that is the look of Esau today.

Aaron, who had spoken against Moses, now called him lord. Murmuring against the man of the Lord is sin, and Aaron confessed it (Numbers 12:11). Moses cried to the Lord to heal her (Numbers 12:13). Miriam’s judgment was worse than Aaron’s because she was the instigator and because she was the woman: she stepped out of her place, and the Lord told her to go back.

The Lord answered that if her father had but spit in her face, she should be ashamed seven days (Numbers 12:14). The spit is correction, a father putting his child in her place; had she been raised to respect the men of the Lord, this would not have befallen her. She should have been humbled from a child: had her father chastised her and rebuked her sharply she would not have had that tongue. She was shut out from the camp seven days, the same law by which the leper dwells alone without the camp, and the people journeyed not till Miriam was brought in again (Numbers 12:15; Leviticus 13:46).

This is a charge to raise children in the fear of the Lord and to teach them to respect the elders and the men of the Lord; parents who let their children speak evil to the men of the Lord provoke them to wrath and bring judgment on the household (Ephesians 6:1-4). Israel was to remember what the Lord their God did unto Miriam by the way (Deuteronomy 24:9). When God changed her complexion Miriam humbled herself and got back right with the Lord, and he names her among those he sent before Israel out of Egypt (Micah 6:4).

cases.name: The ten spies
cases.charge: Bringing up an evil report of the land the Lord had given, putting the spirit of fear on the people, and making all the congregation to murmur against Moses
cases.summary: Twelve rulers, heads of the children of Israel, searched the land the Lord was giving them forty days and brought back its fruit (Numbers 13:1-26). Ten put a nevertheless after the promise: the people were strong, the cities walled, the giants were there, and they were as grasshoppers in their own sight (Numbers 13:27-33). The men that brought up the evil report died by the plague before the Lord (Numbers 14:36-37).
offenseFull: The Lord told Moses to send men to search the land of Canaan, which he was giving to the children of Israel, a ruler of every tribe of their fathers (Numbers 13:1-2). Which I give: the fight was already the Lord’s, and the land already given. Every man sent was a ruler among them, a head of the children of Israel, a man of renown who could lead other men. Sending out spies to learn the landscape, the people, and their strength is the wisdom of war; Moses had learned such things as a leader in Egypt.

They searched the land forty days, and at the brook of Eshcol they cut down a branch with one cluster of grapes so great it took two men to carry it upon a staff, for the earth was younger then and brought forth greater stature in its fruit and its men (Numbers 13:17-25; 2 Esdras 5:52-55). They returned and agreed the land flowed with milk and honey; then the report turns on one word: nevertheless (Numbers 13:27-28). The people were strong, the cities walled, and the children of Anak were there. Doubt entered on the heels of the promise.

Caleb stilled the people and told them to go up at once and possess it, for they were well able to overcome it (Numbers 13:30); the Most High had already said he would deliver the enemy into their hands, so their stature did not matter. But the men that went up with him said they were not able, for the people were stronger than they (Numbers 13:31). That is carnal fear, against the word of the Lord, for to take the land they had to fight the people of the land, Africans of great stature. They brought up an evil report, calling it a land that eats up its inhabitants, where they saw the giants, the sons of Anak, and were in their own sight as grasshoppers (Numbers 13:32-33). Bringing it up unto the children of Israel means they spread it and put that fear on all the people.

The Lord had willed them to go up, but these men were so out of the spirit that they forgot he had already destroyed mightier nations before them. Rulers and leaders shook with doubt and fear, and doubt and fear are Satan’s playground. An evil report spreads a spirit of fear, but the Most High has not given his people the spirit of fear (2 Timothy 1:7). The giants were men of great stature, famous from the beginning, yet destroyed because they had no wisdom (Baruch 3:26-28), and by the law of war the fearful were sent back home, lest they put their fear upon the other men (1 Maccabees 3:56). When the leadership says what is going to be done, do not speak against it, for then the spirit of murmuring goes out into the congregation; if you do not understand at that moment, the Most High has not revealed it to you yet.
judgmentFull: The spirit of fear jumped from the leaders onto everybody: all the congregation lifted up their voice and cried, the people wept that night, and all the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron (Numbers 14:1-2). In murmuring against Moses and Aaron they were truly murmuring against the Most High, for the instruction came from him. They said one to another to make a captain and return into Egypt, forgetting there was nothing to return to, for Pharaoh and his army were destroyed and Egypt laid waste (Numbers 14:3-4). Promotion comes from the Lord; when man picks the leader, the people stay in captivity.

Joshua and Caleb rent their clothes, for the people were about to bring death upon themselves, and exhorted them not to rebel against the Lord nor fear the people of the land, who were bread for them, for the Lord was with them (Numbers 14:6-9). But all the congregation bade stone them with stones, and the glory of the Lord appeared in the tabernacle (Numbers 14:10). It is the same today: when the truth is brought that the Most High loves the people and has something great for them if they repent, they do not believe it and are ready to kill the messenger, hating him that rebuketh in the gate (Amos 5:10).

The tenth provocation was the report of the spies, and it was the last (Numbers 14:22-23; Numbers 14:27). After the number of the days in which they searched the land, forty days, each day for a year, they would bear their iniquities forty years (Numbers 14:34): that is how the Most High deals in numbers, the forty years matching the forty days exactly.

The very men that brought up the evil report, who made all the congregation murmur against Moses, died by the plague before the Lord, but Joshua and Caleb lived still (Numbers 14:36-38). The Lord never liked anyone speaking against his prophets, and he is faithful to do what he says. Be mindful who you give ear to. The giants the ten feared are the ones Caleb went up and took his land from (Joshua 14:12-15).

cases.name: Caleb and Joshua
cases.charge: Wholly following the Lord, with faith and courage to go up and possess the land he had given, when ten spies and the whole congregation would not
cases.summary: Twelve men searched the same land and saw the same walled cities and the same giants; ten said they were not able (Numbers 13:25-33). Joshua and Caleb rent their clothes before a congregation that bade stone them (Numbers 14:6-10). Caleb had another spirit with him and followed the Lord fully, and of six hundred thousand on foot these two were preserved to go into the land (Numbers 14:24; Numbers 14:30).
offenseFull: Joshua was among the spies: of the tribe of Ephraim, Oshea the son of Nun, whom Moses called Jehoshua; and of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh (Numbers 13:6; Numbers 13:8; Numbers 13:16). The land was the Lord’s gift to the children of Israel (Numbers 13:2): the fight was already the Lord’s, and the land already given.

Caleb stilled the people before Moses and told them to go up at once and possess it, for they were well able to overcome it (Numbers 13:30). Caleb showed faith and courage: the Most High had already said he would deliver the enemy, the Hamites of the land, into their hands, so it did not matter how tall they were. Caleb was not playing any games; he was about that business, ready to go and take the land, because he understood the Most High had already promised the land, so he had no fear. His brethren that went up with him made the heart of the people melt, but he wholly followed the Lord his God (Joshua 14:8).

When the congregation wept and spoke of a captain to take them back to Egypt, Joshua and Caleb rent their clothes and told all the company that the land was exceeding good, and that they were not to rebel against the Lord nor fear the people of the land, who were bread for them (Numbers 14:6-9). Those were young men with faith, speaking to older men whose faith was weak. All the congregation bade stone them with stones (Numbers 14:10): that is what faith got them from their own people. In the time of Moses they did a work of mercy, in that they withstood the congregation, withheld the people from sin, and appeased the wicked murmuring (Ecclesiasticus 46:7).

There has to be something different about a man in regard to faith; he cannot move in a faithless spirit, for that will not profit the people at all. The Lord’s servant Caleb had another spirit with him and followed him fully (Numbers 14:24). That is what the Lord wants: a different spirit about faith, following fully whatever everybody else is doing, whatever the peer pressure, the trial or the temptation. If the Lord finds a man lukewarm, choosing his children, his parents or his spouse over following God and Christ and keeping the commandments wholly, he will not enter into the land; he must follow fully like Caleb (Matthew 10:37).
judgmentFull: None of that generation would come into the land, save Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun (Numbers 14:30). Out of all the people that came out of Egypt, only Caleb and Joshua saw that land; the men that came out died in the wilderness and their children went in. That is how rebellious Israel was, and how rebellious Israel still is. Of six hundred thousand people on foot, they two were preserved to bring the people into the heritage (Ecclesiasticus 46:8).

The Most High kept Caleb alive forty and five years, and at fourscore and five he was as strong as in the day Moses sent him, for war, both to go out and to come in (Joshua 14:10-11). This man was eighty-five years old and in perfect health; he kept that strength to fight, and he was not retired from battle at eighty-five. He asked for the very mountain the Anakims were in, where the cities were great and fenced: if the Lord were with him, he would drive them out (Joshua 14:12). Joshua blessed him and gave him Hebron for an inheritance, because he wholly followed the Lord God of Israel (Joshua 14:13-14). Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak: he was promised Hebron, and he went and claimed it himself (Joshua 15:14).

The Lord gave strength also unto Caleb, which remained with him unto his old age, so that he entered upon the high places of the land and his seed obtained it for a heritage (Ecclesiasticus 46:9). Everybody does not get that strength, and strength is not shown when everything is good; it shows when a man is going through something. His life was put there as the example, that all the children of Israel might see that it is good to follow the Lord (Ecclesiasticus 46:10).

Joshua, a man in whom is the spirit, was set before Eleazar the priest and before all the congregation and given some of Moses’ honour, so all Israel could see with their own eyes the man the Most High ordained to lead the nation after the death of Moses (Numbers 27:18-23). Joshua of Ephraim and Caleb of Judah, the only two that came out of Egypt to go in and possess the land, are of the head tribes of the northern and southern kingdoms.

cases.name: The generation that died in the wilderness
cases.charge: Tempting the Lord ten times and not hearkening to his voice; unbelief at Kadesh-barnea; seeking a captain to return into Egypt
cases.summary: All the men who had seen the Lord’s glory and his miracles in Egypt and in the wilderness tempted him ten times, the tenth and last at the report of the spies, when they wept at the border of the land and spoke of making a captain to return into Egypt (Numbers 14:1-4; Numbers 14:22). The Lord did to them as they had spoken in his ears: their carcasses fell in the wilderness, all numbered from twenty years old and upward, save Caleb and Joshua, and their little ones went in (Numbers 14:28-31).
offenseFull: The Lord gave the count himself: all those men which had seen his glory and his miracles had tempted him now ten times and had not hearkened to his voice (Numbers 14:22). Write the ten down; the Most High deals in numbers, and nothing in the Bible is insignificant.

One, at the Red Sea: because there were no graves in Egypt, they said it had been better to serve the Egyptians (Exodus 14:11-12). Two, at Marah, over the bitter waters (Exodus 15:23-24). Three, in the wilderness of Sin, for the flesh pots (Exodus 16:2-3). Four, hoarding the manna against a specific instruction, and it bred worms and stank (Exodus 16:19-20). Five, gathering on the sabbath after the Lord had given two days of bread on the sixth day: no gratitude at all (Exodus 16:27-29). Six, Massah and Meribah, where they chode with Moses, contentious, going back and forth, almost ready to stone him over water, tempting the Lord whether he was among them or not (Exodus 17:2-7). Seven, the golden calf, with disrespect in their words toward the man who led them out (Exodus 32:1-10). Eight, Taberah, where the fire of the Lord burnt among them, the same thing he is going to do in America. Nine, the lusting for flesh, ungrateful, weeping for the food of Egypt and complaining about the manna of heaven (Numbers 11:1-6; Numbers 11:34). Ten, the report of the spies, and it was the last (Numbers 14:1-4).

Israel was rebellious against God’s laws before it even left Egypt, and today is no different; those rebellious spirits from back then are still in the earth today. Aaron made the calf out of fear, knowing better as high priest, and it is no different with our people today who prefer white Jesus or run to a stone in the east that cannot answer prayers.

At the border of the land the whole congregation wished they had died in Egypt, and said one to another to make a captain and return into Egypt (Numbers 14:2-4). Were they loved by the Egyptians? No; the same way Israel is hated in America, Israel was hated in Egypt also. They had cried to the Most High under the taskmasters; now they were in the wilderness and wanted to go back to master. Harriet Tubman could have saved thousands more if they had known they were slaves, and our people who still want to stay with master in Babylon America have the same thought. America is the spiritual Egypt today, and some of our people want it to go on forever. It was a no to the leaders God appointed, and a search for somebody to give heed unto their itching ears.

Do not say you would never have complained; you would do exactly the same thing. Some will say the same when Christ brings the people back into the wilderness, and the complaints are heard every year at the Feast of Tabernacles: the Lord hears the murmuring in the tents. They could not enter in because of unbelief (Hebrews 3:19).
judgmentFull: Moses stood as the mediator between the people and God, and the Lord pardoned according to his word: that is how much the Most High loved Israel and loved Moses (Numbers 14:18-20). He asked how long he should bear with this evil congregation and swore that as they had spoken in his ears, so he would do to them: their carcasses would fall in this wilderness, all numbered from twenty years old and upward that murmured against him, save Caleb and Joshua (Numbers 14:26-30). He was speaking not just to the ten but to the whole congregation that joined in the murmuring. The little ones the doubters said would be a prey were the ones brought in, to know the land their fathers despised (Numbers 14:31). After the number of the days they searched the land, each day for a year, they bore their iniquities forty years, and the forty years matched the forty days exactly (Numbers 14:33-34).

Told these sayings, they mourned, then presumed to go up to the top of the mountain, though the Lord was not among them and the ark and Moses departed not out of the camp, and the Amalekites and the Canaanites smote them even unto Hormah (Numbers 14:39-45). All they had to do was follow counsel. Their refusal was written for us, that we would learn to follow the counsel of the men the Most High sets up rather than lean on our own presumption.

From Kadesh-barnea to the crossing of the brook Zered was thirty and eight years, until all the generation of the men of war were wasted out from among the host, as the Lord sware unto them; the hand of the Lord was against them to destroy them until they were consumed (Deuteronomy 2:14-16). He pitied not the six hundred thousand footmen who were gathered together in the hardness of their hearts (Ecclesiasticus 16:10). The saying that God is good all the time is not scriptural: the same God drowned the whole earth, swallowed rebels alive, and left a generation in the wilderness for forty years; God is good all the time to the people that keep his commandments.
They murmured and were destroyed of the destroyer, and all these things happened unto them for ensamples, written for our admonition (1 Corinthians 10:10-11).

cases.name: The man gathering sticks on the Sabbath
cases.charge: Gathering sticks on the sabbath day to kindle a fire and cook, presumptuously, when he was commanded to rest
cases.summary: Numbers 15 sets the sin of ignorance, which an offering covered, beside the sin done presumptuously, which a man thought about before he did it and for which he was cut off (Numbers 15:27-31). The man found gathering sticks on the sabbath is the example: he was gathering them to kindle a fire and cook on the day he was commanded to rest (Numbers 15:32). The Lord commanded that he be surely put to death, and all the congregation stoned him without the camp (Numbers 15:33-36). Because of that act the Most High gave Israel the fringes (Numbers 15:37-41).
offenseFull: Israel was to keep the Lord’s sabbaths, a sign between him and them throughout their generations, that they might know that he is the Lord that sanctifies them (Exodus 31:13). Keeping the weekly sabbath and the feast days shows that Israel are his children and he is their God; the nations do not have this sabbath, and adopted Sunday worship is not the true sabbath given to the children of Israel. Every one that defiled it was surely to be put to death (Exodus 31:14-15).

No fire was to be kindled throughout their habitations on the sabbath day, and kindling fire goes to cooking (Exodus 35:2-3). What was to be baked was baked the day before and the rest laid up, so the day before is the prep day, and what is prepared that day is what is eaten (Exodus 16:23). Eating is allowed on the sabbath, but not cooking, and what could be called work opens the door to every man excusing his trade on the sabbath.

One law covered the soul that sinned through ignorance, born in Israel or a stranger: he brought a she goat of the first year, the priest made an atonement for him, and it was forgiven him (Numbers 15:27-29). But the soul that does aught presumptuously sins willfully; he thought about what he was doing before he did it. Whether born in the land or a stranger, that soul reproached the Lord; because he despised the word of the Lord and broke his commandment, he was utterly cut off, meaning put to death, and his iniquity was upon him (Numbers 15:30-31). For some sins under the law of Moses there was no forgiveness, and for them a man was put to death.

While the children of Israel were in the wilderness they found a man gathering sticks on the sabbath day (Numbers 15:32). He is the example of the presumptuous sin just described. He was not picking up sticks just to pick up sticks; he was gathering them to kindle a fire and cook on the sabbath, when he was supposed to be resting, and he knew better. Moses had told them to stay home and prepare enough food, and there was no reason for them to go out of their houses; this man had no respect for the sabbath, did not care, and wanted to do his own thing.
judgmentFull: They that found him brought him unto Moses and Aaron and unto all the congregation, and they put him in ward, meaning they locked him up in prison, because it was not declared what should be done to him (Numbers 15:33-34). Then the Lord commanded Moses that the man be surely put to death, and all the congregation stoned him with stones without the camp, and he died (Numbers 15:35-36). He did not even get to the act itself; he had the intention, and for that willful intent he was put to death. He was killed without mercy, to make him an example.

Because of that act the Most High gave Israel the commandment to make fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and to put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue (Numbers 15:37-38). The fringe is to look upon and remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them, and not to seek after your own heart and your own eyes; so that when we think of sin, we look at the fringes and remember the laws of the Most High instead of going and picking up sticks (Numbers 15:39-41). Fringes were the fashion of the Near East, but Israel’s had blue on them to distinguish Israel from everybody else, and they went all around the border of the garment, not on four corners.

The stoning was done away in Christ, but the judgment for breaking the sabbath still stands, and people still die on the sabbath day, Friday sundown to Saturday sundown; the Most High is justified, because it is his sign between him and his people. By Christ all that believe are justified from all things from which they could not be justified by the law of Moses (Acts 13:39), but grace is not a licence to stay in sin. He that despised Moses’ law died without mercy under two or three witnesses, and he that has trodden underfoot the Son of God is worthy of a sorer punishment (Hebrews 10:28-29). Under grace there is a grace period to get right; he who does not use it to fix himself receives eternal fire, not only a stoning.

The sabbath was made for man, the children of Israel, and the Son of man is Lord of the sabbath because Christ instituted it (Mark 2:27-28). The Lord gives no man licence to sin, but Christ is Lord of the sabbath and brought grace for necessities out of a man’s control, a blown tire or an empty tank on the way to keep the sabbath, or medicine when the body is in danger; it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days (Matthew 12:8-12).

cases.name: Korah, Dathan, and Abiram
cases.charge: Rising up against Moses and Aaron, the men the Lord chose, with two hundred and fifty princes, and seeking the priesthood also
cases.summary: Korah of Levi, with Dathan, Abiram and On of Reuben and two hundred and fifty princes, famous in the congregation and men of renown, rose up against Moses and Aaron and charged them with lifting themselves above the congregation (Numbers 16:1-3). They had the service of the tabernacle and it was not enough; they sought the priesthood also (Numbers 16:9-10). The earth opened her mouth and swallowed them alive, and a fire from the Lord consumed the two hundred and fifty (Numbers 16:31-35).
offenseFull: Korah was of Levi, and Dathan, Abiram, and On were of Reuben; with them rose up two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown, two hundred and fifty three in all against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16:1-2). These were known and powerful men among the congregation, and their influence, because of who they were, is how they were able to persuade people. They took men: that was the cliques, and to gather men against Moses a man must have been gossiping and talebearing for a long time.

When division, heresies and offences come to draw away the brothers and sisters, the man who rises up to do it is never a regular officer or a regular soldier; it is a brother well known and loved by the people, a man put in a high position who was not faithful over what he was over, and because of the love some have for that person, they will leave with him. Of their own selves shall men arise to draw away disciples after them (Acts 20:30).

They charged Moses and Aaron with taking too much upon themselves, saying all the congregation was holy and the Lord among them (Numbers 16:3). They thought Moses and Aaron carried themselves as better than the rest, but the Most High is the one who chose them as leaders and was dealing with them; the accusers were jealous of them. The same spirits are back on the earth today, coming into the congregation and after a season rising up to think themselves wiser than the leadership, the bishop and the deacons (Deuteronomy 11:6).

Moses asked whether it seemed a small thing that the God of Israel had separated them from the congregation to bring them near to himself, to do the service of the tabernacle (Numbers 16:9). Only Levi could do that service, and it was a heavy job in itself. But they sought the priesthood also, and for that cause Korah and all his company were gathered together against the Lord (Numbers 16:10-11). They did not see the honour in their position. Whatever position God gives, officer, soldier, captain, deacon or bishop, even the man mopping the floor, there is honour in it, and he who covets another man’s position will line him up to destroy him by slander. Dathan and Abiram would not come up when Moses called them, because they wanted his spot (Numbers 16:12-14).
judgmentFull: The test was censers: the man whom the Lord would choose, he would be holy (Numbers 16:6-7). The Lord told Moses and Aaron to separate themselves, that he might consume them in a moment, and Moses and Aaron fell upon their faces and pleaded that he not be wroth with all the congregation over one man’s sin; they still had that love for their people (Numbers 16:20-22).

The congregation was commanded to get up from about the tabernacle of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, to depart from the tents of these wicked men, and to touch nothing of theirs, lest they be consumed in all their sins (Numbers 16:23-27). Move away from those who have the spirit of gossip. Moses put the proof on the Most High: if these men died the common death of all men, the Lord had not sent him; but if the Lord made a new thing, and the earth opened her mouth and swallowed them up, they would understand that these men had provoked the Lord (Numbers 16:28-30).

As he made an end of speaking, the ground clave asunder, and the earth opened her mouth and swallowed them up, their houses, all the men that appertained unto Korah, and all their goods (Numbers 16:31-33). They went down alive into the pit: God buried them alive. The two hundred and fifty that followed them did not escape either: there came out a fire from the Lord and consumed them (Numbers 16:34-35). God killed them, their wives and their children; it is hard, terrible history, but it was written for us to learn from, not to murmur.

The censers of these sinners against their own souls were made broad plates for a covering of the altar, a sign that no stranger not of the seed of Aaron come near to offer incense before the Lord (Numbers 16:36-40). They envied Moses and Aaron the saint of the Lord, and the earth swallowed Dathan and the company of Abiram for their insurrection (Psalms 106:16-18). Rising against the men God sent is rising against God. They were as natural brute beasts made to be taken by Satan and destroyed, made to be an example to us today not to go against the leadership God set before us (2 Peter 2:12). Those that perish in the gainsaying of Core want position, rank and preeminence (Jude 1:11).

cases.name: The congregation, the day after Korah
cases.charge: Murmuring against Moses and Aaron the day after Korah, saying they had killed the people of the Lord, when it was God who opened the earth
cases.summary: On the morrow after the earth swallowed Korah’s company and fire consumed the two hundred and fifty, all the congregation murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying they had killed the people of the Lord (Numbers 16:41). Moses did not open the earth; God did. Wrath went out from the Lord, Aaron stood with incense between the dead and the living, and fourteen thousand seven hundred were put to death before the plague was stayed (Numbers 16:46-49). Aaron’s rod that budded was then kept for a token against the rebels, that they die not (Numbers 17:10).
offenseFull: On the morrow, the very next day, all the congregation murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying they had killed the people of the Lord (Numbers 16:41). The day before, they had seen the Most High open up the earth, swallow Korah, Dathan and Abiram, and have fire come down and consume two hundred and fifty men, and still they would not let it go; that is just how rebellious we are. Look at who they blamed. Moses did not open the earth; God did, and now Moses was the killer. So it is in Israel: when people are checked for their own fault, they blame somebody else.

Korah and his company were put out permanently, and Israel murmured over them, as people put out of the congregation today have others come around them and say they were put out unjustly. Even when men were causing confusion in the body and their removal was justified, Israel still found a way to justify the wicked. Korah had the same spirit as Cain and Balaam: he was covetous and desired the power that Moses had (Jude 1:11). To murmur is to speak evil secretly, in the form of backbiting, and those who murmured against Moses and Aaron were destroyed; it was written for us to learn from, not to murmur (1 Corinthians 10:10-11).

The cloud covered the tabernacle and the glory of the Lord appeared, and the Lord came down ready to put them to death again, telling Moses and Aaron to get up from among the congregation that he might consume them in a moment (Numbers 16:42-45). They fell upon their faces, still pleading for their people because they loved them so much. That is the character of Moses: no matter what was against him, he loved his people and stood up for them.
judgmentFull: Wrath had gone out from the Lord and the plague was begun; the Most High was already putting them to death (Numbers 16:46). Aaron ran into the midst of the congregation, put on incense, made an atonement, and stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stayed (Numbers 16:47-48). It was like a wave of death, and Aaron ran in front of it, the dead on one side and the living on the other. The blameless man who made haste was Aaron: with prayer and incense he overcame the Destroyer, the Most High’s death angel, not with strength of body but with a word, while the dead fell down by heaps (Wisdom of Solomon 18:20-23). In his garment was the whole world, the twelve tribes of Israel in the four rows of stones (Wisdom of Solomon 18:24). Even in the midst of that rebellion the Most High still had mercy and sent Aaron to defend the people, though the judgment was well deserved.

Beside the two hundred and fifty three who died with Korah, fourteen thousand seven hundred more were put to death (Numbers 16:49-50). Those who escaped the fire and the earth but still sided with Korah died in the plague. No one escapes when there is rebellion and disrespect: it took until the next day, but those who are loyal to wickedness are revealed after a while.

Then every prince wrote his name upon a rod, twelve rods, with Aaron’s on the rod of Levi, and they were laid up before the testimony, the ark of the covenant (Numbers 17:1-7). By the rod that blossomed the Most High would make the murmurings cease, showing that he was dealing with Moses and Aaron and them alone. On the morrow Aaron’s rod had budded, bloomed blossoms and yielded almonds (Numbers 17:8-9): a staff detached from its tree a long time, and overnight it budded.

The rod was kept before the testimony for a token against the rebels, that they die not, so that the Lord would not have to put them to death again for murmuring (Numbers 17:10-11). It was a remembrance for those who murmur and have their little things to say: remember Aaron’s rod that budded, because you could have died. The people cried that whoever came near the tabernacle would die (Numbers 17:12-13); a man had to be of Levi to go near it; that had to be his office.

cases.offense: On the morrow, the very next day, all the congregation murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying they had killed the people of the Lord (Numbers 16:41). The day before, they had seen the Most High open up the earth, swallow Korah, Dathan and Abiram, and have fire come down and consume two hundred and fifty men, and still they would not let it go; that is just how rebellious we are. Look at who they blamed. Moses did not open the earth; God did, and now Moses was the killer. So it is in Israel: when people are checked for their own fault, they blame somebody else.
cases.judgment: Wrath had gone out from the Lord and the plague was begun; the Most High was already putting them to death (Numbers 16:46). Aaron ran into the midst of the congregation, put on incense, made an atonement, and stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stayed (Numbers 16:47-48). It was like a wave of death, and Aaron ran in front of it, the dead on one side and the living on the other. Even in the midst of that rebellion the Most High still had mercy and sent Aaron to defend the people, though the judgment was well deserved.

cases.name: Moses at the waters of Meribah
cases.charge: Smiting the rock twice in anger when commanded to speak to it, and saying must we fetch you water, so that the Lord was not sanctified in the eyes of the children of Israel
cases.summary: In the desert of Zin there was no water, and the people chode with Moses (Numbers 20:1-5). Commanded to speak to the rock before their eyes, Moses got out of the spirit, called the people rebels, asked whether he and Aaron must fetch them water out of this rock, and smote it twice (Numbers 20:7-11). That we is how you know he was off. The water still came, and for that one deed Moses and Aaron did not bring the congregation into the land (Numbers 20:12).
offenseFull: In the desert of Zin there was no water, and the people gathered against Moses and Aaron again. The people chode with Moses: they raised their voices in a loud, angry, shouting argument, wishing they had died when their brethren died, and asking why they had been brought into this evil place with no seed, figs, vines or pomegranates, and no water (Numbers 20:2-5).

This is us, the blacks and Hispanics. We were taken out of Egypt by the hand of the Most High, headed to the promised land, and we forgot so quickly how we were brought out; anything out of the ordinary, we complained about it. That constant complaining is one of the marks that this book is speaking of this people. Moses had to deal with all twelve tribes at once, twelve personalities and twelve attitudes; give that brother all the honour he deserves.

The order was to take the rod and speak to the rock before their eyes, nothing else, and it would give forth his water (Numbers 20:7-8). At Horeb the Lord had said to smite the rock; now he said to speak to it (Exodus 17:6). The rock gives forth his water because the rock represents Christ: the spiritual Rock that followed Israel was Christ, who calls any man who thirsts to come unto him and drink (1 Corinthians 10:4; John 7:37). The people would have seen Moses speak to the rock and the rock let go with that water; it was a symbol.

At this point Moses got out of the spirit; a stomach can only take so much of a rebellious people. Pressed by Israel and angry, he called them rebels and asked whether he and Aaron must fetch them water out of this rock (Numbers 20:9-10). The Lord never told him to say that. That we is how you know Moses was off: he included himself with the Most High and forgot who was giving the water; it was the Lord, not Moses and not Aaron. Then he smote the rock twice with his rod (Numbers 20:11); so angry he was not hearing the instruction, he did not hit it once, but twice.

Anger will take a man out of the spirit. Moses was the meekest man on the whole earth and always listened to God, but that time he reacted out of anger, on his emotions instead of the instructions he was given, leaning on his own understanding instead of trusting in the Lord with all his heart (Proverbs 3:5). The wrathful man stirs up strife (Proverbs 15:18), and Moses’ anger at the children of Israel clouded his judgment. Every one of us probably would have struck the rock, which is why those who grow in this truth and become leaders must learn to control their emotions. They angered him at the waters of strife, so that it went ill with Moses, who spoke unadvisedly with his lips (Psalms 106:32-33).
judgmentFull: The water still came out abundantly (Numbers 20:11). Because they believed him not, to sanctify him in the eyes of the children of Israel, the Lord told Moses and Aaron that they would not bring the congregation into the land (Numbers 20:12). They believed in the Lord, but they did not take heed to what he told them: they let their anger, and the hatred they had toward their brethren, override the commandment, and did not follow it wholly. The Lord called that one time a lack of belief. This is the water of Meribah, which means strife (Numbers 20:13).

Moses took the credit and became high minded instead of sanctifying the Most High. The contrast is the war with Og: afterward the people said the Lord their God delivered the king of Bashan into their hands (Deuteronomy 3:3). They did the fighting but gave the praise, the glory and the victory to the Most High and did not boast in their own swords; that is how you sanctify the Most High, and Moses at the rock did the opposite.

Moses had good character, and that one mistake meant he was not making it across. At mount Hor Aaron was gathered unto his people for the rebellion at Meribah; Moses stripped him of his garments and put them upon Eleazar, the priesthood passed to Eleazar, Aaron died in the top of the mount, and all Israel mourned him thirty days (Numbers 20:23-29). Moses was told to go up into mount Abarim and see the land but not enter it, and then be gathered unto his people as Aaron was, because the Lord gave a specific commandment to speak unto the rock and Moses instead smote it twice (Numbers 27:12-14).

Moses begged to go over and see the good land, trying to get the Lord to repent of his word, and laid it on stiffnecked Israel (Deuteronomy 3:23-26). The answer was final: let it suffice, speak no more of this matter, as a parent tells a child that keeps begging that the matter is closed. He was to see the land from Pisgah and to charge, encourage and strengthen Joshua, the man chosen to replace him, for promotion comes from the Most High (Deuteronomy 3:27-28). The Lord had to deal with Moses here, yet Moses is getting the Kingdom.

cases.name: Israel and the fiery serpents
cases.charge: Speaking against God and against Moses, and loathing the light bread, the angels’ bread, rained on them in the wilderness
cases.summary: Edom refused Israel passage, and the way around was longer than the people wanted it to be, and their soul was much discouraged (Numbers 21:4). They spoke against God and against Moses: no bread, no water, and their soul loathed this light bread, which was angels’ bread (Numbers 21:5). The Lord sent fiery serpents, and much people of Israel died; the people confessed, Moses prayed, and every one bitten who beheld the serpent of brass lived (Numbers 21:6-9). That serpent was for the Israelites, to heal the Israelites, and Christ brought it to Nicodemus: so must the Son of man be lifted up (John 3:14-15).
offenseFull: They journeyed from mount Hor by the way of the Red sea to compass the land of Edom, and the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way: since Edom refused passage, Israel had to go around, and the way was longer than they wanted it to be (Numbers 21:4). Edom is the people called the white man today. That hatred goes back to Esau, who hated Jacob because of the blessing; it is perpetual, and it shows to this day in Edom still rejecting Israel (Genesis 27:41; Ezekiel 35:5).

The people spoke against God and against Moses, asking why they had been brought up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness, with no bread and no water, and saying that their soul loathed this light bread (Numbers 21:5). They hated that manna. The bread they were loathing was angels’ bread, and they complained about it anyway (Psalms 78:25). No other nation on this earth takes food as seriously as Israel; even the complaints over bread and water are a familiar mark of this people to this day, and you cannot put another nation in these scriptures. Murmuring against God and Moses over the bread brought the fiery serpents, and there will be no Popeyes or McDonald’s in the wilderness either.
Paul set it among the examples written for Israel’s admonition: they tempted Christ, for it was Christ with them in the wilderness, and were destroyed of serpents (1 Corinthians 10:9-11).
judgmentFull: The Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people, and much people of Israel died (Numbers 21:6). Fiery means poisonous. Read it with the nation in view: the people being bitten, the people dying, all of it is Israel. A mixed multitude came out of Egypt with Israel, and some argue from that, but the Lord was not judging the mixed multitude on keeping the commandments; he gave his law unto Jacob and his judgments unto Israel, and no nation has known them, and it was much people of Israel that died (Psalms 147:19-20).

Once the serpents started biting and much people died, the people came back into the spirit: they confessed that they had sinned in speaking against the Lord and against Moses, and asked him to pray that the Lord would take away the serpents; and Moses prayed for the people, for the nation of Israel, because they had broken God’s commandments and murmured against the Most High and against him (Numbers 21:7).

Moses was told to make a fiery serpent and set it upon a pole, and every one that was bitten, when he looked upon it, would live: every one of the twelve tribes, because all twelve tribes were there. Moses made a serpent of brass, and any man a serpent had bitten, when he beheld the serpent of brass, lived (Numbers 21:8-9). That pole with the snake wrapped around it, which you see today in hospitals and on the side of the ambulance, comes from this scripture, and it is supposed to represent healing.

The wrath did not endure for ever, because they repented; they were troubled to be admonished, that is, corrected, having a sign of salvation to put them in remembrance of the commandment of the law (Wisdom of Solomon 16:5-6). The sign of salvation was the brass serpent, and the salvation is Christ. Looking on it was not the whole of it; there was repentance with it, and Christ brings the understanding that the laws must be kept.

That brass serpent on the pole was for the Israelites, to heal the Israelites, because it was the Israelites being bitten for rebelling against God and against Moses. Christ brought this same passage to Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews, two Israelites speaking together about the history of Israel: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up, that whosoever believes in him should not perish (John 3:1, 14-15). The whosoever, when you go back to Moses, was not all nations and all races; it was whosoever of the Israelites, and Peter defines it: whosoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved, ye men of Israel (Acts 2:21-22). The world that God so loved, in the next verse, is the world of Israel, the same people in view (John 3:16).
In time the people started worshipping the serpent that Moses made as a god, and Hezekiah broke the brasen serpent in pieces (2 Kings 18:4).

cases.name: Sihon and Og
cases.charge: Refusing Israel passage on the king’s highway and coming out to battle against them, when the iniquity of the Amorites was full
cases.summary: Israel was forbidden to meddle with Esau, Moab or Ammon, for the Most High had appointed their possessions (Deuteronomy 2:4-19). Sihon king of the Amorites refused Israel passage on the highway, for the Lord hardened his spirit, as he hardened Pharaoh’s, that he might deliver him into Israel’s hand; the iniquity of the Amorites was full (Deuteronomy 2:26-30). Og king of Bashan, of the remnant of giants, came out after him. Both kingdoms were utterly destroyed at the command of the Most High (Deuteronomy 2:33-34; Deuteronomy 3:3-6).
offenseFull: Israel had compassed mount Seir long enough and was charged to turn northward and pass through the coast of their brethren the children of Esau, the people called the white man today, and not meddle with them (Deuteronomy 2:2-6). The Most High put fear upon Esau so they would not trouble Israel, because he did not want a war; mount Seir was given to Esau, not so much as a foot breadth for Israel. The same order came for Moab and Ammon, the children of Lot, the nations called the Chinese and the Japanese today: for Lot’s sake the Most High secured their land to his children (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19; Numbers 21:10-13).

Then the word changed: rise up and pass over the river Arnon, for the Lord had given Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land into Israel’s hand (Deuteronomy 2:24-25). That day he would begin to put the dread of Israel upon the nations under the whole heaven. The Most High never gave Israel the spirit of fear, but when it was time to conquer he put the fear of Israel on the nations, so that they trembled and were in anguish. The book of the wars of the Lord recorded what he did in the brooks of Arnon (Numbers 21:14), and the Lord there is Christ, who has been warring ever since the Exodus.

Moses sent messengers to Sihon with words of peace: let Israel pass through by the highway, buying meat and water for money, only passing through on foot, as was done passing Esau in Seir and Moab in Ar (Deuteronomy 2:26-29). But Sihon would not, for the Lord hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, that he might deliver him into their hand. It is the same dealing as with Pharaoh: the Lord hardened his heart so the judgment could land, for the iniquity of the Amorites was full and their land was appointed to Israel (Deuteronomy 2:30; Genesis 15:16). Sihon came out against Israel to fight at Jahaz (Numbers 21:23).

Then Og the king of Bashan came out against them to battle at Edrei (Deuteronomy 3:1). Og was an Amorite, and the Amorites are a Hamitic tribe of the lineage of Canaan (Genesis 10:6, 16); Ham, the youngest son of Noah, is the progenitor of the dark nations. The Hamitic nations were known for great stature, and to this day the tallest peoples on earth, the Watusi, the Dinka, and the Nilotic tribes of Sudan, Ethiopia and Kenya, are Hamites. Only Og remained of the remnant of giants; his bedstead of iron was about thirteen feet long and six feet wide, near the size of two king beds (Deuteronomy 3:11).
judgmentFull: The Lord delivered Sihon before Israel: they smote him and his sons and all his people, took all his cities, and utterly destroyed the men, women and little ones of every city (Deuteronomy 2:31-34; Numbers 21:24-26). That is how thorough the judgment of the Most High was for Israel’s sake; that is how specially privileged Israel was, and still they struggled to believe and obey him. Only the cattle and the spoil were taken for a prey. From Aroer by the river Arnon unto Gilead there was not one city too strong, and Israel touched nothing the Lord withheld, coming not unto the land of the children of Ammon (Deuteronomy 2:35-37).

Of Og the Lord said fear him not, for he had delivered him into their hand (Deuteronomy 3:2; Numbers 21:33-35). Threescore cities were taken, all fenced with high walls, gates and bars, and not one was left untaken; they utterly destroyed the men, women and children of every city, as they did unto Sihon (Deuteronomy 3:4-6). That command came from the Most High himself; this is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God of the Bible, not the invented gospel that says he loves everybody no matter what. All Bashan was called the land of giants, because the giants there were of Og’s kin (Deuteronomy 3:13). The giants were of great stature and expert in war, yet the Lord chose them not; they perished through their own foolishness, and stature and skill in war saved none of them (Baruch 3:26-28).

Always remember, the battle is the Lord’s; this fight is spiritual. Israel does not need weapons of mass destruction: the Bible is the weapon, and when Israel keeps the commandments the Most High fights for his people. After the war the people said the Lord their God delivered the king of Bashan into their hands (Deuteronomy 3:3): they did the fighting, but they gave the praise, the glory and the victory to the Most High and did not boast in their own swords; that is how you sanctify the Most High.

Joshua was told that as the Lord did unto these two kings, so he would do unto all the kingdoms whither he passed, and he was not to fear them (Deuteronomy 3:21-22). The nations heard it: in Jericho Rahab told the spies that when they heard what Israel did to Sihon and Og, their hearts melted (Joshua 2:10-11). The heathen know that Israel has the only true living God. It was the Lord’s good pleasure to give Israel that land: he smote great nations and mighty kings, Sihon and Og, and gave their land to Israel his people for an inheritance (Psalms 135:6-12).

cases.name: Balaam
cases.charge: Divination for hire against Israel; counselling Balak to make Israel fall through the women of Moab and their gods
cases.summary: Balak king of Moab feared that Israel was too big and hired Balaam the son of Beor, a soothsayer, a diviner, to curse them (Numbers 22:2-6; Joshua 13:22). He could not curse what God had blessed, for there is no enchantment against Jacob (Numbers 23:8, 23); so his counsel was the best the enemy can ever do: throw another god in front of Israel and send the women (Numbers 31:16). That counsel is why the Lord put Balaam to death; he was slain with the sword with the kings of Midian (Numbers 31:8).
offenseFull: Balak was the king of the Moabites, the people called the Chinese today. Israel was finally coming into the land, and his fear was that they were too big, so he hired Balaam to do the work (Numbers 22:2-6; Deuteronomy 23:4). Balaam was paid to curse the children of Israel; that was his attribute: he was covetous, and money was his focus. He was a soothsayer, a diviner, a witch so to speak, and his people were the Midianites, of the lineage of Ishmael, the people known today as the Arab man (Numbers 24:14; Numbers 31:8).

His ass saw the angel standing there to kill him when he could not see it himself (Numbers 22:22-33). He could not curse whom God had not cursed (Numbers 23:8). God is not a man that he should lie: Balaam had received commandment to bless, and he could not reverse it (Numbers 23:19-20). There is no enchantment against Jacob, neither any divination against Israel (Numbers 23:23): those enchantments, spirits and spells will not affect Israel while they keep God’s commandments; once you repent, there is no hex, divination or curse of bad luck anyone can put on you.

The spirit of God coming upon him did not make him a prophet: prophets are raised up of the sons of Israel, and the Lord used Balaam to show the nations there is nothing they can do against Israel when the Lord is on Israel’s side (Numbers 24:2; Amos 2:11). Balak offered him honour, and that was Satan speaking through Balak, the same device he tried on Christ (Numbers 24:10-11; Luke 4:6-8). Balaam told Balak what Israel would do to his people in the latter days: a Star out of Jacob, which is Christ, and a Sceptre out of Israel, the King, to smite the corners of Moab (Numbers 24:14-17). Balaam saw Christ destroying the nations.

The nations took this history and understood it: in the latter end Israel would rule over them, and they asked how to stop it from being fulfilled. Balaam could not curse Israel, so his counsel was to throw another god in front of Israel and send the women (Numbers 25:1-3). He told Balak he could not curse them, but he could tell him how to make them fall: whoredom. Through his counsel the women caused the children of Israel to commit trespass against the Lord in the matter of Peor (Numbers 31:16). That is the doctrine of Balaam that Christ held against the church at Pergamos, who taught Balak to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed unto idols and to commit fornication (Revelation 2:14).
judgmentFull: The Most High told Israel to avenge the children of Israel of the Midianites for Peor (Numbers 31:1-2). They slew the five kings of Midian, and Balaam also the son of Beor they slew with the sword (Numbers 31:7-8). That counsel is why the Lord put Balaam to death. Balaam the soothsayer, whose ass saw the angel, went after the lust of greed, and he ended up getting put to death (Joshua 13:22).

The men like Balaam run greedily for money, to be paid to curse Israel, and such men creep in unawares among the people (Jude 1:4).

He asked to die the death of the righteous and to have his last end like Israel’s (Numbers 23:10). The last end of Israel is a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord: the land married, double for our shame, everlasting joy, and a seed acknowledged among the Gentiles as the seed which the Lord hath blessed (Isaiah 62:3-4; Isaiah 61:7-9). Balaam would behold the Star, but not nigh, raised in the last days as a servant far off from the King, because the redeemer is not his (Numbers 24:17).

The same crafty counsel is taken against Israel today, and the pornography industry is one of them. As long as Israel continues in whoredom, with pornography or whatever people are doing, Israel will not build healthy marriages; without healthy marriages there are no spiritually healthy children, and the generational curses keep going. The strength is to come back to the laws of God: that unifies husbands and wives, the children come up in the right frame of mind, prepared to marry other believers’ children, and a nation comes back (Numbers 31:16; Psalms 83:3).

cases.name: Israel at Baal-peor
cases.charge: Whoredom with the daughters of Moab, eating the sacrifices of their gods and bowing down to them, and joining themselves unto Baal-peor
cases.summary: Balaam could not curse Israel, so his counsel was the best the enemy can ever do: throw another god in front of Israel and send the women (Numbers 31:16). In Shittim the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab, ate the sacrifices of their gods and bowed down, and Israel joined himself unto Baal-peor (Numbers 25:1-3). It was sex that got the people to worship another god. The heads of the people were hanged up before the Lord, and twenty-four thousand died in the plague (Numbers 25:4-9).
offenseFull: Israel abode in Shittim, and the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab, who called the people unto the sacrifices of their gods; the people did eat and bowed down, and Israel joined himself unto Baal-peor (Numbers 25:1-3). Moab is the ancient name of China: the Israelites started coming home with the Moabites, the so-called Chinese today, and went and sacrificed to their gods. When they go to those women, they start to worship their gods. The worship of Baal-peor went into whoredom, that orgy worship. That was willingly: syncretism, the blending of religions, by which the nations pulled Israel away from the Most High from the beginning, from Baal-peor to the golden calves to Hellenization to modern day Christianity.

What would cause Israel to bow down to their gods? It was sex that got the people to worship another god. The nations knew: they vexed Israel with their wiles, wherewith they beguiled them in the matter of Peor (Numbers 25:18). Wiles are stratagems, something well planned out, whose result may not come right away. They knew they had to get this people to sin against their God, and they used this stratagem to move them away from him. The Lord would not allow Balaam to curse Israel, but Balaam told Balak how to make them fall: whoredom (Numbers 31:16; Revelation 2:14).

The nations hate God because he chose Israel, and they have taken crafty counsel against his people, with one consent, to cut them off from being a nation (Psalms 83:3-5). Today the pornography industry is one of those crafty counsels, and every video is oversexualised, aimed at destroying the young people’s minds. The Lord never said not to deal with the other nations because they are ugly; he said not to make marriages with them because they will turn the heart after their gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4).

They joined themselves to Baal-peor and ate the sacrifices of the dead, and the plague broke in upon them (Psalms 106:28-29). It was the golden calf again: the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play, and that play means sex. Idolatry leads to whoredom, spiritual whoredom against the Most High and physical whoredom with it (1 Corinthians 10:6-8).
judgmentFull: The Lord told Moses to take all the heads of the people and hang them up before the Lord against the sun, that his fierce anger might be turned away, and Moses told the judges each to slay his men that were joined unto Baal-peor (Numbers 25:4-5). Every one his man means every judge by his rank: the officer over ten took ten, the officer over fifty took fifty. Moses was not running around killing thousands of people; each officer had to put his own men to death, set facing the sun that all might see. With the Most High it is two options only, life and death.

Under the old covenant there was no winking at ignorance; judgment was instant, and this God does not change (Malachi 3:6). The only reason the gods served in this captivity are not judged that way now is the grace and mercy given through Christ: the times of this ignorance God winked at, the Christianity with the white Jesus, the Islam, the Buddhism, the Hinduism, the Egyptology, the atheism; but now he commands all men everywhere to repent, for he has appointed a day in which he will judge the world by Jesus the Christ (Acts 17:29-31). Do not take that mercy lightly, and do not frustrate the grace of God.

While the congregation wept before the tabernacle, a man of Israel brought a Midianitish woman unto his brethren in the sight of all, a man that did not care about his people while everyone around him mourned; Phinehas thrust both of them through, and the plague was stayed (Numbers 25:6-8). Those that died in the plague were twenty and four thousand; Paul counts three and twenty thousand who fell in one day, and either way more than twenty thousand were put to death (Numbers 25:9; 1 Corinthians 10:8).

Their eyes had seen what the Lord did because of Baal-peor: all the men that followed Baal-peor were destroyed from among them, but those that did cleave unto the Lord were alive every one (Deuteronomy 4:3-4). The Bible is that simple: keep the commandments and live, or break them and die. Follow after the ways of the nations and be put to death; keep the laws, statutes and commandments and have life. Then the Lord told Moses to vex the Midianites and smite them, for they had vexed Israel with their wiles (Numbers 25:16-18).

cases.name: The Midianites, in the matter of Peor
cases.charge: Beguiling Israel with their wiles, on Balaam’s counsel, into whoredom and the worship of Baal-peor
cases.summary: On Balaam’s counsel the daughters of Moab and Midian drew Israel to the sacrifices of their gods, and Israel joined himself unto Baal-peor (Numbers 25:1-3; Numbers 31:16). The Lord commanded Moses to vex the Midianites and smite them, because they had beguiled Israel with their wiles (Numbers 25:16-18). Twelve thousand went out with Phinehas, slew all the males, the five kings of Midian and Balaam, and burnt their cities and their goodly castles (Numbers 31:1-10).
offenseFull: Balaam could not curse Israel, because God said you cannot curse what is blessed; so his counsel was the best the enemy can ever do: throw another god in front of Israel and send the women, and let Israel bring the trespass on himself (Numbers 25:1; Numbers 31:16). Israel began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab, the Moabites, who are the so-called Chinese today (Numbers 25:1). The worship of Baal-peor went into whoredom, that orgy worship: Israel started worshipping another god and going after the women together, and it was sex that got the people to bow down to another god (Numbers 25:2-3).

The Lord told Moses to vex the Midianites and smite them, for they vexed Israel with their wiles, wherewith they had beguiled them in the matter of Peor and in the matter of Cozbi (Numbers 25:16-18). Wiles are stratagems, something well planned out. The enemies knew they had to get this people to sin against their God, so they used this stratagem to move them away from God; that was the popular plan. As long as Israel continues in whoredom it will not build healthy marriages, and the generational curses keep going; its strength is to come back to the laws of God.
Midian comes from the lineage of Ishmael, the people known today as the Arab man, and Balaam himself was a Midianite, an Ishmaelite (Deuteronomy 4:3).
judgmentFull: The Lord told Moses, as his last set of instructions, to avenge the children of Israel of the Midianites, and the reason for this vengeance is the history of Peor (Numbers 31:1-2). A thousand of every tribe, twelve thousand armed for war, went out with Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, with the holy instruments and the trumpets to blow (Numbers 31:3-6). This is the Phinehas who killed the man of Israel that was fornicating with the woman of the other nation.

They warred against the Midianites as the Lord commanded Moses, slew all the males and the five kings of Midian, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba, and slew Balaam the son of Beor with the sword (Numbers 31:7-8; Joshua 13:22). Balaam was a soothsayer, a diviner, a witch so to speak, and his counsel is why the Lord put him to death. They took the women of Midian captive with their little ones and the spoil, and burnt all their cities and all their goodly castles with fire (Numbers 31:9-10). Esau was not the one who first came up with castles; the castles seen in the movies were conquered from other nations. The Midianites had captives of their own, and Israel took over both the men and the beasts when they overcame them (Numbers 31:11-12).

Moses was wroth with the officers of the host for saving all the women alive, for these, through the counsel of Balaam, had caused the children of Israel to trespass in the matter of Peor, and the Lord began putting the people to death, over twenty and four thousand (Numbers 31:14-16). Every male among the little ones was to be killed, and every woman that had known a man, because such a woman, seeking to preserve her life, might seduce a young man to get him in a vulnerable place and kill him (Numbers 31:17). The women children that had not known a man were kept alive; Moses allowed the men to keep them so they would not commit sin and go raping the women while out at war. That does not mean it is done today; it was a time the Most High allowed it, so the men would not be in the midst of sin (Numbers 31:18). Israel does not have that spirit now, nor should anyone be doing that today, and will not have it until Christ returns; the scripture says live peaceably with all men, and vengeance belongs to the Lord, the judge of the earth, against the wicked who break his people in pieces (Romans 12:18; Psalms 94:1-5).

The men of war and their captives abode without the camp seven days, by the law that puts the defiled by the dead out of the camp (Numbers 31:19-24; Numbers 5:2). The prey was divided between the army that went out to battle and the congregation that stayed, for the nation looked out for each other, and the Lord’s tribute went to the priest and the Levites, who have no inheritance in the land (Numbers 31:25-41; Numbers 18:19-21).
