cases.name: Phinehas
cases.charge: Zealous for his God at Peor; rising up against the evildoers and making an atonement for the children of Israel
cases.summary: While the whole congregation wept before the door of the tabernacle, a man of Israel brought a Midianitish woman before them all, a man who did not care about his people while everyone around him mourned (Numbers 25:6). Phinehas the son of Eleazar rose up from among the congregation, took a javelin, and thrust them both through, and the plague was stayed (Numbers 25:7-8). He stands third in glory: because he had zeal in the fear of the Lord, a covenant of peace and of an everlasting priesthood was made with him, and it was counted to him for righteousness unto all generations (Ecclesiasticus 45:23-24; Psalms 106:30-31).
offenseFull: Israel had joined himself unto Baal-peor, and while the Most High was passing judgment and the congregation was weeping before the door of the tabernacle, one of the children of Israel brought a Midianitish woman in the sight of Moses and all the congregation (Numbers 25:3-6). He had no fear; all he cared about was fulfilling his lust. When Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose up from among the congregation, took a javelin in his hand, went after the man of Israel into the tent, and thrust both of them through, the man of Israel and the woman through her belly (Numbers 25:7-8). The man was lying with the woman at that moment: the javelin went through his back and right through the woman’s belly, which is why it says through the belly, and Phinehas put both of them to death right there. The atonement was blood, death.

The psalm asks who will rise up for the Lord against the evildoers; Phinehas rose up (Psalms 94:16). Where Phinehas showed up, the zeal of the Most High showed up with him. The name Phinehas means the black man; he was a very dark man. This is what the churches do not want to talk about: he thrust through a heathen woman and one of Israel.

In the praise of famous men Phinehas stands third in glory, because he had zeal in the fear of the Lord and stood up with good courage of heart when the people were turned back, and made reconciliation for Israel; therefore a covenant of peace was made with him, that he and his posterity should have the dignity of the priesthood for ever (Ecclesiasticus 44:1; Ecclesiasticus 45:23-24). Stand firm for the laws of God when the people are turning. Mattathias, a Levite inspired by his own Levite kinsman, slew the apostate on the altar at Modin as Phinehas did, and charged his sons to be zealous for the law and give their lives for the covenant of their fathers, for Phinehas their father, in being zealous and fervent, obtained the covenant of an everlasting priesthood (1 Maccabees 2:23-26; 1 Maccabees 2:50, 54).
judgmentFull: So the plague was stayed, and those who died in the plague were twenty and four thousand: in one day God killed twenty-four thousand, because of sin (Numbers 25:8-9). Phinehas turned the wrath of the Most High away from the children of Israel, because he was zealous for his God’s sake among them; wherefore the Lord gave him His covenant of peace, and to his seed after him the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he made an atonement for the children of Israel (Numbers 25:10-13). He stood up and executed judgment, and the plague was stayed; it was counted to him for righteousness unto all generations, for he had zeal in the fear of the Most High (Psalms 106:30-31).

That covenant of peace is what all of Israel is striving for, rest from this servitude of bondage; but the wisdom in reading the acts of Phinehas is that a man must be zealous for the law of the Most High to obtain it. Being zealous today is confessing Christ before men, and a man confesses him mainly through his actions. Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example that we should follow his steps, and his steps were keeping the commandments of God; the first way a man denies Christ is by rejecting the commandments (1 Peter 2:21). Whoever confesses him before men he will confess before his Father; he came not to send peace on earth but a sword, setting a man at variance against his own household, and he that loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him (Matthew 10:32-37). We stay zealous by letting nothing separate us from following Christ in his steps: keeping the laws of God, teaching the gospel, and spreading the word with wisdom.

cases.name: Zimri and Cozbi
cases.charge: Bringing a Midianite woman into the camp in the sight of Moses and the weeping congregation, while the plague ran
cases.summary: While the whole congregation wept at the door of the tabernacle and the plague ran, Zimri the son of Salu, a prince of a chief house among the Simeonites, brought Cozbi the daughter of Zur, of a chief house in Midian, in the sight of Moses and all the congregation (Numbers 25:6, 14-15). He had no fear; all he cared about was fulfilling his lust. Phinehas thrust them both through, and the plague was stayed (Numbers 25:7-8). The charge stands to Simeon to get it together; Simeon is coming back with the rest of the tribes.
offenseFull: Israel had committed whoredom with the daughters of Moab, eaten the sacrifices of their gods and bowed down, and joined himself unto Baal-peor (Numbers 25:1-3). Idolatry leads to whoredom, spiritual whoredom against the Most High and physical whoredom with it, and these things are written for our admonition (1 Corinthians 10:6-11). Moses had told the judges to slay every one his men that were joined unto Baal-peor, and here came a man who acted as if he did not know what Moses was talking about (Numbers 25:4-6).

The Israelites at that door were trying to repent, worshipping and praying to the Lord, and while they did so this man came hopping, skipping and jumping in with a woman of another nation, clueless, because it had been going on so long that he no longer cared (Numbers 25:6). It was once a shameful thing for the men of Israel to be seen like that; today men and women of Israel walk boldly and proudly with the nations, and it is that same spirit.

The Israelite who was slain was Zimri the son of Salu, a prince of a chief house among the Simeonites, and the woman was Cozbi the daughter of Zur, head over a people of a chief house in Midian (Numbers 25:14-15). He was of one of the chief houses of Simeon, and the example he was leaving was that it is all right to do the same thing.

The Lord never said not to deal with the other nations because they are ugly; that is not in the Bible. He said not to do it because they will turn Israel away from him (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). The Most High forbids marrying outside the nation. The seed of the fathers today is found among the so-called blacks, Hispanics and Native Indians, who make up the twelve tribes of Israel; a spouse may come from any of the twelve tribes, but from within the tribes only (Deuteronomy 7:3). There are all kinds of men and women within the nation of Israel, and Israel cannot go outside its race. Chiefly take a wife of the seed of the fathers, for the fathers from the beginning all married wives of their own kindred and were blessed in their children (Tobit 4:12).
judgmentFull: Phinehas rose up from among the congregation, went after the man of Israel into the tent, and thrust both of them through, the man of Israel and the woman through her belly; so the plague was stayed, and those who died in the plague were twenty and four thousand (Numbers 25:7-9). That is how bad it had become: a man walking in with another nation to fornicate with them, and the Lord said it was time for them to die. Under the old covenant there was no winking at ignorance; judgment was instant. The only reason Israel is not judged that way now for the gods it served is the grace and mercy given through Christ. Phinehas turned away the wrath of the Most High, being zealous for His sake, so that He did not consume the children of Israel in His jealousy; he stood up and executed judgment, and the plague was stayed (Numbers 25:10-11; Psalms 106:30).

The Lord commanded Moses to vex the Midianites and smite them, for they vexed Israel with their wiles, wherewith they had beguiled them in the matter of Peor and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of a prince of Midian, their sister, who was slain in the day of the plague for Peor’s sake (Numbers 25:16-18). Their wiles were sexual wiles.

cases.offense: Israel had committed whoredom with the daughters of Moab, eaten the sacrifices of their gods and bowed down, and joined himself unto Baal-peor (Numbers 25:1-3). Idolatry leads to whoredom, spiritual whoredom against the Most High and physical whoredom with it, and these things are written for our admonition (1 Corinthians 10:6-11). Moses had told the judges to slay every one his men that were joined unto Baal-peor, and here came a man who acted as if he did not know what Moses was talking about (Numbers 25:4-6).
cases.judgment: Phinehas rose up from among the congregation, went after the man of Israel into the tent, and thrust both of them through, the man of Israel and the woman through her belly; so the plague was stayed, and those who died in the plague were twenty and four thousand (Numbers 25:7-9). That is how bad it had become: a man walking in with another nation to fornicate with them, and the Lord said it was time for them to die. Under the old covenant there was no winking at ignorance; judgment was instant. The only reason Israel is not judged that way now for the gods it served is the grace and mercy given through Christ. Phinehas turned away the wrath of the Most High, being zealous for His sake, so that He did not consume the children of Israel in His jealousy; he stood up and executed judgment, and the plague was stayed (Numbers 25:10-11; Psalms 106:30).

cases.name: The daughters of Zelophehad
cases.charge: Asking rightly for their father’s inheritance, and marrying within their father’s tribe as the Lord commanded
cases.summary: Five sisters of the tribe of Manasseh, whose father had died in the wilderness with no son, asked at the door of the tabernacle the question of the lineage: why should their father’s name be done away from among his family because he had no son (Numbers 27:1-4)? Moses did not do his own thing; he brought their cause before the Lord, and the Lord said the daughters of Zelophehad spoke right (Numbers 27:5-7). When the chief fathers of Gilead raised the matter of the tribe, the daughters married within the families of their father’s tribe as the Lord commanded, and the inheritance stayed in Manasseh (Numbers 36:1-12).
offenseFull: The daughters of Zelophehad, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, of the tribe of Manasseh, stood before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the princes and all the congregation by the door of the tabernacle (Numbers 27:1-2). Manasseh, the firstborn of Joseph, held Bashan and a portion by Gilead on the other side of Jordan; the so-called Cubans come from this tribe, and this is their history that their enemies do not want them to know (Joshua 17:1). Their father died in the wilderness in his own sin; he was not in the company of Korah that gathered together against the Lord, and he had no sons, only these five daughters (Numbers 27:3). Their question was the question of the lineage: since the man puts the seed in the woman, if a man had only daughters, why should his name be done away from among his family? So they asked for a possession among the brethren of their father (Numbers 27:4). Moses brought their cause before the Lord; he did not do his own thing, he sought counsel and asked the Most High what to do in this instance (Numbers 27:5).

The chief fathers of the families of Gilead then brought an issue rising out of what was already ruled: if the daughters married men of another tribe, their father’s inheritance would pass with them to the husband’s tribe and at the jubilee be fixed to that tribe, so Manasseh would lose that land for ever (Numbers 36:1-4). The jubilee would not cancel it: if she married into Judah, the land would not go back to Manasseh but would stay with Judah. The daughters did as the Lord commanded Moses: Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah and Noah married their father’s brothers’ sons within the families of Manasseh, and their inheritance remained in the tribe of the family of their father (Numbers 36:10-12).
judgmentFull: The Lord said the daughters of Zelophehad speak right: give them a possession of an inheritance among their father’s brethren, and cause the inheritance of their father to pass unto them (Numbers 27:6-7). Here the Lord set the order of inheritance for all Israel: if a man die and have no son, it passes to his daughter; if no daughter, to his brethren; if no brethren, to his father’s brethren; and if his father had no brethren, to the kinsman that is next to him of his family. Every angle was covered so the inheritance stayed within the tribe (Numbers 27:8-11).

The Most High affirmed the tribe of the sons of Joseph: they had said well. The daughters might marry whom they thought best, only within the family of the tribe of their father, so that the inheritance of the children of Israel would not remove from tribe to tribe; the marriage boundary here was instituted because of land inheritance (Numbers 36:5-9). This is not saying no one ever married from Judah to Benjamin or Levi to Ephraim; it shows that where an inheritance rode on the marriage, the woman married within her father’s tribe. That is why Raguel could not marry his daughter to another according to the law of Moses, for the right of inheritance belonged to Tobias rather than to any other (Tobit 6:12).

The tribal restriction belonged to the time when Israel dwelt in the land. Today Israel has no inheritance in the lands of captivity, so the rule that still applies is marrying within the nation of Israel, not tribe-only marriage. No one today knows his exact tribe with certainty; a Judahite could have been dropped off anywhere in the captivity. Without the history of Numbers 36, Tobit 4:12 gets twisted into a doctrine that a man may only marry his own tribe, and that is a heresy born of not knowing why the law was given. The command to take a wife of the seed of the fathers and not a strange woman still stands (Tobit 4:12). There was never a case where an inheritance in Israel passed to an Edomite, an Ammonite, or a Moabite. The fathers from the beginning took wives of their own kindred, and interracial marriage is not of the scriptures. Not to take a wife of one’s own people is to despise one’s brethren in the heart, and it is pride not to want to marry a woman of one’s own race, for in pride is destruction (Tobit 4:13). Joshua gave the five an inheritance among the brethren of their father according to the commandment of the Lord, and the daughters of Manasseh had an inheritance among his sons; the chronicler still notes the daughters of Zelophehad (Joshua 17:3-6; 1 Chronicles 7:15).

cases.name: Rahab
cases.charge: Receiving the spies with peace and hiding them, believing that the Lord had given Israel the land
cases.summary: Rahab, a harlot of Jericho and a Hamite of the land of Canaan, hid the two spies under the flax on her roof and sent the king’s men the wrong way (Joshua 2:1-7). She confessed that the Lord had given Israel the land, for the report of what He had done had melted the hearts of her city (Joshua 2:8-11). She bound the scarlet line in the window, and when Jericho fell she and her father’s household were saved alive, because she hid the messengers (Joshua 2:21; Joshua 6:22-25).
offenseFull: Joshua sent two men out of Shittim to spy secretly and view the land, even Jericho, and they came into the house of a harlot named Rahab and lodged there; when the king of Jericho sent to bring them out, she had hidden them on the roof under the stalks of flax (Joshua 2:1-6). She told the king’s men the truth in part and misdirection in the rest, saying the men had gone out about the time of the shutting of the gate and urging a quick pursuit; she lied to her own people concerning who these men were (Joshua 2:4-5). The pursuers chased toward Jordan after men who had gone nowhere, the gate was shut behind them, and the spies had clearance to escape. A heathen woman looked out for Israel, and she did it out of the fear of the Lord, as her own words show (Joshua 2:7).

Before the spies lay down, she confessed that the Lord had given them the land, that their terror had fallen upon the city, and that all its inhabitants fainted because of them (Joshua 2:8-9). That is faith and belief; a heathen acknowledged that the God of Israel had ordained them to conquer her land. Her faith came by report: they had heard how the Lord dried up the Red Sea and what Israel did to Sihon and Og, and as soon as they heard it their hearts melted and no courage remained in any man (Joshua 2:10-11). The Lord had said that day he would begin to put the dread and fear of Israel upon the nations who heard the report, and Rahab’s melted heart is that word fulfilled (Deuteronomy 2:25). Faith and fear go hand in hand. Rahab knew the Lord is not to be played with when it comes to this people, and that fear gave her the faith to put her life on the line; she might be caught by her own king for hiding the spies, but what she really feared was the judgment of their God if she did not help them.

She asked them to swear by the Lord, since she had shown them kindness, to show kindness to her father’s house and save her father, mother, brethren and sisters alive, and the men answered with their lives for hers if she uttered not their business (Joshua 2:12-14). Nothing about the kingdom of heaven was mentioned in that covenant. Her faith was not that she would gain eternal life, but that if she kept her mouth shut she would be spared when the destruction came; the faith of the nations is that they will be spared when the destruction comes if they deal right with the nation of Israel. Rahab the harlot was justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out another way (James 2:24-26). She did not only have to believe; she had to do something, and she followed their directions and bound the thread in the window. Even the heathen had enough sense to understand that faith can only be proven by works. Works by the Bible’s own dictionary is keeping his commandments, and by him actions are weighed (Psalms 78:7; 1 Samuel 2:3).
judgmentFull: The token was the line of scarlet thread bound in the window by which she let them down, for her house was upon the town wall. That scarlet line marked her house so no one in it would be slain when Israel came into the land; whoever went out into the street, his blood would be on his own head, and whoever stayed within, on Israel’s head if any hand touched him (Joshua 2:15-21). The spies abode in the mountain three days, then reported to Joshua that all the inhabitants fainted because of them; the land was theirs for the taking, exactly as the Lord had promised (Joshua 2:22-24).

The city was accursed to the Lord, and only Rahab the harlot would live, she and all that were with her in the house, because she hid the messengers (Joshua 6:17). Joshua sent the two spies to bring out Rahab, her father, mother, brethren and all her kindred, and saved her alive with her father’s household, and she dwelt in Israel (Joshua 6:22-25). She came in under the law of the stranger, by which a stranger who wanted to serve the one true God under the children of Israel was allowed to be with them. Rahab was a Canaanite, a heathen, yet the heathen can be blessed when they do it to benefit Israel; blessed is he that blesses Israel (Genesis 12:3). She helped the nation of Israel toward rulership, and that is the only help Israel wants from the other nations: not food stamps, welfare, or reparations, but to tell this people who they are, the Israelites the Bible speaks of, the so-called Blacks, Hispanics and Native Americans, and that they must keep the commandments of the Most High. Whoever does that will receive mercy just as Rahab did.

By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace (Hebrews 11:31). That does not mean all nations can be saved; the Lord spared that heathen because she helped the children of Israel when they came in to overthrow the city. Like her is the woman of Canaan who answered that the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table, and Christ said great is her faith (Matthew 15:27-28). Achan, an Israelite of Judah, lacked faith and was put to death, while Rahab the Canaanite harlot was saved alive for her faith (Joshua 7:25).

cases.name: Achan
cases.charge: Coveting and taking of the accursed spoil of Jericho, consecrated to the Lord’s treasury, and hiding it in his tent, so that the children of Israel trespassed and fell before Ai
cases.summary: The children of Israel committed the trespass in the accursed thing, for Achan of the tribe of Judah took of it (Joshua 7:1). One man’s secret sin cost thirty-six men their lives before Ai, and the Lord would not be with Israel until the accursed was destroyed from among them (Joshua 7:2-12). Taken by lot, Achan confessed that he saw, coveted, took and hid; he was stealing from the Most High (Joshua 7:16-21). He and his sons and daughters and all he had were stoned and burned in the valley of Achor (Joshua 7:24-26).
offenseFull: Many will answer that Achan committed the trespass, but the first sentence says the children of Israel did; one person took of the accursed thing, and all of Israel was blamed (Joshua 7:1). Your individual sins can hurt the rest of the nation. You can be the hindrance to why your camp is not growing, why your family, your marriage, or your children have issues, when you have a spirit on you that you know about and keep secret, not praying, not fasting, not seeking counsel. That is the spirit of Achan, and the children of Israel pay for it, for we are supposed to be one mind, one body, one spirit.

At Jericho Joshua had charged the people to keep from the accursed thing (Joshua 6:17-19). All the silver and gold and vessels of brass and iron were consecrated unto the Lord, separated and sanctified for his treasury alone: nobody was to gain personally from this war. The command was to take nothing and burn everything, and one man took.

Achan saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, two hundred shekels of silver and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels, coveted them, took them, and hid them in the earth in the midst of his tent (Joshua 7:20-21). He was not stealing from men; he was literally stealing from the Most High. As a father saves the weightiest warning for last, the Lord ends the ten commandments with covetousness (Exodus 20:17). To covet is to carry the spirit of jealousy and envy, and the covetous man sets his own soul to sale, selling out his dignity and self-respect to fulfil his desires no matter what it takes (Ecclesiasticus 10:9). He hid it because he knew he was not supposed to take it, the self-willed brother doing presumptuously when the Lord had already warned the whole camp: he saw the garment and had to have it (Leviticus 4:13; Numbers 15:30-31).
judgmentFull: About three thousand went up and fled, and the men of Ai smote thirty-six of them: thirty-six Israelites died because of one man, and it only takes one (Joshua 7:4-5). The Lord is the one who wins the battles and gets the victory, not us. No matter how strong Israel is physically, if we are not spiritually right with the Lord, he will make us lose, for this fight is not carnal. Hearts melting as water is the curse for disobedience: the Most High sends a faintness into the heart, like the athlete in the scary movie suddenly stumbling from sheer fear (Leviticus 26:36).

Joshua rent his clothes and fell before the ark until evening, for he understood what the nations do when they see Israel take a loss: the Canaanites would hear of it, surround us, and cut off our name from the earth (Joshua 7:6-9).

The Lord told him to get up: Israel had sinned (Joshua 7:10-11). It does not say Achan sinned; it says Israel. This walk is not selfish or individual: when you are in sin you hurt your wife, your husband, your children, the congregation, and the leadership, for we are all our brother’s keeper. As a father who finds mischief chastens all his children together when none confesses, so the Most High deals with his children as one house; we pay for one another’s sins. The Lord put a mightier warring spirit on the men of Ai, and he would not be with Israel until they destroyed the accursed from among them, meaning that accursed man (Joshua 7:12).

The lot took Judah, then the Zarhites, then the household of Zabdi, then Achan man by man, and Joshua told him to give glory to God and make confession (Joshua 7:16-19). No man saw Achan, but God did: Joshua told him to hide nothing because it was already not hidden from One mightier than he (Jeremiah 23:24; Numbers 32:23).

They found it hid in his tent, and Joshua and all Israel took Achan, the silver, the garment, the gold, his sons and daughters, his oxen, asses and sheep, his tent and all he had to the valley of Achor (Joshua 7:22-24). His sons and daughters did not steal it, yet because he lacked knowledge and understanding they paid for the covetous spirit he carried (Hosea 4:6). The Lord hits where it hurts, and your sin reaches your children, your wife, your husband, your brothers and sisters. The household also had to have known about it and said nothing, so none of them was innocent. Whoever sees sin or hears of sin must speak up, because silence is agreement.

Joshua said the Lord would trouble him that day, and all Israel stoned and burned them (Joshua 7:25). Into the hands of the living God is where Achan fell, and unfortunately his sons and daughters and all he had with him (Hebrews 10:31). Some of our people in the islands and elsewhere still ignorantly carry out such public executions to this day; we do not condone it, for we are not under the law of sacrifice now but under grace, and the judgment is of the Lord. Achan, an Israelite of Judah, lacked faith and was put to death, while Rahab the Canaanite harlot was saved alive for her faith; when Israel will not obey his voice, the Lord likens the house of Judah unto all the heathen (Ezekiel 25:8). They raised a great heap of stones over him, the Lord turned from the fierceness of his anger, and righteous judgment lifted the wrath (Joshua 7:26).

cases.name: The Gibeonites, and Israel’s oath
cases.charge: Obtaining a league by fraud as from a far country; and Israel making it without asking counsel at the mouth of the Lord
cases.summary: The Hivites of Gibeon, of the nations Israel was commanded to destroy, came to Gilgal with old sacks, rent wine bottles and mouldy bread, claiming a far country, because their only hope was to pretend they were not of the land (Joshua 9:3-6). The men of Israel took of their victuals and asked not counsel at the mouth of the Lord, and that first mistake became a snare and a trap to Israel as a people (Joshua 9:14). The princes held to the oath, and Joshua pronounced the Gibeonites cursed: bondmen for ever, hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God (Joshua 9:18-23).
offenseFull: The kings on this side Jordan, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite and the Jebusite, gathered to fight with Joshua and with Israel with one accord, confederate against Israel as in Psalms 83; these are Hamites, better known as Nilotic Africans (Joshua 9:1-2; Psalms 83:5). These are the nations whose land Israel was to possess. The people fighting in that land today, the Israelis and the Palestinians, are not the Israelites; the land does not belong to them, for it was promised to Israel’s forefathers. The inhabitants of Gibeon, Hivites of the sons of Canaan, heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai and worked wilily: they made as if they had been ambassadors, with old sacks upon their asses, wine bottles old and rent and bound up, old shoes and old garments, and bread dry and mouldy (Joshua 9:3-5; Genesis 10:15-17). Their props sold the story.

There is a law pertaining to war: a city very far off that answered peace became tributary and served Israel, but of the cities of these nations Israel was to save alive nothing that breathed (Deuteronomy 20:10-17). The Gibeonites understood the rules of war, so they made as if they came from a long journey and submitted themselves as servants. No covenant was to be made with these nations nor mercy shown them; since the days of old the Most High has never been about the love-of-the-world gospel (Deuteronomy 7:2).

The men of Israel were suspicious at first, saying the strangers might dwell among them, and Joshua pressed them on who they were and whence they came (Joshua 9:7-8). The Gibeonites leaned on the fame of the Most High: they had heard all that he did in Egypt and to Sihon and Og (Joshua 9:9-10). The men took of their victuals and asked not counsel at the mouth of the Lord. That is the first mistake, and not asking counsel of the Most High at that moment ended up being a snare and a trap to Israel as a people, as the rest of the scriptures show (Joshua 9:14-15). Let reason think on whether it is the right move, and even before reasoning within oneself, the Most High says counsel before every action (Ecclesiasticus 37:16).
judgmentFull: At the end of three days Israel heard that they were neighbours dwelling among them, and the children of Israel smote them not, because the princes of the congregation had sworn unto them by the Lord God of Israel (Joshua 9:16-18). All the congregation murmured against the princes, for Israel was supposed to put them to death, but the princes held the line: they had sworn by the Lord God of Israel and could not touch them. The forefathers were wrong in one situation, but they were upright men in holding to their word (Joshua 9:18-19). When a man vows a vow unto God he is not to defer to pay it; what comes out of the mouth, be sure to do it (Ecclesiastes 5:4-6). Israel let them live lest wrath be upon them because of the oath; a vow made before the Most High stands, even one gotten by guile (Joshua 9:20).

Joshua called for them, asked why they had beguiled Israel, saying they were very far off when they dwelt among them, and pronounced them cursed: none of them would be freed from being bondmen, hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of his God; they were servants all the way up and through (Joshua 9:22-23). Hewers of wood and drawers of water means slaves. This is according to the law of the Most High pertaining to other nations: the bondmen and bondmaids of Israel were to be of the heathen round about, but over their brethren the children of Israel were not to rule with rigour (Leviticus 25:44-46). Canaan was to be the servant of Shem, and the Hivite is of the sons of Canaan (Genesis 9:26; Genesis 10:17). In the Old Testament there was no equality among the nations, and there is still no equality among nations: they were made for a certain purpose. The reason they are not in that purpose now is that Israel sinned and failed, and one day Israel will rise again to put them back in their rightful places.

The Gibeonites answered honestly that it had been told them how the Lord commanded Moses to give Israel all the land and destroy all its inhabitants, so they were sore afraid of their lives; Joshua delivered them and made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the Lord (Joshua 9:24-27). They did not have equal citizenship: rather than be killed, they acknowledged that they would be Israel’s servants. Nor will the kingdom of heaven be all nations ruling equally as joint heirs with Christ. When Saul broke his word and slew the Gibeonites in his zeal, a famine came three years in the days of David for Saul and his bloody house, and Israel learned to pay what it vows unto the Most High (2 Samuel 21:1). This type of ordeal will play out again when Christ returns: the sons of strangers shall build up Israel’s walls, their kings shall minister unto Israel, and the nation and kingdom that will not serve Israel shall perish (Isaiah 60:10-12). To him that overcomes and keeps his works unto the end he will give power over the nations; as it was then, so it will be (Revelation 2:26-27). There is nothing new under the sun.

cases.offense: The kings on this side Jordan, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite and the Jebusite, gathered to fight with Joshua and with Israel with one accord, confederate against Israel as in Psalms 83; these are Hamites, better known as Nilotic Africans (Joshua 9:1-2; Psalms 83:5). These are the nations whose land Israel was to possess. The people fighting in that land today, the Israelis and the Palestinians, are not the Israelites; the land does not belong to them, for it was promised to Israel’s forefathers. The inhabitants of Gibeon, Hivites of the sons of Canaan, heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai and worked wilily: they made as if they had been ambassadors, with old sacks upon their asses, wine bottles old and rent and bound up, old shoes and old garments, and bread dry and mouldy (Joshua 9:3-5; Genesis 10:15-17). Their props sold the story.
cases.judgment: At the end of three days Israel heard that they were neighbours dwelling among them, and the children of Israel smote them not, because the princes of the congregation had sworn unto them by the Lord God of Israel (Joshua 9:16-18). All the congregation murmured against the princes, for Israel was supposed to put them to death, but the princes held the line: they had sworn by the Lord God of Israel and could not touch them. The forefathers were wrong in one situation, but they were upright men in holding to their word (Joshua 9:18-19). When a man vows a vow unto God he is not to defer to pay it; what comes out of the mouth, be sure to do it (Ecclesiastes 5:4-6). Israel let them live lest wrath be upon them because of the oath; a vow made before the Most High stands, even one gotten by guile (Joshua 9:20).

cases.name: The five kings at Makkedah
cases.charge: Confederating against Gibeon and making war against it because it had made peace with Joshua and with the children of Israel
cases.summary: Five kings of the Amorites, gathered by Adoni-zedec king of Jerusalem, made war against Gibeon because it had made peace with Joshua and the children of Israel, and Gibeon sent to Joshua at Gilgal for help (Joshua 10:1-6). The Lord told Joshua not to fear them, cast down great stones from heaven upon them, and held the sun still at Joshua’s word until the people had avenged themselves, for the Lord fought for Israel (Joshua 10:8-14). The five hid in a cave at Makkedah; Joshua brought them out, had the captains put their feet upon their necks, slew them, and hanged them on five trees until the evening (Joshua 10:16-27). What we read in Joshua is future prophecy.
offenseFull: When Adoni-zedec king of Jerusalem heard how Joshua had taken Ai and utterly destroyed it, as he had done to Jericho, and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel, they feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, as one of the royal cities, greater than Ai, and all its men were mighty (Joshua 10:1-2).

The five kings of the Amorites, of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon, gathered themselves with all their hosts, encamped before Gibeon, and made war against it, because it had made peace with Joshua and with the children of Israel (Joshua 10:3-5). They made war against their own brethren, because their brethren had decided they did not want to be wiped off the map and had made a league with Israel; it was by deception, but nonetheless the league was made (Joshua 9:3-15).

The men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at Gilgal to come up quickly and save them (Joshua 10:6). The Lord told Joshua not to fear them, for He had delivered them into his hand, and not a man of them would stand before him (Joshua 10:8). It is not by Israel’s might or strength: the Lord goes with Israel to fight for them, but Israel had to be in its righteousness, as at Ai, where men were lost because of Achan’s sin (Deuteronomy 20:4; Joshua 7:5).
judgmentFull: Joshua went up from Gilgal all night and came upon them suddenly; as they fled the Lord cast down great stones from heaven upon them unto Azekah, and more died with hailstones than the children of Israel slew with the sword (Joshua 10:9-11). The Most High was up in heaven aiming the hailstones right at the people, and nobody could escape. He did the same in Egypt, where the elements were changed in themselves to fight for Israel (Wisdom of Solomon 19:18-20). Fire and hail, famine and death were all created for the Lord’s vengeance (Ecclesiasticus 39:28-29). The Lord killed more than Israel killed: these are the wars of the Lord.

Joshua spoke to the Lord in the sight of Israel, and the sun stood still upon Gibeon and the moon in the valley of Ajalon until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies; there was no day like it before or after, that the Lord hearkened unto the voice of a man, for the Lord fought for Israel (Joshua 10:12-14). Time stopped, and the reason it stopped for him is his faith: he believed the Lord would do it.

The five kings fled and hid themselves in a cave at Makkedah, and were shut in with great stones while Israel pursued the hindmost until they were consumed (Joshua 10:16-20). Joshua was a real warrior, an Ephraimite, what is called a Puerto Rican today (Numbers 13:8). All the people returned to the camp in peace, and none moved his tongue against any of the children of Israel (Joshua 10:21): they destroyed five kings and did not lose a man. Against Israel not a dog would move his tongue, and the dogs are the other nations; Christ used the same word when he said he was not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel, for he came for one people (Exodus 11:7; Matthew 15:24-26).

Joshua had the five kings brought out of the cave and told the captains of the men of war to come near and put their feet upon their necks, and told them to fear not, nor be dismayed, for thus would the Lord do to all their enemies (Joshua 10:22-25). Joshua was operating in the spirit of the Lord. The other nations have had no problem doing the same to Israel: hanging us, shooting us down in the streets, putting a knee on the neck of George Floyd. Oppression makes a wise man mad (Ecclesiastes 7:7), but that is not to say wage physical war against anybody: in the land of its oppressors Israel recompenses to no man evil for evil and lives peaceably with all men (Romans 12:17-18), for vengeance belongs to the Lord (Psalm 94:1). The nations are taken down with the word of God and with Israel’s obedience. They hid in caves, and the nations will do it again: in the day of the Lord men shall go into the holes of the rocks and the caves of the earth for fear of the Lord, when He ariseth to shake terribly the earth (Isaiah 2:19-21). What we read in Joshua is future prophecy.

Joshua slew them and hanged them on five trees until the evening, and at sundown took them down according to the law, for he that is hanged is accursed of God, and cast them into the cave (Joshua 10:26-27; Deuteronomy 21:22-23). Everyone hanged on a tree is cursed: that shows that all the nations are cursed, and Israel fell under the curses also.

So Joshua smote all the country and all their kings, left none remaining, and utterly destroyed all that breathed, as the Lord God of Israel commanded, because the Lord God of Israel fought for Israel (Joshua 10:40-42). The Lord is a man of war: the Lord is His name (Exodus 15:3). Do not think the Most High unjust. No one taught Him or took counsel with Him; all nations before Him are as a drop of a bucket and the small dust of the balance, counted to Him less than nothing, and vanity (Isaiah 40:13-17). He increases the nations and destroys them (Job 12:23).

cases.name: Othniel and Achsah
cases.charge: Taking Kirjath-sepher for Caleb, who wholly followed the Lord; Achsah asking her father for a blessing; and Othniel judging Israel and going out to war when the Spirit of the Lord came upon him
cases.summary: Caleb was given Hebron because he wholly followed the Lord; he drove out the three sons of Anak and offered his daughter Achsah to the man who would smite Kirjath-sepher, and Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, took it and was given Achsah (Joshua 15:13-17). She asked her father for a blessing, and Caleb gave her the upper springs and the nether springs (Joshua 15:18-19). When Israel served Chushan-rishathaim eight years and cried unto the Lord, the Lord raised up Othniel as a deliverer; the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, he judged Israel and went out to war, and the land had rest forty years (Judges 3:8-11).
offenseFull: Unto Caleb the son of Jephunneh was given a part among the children of Judah according to the commandment of the Lord to Joshua, the city of Arba the father of Anak, which is Hebron, and Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai (Joshua 15:13-14). He was promised Hebron, and he went and claimed it himself. Those are the giants of the evil report, before whom the spies were in their own sight as grasshoppers, while Caleb stilled the people and said, let us go up at once and possess it (Numbers 13:30-33). He had another spirit with him and followed the Lord fully: that is what the Lord wants from us, a different spirit about faith, following Him fully whatever the peer pressure, the trial or the temptation, and he was rewarded for it (Numbers 14:24; Joshua 14:14).

He went up against the inhabitants of Debir, whose name before was Kirjath-sepher, and promised Achsah his daughter to wife to the man who would smite it and take it; Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, took it, and got Achsah to wife (Joshua 15:15-17). Othniel is the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother: see the connection (Judges 3:9; 1 Chronicles 4:13).

Achsah moved him to ask of her father a field, and she asked Caleb for a blessing: he had given her a south land, so she asked also for springs of water (Joshua 15:18-19). The account repeats at the opening of Judges as a review of the history just read in Joshua (Judges 1:12-15).
judgmentFull: Caleb gave her the upper springs and the nether springs (Joshua 15:19). After Joshua the Lord left nations to prove Israel, as many as had not known all the wars of Canaan, that the generations of the children of Israel might know war and be taught it, and that it might be known whether they would hearken unto His commandments (Judges 3:1-4).

The children of Israel dwelt among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, the same people the Most High said to utterly destroy, took their daughters to be their wives, gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods (Judges 3:5-6). The law had said it plainly: no covenant and no marriages with them, for they will turn away thy son from following the Lord (Deuteronomy 7:1-4; Deuteronomy 20:16-18). The anger of the Lord was hot against Israel, and He sold them into the hand of Chushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia, and they served him eight years (Judges 3:8).

When the children of Israel cried unto the Lord, He raised up a deliverer, Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother (Judges 3:9). Whenever Israel cries unto the Lord, He sends a deliverer; He always remembers their cry, as in Egypt He heard it and sent Moses. That is why Israel cannot live comfortably in Babylon today: we must cry unto the Lord so He can make the time short.

The Spirit of the Lord came upon Othniel, and he judged Israel, but today our people say, you can’t judge me (Judges 3:10). He judged Israel and went out to war, because the Lord is a man of war (Exodus 15:3). That answers those who ask, when the men are out on the streets teaching, where the women are: they are not at war; the Lord is a man of war. And for those who do not think we are at war now: though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh (2 Corinthians 10:3-5). It is a spiritual war, but we are nonetheless at war, and the weapon of our warfare today is this Bible, mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds, exposing all the lies on the earth.

The Lord delivered Chushan-rishathaim into his hand, his hand prevailed, and the land had rest forty years, until Othniel the son of Kenaz died (Judges 3:10-11). Concerning the judges, every one by name, whose heart went not a whoring nor departed from the Lord, let their memory be blessed (Ecclesiasticus 46:11).

cases.name: Adoni-bezek
cases.charge: Cutting off the thumbs and great toes of seventy kings, who gathered their meat under his table
cases.summary: After the death of Joshua, Judah went up first at the Lord’s word, with Simeon his brother, and slew ten thousand of the Canaanites and Perizzites in Bezek (Judges 1:1-4). Adoni-bezek fled and was caught, and his thumbs and great toes were cut off; he confessed it himself, that seventy kings with their thumbs and great toes cut off had gathered their meat under his table, and as he had done, so God had requited him (Judges 1:6-7). They brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died.
offenseFull: After the death of Joshua the children of Israel asked the Lord who should go up first against the Canaanites, and the answer was Judah, for He had delivered the land into his hand (Judges 1:1-2). Israel was taking the land of Canaan, the promised land. Judah asked Simeon his brother to come up with him into his lot, and Simeon went with him (Judges 1:3), for Simeon’s inheritance was within the inheritance of Judah; Judah was being his brother’s keeper (Joshua 19:1-9). The so-called Dominicans, of Simeon, were living within the land of the so-called African Americans, of Judah: this is our history and where we lived.

The Lord delivered the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand, and they slew ten thousand men in Bezek (Judges 1:4). Adoni-bezek was the king of that land, and he was known for cutting off thumbs and great toes: he gives the number himself, seventy kings with their thumbs and great toes cut off, who gathered their meat under his table (Judges 1:7).

The law keeps the measure: if a man cause a blemish in his neighbour, as he hath done, so shall it be done to him again, breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and one manner of law stood for the stranger as for one of the country (Leviticus 24:19-22; Exodus 21:23-25). When Christ came he taught the proper understanding of eye for eye for dealing inside the nation, resist not evil (Matthew 5:38-42).
judgmentFull: They pursued after him, caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his great toes (Judges 1:6). When Israel went to war, terrible things were done to people. He was known for cutting off thumbs and great toes, so his were cut off, and he was rewarded according to his actions.

Adoni-bezek confessed it: as he had done, so God had requited him (Judges 1:7). What he did to others was done to him. They brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died; and the children of Judah fought against Jerusalem, took it, smote it with the edge of the sword, and set the city on fire (Judges 1:7-8).

Israel made unspeakable slaughters in those wars. David put the people of the cities of Ammon under saws and harrows and axes of iron and made them pass through the brickkiln, which is a furnace; the same account says he cut them with saws (2 Samuel 12:31; 1 Chronicles 20:3). He measured Moab with lines, one line to put to death and one full line to keep alive (2 Samuel 8:2), and Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord, for as his sword had made women childless, so was his mother made childless among women (1 Samuel 15:33). The fathers did not deal lightly with the nations when it came to war. The history shows the same measure: the measure of atrocity done to Israel will be met with the same.

Were it not for God, the nations would have cut Israel off from being a nation (Psalm 83:4). They keep Israel down because they know what Israel did before: the two prophets, Judah and Israel, tormented them that dwelt on the earth (Revelation 11:10).

cases.name: Jabez
cases.charge: Calling on the God of Israel to bless him indeed, enlarge his coast, keep His hand with him, and keep him from evil
cases.summary: Among the families of Judah, Jabez was more honourable than his brethren, and his mother called his name Jabez because she bore him with sorrow, the meaning of the name matching the scripture itself (1 Chronicles 4:9). He called on the God of Israel and asked that He would bless him indeed, enlarge his coast, keep His hand with him, and keep him from evil, and the Most High granted him what he requested (1 Chronicles 4:10). The blessing rested heavily on Judah, who multiplied above his brethren.
offenseFull: The chapter gathers more of the families of Judah: the sons of Judah and the families that came from them, including the line of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah, the father of Bethlehem (1 Chronicles 4:1-4). The names here carry meaning, and the record keeps the families in order down to the sons of Coz (1 Chronicles 4:5-8).
Jabez was more honourable than his brethren, and his mother called his name Jabez because she bare him with sorrow, the meaning of the name matching the scripture itself (1 Chronicles 4:9).
Jabez called on the God of Israel and asked that He would bless him indeed, enlarge his coast, keep His hand with him, and keep him from evil, that it might not grieve him (1 Chronicles 4:10).

The families of Judah are traced further through Chelub, Kenaz and Othniel, and the sons of Ezra and their households (1 Chronicles 4:11-17). The record names the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took, and the names in this stretch carry meaning, as Jekuthiel points to the hope of the congregation of God (1 Chronicles 4:18). The sons of Shelah the son of Judah are named, with the families that wrought fine linen and the potters that dwelt with the king for his work; these are called the ancient things, the old record of the trades and dwellings of these families (1 Chronicles 4:21-23).
judgmentFull: The Most High granted him what he requested (1 Chronicles 4:10).

The blessing rested heavily on Judah, who multiplied above his brethren. The sons of Simeon are set down, and Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters, but his brethren had not many children, and Simeon did not multiply like the children of Judah: the blessing of increase rested on Judah (1 Chronicles 4:24-27). The dwellings of Simeon at Beersheba and the cities round about are the same inheritance given to Simeon in Joshua, within the inheritance of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:28-33; Joshua 19:1-9). The so-called Dominicans, of Simeon, were living within the land of the so-called African Americans, of Judah.

The princes of Simeon, whose houses increased greatly, went to seek pasture for their flocks, and found fat and quiet pasture in a land where the sons of Ham had dwelt of old; in the days of Hezekiah they smote those habitations and dwelt in their place, so the tribe of Simeon took land that had belonged to the sons of Ham (1 Chronicles 4:38-41). Five hundred of the sons of Simeon went to mount Seir, smote the remnant of the Amalekites that had escaped, and dwelt there, showing the Most High’s blessing on them in war (1 Chronicles 4:42-43).

cases.name: Israel in the days of the Judges
cases.charge: Making leagues with the inhabitants of the land; marrying their daughters and serving their gods; every man doing that which was right in his own eyes
cases.summary: An angel of the Lord came up from Gilgal to Bochim and rehearsed the covenant: the Lord would never break it, Israel was to make no league with the inhabitants of the land and to throw down their altars, and they had not obeyed His voice (Judges 2:1-2). The sentence was that He would not drive those nations out, but they would be thorns in Israel’s sides and their gods a snare (Judges 2:3). Another generation arose which knew not the Lord, dwelt among the very nations it was commanded to destroy, married their daughters, served their gods, and was sold into the hands of its enemies (Judges 2:10-14; Judges 3:5-8). The key to the whole book is that there was no king in Israel, and every man did that which was right in his own eyes (Judges 17:6).
offenseFull: At Bochim the angel rehearsed that the Lord had brought them out of Egypt into the land He sware unto their fathers, and they had not obeyed His voice (Judges 2:1-2). The Most High had warned against letting them dwell in the land, because they would make Israel sin against Him (Exodus 23:32-33). Dwelling among them breeds curiosity after their gods: how did these nations serve their gods, what is that thing they are doing with that tree, what are they hanging on the tree, why are they giving each other gifts? That curiosity is the snare, and we are not to add to His commandments or take away from them (Deuteronomy 12:30-32). Throwing down their altars meant burning their graven images with fire, not even desiring the silver or gold on them, lest it become a snare (Deuteronomy 7:25).

The same is true today in the places where we are scattered: we have made leagues with the inhabitants of the land. We find ourselves in their sports leagues and bowling leagues and at their dinner parties, when the scripture says not to envy the oppressor nor choose any of his ways (Proverbs 3:31).

The people served the Lord all the days of Joshua and of the elders that outlived him (Judges 2:7). Joshua was righteous, and the men around him were righteous, and they judged the people and kept them in order, for as the judge of the people is himself, so are his officers (Ecclesiasticus 10:1-2). That is why the nation is in chaos when our people say, you can’t judge me; the scriptures say we are to judge. When that generation was gathered unto their fathers, another arose which knew not the Lord nor His works for Israel, and they served Baalim and Ashtaroth (Judges 2:10-13). Here a pattern starts: when a judge in Israel dies, the people just go off. It shows we are a people that need leadership, which is why we are told to trust in the Lord (Proverbs 3:5-6). Brothers and sisters today come with theories they think are their own thoughts, but those thoughts were given to them, mostly by the television. You are either going to follow the one true living God of Israel or the prince of the power of the air, Satan the devil.

Israel dwelt among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, the very people the Most High said to utterly destroy, took their daughters to wife and served their gods (Judges 3:5-6; Deuteronomy 7:1-4; Deuteronomy 20:16-18). Joshua had warned before he died that if they made marriages with the remnant of these nations, the Lord would no more drive them out, but they would be snares and traps until they perished from off the good land (Joshua 23:12-13). The key to understanding the whole book is that there was no king in Israel, and every man did that which was right in his own eyes (Judges 17:6). With no king and no government Israel was sheep without a shepherd, and the same individual spirit is around today in those who say join no camp and let no man teach you.
judgmentFull: The sentence at Bochim was that the Lord would not drive those nations out; they would be thorns in Israel’s sides and their gods a snare (Judges 2:3-5). Because Israel forsook Him, His anger was hot, and He delivered them into the hands of spoilers and sold them into the hands of their enemies, so that they could no longer stand before them (Judges 2:14). The Lord fights Israel’s battles; when the nation is in sin He leaves and takes His strength with Him, and Israel has no power against its enemies. Look at us today: Black Lives Matter, hands up don’t shoot. We cannot stand before our enemies, so now we beg our enemies to see us as people.

Whithersoever they went, the hand of the Lord was against them for evil (Judges 2:15). We wonder why we cannot get anywhere as a people, with individual millionaires and no farms, no distribution, no hospitals, no textiles, none of the things a nation needs to sustain itself. The curse was to be cursed coming in and cursed going out, coming in from war and going out to war, and the same is happening to this day (Deuteronomy 28:19). Our people do not think we are at war, but when the enemy gives you a false image, a false religion and a false education, slums and ghettos to live in, and bad foods, he is at war with you. Our offence is leaving off the commandments to serve other gods, and the Most High has returned to His place until we acknowledge it (Hosea 5:15).

Nevertheless He raised up judges which delivered them, for it repented Him because of their groanings under those that oppressed them (Judges 2:16-18), as in Egypt, where He saw the affliction of His people and knew their sorrows (Exodus 3:7). We are the apple of His eye (Zechariah 2:8). The Most High does not want to see us on the bottom, but we trespassed against His commandments, so we have to be punished for it. Yet they would not hearken unto their judges, and when the judge was dead they corrupted themselves more than their fathers (Judges 2:17-19). As soon as we got out of the condition we were in, we went right back to doing the same thing, because this is a rebellious and stubborn people, even to this day. So He left the nations Joshua had not driven out, to prove Israel whether they would keep His way, and to teach the generations war (Judges 2:20-23; Judges 3:1-4). Judges is the record of that affliction beginning to come upon our people for turning our backs on the one true living God.

cases.name: Eglon king of Moab
cases.charge: Smiting Israel with Ammon and Amalek, possessing the city of palm trees, and holding Israel in service eighteen years
cases.summary: Israel did evil again, and the Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab against them; Eglon gathered Ammon and Amalek, possessed the city of palm trees, and Israel served him eighteen years (Judges 3:12-14). The same nations whose hearts melted in Joshua’s day were now strengthened against Israel for breaking the commandments. When the people cried, the Lord raised up Ehud the son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite, who brought Eglon a message from God with a two-edged dagger, and Moab was subdued that day, and the land had rest eighty years (Judges 3:15-30).
offenseFull: The children of Israel did evil again in the sight of the Lord, and He strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel because they had done evil (Judges 3:12). It says the Most High strengthened him. In Joshua the hearts of the peoples melted because they heard of the things the Most High did for Israel (Joshua 2:9-11); now He was strengthening them against Israel for breaking His commandments.

Eglon gathered unto him the children of Ammon and Amalek, smote Israel, and possessed the city of palm trees, and the children of Israel served Eglon eighteen years (Judges 3:13-14). It is a constant cycle: Israel does evil, the Most High strengthens an enemy against them, and they are put under him. For eighteen years Israel watched that man walk down the street taking their taxes.

Israel had many captivities, and there is not one nation that has nothing to pay for. While our people want to hold hands and sing along with everybody, all nations play a part unto this day in our demise.
judgmentFull: When the children of Israel cried unto the Lord, He raised them up a deliverer, Ehud the son of Gera, a Benjamite, a man lefthanded (Judges 3:15). The Most High raised up judges of different tribes: Othniel of Judah, now Ehud of Benjamin, and Benjamin were warriors.

Ehud made a dagger with two edges, a cubit long, and girded it under his raiment on his right thigh, and brought the present to Eglon, who was a very fat man (Judges 3:16-17). He concealed it: that was strategy, and when our people are in the right mind, we think with strategy.

With a secret errand for the king he got Eglon alone in his summer parlour, told him he had a message from God unto him, and thrust the dagger into his belly with his left hand, and the fat closed upon the blade so that he could not draw it out; he locked the doors of the parlour and went out (Judges 3:19-23). Ehud had the tact to earn an audience and then a private room with the king, the same way Nehemiah the cupbearer had the ear of the king over him (Nehemiah 2:1). The servants found the doors locked and thought he was relieving himself in his summer chamber, tarried till they were ashamed, then took a key and found their lord fallen down dead (Judges 3:24-25).

Ehud escaped while they tarried, passed the quarries, and nobody saw him leave. He blew a trumpet in the mountain of Ephraim, a plan agreed beforehand, and he went before the children of Israel, a leader who went in front, and we have to lead by example in this truth; he told them to follow, for the Lord had delivered their enemies the Moabites into their hand (Judges 3:26-28). They took the fords of Jordan, suffered not a man to pass over, and slew of Moab about ten thousand men, all lusty and all men of valour, and not a man escaped; so Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel, and the land had rest fourscore years (Judges 3:29-30).

The Lord always sends Israel deliverers. In each captivity He raises up men to stand between Him and the children of Israel and fight for them; it never fails, and the same will happen today, for saviours shall come up on mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau (Obadiah 21). After Ehud was Shamgar the son of Anath, which slew of the Philistines six hundred men with an ox goad, and he also delivered Israel (Judges 3:31). The goad is a formidable weapon, sometimes ten feet long with a sharp point, and it does not say he had a troop with him: the spirit of the Lord was on him.

cases.name: Jabin and Sisera
cases.charge: Mightily oppressing the children of Israel twenty years with nine hundred chariots of iron, when the Lord sold them into his hand for their evil
cases.summary: When Ehud was dead the children of Israel again did evil, and the Most High sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, whose captain Sisera had nine hundred chariots of iron and mightily oppressed Israel twenty years, until they cried unto the Lord (Judges 4:1-3). Every time Israel sins against God, he allows the other nations to enslave them. The Lord discomfited Sisera and all his host before Barak, and there was not a man left; Sisera died in the tent of Jael, and Israel prevailed against Jabin until they had destroyed him (Judges 4:15-24).
offenseFull: The children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the Lord when Ehud was dead, and the Lord sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, that reigned in Hazor, whose captain Sisera dwelt in Harosheth of the Gentiles (Judges 4:1-2). This captivity was around the twelfth century before Christ, when Israel had to serve the Canaanites. Sisera had nine hundred chariots of iron, and twenty years he mightily oppressed the children of Israel (Judges 4:3).

The account carries the same cycle laid out in chapter two: Israel does evil, is sold into an oppressor’s hand, cries unto the Most High, and a deliverer is raised up. When the judge was dead, they returned and corrupted themselves more than their fathers, for this is a rebellious and stubborn people, even to this very day (Judges 2:19). Israel cannot be left to itself. Whoever plays with God pays.

Every time Israel sins against God, he allows the other nations to enslave them. The other nations do not have power over Israel because Israel is weak; the Lord uses the other nations to break Israel. Because Israel forsook the Most High, he sold them into the hands of their enemies, so that they could not any longer stand before them, and so it is today: Israel cannot stand before its enemies, and begs its enemies to see it as human (Judges 2:14).

Jabin was king of Canaan, and Sisera is the general of the Canaanite host, not Syria. The Canaanites come of Ham through Canaan; they are a dark nation, the same colour as Israel but a different people, whom Israel fought in the land and forced into West Africa, where they later enslaved Israel with the help of the Arabs (Genesis 10:15-18).
judgmentFull: Deborah gave Barak the commandment of the Most High: draw toward mount Tabor with ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun, and he would draw Sisera with his chariots and his multitude to the river Kishon and deliver him into his hand (Judges 4:6-7).

The Most High discomfited Sisera and all his chariots and all his host with the edge of the sword before Barak; Sisera lighted down off his chariot and fled away on his feet, and all his host fell upon the edge of the sword (Judges 4:15-16). Not one was spared. The stars in their courses fought against Sisera, and the river Kishon swept them away (Judges 5:19-21).

Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin and the house of Heber, and there he died with the nail in his temples; the word through Deborah stood, and Sisera was sold into the hand of a woman. So God subdued that day Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel, and their hand prospered and prevailed until they had destroyed him (Judges 4:17-24).

The mother of Sisera looked out at a window for his chariot, looking for a son who was never coming home; he lay dead in Jael’s tent. The song asks that all the Lord’s enemies perish, and the land had rest forty years (Judges 5:28-31).

Asaph prayed the Most High to do unto the nations confederate against Israel as unto the Midianites, as to Sisera and as to Jabin at the brook of Kison, who perished at Endor (Psalms 83:5-10). The tabernacles of Edom, the so-called white man, stand at the top of that list, and the Ishmaelites, the Arabs, after them. That is righteous prayer. The Most High will enforce that judgment when Christ returns; none of those nations will escape for the evil they have done to Israel, for nobody escapes justice (Joel 3:2-3).

cases.name: Deborah
cases.charge: Judging Israel under the palm tree in subjection and in order; confirming to Barak the commandment the Lord had already given him, and going up with him, giving the honour to the Lord
cases.summary: Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, judged Israel at that time under the palm tree between Ramah and Bethel, and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment (Judges 4:4-5). She was a married woman in subjection to a husband, placed there by the Most High to judge the matters between the children of Israel. The men were weak, and the Lord revealed the mission to her; she called Barak, confirmed what the Lord had already commanded him, and went with him, saying the honour would be neither his nor hers (Judges 4:6-9). A mother in Israel, her heart was toward the governors of Israel; she kept the order and did not usurp authority over the man (Judges 5:7-9).
offenseFull: Deborah judged Israel at that time; she dwelt under the palm tree of Deborah in mount Ephraim, and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment (Judges 4:4-5). There was never a time when a woman led the Israelites; she was always under an authority. The men were spiritually weak, and God will deal with specific women when he is fed up with weak men. The Lord revealed the mission to Deborah because she was obedient and had a spirit of order according to the scriptures, and the men at the time were weak.

She could be called a prophetess because she was in order: not doing what she wanted and giving her own sermon, but in subjection to the men of Israel, the leaders of Israel. Miriam the prophetess led the women in song with timbrels; she could lead the women, but not the man (Exodus 15:20). Anna the prophetess departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day (Luke 2:36-37). A prophetess is not someone in the pulpit trying to be over men; that is the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess to teach and seduce the Lord’s servants (Revelation 2:20). The woman is to learn in silence with all subjection, not to teach nor to usurp authority over the man (1 Timothy 2:11-12). A sister puts in her brick by supporting the men.

She sent and called Barak, and asked whether the Lord God of Israel had not commanded him to go to mount Tabor with ten thousand men (Judges 4:6-7). She asked him the question because the Most High had revealed it to her, but the Most High had already told him to do it, for he reveals his secret unto his servants the prophets (Amos 3:7). Barak was slothful, so the Most High spoke to his prophetess to confirm it. When Barak would not go unless she went, she said she would surely go, but the journey would not be for his honour, for the Lord would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman (Judges 4:8-9). Barak was not getting the glory and she was not getting the glory; it was for the Lord. A wise woman does not put herself in authority. On the day she told him to rise, for the Lord had delivered Sisera into his hand; she gave the credit to God (Judges 4:14). She was used as a vessel to get him off his seat so he could fulfil the will of God; she put a backbone back in him.
judgmentFull: This passage is for all the closet feminists who think Deborah justifies women leading men. She did not lead men into any kind of war; she did not put on body armour and a breastplate, rise up on a horse, and lead the charge. She was the motivating factor to men that were shaky and fearful during that time, a mother in Israel, a guiding light (Judges 5:7). To be a mother is to feel the pain of your people, and she saw her nation struggling and stood up in faith. Verse nine proves it: her heart was toward the governors of Israel, the leaders who offered themselves willingly; she was not ruling over them (Judges 5:9).

Judith did the same in her day. She heard the governors speak wrongly before the people and told them plainly their words were not right; she did not usurp authority over the men, but spoke good words to encourage them, and Ozias answered that she had spoken with a good heart (Judith 8:9-31).

Deborah and Barak sang praise to the Lord for the avenging of Israel, when the people willingly offered themselves (Judges 5:1-2). That is what the Most High wants from us: a willing heart in the keeping of the commandments, of the feast days, and in his praise, the heart of the men and women who brought their gold for the tabernacle (Exodus 35:22). We willingly offer ourselves today by giving up whatever stands between us and the Lord, whether father, mother, husband, wife or children, drugs, money, or working on the sabbath (Matthew 10:34-39). They that are delivered from the noise of archers in the places of drawing water rehearse the righteous acts of the Lord, and that is where Israel is now, yet in captivity for the iniquities of the fathers, enduring and keeping the commandments until Christ redeems us (Judges 5:11; Baruch 3:8).

The song gets on the tribes that stayed home; Zebulun and Naphtali jeoparded their lives unto the death, and Meroz was cursed bitterly for not coming to the help of the Lord against the mighty (Judges 5:15-23). Sitting out the battle of the Lord brings a curse. The Lord marching out of Seir, out of the field of Edom, with the earth trembling and the mountains melting, is future prophecy that has not happened yet; Deborah saw in the spirit what is about to happen, and it is the same picture as the one who comes from Edom with dyed garments, treading the winepress alone in the day of vengeance (Judges 5:4-5; Isaiah 63:1-4). And the land had rest forty years (Judges 5:31).

cases.name: Barak
cases.charge: Going down from mount Tabor at the word of the Lord against nine hundred chariots of iron, after refusing to go unless Deborah went with him
cases.summary: The Most High had already commanded Barak to go to mount Tabor with ten thousand men and had already told him he would win the battle, but he was slothful and fearful, so the Lord sent his prophetess to confirm it to him (Judges 4:6-7). He answered that he would go only if Deborah went with him, and because of the spirit he was in, the journey was not for his honour: the Lord sold Sisera into the hand of a woman (Judges 4:8-9). Strengthened up, he went down, and the Lord discomfited Sisera before him until not a man was left (Judges 4:14-16).
offenseFull: Deborah called Barak the son of Abinoam out of Kedesh-naphtali and asked whether the Lord God of Israel had not commanded him to draw toward mount Tabor with ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun, and promised to draw Sisera to the river Kishon and deliver him into his hand (Judges 4:6-7). She asked him the question because the Most High had revealed it to her, but the Most High had already told him to do it, and had already told him he was going to win the battle. He was being slothful, so the Most High spoke to the prophetess to tell him the same thing and confirm it. At this time Israel was not in its glory.

Barak said that if she would go with him he would go, and if she would not go with him he would not go (Judges 4:8). He had fear, uncertainty, and doubt. He was already told by the Lord, Deborah came and confirmed it, and he was still fearful. The leader of the army asking a woman to go with him to battle is a weak spirit, and that is why the Lord had to deal with Deborah: he could not find a brother fearless to do the mission. That is the man a brother does not want to be. Everybody’s faith is not the same, and the only safety net is godly men and women around you who will tell you what God says, not what they feel.

She said she would surely go, but the journey would not be for his honour, for the Lord would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman (Judges 4:9). That was because of the spirit he was in: because of his weakness the Most High told Barak he would not get the victory, and Jael is the one Deborah prophesied about.

Barak called Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh and went up with ten thousand men at his feet, and Deborah went up with him (Judges 4:10). Zebulun and Naphtali jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field; those tribes are warriors, and they are in the South Americas right now, with that warrior spirit still in them (Judges 5:18).

Deborah told him to rise, for this was the day the Lord had delivered Sisera into his hand, and the Lord had gone out before him; so Barak went down from mount Tabor with ten thousand men after him (Judges 4:14). She put a backbone back in him. He needed that push; he did not want to go by himself. He had to get strengthened up, and then he went on and did what he had to do. When Israel goes to battle against horses and chariots and a people more than they, they are not to be afraid, for the Lord their God goes with them to fight for them (Deuteronomy 20:1-4). Fear will make you not keep the commandments of the Lord, and the fearful and unbelieving have their part in the lake of fire (Revelation 21:8).
judgmentFull: The Lord discomfited Sisera and all his chariots and all his host with the edge of the sword before Barak, so that Sisera fled away on his feet; Barak pursued after the chariots and the host unto Harosheth of the Gentiles, and all the host of Sisera fell upon the edge of the sword, and there was not a man left (Judges 4:15-16). The stars in their courses fought against Sisera, and the river Kishon swept them away (Judges 5:20-21).

As Barak pursued Sisera, Jael came out to meet him and showed him the man he sought, lying dead with the nail in his temples (Judges 4:22). The battle was over; the Most High had used her. So God subdued on that day Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel (Judges 4:23).

Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day, praising the Lord for the avenging of Israel, when the people willingly offered themselves (Judges 5:1-2). That is what the Most High wants from us: a willing heart in all that we do. And the land had rest forty years (Judges 5:31).
