cases.name: Jael
cases.charge: Smiting the nail into the temples of Sisera, the captain of Jabin’s host, when he fled to her tent; the woman into whose hand the Lord sold Sisera
cases.summary: Sisera fled away on his feet to the tent of Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin and the house of Heber (Judges 4:17). She covered him with a mantle and gave him milk, and when he was fast asleep and weary she smote the nail into his temples and fastened it into the ground, and he died (Judges 4:18-21). Barak was weak and fearful, and the Lord used a woman to deliver Sisera; Jael is the one Deborah prophesied about (Judges 4:9). She was committed to God and to her people, and the song pronounces her blessed above women in the tent (Judges 5:24).
offenseFull: Heber the Kenite, of the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses, had severed himself from the Kenites and pitched his tent by Kedesh (Judges 4:11). After the Lord discomfited Sisera’s host before Barak, Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael, Heber’s wife, for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber (Judges 4:15-17).

Jael went out to meet him, invited him in, told him to fear not, and covered him with a mantle; he asked for water, and she gave him milk to drink and covered him again (Judges 4:18-19). He told her to stand in the door and say no man was there (Judges 4:20). She made him feel comfortable; she made him believe that everything was all right before he fell into his sleep.

Then Jael took a nail of the tent and an hammer in her hand, went softly unto him as he slept fast and weary, smote the nail into his temples and fastened it into the ground, and he died (Judges 4:21). That must have been a mighty blow, for the tent nails were huge, and she struck it so hard that it went through his head into the ground. Barak did not want to do it, and she did it. Her mind was to deliver the people out of that man’s hand; she knew he was the enemy of the people.

Because Barak was weak and fearful, the Lord said he would use a woman to deliver Sisera, and the word Deborah spoke stood: the Lord sold Sisera into the hand of a woman (Judges 4:9). As Barak pursued Sisera, Jael came out to meet him and showed him the man he sought, lying dead with the nail in his temples; the battle was over, and the Most High had used her to kill him (Judges 4:22). So God subdued on that day Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel (Judges 4:23).
judgmentFull: The song pronounces Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite blessed above women, blessed above women in the tent: he asked water and she gave him milk; she took the nail in one hand and the workman’s hammer in her right, and he fell down dead where he bowed (Judges 5:24-27).

She was committed to God and committed to her people, and the Lord used a sister to do that thing; sisters are not to sleep on the work the Most High has given them. Judith did the same in her day, praying the Lord God of all power to look upon the works of her hands for the exaltation of Jerusalem before she smote Holofernes (Judith 13:4-8). Esther used her power and authority as queen to protect her people, and that is why she was honoured (Esther 9:32).

It was counted a shame for a man of war to die by the hand of a woman, as when Jael put Sisera to death. When a woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech’s head at Thebez, he called hastily to his armourbearer to slay him, so that men would not say a woman slew him (Judges 9:53-54).

The mother of Sisera looked out at a window and cried, asking why his chariot was so long in coming, and her wise ladies answered her with imaginations of victory, that they were dividing the prey and the needlework spoil. She was looking for a son who was never coming home; he lay dead in Jael’s tent (Judges 5:28-30). The song ends asking that the Lord’s enemies perish and that those who love him be as the sun going forth in his might (Judges 5:31).

cases.name: Gideon
cases.charge: Throwing down his father’s altar of Baal and cutting down the grove at the Lord’s word; going against Midian with three hundred men, as the Lord said
cases.summary: Israel did evil, and the Lord delivered them into the hand of Midian seven years; they hid in dens and caves in the mountains of their own land, and Midian and the children of the east destroyed the increase of the earth (Judges 6:1-6). An angel of the Lord greeted Gideon, threshing wheat by the winepress to hide it, as a mighty man of valour; the Most High already saw the warrior in the man hiding wheat (Judges 6:11-12). He threw down his father’s altar of Baal, and with three hundred men the Lord saved Israel (Judges 6:25-27; Judges 7:7). The victory of battle comes from the Lord.
offenseFull: Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hand of Midian seven years (Judges 6:1). That is our manner: the Most High delivers us, we get a little freedom, and we go right back to wickedness, and the Lord has to put us right back into hard bondage to remind us that this is not our rest. When Israel had sown, the Midianites, the Amalekites and the children of the east came up as grasshoppers for multitude and left no sustenance, and Israel was greatly impoverished; that goes right into the curses of blasting and mildew, which go into famine (Judges 6:3-6; Deuteronomy 28:22). All their planning, calculating and saving was taken: no one hides from what the Lord sends the nations to do. He will break us before he takes us, and if we do not listen he will forsake us.

When Israel cried, the Lord sent a prophet to remind them that he had brought them out of the house of bondage and told them not to fear the gods of the Amorites, but they had not obeyed his voice (Judges 6:7-10). The judgment came with a reason attached, and the Amorites go back through Canaan into the Hamites (Genesis 10:15-16). Then an angel of the Lord sat under an oak in Ophrah while Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress to hide it from the Midianites, and greeted him as a mighty man of valour with the Lord at his side (Judges 6:11-12). The Most High already saw the warrior in the man hiding wheat.

Gideon asked why, if the Lord was with them, all this had befallen them, and where were all his miracles (Judges 6:13). A lot of us ask the same today when we watch our people judged in the streets over and over. Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth; the other nations never suffer the judgments we suffer, because his chastening does not pertain to them (Hebrews 12:6-8). God has not forsaken us; we have forsaken God, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out broken cisterns, the religions, Christianity, Islam, and now politics (Jeremiah 2:13).

Sent to save Israel, Gideon answered with his pedigree: his family poor in Manasseh, himself the least in his father’s house (Judges 6:14-15). That is a defeated mentality, and we all have to overcome it, for God hath chosen the foolish, the weak and the base of the world to confound the mighty (1 Corinthians 1:26-28). The same night the Lord told him to throw down his father’s altar of Baal and cut down the grove by it (Judges 6:25). He did it by night, for fear of his father’s household and the men of the city, and when they demanded his death, Joash answered that if Baal were a god he should plead for himself; obviously he is no god, he is an idol (Judges 6:27-32). Gideon asked the fleece signs (Judges 6:36-40), but we are not to ask for signs like that any more; the walk we are in now is by faith (Matthew 12:39).
judgmentFull: The Lord told Gideon the people were too many, lest Israel vaunt themselves and say their own hand had saved them (Judges 7:2). That is Israel: look at what I did. They were warned before they entered the land (Deuteronomy 8:14-18). The fearful returned, twenty and two thousand, and ten thousand remained (Judges 7:3). God always lowered the numbers going into battle so Israel would know it was by the Lord’s strength, and it will be the same again, few against the nations, when that time comes.

The Lord tried the rest at the water (Judges 7:4-7). Nine thousand seven hundred bowed down to drink with their minds on themselves; the three hundred put their hand to their mouth and kept their eyes up, still alert, surveying everything around them, men of vision who understand the mission. You have to be willing to let go of some people (Matthew 10:34-36). Those who are not the three hundred must be the support.

That night the Lord sent Gideon down to the host, which lay along the valley like grasshoppers for multitude, and there he heard a man tell a dream of a cake of barley bread overturning a tent, and his fellow say it could only be the sword of Gideon (Judges 7:9-14). Is that not what is going on today, enemies all around us? The Lord put that dream into the mind of the enemy and sent Gideon to hear it, so he could go into the battle without any doubt, and Gideon worshipped (Judges 7:15).

He divided the three hundred into three companies with trumpets, and lamps within empty pitchers, and struck in the beginning of the middle watch, right between the changing of the watchmen (Judges 7:16-19). They blew the trumpets, broke the pitchers, and cried out for the sword of the Lord and of Gideon; the Lord set every man’s sword against his fellow, and the enemy destroyed itself: that is the Lord fighting the battle (Judges 7:20-22). When Israel goes to war against the enemy that oppresseth them they blow an alarm with the trumpets, and the Lord remembers them and saves them (Numbers 10:9). The famous story of the three hundred was taken from Gideon, and those three hundred were Israelites.

Midian was subdued and lifted up their heads no more, and the country was in quietness forty years (Judges 8:28). The victory does not come in the strength of numbers, in how many guns or how many bullets you have; it is no hard matter for many to be shut up in the hands of a few, for strength cometh from heaven (1 Maccabees 3:18-19).

cases.name: The men of Succoth and Penuel
cases.charge: Refusing bread to the three hundred, faint yet pursuing the kings of Midian, and playing neutral ground for fear of Zebah and Zalmunna
cases.summary: Gideon and the three hundred passed over Jordan, faint, yet pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna the kings of Midian, and asked the men of Succoth for loaves of bread; the princes of Succoth asked whether the kings were already in his hand, and the men of Penuel answered him the same way (Judges 8:4-8). They played neutral ground for fear the kings might come against them if they helped. The Lord gave the kings into his hand, and Gideon taught the men of Succoth with the thorns and briers of the wilderness, beat down the tower of Penuel and slew the men of the city (Judges 8:10-17).
offenseFull: Succoth, which means booths, is where Jacob built him an house and made booths for his cattle, and Penuel is where Jacob saw God face to face (Genesis 33:17; Genesis 32:30). Gideon and the three hundred came to Jordan and passed over, faint, yet pursuing, and he asked the men of Succoth for loaves of bread for the people that followed him, for they were faint, and he was pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian (Judges 8:4-5).

The princes of Succoth asked whether he already had Zebah and Zalmunna in his hand, that they should give bread to his army; he went up to Penuel and asked the same, and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had (Judges 8:6-8). They tried to play neutral ground, for fear the kings might come against them if they helped.

Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that were left of the host of the children of the east, for there fell an hundred and twenty thousand men that drew sword (Judges 8:10). Three hundred against those numbers: you know God was with them. Those are the princes of Asaph’s prayer, that the Most High make the nobles of the nations confederate against Israel like Oreb and Zeeb, and all their princes as Zebah and Zalmunna, who said, let us take to ourselves the houses of God in possession (Psalms 83:11-12). Those nations were destroyed, and the prayer asks that their faces be filled with shame, that men may know that he whose name alone is Jehovah is the Most High over all the earth (Psalms 83:16-18).
judgmentFull: Gideon promised Succoth that when the Lord had delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into his hand he would tear their flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers, and promised Penuel that when he came again in peace he would break down their tower (Judges 8:7-9).

He went up by the way of them that dwelt in tents and smote the host while it was secure, and when the two kings fled he pursued and took them, and discomfited all the host (Judges 8:11-12). Returning from battle, he caught a young man of Succoth who described unto him the princes and elders of the city, and he came back to Succoth with the kings in hand and showed them the kings with whom they had upbraided him (Judges 8:13-15). Gideon and his men had finished off Midian on an empty stomach because of them.

He took the elders of the city, and with the thorns of the wilderness and briers he taught the men of Succoth (Judges 8:16). He taught them a lesson: when the army of the Lord comes through faint and weary and asks for bread, you do not turn them away. And he beat down the tower of Penuel and slew the men of the city (Judges 8:17).

Zebah and Zalmunna said that the men they slew at Tabor each resembled the children of a king; they were Gideon’s brethren, the sons of his mother, and he told the kings that if they had saved them alive he would not slay them (Judges 8:18-19). He told Jether his firstborn to rise up and slay them, but the boy did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, being yet a youth (Judges 8:20). We have all had that moment of getting the nudge from our father and being nervous; the son was young, and that is understandable, but Gideon was being a father, taking his son to the war and teaching him the ways he must walk. That is exactly what we have to do with our young men: train up a child in the way he should go (Proverbs 22:6). Children are like a blank canvas; whatever you put into them and whatever they witness growing up is the type of person they become.

Zebah and Zalmunna told Gideon to rise and fall upon them himself, for as the man is, so is his strength; they wanted to die quickly at the hand of a warrior rather than suffer under the sword of a boy. So Gideon arose and slew them, and took away the ornaments that were on their camels’ necks (Judges 8:21).

cases.name: Gideon’s ephod
cases.charge: Making an ephod of the golden earrings of the spoil and putting it in his city Ophrah, so that all Israel went a whoring after it, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house
cases.summary: The men of Israel asked Gideon to rule over them, he and his son and his son’s son, for delivering them from Midian, and he refused: the Lord would rule over them (Judges 8:22-23). He then asked every man for the golden earrings of his prey, made an ephod of the gold and put it in Ophrah, and all Israel went a whoring after it, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house (Judges 8:24-27). As soon as he was dead, Israel went a whoring after Baalim and made Baal-berith their god (Judges 8:33).
offenseFull: The men of Israel asked Gideon to be their king, and his sons after him in order, his son and his son’s son, because he had delivered them from the hand of Midian (Judges 8:22). Israel has always needed a leader, because we are lost sheep; we need somebody to guide us in the way we must go, or we wander off the path of righteousness.

Gideon refused: he would not be their king, his sons would not be their king, and the Lord would rule over them (Judges 8:23). He knew that if thrones were set up, the people would put their trust and faith in the king instead of the Most High; it was never the Lord’s intention to set kings in the flesh over Israel, for he was to be our king. Nobody of Gideon’s line wanted to be king, because Gideon said the Lord would be king: in Jotham’s parable the olive tree is Gideon, and the fig tree and the vine are Gideon’s sons (Judges 9:8-13).

Gideon asked of every man the golden earrings of his prey, for the enemy were Ishmaelites, and they gave them willingly: seventeen hundred shekels of gold, beside the ornaments and purple raiment of the kings of Midian and the chains about their camels’ necks (Judges 8:24-26).

Gideon made an ephod of it and put it in his city, Ophrah, and all Israel went a whoring after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house (Judges 8:27). The love of money is the root of all evil; the gold that Gideon gathered turned into the very snare that trapped his own house (1 Timothy 6:10).
judgmentFull: Midian was subdued and lifted up their heads no more, and the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon. Gideon had seventy sons, for he had many wives, and his concubine in Shechem bore him a son whose name he called Abimelech; and Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age (Judges 8:28-32). The sum of the history of Gideon, also named Jerubbaal, is this: the victory does not come in the strength of numbers, in how many guns or how many bullets you have. The victory of battle comes from the Lord, and that is why we have to trust in the Lord with all our heart and endure to the end, keeping these commandments until the return of our King of kings.

As soon as Gideon was dead, the children of Israel turned again and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baal-berith their god (Judges 8:33). Baal means lord and berith means covenant, so Baal-berith together means lord of the covenant. They remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side, and showed no kindness to the house of Jerubbaal, namely Gideon, the same person, for all the goodness he had shown Israel (Judges 8:34-35). Out of the house of Baal-berith they gave Abimelech seventy pieces of silver, money out of their idol’s house to back his rise (Judges 9:4).
The same cycle turns again the moment the judge is gone. That is the whole lesson of the book: our deliverance is never our own hand, and our downfall is always our own forgetting.
No sentence on Gideon is recorded beyond the snare to him and to his house.

cases.offense: The men of Israel asked Gideon to be their king, and his sons after him in order, his son and his son’s son, because he had delivered them from the hand of Midian (Judges 8:22). Israel has always needed a leader, because we are lost sheep; we need somebody to guide us in the way we must go, or we wander off the path of righteousness.
cases.judgment: Midian was subdued and lifted up their heads no more, and the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon. Gideon had seventy sons, for he had many wives, and his concubine in Shechem bore him a son whose name he called Abimelech; and Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age (Judges 8:28-32). The sum of the history of Gideon, also named Jerubbaal, is this: the victory does not come in the strength of numbers, in how many guns or how many bullets you have. The victory of battle comes from the Lord, and that is why we have to trust in the Lord with all our heart and endure to the end, keeping these commandments until the return of our King of kings.

cases.name: Abimelech son of Gideon
cases.charge: Slaying his seventy brethren, the sons of Jerubbaal, upon one stone with silver out of the house of Baal-berith, and making himself king at Shechem by kinship
cases.summary: Abimelech, Gideon’s son by his concubine in Shechem, reminded his mother’s kin that he was their bone and their flesh, and they chose him by kinship, not by righteousness (Judges 9:1-3). With silver out of the house of Baal-berith he hired vain and light persons and slew his seventy brethren upon one stone (Judges 9:4-5). Jotham prophesied that Abimelech and the men of Shechem would destroy one another, and it came to pass: God sent an evil spirit between them, and a woman broke Abimelech’s skull with a piece of a millstone (Judges 9:7-57).
offenseFull: Abimelech, the son of Jerubbaal by his concubine in Shechem, went to his mother’s brethren and had them ask the men of Shechem whether it was better for all seventy sons of Jerubbaal to reign over them, or one man (Judges 9:1-2). Abimelech means my father is king. He reminded them that he was their bone and their flesh; when people do that, they want you to remember that blood is thicker than water, so you will back them whether or not it is right.

Their hearts inclined to follow him, for they said he is our brother, and that was the whole of their reasoning: they chose him by kinship, not by righteousness (Judges 9:3). They gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith, money out of their idol’s house to back his rise (Judges 9:4).

With that money he hired vain and light persons, wicked and empty men, to follow him. A man with that lust for power, money or preeminence picks foolish people to put around him, not anybody intelligent who will pick up on his nonsense; he wants yes men.

He went to his father’s house at Ophrah and slew his brethren, seventy persons, upon one stone (Judges 9:5). To kill seventy of your own brothers, you know how evil and how lustful for power you have to be. Only Jotham the youngest was left, for he hid himself; the Lord preserved one of them for a purpose. The men of Shechem and all the house of Millo made Abimelech king, endorsing the man who had just used their money and his hired men to murder his seventy brothers (Judges 9:6).

Jotham stood on the top of mount Gerizim and cried to the men of Shechem to hearken to him, that God might hearken to them (Judges 9:7). In his parable the olive tree is Gideon, and the fig tree and the vine are Gideon’s sons: the profitable trees refused to be promoted over the trees, and only the bramble accepted (Judges 9:8-15).

Jotham reminded them that his father had fought for them and adventured his life to deliver them from Midian, and they had slain his sons upon one stone and made the son of his maidservant king; they did it only because he was kin to them (Judges 9:16-18). If they had not done it in truth, fire would come out from Abimelech and devour the men of Shechem, and fire from the men of Shechem would devour Abimelech (Judges 9:19-20). He prophesied that they would destroy one another.
judgmentFull: When Abimelech had reigned three years, God sent an evil spirit between him and the men of Shechem, and they dealt treacherously with him; the Lord flipped the switch on them (Judges 9:22-23). The Lord sent the evil spirit. War and strife between nations are not coincidence, karma, or mother nature; those are the world’s false ideas and idols. The Most High is in the midst of the armies, mustering the host of the battle; he makes peace and creates evil, and he put a lying spirit in the mouth of all Ahab’s prophets (Isaiah 13:3-4; Isaiah 45:7; 1 Kings 22:22-23).

The cruelty done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal was laid upon Abimelech their brother, and upon the men of Shechem who aided him: guilty by association and by action; the blood cried, and the Lord put it back on them (Judges 9:24). That is the warning: choose your friends carefully. When you pair up with somebody in evil, the Lord will have you at each other’s throats down the line.

Gaal the son of Ebed talked big against Abimelech with wine in him, and all of that big talk disappeared when the fight showed up (Judges 9:26-41). The Lord was in the midst of this whole treachery, turning it back on all of them.

Abimelech took Shechem, slew the people, beat down the city and sowed it with salt, and when the men of the tower of Shechem entered a hold of the house of the god Berith, he set the hold on fire upon them, about a thousand men and women (Judges 9:42-49). These are the people whose money and endorsement made him king; now he turned on Shechem itself and burned them, and the fire out of the bramble that Jotham prophesied was devouring the men of Shechem.

At Thebez a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon his head and broke his skull, and he called hastily to his armourbearer to slay him, so that men would not say a woman slew him; and the young man thrust him through (Judges 9:50-54). It was counted a shame for a man of war to die by the hand of a woman, as when Jael put Sisera to death (Judges 4:21). Killing his seventy brothers bought him a three year reign and a crushed skull; it was to no profit. Be sure your sin will find you out; that is exactly what happened to Abimelech (Numbers 32:23).

Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech and all the evil of the men of Shechem upon their heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham (Judges 9:56-57). If there is evil being done behind closed doors, the Most High will judge it in front of everybody, as he judged Abimelech. Traitors can never be trusted, whether in the faith or out of it, male or female. The spirit of Abimelech is preeminence, manipulation, hatred and murder, and it must be overcome: let nothing be done through strife or vain glory (Philippians 2:3).

cases.name: Jephthah’s vow
cases.charge: Vowing a vow to the Lord before the battle, with good intentions, that whatever came out of his doors to meet him should be the Lord’s, and keeping it when his only daughter came out
cases.summary: Jephthah the Gileadite, a mighty man of valour and the son of a harlot, was thrust out of his father’s house by his brothers, and the elders of Gilead fetched him back as captain when Ammon made war (Judges 11:1-11). Before the battle he vowed that whatever came out of his doors to meet him would be the Lord’s; the Lord delivered Ammon into his hands, and his only daughter came out (Judges 11:29-35). He had good intentions, but when you vow you keep that vow, and he could not go back. She was given over to the Lord and knew no man (Judges 11:36-40).
offenseFull: Jephthah’s mother was a harlot, but he himself was a mighty man of valour (Judges 11:1). His father’s wife’s sons thrust him out, saying he would not inherit in their father’s house because he was the son of a strange woman (Judges 11:2). Strange woman here does not mean his mother was of another nation; the scripture says only that she was a harlot. He fled to the land of Tob, and vain men gathered to him (Judges 11:3). When the ones trying to do right do not get the love and support they need from their own family, they go looking for love in the wrong places, and you see the kind of men they gravitate to. We all have backgrounds; do not think the Lord cannot use who he wants to use.

When Ammon made war, the elders of Gilead came to fetch the man of valour they had cast out (Judges 11:4-6). Jephthah did not forget: you hated me, you put me out, and now that trouble has come, you need me (Judges 11:7). He set the terms; the people made him head and captain (Judges 11:8-11).

The king of Ammon claimed Israel had taken his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan when they came up out of Egypt (Judges 11:12-13). That claim was a lie, and Jephthah knew it. He broke down the whole history: Edom and Moab refused Israel passage, and Israel went around their land and came not within the border of Moab (Judges 11:14-18; Numbers 20:21). Sihon king of the Amorites came out and fought against Israel, and the Lord delivered him and his land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, into Israel’s hand (Judges 11:19-22; Deuteronomy 2:30-36). Israel never touched Ammon’s land, which proves the king’s claim false (Deuteronomy 2:37), and for three hundred years Israel held that land and nobody came to claim it (Judges 11:26).

This is why we must know our history. The king of Ammon could have pulled that on somebody ignorant and been given the land. People try to confuse us about the Bible in the street the same way, so prepare yourself to the search of the fathers; we are supposed to know these things so nobody can pull the wool over our eyes (Job 8:8; Deuteronomy 32:7).

The Lord is in the midst of every battle, and whoever he has destined to win is going to win (Judges 11:27; Isaiah 46:10). The king of Ammon hearkened not, for the Lord had hardened their hearts not to listen, the same as he did with Sihon (Judges 11:28).

Then the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah, and he vowed a vow before the battle: if the Lord delivered Ammon into his hands, whatever came out of the doors of his house to meet him would surely be the Lord’s, an offering promised to the Lord for the victory (Judges 11:29-31). He had good intentions, and Christ teaches not to swear at all; Jephthah is the example of one who swore (Matthew 5:34-37).
judgmentFull: The Lord gave him the victory he asked for: he smote Ammon and Ammon was subdued before Israel (Judges 11:32-33).

His only child came out to meet him at Mizpeh with timbrels and dances, happy that he had won the battle; beside her he had neither son nor daughter (Judges 11:34). He rent his clothes, for he had opened his mouth to the Lord and could not go back (Judges 11:35). When you vow you keep that vow. Watch how you talk to God: you cannot make a vow to God and then turn back.

She did not plead for her life; she accepted that her life was now vowed to the Lord, since the Lord had taken vengeance for him on Ammon (Judges 11:36). She asked one thing, two months to go up and down on the mountains with her companions and bewail her virginity, because being given over to the Lord she would never know a man (Judges 11:37-38). Her respect for her father and for God was so great that she left for two months knowing she would never be held by a man.

Jephthah did not burn his daughter as a human sacrifice. Israel did not do human sacrifices; that was Molech worship among the Canaanites. At the end of two months she returned to her father, who did with her according to his vow, and she knew no man (Judges 11:39). If she had been put to death, there would be no reason for the scripture to say she knew no man; her life was committed to the Lord and she remained a virgin. It is a translation difference around the word offering: she was presented to the Lord to serve him, not sent up as a burnt sacrifice. He offered her up to the Lord as a living sacrifice. The vow was also her death: she mourned that she would leave the earth without being a wife or a mother, and the mistake was her father’s.

The sorrow was that she could never marry or bear children. In those days our women wanted to bring children into the world and continue the lineage; to be without children was counted a shame and a dishonour among the daughters of Israel. Rachel’s cry to Jacob for children shows how heavy childlessness sat upon our foremothers (Genesis 30:1). It became a custom that the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah four days in a year (Judges 11:40).

cases.name: Manoah and his wife
cases.charge: Entreating the Lord to send the man of God again to teach them what to do unto the child, and observing all that the angel commanded, offering the burnt offering unto the Lord
cases.summary: When Israel did evil again and was delivered to the Philistines forty years, the angel of the Lord appeared to the barren wife of Manoah of Zorah, of the Danites, and told her she would bear a son who would be a Nazarite unto God from the womb (Judges 13:1-7). Manoah entreated the Lord to send the man of God again to teach them, and the Lord hearkened (Judges 13:8-14). The angel directed their offering to the Lord and ascended in the flame, and his wife reasoned rightly that the Lord would not have received their offering if he meant to kill them (Judges 13:15-23).
offenseFull: The children of Israel did evil again in the sight of the Lord, and he delivered them into the hand of the Philistines forty years (Judges 13:1). This is the pattern of the book of Judges: after Joshua’s death Israel went off, and nation after nation was given power over them before the great captivities ever came.

His wife was barren, and the angel of the Lord told her plainly that she would conceive and bear a son (Judges 13:2-3). This is one of many examples in the Bible of our foremothers going through barrenness, and when the Most High was ready he enabled them to conceive (Psalms 113:9). Sisters who have tried for years without children should in patience possess their souls, take comfort of the scriptures, meditate on the foremothers, and believe what the Bible says.

The angel commanded the mother herself to drink no wine nor strong drink and to eat no unclean thing, because the child would be a Nazarite unto God from the womb; even in the womb he was to be kept pure (Judges 13:4-5). No razor was to come on his head, and he would begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines. This is one of the first examples in scripture of somebody actually living the Nazarite vow laid out in the law, another level of dedication to the Lord (Numbers 6:1-5). Samson was a Nazarite from birth, just like Samuel and John the Baptist (Luke 1:15).

Understand the difference between a Nazarite and a Nazarene. Christ was a Nazarene because he was from the city of Nazareth, not a Nazarite; he drank wine, and Nazarites could not drink the blood of the grape at all. The locks of the Nazarite also witness to who Israel is; the hair of Israel naturally grows into locks.

The woman told her husband that a man of God had come to her whose countenance was like the countenance of an angel of God, very terrible (Judges 13:6-7). Angels are called men here, as at Christ’s sepulchre and with Lot, because that is their appearance (Luke 24:4). The popular pictures of angels as cute babies with smooth cheeks and little white wings do not match the biblical descriptions at all; there is no such thing as a naked white baby angel. To see an angel of the Most High was a terrifying sight, and the keepers at the sepulchre became as dead men for fear of him (Matthew 28:1-4).

Manoah entreated the Lord to send the man of God again to teach them what to do unto the child, and the Most High hearkened to the voice of Manoah (Judges 13:8-9). Manoah asked how they should order the child, and the angel reiterated the instructions he had already given: all that he commanded the woman, she was to observe while she carried this son (Judges 13:11-14).
judgmentFull: Manoah tried to detain the angel and make ready a kid for him; angels eat, walk, and have physical bodies to eat and walk with. But the angel refused to eat of his bread, and said that if he offered a burnt offering, he must offer it unto the Lord (Judges 13:15-16). The angel knew Manoah might try to offer it up to him, since he appeared like a god, so he directed the offering to the Lord. Israel is quick to worship anything that looks like it could be God because we cannot see the Most High, which is why the scriptures warn against the worshipping of angels (Colossians 2:18).

Manoah still did not know that he was an angel of the Lord. Lot knew and Abraham knew, but Manoah and his wife did not, and most of the time we do not know; some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2). Manoah asked his name, and the angel asked why he asked after his name, seeing it is secret (Judges 13:17-18). His name was too wonderful to be uttered to him.

Manoah took a kid with a meat offering and offered it upon a rock unto the Lord, and when the flame went up toward heaven from off the altar, the angel of the Lord ascended in the flame and went out of their sight (Judges 13:19-20). Angels are spirits and ministers of flaming fire (Psalms 104:4); they have bodies, but celestial bodies, a different kind from ours. Manoah and his wife fell on their faces to the ground. Then Manoah knew that he was an angel of the Lord (Judges 13:21).

Manoah said they would surely die, because they had seen God (Judges 13:22). This is a passage the contradictors point to, since the Bible says no man has seen God; but God here is Elohim, which is plural and speaks of heavenly beings. They saw an angel, not the Most High God. No flesh can look upon the Most High God, and the furthest anybody got was Moses seeing his back parts.

His wife reasoned rightly: if the Lord were pleased to kill them, he would not have received a burnt offering and a meat offering at their hands, nor shown them all these things (Judges 13:23). The woman bore a son and called his name Samson, the child grew, and the Lord blessed him; the Spirit of the Lord began to move him at times in the camp of Dan between Zorah and Eshtaol, and the Most High began to deal with him (Judges 13:24-25).

cases.name: Samson
cases.charge: Lusting after the heathen women of the Philistines, a wife at Timnath against his parents’ charge, a harlot at Gaza, and Delilah, to whom he told all his heart and broke his Nazarite vow
cases.summary: Samson, a Nazarite unto God from the womb, had a lust issue with heathen women; that is the infamy his story is known for, and the Lord used the flaw as an occasion against the Philistines who had dominion over Israel (Judges 14:1-4). Three times Delilah attempted to have his life taken and he stayed; then he told her all his heart, was shaven, and knew not that the Lord had departed from him (Judges 16:4-20). Blinded and grinding in the prison at Gaza, he called on the Lord once more, and slew more at his death than in his life (Judges 16:21-30).
offenseFull: Samson saw a woman of the daughters of the Philistines at Timnath and told his father and mother to get her for him to wife (Judges 14:1-2). Samson never wanted an Israelite woman; he always wanted a Hamite. His parents answered him rightly, asking whether there was never a woman among his brethren: there were twelve tribes, and no shortage of women in all the coasts of Israel (Judges 14:3). Samson insisted, for she pleased him well. The forefathers always charged their sons not to do this (Genesis 28:1).

His father and mother knew not that it was of the Lord, who sought an occasion against the Philistines, for at that time they had dominion over Israel (Judges 14:4). The Most High was using Samson’s flaw, his lust after Philistine women, to destroy them for oppressing his people. His thoughts are higher than our thoughts, and the deceived and the deceiver are his: he used these heathen women, and later Delilah, to get Samson caught up with the Philistines so that he would destroy them (Isaiah 55:8-9; Job 12:16).

At the wedding feast the thirty companions threatened to burn Samson’s wife unless she enticed his riddle out of him, and she wept before him that he did not love her; she cared more about her people than about him, and that is why he should never have married outside the nation (Judges 14:15-17). This big strong mighty brother caved in because of the tears of a woman. Samson knew exactly what happened: they had plowed with his heifer (Judges 14:18). Never trust your enemy. That is why it makes no sense to marry the enemy.
At Gaza he saw a harlot and went in unto her; once again the whoremongering spirit had hold of this brother (Judges 16:1).

Afterward he loved Delilah, another heathen woman. The lords of the Philistines each offered her eleven hundred pieces of silver to entice him and learn wherein his great strength lay (Judges 16:4-5). It was a setup the whole time. The scheme never changed: when the devil wants to attack a strong Israelite man, he uses the woman. Once they learn where our strength lies, as Delilah was sent by the Philistines to learn Samson’s, that is how they subdue us; you bind a strong man, and you can go in and spoil his goods. The strength of Israel is the Bible, the laws of God recorded in it.

Delilah asked him outright wherein his strength lay and how he might be bound; she was literally asking him for the formula to get him killed (Judges 16:6). Three times she bound him and three times he broke free (Judges 16:7-14). A man of war should have recognized right there that this was a setup and cut her off, but he stayed.
judgmentFull: She said his heart was not with her; but her heart was not with him, her mind was with the enemy, and Samson was sleeping with the enemy (Judges 16:15). She pressed him daily, and he told her all his heart, and that is where he messed up: he was a Nazarite unto God from his mother’s womb, and if shaven his strength would go from him (Judges 16:16-17). This is a scriptural example of why a man cannot tell his wife every single thing in his heart. We do not go by the philosophies of men that say your wife is your best friend you tell everything to. Keep the doors of your mouth from her that lies in your bosom, and do not counsel with your wife about such things (Micah 7:5).
Samson’s downfall was compromise: emotional attachment, physical relationship, and he ignored all the warning signs.

She made him sleep upon her knees and called for a man to shave off the seven locks of his head, and his strength went from him (Judges 16:18-19). He awoke thinking he would go out as at other times before, but it was over, because he had broken his vow; he knew not that the Lord was departed from him (Judges 16:20). The Philistines put out his eyes, and he did grind in the prison house at Gaza. But the hair of his head began to grow again (Judges 16:21-22).

The lords of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice unto Dagon their god, saying their god had delivered Samson into their hand (Judges 16:23-24). They gave the praise and the glory to their idol, a devil that had not done a thing. It was Samson’s own transgression that caused the Most High to allow the Philistines to bind and afflict him, and that praise to a fake god did not please the Most High. They called him out to make them sport, using the Israelite man for mockery (Judges 16:25-27).

Samson called unto the Lord to strengthen him only this once, bowed himself between the two middle pillars, and died with the Philistines, and the dead he slew at his death were more than those he slew in his life (Judges 16:28-30). Even with Samson’s failings and flaws the Most High used him as a vessel of vengeance on the heathen who oppressed his people and gave the glory of their victory to a fake god. Israel’s salvation in scripture is always joined with the destruction of the enemy (Wisdom of Solomon 18:7); the avenging of what has been done to Israel does not come by striving for equality, but by the destruction the Most High brings on the oppressor.

He had judged Israel twenty years (Judges 16:31). When Satan whispers in your ear that you are no good and the Lord cannot use a person like you: he used Samson, and he used a lot of our forefathers that fell to sin.

cases.offense: Samson saw a woman of the daughters of the Philistines at Timnath and told his father and mother to get her for him to wife (Judges 14:1-2). Samson never wanted an Israelite woman; he always wanted a Hamite. His parents answered him rightly, asking whether there was never a woman among his brethren: there were twelve tribes, and no shortage of women in all the coasts of Israel (Judges 14:3). Samson insisted, for she pleased him well. The forefathers always charged their sons not to do this (Genesis 28:1).
cases.judgment: She said his heart was not with her; but her heart was not with him, her mind was with the enemy, and Samson was sleeping with the enemy (Judges 16:15). She pressed him daily, and he told her all his heart, and that is where he messed up: he was a Nazarite unto God from his mother’s womb, and if shaven his strength would go from him (Judges 16:16-17). This is a scriptural example of why a man cannot tell his wife every single thing in his heart. We do not go by the philosophies of men that say your wife is your best friend you tell everything to. Keep the doors of your mouth from her that lies in your bosom, and do not counsel with your wife about such things (Micah 7:5).

cases.name: Micah’s idols and the tribe of Dan
cases.charge: Making a house of gods with a graven image and a molten image, consecrating a son and hiring a Levite as priest to the idols; and the tribe of Dan stealing both and setting up the graven image in Dan until the captivity of the land
cases.summary: Micah of mount Ephraim stole eleven hundred shekels of silver from his own mother, and when he restored it she blessed him instead of rebuking him and had idols made for his house (Judges 17:1-4). He consecrated one of his sons and hired a Levite as priest, expecting the Lord to do him good (Judges 17:5-13). Six hundred Danites took the gods and the priest, burned Laish, and set up the graven image, with priests until the day of the captivity of the land; Dan stayed heavy in idolatry and is not named among the sealed tribes (Judges 18:1-31).
offenseFull: A man of mount Ephraim named Micah stole eleven hundred shekels of silver from his own mother, and restored it when he heard her cursing (Judges 17:1-2). Instead of rebuking her son, his mother blessed him of the Lord and told him she had wholly dedicated the silver for him to make a graven image and a molten image. She had idols made to set up in her son’s house (Judges 17:3-4). A mother buying her son idols was nothing new in Israel: later king Ahaziah walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counsellor to do wickedly (2 Chronicles 22:3).
Micah had a whole house of gods. He made an ephod and teraphim and consecrated one of his own sons to be his priest, a counterfeit priesthood serving counterfeit gods (Judges 17:5).

There was no king in Israel, and every man did that which was right in his own eyes (Judges 17:6). This verse is the key to understanding the whole book of Judges. With no king and no government, Israel was sheep without a shepherd. The same individual spirit is around today in those who say join no camp and let no man teach you. Every time the scripture shows Israel without a leadership structure, all manner of wickedness follows, primarily idolatry.

A young Levite of Bethlehem-judah came to the house of Micah, and Micah offered him ten shekels of silver by the year, a suit of apparel and his victuals to be unto him a father and a priest (Judges 17:7-10). Nothing says the Levite was already in idolatry, but when money was offered he went right along with it; being corrupted for reward was always the Levites’ weakness (Judges 17:11-12). Micah was sure the Lord would do him good (Judges 17:13): a house full of idols and a hired priest over them, yet he expected the Most High to bless him because a Levite was on the payroll. That is how sick in the mind Israel was without leadership.

The tribe of Dan was still seeking an inheritance; they had conquered in Joshua’s day but never attained all their land (Judges 18:1; Joshua 19:47). Their five spies lodged at Micah’s house and questioned the young Levite, for a Levite serving in a house of idols raised questions (Judges 18:2-6).

At Laish they saw a people dwelling careless, quiet and secure, not even watching for anyone to come in and conquer them. There was no magistrate, no judicial system to convict a man for a crime; they were too far from Zidon for Zidon to interfere, and had no business with any man, no allies (Judges 18:7-10). The spies peeped all of it.

Six hundred armed Danites passed by the house of Micah (Judges 18:11-13). The first time Micah let the five spies lodge in his house, they saw his expensive looking gods and got covetous (Judges 18:14). On the way to the lick they spotted another lick. Do not bring just anybody into your house, even brethren, because the deceitful man has many tricks and approaches to finesse you out of the goods in your house (Ecclesiasticus 11:29).

While the six hundred armed men stood by the gate keeping the priest occupied, the five spies took the graven image, the ephod, the teraphim and the molten image (Judges 18:15-17). When the priest objected, they told him to hold his peace and asked whether it was better to be a priest to one man’s house or to a tribe in Israel (Judges 18:18-19). The priest’s heart was glad (Judges 18:20). His covetous spirit was plain: already sold out to serve idols for Micah’s silver, he dropped the man who treated him as a son the moment a bigger position was offered.
judgmentFull: Micah and his neighbours overtook the children of Dan, and he complained that they had taken away the gods which he made, and the priest, and what more did he have (Judges 18:22-24). Examine how foolish that sounds: my gods which I made. How can a man make his own god? That is how simple we had become without leadership. Dan warned him to hush, lest he and his household lose their lives, and Micah turned back to his house (Judges 18:25-26).
The Danites smote Laish with the sword and burnt the city, and there was no deliverer, exactly what the spies had scoped out; no neighbour and no ally came to save them (Judges 18:27-29).

The first thing the children of Dan did in the land the Most High allowed them to take was set up the graven image, a god made by the hands of a man they had just robbed. Jonathan the son of Gershom and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land (Judges 18:30-31).

Dan stayed heavy in idolatry all the way through history and never changed. After the kingdom split, Jeroboam feared the people’s heart would turn again to Rehoboam if they kept going up to Jerusalem, so he made two calves of gold, doubling the iniquity of the wilderness, and set one in Bethel and the other in Dan, and this thing became a sin (1 Kings 12:27-30).

Those who swear by the sin of Samaria and by the god of Dan as living shall fall and never rise up again; it is an idol made with hands, yet they called it living (Amos 8:14). That is why, when the tribes are sealed, Dan is not named among them; Dan was discontinued as a tribe of itself and intertwined with Benjamin for the most part (Revelation 7:5-8).

cases.name: The men of Gibeah, and Benjamin
cases.charge: Sons of Belial besetting the house to know the Levite and forcing his concubine all night until she was dead; and Benjamin refusing to deliver up the guilty and going out to battle against their brethren
cases.summary: With no king in Israel, a Levite would not lodge in Jebus, a city of strangers, and turned in to Gibeah of Benjamin, where only an old man took them in (Judges 19:1-21). Sons of Belial beset the house demanding the man, a rerun of Sodom, and forced his concubine all night until she was dead (Judges 19:22-28). Benjamin would not deliver up the guilty, and the Lord smote Benjamin before Israel until six hundred were left (Judges 20:12-48).
offenseFull: In those days there was no king in Israel, sheep without a shepherd. A Levite of mount Ephraim took a concubine, a woman dealt with on the level of a servant; she played the whore against him and went back to her father’s house, and instead of letting her go he went after her to bring her again (Judges 19:1-3). A woman who is put away and becomes another man’s is defiled to her former husband, and taking her back is abomination and causes the land to sin (Deuteronomy 24:4; Jeremiah 3:1); with no king and no enforcement of the law, this is what men did. He went back for a defiled wife, and that is why she was later ravished and killed: God does not like it.

On the fifth day her father pointed out that the day was drawing toward evening and coming to an end (Judges 19:9): the day ends at evening, so it begins at evening, and a day, the sabbath included, runs from evening to evening, not sunrise to sunrise. Passing Jebus, still held by the Jebusites (Joshua 15:63), the Levite would not lodge in a city not of the children of Israel; even in those wild days he would lodge only with his brothers (Judges 19:10-13). In Gibeah no man took them in: no charity from Benjamin, a brother travelling and nobody showing hospitality (Judges 19:15). An old man of mount Ephraim took them in, for he knew what the streets of Gibeah held at night (Judges 19:16-21).

Certain sons of Belial, children of the devil, demon seed, beset the house and beat at the door demanding the man, that they might know him (Judges 19:22). To know here is sexual, as Adam knew his wife (Genesis 4:1); the men of Gibeah were howling for the man himself. It is a rerun of Sodom at Lot’s door (Genesis 19:4-9), and the scripture names the vile thing they were after, men with men working that which is unseemly (Romans 1:26-27). All the tribes have shameful history somewhere down the line; this night is Benjamin’s.

The man brought his concubine out, and they abused her all the night (Judges 19:25). They is plural: a gang rape, forced, nothing voluntary about it, done in the anger of men who could not get the man they wanted. At dawn she fell at the door with her hands upon the threshold, and there was no more spirit left in her (Judges 19:26-28). Rape is a sin worthy of death: the man who forces a damsel shall die, as when a man rises against his neighbour and slays him (Deuteronomy 22:25-26); the Most High counts rape the equivalent of murder, and here the victim was literally murdered. Marriage is the only honourable bed (Hebrews 13:4); men calling themselves Israelites and teaching otherwise give Israelites a bad name. He divided her into twelve pieces and sent her into all the coasts of Israel, to make the twelve tribes aware of what was done in Gibeah (Judges 19:29-30).
judgmentFull: All Israel gathered as one man at Mizpeh, four hundred thousand that drew sword (Judges 20:1-2). Israel got ready for war behind one woman. There is no hatred of women in this truth; a crime against one sister moved the whole nation to arms. The Levite testified that they had forced his concubine until she died (Judges 20:5); forced is the Bible’s word for rape, nowhere can rape be called lawful, and whether the victim lives or dies it is counted as murder. Be very mindful of sick, perverted camps that teach otherwise.

They demanded that Benjamin deliver up the children of Belial to be put to death, but Benjamin would not hearken, riding for their own no matter the crime (Judges 20:12-13). He who is a witness and does not utter it shall bear his iniquity (Leviticus 5:1): by not turning them over Benjamin became guilty of the same sin, and they doubled down, gathering to fight their brethren (Judges 20:14). This is the civil war in Israel; some of our people do not know we had one. With seven hundred left-handed slingers who could hit a hair’s breadth and not miss, Benjamin destroyed twenty-two thousand the first day and eighteen thousand the second (Judges 20:15-25). Then the whole nation wept, fasted and offered before the Lord, humbled itself, and through Phinehas at the ark the Lord promised them victory (Judges 20:26-28).

No more going head up against slingers they could not beat straight on: Israel set liers in wait, drew Benjamin onto the highways, and burned Gibeah as the appointed sign, (Judges 20:29-41). The Lord smote Benjamin before Israel, twenty-five thousand one hundred that day, and the victory belonged to the Most High as he had promised (Judges 20:35). Because Benjamin would not deliver the guilty and fought the brethren who came to judge the matter, all the city bore that same judgment (Judges 20:37, 48).

Six hundred fled to the rock Rimmon; only that remnant kept the tribe from being utterly destroyed (Judges 20:47). The Most High pushed the reset button on the tribe for the sodomite and rape activity that came out of Gibeah, and drastic measures had to be taken so Benjamin could continue, for Israel had sworn not to give them their daughters, and a sworn oath must be performed (Judges 21:1-7; Numbers 30:2). Four hundred virgins did not suffice the six hundred, for there was no sharing: one man, one woman (Judges 21:12-14). That war is why Saul called himself of the smallest of the tribes (1 Samuel 9:21). There have been mighty and righteous Benjamites since, Paul chief among them, but we learn the history as it is written: there was no king in Israel, every man did what was right in his own eyes, and most of our people are still in that state (Judges 21:25).

cases.name: Ruth and Boaz
cases.charge: Ruth: cleaving to Naomi and joining herself under Israel and Israel’s God. Boaz: the law of the land conducted at the gate before witnesses, and love thy neighbour as thyself
cases.summary: In the days when the judges ruled, a Moabite widow would not go back to her people and to Chemosh, but bound herself to Naomi’s road, Naomi’s people and Naomi’s God. She came to Bethlehem with a mother in law who called herself Mara, gleaned in the field of Boaz, and called herself what she was to Israel, a stranger. Boaz went up to the gate, called ten elders as witnesses, carried out the law of inheritance and the law of the husband’s brother, and bought the field and Ruth with it, to keep the dead man’s name alive. Their son was Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David.
offenseFull: When the judges ruled, famine drove Elimelech of Bethlehem-judah to Moab with Naomi and their two sons, who married the Moabite women Orpah and Ruth and died there (Ruth 1:1-9). Were the sons of Israel supposed to marry the women of Moab? No. A Moabite was not to enter the congregation of the Lord (Deuteronomy 23:3), and Israel had already gone whoring with the daughters of Moab at Shittim (Numbers 25:1-2); but this was the era of no king, when every man did what was right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25), and even in Ezra’s day the Moabites had not been put away (1 Esdras 8:69). Naomi prayed that each daughter in law find rest in a husband’s house. That rest is an inheritance; a good man leaves one to his children’s children, not a gang of bills (Proverbs 13:22). Behind her words stands the law of the husband’s brother, the widow’s firstborn carrying on the dead man’s name (Deuteronomy 25:5-10). We are not under that
law now, having no land inheritance in this captivity, and it is wicked to pull that scripture today to get with a brother’s widow; but we are still to build a legacy and pass it down.

Orpah went back to her people and her gods, to Chemosh (Numbers 21:29), for all the gods of the nations are idols (Psalms 96:5). Ruth clung to Naomi, her people and her God until death (Ruth 1:14-22). Does that make her an Israelite, or an heir of the kingdom? No. Both daughters in law knew exactly what they were, and Ruth never claimed otherwise. She joined herself under Israel and acknowledged her place, like the woman of Canaan who accepted the crumbs from the masters’ table (Matthew 15:24-28), and like Rahab, who knew the God of Israel was the true living God (Joshua 6:25). Naomi came home to Bethlehem calling herself Mara, bitter.

Ruth gleaned in the field of Boaz, a wealthy kinsman of Elimelech, who kept her with his young women and charged his men not to touch her (Ruth 2:1-16). She asked why he took notice of her, since she was a stranger, the word the law uses for the nations round about (Leviticus 25:44-46). Boaz had heard how she left her own parents and land for her mother in law, prayed that the Lord under whose wings she had taken refuge would reward her, and had handfuls dropped on purpose for her. Naomi then sought that same rest for her, sending her to lie at Boaz’s feet on the threshing floor (Ruth 3:1-18), where Ruth asked him to spread his skirt over her as near kinsman. The skirt is male clothing, the edge of the garment; she was asking the near kinsman to take her under his covering. He blessed her for not going after young men: even as a Moabitess she was keeping the customs of Israel, seeking her dead husband’s kinsman to keep his name in the earth.
judgmentFull: Boaz sat at the gate with the nearer kinsman and ten elders as witnesses, for the record (Ruth 4:1-12). The kinsman had first right to redeem Elimelech’s land, under the law that no inheritance pass from tribe to tribe (Numbers 36:5-9); a man could marry outside his own tribe but not outside the nation. But whoever took the land took the dead man’s wife with it, to keep his name on his inheritance, the duty of the husband’s brother and the loosed shoe. The kinsman declined and drew off his shoe, and Boaz bought all that was Elimelech’s and took Ruth, Mahlon’s widow, as his wife. What law was Boaz exercising in all of that? Loving his neighbour as himself (Leviticus 19:18). That is why he is mentioned in the scriptures.

The elders blessed the marriage, naming Rachel and Leah who built the house of Israel and Pharez whom Tamar bore to Judah; in that blessing they were prophesying of David to come. Ruth bore a son, and Naomi took the child to her bosom and became his nurse (Ruth 4:13-22). Why? Because it is not the custom of Israel to allow a child to be raised under the hand of a heathen. A child’s first teacher is the mother; he takes on her ways, which is what Nehemiah found among the children of the wives of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab, who could not speak the Jews’ language (Nehemiah 13:23-24). Ruth was brought in to keep Mahlon’s name alive in Israel, and she had no hand in raising the child; Naomi raised him so he would learn the ways of Israel. His name was Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David, the line of Judah running down to the king and on to Christ (Matthew 1:5-6).

cases.name: Hannah
cases.charge: Pouring out her soul before the Lord, vowing her son to him under the vow of the Nazarite, and paying her vow by lending him to the Lord as long as he lived
cases.summary: Elkanah of mount Ephraim had two wives; Peninnah had children, but the Lord had shut up Hannah’s womb, and her adversary provoked her year by year until she wept and would not eat (1 Samuel 1:1-8). At Shiloh she poured out her soul before the Lord and vowed a man child to him all his days, with no razor upon his head; Eli took her for drunk, then blessed her petition, and she believed and was no more sad (1 Samuel 1:9-18). She bore Samuel, weaned him, and lent him to the Lord as long as he lived, and the Lord gave her three sons and two daughters more (1 Samuel 1:19-28; 1 Samuel 2:21).
offenseFull: At Shiloh, another name for Jerusalem, Elkanah gave Hannah a worthy portion, for he loved her, but the Lord had shut up her womb, as with Rachel, and her adversary mocked her for it, as Hagar did Sarah (1 Samuel 1:4-6). The women of Israel have not changed one bit: even in the times of Samuel there was a sister vexing a barren woman and rubbing it in her face, and sisters of Israel have to get their spirits right.

In bitterness of soul she prayed and wept sore, and vowed that if the Lord of hosts would remember his handmaid and give her a man child, she would give him to the Lord all the days of his life, and no razor would come upon his head (1 Samuel 1:9-11). Sometimes you go before the Lord and let it go. That vow goes back to the law of the Nazarite, who is holy and lets the locks of his hair grow (Numbers 6:5). The locks are hair braided so that it locks into place as it grows, the same seven locks of Samson (Judges 16:13), and that is how you know these were black men.

Only her lips moved, and Eli thought she was drunk; she answered that she had drunk nothing but had poured out her soul before the Lord, and Eli prayed that God grant her petition (1 Samuel 1:12-17). She went her way and ate, and her countenance was no more sad: she believed when she heard the word of Eli (1 Samuel 1:18). Why was the petition granted? It was the will of the Most High for Samuel to come through Hannah, in his time, and she was granted it because of what she did before she even asked: we receive whatsoever we ask because we keep his commandments and do what is pleasing in his sight (1 John 3:22), and if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us (1 John 5:14-15). A lot of us pray for things the Lord has not given us; he has the infinite wisdom and knows what is best, so some things he keeps back, and we have to accept that. If you are in sin, he is not hearing your prayers.

The Lord remembered her, and she bore a son and called him Samuel, asked of the Lord (1 Samuel 1:19-20). Hannah did not have to go up to the yearly sacrifice, for the law said all thy males (Deuteronomy 16:16), and she stayed until the child was weaned, about three or four years old, the last time he would be under her care (1 Samuel 1:21-23). Then she brought him to Eli with three bullocks, flour and wine, told him this was the child she had prayed for, and lent him to the Lord as long as he lived (1 Samuel 1:24-28). That is great faith, and she kept her promise; Hannah was an upright and honest woman. When you vow a vow to God, defer not to pay it, and do not say before the angel that it was an error (Ecclesiastes 5:4-6): that is your guardian angel, who recorded it and knew exactly what it was. Let your yea be yea and your nay be nay (Matthew 5:37).
judgmentFull: Hannah rejoiced in the Lord’s salvation: there is none holy as the Lord, and no rock like our God (1 Samuel 2:1-2). She warned against arrogancy, for the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed: if it came out of your mouth, are you going to do it (1 Samuel 2:3)? Why call him Lord and not do the things he says (Luke 6:46)? The Lord does not like a people that only talk; he wants to see faith and actions (Isaiah 29:13). To say God knows my heart and loves me no matter what is arrogancy coming out of the mouth; he loves you if you keep the commandments.

The Lord was prophesying through Hannah: the bows of the mighty are broken and they that stumbled are girded with strength, and he that is feeble shall be as David, which is the house of Israel (1 Samuel 2:4; Zechariah 12:7-8). The Lord kills and makes alive, decides who wakes up and who passes, and there is no god with him (1 Samuel 2:6; Deuteronomy 32:39). He raises the poor out of the dust, out of confusion, and lifts the beggar from the dunghill to set them among princes (1 Samuel 2:8). Why beggars? Because we are the ones always begging another race of people for reparations, for jobs, for services, instead of building with our own. The dunghill is not just one poor country; wherever we live in this captivity has been made a dunghill compared to what we came from, because we came from ruling, and from the dunghill to the throne of glory is planet rulership. He gives strength unto his king, which is Christ, and exalts the horn of his anointed (1 Samuel 2:10).

Samuel ministered before the Lord as a child, and his mother brought him a little coat year by year; Eli blessed her for the loan lent to the Lord, and she bore three sons and two daughters (1 Samuel 2:18-21). She kept her end of the bargain, and the child grew up to be a powerful prophet.

cases.name: Eli and his sons
cases.charge: Sons of Belial in the priest’s office, taking the offering of the Lord by force and lying with the women at the door of the tabernacle; and a father who honoured his sons above the Lord and restrained them not
cases.summary: The sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the Lord (1 Samuel 2:12). Priests in the house of the Lord, they took the sacrifice by force, so that men abhorred the offering of the Lord, and lay with the women at the door of the tabernacle (1 Samuel 2:13-22). Eli spoke to them but did not remove them from the priesthood (1 Samuel 2:23-25). In one day both sons were slain and the ark was taken, and Eli fell backward from his seat and broke his neck (1 Samuel 4:10-18).
offenseFull: The sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the Lord. They were the devil (1 Samuel 2:12). They were Levites, priests in the house of the Lord doing the work of the Lord, and yet they did not know him, because they did not keep the commandments true in their spirit; they kept them on the surface where you can see it. They looked the part, with the fringes, the beard, and showing up on the sabbath day, but their spirit was not right with the Lord. Knowing you are Israel does not mean you are righteous, and congregating on the sabbath does not mean you go into the kingdom.

The custom was that while the flesh was seething, the priest’s servant struck a fleshhook of three teeth into the pot, and all that it brought up the priest took (1 Samuel 2:13-14). That is how the Lord took care of Levi: Levi had no inheritance of land among the tribes, and the Lord provided for them through the sacrifices Israel brought, so that they had need of nothing. But before the fat was burned the servant demanded raw flesh to roast, and if the man asked him to wait he would take it by force (1 Samuel 2:15-16). These were devils strong-arming the offerings; the sin of the young men was very great before the Lord, for men abhorred the offering of the Lord (1 Samuel 2:17). Men hated offering to the Lord because the sons of Eli would get physically abusive with them.

Eli was very old and heard all that his sons did to all Israel, and how they lay with the women that assembled at the door of the tabernacle (1 Samuel 2:22). These were the harlots hanging around the temple, and other men’s wives: the sons of Eli used their privilege and their authority to sleep with whom they wanted and eat what they wanted. He asked why they did such things and told them they made the Lord’s people transgress (1 Samuel 2:23-24). The Levites were the leaders, so the people followed their actions: they saw the sons of Eli with the harlots and said, it must be all right, look how they live in the temple.

Eli said something, but he did not remove them and put them out of the priesthood; he did not go further than words, and he took no action. That is the soft correction many give today: they said what Eli said. Correction is to be given with a forehead set hard against their foreheads (Ezekiel 3:8-9), or the wicked think what they are doing is all right and keep on doing it, and next you have a whole people full of wickedness.
judgmentFull: A man of God reminded Eli that the Lord chose the house of his father, Levi, out of all the tribes to be his priest and gave it all the offerings made by fire, and asked why they kicked at his sacrifice and why Eli honoured his sons above him (1 Samuel 2:27-29). Take that into account: do you honour your children above what the Lord says to do? Can they do no wrong while keeping no commandments, never showing up on the sabbath day, and living grown under your roof? As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord (Joshua 24:15).

The Lord had said Eli’s house would walk before him for ever, but now he would honour them that honour him, and they that despise him would be lightly esteemed (1 Samuel 2:30). Lightly esteemed means the Lord is not looking out for you: you are not thinking about me, so I am not thinking about you. He would cut off the arm of Eli’s house, so that there would not be an old man in it (1 Samuel 2:31-33); the arm is the strength, his children, who would die in the flower of their age. That is not the sons dying for the father: the son that continues in his father’s sins dies for his own doings (Ezekiel 18:10-17), and because Eli did not reprove his sons, the generations after would follow right in their footsteps.

The sign was that Hophni and Phinehas would both die in one day, and the Lord would raise up a faithful priest to do according to his heart and mind (1 Samuel 2:34-35). Whoever was left in Eli’s house would crouch for a piece of silver and a morsel of bread (1 Samuel 2:36); Levi had no land, and cut off from the priesthood, Eli’s house was left to beg. The Lord told Samuel he would judge Eli’s house for ever, because his sons made themselves vile and he restrained them not, and its iniquity would not be purged with sacrifice nor offering (1 Samuel 3:11-14). Eli accepted it: it is the Lord, let him do what seemeth him good (1 Samuel 3:18).

Israel fetched the ark into the camp, thirty thousand fell, the ark of God was taken, and Hophni and Phinehas were slain (1 Samuel 4:3-11): in this battle the Most High allowed their lives to be taken, exactly as was prophesied against the house of Eli. Eli was righteous as far as himself, but he honoured his sons above the Most High by not rebuking them as a true leader should. When he heard that the ark was taken, he fell backward from his seat, broke his neck and died, for he was old and heavy (1 Samuel 4:12-18). He had judged Israel forty years, and his death was part of the judgment for how he dealt with his sons. His daughter in law named her child Ichabod: the glory, the ark that held the commandments, was departed (1 Samuel 4:19-22).

cases.name: The Philistines and the captured ark
cases.charge: Taking the ark of God and setting it in the house of Dagon beside their idol, and carrying it from city to city seven months
cases.summary: The Philistines took the ark of God from Ebenezer to Ashdod and had the audacity to set it in the house of Dagon, a fake god the Lord had already exposed (1 Samuel 5:1-2). Dagon fell on his face before the ark, and the next morning his head and hands lay cut off upon the threshold (1 Samuel 5:3-5). The hand of the Lord smote Ashdod, Gath and Ekron with emerods and deadly destruction, until after seven months their own priests warned them not to harden their hearts as Pharaoh did, and they sent the ark home with a trespass offering (1 Samuel 5:6-6:18).
offenseFull: The Philistines never wanted to leave Israel alone (1 Samuel 4:1). They came of Mizraim, the son of Ham (Genesis 10:6, 13-14); the sons of Ham are the Ethiopians, Egyptians, South Africans and Libyans today (1 Chronicles 1:8). When the ark came into Israel’s camp they were afraid, for these were the Gods that smote the Egyptians with all the plagues: the nations knew what the Most High did to Egypt (1 Samuel 4:6-8). They had served Israel in the days of the judges, so they quit themselves like men and fought (1 Samuel 4:9; Judges 13:1).

Israel was smitten, thirty thousand footmen fell, and the ark was taken (1 Samuel 4:10-11). Every time you see this judgment it is because of sin: God allowed those numbers to die because we turned our back on the Most High, just as today. The ark did not have the effect Israel expected because there were still Israelites with idols among them, and until those idols were put away we could not be delivered from our enemies. The ark contained the commandments God wrote with his own finger, and the commandments have always been the nation’s source of power (Deuteronomy 10:1-5).

The Philistines carried the ark from Ebenezer to Ashdod and had the audacity to bring it into the house of Dagon and set it by Dagon (1 Samuel 5:1-2). Samson had already brought Dagon’s house down on the lords of the Philistines (Judges 16:29-30); they rebuilt this fake god, and the Most High humiliated him again. The ark is serious to the Most High; he does not play when it comes to his holy vessels. He allowed it to be taken, but if it is mistreated or mishandled, the Most High will kill you.
judgmentFull: When they of Ashdod rose early, Dagon had fallen on his face before the ark of the Lord (1 Samuel 5:3). This was no little souvenir you could knock over; it was a large statue, and nobody had been in there to touch it. They set him in his place again, as if maybe the wind blew a little harder, and the next morning he had fallen again, with his head and both palms of his hands cut off upon the threshold and only the stump left (1 Samuel 5:4). No man did this: that is the power of the ark of God.

The hand of the Lord was heavy upon Ashdod, and he smote them with emerods, what we know today as hemorrhoids (1 Samuel 5:6). The Most High was not playing games with the heathen; he afflicted them in their behinds for stealing the ark, smiting his enemies in the hinder parts and putting them to a perpetual reproach (Psalms 78:66). Ashdod would not keep the ark, and the lords carried it to Gath, where the Lord smote small and great; moving it to another city changed nothing, for the affliction went with it (1 Samuel 5:7-9). At Ekron the people cried out that it was brought to slay them, there was a deadly destruction throughout the city, and the cry of the city went up to heaven (1 Samuel 5:10-12).

After seven months they asked their priests and diviners how to send it back (1 Samuel 6:1-2). The priests said to send it with a trespass offering, which acknowledges you did wrong: five golden emerods and five golden mice for the five lords, images of the very things that marred the land, giving glory to the God of Israel (1 Samuel 6:3-5). One plague was on them all, and everybody got it, just as in Egypt, and when Christ returns everybody is going to get it. Every knee shall bow, and not willingly. That is why Israel was commanded not to fear nor serve other gods. Their own priests warned them from Israel’s history not to harden their hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh did, for they did not want to end up like Egypt (1 Samuel 6:6).

The test was a new cart drawn by two milch kine that had never borne a yoke, their calves shut up at home: if they went up toward Beth-shemesh, the God of Israel had done this; if not, it was chance (1 Samuel 6:7-9). The kine took the straight way to Beth-shemesh, lowing as they went, turning neither to the right nor the left, with the lords of the Philistines following to the border (1 Samuel 6:12). Cows with no yoke, separated from their calves, walking a straight line home to Israel: that settled that it was the hand of the Lord. The five lords returned to Ekron the same day, understanding it really was the Lord that had afflicted them (1 Samuel 6:16-18). Israel learned its part later at Mizpeh: deliverance is not just having the ark but applying the commandments in it, so they put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth, and the Lord thundered upon the Philistines (1 Samuel 7:3-10).
