cases.name: The men of Beth-shemesh
cases.charge: Looking into the ark of the Lord, which no man of any tribe, even Levi, might look upon unless the Lord gave him authority
cases.summary: The men of Beth-shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest when they saw the ark coming home on the Philistines’ cart, and they rejoiced; the Levites took it down, and the kine were offered as a burnt offering (1 Samuel 6:13-15). Then they got nosy and looked into the ark of the Lord, and he smote fifty thousand and seventy men (1 Samuel 6:19). The people lamented, asked who was able to stand before this holy Lord God, and sent to Kirjath-jearim to fetch the ark up (1 Samuel 6:20-21).
offenseFull: They of Beth-shemesh lifted up their eyes and saw the ark, and they rejoiced to see it (1 Samuel 6:13). As soon as the ark crossed that border coming home, it was rejoicing time in Israel. The cart came into the field of Joshua the Beth-shemite and stood by a great stone; they clave the wood of the cart and offered the kine a burnt offering unto the Lord, and the Levites took down the ark and the coffer with the jewels of gold (1 Samuel 6:14-15).

Then the men of Beth-shemesh looked into the ark of the Lord (1 Samuel 6:19). It was not just the other nations that had to keep discretion with the ark of the covenant; it was forbidden to touch it or look into it unless the Lord gave you authority, no matter what tribe you were, even Levi. The Kohathites, who bore the most holy things, were not to go in to see when the holy things were covered, lest they die (Numbers 4:17-20), and the stranger that came nigh the service of the tabernacle was to be put to death (Numbers 3:5-10). Every family of the Levites had its own specific task. You cannot open the ark and see the holy things that are in it. These men got too excited and got nosy, taking a peek to see what the writing of God looked like.
judgmentFull: He smote the men of Beth-shemesh because they had looked into the ark of the Lord, fifty thousand and threescore and ten men, and the people lamented the great slaughter (1 Samuel 6:19). Fifty thousand and seventy, just for peeking. That shows us we have to have a level of discipline over our eyes: with these devices today it is very easy to take a two second look at what you know you should not be looking at. Guard your eyes.

The people lamented, asking who could stand before so holy a Lord God, and where the ark should go from them (1 Samuel 6:20). The Bible acknowledges the Most High God as the king of terrors: he was killing thousands at a time, and his judgments are terrifying. The confidence of the wicked is rooted out of his tabernacle and brings him to the king of terrors (Job 18:14), and God is terrible in his doing toward the children of men (Psalms 66:5), heathen and wicked Israelite alike. He is a holy God and a jealous God, who will turn and consume those who forsake him and serve strange gods (Joshua 24:19-20).

They sent messengers to Kirjath-jearim, and the men of Kirjath-jearim fetched up the ark into the house of Abinadab in the hill and sanctified Eleazar his son to keep it (1 Samuel 6:21-7:1). The ark abode there twenty years, and all the house of Israel lamented after the Lord (1 Samuel 7:2). Deliverance was not just having the ark back but applying the commandments in it, the first of which is to have no other gods before him (Exodus 20:3). Samuel told all Israel that if they returned to the Lord with all their hearts they must put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth and serve him only, and he would deliver them out of the hand of the Philistines; and the children of Israel put away Baalim and Ashtaroth and served the Lord only (1 Samuel 7:3-4). That is repentance. The message had to be repeated over and over because Israel is rebellious and stiffnecked.

cases.name: Samuel
cases.charge: Answering the Lord when He called; telling Eli all the judgment against his house and hiding nothing; praying for Israel without ceasing and judging the congregation by the law all his days, taking nothing from any man
cases.summary: When the word of the Lord was precious, the Lord came and stood and called the child Samuel by name (1 Samuel 3:1-10). His first test as a judge was the word against the house of Eli, and he told Eli all of it and hid nothing (1 Samuel 3:11-18). The Lord let none of his words fall to the ground; he judged the congregation by the law of the Lord all his life, and by his faithfulness was found a true prophet (1 Samuel 3:19-21; Ecclesiasticus 46:13-15).
offenseFull: The child Samuel ministered unto the Lord before Eli when the word of the Lord was precious and there was no open vision (1 Samuel 3:1). Precious means the Lord was not dealing with everybody: not with the priests, and there were no prophets around saying thus saith the Lord.

Twice the Lord called and the child ran to Eli, because Samuel did not yet know the Lord, neither was the word of the Lord yet revealed unto him (1 Samuel 3:4-7). He had been in the house of the Lord since he was weaned and he still did not know the Lord. This goes in on those playing church with their children: just because your children come and sit and listen to the teaching does not mean they know the Lord; they are there because you brought them. Your job is the training; the revealing belongs to the Most High (Proverbs 22:6). No one knows the Father until Christ reveals Him, because Christ is the mediator, and that is why our brothers and sisters caught up in Christianity and Islam do not know the Most High (Matthew 11:27). In these last days God speaks by His Son, and the scriptures are all about Christ; the pastors whose word from the Lord has nothing to do with what is written prophesy out of their own minds (Hebrews 1:1-2).

The third time Eli perceived that the Lord had called the child and taught him how to answer (1 Samuel 3:8-9). The Lord is merciful with us even in these days, in this wickedness: He calls out to us numerous times until we wake up. The Lord came and stood and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel (1 Samuel 3:10). He did not just call from the heavens; He came down and stood by Samuel. Samuel could not see Him, but he heard Him, and that is what happens in the spirit to all of us. He stands at the door and knocks, and that door is your spirit (Revelation 3:20).

The word given to Samuel was that the Lord would judge Eli’s house for ever for the iniquity which he knew, because his sons made themselves vile and he restrained them not, and that its iniquity would not be purged with sacrifice nor offering for ever (1 Samuel 3:11-14). When the Lord is mad, the Lord is mad. Samuel feared to show Eli the vision, but Eli charged him to hide nothing, and Samuel told him all of it (1 Samuel 3:15-18). Samuel was going to be a judge of Israel, and this was his first test as a judge: do not sugarcoat what the Lord has said, and do not trim your words to seek love.

Before he reasoned with Israel at the crowning of Saul, Samuel established his blamelessness: whose ox or ass had he taken, whom had he defrauded or oppressed, from whose hand had he taken any bribe? The people answered that he had taken nothing from any man’s hand (1 Samuel 12:3-5). Marinate on his next words: God forbid that he should sin against the Lord in ceasing to pray for them, but he would teach them the good and the right way (1 Samuel 12:23). For a leader of Israel to stop praying for the nation is a transgression.
judgmentFull: Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and did let none of his words fall to the ground: what Samuel said, it came to pass. All Israel from Dan even to Beersheba knew that he was established to be a prophet of the Lord (1 Samuel 3:19-21).

At Mizpeh Samuel told all the house of Israel that if they returned unto the Lord with all their hearts, they must put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth and serve Him only (1 Samuel 7:3-4). Deliverance is not just having the ark; it is applying the commandments that are in the ark, thou shalt have no other gods before me. The children of Israel put away Baalim and Ashtaroth and served the Lord only: that is repentance. They fasted at Mizpeh, for fasting and supplication is a means of getting the Lord to hear you (1 Samuel 7:5-6).

When the Philistines came up, this time Israel did not run for the ark; they charged Samuel not to cease crying unto the Lord for them, for the prayer of a righteous man reaches the ears of the Most High (1 Samuel 7:7-8; James 5:16). Samuel offered a sucking lamb and cried unto the Lord for Israel, and the Lord thundered with a great thunder upon the Philistines and discomfited them (1 Samuel 7:9-10). That was no regular thunder; it was the Lord entering the battle Himself. The hand of the Lord was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel (1 Samuel 7:12-13). The cities they had taken from Ekron to Gath were restored to Israel, for that land belongs to Israel, and those in the land today are not the Israelites (1 Samuel 7:14; Joel 3; Ezekiel 36:5).

Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life, going in circuit year by year and returning to Ramah: leadership making its rounds, establishing the people and coming back to check on them (1 Samuel 7:15-17). He was beloved of his Lord, established the kingdom, and judged the congregation by the law of the Lord (Ecclesiasticus 46:13-14). By his faithfulness he was found a true prophet, and faithfulness translates loyalty (Ecclesiasticus 46:15). He came up under Eli, watched Eli’s sons go wicked, and stayed loyal to the Most High. Prayer is a superpower, and that is how our mighty forefathers rolled, from Moses to Samuel all the way to Christ.

cases.name: Joel and Abiah, the sons of Samuel
cases.charge: Walking not in their father’s ways as judges in Beersheba: turning aside after lucre, taking bribes, and perverting judgment
cases.summary: When Samuel was old he made his sons judges over Israel, Joel the firstborn and Abiah the second, judges in Beersheba, and they turned aside after lucre, took bribes, and perverted judgment (1 Samuel 8:1-3). The elders of Israel came to Samuel at Ramah: their complaint was that his sons walked not in his ways, and their demand was a king to judge them like all the nations (1 Samuel 8:4-5). No sentence upon the two men is recorded.
offenseFull: When Samuel was old he made his sons judges over Israel, Joel the firstborn and Abiah his second, judges in Beersheba. But his sons walked not in his ways; they turned aside after lucre, took bribes, and perverted judgment (1 Samuel 8:1-3).

The law set judges and officers in all the gates to judge the people with just judgment, without wresting judgment, respecting persons or taking a gift, because a gift blinds the wise; what is altogether just they were to follow, that they might live and inherit the land (Deuteronomy 16:18-20). There is nothing new under the sun: when you see judges and officers among us today, know that we are following the things that are written within this book. The gift the law forbids is what goes into bribes: do not take a bribe when it comes to judgment; be upright and honest (Exodus 23:8).

We see that same thing going on now in this political climate, and even in the church system. This is why the churches will not teach us who we are or teach the commandments of the Most High; when riots and unrest break out, it is those same pastors who go out to calm the people down.

Their father walked before Israel from his childhood, and when he asked whose ox or ass he had taken, whom he had defrauded or oppressed, and from whose hand he had taken any bribe, the people answered that he had taken nothing from any man’s hand (1 Samuel 12:2-5). Samuel was never a bad guy to the nation of Israel, and the whole congregation confirmed it. His sons did not walk in his ways.
judgmentFull: All the elders of Israel gathered themselves together and came to Samuel at Ramah, saying that he was old and his sons walked not in his ways, and asked him to make them a king to judge them like all the nations (1 Samuel 8:4-5). Your sons are not righteous like you, so instead of them judging us, give us a king like the other nations have. They were not looking to Samuel’s sons to lead; they wanted a king. Samuel’s sons took bribes, and so the elders asked for a king like all the nations, and it displeased Samuel; the Lord said they had not rejected Samuel but had rejected Him, that He should not reign over them (1 Samuel 8:6-7).

The oppression of the poor and the violent perverting of judgment in a province are no cause to marvel, for One higher than the highest regards it (Ecclesiastes 5:8). What Samuel’s sons did is what we see today. God is paying attention to this; He is keeping a watchful eye, because there might be some things that we miss, but God misses nothing. He sees every hiding of evidence, He sees the perverting of judgment, and He sees who is on the payroll.
No sentence upon Joel or Abiah is recorded.

cases.name: Israel asking for a king
cases.charge: Rejecting the Lord, that He should not reign over them, by demanding a king to judge them and fight their battles like all the nations
cases.summary: The elders asked Samuel for a king to judge them like all the nations, and the Lord told him they had rejected not him but the Lord (1 Samuel 8:4-9). Warned of the manner of the king, they would have one anyway (1 Samuel 8:10-20); it came to pass under Solomon and Rehoboam. Yet the Lord would not forsake His people: if they and their king obeyed they would be all right, and if they did wickedly they would be consumed (1 Samuel 12:20-25).
offenseFull: All the elders of Israel came to Samuel at Ramah, saying he was old and his sons walked not in his ways, and asked him to make them a king to judge them like all the nations (1 Samuel 8:4-5). Moses prophesied it: he was shown from the beginning to the end, saw Israel rejecting the Lord, and wrote that the king must be one the Lord would choose, from among their brethren, never a stranger (Deuteronomy 17:14-15). For those who say there is no prophecy in the laws, here is one: even in our own land we wanted to mimic the customs of the other nations.

Where do we see that today? Voting. We are saying the same thing today when we vote, looking to a ruler like the nations instead of to the Most High. Now you hear people say this one is the lesser of two evils, but they are both evil. We reject the Lord by not keeping His commandments and by trusting in the nations that have subdued us, by voting and by keeping their holidays and their ways; we have made a covenant with them.

The thing displeased Samuel, and he prayed unto the Lord, and the Lord told him that the people had not rejected him but had rejected the Lord, as they had done since the day He brought them out of Egypt, forsaking Him and serving other gods (1 Samuel 8:6-8). Just as they rejected the Most High, they were rejecting Samuel and his counsel. Samuel was appointed of God and was not speaking his own thoughts, so to reject him was to reject the Most High; and whoever murmurs against the leaders the Most High has set over Israel today speaks directly against the Most High (2 Peter 2:10).

Joshua warned us about this. At Shechem Israel made the covenant with its own mouth to serve the Lord and obey His voice, and became witnesses against itself that it had chosen the Lord (Joshua 24:21-24); asking for a king was breaking the choice we ourselves made. Christ gave the same picture in the nobleman who went into a far country to receive a kingdom, whose citizens sent a message after him that they would not have this man to reign over them (Luke 19:12-14). The same spirit that said set a king over us says, we will not have Christ to reign over us.

Samuel told them the manner of the king: he would take their sons, their daughters, the best of their fields and the tenth of their seed and sheep, and they would be his servants and cry out in that day, and the Lord would not hear them (1 Samuel 8:10-18). Nevertheless the people refused, and would have a king to judge them and go out before them and fight their battles (1 Samuel 8:19-20). That is why Samuel was displeased: all this time the Lord had been fighting their battles (Deuteronomy 20:1-4). Under Joshua Israel destroyed thirty-one kings, and lost men only when in sin; in the Judges the Lord raised up judges who fought for them. It has always been of the Lord.
judgmentFull: Samuel rehearsed the people’s words in the ears of the Lord, and the Lord told him to hearken unto their voice and make them a king (1 Samuel 8:21-22): you want a king, I will give you a king. At Mizpeh Samuel told them they had that day rejected the God who saved them out of all their adversities (1 Samuel 10:18-19). Every time one of our judges rose up and delivered us, we got right during the life of that judge, and when that judge died we went right back into our falling.

The manner of the king came to pass under Solomon: he levied a tax, and the tax was men, sent to Lebanon a month on and two months off (1 Kings 5:13-14). Under Rehoboam the yoke grew heavier still (1 Kings 12:13-14). We rejected the Lord and wanted a king like all the other nations, and this is what we got; look at our condition today, ruler after ruler, and things do not get any better for us. We are getting what we deserve, because we rejected the Lord. When we rejected the Lord in our own land, that also set us up to be taken out of our own land and set in a land we did not know, under oppressors, you and the king you set over you (Deuteronomy 28:36).

To demonstrate how wicked Israel was for asking a king, Samuel called for thunder and rain in wheat harvest, the very day they expected clear skies, and the people, in great fear, confessed they had added this evil to all their sins (1 Samuel 12:16-19). Now they confessed they were dead wrong for asking for a king.

Samuel told them to fear not: they had done all this wickedness, yet they were not to turn aside from following the Lord, but serve Him with all their heart (1 Samuel 12:20). After all the wickedness you have done, still serve the Lord. The Lord will not forsake His people for His great name’s sake (1 Samuel 12:22). He may purge His people, but He will never exterminate the Israelites (Romans 11:1-2). If both they and their king feared the Lord and did not rebel against His commandment, they would be all right; but if they still did wickedly, after the speech, the warning and the thunder, they would be consumed, both they and their king (1 Samuel 12:14-15, 24-25). You asked for the wrong thing, but now that you have it, keep the commandments and you will be all right.

cases.name: King Saul
cases.charge: Offering the burnt offering himself at Gilgal instead of waiting for the prophet; sparing Agag and the best of the spoil of Amalek against the commandment; and at the last asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit
cases.summary: Chapter thirteen is the beginning of Saul showing his simplicity, the proof that he was not fit to be king over Israel. Told to tarry at Gilgal, he offered the burnt offering himself (1 Samuel 13:8-14); sent to utterly destroy Amalek, he spared Agag and the best of the spoil and laid it on the people (1 Samuel 15:1-24). The Lord rejected him from being king, and when he sought a woman with a familiar spirit, the Most High slew him (1 Chronicles 10:13-14).
offenseFull: Samuel had told Saul to tarry seven days at Gilgal until he came (1 Samuel 10:8). When the Philistines gathered as the sand of the seashore, the men of Israel hid in caves and pits (1 Samuel 13:5-7). If we really have faith we should be fearless; to still fear the enemy shows that you really do not believe in your God (2 Timothy 1:7).

Samuel came not at the moment expected and the people were scattered, so Saul offered the burnt offering himself, and Saul was not the priest; that was Samuel’s office. As soon as he had made an end, Samuel came (1 Samuel 13:8-10). Brothers do the same thing today: leadership said ten o’clock, it is five past ten, so we cancel the plan and go home. The Lord may be testing your patience (Ecclesiasticus 2:2). Not only was Saul bashful; that bashful spirit made him self-willed.

He went out to meet Samuel: when you are dead wrong and try to cover it up, you meet the man before he gets to where you messed up. Then came the excuses: the people scattered, Samuel late, the Philistines gathering (1 Samuel 13:11-12). This is Saul’s pattern; he never holds himself accountable and always deflects. Samuel told him he had done foolishly and had not kept the commandment of the Lord; disobeying the prophet’s instruction was disobeying the commandment of the Lord. His kingdom would not continue, and Samuel named the replacement without ever having met him, a man after the Lord’s own heart (1 Samuel 13:13-14; Acts 13:22).

Then Saul was sent to smite Amalek and utterly destroy all that they had, for what Amalek did to Israel in the way from Egypt (1 Samuel 15:1-3; Deuteronomy 25:17-19). Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High God said remember. That war continues from generation to generation and is now more spiritual than ever, because the adversary has established the imagination that they are the Jews; the walk commanded now is to live peaceably with all men (Exodus 17:16; Romans 12:18).

Saul took Agag alive and spared the best of the sheep and oxen, and destroyed only what was vile and refuse (1 Samuel 15:7-9). Saul did most of what was said, yet the Lord counted it as not performing His commandments at all (1 Samuel 15:10-11). Whenever there is a but in your obedience, you did not perform the orders given unto you. The first thing out of Saul’s mouth to Samuel was a fabrication, that he had performed the commandment, while the sheep were bleating in the prophet’s ears; then he deflected again, the same blame game as chapter thirteen: it was the people (1 Samuel 15:12-15). He could have corrected the people and sent them back to destroy it, and he would have been justified; but he hearkened unto the people, because he was weak and bashful.
judgmentFull: Samuel made it plain that the Lord delights in obedience more than in burnt offerings, for the spoil was wrongfully gotten and the offering was ridiculous (1 Samuel 15:22; Ecclesiasticus 34:18-19). Rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness as iniquity and idolatry (1 Samuel 15:23). A brother who would never touch voodoo will sit through a whole counsel of do not do this, and call two weeks later saying he did it anyway; that rebellion is the same as witchcraft. Stubbornness is idolatry because the instruction is the commandment of the Lord that leadership carries: when you are stubborn against it, what I want comes before what God wants. Because he rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord rejected him from being king.

The confession finally came and was still not sincere: he feared the people and obeyed their voice (1 Samuel 15:24). If you are a leader in fear of your people, they can manipulate you; you are not leading the people, you are being led by them (Proverbs 29:25). Saul laid hold on Samuel’s mantle and it rent, and as he tore the garment, the Lord tore the throne from him for a neighbour better than he (1 Samuel 15:27-29). Then he asked to be honoured before the elders anyway: the spirit of vanity, caught up in a title and forgetting the title came for pleasing the Lord (1 Samuel 15:30-31).

As the Spirit of the Lord came on David it departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him; that it came from the Lord is what the church world leaves out (1 Samuel 16:14). It all went back to bashfulness. God said Saul was the goodliest in Israel, but when Saul looked in the mirror he did not see the lion, he saw the kitty cat; he never believed God, and he never listened to the prophet who was there to guide him. There is that destroyeth his own soul through bashfulness (Ecclesiasticus 20:22).

When the Lord answered him no more, the king who had put the familiar spirits out of the land sought a woman with a familiar spirit at Endor (1 Samuel 28:3-8). That was the last straw. Samuel told him the Lord was become his enemy, because he obeyed not the voice of the Lord nor executed His fierce wrath upon Amalek, and that tomorrow he and his sons would be with him (1 Samuel 28:16-19). On mount Gilboa, wounded by the archers, Saul fell upon his own sword, and his three sons died that same day (1 Samuel 31:3-6). Saul died for his transgression against the Most High, for not keeping His word, and for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit; therefore the Most High slew him and turned the kingdom to David (1 Chronicles 10:13-14).

cases.name: David
cases.charge: A man after the Lord’s own heart: twice sparing the Lord’s anointed and leaving vengeance with the Lord, judging those who shed blood in his name, and repenting with godly sorrow when he fell
cases.summary: Samuel named a man after the Lord’s own heart before he had ever met him (1 Samuel 13:14). Twice Saul was delivered into David’s hand, and twice David would not stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed, but left the judgment with the Most High (1 Samuel 24; 1 Samuel 26). He did not accept wickedness done in his name, and when he fell he had godly sorrow and rose again; his great fall is its own case.
offenseFull: The Lord had sought a man after His own heart to be captain over His people; Samuel prophesied this without ever having met the replacement, David, predestined before he is even introduced in the scriptures (1 Samuel 13:14; Acts 13:22).

Saul was hunting David to kill him, because Saul was dealing with bitterness, envy and hatred. He took three thousand chosen men to the rocks of the wild goats and went into a cave to cover his feet: that means he was in there relieving himself (1 Samuel 24:1-3). See the vulnerable position Saul was in, and yet David spared his life. David cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe privily, the bottom part of the robe where we have our fringes attached, and afterward his heart smote him even for that, and he stayed his servants, for Saul was the Lord’s anointed (1 Samuel 24:4-7).

When Saul rose out of the cave, David went out after him, cried, my lord the king, and bowed with his face to the earth (1 Samuel 24:8). He reverenced Saul even though Saul was trying to kill him; that is why the Most High said David is a man after His own heart. David maintained his integrity. He laid the proof before Saul and left the judgment with the Most High: the Lord judge between them, but his hand would not be upon him (1 Samuel 24:9-15). Saul wept and said David was more righteous than he, and that he knew well David would surely be king (1 Samuel 24:16-20). David showed so much restraint and respect unto his elder; that is something some of us struggle with today.

In the wilderness of Ziph, Saul lay sleeping in the trench with his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster and Abner and the people round about him, and Abishai asked leave to smite him to the earth at once (1 Samuel 26:7-8). David said no man could stretch forth his hand against the Lord’s anointed and be guiltless; the Lord would smite him, or his day would come to die, or he would descend into battle and perish (1 Samuel 26:9-11). That is the kind of love David had toward his people. Even if somebody does you wrong, you do not have to do evil back; sometimes it is good to leave it in God’s hands. Whoever takes vengeance finds vengeance from the Lord, and if David had taken vengeance, he would have found vengeance from the Lord (Ecclesiasticus 28:1).

David cried from the hill that if the Lord had stirred Saul up against him, let Him accept an offering, but if it were the children of men, cursed be they before the Lord (1 Samuel 26:19). Sometimes the Lord puts a spirit on somebody to deal with you wrongfully, to try you, and how you deal with it tells whether you get the kingdom or not. There were men around Saul whispering that David thought himself better and wanted the kingdom; Satan was in certain men around Saul, and Saul fed into it instead of saying David was a man of God. Saul confessed that he had played the fool and erred exceedingly (1 Samuel 26:21). Your enemy is like King Saul was to King David, and David still loved him: that is how you get rid of bitterness (Matthew 5:44). When Shimei came out cursing, David would not let Abishai take his head: if it was of the Most High, let him curse (2 Samuel 16:5-12).
judgmentFull: The Amalekite who said he had slain the Lord’s anointed, his own mouth testifying against him, and Rechab and Baanah, who brought the head of Ishbosheth, David had put to death (2 Samuel 1:14-16; 2 Samuel 4:9-12). This is why David is called a man after the Most High’s own heart: he did not accept wickedness done in his name or let the murderers slide, and they received judgment for taking a man’s life not ordained of the Lord nor commanded by the king. Let all things be done decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40).

The Lord promised that His mercy would not depart from David as it did from Saul, and that his house, kingdom and throne would be established for ever (2 Samuel 7:15-16). Solomon’s kingdom was not established for ever; the phrase for ever points to Jesus Christ, the black Messiah, who came through David’s lineage, to whom the Lord God gives the throne of his father David, and of whose kingdom there shall be no end (Luke 1:32-33).

David slipped and fell; he had godly sorrow, and in that godly sorrow he was not put to death (2 Samuel 12:13; 2 Corinthians 7:10). If he had been, there would be no Solomon, and through that no Christ. God still dealt with David because David repented, and the sure mercies of David are the mercies the Lord gives unto us: many of us are supposed to be dead for the evil we did in the past, but through the mercies of David we are still here and able to repent in Christ (Isaiah 55:3). The Lord took away his sins and exalted his horn for ever, giving him a covenant of kings, for David repented (Ecclesiasticus 47:11).

Fleeing from Absalom, David sent the ark back into the city in faith: if he found favour in the eyes of the Lord, he would be brought again to see it, and if not, let the Lord do as seemed good (2 Samuel 15:25-26). That is how much faith David had. At the last he charged Solomon to keep the law of Moses, for there was a stipulation for the throne to continue: if his children walked before the Most High in truth, the throne stood (1 Kings 2:2-4).

cases.name: Saul’s rash oath, and the people at the blood
cases.charge: A strange oath that distressed the army; the people flying upon the spoil and eating flesh with the blood; and the king ready to kill the son who had wrought the salvation
cases.summary: While the Lord saved Israel by Jonathan and his armourbearer, Saul put out a strange order, a curse on any man who ate before evening (1 Samuel 14:6-24). Jonathan, who had not heard it, tasted honey and argued against the order, and the faint people ate the spoil with the blood (1 Samuel 14:27-32). When the lot took Jonathan the king swore he should die, and the people rescued him, for he had wrought with God that day (1 Samuel 14:36-45).
offenseFull: Jonathan told the young man that bore his armour to come over to the garrison of the uncircumcised, for it might be that the Lord would work for them, there being no restraint to the Lord to save by many or by few (1 Samuel 14:6). Jonathan was in the spirit; he understood totally where his strength lies. The Lord put that spirit on him. That is how the Most High operates: He loves to show His power by having a small number defeat a very large number, and that is why it will be the hundred and forty-four thousand taking over the whole world. With the God of heaven it is all one to deliver with a great multitude or a small company (1 Maccabees 3:18-19).

Jonathan climbed up upon his hands and his feet, his armourbearer after him, and that first slaughter was about twenty men within about half an acre of land: two men against a garrison (1 Samuel 14:13-14). Some hold a doctrine that Jonathan was a homosexual; this act answers it, for scaling a rock face to rush a garrison two deep is a bold, manly act of war that most men are not cut out for. There was trembling in the host, the earth quaked, and the Philistines went on beating down one another (1 Samuel 14:15-16). That is what happens when a few beat many: their hearts melted, because they knew the Spirit of the Lord was on this one. So the Lord saved Israel that day (1 Samuel 14:20-23).

Saul had adjured the people with a curse on the man that ate any food until evening, that he might be avenged on his enemies (1 Samuel 14:24). Saul put out a strange order, and the men of Israel were distressed that day. He vowed a vow: a man that vows unto the Lord shall not break his word, and it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay, for God has no pleasure in fools (Numbers 30:2; Ecclesiastes 5:2-5). Christ said, let your yea be yea and your nay be nay; do not even make vows (Matthew 5:37).

In the wood the honey dropped, and no man put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath; but Jonathan was not there when the order came out (1 Samuel 14:25-26). He dipped the end of his rod in a honeycomb and his eyes were enlightened (1 Samuel 14:27). Told of the oath, he said his father had troubled the land, and that the slaughter would have been far greater had the people eaten freely of the spoil; he began to convince the people that eating was the better idea and that the king’s order was folly (1 Samuel 14:28-30). Israel is to fear the Lord and the king and not meddle with those given to change (Proverbs 24:21): Saul was the king and put out an order, and when someone among you tries to change the orders of the king, do not meddle with him, because he will lead you into error, which is exactly what happened next.

The people were very faint, and they flew upon the spoil, slew sheep, oxen and calves on the ground, and ate them with the blood (1 Samuel 14:31-32). That was the transgression Jonathan’s talk led the people into. In the law we are not supposed to eat blood, for the life is in the blood (Leviticus 17:11).
judgmentFull: When they told Saul the people sinned against the Lord in eating the blood, he said they had transgressed, had a great stone rolled to him, and had every man bring his ox and his sheep and slay them there, and not sin against the Lord in eating with the blood; and Saul built an altar unto the Lord, the first altar he built unto the Lord (1 Samuel 14:33-35).

Saul proposed going down after the Philistines by night, and he asked counsel of God, but He answered him not that day (1 Samuel 14:36-37). The Lord was not dealing with him; He was starting to withdraw from Saul. If you are spiritual, when the Lord ignores you, you understand at that point what it reveals: it is sin. The Lord does not hear the one who regards iniquity in his heart, and somewhere in the camp there was iniquity (Psalms 66:18). Sin and iniquity are what cause the Most High not to hear you, plain and clear (Isaiah 59:2).

Saul swore that the one in whom the sin was found should surely die, though it were Jonathan his son; the lot took Jonathan, and though he had but tasted a little honey, Saul swore that he should surely die (1 Samuel 14:38-44). Saul was ready to kill his own son over the oath.

The people would not have it: Jonathan had wrought this great salvation in Israel, and not one hair of his head would fall to the ground, for he had wrought with God that day; so the people rescued Jonathan, and kept him from the wrath of his father (1 Samuel 14:45). Think about the contrast: in chapter thirteen Saul was the one disobeying the voice of the Lord and getting rebuked, while Jonathan was brave and mighty and had just saved Israel out of the hand of its enemies; now the coward wanted to kill the deliverer. In some situations you have to weigh it as the people did: yes, he made a mistake and crossed the order, but he just saved all our lives. Judgment without mercy comes on the one who has shown no mercy, and mercy rejoices over judgment (James 2:13). Saul had just been shown mercy for his own failure, so passing merciless judgment on his own son would have left no mercy for Saul the next time he fell.

cases.name: Agag king of the Amalekites
cases.charge: Smiting the hindmost of Israel, the feeble, faint and weary, when they came out of Egypt, a war the Lord swore from generation to generation; and the sword that made women childless
cases.summary: Amalek, Esau’s grandson, was the first nation to come against Israel after Egypt; he did not meet the mighty men in front but smote the hindmost, the feeble, when Israel was faint and weary, and he feared not God (Exodus 17:8; Deuteronomy 25:17-18). The Lord swore war with Amalek from generation to generation, and generations later He sent Saul to utterly destroy them (Exodus 17:16; 1 Samuel 15:1-3). Saul spared Agag the king, presuming to find something good in what God had condemned. Agag came to Samuel delicately, thinking himself safe, and the old prophet hewed him in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal, measure for measure (1 Samuel 15:32-33).
offenseFull: Amalek came and fought with Israel in Rephidim (Exodus 17:8). Amalek was the first nation to come against Israel after Egypt; he was Esau’s grandson, born to Eliphaz of Timna the concubine, a duke in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:12). Amalek is the children of Esau, the dukes, the elite of Esau’s line.

Moses gave the detail of the attack (Deuteronomy 25:17-18). In a caravan the strong men walk in front; in the back are the elderly, the women, the babies and the lame. Rather than attack head on, Amalek crept up behind, killed the feeble, and waited until Israel was tired to do it. He feared not God: they knew exactly who Israel was, for those are Israel’s cousins.

The Lord told Moses to write it for a memorial in a book and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, and swore that He would have war with Amalek from generation to generation, meaning for ever, the same thing Malachi said (Exodus 17:14-16; Malachi 1:2-4). Amalek was the first of the nations, but his latter end is that he perish for ever (Numbers 24:20). God does not forget; we do. Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High said remember; this is a righteous grudge, and the law against bearing a grudge applies to the children of thy people (Leviticus 19:18; Deuteronomy 25:19).

Generations later the Lord of hosts sent Saul by Samuel: He remembered what Amalek did when Israel came up from Egypt, and He commanded Saul to smite Amalek, utterly destroy all that they had, and spare none (1 Samuel 15:1-3). The generation under that sword had not personally done the deed in the wilderness, and that answers the argument heard today: that was not me; I never held anyone in slavery. The Most High Himself commanded recompense for what was done to the forefathers. The nations pay for the sins of their fathers, the same way Israel is paying for the sins of hers: the fathers refused God’s commandments, the curses fell on them and their seed, and here Israel is, generations of oppression later. Israel does not get a pass, so nobody else gets a pass either.

The Most High discriminates righteously: the Kenites, who had shown kindness to all the children of Israel when they came up out of Egypt, were told to depart from among the Amalekites, and they were spared out of the judgment (1 Samuel 15:6). Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah to Shur, halfway fulfilling the order (1 Samuel 15:7-8): he and the people, presumptuous and covetous, spared Agag and the best of the sheep and oxen and all that was good, and destroyed only what was vile and refuse (1 Samuel 15:9). Agag was a king of Edom, a descendant of Esau the despiser of the birthright, whom God had sentenced to death, and Saul presumed to find something good in what God had condemned. He kept him because he liked him: there is always that one Edomite at work or at school that a man might like and who might like him, and God does not care about that.
judgmentFull: Samuel called for Agag, and Agag came unto him delicately, crouching and speaking softly (1 Samuel 15:32). With Saul under rebuke, Agag figured nobody was angry at the Amalekites any more and he was safe. Saul trusted the enemy; Samuel did not. Never trust the enemy: though he humble himself and go crouching, as Agag came delicately, his rust has not been altogether wiped away (Ecclesiasticus 12:10-11).

Samuel told him that as his sword had made women childless, so his mother would be childless among women, and he hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal (1 Samuel 15:33). That is the punishment of Esau: the same thing he does to people, the Lord does to him. The old prophet did not play; he finished the commandment himself, measure for measure for what Amalek’s sword had done. Samuel followed instructions; Saul played games.

Saul did not finish Agag’s line, and in Esther’s day Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, a descendant of the same Agag, an Amalekite of the royal line of the dukes of Esau, was set above all the princes of Persia, and he sought to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom of Ahasuerus for what one Jew would not do (Esther 3:1-6). Haman’s people kept the records; he knew Mordecai was of the line of Kish, the line sent to destroy his forefathers. Esau forgave Jacob, but his children hold the grudge from generation to generation; they do not forget, and we do.

The same war continues to this day, and it is more spiritual than ever, because the adversary has established the imagination that they are the Jews, and that imagination is cast down every day. That seed says they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan, robbing Israel of identity and prospering off the oppression (Revelation 2:9; Revelation 3:9). The whole world is set up between Jacob and Esau, and Esau is the end of this world, the so-called white man, with Amalek leading. Understand the frame: Israel lives peaceably with all men and lays hands on no one, and does not incite or condone any violence (Romans 12:18). The day when Edom, who cheered Babylon on when Jerusalem burned, is paid back has not yet come; it belongs to the return of the Lord (Psalms 137:7-9).

cases.name: Goliath of Gath
cases.charge: Defying the armies of the living God morning and evening for forty days, trusting in his weapons and boldness, and cursing David by his gods
cases.summary: Out of the camp of the Philistines came Goliath of Gath, a giant remaining from the Anakims, six cubits and a span high, and for forty days he defied the armies of Israel and demanded a man (1 Samuel 17:4-16). Saul and all Israel were dismayed and greatly afraid, measuring his height and his reach in a carnal spirit. David, a sheep keeper sent on an errand, knew that Israel was the army of the living God; he came against the giant in the name of the Lord of hosts and cut off his head with Goliath’s own sword (1 Samuel 17:45-51).
offenseFull: The Philistines, who would not leave Israel alone, pitched between Shochoh and Azekah, and Israel by the valley of Elah, a mountain on either side with a valley between them (1 Samuel 17:1-3). Out of their camp came a champion named Goliath of Gath, six cubits and a span high, in a mighty costume of armour; he did not even carry his own shield (1 Samuel 17:4-7). Goliath was a giant remaining from the Anakims, whom Joshua cut off from the mountains; none were left in the land but in Gaza, in Gath and in Ashdod, and that is where Goliath came from (Joshua 11:21-22).

He cried to the armies of Israel to choose a man, the loser’s people to serve the winner’s, and he defied the armies of Israel that day (1 Samuel 17:8-10). He trusted in his weapons and boldness, and boldness is pride: he was undefeated, ten feet tall in his battle array, ready for war (2 Maccabees 8:18). That boasting, that pride, is what the nations are today; they are on high, but the Son of the Most High is coming back to the earth, and He will destroy all these nations and put them in subjection.

When Saul and all Israel heard him they were dismayed and greatly afraid (1 Samuel 17:11). They were in a carnal spirit, measuring his height, his armour and his reach; the spirit had departed, and fear is not the spirit of the Most High (2 Timothy 1:7). The Most High put laws in the book about going to battle: Israel was not to be afraid of a people more than they, for the Lord went with them to fight for them, and the fearful and fainthearted were to return home, lest that fearful spirit jump from one man to another (Deuteronomy 20:1-8). Israel had asked for a king because they were not content to have the Lord fight their battles; the Lord does not fear men, but the king they chose feared a man, and that man was Goliath (1 Samuel 8:5-20). The fear showed that they lacked faith; the God that destroyed Pharaoh was with them, and a trial of faith was set before them in the form of one big intimidating man with a big mouth.

The Philistine drew near morning and evening and presented himself forty days, forty days straight of big talk to scare Israel (1 Samuel 17:16). All the men of Israel fled from him and were sore afraid; the whole nation’s freedom was on the line, and they ran scared (1 Samuel 17:24). David’s three eldest brothers were there and did not have the spirit to rise up; that is why the Most High had refused them. Who will rise up for Him against the evildoers? That is the spirit the Most High looks for (Psalms 94:16).
judgmentFull: David, sent with corn and loaves for his brethren, heard the same words and asked who this uncircumcised Philistine was, that he should defy the armies of the living God (1 Samuel 17:17-26). The soldiers themselves did not understand that they were the armies of the living God; David, a sheep keeper sent on an errand, knew it. The Most High calls His people, the children of Israel, His armies (Exodus 7:4).

Saul told him he was but a youth against a man of war (1 Samuel 17:33). If the Most High is dealing with a young person in a special way, let nobody discourage him or tell him he is too young to be a mighty man of the Lord; the nation had no example of faith that day, so a young youth had to be that example (1 Timothy 4:12). David gave Saul his resume: he had smitten the lion and the bear that took a lamb out of the flock, and the Lord that delivered him from them would deliver him from this Philistine; same God, no difference (1 Samuel 17:34-37). He played with lions as with kids and with bears as with lambs (Ecclesiasticus 47:3).

David put off Saul’s armour, for he had not proved it, and took his staff, five smooth stones and his sling (1 Samuel 17:38-40). What he put on instead was the whole armour of God, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, the word of God (Ephesians 6:16-17). The Philistine disdained him and cursed him by his gods, and David answered that he came in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom Goliath had defied (1 Samuel 17:41-45). David did not need the sword, the spear or the shield; he had the spirit of the living God. No amount of carnal firepower overcomes the enemies of Israel; this is spiritual warfare, not by might nor by power but by His spirit, the only way Israel overcomes (Zechariah 4:6; Hosea 1:7).

David prophesied the outcome before the fight, that all the earth might know there is a God in Israel, for the battle is the Lord’s (1 Samuel 17:46-47). It was a fixed fight, preordained: the Most High knew Israel would be fearful, and He sent the little one, mighty in spirit, to kill Goliath. David slung one stone, and it sank into the Philistine’s forehead, and he fell on his face to the earth; with no sword in his hand David stood upon him, drew Goliath’s own sword and cut off his head (1 Samuel 17:48-51). David called upon the Most High, and it was the Most High who gave his right hand strength to slay that mighty warrior and beat down the boasting of Goliath (Ecclesiasticus 47:4-5); the Lord taught his hands to war (Psalms 144:1). When the Philistines saw their champion dead they fled from a young youth, because they knew something supernatural was going on.

cases.name: Jonathan
cases.charge: Loving David as his own soul, the king’s son and heir stripping himself of his robe for the armourbearer; defending David against his father at any time and anywhere, and keeping the covenant of the Lord between their seed
cases.summary: The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul; the prince and heir stripped off his robe and gave it to the armourbearer, with his garments, his sword, his bow and his girdle (1 Samuel 18:1-4). He spoke good of David to Saul and had a javelin cast at him for it (1 Samuel 19:4; 1 Samuel 20:33). His loyalty exceeded his own desires: there would not have been a King David without the strong defence of Jonathan, and his loyalty extended beyond his life into his son at the king’s table (2 Samuel 9:1-13).
offenseFull: When David had made an end of speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and they made a covenant, and Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him and gave it to David (1 Samuel 18:1-4). Souls being knit is not speaking of anything unnatural between the two men. The same word describes the church, hearts knit together in love, as joints and bands in one body; Jonathan and David were on one accord, they had the same spirit (Colossians 2:2; Colossians 2:19). David was an armourbearer taken in by the king; Jonathan was Saul’s son, the heir, the prince, above David in estate. A true friend is not going to rejoice in being in a higher estate than his friend; he is going to love him as his own soul.

Saul spoke to Jonathan and to all his servants that they should kill David; the Philistines could not get him, so now the king wanted Israelites to kill an Israelite (1 Samuel 19:1). But Jonathan delighted much in David and told him to take heed and hide himself until the morning (1 Samuel 19:2-3). Jonathan would have been next in line for the throne, but he saw that the spirit was not on his father; it was on his brother David. His loyalty exceeded his own desires. Jonathan had the courage to hide David not only from his father but from all the servants Saul told to kill him; he put himself against everybody to save David’s life, for a true friend will defend a man at any time and anywhere. He would not be ashamed to defend a friend nor hide from him (Ecclesiasticus 22:25).

He spoke good of David to Saul: let not the king sin against his servant, whose works had been very good, who put his life in his hand and slew the Philistine; why sin against innocent blood to slay David without a cause (1 Samuel 19:4-5)? The innocent and righteous are not to be slain, and hands that shed innocent blood are among the things the Lord hates (Exodus 23:7; Proverbs 6:16-17). Saul hearkened and swore that David would not be slain (1 Samuel 19:6); the faithful friend, by defending his friend, turned his father’s mind from wanting to kill him in that instance.

At the new moon, when David’s place was empty and Jonathan covered for him, Saul’s anger was kindled against his own son: as long as the son of Jesse lived on the ground, Jonathan would not be established, nor his kingdom (1 Samuel 20:24-31). Jonathan did not fold; he asked his father what David had done that he should be slain, and Saul cast a javelin at him, whereby Jonathan knew it was determined of his father to slay David (1 Samuel 20:32-33). He arose from the table in fierce anger and did eat no meat, grieved for his friend (1 Samuel 20:34). He knew he would lose his position, and he did not care, because above riches is character. Had he broken that friendship and had David killed, he would have sat on the throne, but he would have had to look at himself and know his character was foul. A faithful friend is a strong defence, and he that has found such a one has found a treasure; nothing countervails a faithful friend, not the promise of a throne, not even his own life (Ecclesiasticus 6:14-15).

In the wood of Ziph Jonathan went to David and strengthened his hand in God, telling him that Saul’s hand would not find him, that David would be king over Israel and Jonathan next to him, and they made a covenant before the Lord (1 Samuel 23:16-18).
judgmentFull: Jonathan had made David swear that he would not cut off his kindness from Jonathan’s house for ever, and that the Lord would be between their seed for ever (1 Samuel 20:14-17; 1 Samuel 20:42). This is real brotherhood: if I am not here, stay loyal to my son, and I will tell my son to be loyal to you.

The Philistines followed hard after Saul and his sons and slew Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua in mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:2). Jonathan’s body had been hanged in the temple of Dagon, the fish god of the Hamites. David’s lament is a prophecy given in the spirit, almost a eulogy: Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided; (2 Samuel 1:23). David was distressed for his brother Jonathan, whose love to him was wonderful, passing the love of women, because it was a real friendship, with no end in view but friendship (2 Samuel 1:26). There is a friend that sticks closer than a brother; so was Jonathan to David, knit at the soul. (Proverbs 18:24).

When David was king he asked whether any of the house of Saul was left, that he might show him the kindness of God for Jonathan’s sake, fetched Mephibosheth, lame on his feet, out of Lodebar, restored him all the land of Saul, and set him at the king’s table continually (2 Samuel 9:1-13). David’s loyalty extended beyond Jonathan’s life into his son, because he swore that their seed would be loyal. This same love and care for the people Israel loses is what must be brought back into Israel: to take care of their family as if they were there themselves. When the sons of Saul were delivered to the Gibeonites, the king spared Mephibosheth because of the Lord’s oath between David and Jonathan; David did not go back on his oath (2 Samuel 21:7). Thousands of years later Jonathan’s loyalty is still read: this man was great.

cases.name: Saul and Doeg at Nob
cases.charge: Slaughter of eighty-five priests of the Lord and the city of Nob: a king who read loyalty to David as treason, and an Edomite set over his servants who informed and did what Israel’s own men would not
cases.summary: Saul had set an Edomite over his servants, though the scriptures say never trust an enemy. Doeg the Edomite, detained before the Lord at Nob, saw Ahimelech give David the hallowed bread and the sword of Goliath, and he informed Saul (1 Samuel 21:6-7; 1 Samuel 22:9-10). Saul, desperate, read loyalty to David as betrayal of himself. His own footmen would not put forth their hand against the priests of the Lord, so Saul got the Edomite to do what his own men would not: Doeg slew eighty-five men that wore a linen ephod and smote Nob, all out of hatred and envy (1 Samuel 22:17-19). David wrote the Edomite’s sentence in a psalm: God shall destroy him for ever (Psalms 52:5).
offenseFull: David came to Nob, three days out in the field and fearful of king Saul, and Ahimelech the priest gave him hallowed bread, for there was no bread there but the shewbread taken from before the Lord (1 Samuel 21:1-6). Christ recounted this very history when the Pharisees challenged his disciples for plucking the ears of corn on the sabbath day (Mark 2:23-26); precept it in the Bible if it is not there already.

A certain servant of Saul was detained before the Lord that day: Doeg, an Edomite, the chiefest of Saul’s herdmen (1 Samuel 21:7). His presence was not accidental; his forced stay kept him in position to observe David, and he became an informant. The house of God is not immune to treachery: while Doeg was physically before the Lord, his heart was far from Him. The name Edomite ties him to Esau’s line, historically hostile toward Israel, an outsider holding power in Saul’s court. The scriptures say Israel is never to trust its enemies, yet here is a king of Israel with an Edomite set over his servants (Ecclesiasticus 12:10). Israel has always kept Esau in its midst and in high positions, as Haman was in the Persian court. That foreshadowed Saul’s spiritual drift: he that contemns small things shall fall by little and little (Ecclesiasticus 19:1). Saul was continually disobedient from the time he became king, because he feared the people and looked to please man, disobeying God’s laws, and in doing so he put an Edomite in a high position.

Doeg reported that he saw the son of Jesse come to Nob, and that Ahimelech enquired of the Lord for him, gave him victuals and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine (1 Samuel 22:9-10). Saul charged Ahimelech and all his father’s house with conspiracy; Ahimelech answered that none of the king’s servants was as faithful as David, the king’s son in law (1 Samuel 22:11-15). Saul had become so desperate that he interpreted loyalty to David as betrayal of himself, because he wanted everybody against David. It is no new thing under the sun: men put slander out to turn whole congregations to hate a man they have never sat down and broken bread with, because of hatred.
judgmentFull: Saul told his footmen to turn and slay the priests of the Lord, but the servants of the king would not put forth their hand against them (1 Samuel 22:17). Saul was able to get the Edomite to do what his own men would not do: Doeg turned and fell upon the priests and slew on that day eighty-five persons that did wear a linen ephod, because they showed affinity to David, and he smote Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword, men and women, children and sucklings (1 Samuel 22:18-19). All because of hatred and envy.

Go back to Genesis and see the spirit that has been on this man from the beginning: Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing and comforted himself, purposing to kill his brother (Genesis 27:41-42). Just as in the time of Saul, even to this very day, when Israel suffers violence at the hands of the other nations, especially Esau, he gets comfort out of it; when Saul appointed Doeg to that task, he was quite happy over it and most likely found much pleasure in killing the priests. The servant is not greater than his lord: if they persecuted Christ, Israel will be persecuted, by the heathen and by its own kinsmen as well, and that is what Jacob’s trouble is about (John 15:20).

Abiathar the son of Ahimelech escaped and fled after David and told him that Saul had slain the Lord’s priests. David answered that he knew that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul, and that he had occasioned the death of all his father’s house; Abiathar was to abide with him and fear not (1 Samuel 22:20-23).

David wrote the psalm when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul that David was come to the house of Ahimelech (Psalms 52:1). His tongue devised mischief like a sharp razor, working deceitfully, and he loved evil more than good and lying rather than righteousness (Psalms 52:2-4). The deceitful tongue today is the one that puts forth a white Christ, when Christ is black. God shall likewise destroy him for ever, take him away, pluck him out of his dwelling place and root him out of the land of the living, meaning he will no longer exist (Psalms 52:5). David did not tell Doeg the Edomite he could come and rule with him in the kingdom. The psalm speaks of Doeg and also of Esau as a whole: it is future prophecy that the Lord will destroy all of Esau from the face of the earth for ever. Esau’s nations, the so-called white man, will have no place in the kingdom; there will be a period of servitude, and then they die and it is over. He is the man that made not God his strength but trusted in the abundance of his riches, his slave trades and his riches (Psalms 52:7). Israel is the green olive tree in the house of God, trusting in the mercy of God for ever (Psalms 52:8; Jeremiah 11:16).

cases.name: Nabal
cases.charge: Railing on the Lord’s anointed and requiting evil for good to the men who had been a wall to his shepherds: who is David?
cases.summary: Nabal was a very great man in Maon, rich in sheep and goats, churlish and evil in his doings, and such a son of Belial that a man could not speak to him (1 Samuel 25:2-3, 17). David’s men had been a wall to his shepherds by night and by day, and at the shearing David sent ten young men in peace to ask whatever came to his hand. Nabal asked who David was and railed on them (1 Samuel 25:4-14). Loyalty is a two-way street, and Nabal never requited it. When the wine was gone out of him and his wife told him how close he had come to death, his heart died within him, and about ten days after the Lord smote him (1 Samuel 25:36-38).
offenseFull: There was a very great man in Maon whose possessions were in Carmel, three thousand sheep and a thousand goats; his name was Nabal, and his wife was Abigail, a woman of good understanding and of a beautiful countenance, but the man was churlish and evil in his doings, and he was of the house of Caleb (1 Samuel 25:2-3). Nabal means folly, or fool.

David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing and sent ten young men to greet him in peace, peace to him, to his house and to all that he had (1 Samuel 25:4-6). The request was righteous: Nabal’s shepherds had been with David’s men in Carmel, nothing of theirs was hurt or missing, and Nabal could ask his own young men; so let him give whatever came to his hand to his servants and to his son David (1 Samuel 25:7-8). David’s men had looked out for his shepherds and protected them; they had been loyal and had helped them, and now they asked a favour back in a good day. It is a two-way street.

Nabal answered, who is David, and who is the son of Jesse? There were many servants nowadays, he said, that break away every man from his master, and he would not give his bread, his water and the flesh he had killed for his shearers to men he knew not (1 Samuel 25:10-11). He was talking much big talk, as if he did not even know who David was. Nabal was rich, a very wealthy man, and a lot of times what comes with that is an arrogant spirit.

One of the young men told Abigail that David had sent messengers out of the wilderness to salute their master and he railed on them; yet the men had been very good to them, and they were a wall unto them both by night and day while they kept the sheep (1 Samuel 25:14-16). David’s men had been giving Nabal’s shepherds protection from their enemies. Evil was determined against their master and all his household, for he was such a son of Belial that a man could not speak to him (1 Samuel 25:17). Some people are like that: a man cannot talk to them, and they will not reason with him. Nabal was reckless, and he was trying to get his whole house killed.
judgmentFull: David told his men to gird on every man his sword, and about four hundred went up after him, while two hundred abode by the stuff (1 Samuel 25:13). He said he had kept all that this fellow had in the wilderness in vain, for he had requited him evil for good, and he swore to leave him not one male of all that pertained to him by the morning light (1 Samuel 25:21-22). David was coming with intent to destroy the men of that house. Abigail met him on the road, and David blessed the Lord who sent her, and blessed her advice, that kept him that day from coming to shed blood and from avenging himself with his own hand (1 Samuel 25:32-35).

Abigail came home, and Nabal held a feast in his house like the feast of a king, and his heart was merry within him, for he was very drunken; so she told him nothing, less or more, until the morning light (1 Samuel 25:36). She had enough sense not to come to him boasting that she had saved his life; she still respected him. In the morning, when the wine was gone out of Nabal and his wife told him these things, his heart died within him, and he became as a stone (1 Samuel 25:37). He had railed, asking who David was; but when he sobered up and heard that the coming king had come down to destroy everybody in his house, fear came over him, because he realized how close he had been to his death. He thought he was being clever; he would have been caught off guard and put to death.

About ten days after, the Lord smote Nabal, that he died (1 Samuel 25:38). He was wicked; she was righteous and patient, and the Lord delivered her. The loyalty David had shown to Nabal, Nabal never requited, and he ended up losing his life. When David heard that Nabal was dead, he blessed the Lord, who had pleaded the cause of his reproach from the hand of Nabal and kept His servant from evil, for the Lord had returned the wickedness of Nabal upon his own head (1 Samuel 25:39). Sometimes a man has to let God handle his quarrel; the Lord returns the wicked’s wickedness on their own head. Then David sent and communed with Abigail to take her to him to wife (1 Samuel 25:39-42).

cases.name: Abigail
cases.charge: Taking her husband’s iniquity upon herself and, by her deeds, sparing her lord’s house; keeping David from shedding blood and from avenging himself with his own hand
cases.summary: Abigail was a woman of good understanding attached to a son of Belial (1 Samuel 25:3). When she heard that David was coming with four hundred swords for her husband’s railing, she made haste with a gift to appease David and save her house, and she told not her husband (1 Samuel 25:14-19). She fell at David’s feet, took the iniquity upon herself, named her husband’s folly without defending it, and told the coming king what the Lord would do for him (1 Samuel 25:23-31). The Lord put the spirit on her, and David changed his mind. She by her deeds spared her lord’s house; about ten days later the Lord smote Nabal, and David sent for her (1 Samuel 25:32-42).
offenseFull: One of the young men told Abigail that David had sent messengers to salute their master and he railed on them, though David’s men had been a wall to the shepherds by night and by day; evil was determined against their master and all his household (1 Samuel 25:14-17). She was of good understanding: they went to her, because Nabal was reckless and was trying to get them killed. She made haste and took two hundred loaves, two bottles of wine, five sheep ready dressed, parched corn, raisins and cakes of figs, laid them on asses, and sent her servants on before her, but she told not her husband Nabal (1 Samuel 25:18-19). Abigail went to present a gift to appease David and save her house; Jeroboam’s wife, by contrast, worked deceit hand in hand with Jeroboam (1 Kings 14:1-6).

When she saw David she hasted, lighted off the ass, fell before him on her face and bowed to the ground; she reverenced him and respected him, and at his feet she asked that the iniquity be upon her (1 Samuel 25:23-24). She was not the one who did anything wrong, but she took that iniquity upon herself; she was being the pillar of her house, using wisdom to protect it, for the scripture says she was a woman of good understanding.

She did not turn her lord over to be destroyed, as some women today would be ready to do, and she did not defend him either: she asked David not to regard this man of Belial, for as his name is, so is he, and folly is with him (1 Samuel 25:25). Belial means a child of Satan; she said openly that her husband was the devil the Bible speaks of. Every wise woman who was with a wicked man was not taking him by the hand and following his plan. It was Nabal who was out of the spirit, yet she asked forgiveness for the trespass of her handmaid, the same chaste conversation, stepping up for her household (1 Samuel 25:28).

Then she told the coming king who he was: the Lord had withheld him from shedding blood and avenging himself; the Lord would make him a sure house, because he fought the battles of the Lord; his soul would be bound in the bundle of life with the Lord his God, and his enemies slung out as from a sling; and when he was ruler over Israel he would have no grief for blood shed causeless (1 Samuel 25:26-31). This is a woman who knows how to speak and how to deal with situations, when David was coming to kill everything moving.
judgmentFull: David blessed the Lord God of Israel who sent her to meet him, blessed her advice and blessed her, which kept him that day from coming to shed blood and from avenging himself with his own hand; he received what she brought and told her to go up in peace, for he had hearkened to her voice and accepted her person (1 Samuel 25:32-35). The Lord put the spirit on her, she spoke eloquently, and he changed his mind. That is why it is important for women to know how to speak, when to speak and how to speak. Submission does not mean a woman cannot give advice to her husband: Abigail was intelligent, decisive, articulate and courageous, and she gave David counsel that prevented bloodshed. A godly woman knows how to communicate wisdom without abandoning order, respect, discretion and self-control.

Wives are to be in subjection to their own husbands, that those who obey not the word may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives, beholding their chaste conversation coupled with fear (1 Peter 3:1). That is what Abigail was putting in place, one of the holy women of old who trusted in God (1 Peter 3:5). Her chaste conversation was her behaviour: if her lord is out of the spirit, instead of going railing for railing with him, a wife’s behaviour should be able to win him over; provoking with the mouth only leaves an unhappy household. Even when the man is out of the spirit, that does not give the woman licence to be out of the spirit also. She was loyal to her husband even though he was not right, because that is a commandment of God; being loyal to her lord, she was being loyal to God.

Nabal held a feast like the feast of a king and was very drunken, so she told him nothing until the morning light; she had enough sense not to come to him boasting that she had saved his life (1 Samuel 25:36-37). About ten days after, the Lord smote Nabal, that he died; he was wicked, she was righteous and patient, and the Lord delivered her (1 Samuel 25:38). David sent and communed with Abigail to take her to wife, and she bowed herself to the earth and said her handmaid would be a servant to wash the feet of the servants of her lord, a very humble act; even attached to a wicked man, she was still in a place of humility (1 Samuel 25:39-41). She was probably very glad to go, relieved of a man who would not listen, would not take advice, and was arrogant, and she hasted with five damsels and became David’s wife (1 Samuel 25:42). Some women are not wicked; they get the title because of who they are attached to.

cases.name: Saul and the witch of Endor
cases.charge: Seeking counsel of a woman with a familiar spirit, after he had put them out of the land, when the Lord would not answer him
cases.summary: Samuel was dead, and Saul had put away those that had familiar spirits and the wizards out of the land; when he saw the host of the Philistines he was afraid, and when the Lord answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets, he sought a woman with a familiar spirit (1 Samuel 28:3-7). Cut off from the Most High for his disobedience, he heard his own death prophesied: the Lord was become his enemy, and the next day he and his sons would be with Samuel (1 Samuel 28:16-19). Saul died for his transgression and for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, and the Most High slew him (1 Chronicles 10:13-14).
offenseFull: Samuel was dead and buried in Ramah, and Saul had put away those that had familiar spirits and the wizards out of the land (1 Samuel 28:3). They were put to death, for the law says that a man or a woman that has a familiar spirit or is a wizard shall surely be put to death, and a witch is not to be suffered to live: that was the cleaning of the land (Leviticus 20:27; Exodus 22:18).

When the Philistines pitched in Shunem, Saul saw their host, was afraid, and his heart greatly trembled (1 Samuel 28:4-5). This is the king: if the king is afraid, the fear spreads to the men under him, for as the judge of the people is himself, so are his officers (Ecclesiasticus 10:2). Fear is a betraying of the succours which reason offers: a man tricks himself into being afraid of things that are not really there, because his faith is only in what he can see with his eyes (Wisdom of Solomon 17:12). Saul had been little in his own sight from the beginning, and that bashful spirit made him self-willed, full of excuses, fearful of the people and easily manipulated (1 Samuel 15:17; 1 Samuel 13:11-12; 1 Samuel 15:24).

When Saul enquired of the Lord, the Lord answered him not, for the Lord does not hear the prayers of sinners (1 Samuel 28:6). He had just rid the land of the familiar spirits and the wizards, and now he told his servants to find him one; he was double minded (1 Samuel 28:7). He was going through the back door, trying to get wisdom by a sinful means, from a witch, when the law says not to regard them that have familiar spirits nor seek after wizards, to be defiled by them (Leviticus 19:31). What he was doing is called necromancy, going to somebody that conjures up spirits, the commandment he turned around and broke (Deuteronomy 18:10-11). Rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft (1 Samuel 15:23): Saul’s first sins were rebellion, and the latter sin that got him killed was witchcraft.

Saul disguised himself and came to the woman by night with two men, and when she asked why he laid a snare for her life, he swore to her by the Lord that no punishment would happen to her for this thing (1 Samuel 28:8-10). The Lord had already said to put witches to death in the land, and Saul swore falsely by the Lord; a man who swears by the Lord over sin is not examining himself.
judgmentFull: Samuel asked why Saul had disquieted him, and Saul answered that he was sore distressed, for God was departed from him and answered him no more (1 Samuel 28:15). Samuel asked why he asked of him, seeing the Lord was become his enemy (1 Samuel 28:16): imagine that, the Lord is your enemy now; it all went back to Saul being bashful.

The Lord had rent the kingdom out of his hand and given it to his neighbour David, because he obeyed not the voice of the Lord nor executed His fierce wrath upon Amalek (1 Samuel 28:17-18). The Most High gave a law concerning Amalek, that Israel blot out his remembrance from under heaven, and Saul did not carry it out (Deuteronomy 25:17-19). It was his own fault the whole time that the Lord was not answering him.

Moreover the Lord would deliver Israel with him into the hand of the Philistines, and the next day he and his sons would be with Samuel (1 Samuel 28:19). That means the next day he and his sons were going to die; Samuel prophesied from his grave. Saul fell all along on the earth, sore afraid, with no strength in him (1 Samuel 28:20).

The Philistines slew Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua, and the archers sore wounded Saul (1 Samuel 31:2-3). Fearing how men abuse their captives in war, he asked his armourbearer to thrust him through rather than be taken (1 Samuel 31:4). When the man would not, Saul took a sword and fell upon it; he took his own life, and he and his three sons and all his men died that same day together, the fulfilment of the prophecy (1 Samuel 31:4-6).

Saul died for his transgression against the Most High, for not keeping His word, and for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit rather than enquiring of the Lord; therefore the Most High slew him and turned the kingdom to David the son of Jesse (1 Chronicles 10:13-14). The last straw for Saul was seeking that familiar spirit. The left hand of the Most High is real; people who meddle with it get entangled and get spirits put on them, and it is not Israel’s custom. Saul would join Samuel the next day; the difference is that Samuel died righteously.

The Philistines fastened his body to the wall of Bethshan, and the men of Jabesh-gilead took it down, buried the bones and fasted seven days (1 Samuel 31:8-13); it has always been in Israel to mourn the dead, for no matter what a person has done, it does not sit right to see a brother put to death.
