cases.name: The Amalekite who claimed to kill Saul
cases.charge: Claiming to have slain the Lord’s anointed, and bringing his crown and bracelet to David
cases.summary: After the death of Saul a young man came out of the camp of Israel to Ziklag with his clothes rent and earth upon his head, and told David that he had come by chance upon mount Gilboa and slain Saul at his own asking, and brought him the crown and the bracelet (2 Samuel 1:1-10). He was an Amalekite, of the seed of Esau, of the nation that from the beginning feared not God (Genesis 36:12; Deuteronomy 25:18). David asked how he was not afraid to destroy the Lord’s anointed, and had him slain, for his own mouth had testified against him (2 Samuel 1:14-16).
offenseFull: When David had returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites and abode two days in Ziklag, a man came out of the camp from Saul with his clothes rent and earth upon his head and fell to the earth before David to do him honour (2 Samuel 1:1-2). He said the people were fled from the battle and Saul and Jonathan were dead; he had found Saul leaning upon his spear with the chariots and horsemen pressing hard after him, Saul had asked him to stand upon him and slay him, and he slew him and took the crown from his head and the bracelet from his arm (2 Samuel 1:4-10). In the earlier account Saul fell upon his sword but did not die at that moment (1 Samuel 31:4-5). Saul took his own life; he was not killed by the Edomite.

The man was an Amalekite, and the Amalekites are the seed of Esau, of Eliphaz his son: Amalek is Esau’s grandson, and his lineage is a thing to know when reading of Israel’s enemies (Genesis 36:12). Esau came out red, not white; there are no white people on the earth, and to be perceived as white, as pure, is one of the lies (Genesis 25:25). He is a liar from the womb, who sold his birthright and then cried for the blessing, and by his sword he would live: the same man is the liar and the murderer, who purposed in his heart to slay his brother (Hebrews 12:16; Genesis 27:37-41). Esau has had a perpetual hatred and shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity, and that is a murderer; he pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity, and the Lord will not turn away his punishment (Ezekiel 35:5; Amos 1:11). Never trust the enemy: though he humble himself and go crouching, beware of him, for he stands up in Israel’s place and takes their identity (Ecclesiasticus 12:10-12; Revelation 2:9).

David took hold on his clothes and rent them, and all the men with him, and they mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul, for Jonathan and for the house of Israel (2 Samuel 1:11-12). The renting of garments was the sign of mourning, but the Most High looks for a rent heart and not rent garments only; true repentance is inward, not just an outward show (Joel 2:13).
judgmentFull: David asked him whence he was, and he answered that he was the son of a stranger, an Amalekite; and David asked how he was not afraid to stretch forth his hand to destroy the Lord’s anointed (2 Samuel 1:13-14). Why he was not afraid is written in the law: Amalek met Israel by the way and smote the hindmost, all that were feeble behind, when they were faint and weary, and he feared not God; from the beginning he did not fear God (Deuteronomy 25:18). Even a man about to die was not to be touched; the judgment of the Lord was to be let play out.

David called one of his young men and told him to go near and fall upon him, and he smote him that he died, for his own mouth had testified against him (2 Samuel 1:15-16). He that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword; that is the punishment, and they will not escape it (Revelation 13:10). The Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation, and Israel is commanded to blot out his remembrance from under heaven and not to forget it (Exodus 17:16; Deuteronomy 25:19). When Rechab and Baanah later brought him the head of Ishbosheth, David reminded them that the man who thought to bring good tidings of Saul’s death he had taken hold of and slain in Ziklag, and that was the reward he gave for such tidings (2 Samuel 4:10).

David lamented over Saul and Jonathan and bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow, which is written in the book of Jasher (2 Samuel 1:17-18). The book of Jasher is not in the canon because the Most High did not will His people to have it; He put in the book exactly what He wanted them to read in the last days. This walk in the last days is not by might nor by power but by His spirit; the captivity is not overthrown by rising up with the bow or the gun, for this is spiritual war and not physical (Zechariah 4:6; Revelation 14:12). There is nothing wrong with knowing how to defend yourself, but the redemption of Israel does not come by force of arms.

The lament is a prophecy given in the spirit, almost a eulogy: Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided (2 Samuel 1:23). Before the devil jumped on Saul he was good, and the two of them were good together; Israel’s forefathers died only when the Most High said it was time, and that is the only way any of them died.

cases.name: Joab
cases.charge: Shedding the blood of war in peace: slaying Abner in the gate of Hebron for his brother’s blood, and Amasa with a kiss, without the king’s knowledge
cases.summary: Abner slew Asahel in open battle at Gibeon after warning him again and again to turn aside (2 Samuel 2:19-23). When Abner came to David to bring all Israel to him and went away in peace, Joab, without David’s knowledge, brought him back, took him aside in the gate to speak quietly and smote him under the fifth rib for the blood of Asahel his brother: it was payback, premeditated murder (2 Samuel 3:20-27). Years later he took Amasa by the beard as if to kiss him and shed his bowels to the ground at one stroke (2 Samuel 20:9-10). David left the reward of the doer of evil with the Lord, and it came through Solomon: Joab died at the horns of the altar for the innocent blood he shed (1 Kings 2:28-34).
offenseFull: When Abner’s men were beaten at Gibeon, Asahel, as light of foot as a wild roe, pursued Abner, and Abner warned him again and again to turn off and take another man’s armour, not wanting to kill him and face Joab his brother, for everybody knew the spirit that was on Joab (2 Samuel 2:17-22). When Asahel refused, Abner smote him with the hinder end of the spear under the fifth rib, and he died there; the lesson is to take heed to the warning and not keep testing a man (2 Samuel 2:23).

Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men to bring all Israel over to him, David made them a feast, and Abner went in peace (2 Samuel 3:20-21). Joab came in from pursuing a troop, as he always was, pursuing troops and finding somebody to fight, and demanded of the king why he had sent Abner away, saying Abner came to deceive him and to know his going out and his coming in (2 Samuel 3:22-25). He did not trust Abner, and there was already blood between them; he did not care about the king, for all he knew was that the man who killed his brother had been fed and let go, and Joab knew that what he said was not true, but he was angry and trying to make David see things his way.

He sent messengers after Abner, took him aside in the gate to speak quietly, and smote him under the fifth rib (2 Samuel 3:26-27). It was payback; Joab’s blood was burning for revenge; Abner was unwise to return to that place, knowing what Joab would do, but it was of the Lord. It was not the avenger of blood, and it was not manslaughter; it was premeditated murder: he thought it out, conceived it in his mind, and got it done. The man who kills his neighbour ignorantly, as when the axe head slips from the helve, flees to the appointed city and lives; but he who comes presumptuously to slay with guile is taken from the altar that he may die, for wilful murder found no refuge there (Exodus 21:13-14).

David declared himself and his kingdom guiltless of the blood of Abner, for it looked as though the king had set him up, and laid it on the head of Joab (2 Samuel 3:28-29). Abishai was there too, but it rested on Joab as the ringleader: Joab had his own band of killers under King David, all of the same murderous mind (2 Samuel 3:30). David lamented over Abner in the spirit, another eulogy and prophecy: Abner died as a fool dies, coming back thinking he was going to speak with the king again, and fell as a man falls before wicked men (2 Samuel 3:33-34). David said he was weak that day though anointed king, and the sons of Zeruiah, ruthless men he could not bring under, were too hard for him; but the Lord would reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness (2 Samuel 3:39).

At the great stone in Gibeon, Joab came to Amasa with a sword secretly fastened, took him by the beard with his right hand as if to kiss him, and smote him in the fifth rib so that his bowels shed to the ground, and he died at one stroke (2 Samuel 20:8-10). Joab was crooked and underhanded, murdering the man who had been named captain in his place.
judgmentFull: On his deathbed David charged Solomon with what Joab did to the two captains of the hosts of Israel, Abner and Amasa, whom he slew and shed the blood of war in peace (1 Kings 2:5). The only reason Asahel was killed was that a war was going on, not a personal matter, and Joab went about it all wrong, emotional, in premeditated murder. Joab was putting people to death he was not supposed to; David knew, stood quiet, and would deal with him in his own time. David could not do it himself, for he had given men commandments to kill on his behalf, Uriah among them; his hands were full of blood, and he left it to his son, leaving behind him an avenger (1 Kings 2:6; 2 Samuel 11:14-17).

Joab had turned after Adonijah, and when the tidings came he fled to the tabernacle of the Lord and caught hold on the horns of the altar, as men sometimes did to get mercy (1 Kings 2:28). When Joab said he would die there, Benaiah brought the word back to the king, for they all revered Joab, a real star in Israel (1 Kings 2:30). Solomon told him to do as Joab had said and fall upon him, and to take away from the house of his father the innocent blood Joab shed (1 Kings 2:31).

Joab died for the innocent blood he shed when he slew Abner and Amasa, two men more righteous and better than he, without David’s knowledge; the blood returned upon his own head and upon his seed, while upon David and his seed and throne there would be peace for ever from the Lord, and Benaiah was set over the host in his place (1 Kings 2:32-35). David also did a premeditated murder, and he was not put to death, for David was a man that repented, and Joab was not a man to repent (2 Samuel 12:13).

cases.name: Mephibosheth
cases.charge: What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am? and, let him take all, forasmuch as my lord the king is come again in peace
cases.summary: He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan, and his nurse fled with him because a new king customarily killed the descendants of the former king, and in her haste he fell and became lame (2 Samuel 4:4). For Jonathan’s sake David fetched him out of Lodebar, restored him all the land of Saul, and set him at the king’s table continually (2 Samuel 9:1-13). When Ziba slandered him and took his estate, Mephibosheth met the returning king and said Ziba could take it all, for it was enough that the king had come again in peace (2 Samuel 16:1-4; 2 Samuel 19:24-30).
offenseFull: Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth was lame of his feet: when the tidings came out of Jezreel he was five years old, and his nurse took him up and fled, and in her haste he fell and became lame (2 Samuel 4:4). She fled because a new king taking over would customarily kill all the descendants of the former king, to make sure none could overthrow him.

David asked whether there was yet any left of the house of Saul, that he might show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake (2 Samuel 9:1). Jonathan and David were always very close, and Jonathan was always there for David; they made a covenant, for Jonathan loved him as his own soul (1 Samuel 18:3). Souls being knit is not anything unnatural between the two men: Jonathan and David were on one accord and had the same spirit (1 Samuel 18:1). That covenant was a binding agreement, a bond, and David was a surety for Jonathan’s house; his word was his bond, for an honest man is surety for his neighbour (Ecclesiasticus 29:14-15).

Ziba, a servant of the house of Saul, told the king that Jonathan had yet a son, lame on his feet, in the house of Machir in Lodebar, and the king sent and fetched him (2 Samuel 9:2-5). Mephibosheth fell on his face and did reverence, thinking David would do something evil because he was of the house of Saul; it was a time when David could have paid back the house that had tried to murder him (2 Samuel 9:6). David told him to fear not, for he would surely show him kindness for Jonathan his father’s sake, restore him all the land of Saul, and have him eat bread at the king’s table continually (2 Samuel 9:7). Not everybody was allowed to eat bread at the king’s table, yet the grandson of the man who hated David would eat there. He bowed himself and asked what David saw in such a dead dog as he was (2 Samuel 9:8).

During Absalom’s rebellion Ziba met David with saddled asses and bread and fruit and wine, and claimed that Mephibosheth abode in Jerusalem thinking the kingdom was about to be restored to him, which was not true; on that word David handed Ziba everything that belonged to Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 16:1-4).

When the king came again, Mephibosheth came down to meet him, having neither dressed his feet, trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes from the day the king departed until he returned in peace, showing his mourning for David (2 Samuel 19:24). Going so unkempt is also not the spirit of Israel, who were always a clean people: a man going before the king, who was also the judge, presents himself groomed (Exodus 19:14). He said his servant Ziba had deceived and slandered him, since he was lame and could not saddle his own beast; he acknowledged that all his father’s house were dead men before the king, yet David had set him to eat at his own table, so he had no further right to cry to the king (2 Samuel 19:26-28). When David said that he and Ziba should divide the land, Mephibosheth answered that Ziba could take it all, for it was enough that his lord the king had come again in peace to his own house (2 Samuel 19:29-30).
judgmentFull: David gave Mephibosheth all that pertained to Saul, and charged Ziba, his sons and his servants to till the land and bring in the fruits, that Mephibosheth might have food, though he himself would eat at the king’s table always (2 Samuel 9:9-10). Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants, and that shows the level of riches Israel had as a nation: Saul’s servant had servants of his own, and all of them were set to till the land and take care of the house for Mephibosheth, out of the respect David had for Jonathan (2 Samuel 9:10). So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem and did eat continually at the king’s table, and was lame on both his feet (2 Samuel 9:13).

This is what Israel needs to bring back: the same love, care and admiration for the people it loses; it is unfortunate, but Israel does lose people, and their family must be taken care of as if they were there themselves. That is why the Most High called David a man after his own heart: even though things did not go well between him and Saul, he still had enough love for Jonathan to take care of his seed.

A famine of three years came for Saul and his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites; Saul broke his word, and the Gibeonites asked for seven of his sons (2 Samuel 21:1-6). The lesson the Most High taught Israel is to pay what you vow and let your yea be yea and your nay be nay: Saul went back on his word after he had given his yea, and the whole house paid for it (Ecclesiastes 5:4-6; Matthew 5:37). The king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, because of the Lord’s oath that was between David and Jonathan; David did not go back on his oath, for he had promised Jonathan that his seed would always eat at David’s table (2 Samuel 21:7).

cases.offense: Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth was lame of his feet: when the tidings came out of Jezreel he was five years old, and his nurse took him up and fled, and in her haste he fell and became lame (2 Samuel 4:4). She fled because a new king taking over would customarily kill all the descendants of the former king, to make sure none could overthrow him.
cases.judgment: David gave Mephibosheth all that pertained to Saul, and charged Ziba, his sons and his servants to till the land and bring in the fruits, that Mephibosheth might have food, though he himself would eat at the king’s table always (2 Samuel 9:9-10). Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants, and that shows the level of riches Israel had as a nation: Saul’s servant had servants of his own, and all of them were set to till the land and take care of the house for Mephibosheth, out of the respect David had for Jonathan (2 Samuel 9:10). So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem and did eat continually at the king’s table, and was lame on both his feet (2 Samuel 9:13).

cases.name: Baanah and Rechab
cases.charge: Murdering Ishbosheth on his bed at noon, and carrying his head to David as the Lord’s vengeance on Saul’s seed
cases.summary: When Saul’s son Ishbosheth heard that Abner was dead in Hebron, his hands were feeble and all the Israelites were troubled (2 Samuel 4:1). Two captains of his bands came in the heat of the day as though they would fetch wheat, smote him under the fifth rib as he lay on his bed at noon, beheaded him, and brought the head to David, claiming that the Lord had avenged the king of Saul and his seed (2 Samuel 4:5-8). They did too much; David required the blood of a righteous man slain on his bed at their hand, and they were slain, their hands and feet cut off, and hanged up over the pool in Hebron (2 Samuel 4:9-12).
offenseFull: Ishbosheth had two men that were captains of bands, Baanah and Rechab, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, of the children of Benjamin (2 Samuel 4:2-3).

The sons of Rimmon came about the heat of the day to the house of Ishbosheth, who lay on a bed at noon in the hottest part of the day, and came into the midst of the house as though they would have fetched wheat, and smote him under the fifth rib (2 Samuel 4:5-6). Having smitten and slain him on his bed, they beheaded him, took his head, and got away through the plain all night (2 Samuel 4:7).

They brought the head to David at Hebron and presented it as the head of Ishbosheth his enemy, who sought his life, and said that the Lord had avenged the king that day of Saul and of his seed (2 Samuel 4:8). They did too much; they went overboard. Israel, being out of order, took the matter upon themselves. David had no quarrel with Saul’s sons; it was Saul who sought his life. Men who take vengeance and shed blood by their own hand, out of order and not ordained of the Lord, answer for it.
judgmentFull: David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, as the Lord liveth, who had redeemed his soul out of all adversity: the man who told him Saul was dead, thinking to bring good tidings, he had taken hold of and slain in Ziklag, and that was the reward he gave for such tidings (2 Samuel 4:9-10). How much more, when wicked men had slain a righteous person in his own house upon his bed, should he not require his blood of their hand and take them away from the earth (2 Samuel 4:11). The man was at rest, asleep, and it was not even a man-to-man contest for the kingdom; that is not how the Most High brings His purpose to pass.

David commanded his young men, and they slew Rechab and Baanah, cut off their hands and their feet, and hanged them up over the pool in Hebron, but took the head of Ishbosheth and buried it in the sepulchre of Abner (2 Samuel 4:12). The Most High has His own way of doing things; His people are not to put the cart before the horse.

If a man comes presumptuously upon his neighbour to slay him with guile, he is to be taken from the altar of the Lord that he may die; that is known as premeditated murder, and wilful murder found no refuge at the altar (Exodus 21:14). A curse stands on him that smites his neighbour secretly (Deuteronomy 27:24).

This is why David is called a man after the Most High’s own heart: he did not accept wickedness done in his name or let the murderers slide; he called them out, and they received judgment for taking a man’s life not ordained of the Lord nor commanded by the king. Let all things be done decently and in order, for the Most High is not the author of vengeance taken out of order (1 Corinthians 14:40). So David charged Solomon concerning the blood Joab shed, and the doer of evil was rewarded according to his wickedness (1 Kings 2:5-6).

cases.name: Uzzah and the ark
cases.charge: Putting forth his hand to the ark of God, which was carried on a new cart and not borne by the Levites after the due order
cases.summary: David and all Israel went to bring again the ark of God, which had been neglected in the days of Saul, and set it upon a new cart out of the house of Abinadab, with Uzzah and Ahio driving (2 Samuel 6:1-4; 1 Chronicles 13:3-7). At Nachon’s threshingfloor the oxen shook it, Uzzah put forth his hand and took hold of the ark, and God smote him there for his error (2 Samuel 6:6-7). Grabbing the ark was a natural reaction, but the Most High had already declared it holy and untouchable. When David came back for it, the Levites sanctified themselves and bore it upon their shoulders with the staves, after the due order (1 Chronicles 15:12-15).
offenseFull: David consulted the leaders and proposed to the congregation to bring again the ark, for they had not enquired at it in the days of Saul, and all agreed, for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people (1 Chronicles 13:1-4). The ark had been taken from Israel by the Philistines in the days of the judges because of sin and left in the house of Abinadab; through the wilderness there had been no house for the Lord, and the ark was moved from place to place.

They set the ark upon a new cart, and Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, drove it, with Ahio going before the ark, while David and all the house of Israel played before the Lord on harps, psalteries, timbrels, cornets and cymbals (2 Samuel 6:3-5).

The staves are set in the rings so that the ark is borne, and the staves are not to be taken out (Exodus 25:14-15). When the camp set forward, Aaron and his sons wrapped and covered the holy things, and then the sons of Kohath came to bear them, the movers of the sanctuary; but they were not to touch any holy thing, lest they die, for only the sons of Aaron handled the most holy things: handle not (Numbers 4:15). Only chosen men could come near the ark; it was only to be touched by the Levites.
judgmentFull: When they came to Nachon’s threshingfloor the oxen shook the cart, and Uzzah put forth his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it; the anger of the Lord was kindled, God smote him there for his error, and he died there by the ark (2 Samuel 6:6-7). The animal bumped the cart and he reached to stop it from falling; it does not matter. That was the most holy thing, it was not his place to touch it, and even Uzzah, who meant well, could not get away with it. Israel learned that day not to touch the ark: if you mean well, it is still not going to go well.

He had good intentions but poor judgment, for only Aaron and his sons, the high priest, could deal with the ark; it may be a knee-jerk reaction to a sudden fall, but the Lord said that nobody could touch the ark of the covenant. Most of the time good intentions are bad judgments, and many keep them as a backup for doing the wrong thing, so that they can say they meant well. So Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire before the Lord, which He commanded them not, and there went out fire from the Lord and devoured them (Leviticus 10:1-2).

The Lord had warned Aaron not to come at all times into the holy place before the mercy seat, that he die not, and had set many stipulations upon it, even after the two sons of Aaron died for offering strange fire (Leviticus 16:2-4). The Most High is holy and not to be handled carelessly. Everything in that day had to be done to a T, and thanks are owed that there is mercy through Christ, for the Lord was not playing about His commandments. If it falls, let it fall, and get a Levite to lift it.

David was displeased that the Lord had made a breach upon Uzzah, and called the place Perez-uzzah, and he was afraid of the Lord that day and asked how the ark of the Lord should come to him (2 Samuel 6:8-9). David had seen the power of the Lord, and his flesh trembled for fear of Him and His judgments (Psalms 119:120): to see a man touch the ark and drop dead on the spot was a fearful thing, and he knew that the Lord was not playing, good intentions or not. He carried the ark aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, where it remained three months, and the Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household (2 Samuel 6:10-11). The ark blesses when it is with Israel and afflicts those who wrongly hold it, as when the Philistines were struck with emerods for taking it (1 Samuel 5:6-9).

David declared that none ought to carry the ark but the Levites, for the Most High had chosen them to carry it and to minister unto Him for ever (1 Chronicles 15:2). He charged the chief fathers of the Levites to sanctify themselves before bringing up the ark, because the first attempt failed when they did not seek Him after the due order, and the Levites bore the ark upon their shoulders with the staves, as Moses commanded according to the word of the Most High (1 Chronicles 15:12-15).

cases.name: Obed-edom the Gittite
cases.charge: Receiving the ark of God into his house three months, after the Lord had smitten Uzzah for touching it, and keeping it until the Lord blessed him and all his household
cases.summary: Uzzah had just died by the ark for putting forth his hand to it, and David was afraid of the Lord that day (2 Samuel 6:6-9). He would not remove it into the city of David but carried it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, where it remained three months, and the Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household because of the ark (2 Samuel 6:10-11). The ark blesses when it is with Israel and afflicts those who wrongly hold it.
offenseFull: When the oxen shook the cart at Nachon’s threshingfloor, Uzzah put forth his hand and took hold of the ark, and God smote him there for his error, and he died by the ark (2 Samuel 6:6-7). Grabbing the ark was a natural reaction, for he did not want it to fall to the ground; but the Most High had already declared it holy and untouchable. Whoever handled the ark when that service did not pertain to him was to be put to death; the sons of Kohath were forbidden to touch the holy things lest they die, and the ark was only to be touched by the Levites (Numbers 4:15). The Most High is holy and not to be handled carelessly; everything in that day had to be done to a T, and the Lord was not playing about His commandments. If God did this to an Israelite, imagine what He would do to a heathen.

David was displeased that the Lord had made a breach upon Uzzah, and he was afraid of the Lord that day (2 Samuel 6:8-9). He had seen the power of the Lord, and his flesh trembled for fear of Him and His judgments (Psalm 119:120).

The ark blesses when it is with Israel and afflicts those who wrongly hold it (1 Samuel 5:6-9). The Philistines set it by Dagon, and Dagon fell on his face before it; no man did this, and that is the power of the ark of God. The hand of the Lord was heavy upon them and smote them with emerods, and the punishment followed the ark from city to city (1 Samuel 5:1-12). If it falls, let it fall, and get a Levite to lift it.

When the ark went on to the city of David it went after the due order, for none ought to carry it but the Levites, whom the Most High had chosen (1 Chronicles 15:2). The first attempt failed because they did not seek Him after the due order, so the Levites sanctified themselves and bore the ark upon their shoulders with the staves, as Moses commanded according to the word of the Lord (1 Chronicles 15:12-15; Exodus 25:14-15).
judgmentFull: The Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household, the house of Obed-edom and all that he had, because of the ark (2 Samuel 6:11; 1 Chronicles 13:14). When David heard it, he and the elders and captains went and brought up the ark from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David with joy, and when they that bore it had gone six paces he sacrificed oxen and fatlings (2 Samuel 6:12-13; 1 Chronicles 15:25-26).

The sons of Obed-edom are numbered among the porters, for God blessed him: he and his sons and his brethren were threescore and two, able men for strength for the service, and the lot for the south gate fell to Obed-edom, and to his sons the house of Asuppim (1 Chronicles 26:4-8; 1 Chronicles 26:15).

Do not let anyone claim the ark is in Ethiopia or anywhere else on show. The prophet Jeremiah hid the tabernacle, the ark and the altar of incense in a cave, hidden by the Most High; the place is to be unknown until God gathers His people together again (2 Maccabees 2:5-7). The ark is hidden until Christ returns. It is not under the Al Aqsa; not just anybody can put their hands on the ark of God, and while the earth is defiled and the wicked are in rulership it will stay hidden, until the Lord gathers His people together and reveals it.

cases.name: Michal
cases.charge: Despising the king in her heart for dancing before the ark, and meeting him with sarcasm when he returned to bless his household
cases.summary: As the ark of the Lord came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked through a window, saw king David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and despised him in her heart (2 Samuel 6:16). In the midst of pure righteousness she was out of the spirit, hating him instead of rejoicing. She had once been a tower against death to him; now she met him with sarcasm when he came home to bless his household (2 Samuel 6:20). Michal had no child unto the day of her death; the Lord shut her womb (2 Samuel 6:23).
offenseFull: David danced before the Lord with all his might, girded with a linen ephod, and he and all the house of Israel brought up the ark with shouting and with the sound of the trumpet (2 Samuel 6:14-15). He was happy and in the spirit, because the Lord had chosen him to bring the ark back among the people.

Michal loved David, and Saul gave her to him that she might be a snare to him; he set his own daughter as a trap (1 Samuel 18:20-21). She loved him until she married him: she loved the mystique of who David was, and when she got him she did not know how to keep him. Yet when Saul sent messengers to slay David in the morning, she warned him, let him down through a window, and laid an image in the bed, looking out for her husband (1 Samuel 19:11-17). At that time Michal was a righteous example; a married woman is a tower against death to her husband, and that is what she was to David that night (Ecclesiasticus 26:22). She turned sour some chapters down the line.

Michal looked through a window, saw the king leaping and dancing before the Lord, and despised him in her heart (2 Samuel 6:16; 1 Chronicles 15:29). To despise him is to hate him: the Michal who had loved David now hated him. This is a spirit to be careful of: coming out of the spirit on the Lord’s day and murmuring against a brother who is rejoicing in the Most High. She did not want to see him rejoice before the Lord for the victory the Lord had brought him through; she had no love for him and was emotionally cut off from him, and he was the king.

When he had done the work and blessed all the people with bread, flesh and wine (2 Samuel 6:17-19), he came home to bless his own household, still in a good mood (2 Samuel 6:20). Michal came out to meet him and said sarcastically how glorious the king of Israel had been that day, uncovering himself in the eyes of the handmaids of his servants as one of the vain fellows (2 Samuel 6:20). She had watched from a distance and could think only of the king dancing with his clothes falling, when the Most High had just brought the ark of God back among Israel; she forgot the greatness of the day and let a murmuring spirit take her. That was all she saw; she did not see the good of that man, and she opened her mouth not with kindness but with bitterness, hatred and malice against her own husband.
judgmentFull: David answered that it was before the Lord, who chose him before her father and before all his house to appoint him ruler over Israel; therefore he would play before the Lord, and would yet be more vile and base in his own sight, and of the maidservants she had spoken of he would be had in honour (2 Samuel 6:21-22). She was angry because David had replaced her father: God made him king instead of her father; he did not make himself king.

Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death (2 Samuel 6:23). The Lord shut her womb. Do not play with the Most High. She died childless for disrespecting her husband: David would not deal with her any more, and his honour would come from the maidservants, not from her. The ungodly are punished according to their own imaginations, and whoever despises wisdom and nurture is miserable, and his hope is vain (Wisdom of Solomon 3:10-11).

The earth cannot bear an odious woman when she is married, a woman unpleasant and disrespectful toward her husband and his family (Proverbs 30:21-23). The adulterous woman eats, wipes her mouth and claims she has done nothing wrong: she does not hold herself accountable (Proverbs 30:20). Where there is an evil wife it is good to keep her shut up, away from the many, so that she does not spread her evil among everybody else (Ecclesiasticus 42:6). The bitter woman’s heart is snares and nets, and the man who pleases the Most High escapes her (Ecclesiastes 7:26).

cases.name: David and Bathsheba
cases.charge: Adultery with the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and setting Uriah up to be murdered on the battlefield by the sword of the children of Ammon to cover it
cases.summary: While Joab and all Israel were at war, David tarried at Jerusalem, saw from his roof a woman washing herself, learned that she was the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and sent and took her (2 Samuel 11:1-4). When she conceived he schemed to cover it, and when the loyal Uriah would not go down to his house, he sent him back to the front with a letter ordering his death (2 Samuel 11:5-17). David was judged; he did not get off scot-free, but because he had godly sorrow he was not put to death: the child died, and the sword never departed from his house (2 Samuel 12:10-14).
offenseFull: Somebody with a spiritual mind made it plain that she was Bath-sheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite: this was somebody’s wife. Wisdom and understanding were right there, and he ignored them; he sent messengers and took her anyway, and lay with her, and she conceived (2 Samuel 11:4-5). Satan put that lust in him to where he did not care: what he saw became desire, desire became action, he tried to cover it up, and the consequences came. Bath-sheba was not innocent either; she was complicit: when David called for her she went, she did not refuse because she was married, and it was consensual, not rape.

David sent for Uriah, asked how the war prospered, and told him to go down to his house and wash his feet, sending a mess of meat after him (2 Samuel 11:6-8). His plan, which nobody was privy to, was that if Uriah went down and lay with his wife, they could say the child was his; he was trying to make her bring an heir by another (Ecclesiasticus 23:22). But Uriah slept at the door of the king’s house, and even when David made him drunk he would not go down (2 Samuel 11:9-13). All the wisdom and understanding of the law he had departed from him in that moment; he was not fasting, not praying, and all his thinking was to cover his crime.

In the morning David wrote to Joab and sent the letter by Uriah’s own hand, ordering that he be set in the forefront of the hottest battle and abandoned there, and Uriah died, and some of David’s servants with him (2 Samuel 11:14-17). David set this man up to be murdered; this was premeditated murder. This goes back to Deuteronomy 27: a curse lies on the man who strikes his neighbour in secret, for nobody knew what David was doing, and on the man who takes a reward to kill an innocent person; the reward was that woman (Deuteronomy 27:24-25). Other men of Israel died too, so with David’s sin other men died as well. When her mourning was past he took her to wife, but the thing that David had done displeased the Most High, because it was murder (2 Samuel 11:26-27).
judgmentFull: The Lord sent Nathan with a parable of a rich man who spared his own flock and took the poor man’s one little ewe lamb, and David swore that the man should die and restore fourfold, because he had no pity (2 Samuel 12:1-6). In judging that man he was unknowingly pronouncing sentence on himself; the rich man was David, the poor man was Uriah, and the ewe lamb was his wife. Nathan told him he was the man: the Most High had given him the kingdom, Saul’s house and protection from Saul, and if David had only asked, He would have given him anything (2 Samuel 12:7-9). There is a term called suicide by cop; David committed murder by the hand of another nation, for he set the whole thing up.

Therefore the sword would never depart from his house: the Lord would raise up evil against him out of his own house and give his wives to his neighbour in the sight of the sun, for what he did secretly would be done before all Israel (2 Samuel 12:10-12). The baby was put to death, his son raped his daughter, another son killed that son, and that son rose up for the throne, lay with his wives, and had David on the run. Had the Lord asked David whether he wanted to be put to death that day or to take this, he would have begged for death; it is a terrible thing to fall into the hands of the Lord (Hebrews 10:31).

David did not answer that he was king; he confessed his sin against the Lord and accepted the judgment (2 Samuel 12:13). Nathan said the Lord had put away his sin and he would not die, but because the deed had given the enemies of the Lord great occasion to blaspheme, the child would surely die (2 Samuel 12:13-14). The judgment of David was that child being put to death: the Most High keeps mercy and forgives iniquity, yet does not clear the guilty, and visits the fathers’ iniquity upon the children (Exodus 34:7). David got pardoned, but he did not get cleared.

While the child lived David fasted and lay all night upon the earth; when it died he rose, washed, worshipped and ate, for he knew it was of the Most High and no amount of prayer would bring the child back (2 Samuel 12:15-23). Through the judgment Solomon was still born, and through David’s lineage Christ (2 Samuel 12:24-25). People who want to justify wrongdoing always run to David and Bath-sheba, but you are not King David: he was a man like the rest of us, and this was his mess up.

cases.offense: Somebody with a spiritual mind made it plain that she was Bath-sheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite: this was somebody’s wife. Wisdom and understanding were right there, and he ignored them; he sent messengers and took her anyway, and lay with her, and she conceived (2 Samuel 11:4-5). Satan put that lust in him to where he did not care: what he saw became desire, desire became action, he tried to cover it up, and the consequences came. Bath-sheba was not innocent either; she was complicit: when David called for her she went, she did not refuse because she was married, and it was consensual, not rape.
cases.judgment: The Lord sent Nathan with a parable of a rich man who spared his own flock and took the poor man’s one little ewe lamb, and David swore that the man should die and restore fourfold, because he had no pity (2 Samuel 12:1-6). In judging that man he was unknowingly pronouncing sentence on himself; the rich man was David, the poor man was Uriah, and the ewe lamb was his wife. Nathan told him he was the man: the Most High had given him the kingdom, Saul’s house and protection from Saul, and if David had only asked, He would have given him anything (2 Samuel 12:7-9). There is a term called suicide by cop; David committed murder by the hand of another nation, for he set the whole thing up.

cases.name: Uriah the Hittite
cases.charge: Refusing to go down to his house to eat and drink and lie with his wife while the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents and his brethren were encamped in the field, even when made drunk
cases.summary: Uriah the Hittite, one of David’s mighty men, was called home from the siege of Rabbah so that the king’s sin could be covered (2 Samuel 11:6; 2 Samuel 23:39). He would not go down to his house but slept at the door of the king’s house, for the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents and his lord Joab was encamped in the open fields (2 Samuel 11:9-11). Made drunk, he still would not go, and he was sent back carrying the letter that ordered his death (2 Samuel 11:13-15). David slew an innocent man who had done nothing, and the Lord named him in the judgment (2 Samuel 12:9).
offenseFull: David sent to Joab for Uriah, and when he came, asked him how Joab did and how the people did and how the war prospered, then told him to go down to his house and wash his feet, and a mess of meat from the king followed him (2 Samuel 11:6-8). Uriah was a soldier and a warrior, not part of the king’s circle, and now the king was making small talk with him as if they were good friends. He is listed among the mighty men, and not everybody gets that significance (2 Samuel 23:39). The names Hittite and Ammonite among the thirty do not mean they were Hamites in David’s army; they dwelt in those lands after Israel removed the nations from the coasts.

But Uriah slept at the door of the king’s house with all the servants of his lord and went not down to his house (2 Samuel 11:9). Asked why, he answered that the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents and Joab and the servants of his lord were encamped in the open fields, so how could he go into his house to eat and drink and lie with his wife; as the king lived, he would not do it (2 Samuel 11:10-11). That is what Moses asked the children of Gad and of Reuben, whether their brethren should go to war while they sat still (Numbers 32:6). His brothers were at war, and he would not be home and comfortable with his wife; he would be on the battlefield with his brothers. He was a faithful brother, faithful to the mission, and he understood the mission; that is real brotherhood.

David kept him another day, called him to eat and drink before him, and made him drunk, and at evening he went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house (2 Samuel 11:12-13). Even drunk, when a man might just go home to sleep it off, he still slept at the king’s house and would not go down; his wife was there, and she never even saw him. He was a real soldier. That loyalty was probably killing David all the more, because David could not deceive this man into lying with his wife. In the spirit Uriah was telling the king that the only way to be rid of him was to kill him, for he was a loyal soldier to the end.

In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah, ordering that he be set in the forefront of the hottest battle and abandoned, that he might be smitten and die (2 Samuel 11:14-15). Uriah went with his own death notice and handed it to Joab; the brother was sent to deliver his own death sentence to his executioner. Joab assigned him to a place where he knew the valiant men were, the hardest fighters of the adversary, and some of David’s servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite died also (2 Samuel 11:16-17). This was premeditated murder.
judgmentFull: Joab knew what the king really wanted, so he made sure the messenger named Uriah as dead, and David answered that the sword devours one as well as another (2 Samuel 11:18-25). Being content with murder is a wicked thing to do. But the thing that David had done displeased the Most High, because he set the man up to be murdered on a battlefield; the Lord sees all things (2 Samuel 11:27).

The Lord sent Nathan with the parable of the rich man who took the poor man’s one little ewe lamb: the rich man was David, the poor man was Uriah the Hittite, and the ewe lamb was his wife (2 Samuel 12:1-6). Nathan named him to the king’s face: David had killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword, taken his wife, and slain him with the sword of the children of Ammon (2 Samuel 12:9). That is murder by the hand of another nation. A curse lies on the man who strikes his neighbour in secret and on the man who takes a reward to kill an innocent person; the reward was that woman, and that is a hitman (Deuteronomy 27:24-25).

What Uriah did before is in the Most High’s hands; what is known is what is written here. The record of the kings keeps his name: David did right all his days except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite, a wrong from which David repented (1 Kings 15:5). In his psalm of repentance David asked to be delivered from bloodguiltiness, and that is Uriah (Psalm 51:14). The genealogy of Christ keeps it too: David fathered Solomon by the woman who had been the wife of Urias (Matthew 1:6).

cases.name: Amnon
cases.charge: Forcing his half sister Tamar by subtlety and strength, then hating her and putting her out and bolting the door after her
cases.summary: Amnon the son of David was so vexed for his half sister Tamar that he fell sick, and his subtle friend Jonadab told him to feign sickness and ask for her to be sent to him (2 Samuel 13:1-6). He cleared the room so there would be no witnesses, and being stronger than she, forced her; then he hated her more than he had loved her and had her put out and the door bolted (2 Samuel 13:9-18). David was very wroth and did nothing about it, and after two full years Absalom killed him for what he did to Tamar (2 Samuel 13:21-29).
offenseFull: Amnon loved Absalom’s fair sister Tamar and was so vexed that he fell sick, for she was a virgin and he thought it hard to do anything to her (2 Samuel 13:1-2). She was his half sister: they had the same father, King David, but different mothers, and Tamar and Absalom had the same mother. Jonadab, his cousin, was a very subtle man who knew exactly how to get over on somebody; the counsellor who is supposed to give godly counsel can tell you how to be the devil (2 Samuel 13:3).

Jonadab told him to lie down and make himself sick, and when his father came, to ask that Tamar come and dress meat in his sight, that he might eat at her hand (2 Samuel 13:4-5). She made cakes in his sight, but he refused to eat and sent every man out; he cleared the room first so there would be no witnesses, then seized his own sister (2 Samuel 13:8-11).

She begged him not to force her, for no such thing ought to be done in Israel, and not to do this folly, for he would be as one of the fools in Israel; let him rather speak to the king (2 Samuel 13:12-13). He would not hearken, because the lust demon was on him, and being stronger than she, he forced her (2 Samuel 13:14). Tamar herself calls it folly, a sin, a thing that ought not to be done in Israel. Any man talking about forcing a woman is wicked; rape is not good in the Bible, and it is the same as murder. When a man forces a betrothed young woman in the field, only the man dies and nothing is done to her, for the case is like a man attacking his neighbour and killing him; she cried, and it was done where no one could hear her (Deuteronomy 22:25-27). The law lays the whole weight of the crime on the man. On top of that she was his sister, and the curse stands on the man who lies with his sister (Leviticus 18:9; Deuteronomy 27:22).

Then Amnon hated her exceedingly, more than he had loved her, and told her to be gone (2 Samuel 13:15). She answered that sending her away was a greater evil than the other: the disrespect was worse than the rape (2 Samuel 13:16). He had his servant put her out and bolt the door after her, so that she could not come back in (2 Samuel 13:17-18). She wore a garment of diverse colours, the dress of the king’s virgin daughters, those able to be married; that was part of the order in the kingdom, and it is why we wear garments today, rehearsing the righteous acts (2 Samuel 13:18).
judgmentFull: Tamar put ashes on her head, rent her garment and went out crying; Absalom told her to hold her peace for now, since he was her brother, and she remained desolate in his house (2 Samuel 13:19-20).

David was upset at what happened to Tamar but did nothing about it. He could easily have put Amnon to death, but he was guilt-stricken for what he did with Bath-sheba and Uriah; the Lord had said He would bring evil into his house, and David felt he was being judged and could not judge what he was just as guilty of (2 Samuel 12:10-11). By the law the man who forced her was to die, and David was passive as a leader. Absalom was one of those men who holds a grudge for years just to get someone back, and these are people who know the law and know they are Israel.

After two full years Absalom held a sheepshearing at Baal-hazor and pressed the king until Amnon and all the king’s sons went with him; he was setting Amnon up, maneuvering him out of the city and among his own servants (2 Samuel 13:23-27). He told them to wait until Amnon was merry with wine, then to strike, and they killed him for what he did to Tamar (2 Samuel 13:28-29).

A man may kill through his malice, but no one escapes the Lord’s hand; the rapist is going to be judged one way or the other, for the Most High will find him at some point (Wisdom of Solomon 16:14-15). This was the working out of the judgment that the sword would never depart from David’s house; none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did, but he did it, and this is the punishment (2 Samuel 12:10). The Most High had those things play out for a reason, to weed out the undesirable among those around David in his kingdom. David mourned for his son every day, and even through all of it he still showed compassion (2 Samuel 13:37-39).

cases.name: Absalom
cases.charge: Murder of his brother Amnon in his own vengeance; stealing the hearts of the men of Israel by flattery; conspiracy and rebellion against the king his father; lying with his father’s concubines before all Israel
cases.summary: Absalom killed his brother Amnon for forcing their sister Tamar, fled, and was brought home (2 Samuel 13:28-14:33). Then he stood by the gate and stole the hearts of the men of Israel (2 Samuel 15:1-6). He raised a conspiracy at Hebron with Ahithophel, drove his father out of Jerusalem, and went in unto his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel (2 Samuel 15:7-16:22). Caught by the head in an oak, he was slain by Joab; the Lord also put him to death (2 Samuel 18:9-15).
offenseFull: Absalom was upset with his father because Amnon forced their sister and David was passive toward judgment upon him. By the law the man who forced her was to die, and whoever kills a man is to be put to death, so his anger had cause (Deuteronomy 22:25; Leviticus 24:17). But he rendered justice on his own, killing his brother at the sheepshearing, and ran away to Geshur (2 Samuel 13:23-38). Vengeance belongs to the Lord, who will repay; instead of waiting for the Lord’s judgment he avenged himself on his own brother, which is against the law (Romans 12:19). In all Israel none was so praised as Absalom for his beauty; beauty became his identity, and behind it came ambition, rebellion against his father, civil war, and death hanging by that very hair (2 Samuel 14:25-26).

He prepared chariots and horses and fifty men to run before him, stood beside the way of the gate, told every man who came for judgment that his matters were good and right but no man was deputed of the king to hear him, and wished that he were made judge in the land (2 Samuel 15:1-4). He was still angry with the king over Tamar; now he wanted to be the judge and wanted the throne, saying that King David was an unjust king. When any man bowed to him he took his hand and kissed him, and so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel (2 Samuel 15:5-6). That is the sneakiness: instead of going to the king and resolving things, he got into the king’s good graces, then went around patting people on the back behind the king’s back, so that he could later betray him. That is being friendish, showing people friendship without being a true friend.

After forty years he asked leave to pay a vow at Hebron and sent spies through all the tribes to proclaim at the sound of the trumpet that Absalom reigned in Hebron, and two hundred men went with him in their simplicity, knowing nothing (2 Samuel 15:7-11). That is the simplicity of a lot of brothers in Israel: a man who says all the nice things goes completely against leadership and out of order, and men follow him carnally, not spiritually, because he kissed their hand. He sent for Ahithophel, David’s counsellor, and the conspiracy was strong (2 Samuel 15:12). Ahithophel was Bath-sheba’s grandfather, for Eliam her father was his son, and he was angry with David for destroying his granddaughter’s marriage and killing her husband (2 Samuel 23:34; 2 Samuel 11:3).

David fled barefoot and weeping up Olivet (2 Samuel 15:13-30). Absalom wanted the kingdom from his father because he had envy and jealousy and hatred, and Ahithophel counselled him to go in unto his father’s concubines and shame him openly, so that all Israel would hear he was abhorred of his father; they spread a tent on the top of the house, and he went in unto them in the sight of all Israel (2 Samuel 16:21-22). This is the exact fulfilment of what the Most High spoke by Nathan, that what David did secretly would be done before all Israel and before the sun; it was not coincidence, it was prophesied (2 Samuel 12:11-12). A curse lies on the man who lies with his father’s wife (Deuteronomy 27:20).
judgmentFull: David prayed that the Lord would turn Ahithophel’s counsel into foolishness and sent his friend Hushai back to defeat it; Hushai was a real friend, not a friendish one (2 Samuel 15:31-37; 2 Samuel 16:16-19). The Lord had ordained that the good counsel of Ahithophel be defeated, so as to bring evil upon Absalom; the Most High moved Absalom’s heart to listen to Hushai, which would be his demise (2 Samuel 17:14). The Lord was working with Hushai and David, while Satan was in the spirit of Absalom and Ahithophel. When his counsel was not followed, Ahithophel hanged himself as a traitor (2 Samuel 17:23).

David charged Joab, Abishai and Ittai to deal gently with the young man for his sake; even after Absalom defiled his concubines and stole the people’s hearts, David still sought to make amends with his son (2 Samuel 18:1-5). The wood devoured more people that day than the sword, and Absalom, riding on a mule, was caught by the head in a great oak and left hanging, yet alive (2 Samuel 18:6-9).

The man who saw him would not touch the king’s son for a thousand shekels, because of the king’s charge; Joab took three darts and thrust them through Absalom’s heart while he was yet alive in the oak, and ten of his armourbearers slew him (2 Samuel 18:10-15). Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder; he could have brought Absalom back alive for his father to make amends, but he did what he wanted. The Lord also put Absalom to death; the Lord killed two birds with one stone, Ahithophel and Absalom. When brothers betray their own brothers there is nothing else for them; as Christ said, it would be better for him to have a millstone hung about his neck and be drowned, for he is a traitor (Matthew 18:6).

When Cushi brought the news, David went up to the chamber over the gate and wept for his son, wishing he had died in his place (2 Samuel 18:31-33). A man’s heart has many devices, but the Lord’s counsel stands; promotion comes from the Most High, who places every member in the body as He pleases, not from a man taking the seat himself (Proverbs 19:21; 1 Corinthians 12:18).

cases.name: Ahithophel
cases.charge: Treason against King David his master; counselling Absalom to go in to his father’s concubines and asking for twelve thousand men to smite the king; carrying secret hatred and a grudge for years, until it ended in his hanging himself
cases.summary: Ahithophel the Gilonite was David’s counsellor, whose counsel was as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God, and he joined the conspiracy of Absalom (2 Samuel 15:12; 2 Samuel 16:23). He counselled Absalom to go in to his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel, and asked for twelve thousand men to pursue David that night and smite the king only (2 Samuel 16:21-22; 2 Samuel 17:1-3). Bath-sheba was his granddaughter, and he carried that grudge for years (2 Samuel 23:34; 2 Samuel 11:3). The Lord turned his counsel into foolishness, and when it was not followed he put his household in order and hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:14; 2 Samuel 17:23).
offenseFull: Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counsellor, from his city Giloh while he offered sacrifices, and the conspiracy was strong (2 Samuel 15:12). His counsel in those days, both with David and with Absalom, was as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God (2 Samuel 16:23): he had the gift of gab, so persuasive that his advice sounded almost biblical, like talking to an angel of the Most High. He was David’s own counsellor turned traitor, the devil the Bible speaks of, working deceit and betrayal from inside the gates of Israel (Micah 2:8). It was betrayal by a familiar friend who did eat of David’s bread, and it is prophetic of somebody else (Psalms 41:9; Psalms 55:12-14).
David knew Ahithophel was an eloquent, spiritual man whose counsel was always on point, and he prayed that the Lord would turn it into foolishness (2 Samuel 15:31).

Ahithophel’s first counsel was that Absalom go in to his father’s concubines, left to keep the house, so that all Israel would hear he was abhorred of his father; they spread a tent on the top of the house and it was done in the sight of all Israel (2 Samuel 16:20-22). It shamed David openly, and it was the exact fulfilment of the word in chapter 12, that what David did secretly would be done before all Israel and before the sun (2 Samuel 12:11-12). It was not coincidence; it was prophesied, and none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did, for the Most High keeps mercy but by no means clears the guilty (Exodus 34:7).

Then he asked for twelve thousand men to pursue David that night while he was weary and weak handed, and smite the king only (2 Samuel 17:1-3). He wanted the victory and the bragging rights of being the one who killed King David. Though it is wrong to kill your own brother, it was good war counsel to overcome David.

When people do things there is a reason. Eliam the son of Ahithophel was a mighty man in David’s army, and Bath-sheba was the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite (2 Samuel 23:34; 2 Samuel 11:3): Ahithophel was her grandfather. He was counselling David while Joab besieged Rabbah and would have been in the throne room when Uriah was called home (2 Samuel 11:1-17). He was angry with David for destroying his granddaughter’s marriage and killing his grandson-in-law. He lived with that for years, carried the grudge and bare hatred, lying in wait, and when he saw the opportunity he used Absalom to disgrace David’s household. Absalom and Ahithophel flocked together because both were angry at King David. Secret hatred can take years to be revealed; brothers can sit next to you and hold personal hatred for you.
judgmentFull: Absalom wanted a second opinion and called Hushai the Archite. There is safety in a multitude of counsellors, but only where the counsel is according to thus saith the Lord. Hushai said Ahithophel’s counsel was not good at this time, and counselled that all Israel be gathered from Dan to Beer-sheba with Absalom going to battle in his own person (2 Samuel 17:5-13). It was deliberately inaccurate counsel to give David room to escape; Hushai was a counterintelligence agent, a spy planted in righteousness, always siding with King David.

Absalom and Israel preferred it, for the Lord had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to bring evil upon Absalom (2 Samuel 17:14). The Lord was working with Hushai and David, while Satan was in the spirit of Absalom and Ahithophel. There are many devices in a man’s heart, but it is the counsel of the Lord that stands (Proverbs 19:21).

When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his ass, went home to his city, put his household in order, and hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23). The Lord turned his counsel into foolishness, and he killed himself as a traitor; Absalom also the Lord put to death, two at one stroke. For brothers who betray their own brothers there is nothing else, as Christ said of the millstone (Matthew 18:6). The evil counsel he devised bit its author: evil pursues sinners, but to the righteous good is repaid (Proverbs 13:21). To be righteous is to keep all the commandments (Deuteronomy 6:25). David, who did not want to war against his own son, was repaid good; he was forgiven of God and died as God’s friend.

The grudge was Ahithophel’s ruin. Hatred goes to grudges, and grudges turn to wanting to murder, against the law that forbids hating thy brother in thine heart or bearing any grudge against the children of thy people (Leviticus 19:17-18). Whoever takes vengeance shall find vengeance from the Lord, and a man must forgive his neighbour’s hurt for his own sins to be forgiven (Ecclesiasticus 28:1-2). Hatred, wrath, seditions and murders are works of the flesh that shall not inherit the kingdom of God (Galatians 5:20-21). Ahithophel and Absalom were very eloquent men, with knowledge, understanding and wisdom, but because of their hatred, without charity, they were nothing (1 Corinthians 13:1-2).

He was David’s own counsellor turned traitor, the devil the Bible speaks of, working deceit and betrayal from inside the gates of Israel (Micah 2:8). It was betrayal by a familiar friend who did eat of David’s bread, and it is prophetic of somebody else (Psalms 41:9; Psalms 55:12-14).

cases.name: Ittai the Gittite
cases.charge: Swearing by the Lord and by the king’s life to be with the king in death or in life, and passing over with him when he fled from Absalom
cases.summary: As David fled from Absalom, the six hundred Gittites who came after him from Gath passed on before the king (2 Samuel 15:18). David told Ittai the Gittite to return, since he was a stranger and an exile who had only just come, and wished him mercy and truth; but Ittai swore that wherever the king was, in death or life, there would his servant be, and David let him pass over with all his men and little ones (2 Samuel 15:19-22). Ittai showed a level of loyalty that David respected. When the people were set in array, a third part was under his hand (2 Samuel 18:2).
offenseFull: A messenger told David that the hearts of the men of Israel were after Absalom, and David told his servants to arise and flee, lest Absalom overtake them suddenly and smite the city with the edge of the sword (2 Samuel 15:13-14). David, being the man of war that he is, saw everyone starting to follow Absalom, and instead of sitting there like a dummy he chose to leave and strategize while he was out. All his servants passed on beside him, and the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men which came after him from Gath, passed on before the king (2 Samuel 15:16-18).

Then the king asked Ittai the Gittite why he went with them too, and told him to return to his place and abide with the king, for he was a stranger and also an exile (2 Samuel 15:19). He had come but yesterday; should David that day make him go up and down with them, when David himself went wherever he could? David told him to return and take back his brethren, and wished him mercy and truth (2 Samuel 15:20).

Ittai answered with an oath by the Lord and by the life of the king, that in whatever place the king should be, whether in death or life, even there also would his servant be (2 Samuel 15:21). David told him to go and pass over, and Ittai the Gittite passed over, and all his men, and all the little ones that were with him (2 Samuel 15:22). Ittai showed a level of loyalty that David respected, so David let him come. This loyalty in the face of trouble is the same thing seen throughout Israel’s story.

All the country wept with a loud voice, and all the people passed over the brook Kidron toward the way of the wilderness, and the king also passed over (2 Samuel 15:23). David sent the ark back to the city in faith: if he found favour in the eyes of the Most High, he would be brought again to see it and its habitation, and if not, let the Most High do to him as seemed good (2 Samuel 15:25-26). That is how much faith David had.
judgmentFull: David numbered the people that were with him and set captains of thousands and captains of hundreds over them, and sent forth a third part under the hand of Joab, a third under Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and a third under the hand of Ittai the Gittite (2 Samuel 18:1-2). He said he would surely go forth with them himself.

The people answered that he should not go forth, for he was worth ten thousand of them, and it was better that he succour them out of the city, and David hearkened to their counsel and said that what seemed best to them he would do (2 Samuel 18:3-4). He did not run a dictatorship. In a time when he could not trust his own flesh and blood, he trusted the proven men he had warred with for years.

The king charged Joab and Abishai and Ittai to deal gently for his sake with the young man, even with Absalom, and all the people heard when the king gave all the captains charge (2 Samuel 18:5). Even after Absalom defiled his concubines and stole the people’s hearts, David still sought to make amends with his son.

The battle was in the wood of Ephraim, and Israel was slain before the servants of David, twenty thousand men; the wood devoured more people that day than the sword (2 Samuel 18:6-8). A man who saw Absalom hanging in an oak would not put forth his hand against the king’s son, because he had heard the king’s charge (2 Samuel 18:10-13). Joab took three darts and thrust them through Absalom’s heart while he was yet alive (2 Samuel 18:14). Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder; he could have brought Absalom back alive for his father to make amends, but he did what he wanted.

cases.name: Shimei son of Gera
cases.charge: Cursing the Lord’s anointed king and casting stones at him, blaming him for the blood of Saul’s house; and, spared by David’s oath, breaking his own oath to Solomon by going out of Jerusalem to Gath
cases.summary: As David came to Bahurim fleeing from Absalom, Shimei the son of Gera, of the house of Saul, came out cursing him, calling him a bloody man and a man of Belial, and casting stones at him and his servants (2 Samuel 16:5-8). Saul was the wicked one who tried to kill David, yet Shimei cursed David as if David were in the wrong. David would not let Abishai take his head, for the Lord had bidden him curse (2 Samuel 16:9-12). When the king returned, Shimei confessed his sin and David swore he would not die (2 Samuel 19:18-23). Solomon commanded him to dwell in Jerusalem on pain of death; after three years he went to Gath after his runaway servants and broke the oath, and Benaiah put him to death (1 Kings 2:36-46).
offenseFull: When King David came to Bahurim, Shimei the son of Gera, a man of the family of the house of Saul, came out cursing as he came, and cast stones at David and at all his servants, though all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left (2 Samuel 16:5-6). He was a Benjamite, a wicked Benjamite and not a righteous one. He could have died on the spot, for the mighty men were nothing to play with; but sometimes people do things without understanding what they are doing, and Satan is just using them.

He called David a bloody man and a man of Belial, a man of Satan, and said the Lord had returned upon him all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose stead he reigned, and had delivered the kingdom to Absalom his son (2 Samuel 16:7-8). Saul was the wicked one who tried to kill David, and it was by the hand of the Most High that Saul did not succeed. Yet Shimei cursed David as if David were in the wrong, because word gets around, people gossip and blame, and he saw David at a low state and went to rub it in his face. He showed his hatred and disdain for David for the kingdom being translated to him, blaming him for Saul’s death and for everything. He literally thought he was right in cursing David; he thought David was wicked for what he did. But when we read the scripture, we see he was not right.

David did commit murder and adultery, but God forgave him; he was still a prophet of God, righteous because he repented, though he still paid for what he did. The Lord had said he would raise up evil against David out of his own house, and when the leader fell, the enemy used it to throw it in his face. Even today people look for something to happen in IUIC and run their mouths. The law says thou shalt not revile the gods, meaning do not hate or speak evil of your leaders; the gods are the leaders over you, for the Most High calls us gods and children of the Most High (Exodus 22:28; Psalms 82:6). Paul quoted this very law when rebuked for speaking against the high priest (Acts 23:5).

Abishai the son of Zeruiah asked why this dead dog should curse the king, and asked leave to go over and take off his head (2 Samuel 16:9). But the king asked what he had to do with them, the sons of Zeruiah, and said to let him curse, for the Lord had bidden him; if his own son sought his life, how much more this Benjamite (2 Samuel 16:10-11). If it was of the Most High, let him do it, just as the Most High brings people to our forums and classrooms who bicker and bring confusion, sometimes to test the patience of those who pray for patience.

David was in his repentant state. He hoped the Lord would look on his affliction and requite him good for that cursing (2 Samuel 16:12), and that is why he was a man after the Lord’s heart: he could acknowledge his faults, his shortcomings and his sins, and always go to the Lord asking for mercy. He remembered that the sword would never depart from his house because he had killed Uriah and taken his wife (2 Samuel 12:9-10), and he prayed to be delivered from bloodguiltiness (Psalms 51:14). When something happens to you, consider whether it is payback for something you have done; vengeance is the Lord’s, for you do not know why he is doing what he is doing. If you take it patiently when you do well and suffer for it, this is acceptable with God (1 Peter 2:20). Shimei went along the hillside over against him, cursing, throwing stones and casting dust (2 Samuel 16:13).
judgmentFull: When the king returned, Shimei hastened down with a thousand men of Benjamin and fell before him at Jordan, begging him not to impute iniquity to him nor remember the day he did perversely, for he knew he had sinned (2 Samuel 19:16-20). Abishai said he should be put to death for cursing the Lord’s anointed, but David rebuked the sons of Zeruiah as adversaries, asking whether any man should be put to death in Israel that day when he knew he was king, and he swore to Shimei that he would not die (2 Samuel 19:21-23). David understood grace long before the New Testament, for grace has always been around.

At the last David charged Solomon concerning Shimei, who had cursed him with a grievous curse in the day he went to Mahanaim, to whom David had sworn by the Lord that he would not put him to death with the sword: Solomon was not to hold him guiltless, but as a wise man would know what he ought to do to him (1 Kings 2:8-9). David had sworn that he himself would not kill him; Solomon would.

Shimei was commanded to build a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, never crossing the brook Kidron on pain of death, and he agreed (1 Kings 2:36-38). After three years he went to Gath after his runaway servants and broke the oath, so Solomon had Benaiah put him to death, and the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon (1 Kings 2:39-46).

cases.name: Barzillai the Gileadite
cases.charge: Providing the king with sustenance while he lay at Mahanaim, helping him in the time of his need when he fled from Absalom
cases.summary: When David came to Mahanaim fleeing from Absalom, Shobi, Machir and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim brought beds, vessels, grain, honey, butter, sheep and cheese, for they said the people were hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness (2 Samuel 17:27-29). Barzillai was a very aged man of fourscore years and a very great man (2 Samuel 19:32). When the king returned he came down to conduct him over Jordan, declined to be fed in Jerusalem because at eighty he could no longer taste nor hear as he used to, and sent Chimham in his place; the king kissed and blessed him (2 Samuel 19:31-39). David requited his kindness to the next reign (1 Kings 2:7).
offenseFull: Absalom passed over Jordan with all the men of Israel and pitched in the land of Gilead, on the east side of Jordan, while David came to Mahanaim (2 Samuel 17:24-26). There Shobi the son of Nahash of Rabbah of the children of Ammon, Machir the son of Ammiel of Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim brought beds, basons, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched corn, beans, lentiles, parched pulse, honey, butter, sheep and cheese of kine for David and for the people with him to eat, for they said the people were hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness (2 Samuel 17:27-29). Barzillai was one of those that helped King David in the time of his need.

David said he had been young and now was old, yet had never seen the righteous forsaken (Psalms 37:25). He was talking from experience, because all those times he had to flee he never went hungry: when he fled from Saul he ate the shewbread from the temple, and when he fled from Absalom, Barzillai came with cheeses and food for him and his men. The Most High held him down. Those who keep the commandments shall not be ashamed in the evil time, and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied (Psalms 37:18-19). So the church took care of each other, and there was none among them that lacked (Acts 4:34); in evil times like these, Israel holds each other down.

Barzillai was a very aged man, even fourscore years old, and he had provided the king with sustenance while he lay at Mahanaim, for he was a very great man (2 Samuel 19:32). He came down from Rogelim and went over Jordan with the king to conduct him over (2 Samuel 19:31). The king invited him to come over and be fed with him in Jerusalem, and Barzillai asked how long he had to live that he should go up with the king (2 Samuel 19:33-34). At eighty years old he could no longer discern between good and evil, nor taste what he ate or drank, nor hear the voice of singing men and singing women, and he would not be a burden unto the king (2 Samuel 19:35). This tells you some of the things that beset us in our old age: some have heard grandparents who reached extreme age say they cannot taste their food, because at that age the bodily functions start to cease. He could not move around, eat, drink, hear or see as he used to, and he did not want to be a burden.

Man’s days were once hundreds of years; the Most High set them at a hundred and twenty (Genesis 6:3). The number of a man’s days at the most is a hundred years, so to see a hundred is extreme age (Ecclesiasticus 18:9), and the days of our years are threescore and ten, or by reason of strength fourscore (Psalms 90:10): a man is very aged at seventy and eighty. Eleazar was called a very aged man at fourscore and ten (2 Maccabees 6:24). The Lord kept cutting our lifespan down because of sin. By that measure Barzillai had lived a good life.

He asked to go only a little way over Jordan, to turn back and die in his own city and be buried by the grave of his father and his mother, and offered his servant Chimham to go over with the king in his place (2 Samuel 19:36-37).
judgmentFull: The king answered that Chimham should go over with him, that he would do to him whatever seemed good to Barzillai, and that whatever Barzillai required of him he would do. All the people went over Jordan, and the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own place (2 Samuel 19:38-39). King David was requiting the kind acts of this brother and showing his gratitude, because Barzillai was one of those that helped him in the time of his need.

In his last charge to Solomon, David told him to show kindness to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite and let them be of those that eat at his table, for so they came to him when he fled because of Absalom his brother (1 Kings 2:7).
