cases.name: Sheba son of Bichri
cases.charge: Insurrection against King David: blowing a trumpet and crying that Israel had no part in David nor inheritance in the son of Jesse, so that the men of Israel went up from following the king
cases.summary: After Absalom’s revolt the men of Israel and the men of Judah quarrelled over who had the right to bring the king back, the tribe strife that would later split the northern and southern kingdoms (2 Samuel 19:41-43). Sheba the son of Bichri, a Benjamite, a man of Belial, a devil, blew a trumpet and cried that they had no part in David, and the men of Israel followed him (2 Samuel 20:1-2). Joab pursued him to Abel of Beth-maachah and battered the wall; a wise woman of the city spoke with Joab, negotiated, and stopped the onslaught of the city, and the people cut off Sheba’s head and cast it out to Joab (2 Samuel 20:14-22).
offenseFull: A quarrel arose between the men of Israel and the men of Judah over who had the right to bring the king back. Judah claimed the king was near of kin to them, being of the tribe of Judah, while Israel claimed ten parts in the king and more right in David, and the words of Judah were fiercer than the words of Israel (2 Samuel 19:41-43). This was the tribe strife that would later split the northern and southern kingdoms, though they were all Israel.

A man of Belial, a devil, named Sheba the son of Bichri, a Benjamite, blew a trumpet and cried that they had no part in David nor inheritance in the son of Jesse, and every man of Israel went up from David to follow Sheba, while the men of Judah clave unto their king from Jordan to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 20:1-2).

David came to his house in Jerusalem and took the ten concubines Absalom had defiled, put them in ward and fed them, but went not in unto them; they were shut up in widowhood until the day of their death (2 Samuel 20:3).

David told Amasa to assemble the men of Judah within three days, but Amasa tarried longer than the set time. So David sent Abishai with Joab’s men, the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty men to pursue Sheba, lest he escape into fenced cities (2 Samuel 20:4-7). At the great stone in Gibeon, Joab came to Amasa with a sword secretly fastened, took him by the beard with his right hand as if to kiss him, and smote him in the fifth rib, and he died at one stroke (2 Samuel 20:8-10). Joab was grimy and shady, murdering the man who had been named captain in his place.

Joab pursued him through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maachah, and the Berites gathered together and went after him; when the people heard that he was hunting this man, they joined him, because they loved King David. They cast up a bank against the city, and all the people with Joab battered the wall to throw it down (2 Samuel 20:14-15).
judgmentFull: With all those men of war coming to tear the city down, a wise woman cried out of the city and asked that Joab come near so she could speak with him (2 Samuel 20:16). She had enough respect to come to the leader who was bringing all this harm on the city and ask him to hear her. She asked whether he was Joab, and so showed him that she recognised his authority (2 Samuel 20:17). She asked him to hear the words of his handmaid, speaking to him respectfully; she was not all up in his space, but was humbling herself to him, and he gave her a chance to speak.

She reminded him of the old saying that men would surely ask counsel at Abel and so end the matter, and told him she was one of them that were peaceable and faithful in Israel (2 Samuel 20:18-19). So she let him know her character, and that she had a good reputation among the Israelites and her people. Then she asked why he sought to destroy a city and a mother in Israel, and swallow up the inheritance of the Lord; we are the Most High’s people. In war a man comes in wanting to take that head, so she calmed him down first and spoke to him reasonably and peaceably.

Joab answered that far be it from him to swallow up or destroy: a man of mount Ephraim, Sheba the son of Bichri, had lifted up his hand against the king, even against David; deliver him only, and he would depart from the city (2 Samuel 20:20-21). She negotiated with Joab: a woman came out in wisdom, negotiated, and stopped the onslaught of the city. She promised that Sheba’s head would be thrown to him over the wall, and went to all the people in her wisdom; they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and cast it out to Joab, and he blew a trumpet and they retired from the city every man to his tent, and Joab returned to Jerusalem unto the king (2 Samuel 20:21-22).

That is why wise women are wanted among the people, why their talents are praised and honour shown to them, and why they are not kept beneath, for the people know the history of their foremothers. The Most High will put that kind of spirit on sisters, so that they know how to talk to men and how to become peacemakers, and a man who is supposed to have wisdom should be able to spot that, and not let a whole house be destroyed because he has a big mouth. There are sisters with gifts that can do certain things that the brothers cannot. Such a sister is not trying to usurp authority over anyone; she is trying to help the nation. Know the difference between help and usurping authority over the man; it is a big difference.
Joab was over all the host of Israel, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and the officers of David were set in order (2 Samuel 20:23-26).

cases.name: Rizpah
cases.charge: Spreading sackcloth upon the rock from the beginning of harvest until water dropped out of heaven, suffering neither the birds by day nor the beasts by night to touch the hanged of Saul’s house
cases.summary: Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, Saul’s concubine, lost her two sons when seven of Saul’s house were delivered to the Gibeonites and hanged before the Lord at the beginning of barley harvest, because Saul broke Israel’s oath and slew the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1-9). She spread sackcloth upon the rock and kept the birds off them by day and the beasts by night until the rain fell (2 Samuel 21:10). When David was told, he took the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead and buried them with the bones of the hanged in the sepulchre of Kish, and after that the Most High was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:11-14).
offenseFull: Rizpah was Saul’s concubine. After Saul’s death, when Abner made himself strong for the house of Saul, Ishbosheth charged him over Rizpah, and Abner was very wroth: he had shown kindness to the house of Saul and not delivered them to David, and now was charged with a fault concerning this woman. Abner then turned to go with David and the Lord (2 Samuel 3:6-10).

There was a famine in the days of David three years, year after year, and the Lord answered David that it was for Saul and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites. Saul broke his word: the Gibeonites were not of the children of Israel but of the remnant of the Amorites, and Israel had sworn unto them, yet Saul sought to slay them in his zeal (2 Samuel 21:1-2). The blessing was not truly coming from the Gibeonites; it was coming from the Most High, who was teaching Israel a lesson through this famine: pay what you vow. Let your yea be yea and your nay be nay; Saul went back on his word, and the whole house paid for it (Ecclesiastes 5:4-6; Matthew 5:37). The Gibeonites would take no silver nor gold, but asked for seven of Saul’s sons to be hanged unto the Lord in Gibeah of Saul (2 Samuel 21:3-6).

The king spared Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan because of the Lord’s oath between David and Jonathan; David did not go back on his oath (2 Samuel 21:7). But he took the two sons of Rizpah, Armoni and Mephibosheth, whom she bare unto Saul, and the five sons of Michal, and delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, who hanged them in the hill before the Lord. They fell all seven together and were put to death in the days of harvest, in the first days, in the beginning of barley harvest (2 Samuel 21:8-9).

Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for her upon the rock from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and she suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day nor the beasts of the field by night (2 Samuel 21:10).
judgmentFull: It was told David what Rizpah had done, and he went and took the bones of Saul and of Jonathan his son from the men of Jabesh-gilead, which had stolen them from the street of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them when they slew Saul in Gilboa (2 Samuel 21:11-12).

On the morrow of the battle the Philistines found Saul and his three sons fallen in mount Gilboa. They cut off his head, stripped off his armour, and sent into the land of the Philistines round about to publish it in the house of their idols (1 Samuel 31:8-9). They put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth, the fertility goddess; it is the same thing as Easter, the god that Christianity worships every April. They fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31:10). The Canaanites resided in that area, and the Philistines and Canaanites were pretty much the same people, Hamites in league together. Jonathan’s body had been hanged in the temple of Dagon, the fish god of the Hamites.

When the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, all the valiant men arose and went all night, took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, came to Jabesh and burnt them there, for they were defiled from that idol place; they buried the bones under a tree at Jabesh and fasted seven days, for they were now unclean from being in that area (1 Samuel 31:11-13).

David brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan, and they gathered the bones of them that were hanged, and buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish his father; they performed all that the king commanded, and after that the Most High was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:13-14). They took the bones down from Beth-shan and buried Saul and his sons in his home of inheritance.

cases.name: Saul’s house and the Gibeonites
cases.charge: Breaking the oath Israel sware to the Gibeonites by the Lord God of Israel, slaying them in his zeal to the children of Israel and Judah
cases.summary: A famine came in the days of David three years, year after year, and the Lord answered that it was for Saul and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites, to whom Israel had sworn in Joshua’s day (2 Samuel 21:1-2; Joshua 9:15). Saul broke his word, and the lesson the Most High was teaching Israel through the famine was to pay what you vow. The Gibeonites would take no silver nor gold and asked for seven of Saul’s sons; David spared Mephibosheth for the Lord’s oath, delivered the seven to be hanged before the Lord, and after the burial of Saul and Jonathan the Most High was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:3-14).
offenseFull: There was a famine in the days of David three years, year after year, and David enquired of the Lord, who answered that it was for Saul and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1). The Gibeonites were not of the children of Israel but of the remnant of the Amorites, and Israel had sworn unto them, yet Saul sought to slay them in his zeal (2 Samuel 21:2). Saul broke his word.

The oath went back to the conquest. The kings of the land, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite and the Jebusite, gathered to fight with Israel; these are Hamites, better known as Nilotic Africans (Joshua 9:1-2). The inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai and did work wilily, with old sacks, old and rent wine bottles, old shoes and garments, and dry and mouldy bread (Joshua 9:3-6). Israel was commanded to destroy all the inhabitants of the land, so their only hope was to pretend they were not of the land, and their props sold the story (Joshua 9:7-13).

The men took of their victuals and asked not counsel at the mouth of the Lord (Joshua 9:14). That is the first mistake, and it became a snare and a trap to Israel as a people; the Most High says counsel before every action (Ecclesiasticus 37:16). Joshua made a league to let them live, and the princes of the congregation sware unto them (Joshua 9:15).

When Israel heard three days later that they dwelt among them, the congregation murmured, but the princes held the line: they had sworn by the Lord God of Israel and might not touch them (Joshua 9:16-19). Our forefathers were wrong in one situation, but they were upright men in holding to their word. A vow made before the Most High stands, even one gotten by guile (Joshua 9:20). The Gibeonites were made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God, which means slaves, according to the law of the Most High pertaining to other nations (Joshua 9:21-27; Leviticus 25:44-46). The nations were made for a certain purpose; they are not in that purpose now because Israel has sinned and failed, and one day Israel will rise again to put them back in their rightful places (Isaiah 60:9-12).

When a vow is made unto God it is not to be deferred, for he has no pleasure in fools; it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay, and a man is not to say before the angel that it was an error (Ecclesiastes 5:4-6). Christ simplified it: let your yes be yes and your no be no, for whatever is more than these comes of evil (Matthew 5:37). Word is bond, and it is better not to swear at all than to cause yourself to sin by making an oath you cannot live up to. Saul went back on his word after he had given his yes to the Amorites, and the whole house paid for it.
judgmentFull: David asked the Gibeonites wherewith he should make the atonement, that they might bless the inheritance of the Lord (2 Samuel 21:3). The blessing was not truly coming from the Gibeonites; it was coming from the Most High, who was teaching Israel a lesson through this famine. They would have no silver nor gold of Saul nor of his house, but asked for seven sons of the man who consumed them, to be hanged unto the Lord in Gibeah of Saul, and the king said he would give them (2 Samuel 21:4-6).

The king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan the son of Saul, because of the Lord’s oath between David and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7). David did not go back on his oath; he had promised Jonathan that his seed would always eat at David’s table (1 Samuel 18:1-3; 2 Samuel 9:1-7). He was a surety for Jonathan’s house, for they made a bond, and his word was his bond.

The king took the two sons of Rizpah and the five sons of Michal and delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, who hanged them in the hill before the Lord; they fell all seven together and were put to death in the days of harvest, in the beginning of barley harvest (2 Samuel 21:8-9).

Rizpah spread sackcloth upon the rock and suffered neither the birds by day nor the beasts by night to touch them, and when David was told, he took the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the street of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them (2 Samuel 21:10-12). Jonathan’s body had been hanged in the temple of Dagon, the fish god of the Hamites. The bones of Saul and Jonathan were buried in the sepulchre of Kish his father, and after that the Most High was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:13-14).

cases.name: David’s numbering of the people
cases.charge: Numbering Israel and Judah in a spirit of pride against Joab’s counsel, when the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel; seventy thousand men dead of the pestilence
cases.summary: The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he moved David to number Israel and Judah; in the Chronicles account Satan stood up against Israel and provoked David to number Israel (2 Samuel 24:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1). The Most High wanted to judge Israel, and he used David and used Satan to do it. The king’s word prevailed against Joab, and as soon as the count was done David’s heart smote him. He chose to fall into the hand of the Lord, seventy thousand men died of the pestilence, and the plague was stayed when David bought the threshing floor of Araunah and offered there (2 Samuel 24:2-25).
offenseFull: Two accounts tell one event: in Second Samuel the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel and he moved David to number Israel and Judah, and in First Chronicles Satan stood up against Israel and provoked David to number Israel (2 Samuel 24:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1). It is all saying the same thing: God has an angel going on his behalf to accomplish his task, for the Lord brings forth his judgment by sending evil angels among them (Psalms 78:49). The issue was with Israel, and the Lord got David to number the children of Israel so that he could bring forth judgment.

There is no fight between God and Satan; Satan is an employee of God, and he cannot come into a man’s life without the okay from God: God chooses him, and Satan uses him. The lust was inside David as king, and Satan feeds on lust, tempting a man until he carries it out; a man in power gets puffed up with pride and wants to know how many people he is over.

Numbering the people in that spirit is unlawful, for the only one who is supposed to know the exact number of the people is God, and numbering was not the king’s job but the work of the Levites. When the Lord counted the children of Israel he started with twenty years old and upward and did not include the children, because the Lord does not want the number of the children of Israel as a whole to be known (Numbers 1:3).

Joab tried to talk sense into the king: God already knew the number, so why did the king delight in this thing and want to supersede God (2 Samuel 24:3)? Joab did not understand that behind it all the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel. The king’s word prevailed against Joab and the captains (2 Samuel 24:4). In Chronicles Joab left Levi and Benjamin out of the count, because the king’s word was abominable to him (1 Chronicles 21:3-6). God can take a man in a position of power and make him do things that are harmful to the people.

It took nine months and twenty days, and Joab brought eight hundred thousand valiant men of Israel that drew the sword and five hundred thousand of Judah, not counting the women and the children (2 Samuel 24:5-9). Today they call that a census. Those who control the earth take one every few years, not for the people’s good, but so that they know what level of force to use if they want to destroy them. A true leader aligned with God does not divulge that number; he does as Joab said, for God’s eyes are upon the nation and only he needs to know how many.
judgmentFull: David’s heart smote him; as soon as it was done it hit him, and he confessed that he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly (2 Samuel 24:10). The prophet Gad, David’s seer, brought three things to choose one: seven years of famine, three months fleeing before his enemies, or three days of pestilence (2 Samuel 24:11-13); in Chronicles the famine is three years (1 Chronicles 21:11-12).

David was in a great strait and chose to fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercies are great, and not into the hand of man (2 Samuel 24:14). He knew man would not show him the mercy the Most High would: whatever judgment the Lord wanted to bring forth, let it be his.

The Lord sent the pestilence upon Israel, not upon David, and there died from Dan to Beer-sheba seventy thousand men (2 Samuel 24:15). The reason for the seventy thousand is verse one: the Most High was angry at Israel. Each of those men individually might have done something wrong, and the Lord would allow some incident to occur and kill those who did wrong in his sight; the Lord still deals the same today. The same way God used the nations back then to correct Israel when they were disobedient, it is the same thing today; every time this judgment is seen, it is because of sin.

When the angel stretched out his hand upon Jerusalem, the Lord repented him of the evil and said it was enough (2 Samuel 24:16). David saw the angel, something we cannot see today, for this walk is by faith and the keeping of the commandments. He and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces, and he pleaded that he had sinned, but these sheep had done nothing (2 Samuel 24:17; 1 Chronicles 21:16-17).

Gad sent David to rear an altar in the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, who offered it freely, but David would not offer unto the Lord of that which cost him nothing; he bought the floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the plague was stayed (2 Samuel 24:18-25). In Chronicles he paid six hundred shekels of gold, and the Most High answered him by fire from heaven (1 Chronicles 21:25-27). True worship costs us something. That threshing floor in mount Moriah is where Solomon built the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 3:1).

cases.name: Adonijah
cases.charge: Exalting himself, saying, I will be king, while David yet lived, to usurp the throne the Lord gave Solomon; and after his pardon at the altar, coming with guile to ask for Abishag the Shunammite
cases.summary: While David was old, his son Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying he would be king; he took the throne to himself rather than receiving it from the Most High, and Joab and Abiathar followed him (1 Kings 1:5-10). David confirmed his oath that Solomon should reign, Solomon was anointed at Gihon, and Adonijah caught hold on the horns of the altar and was spared on condition that he show himself a worthy man (1 Kings 1:29-53). After David’s death he came with guile asking for Abishag the Shunammite to wife, and Solomon, discerning a reach for the throne, had him put to death (1 Kings 2:13-25).
offenseFull: King David was old and could get no heat, so his servants found Abishag the Shunammite, a woman of Issachar, to lie in his bosom; this happens with age, when the body no longer produces heat as in youth, and two that lie together have heat (1 Kings 1:1-3; Ecclesiastes 4:11). He knew her not: he did not have relations with her, and she was there only to keep him warm (1 Kings 1:4). She understood her purpose, to cherish the king and minister unto him, for the woman was created for the man.

Then Adonijah exalted himself, saying he would be king, and prepared chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run before him, and his father had not displeased him at any time by asking why he did so (1 Kings 1:5-6). David was still alive, and this son was already seeking power. He took the throne to himself rather than receiving it from the Most High. He was not the rightful heir, but he wanted the throne; he had a vainglorious and covetous spirit, seeking preeminence as Absalom did, and tried to usurp authority over Solomon.

He conferred with Joab and with Abiathar the priest, but Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan, Shimei, Rei and David’s mighty men were not with him (1 Kings 1:7-8). Joab was David’s right hand man, loyal to him but always doing underhanded evil, and David knew it and stayed quiet, for Joab was a necessary evil. Joab turned not after Absalom, but he turned after Adonijah (1 Kings 2:28): sometimes it takes certain spirits to bring out other spirits.

Adonijah slew sheep and oxen by the stone of Zoheleth and called the king’s sons, but not Nathan, Benaiah, the mighty men, or Solomon his brother (1 Kings 1:9-10). He left them out because he knew what he was doing was wrong; he had heard David tell Bathsheba that Solomon would be king. Nathan sent Bathsheba in to the king and came in after her to confirm her words, two witnesses establishing the matter (1 Kings 1:11-27).

David swore by the Lord that Solomon should reign after him and sit upon his throne that very day (1 Kings 1:29-30). The throne belonged to Solomon by that sworn word, for the Most High chose Solomon among David’s sons to sit upon the throne of the kingdom of the Lord (1 Chronicles 28:5). Solomon was set on the king’s own mule: to be seen on the king’s property meant the king was confirming him, as Christ rode upon an ass because that represents him being the next king. Zadok and Nathan anointed him at Gihon (1 Kings 1:32-40). Adonijah’s guests heard it and went every man his way, knowing they had made the wrong choice, and Adonijah, fearing Solomon, caught hold on the horns of the altar (1 Kings 1:41-50).
judgmentFull: Solomon showed mercy: if Adonijah would show himself a worthy man, not a hair of him would fall to the earth, but if wickedness were found in him, he would die. They brought him down from the altar, he bowed himself to King Solomon, and Solomon sent him to his house (1 Kings 1:51-53). The mercy came with a warning: Solomon was watching him.

After David slept with his fathers, Adonijah came to Bathsheba, whom he had plotted to have killed, and said he came peaceably; then he told her she knew the kingdom was his and that all Israel had set their faces on him to reign, but it was turned about and become his brother’s, for it was his from the Lord (1 Kings 2:10-15). It was never his. He was bitter, and once people are bitter they start running their mouths. He asked her to speak to Solomon to give him Abishag the Shunammite to wife (1 Kings 2:16-17).

He came with guile. It was not that he wanted a wife, for there were many wives to choose from; he asked for his father’s wife, knowing it was a gateway to usurping authority and overthrowing King Solomon. Nobody sits on the king’s mule, takes the crown off his head or takes his ring; to give him the king’s wife would be to confirm him as the rightful heir.

Bathsheba was not able to discern it and carried the request to her son (1 Kings 2:18-21). Solomon answered that she might as well ask the kingdom for him also, for he was the elder brother (1 Kings 2:22). He had the spirit of discernment that he asked God for, and saw through it from the start, for the first thing Adonijah said was that the kingdom was his. The Most High gave him the reasonings of men, what today would be called psychology, spiritual discernment (Wisdom of Solomon 7:20).

Solomon swore by the Lord that Adonijah had spoken this word against his own life, and sent Benaiah, who fell upon him that he died (1 Kings 2:23-25). Abiathar, who had joined with Adonijah to unseat Solomon, was thrust out from the priesthood, fulfilling the word concerning the house of Eli (1 Kings 2:26-27). Joab, who had turned after Adonijah, died at the altar for the innocent blood of Abner and Amasa, two men more righteous and better than he (1 Kings 2:28-34).
Some sit among the congregation for a time, but over time some spirit will come around and gather them, and it is known they were not right from the beginning. It never fails.

cases.name: Solomon at Gibeon
cases.charge: Asking for an understanding heart to judge the people and to discern between good and bad, and not for long life, nor riches, nor the life of his enemies
cases.summary: At Gibeon the Most High appeared to Solomon in a dream and said, ask what I shall give thee; Solomon, calling himself a little child who knew not how to go out or come in, asked for an understanding heart to judge the great people, to discern between good and bad (1 Kings 3:5-9). Because he asked for understanding to discern judgment and not for long life, riches, or the life of his enemies, the Most High gave him a wise and understanding heart like no other before or after, added riches and honour, and promised length of days if he would walk in his ways (1 Kings 3:10-14). The Lord came to him while he was already married to Pharaoh’s daughter and sacrificing in the high places.
offenseFull: Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt and took his daughter. He loved the Lord and walked in the statutes of David his father, though the people still sacrificed in high places because no house was yet built to the name of the Lord; only he too sacrificed and burnt incense in high places, and at Gibeon, the great high place, he offered a thousand burnt offerings (1 Kings 3:1-4).

In marrying Pharaoh’s daughter he married a heathen woman, against the law that forbade marriages with the nations because they would turn the son away from following the Most High to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 7:1-4). The high places were where he afterward built for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom (2 Kings 23:13): as he was loving God, he was serving another god. While he was doing that, the Lord appeared to him at Gibeon in a dream by night and came to his conscience: you are serving another god, but what do you need? The first time, at Gibeon, he was doing something wrong. The Lord appeared unto him twice, and Solomon was still unable to put it away (1 Kings 9:2; 1 Kings 11:9).

Solomon had a bad upbringing. David lived a life of war and was not home to teach his children diligently as the law commands (Deuteronomy 6:7), to bring him up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. The examples he had were brothers who were murderers and rapists and a father who committed adultery; it is not hard to understand why he made some of the mistakes he made.

Solomon began with the great mercy shown to David his father and the kindness of giving him a son to sit on his throne (1 Kings 3:6). He took the throne at an early age, and said he was but a little child who knew not how to go out or come in, in the midst of a people that could not be numbered for multitude, the promise made to Abraham that his children would be as the sand of the sea; and he asked for an understanding heart to judge the people, that he might discern between good and bad (1 Kings 3:7-9). He was a young man saying, Lord, teach me how to serve you; tell me what to do.

This is what we still need to pray for: that the Most High endows our leadership with wisdom, and that we ourselves learn wisdom in these scriptures and how to judge matters among one another. The saints shall judge the world and even angels, so they should be able to judge the smallest matters of this life (1 Corinthians 6:1-3); and the Most High exalts the horn of his people, the children of Israel, a people near unto him, who are the saints (Psalms 148:14).
judgmentFull: The speech pleased the Lord. Because Solomon asked not for long life, nor riches, nor the life of his enemies, but for understanding to discern judgment, the Most High gave him the spirit of understanding, judgment and wisdom: he did not ask amiss to fulfil his lust; he asked for the spirit to judge righteously. There was none like him before him and none should arise after him, and he gave him also what he had not asked, riches and honour (1 Kings 3:10-13).

Length of days was conditional: if he would walk in God’s ways and keep his statutes and commandments as his father David did walk, the Lord would lengthen his days (1 Kings 3:14). Solomon awoke, came to Jerusalem, stood before the ark of the covenant, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings (1 Kings 3:15).

Then came the establishment of government, showing order: the king, then ranking men, each with a position of order, the same pattern of captains and officers set up in the days of Moses (1 Kings 4:1-7). Judah and Israel dwelt safely, every man under his vine and fig tree, because the wars of King David had put down all the surrounding nations and put them to tribute; that is why Solomon was able to rule in a time of peace (1 Kings 4:20-25).

God gave him wisdom and understanding exceeding much, so that his wisdom excelled all the children of the east country and all the wisdom of Egypt; he spoke three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs, which is why there are Proverbs and the Song of Songs (1 Kings 4:29-34). Since his wisdom already excelled Egypt’s, there is no need to dabble in Egyptology or any doctrine outside the scriptures; Israel should want its own understanding and wisdom to pass that nation too. The Most High gave him knowledge of how the world was made, the natures of living creatures, the virtues of roots, and the reasonings of men, what today would be called psychology, spiritual discernment (Wisdom of Solomon 7:17-21).

The Lord appeared to him the second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon, when he had finished the house of the Lord (1 Kings 9:1-3). Yet with all the wisdom God gave him, he gave his heart to know madness and folly, and it was a vexation of spirit, because he knew better (Ecclesiastes 1:16-17).

cases.name: The two women before Solomon
cases.charge: Two harlots claiming one living child before the king with no witness; the false claimant willing to have the child divided
cases.summary: Two women that were harlots, dwelling in one house, each bore a son three days apart; one woman’s child died in the night because she overlaid it, and she exchanged it for the living child while the other slept (1 Kings 3:16-21). There was no witness, and before the king each claimed the living child. Solomon called for a sword and commanded the child divided; the true mother, her bowels yearning upon her son, gave up her claim to save its life, the other would have it divided, and the king gave the child to its mother, so that all Israel saw that the wisdom of God was in him to do judgment (1 Kings 3:22-28).
offenseFull: After Gibeon, Solomon came to Jerusalem, stood before the ark of the covenant, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants; then came two women that were harlots unto the king and stood before him (1 Kings 3:15-16). He was king over all Israel, and whoever was committing wickedness would come before him for judgment.

The first said that she and the other woman dwelt in one house with no stranger with them, that she was delivered of a child, and that the third day after, the other woman was delivered also. The other woman’s child died in the night because she overlaid it: she was sleeping with the baby in the bed and laid on top of it. This is something that happens a lot, unfortunately, and it hurts. She arose at midnight, took the living son from beside the first woman while she slept, laid him in her own bosom, and laid her dead child in the first woman’s bosom (1 Kings 3:17-20). In the morning the first woman rose to give her child suck and found it dead, but when she looked on it she knew it was not her son (1 Kings 3:21). To the untrained eye one small baby can look like another, depending on the features, but the mother knows when it is not her child.

The other woman said the living child was hers and the dead one the first woman’s, and the first said the opposite, and so they spake before the king (1 Kings 3:22). Solomon did not know these women. There was no stranger in the house to bear witness, and he was dealing only with each woman’s version of the story.

That was the Kingdom of Heaven on earth, yet there were still harlots; when Christ, the greater Solomon, comes back there will be no harlots, for all shall be righteous, and harlots who do not repent will burn. They came before the king in a pair because all flesh consorts according to kind (Ecclesiasticus 13:16): this harlot was not with a righteous woman; she was with one just like herself.
judgmentFull: The king repeated both claims, called for a sword, and when it was brought commanded the living child divided in two and half given to each (1 Kings 3:23-25). Then the woman whose the living child was spoke, for her bowels yearned upon her son. No mother would want to see her child split in two, so the real mother was the first to speak up: she begged the king to give the other the living child and in no wise slay it. The other would have it neither hers nor her rival’s, but divided (1 Kings 3:26).

She did not care whether the baby was put to death, because she had already lost her own; she wanted company in her misery, and she had no love for that child. The same spirit is on the earth today in women who have abortion after abortion.

The king answered that the living child be given to the first woman and in no wise slain, for she was the mother thereof (1 Kings 3:27). No law in the scriptures speaks of a woman who snatches another’s baby and gives her own in its place, and no fight was going on that the law of the woman with child would cover (Exodus 21:22). Solomon went off the strength of common sense: from the moment he called for the sword he knew the real mother would react in a way the false one would not, because of what is seen in how a mother deals with her child, a mother’s love.

Wisdom knows things of old and conjectures aright what is to come; she knows the subtilties of speeches (Wisdom of Solomon 8:8). Conjecture is an opinion or conclusion formed on the basis of incomplete information. Solomon did not have everything; by his wisdom, his experience and what was taught him through the law he reached a conclusion, and he recognised the subtlety in the false woman’s speech. The word of God is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart (Hebrews 4:12). When no law speaks to a matter directly, the judge must still discern from what he has, the person’s behaviour and his past experience, and he may create a scenario, as Solomon did with the sword, and see how they react to get to the bottom of it. Most will never be in a position to judge congregational matters, but all still have to understand judgment, and that discernment is gained through the scriptures, examining the law precept upon precept, and study.

All Israel heard of the judgment and feared the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to do judgment (1 Kings 3:28). Solomon had to hear these two women out and look at their countenance. Christ, the greater Solomon, needed not that any should testify of man, for he knew what was in man (John 2:24-25); he knew Nathanael for an Israelite in whom is no guile, and perceived the thoughts of the Pharisees before they spoke, a discernment on a greater level than Solomon’s (John 1:47; Luke 5:22). The record gives no separate punishment for the false claimant; it ends with the living child given to his mother.

cases.name: King Solomon
cases.charge: Loving many strange women of the nations the Lord had forbidden; multiplying wives against the law of the king; going after other gods and building high places for Chemosh and Molech
cases.summary: Solomon loved many strange women together with the daughter of Pharaoh, of the nations the Most High had said Israel should not join with, for surely they would turn their heart after their gods; he had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and it happened exactly as the Most High said it would (1 Kings 11:1-3). When he was old his wives turned his heart after other gods, and he built high places for Chemosh and Molech (1 Kings 11:4-8). The Lord, who had appeared to him twice, said he would rend the kingdom out of his son’s hand, leaving one tribe for David’s sake, and stirred up adversaries against him; this sin divided the kingdom (1 Kings 11:9-40).
offenseFull: Solomon reigned in a peaceable time, all the kings of the earth wondered at his wisdom, and he gathered gold as tin and silver as lead; yet he bowed his loins unto women, was brought into subjection by his body, stained his honour and polluted his seed (Ecclesiasticus 47:13-20).

The Most High gave him to know all things, secret or manifest, and he knew better than to do what he did (Wisdom of Solomon 7:21). One may be wise and teach many and yet be unprofitable to himself (Ecclesiasticus 37:19). He wrote that a man should drink waters out of his own cistern, which is marrying within your race, and not embrace the bosom of a stranger (Proverbs 5:15-20); that the law keeps a man from the flattery of a strange woman (Proverbs 6:23-24); and his own mother told him not to give his strength unto women (Proverbs 31:3). He wrote that the prudent foresee the evil and hide themselves while the simple pass on and are punished (Proverbs 22:3): he foresaw the consequences of falling into subjection to strange women, and he knew better but did not do better.

The law was plain. Israel was to make no marriages with the nations, for they would turn away the son from following the Most High (Deuteronomy 7:3; Exodus 34:16); it was not a maybe but a will. A man is supposed to marry a woman of his own race. The king was not to multiply wives to himself, nor greatly multiply silver and gold, which is exactly what Solomon did (Deuteronomy 17:17). Tobit charged his son to take a wife of the seed of his fathers and not a strange woman; not to take a wife of your own people is to despise them, and in pride is destruction (Tobit 4:12-13).

Nehemiah later saw children of Jews who had married wives of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab who could not speak the Jews’ language, because the fathers were not truly in the house, and he reminded them that Solomon, beloved of his God, was caused to sin by outlandish women (Nehemiah 13:23-26). No one is above the temptation that took Solomon down (1 Corinthians 10:12).

When Solomon was old his wives turned his heart after other gods (1 Kings 11:4). David also sinned, but he repented and turned back, while Solomon kept going into sin (Proverbs 24:16). He went after Ashtoreth of the Zidonians, the fertility goddess, who is Easter, and after Milcom of the Ammonites, who are the Japanese, and built high places for Chemosh and Molech and for all his strange wives (1 Kings 11:5-8). His sin was not his alone, for he was the biggest influence on the earth, and his idolatry seduced many Israelites. The six-pointed star called the star of David is in truth the star of Molech, an idol, the star of Remphan that Israel still carried in the apostles’ time (Amos 5:26; Acts 7:43). He gave his heart to know madness and folly, which in one word is sin (Ecclesiastes 1:17).
judgmentFull: The Most High was angry with Solomon because his heart was turned from him who had appeared to him twice (1 Kings 11:9-10). A heretic is rejected after the first and second admonition (Titus 3:10): the third time is judgment. The Most High said he would rend the kingdom out of the hand of his son, not in Solomon’s days for David’s sake, leaving one tribe for David’s sake and for Jerusalem’s (1 Kings 11:11-13). This is the pivotal moment in the history of Israel, for this sin divided the kingdom under Jeroboam and Rehoboam.

There was peace under Solomon while he kept the commandments, but when he broke them the Most High gave strength to his enemies: Hadad the Edomite, who had fled to Egypt as a child when Joab cut off every male in Edom, for Esau was always the first hater and enemy of Israel; and Rezon, who reigned in Damascus (1 Kings 11:14-25).

The prophet Ahijah rent Jeroboam’s new garment in twelve pieces and gave him ten, for ten tribes, because Israel had forsaken the Most High and worshipped Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom; the house of David held Judah and Benjamin, with Levi. Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam, who fled to Egypt until Solomon died (1 Kings 11:26-40).

Solomon, the peaceable one, was supposed to have peace all his days, but toward the end of his reign things went south, and his son was not raised up in the same estate. Had he walked in the way of God and hearkened to the second admonition, he would have dwelt in peace for ever (Baruch 3:13), and Israel would still be in the blessings of Deuteronomy 28. Wine and women make men of understanding to fall away (Ecclesiasticus 19:2): for the kings it was always women and idols.

Ecclesiastes, written looking back, has a different tone from Proverbs, for dabbling in the dark realm weighed on his mind and spirit (Ecclesiastes 1:18). He found more bitter than death the woman whose heart is snares and nets (Ecclesiastes 7:26), and gave the conclusion of the whole matter: fear the Most High and keep his commandments, for he shall bring every work into judgment (Ecclesiastes 12:13-14).

cases.name: Rehoboam
cases.charge: Forsaking the counsel of the old men for the young men he grew up with and answering the people roughly; and forsaking the law of the Lord, and all Israel with him, once the kingdom was established
cases.summary: All Israel came to Shechem to make Solomon’s son king and asked him to lighten the heavy yoke his father had laid on them (1 Kings 12:1-4). He forsook the counsel of the old men for the young men he grew up with and answered the people roughly, and ten tribes left the house of David, for the cause was from the Lord (1 Kings 12:6-20). When he had established the kingdom he forsook the law of the Lord, and the Lord left Judah in the hand of Shishak king of Egypt until the king humbled himself (2 Chronicles 12:1-12).
offenseFull: Solomon left behind him Rehoboam, the foolishness of the people, one that had no understanding, who turned away the people through his counsel (Ecclesiasticus 47:23). That is his identity and his legacy: the son of the wisest king known as the complete opposite.

At Shechem the congregation asked him to lighten the grievous service and heavy yoke of his father (1 Kings 12:1-4). The heavy yoke was the labour of the building: Solomon did not enslave his own people as he did the other nations, but they did have to put in that work. The yoke was also the taxing Solomon put on the people to finance the temples of his wives. Rehoboam told them to depart three days, which was wisdom, for it is right to take time and get counsel before giving an answer (1 Kings 12:5).

He consulted the old men who had stood before Solomon, who told him that if he would serve the people that day and speak good words to them they would be his servants forever, and he forsook their counsel for the young men who had grown up with him (1 Kings 12:6-8). Solomon was the wisest man on earth and still had counsellors, yet Rehoboam forsook the counsellors of the wisest man for his peers; the problem is getting counsel from those on your own level rather than from elders. Because of pride he went to the young men, and his father, full of pride and given to his pleasures, had not been there to guide him. Counsel with foolish brothers brings foolish results. You are where you are based on the decisions you made.

The young men told him to say that his little finger would be thicker than his father’s loins and that he would chastise them with scorpions, which was disrespectful, and on the third day he answered the people roughly in those words (1 Kings 12:9-14).

He desired many wives, a spirit he got from his father rather than the wisdom, though the law warns the king not to multiply wives, that his heart turn not away (2 Chronicles 11:21-23; Deuteronomy 17:17). When he had established the kingdom and strengthened himself, he forsook the law of the Lord, and all Israel with him (2 Chronicles 12:1). Moses saw it in the spirit: Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked and forsook God (Deuteronomy 32:15). One who leads goes astray and carries many others with him. Judah built high places, images and groves on every high hill, and there were sodomites in the land (1 Kings 14:22-24); the law says there shall be no sodomite of the sons of Israel (Deuteronomy 23:17). His mother was an Ammonitess, and the son of a heathen mother turned after his mother’s gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). He did evil because he prepared not his heart to seek the Lord, as Solomon had when he asked for wisdom (2 Chronicles 12:14).
judgmentFull: The king hearkened not unto the people, for the cause was from the Lord, that he might perform the saying he spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite; the prophecy had to come to pass (1 Kings 12:15). The split is the beginning of the New Testament: the twelve tribes were divided, and the mission of the disciples and apostles was to reunite both kingdoms under Christ (Romans 11; Ephesians 2).

Israel said they had no portion in David and went to their tents; they stoned Adoram, who was over the tribute, and Rehoboam fled to Jerusalem. This is the split, the northern tribes rebelling against the house of David to this day (1 Kings 12:16-20).

If Israel forsakes the Lord, he will turn and do them hurt after he has done them good (Joshua 24:20). In the fifth year, because they had transgressed, Shishak king of Egypt came up with the Lubims, the Sukkiims and the Ethiopians, kindred Hamite nations, and took the fenced cities of Judah (2 Chronicles 12:2-4). The nations are instruments in the Lord’s hand: when Israel keeps the commandments they serve Israel, and when Israel breaks them he uses them to punish Israel.

Shemaiah declared that because they had forsaken the Lord he had left them in Shishak’s hand, and the princes and the king humbled themselves and said the Lord is righteous (2 Chronicles 12:5-6). When correction comes, the right response is to confess that the Most High is righteous in what he does. He would not destroy them, but they would be Shishak’s servants, paying tax and tribute, that they might know his service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries (2 Chronicles 12:7-8). The Lord ordained the nations for judgment and correction (Habakkuk 1:12), and it is the same today: Israel is to submit to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake (1 Peter 2:13-14). The people today must likewise humble themselves; if they confess their iniquity and accept the punishment, the Most High remembers his covenant (Leviticus 26:40-42).

Shishak carried off the treasures and the three hundred shields of gold Solomon had made, about nine hundred pounds of gold, and Rehoboam made shields of brass in their place, a fall from gold to brass (2 Chronicles 12:9-10; 1 Kings 10:17). Because he humbled himself the wrath turned from him, and in Judah things went well (2 Chronicles 12:12); though the Lord punish with adversity, he never forsakes his people (2 Maccabees 6:16). There was war with Jeroboam all his days, and after seventeen years Abijah his son reigned (2 Chronicles 12:13-16).

cases.name: Jeroboam son of Nebat
cases.charge: Setting up two calves of gold in Bethel and Dan as the gods that brought Israel out of Egypt; making priests of the lowest of the people, not of Levi; and ordaining a feast devised of his own heart
cases.summary: Given ten tribes by the word of Ahijah, with the promise of a sure house if he kept the commandments, Jeroboam feared the people’s hearts would turn back to Rehoboam if they went up to Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:29-38; 1 Kings 12:26-27). He made two calves of gold, set one in Bethel and the other in Dan, made priests of the lowest of the people, and devised a feast of his own (1 Kings 12:28-33). He did not turn after the signs at the altar, and the Lord cut off his house and gave Israel up because of his sins (1 Kings 13:33-34; 1 Kings 14:7-16).
offenseFull: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephrathite whose mother was a widow, was Solomon’s servant, and Solomon, seeing he was industrious, made him ruler over the charge of the house of Joseph, the two tribes Ephraim and Manasseh (1 Kings 11:26-28). As the son of a widow he was free from paternal restraint and followed his own impulses uncontrolled; that is why a father is needed in the house, and the people now have spiritual fathers and counsellors in this truth. Told by Ahijah that he would be king, he tried to take it faster and lifted up his hand against Solomon, then fled to Egypt (1 Kings 11:26-40); when Solomon died he stirred up the people against Rehoboam, giving them something to complain about.

Made king, he had no faith in the promise of a sure house (1 Kings 11:38). He said in his heart that if the people went up to sacrifice at Jerusalem they would kill him and go again to Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:26-27). He knew the law that the males appear before the Lord three times a year (Deuteronomy 16:16). So he took counsel, made two calves of gold, told the people it was too much to go up to Jerusalem, and presented the calves as their gods that brought them out of Egypt (1 Kings 12:28). It was what Israel did in the wilderness, when the people were put to death for it, and he doubled that sin (Exodus 32:4, 28). The calf was in honour of Apis, the bull god of Egypt. He set one in Bethel and the other in Dan, and this thing became a sin (1 Kings 12:29-30). The northern kingdom’s inception was idolatry: it became a nation and stayed separate by worshipping golden calves.

He made a house of high places and priests of the lowest of the people, not of the sons of Levi (1 Kings 12:31). He cast the Levites off, and they and all who set their hearts to seek the Lord went to Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 11:13-16); whoever came with a young bullock and seven rams could be a priest of them that are no gods (2 Chronicles 13:9). The great sin the account underlines is casting off the Levites, a law the Most High was very specific about (Deuteronomy 14:27). He ordained a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, a counterfeit of the feast of tabernacles of the seventh month, in a month he devised of his own heart (1 Kings 12:32-33; Leviticus 23:34). Devising your own holy days and throwing off the days of the Most High is the same error men make today.

A man of God cried against the altar, Jeroboam’s hand dried up and was restored, and then the same man of God, for one false move, was slain by a lion (1 Kings 13:1-24). The Lord was warning Jeroboam; yet after this Jeroboam returned not from his evil way, but made whoever would a priest of the high places (1 Kings 13:33). The obstinate heart is laden with sorrows and heaps sin upon sin, and for the proud there is no remedy, for the plant of wickedness has taken root in him (Ecclesiasticus 3:27-28): no punishment would fix him.
judgmentFull: This thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, to cut it off and destroy it from the face of the earth (1 Kings 13:34). When his son Abijah fell sick, the hard man sent his wife disguised to the blind prophet Ahijah (1 Kings 14:1-6). By trouble the Lord makes the heart soft (Job 23:16): the king bent on keeping the people from serving the Lord now sought his help. But the Lord reveals his secrets to his prophets, and Ahijah knew her at the sound of her feet and gave her heavy tidings (Amos 3:7).

The Lord had exalted Jeroboam and rent the kingdom from David’s house to give it to him, yet he made other gods and molten images and cast the Lord behind his back; therefore his house would be swept away as a man sweeps away dung (1 Kings 14:7-11). The child would die when her feet entered the city, the only one of Jeroboam’s house to come to the grave, because in him was found some good thing toward the Lord; at the threshold the child died (1 Kings 14:12-13, 17). This is the God of the Bible, and the Lord dealing with Israel this whole time was Christ.

The sentence reached the nation: the Lord would smite Israel as a reed shaken in the water, root them out of the good land, scatter them beyond the river, and give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam (1 Kings 14:15-16). Defeated by Abijah of Judah, who cried unto the Lord while the north had golden calves, Jeroboam never recovered strength, and the Lord struck him and he died (2 Chronicles 13:13-20).

Baasha killed Nadab his son and left none that breathed of his house, according to Ahijah’s word (1 Kings 15:29). There were no righteous kings in the northern kingdom: they departed not from Jeroboam’s sins until the Lord removed them into Assyria (2 Kings 17:21-23). The calf of Samaria cast them off: they became castaways, not a people, Samaritans and Gentiles (Hosea 8:4-6), which is why the seed of Israel are called heathens and Gentiles in the New Testament. Dan, where the second calf stood, caused many of Israel to sin; those who swore by the sin of Samaria were to fall and never rise again (Amos 8:14). The tribe of Dan was removed and assembled itself among Benjamin, but the Lord will re-establish Dan towards the end (Genesis 49:16).

cases.name: Amaziah the priest of Bethel
cases.charge: Forbidding Amos to prophesy at Bethel, the king’s chapel, and sending to Jeroboam that Amos had conspired against him, to have the prophet put to death
cases.summary: When Amos, a herdman of Tekoa, prophesied at Bethel that the sanctuaries of Israel would be laid waste and the Lord would rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword, Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to King Jeroboam that Amos had conspired against him and the land could not bear his words (Amos 7:7-11). He told the prophet to go and prophesy in Judah and never again at Bethel, the king’s chapel (Amos 7:12-13). Amos answered that the Lord had taken him from the flock to prophesy to Israel, and pronounced the judgment on Amaziah’s house and on Israel’s land (Amos 7:14-17).
offenseFull: Amos prophesied in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and of Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel (Amos 1:1). This is Jeroboam the second, not Jeroboam the son of Nebat of the split; he reigned forty-one years, did evil, and departed not from the sins of the first Jeroboam (2 Kings 14:23-24). The Lord showed Amos grasshoppers eating the grass of the land and a fire devouring the great deep, and twice the Lord repented at Amos’s plea (Amos 7:1-6). Then the Lord stood upon a wall with a plumbline in his hand: he would set a plumbline in the midst of his people Israel and not pass by them any more; the high places of Isaac would be desolate, the sanctuaries of Israel laid waste, and he would rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword (Amos 7:7-9).

Then Amaziah, an idolatrous priest at Bethel, where the first Jeroboam had set his calf, sent to the king that Amos had conspired against him in the midst of Israel and the land could not bear all his words, for Amos said Jeroboam would die by the sword and Israel would surely be led away captive (Amos 7:10-11). He went to slander the prophet to the king so that the king would do something about it, trying to put a lie on Amos to get him put to death. Amos was that direct: he stood before the king’s court and prophesied death and destruction, and the land could not bear his words because he kept bringing judgment. Amaziah also sauced it up: Amos never said Jeroboam would die by the sword, but prophesied that if the northern kingdom did not repent it would go into captivity. They hated those who tried to save them, telling them this was wrong and the Lord would punish them.

Our own people will do this to us. They will try to make it seem that the congregation is a treasonous movement of insurrection and sedition, to knock it off the map. Christ warned that whoever kills you will think he does God service, as Saul thought when he consented to Stephen’s death (John 16:2; Acts 8:1).

Amaziah told Amos, calling him a seer, to flee into the land of Judah, eat bread and prophesy there, but never again at Bethel, for it was the king’s chapel and the king’s court (Amos 7:12-13): go to Judah, we do not want to hear it here. Amaziah was more concerned with protecting the king’s institution than with hearing the word of the Lord, and the same thing goes on today: instead of correcting the leaders and teachers in these congregations with their ridiculous doctrines and accusations, they prefer that we not speak at all. It was the northern kingdom’s way: they gave the Nazarites wine to drink and commanded the prophets not to prophesy, which goes into lies and deceit, doing anything to stop the word of the Most High (Amos 2:11-12). The same passage shows that the children of Israel are the prophets of the Most High.
judgmentFull: Amos answered that he was no prophet nor a prophet’s son, but a herdman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit, and the Lord took him as he followed the flock and sent him to prophesy to his people Israel (Amos 7:14-15). The prophet did not choose himself: the Lord chose and ordained him, as Christ chose and ordained his disciples and as the Lord ordained Jeremiah before he was born (John 15:16; Jeremiah 1:5). Many say they were called into the ministry while keeping no commandments and no Sabbath; that is not biblical, for it is Jacob and Israel whom the Lord calls (Isaiah 48:12). The Most High gives his word to the prophets, and the prophet’s job is to carry out the word of the Lord, no more, no less; if you do not like it, too bad.

Because Amaziah said prophesy not against Israel and drop not thy word against the house of Isaac, the Lord said his wife would be a harlot in the city, his sons and daughters would fall by the sword, his land would be divided by line, he would die in a polluted land, and Israel would surely go into captivity out of its land (Amos 7:16-17). Amaziah was trying to get the brother to stop prophesying, and judgment came upon him for that. True prophets put their lives on the line, for most of our people hate God and his word, and the righteous are hated of all men for his name’s sake (Matthew 10:22).

Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria took Gilead, Galilee and all the land of Naphtali and carried them captive, and in the ninth year of Hoshea Assyria took Samaria and carried Israel away (2 Kings 15:29; 2 Kings 17:6). Israel deserved captivity: they were already wicked, and there was never a good king in the northern kingdom. They sold the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of shoes, so in that day the mighty would not deliver himself (Amos 2:6; Amos 2:14). The reason we are in captivity even today is the same reason our forefathers went into the Assyrian captivity: they were rebellious against the Most High’s laws, would not keep the commandments, and wanted to worship idols.

cases.name: The man of God from Judah
cases.charge: Turning back to eat bread and drink water at Bethel against the word of the Lord, on the word of an old prophet who lied, claiming an angel had spoken to him
cases.summary: A man of God came out of Judah by the word of the Lord to Bethel and cried against Jeroboam’s altar, naming Josiah, a child of David’s house, who would burn the priests of the high places on it; the altar was rent and the king’s hand dried up as the sign declared (1 Kings 13:1-6). He refused the king’s meal, for the Lord had charged him to eat no bread and drink no water there (1 Kings 13:7-10). Then an old prophet of Bethel lied to him, claiming an angel’s word, and he turned back and ate; on the road a lion slew him, and his body lay in the way with the ass and the lion standing by it (1 Kings 13:11-26).
offenseFull: Jeroboam stood by his altar at Bethel burning incense to his idol when the man of God cried against it: a child named Josiah would be born to the house of David and would offer on it the priests of the high places and burn men’s bones upon it; and he gave a sign that the altar would be rent (1 Kings 13:1-3). He prophesied Josiah hundreds of years before the child was born. That is how prophecy works, as Isaiah named Cyrus king of Persia long before he came, for the Lord showed the prophets secrets (Isaiah 44:28).

When Jeroboam put forth his hand to have him seized, it dried up so that he could not pull it in, and the altar was rent (1 Kings 13:4-5). The Lord reproves kings for the sake of his anointed and lets no man do his prophets harm (Psalms 105:14-15). Pain will get a man to change his thoughts: a few minutes before, the king wanted him put to death, and now he wanted him to pray for him; in their affliction they seek the Lord early, and the hand was restored (1 Kings 13:6; Hosea 5:15).

The king invited him home with a reward; he answered that even for half the king’s house he would not go in, eat bread or drink water there, for the Lord had charged him so and not to return by the way he came, and he went home another way (1 Kings 13:7-10). The Lord instructed him what to do and what not to do, specific instructions for this mission, and at first he stood firm.

An old prophet of Bethel rode after him, found him under an oak and invited him home; the man of God repeated his charge; the old man said he was a prophet also and an angel had spoken to him by the word of the Lord to bring him back, but he lied to him (1 Kings 13:13-18). It is like Eve and the serpent: first a little resistance, then the voice that talks a man out of the plain command. Giving reverence to the older prophet, the man of God went back and ate (1 Kings 13:19); a man is not to let the reverence of any man cause him to fall (Ecclesiasticus 4:22). He let his guard down because the old man made himself equal to him.

The Most High is not wishy-washy; he does not tell a man one thing and then go back the other way. What he told you, you stick to; the lie caused confusion. The only one the Lord spoke with mouth to mouth was Moses, and to every other prophet he speaks in visions and dreams; this man said an angel came to him (Numbers 12:6-8). The Lord sends false prophets to prove his people, whether they love him with all their heart and will obey his voice (Deuteronomy 13:3-4), and all of us will be tried like that. Meddle not with them that are given to change, who say they know what was said before, but now it is different (Proverbs 24:21).
judgmentFull: As they sat at the table, the word of the Lord came to the very prophet who had lied, and he cried that because the man of God had disobeyed the mouth of the Lord and eaten and drunk where he was forbidden, his carcass would not come to the sepulchre of his fathers (1 Kings 13:20-22). When he went, a lion met him by the way and slew him, and his carcass was cast in the way with the ass and the lion standing by it (1 Kings 13:23-25). The Most High used the deceiver to prove whether the man would keep the charge, and disobedience under that dispensation carried the penalty of death; the deceived and the deceiver are his (Job 12:16). His brother was put to death because the other lied: it can be that simple, a lie.

It was spiritual. A lion left to itself would have eaten the man and destroyed the donkey, but this lion slew him and then stood by the body beside the ass, eating neither, until the old prophet came (1 Kings 13:28). There are spirits created for vengeance, fire and hail and famine and death, and the teeth of wild beasts (Ecclesiasticus 39:28-30). The Lord put that spirit in the lion’s teeth to take vengeance on a disobedient man of God, and the lion kept the commandment.

The old prophet said it was the man of God who had been disobedient, laid him in his own grave, mourned him as his brother, and told his sons to lay his bones beside his, for the word cried against the altar in Bethel would surely come to pass (1 Kings 13:26-32). Even though he disobeyed, he was a real prophet, and the test of a true prophet is that the thing he speaks comes to pass (Deuteronomy 18:22). It was all to warn Jeroboam, yet he returned not from his evil way (1 Kings 13:33).

Over hundreds of years Israel stayed in that idolatry, because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily (Ecclesiastes 8:11-13). Then the Lord raised up Josiah, who broke down the altar at Bethel and burned bones from the sepulchres on it according to the word of the man of God, and when shown his tomb said to let him alone (2 Kings 23:15-18). Just like that the man of God was killed, because he deviated from the instructions; follow someone who only looks the part, and he will get you killed. The story is a warning not to deviate.

cases.name: The old prophet of Beth-el
cases.charge: Lying in the name of the Lord, claiming an angel’s word, to turn the man of God from Judah from his charge
cases.summary: An old prophet living in Bethel heard from his sons what the man of God from Judah had done at Jeroboam’s altar, rode after him, and brought him back to eat and drink by claiming that an angel had spoken to him by the word of the Lord; but he lied to him (1 Kings 13:11-19). At the table the true word came through the liar himself, the man of God was slain by a lion on the road, and the old prophet buried him in his own grave and asked to be laid beside him, confessing that the word against Bethel would surely come to pass (1 Kings 13:20-32). No sentence on the old prophet is recorded.
offenseFull: The man of God had kept his charge before the king: no bread, no water, and home by another way (1 Kings 13:7-10). He changed his path so that none would know him, but people were watching. There dwelt an old prophet in Bethel, the city of Jeroboam’s calf; his sons told him all the man of God had done and said to the king and showed him which way he went, and he had the ass saddled, rode after him, and found him sitting under an oak (1 Kings 13:11-14). He invited him home to eat bread, and the man of God repeated the word of the Lord: he could not return, go in, eat or drink in that place (1 Kings 13:15-17).

The old man answered that he was a prophet also, and an angel had spoken to him by the word of the Lord to bring him back; but he lied to him (1 Kings 13:18). He was an old prophet, but he was a liar. It was the serpent with Eve again: first a little resistance, then the voice that talks a man out of a plain command. The Lord speaks to his prophets in visions and dreams, and mouth to mouth only with Moses (Numbers 12:6-8); this man said an angel came to him, and he was lying. The prophet who presumes to speak a word in the name of the Most High which he has not commanded him to speak shall die (Deuteronomy 18:20), and by this law many pastors stand condemned, who say Christ said things the Most High never commanded him to say.

So the man of God went back with him and ate (1 Kings 13:19). The scripture does not say who the old prophet was; the moral is not who he was but what he did to the man of God. He made himself equal to him, a fellow prophet with whom the Lord was working too, and the man let his guard down. That is why the congregation does not just join with another camp. Many lying camps expect respect and want you to believe the Lord is working with them; men who have learned a couple of scriptures, quote the same scriptures and set up shop think they are on that level, and they are not. Follow such a man and he will get you killed. Put no trust in any brother, for every brother will utterly supplant (Jeremiah 9:4). The Lord proves his people by such voices, to know whether they love him with all their heart (Deuteronomy 13:3).
judgmentFull: As they sat at the table, the word of the Lord came to the old prophet who had lied, and he had to cry out the sentence on the man he had deceived: because he disobeyed the mouth of the Lord, his carcass would not come to the sepulchre of his fathers (1 Kings 13:20-22). A lion slew the man of God on the road and stood by the body with the ass, and when men told it in the city, the old prophet said it was the man of God who had been disobedient to the word of the Lord (1 Kings 13:23-26). The Most High used the deceiver to prove whether the man would keep his charge, for the deceived and the deceiver are his (Job 12:16). The lie caused confusion and got his brother put to death; that is how dangerous a lie can be.

He found the body untouched, brought it back on the ass, laid it in his own grave, and mourned over him as his brother. He charged his sons to bury him in the same sepulchre and lay his bones beside the bones of the man of God, for the word cried against the altar in Bethel and against the high places of Samaria would surely come to pass (1 Kings 13:27-32). Even though the man of God was disobedient, he was a real prophet, and what he said would come to pass. The Lord was warning Jeroboam, first by the sign on the altar and then by the death of the man who disobeyed; yet Jeroboam returned not from his evil way (1 Kings 13:33).

Over hundreds of years Israel stayed in that idolatry, because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily (Ecclesiastes 8:11). Then the Lord raised up Josiah, who burned bones from the sepulchres of Bethel on its altar according to the word of the man of God, and when shown his tomb said to let him alone; so they let his bones alone, with the bones of the prophet that came out of Samaria (2 Kings 23:15-18).

cases.name: Baasha
cases.charge: Walking in the way of Jeroboam and making Israel to sin after being exalted out of the dust to destroy Jeroboam’s house; building Ramah to keep the people from going over to Asa
cases.summary: Baasha conspired against Nadab the son of Jeroboam, killed him, and destroyed all the house of Jeroboam as Ahijah had foretold, then reigned twenty-four years walking in the same way of Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:27-34). He built Ramah to stop the people of the north, who were turning their hearts back to the Most High, from going over to Asa (2 Chronicles 16:1). The word came by Jehu the son of Hanani that the Lord, who had lifted him out of the dust, would make his house like the house of Jeroboam; Baasha slept with his fathers, and the sentence fell on his house when Zimri killed Elah his son and all his kin (1 Kings 16:1-13).
offenseFull: Nadab the son of Jeroboam reigned two years and did evil, walking in the way and sin of his father. Baasha of the house of Issachar conspired against him, struck him down at Gibbethon, reigned in his place, and struck all the house of Jeroboam, leaving none that breathed, according to the word the Lord spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite (1 Kings 15:25-30). This fulfilled, years later, the judgment that Jeroboam’s descendants would be destroyed for the sins by which he made Israel to sin. Then he reigned twenty-four years in Tirzah and did evil, walking in the way of Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:33-34). The pattern continues: each king who follows takes up the sin of the one before, and the same judgments keep coming.

There was war between Asa and Baasha all their days, and Baasha came up against Judah and built Ramah to let none go out or come in to Asa king of Judah (1 Kings 15:16-17; 2 Chronicles 16:1). He was trying to stop the northern kingdom from coming down to Judah, because tribes out of Israel had been turning their hearts back to the Most High and joining Asa. There were internal battles within the nation of Israel, and it shows how strong the northern kingdom of ten tribes was as it encroached on Judah’s land. The enmity continued, the north trying again and again to uproot Judah (Isaiah 7:1).

Asa, instead of crying to the Most High as he had against Zerah, took silver and gold out of the house of the Lord and hired Benhadad king of Syria to break his league with Baasha; Benhadad smote the cities of Israel, Baasha left off building Ramah (2 Chronicles 16:2-6). So Asa let the heathen come and destroy his brothers, using his finances against them, and Hanani the seer rebuked him for relying on the king of Syria and not on the Lord (2 Chronicles 16:7). Cursed be the man that trusteth in man (Jeremiah 17:5).
judgmentFull: The word of the Lord came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha: the Lord had exalted him out of the dust and made him prince over his people Israel, and he had walked in the way of Jeroboam and made Israel to sin (1 Kings 16:1-2). Out of the dust means he came from nothing, from confusion, a nobody, and the Most High lifted him out of that state, as he has chosen Israel to be a special people unto himself above all people (Deuteronomy 7:6). Therefore the Lord would take away the posterity of Baasha and make his house like the house of Jeroboam; the dogs would eat those of his who died in the city, and the fowls those who died in the field (1 Kings 16:3-4), the curse of the law on the carcasses of the disobedient (Deuteronomy 28:26). The same judgment falls because the same sin is repeated, just as descendants keep the pattern of their fathers though they saw the ruin it brought.

Baasha slept with his fathers and was buried in Tirzah, and Elah his son reigned two years (1 Kings 16:6-8). His servant Zimri conspired against him while he was drinking himself drunk, killed him, and as soon as he sat on the throne slew all the house of Baasha, leaving not one male, nor his kinsfolk nor his friends, according to the word spoken by Jehu (1 Kings 16:9-12). It all came for the sins of Baasha and of Elah his son, who provoked the Most High to anger with their vanities (1 Kings 16:13): Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked, forsook the God who made him, and provoked him with strange gods (Deuteronomy 32:15-21).
A generation later the same sentence was pronounced on Ahab, that his house would be made like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah (1 Kings 21:22).
