cases.name: Zimri
cases.charge: Conspiring against his master Elah while he was drunk and slaying him, coveting power and the throne; slaying all the house of Baasha; treason
cases.summary: Zimri, captain of half the chariots of Elah the son of Baasha, waited until the king was drunk in Tirzah, killed him, took the throne, and slew all the house of Baasha, according to the word of the Lord by Jehu the prophet (1 Kings 16:8-13). His covetousness was power. The Lord cut his reign short in a week; when Omri and all Israel took Tirzah he burnt the king’s house over himself and died for his sins, and his treason is recorded, treason being punishable by death in that time (1 Kings 16:15-20).
offenseFull: While Asa reigned in Judah, Elah the son of Baasha reigned over Israel in Tirzah, and his servant Zimri, one of the captains of Israel, captain of half his chariots, conspired against the king (1 Kings 16:8-9). He waited until the king was drunk in the house of Arza, steward of his house, then went in, smote him, killed him, and reigned in his stead (1 Kings 16:9-10).

As soon as he sat on his throne he slew all the house of Baasha; he left not one male, neither of his kinsfolks nor of his friends; he killed everybody (1 Kings 16:11). Thus Zimri destroyed the house of Baasha according to the word the Lord spoke against Baasha by Jehu the prophet, for all the sins of Baasha and of Elah his son, who provoked the Most High to anger with their vanities (1 Kings 16:12-13; 1 Kings 16:1-4). It is the demise of that king’s kingdom as it was prophesied, judgment brought on him for the evil that was there in the time they ruled. The same judgment falls because the same sin is repeated (1 Kings 16:7).

Some covet clothing, as Achan coveted the Babylonish garment, but not everyone has the same covetous spirit; some covet power and preeminence (Joshua 7:21). Zimri’s covetousness was power. It was not a garment: he wanted to be king, it was good to be the king, and he would kill the king and sit upon the throne. When you read the books of Kings and Chronicles you read about a lot of conspiracy among our people. The same sin was in Diotrephes, who loved to have the preeminence among them: he wanted to be the top teacher in Israel and to be known as number one; he received not the apostles, prated against them with malicious words, and cast the brethren out of the church (3 John 1:9-10). That was his sin, covetousness, and the same evil is seen today.
judgmentFull: Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah (1 Kings 16:15). He took the throne by conspiracy, and the Lord cut his time short in a week: he spent one Sabbath as king over the northern kingdom.

The people encamped against Gibbethon heard that Zimri had conspired and slain the king, and they would not accept it; all Israel made Omri, the captain of the host, king that day in the camp (1 Kings 16:15-16). Omri was a mighty man, reputed for his military mind; he went up from Gibbethon with all Israel and besieged Tirzah (1 Kings 16:17). When Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the palace of the king’s house, burnt the king’s house over himself with fire, and died (1 Kings 16:18). He did not want to face Omri and the army that came against him, so he set the palace on fire and killed himself.
His death came for his sins in walking in the way of Jeroboam, and his treason is recorded, treason being punishable by death in that time (1 Kings 16:19-20).

Years later, when Jehu, anointed to avenge the blood of the prophets shed at the hand of Jezebel, entered in at the gate of Jezreel, Jezebel called down from a window asking whether Zimri had peace, who slew his master (2 Kings 9:6-10; 2 Kings 9:30-31). Jehu asked who was on his side, and at his word she was thrown down; this is the judgment on Jezebel (2 Kings 9:32-33).

cases.name: Omri
cases.charge: Doing worse than all that were before him and walking in all the way of Jeroboam; setting up the statutes that Israel kept to its desolation
cases.summary: When Zimri burnt the king’s house over himself, Israel was divided between Tibni and Omri, the captain the people chose to overthrow the traitor; Omri prevailed and reigned twelve years (1 Kings 16:21-23). He bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver and built there the capital of the northern kingdom, yet he did worse than all before him, walking in the way of Jeroboam (1 Kings 16:24-26). The Lord made Israel a desolation because the statutes of Omri were kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab (Micah 6:16).
offenseFull: Then the people of Israel were divided, half following Tibni the son of Ginath and half Omri, in a power struggle over who would take the throne; the people chose Omri, who led the charge in overthrowing the traitor, and Tibni died, and Omri reigned (1 Kings 16:21-22). He began to reign in the thirty and first year of Asa, twelve years, the first six in Tirzah, the original capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:23). Omri was the sixth king of Israel after the split: Jeroboam, Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, and then Omri.

He bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver, built on the hill, and named the city after Shemer, the owner of the hill (1 Kings 16:24). From that time on Samaria became the capital city of the northern kingdom, the kingdom of the ten tribes that revolted from the house of David. The whole region became known as Samaria and its inhabitants as Samaritans; the Good Samaritan and the Samaritan woman of the New Testament all stem from Omri purchasing this hill. Conscious of the lustre of Jerusalem, the place the Lord chose, Omri set out to build a northern Jerusalem.

He built it up with the alliance of the Zidonians, the Phoenicians of Tyre and Zidon, whose coast and ports were vital for trade, and that is how he became so successful. To seal the league he married his son Ahab to their king’s daughter Jezebel, and that is how all of it got started (1 Kings 16:31). Samaria became a rich city, and with the images and priests of Baal it became a little Zidon in northern Israel.

But Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the Lord and did worse than all that were before him, for he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat and in his sin, idolatry and the lowest of the people set up as priests, wherewith he made Israel to sin and provoked the Lord God of Israel to anger with their vanities (1 Kings 16:25-26). There were no righteous kings in the northern kingdom from Jeroboam all the way down; every time you read about a king of Israel, the record says he wrought evil.
judgmentFull: Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, in the same land he purchased, and Ahab his son reigned in his stead (1 Kings 16:27-28). Ahab was even worse than his father: he married a heathen woman, Jezebel, served Baal, and reared up an altar for Baal in the house of Baal he built in Samaria, establishing idol worship there (1 Kings 16:30-32).

The Most High gave the verdict by the prophet Micah. Because the rich were full of violence and the people spoke lies, he would smite them and make them desolate; they would sow and not reap and tread the olives without oil, for the statutes of Omri were kept and all the works of the house of Ahab, and they would bear the reproach of his people (Micah 6:12-16). The works of idolatry, marriage to the heathen, and all other sorts of wickedness set up in the days of Omri and Ahab were still being kept in the land. Among our people the statutes of Omri are kept, and that is why sin is going to make us desolate and a hissing to the nations.

The northern kingdom dwelt in the land of Samaria that Omri bought, and out of that land the king of Assyria, after a siege of three years, carried Israel away in the ninth year of Hoshea and put other nations there (2 Kings 17:5-6, 24). They rejected his statutes, served Baal, and gave themselves wholly to do evil, and the Lord removed them out of his sight (2 Kings 17:15-18).

cases.name: Ahab
cases.charge: Marrying Jezebel and serving Baal above all the kings before him; letting Jezebel reign through him; letting go Ben-hadad whom the Lord appointed to destruction; selling himself to work wickedness
cases.summary: Ahab the son of Omri did evil above all before him: as if the sins of Jeroboam were a light thing, he took Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians to wife, served Baal, and reared him an altar and a grove in Samaria (1 Kings 16:30-33). He let Jezebel reign through him and slay the prophets, blamed Elijah for the trouble his own sin brought, made a covenant with Ben-hadad whom the Lord had appointed to utter destruction, and took Naboth’s vineyard after Jezebel had him stoned (1 Kings 18:17-18; 1 Kings 20:31-42; 1 Kings 21:1-16). His humbling delayed the evil to his son’s days, but he died at Ramoth-gilead and the dogs licked up his blood according to the word of the Lord (1 Kings 21:27-29; 1 Kings 22:34-38).
offenseFull: Not only did Ahab continue in the sins of Jeroboam, which was idolatry; he married a heathen woman, served Baal, and made a grove, provoking the Lord more than all the kings before him (1 Kings 16:31-33). This mirrors Solomon, who followed Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and the marrying outside the people that the law forbids because it turns the heart to other gods (1 Kings 11:4-5; Deuteronomy 7:3).

Ahab let Jezebel reign through him, and she slew the prophets of the Most High (1 Kings 18:4). She was the boss at that time; Ahab was just there for show, and she was the real king. The Jezebel spirit cannot exist without a weak man who enables it. Jezebel fed the eight hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and of the groves at her table and encouraged them, and Ahab never checked her (1 Kings 18:19).

When Ahab saw Elijah he asked whether he was the one who troubled Israel (1 Kings 18:17). That is the mind of a wicked person: he blamed the trouble on the ordained prophet of God, the messenger, for the consequences of his own disobedience. Elijah answered that Ahab and his father’s house had troubled Israel by forsaking the commandments of the Lord and following Baalim; it was Ahab following the sin of Jeroboam, worshipping the golden calves, that brought the trouble (1 Kings 18:18). Into a malicious soul wisdom shall not enter; sin comes in and wisdom goes out, so Ahab had thoughts without understanding (Wisdom of Solomon 1:3-5).

When Ben-hadad besieged Samaria, it was Ahab’s judgment from the Lord for trying to kill Elijah, for serving Baal, and for letting Jezebel run him and kill the prophets (1 Kings 20:1-6). Yet twice the Lord delivered the great Syrian host into his hand with small numbers (1 Kings 20:13-30). The Most High was giving Ahab a chance to repent, yet he did not repent, did not check Jezebel, and did not destroy the idols of Baal, for his sin had blinded him. When Ben-hadad pleaded for his life, Ahab called him his brother and brought him up into his chariot; look at his wickedness, for this Syrian had just tried to kill him, and he made a covenant with the heathen and sent him away (1 Kings 20:31-34). A prophet declared that because he had let go a man the Lord appointed to utter destruction, his life would go for his life (1 Kings 20:35-42).

He coveted Naboth’s vineyard, the inheritance of his fathers, and sulked because he could not get his way (1 Kings 21:1-4). When Jezebel had Naboth stoned by false witness, Ahab rose up and went down to take the vineyard: this is extortion, seizing what another has by violence and force (1 Kings 21:15-16). Ahab shares the guilt; he sat by and let Jezebel commit the crime because he coveted the field, then went to claim the reward.
judgmentFull: Elijah met him in the vineyard: dogs would lick his blood where they licked the blood of Naboth, and because he had sold himself to work evil the Lord would cut off every male of his house, as the curses of the law spoke (1 Kings 21:17-24; Deuteronomy 28:26). There was none like Ahab, who sold himself to work wickedness, stirred up by Jezebel his wife, because he was weak (1 Kings 21:25). That is the warning: weak men allow wicked women who portray themselves as righteous to manipulate, guide, and rule through them.

When Ahab heard these words he rent his clothes, put on sackcloth, fasted, and went softly, and the Lord said he would not bring the evil in Ahab’s days but upon his house in his son’s days (1 Kings 21:27-29). The judgment was not cancelled but delayed and transferred to the next generation, showing that genuine humbling before the Most High moves his hand.

When four hundred prophets told him with one mouth to go up to Ramoth-gilead, Jehoshaphat asked for a prophet of the Lord, and Ahab answered that there was Micaiah, but he hated him, for he prophesied not good concerning him but evil (1 Kings 22:1-8). They acknowledged that the spirit of the Lord was on this man, yet they hated him; they put him in prison not for adultery or theft or any act, but because they did not like the words of the law that came out of his mouth (1 Kings 22:24-27). Micaiah saw a lying spirit put in the mouth of all Ahab’s prophets; the deceiver and the deceived are under the hand of the Most High, who uses the lie to bring the judgment he has already declared (1 Kings 22:17-23; Job 12:16).

Ahab disguised himself, hoping to escape the word spoken against him; a certain man drew a bow at a venture and smote him between the joints of the harness, and he was held up in his chariot until he died at even (1 Kings 22:30-35). When they washed the chariot in the pool of Samaria the dogs licked up his blood according to the word of the Lord, and the judgment pronounced on Ahab and his house began to be fulfilled exactly as spoken (1 Kings 22:38). In Jehu’s day the seventy sons of Ahab were slain and all that remained of his house, until none remained, according to the word spoken by Elijah (2 Kings 10:1-11).

cases.name: Jezebel
cases.charge: Cutting off the prophets of the Lord; feeding eight hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the groves at her table; ruling through her husband and murdering Naboth by false witness; whoredoms and witchcrafts
cases.summary: Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians was married to Ahab to seal Omri’s league with Zidon; she cut off the prophets of the Lord and fed eight hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and of the groves at her table (1 Kings 16:31; 1 Kings 18:4; 1 Kings 18:19). After Carmel she swore to take Elijah’s life, and she wrote letters in Ahab’s name to have Naboth stoned by false witness: she was ruling through his power (1 Kings 19:1-2; 1 Kings 21:8-16). Jehu was anointed to avenge the blood of the prophets at her hand; she was thrown down from a window at Jezreel and the dogs ate her, as Elijah had said (2 Kings 9:7-10; 2 Kings 9:30-37).
offenseFull: Ahab took Jezebel to wife and went and served Baal (1 Kings 16:31). Her father’s name, Ethbaal, bore the name of the Zidonians’ god. She was a heathen; she caused Ahab to worship Baal, and when she came to Samaria she multiplied that worship vastly throughout the city, until it was a little Zidon in northern Israel.

When Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord, which means she killed them, Obadiah hid a hundred of them by fifty in a cave and fed them, putting his own life in danger (1 Kings 18:4). Ahab searched every nation and kingdom to find Elijah and slay him; that is how badly Jezebel wanted him dead, so she got Ahab to do her bidding (1 Kings 18:10). The prophets of Baal and of the groves ate at her table: she was feeding these eight hundred and fifty false prophets and encouraging them, and Ahab never checked her (1 Kings 18:19). She was the boss at that time; Ahab was just there for show, and she was the real king.

When Ahab told her how Elijah had slain her prophets, she swore by her gods to make his life as one of theirs by the next day (1 Kings 19:1-2). She wanted him dead because he had taken away her power and the name she had gotten in Israel through her idolatry; this is the same wicked spirit named in Revelation, the wicked woman who feared no God at all. She was not trying merely to destroy one prophet; she was trying to stop the whole prophetic voice out of Israel. You would think that the Most High demonstrating his power on Mount Carmel would bring her to repentance, but it increased her fury even more.

When Ahab sulked because Naboth would not give up the inheritance of his fathers, she mocked his weakness, telling him he was king, and promised him the vineyard (1 Kings 21:5-7). She wrote letters in Ahab’s name and sealed them with his seal, the signet of the king’s authority, and had two sons of Belial bear false witness that Naboth blasphemed God and the king, the same thing they did to Christ; they stoned him (1 Kings 21:8-13). She was ruling through his power; really, Jezebel was the king (1 Kings 21:14-15). The Jezebel spirit operates through weak men and exercises her authority through them; when a strong man opposes her she wants to get rid of him, for she resists the authority of holy men of God. There was none like Ahab, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up (1 Kings 21:25). Any woman can become a Jezebel if the man is weak like Ahab.
judgmentFull: Jehu was anointed to smite the house of Ahab, to avenge the blood of the prophets shed at the hand of Jezebel, whose work was to kill the prophets while weak Ahab let it continue; the dogs would eat her in the portion of Jezreel, with none to bury her (1 Kings 21:23; 2 Kings 9:1-10). Jezebel was attacking God’s prophets, so God wanted judgment on her for not listening to what he said.

When Joram the son of Ahab and Jezebel asked whether it was peace, Jehu answered that there could be no peace while the whoredoms and witchcrafts of his mother Jezebel were so many (2 Kings 9:22). There is no peace as long as a wicked woman is in power.

When Jehu came to Jezreel, with armies coming into the city, she painted her face and tired her head and looked out at a window, returning to her seductive ways (2 Kings 9:30). She painted her face to entice the foolish men to her side with her beauty, but her beauty was superficial; that is what the scripture shows of a Jezebel spirit. She called down asking whether Zimri had peace, who slew his master; Jehu asked who was on his side, two or three eunuchs looked out, and at his word they threw her down; her blood was sprinkled on the wall and on the horses, and he trod her under foot (2 Kings 9:31-33). She never thought she would have to pay for what she did. When they went to bury her as a king’s daughter they found only the skull, the feet, and the palms of her hands, fulfilling the word spoken by Elijah that the dogs would eat her flesh and her carcass would be as dung upon the field (2 Kings 9:34-37).
Jehu slew all that remained of the house of Ahab, gathered the worshippers of Baal in subtilty and slew them, and broke down the images and the house of Baal (2 Kings 10:11; 2 Kings 10:18-28).

Christ still names her: he has a few things against the angel of the church in Thyatira, because he suffers that woman Jezebel, which calls herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce his servants (Revelation 2:20). Jezebel was one woman in the time of the kings, but spirits always come back (Ecclesiastes 1:9). The angel is the male leader of the church: the leaders are letting their wives teach through them, so that it comes through the man’s mouth but really from her mouth. Women who call themselves prophetesses and preach out of the order the scriptures set are Jezebels; Deborah was called a prophetess because she was in order, in subjection to the leaders of Israel, her heart toward the governors of Israel (1 Corinthians 14:33-34; Judges 4:4; Judges 5:9).

cases.name: Hiel the Bethelite
cases.charge: Building Jericho again under the curse Joshua adjured before the Lord
cases.summary: When the wall of Jericho fell and the city was burned, Joshua adjured Israel before the Lord: the man who rose up and built Jericho would lay its foundation in his firstborn and set up its gates in his youngest son; the city was not to be rebuilt (Joshua 6:20-26). In the days of Ahab, who provoked the Lord more than all the kings of Israel before him, Hiel of Bethel built Jericho, laying its foundation in Abiram his firstborn and setting up its gates in his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the Lord spoken by Joshua (1 Kings 16:33-34).
offenseFull: Jericho was straitly shut up because of the children of Israel; none went out and none came in. It had a military and a garrison, with the walls shut so nobody could enter or leave (Joshua 6:1). The Lord told Joshua that he had given into his hand Jericho, its king, and the mighty men of valour: the battle was already decided (Joshua 6:2).

The battle plan came from the Lord: the men of war compassed the city once a day for six days, seven priests bearing seven trumpets of rams’ horns before the ark, and on the seventh day seven times (Joshua 6:3-15). The blowing of the trumpets activates the armies of the Lord, the angels, to help in battle, as Elisha’s servant saw when his eyes were opened (2 Kings 6:17). There is something about the number seven that the Lord loves. At the seventh time Joshua told the people to shout, for the Lord had given them the city, and the wall fell down flat; that shout was cry aloud and spare not in action, the sound breaking everything down like thousands of lions roaring at once (Joshua 6:16-20; Isaiah 58:1).

The city was accursed to the Lord, even it and all that were therein; only Rahab the harlot would live, she and all that were with her in the house, because she hid the messengers (Joshua 6:17). Israel was to keep from the accursed thing, lest they make themselves accursed and make the camp of Israel a curse and trouble it, for individual sins affect the whole nation of Israel (Joshua 6:18). All the silver and gold and vessels of brass and iron were consecrated to the Lord, separated and sanctified for his treasury alone: nobody was to gain personally from this war (Joshua 6:19). They utterly destroyed all that was in the city with the edge of the sword and burnt it with fire, and only the silver, gold, and vessels went into the treasury of the house of the Lord (Joshua 6:21-24).

Joshua saved Rahab alive and her father’s household, and she dwelt in Israel, because she hid the messengers (Joshua 6:25). She was a Canaanite, a heathen, yet the heathen can be blessed when they do it to benefit Israel; she was justified by works, for faith without works is dead (James 2:24-26). She helped the nation of Israel toward rulership, and that is the only help Israel wants from the other nations: to tell our people who they are, the Israelites the Bible speaks of, the so-called Blacks, Hispanics, and Native Americans, and that we must keep the commandments of the Most High; whoever does that will receive mercy just as Rahab did.

Then Joshua adjured them at that time: cursed before the Lord be the man that rises up and builds this city Jericho; he would lay the foundation in his firstborn and set up the gates in his youngest son. The city was not to be rebuilt (Joshua 6:26). So the Lord was with Joshua, and his fame was noised throughout all the country (Joshua 6:27).

Generations later, in the days of Ahab, Hiel of Bethel built Jericho (1 Kings 16:34). Ahab had taken Jezebel to wife and served and worshipped Baal, rearing an altar and a grove and provoking the Most High more than all the kings before him (1 Kings 16:31-33).
judgmentFull: Hiel laid the foundation of Jericho in Abiram his firstborn and set up its gates in his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the Lord which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun (1 Kings 16:34). That was Joshua’s curse: whoever rebuilds Jericho lays its foundation in his firstborn and sets its gates in his youngest son.

cases.name: Elijah
cases.charge: Standing before the Lord God of Israel: shutting the heaven by prayer, standing alone against the prophets of Baal at Carmel, and turning the people’s heart back to the Lord
cases.summary: Elijah the Tishbite, of the inhabitants of Gilead, told Ahab by the Lord God of Israel before whom he stood that there would be no dew nor rain but according to his word; he prayed, and it did not rain (1 Kings 17:1). The Lord fed him by ravens and a widow, raised her son at his prayer, and answered him by fire on Carmel, then sent rain (1 Kings 17:2-24; 1 Kings 18:17-46). Fleeing Jezebel he asked to die, but the Lord sustained him, told him seven thousand had not bowed to Baal, and gave him Elisha; he was taken up by a whirlwind (1 Kings 19:1-21; 2 Kings 2:11-12).
offenseFull: The whole account turns on the power of the Most High: he has power over everything, the animals and all creation, and he set that power on display through his prophet. Elijah was of a tempestuous nature, guided by no considerations of expediency: like a tempest he made his entry, thundered forth his execrations against the weak, woman-led Ahab, and rushed away so that no one could seize him. His leather girdle and black hairy cloak stood against the effeminate, luxurious dress of the worshippers of Baal (2 Kings 1:8).

The Lord sent him to hide by the brook Cherith, and the ravens brought him bread and flesh morning and evening, for the Most High can command the ravens to bring a man food if it be his will (1 Kings 17:2-6). At Zarephath the widow fed the man of God first and was sustained for trusting in the Lord and obeying; that is a precept: the man eats first (1 Kings 17:7-16). When her son died, Elijah cried to the Lord and the child revived, for it was not his time to go: a man’s days are determined, and he cannot pass the bound the Most High has set (1 Kings 17:17-24; Job 14:5).

In the third year, when Ahab blamed him for troubling Israel, he answered that Ahab and his father’s house had troubled Israel by forsaking the commandments and following Baalim (1 Kings 18:1; 1 Kings 18:17-18). At Carmel he asked the people how long they would halt between two opinions, for Israel is always double-minded, caught between serving God and serving the devil; and they answered him not a word (1 Kings 18:21). That is a call for all of us to examine ourselves and not keep one foot in and one foot out, for the lukewarm are spewed out (Revelation 3:15-16).

The other nations also sacrificed, but they sacrificed unto devils; God never made a covenant with them, never chose the Hamites or the Ishmaelites, but chose only the Israelites, the so-called Negroes, Hispanics, and Natives of today. The prophets of Baal cried to him from morning until noon; Elijah mocked them, and they cut themselves till the blood gushed out, for cutting the flesh, which the law forbids, was part of their false worship (1 Kings 18:25-28; Leviticus 19:28). Elijah repaired the altar with twelve stones according to the twelve tribes of the sons of Jacob, for the whole Bible is about the twelve tribes of Israel (1 Kings 18:30-31). At the evening sacrifice he prayed to the Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, who created everybody but chose a particular people, that the people might know he is God in Israel and had turned their heart back again (1 Kings 18:32-37).
judgmentFull: The fire of the Lord fell and consumed the sacrifice, the stones, and the dust; the people fell on their faces confessing the Lord, and the prophets of Baal were slain at the brook Kishon (1 Kings 18:38-40). In the last days, when the Most High rains down fire again by the hands of Christ, no false prophet will escape, and the same judgment will fall on the false shepherds today (Jeremiah 23:1-2). He prayed on Carmel with his face between his knees until a great rain came, and the hand of the Lord was on him as he ran before Ahab to Jezreel (1 Kings 18:41-46).

When Jezebel swore to take his life he arose and went for his life (1 Kings 19:1-3). He was an old man and knew she would truly try to kill him. The spirit of fear entered into him, for she had killed prophets before him. Under a juniper tree he asked to die, counting himself no better than his fathers, and an angel fed him for the journey to Horeb (1 Kings 19:4-8). Our forefathers had ultimate faith and understood regeneration: they could ask the Most High to take their life and let them rest in the grave, trusting he would bring them back whenever he chose.

The Lord passed by in a wind, an earthquake, and a fire, and was not in them, and after the fire came a still small voice (1 Kings 19:11-12). We do not know who we are dealing with. Elijah said he alone was left; the Lord sent him to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha, and told him he had left himself seven thousand in Israel whose knees had not bowed unto Baal (1 Kings 19:14-18). Seven represents completion, so it could be more. Elijah was not by himself; the Lord had people reserved who had not yet awakened, and so we pray for more labourers and preach the word, for we never know what video or flyer will wake up the ones the Lord has reserved.

He cast his mantle on Elisha, who destroyed the instruments of his husbandry, fed the people, and followed him without turning back (1 Kings 19:19-21). When he was taken up by a whirlwind, Elisha cried after him as his spiritual father (2 Kings 2:11-12).

Christ said that Elias was come already, and the disciples understood that he spoke of John the Baptist: Elijah came again, for the forefathers understood regeneration (Matthew 17:11-13). The prophecy that the Lord would send Elijah before the great and dreadful day had to occur more than once: in the time of John the Baptist, and in these times, when the truth was revealed to the so-called Negroes and to our Hispanic brothers and sisters that they are the Israelites (Malachi 4:5-6). Many of the elders hold that it was Abba Bivens, whom the Most High moved to teach that not only the so-called Negroes but also the northern kingdom are Israelites. That day has not come yet, so Elijah was sent already; the sign that we are near the end is that the prophet brought this truth back.

cases.name: The widow of Zarephath
cases.charge: Making the man of God a little cake first, out of the last handful of meal, according to the word, and trusting the Lord to sustain her
cases.summary: When the brook Cherith dried up, the Lord sent Elijah to Zarephath of Zidon, where he had commanded a widow woman to sustain him; she had but a handful of meal and a little oil, and was gathering two sticks to dress a last meal for herself and her son (1 Kings 17:7-12). Elijah told her to make him a little cake first; she obeyed, and for trusting in the Lord and obeying she was sustained until the rain came (1 Kings 17:13-16). When her son died, the Lord heard the voice of Elijah, the child revived, and she knew him for a man of God (1 Kings 17:17-24). Christ named her at Nazareth: God was selective about whom he helped (Luke 4:25-26).
offenseFull: The brook dried up for want of rain, and the Lord sent Elijah all the way across the land to Zarephath, which belonged to Zidon on the coast, where he had commanded a widow woman to sustain him (1 Kings 17:7-9). From the east side by Jordan to the west by Sidon was a hard walk of a Sabbath day’s journey or more, with no water anywhere. Zarephath is Lebanon, the bound named when the captivity of the children of Israel shall possess the land of the Canaanites: the twelve tribes are coming back to take the land over once again (Obadiah 1:20).

The Most High has power over everything, the animals and all creation. He who had commanded the ravens to feed Elijah now commanded a woman (1 Kings 17:4-6). That shows how mighty the prophets were: they were not regular men; they were the elect of the nation of Israel. He dried up the brook and sent his prophet to a complete stranger, a woman with no husband and no food in her house. That is how the spirit of God works: things will not always make sense, and you never know where the Lord will put you, or whom you will be sent to help.

At the gate of the city she was gathering sticks. Elijah asked her for a little water, and as she went, for a morsel of bread; she answered that she had only a handful of meal and a little oil, and was gathering two sticks to dress it for herself and her son, that they might eat it and die (1 Kings 17:10-12). She did not even know Elijah was a prophet; others were dying from the famine, and he was sent to her while she was making her last meal.

Elijah told her to fear not, to make him a little cake first and after that for herself and her son, for the Lord God of Israel said the barrel of meal would not waste nor the cruse of oil fail until the day the Lord sent rain (1 Kings 17:13-14). Fear not is the spirit in which a man of God comes. She went and did according to the saying of Elijah (1 Kings 17:15). The instruction to feed the man of God first is a precept: the man eats first. Sisters must trust in the Lord when he tells them to reverence their husbands and be submissive in all things, and not lean to their own understanding; the wife is to see that she reverence her husband, and that reverence goes into the honour of feeding the man first, just as the widow did (Ephesians 5:33). For trusting in the Lord and obeying, she was sustained.
judgmentFull: She and Elijah and her house did eat many days, and the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the Lord by Elijah (1 Kings 17:15-16). The little she had did not end until God sent rain upon the earth again; that is the power God gave his prophets, to do what is not natural.

After these things her son fell sick, so sore that there was no breath left in him, and she asked Elijah whether he had come to call her sin to remembrance and to slay her son (1 Kings 17:17-18). Her thought was that the child was paying for the parent’s sins; the Israelites of the past knew that God could bring judgment on a person for sins committed. When they met she was ready to die with her son; now there was food in the house, her son died, and she turned on the man of God.

Elijah carried the child up to the loft, laid him on his own bed, and cried to the Lord, not knowing what God was doing; he stretched himself upon the child three times, and the Lord heard the voice of Elijah, and the child revived (1 Kings 17:19-23). There are specific men who can talk to God, because spiritually they are where they need to be with God. All praises that Elijah was there to call upon the Lord, for it was not the young man’s time to go. A man’s days are determined and appointed, and he cannot pass the bound the Most High has set; because it was not the child’s time, the Lord let his soul return (Job 14:1-5).

She said that now she knew he was a man of God, and that the word of the Lord in his mouth was truth (1 Kings 17:24). The food that came to her house from nowhere did not settle it for her; had her son died, she would not have believed he was a prophet.

Christ referenced that history at Nazareth: many widows were in Israel when the heaven was shut three years and six months, but Elias was sent to none of them save to a widow of Sarepta, and of the many lepers none was cleansed but Naaman the Syrian (Luke 4:25-27). God was selective about whom he helped. Christ was saying he was not there for everybody, just as Elijah went to that one widow and Elisha dealt with that one man. The synagogue was filled with wrath and sought to cast him down headlong, because he spoke truth; it is the same now, and when the truth is spoken people get angry (Luke 4:28-29).

cases.name: Obadiah, who hid the prophets
cases.charge: Taking an hundred prophets and hiding them by fifty in a cave, and feeding them with bread and water, while governor of Ahab’s house, putting his own life in danger to save them
cases.summary: Obadiah was governor of Ahab’s house and feared the Lord greatly; when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord, he took an hundred of them, hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water, putting his own life in danger to save them (1 Kings 18:3-4). Sent out by Ahab to search for grass in the famine, he met Elijah on the way and was afraid to carry his message, lest the spirit of the Lord carry the prophet away and Ahab slay him; Elijah swore he would show himself that day, and Obadiah went (1 Kings 18:5-16).
offenseFull: In the third year the word of the Lord came to Elijah to show himself unto Ahab, and there was a sore famine in Samaria (1 Kings 18:1-2). Ahab called Obadiah, the governor of his house, the ruler of the king’s house; and Obadiah feared the Lord greatly, for when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord he took an hundred prophets, hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water (1 Kings 18:3-4). To cut off the prophets is not to cut someone off in his speech: she killed the prophets, so that a faithful prophet had to hide them. Obadiah was a prophet himself, and he took care of the servants of the Lord. Jezebel was the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, a Hamite, and she hated the prophets of God (1 Kings 16:31).

There were men in that time who feared the Lord greatly and were there in the famine, and they did not sit on their hands. The famine was so sore it was hitting the animals, so Ahab and Obadiah divided the land between them, each going his own way to every fountain and brook to find grass to save the horses and mules alive (1 Kings 18:5-6). This was the fruit of the drought Elijah had pronounced. The livestock was everything, and in a famine a righteous man has to be smart and plan to keep something alive.

As Obadiah was in the way, Elijah met him; Obadiah fell on his face, asked whether he was his lord Elijah, and was told to go tell his master that Elijah was there (1 Kings 18:7-8). Obadiah was afraid, for Ahab had searched every nation and kingdom to find and slay Elijah and made them swear they had not found him; that is how badly Jezebel wanted him dead, so she got Ahab to do her bidding. This is why Elijah had been on the run, first by Jordan, then years with the widow.

Obadiah feared that the spirit of the Lord would carry Elijah away and Ahab would slay him for a false report, so he pleaded his own record: he feared the Lord from his youth and had hidden an hundred of the Lord’s prophets by fifty in a cave and fed them (1 Kings 18:9-14). The errand put Obadiah’s life in danger, for Ahab hated Elijah and wanted him dead, and Obadiah had managed to spare an hundred prophets alive while the king was killing them. Elijah swore by the Lord of hosts that he would surely show himself to Ahab that day, and Obadiah went to Ahab, and Ahab came to meet Elijah (1 Kings 18:15-16).
judgmentFull: An hundred prophets of the Lord lived through Jezebel’s killing and the famine. Jezebel was not trying merely to destroy one prophet; she was trying to stop the whole prophetic voice out of Israel, the whole movement. It is the same today: when those who oppose the congregation speak against one specific person, their objective is to destroy the whole movement, for when the shepherd is smitten the flock flees (Zechariah 13:7). Jezebel’s spirit is the spirit that wants to stop the man from doing the work, and to stop the prophets from going out to teach.

Obadiah’s errand brought the king face to face with Elijah, and from that meeting came the gathering of all Israel to Mount Carmel with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of the groves that ate at Jezebel’s table (1 Kings 18:17-19).

When Elijah fled from Jezebel he said he alone was left, for the spirit of fear had entered into him (1 Kings 19:3; 1 Kings 19:10). In his panic he forgot what Obadiah had told him, that an hundred prophets were hidden away. The Lord answered that he had left himself seven thousand in Israel whose knees had not bowed unto Baal (1 Kings 19:18). Elijah was not by himself; the Lord had people reserved who had not yet awakened, ordained to come in at a certain time for a certain purpose. It is the same today: our job is to preach the word, for we never know what video or flyer will wake up the ones the Lord has reserved.

cases.name: The prophets of Baal at Carmel
cases.charge: Prophesying in the name of Baal, the devil, and eating at Jezebel’s table; crying from morning to noon to a god that could not answer
cases.summary: The four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, with the four hundred prophets of the groves, ate at Jezebel’s table, and Elijah called them to Mount Carmel before all Israel to see who was the true God (1 Kings 18:19-24). They dressed their bullock and cried to Baal from morning until past noon, leaped on their altar and cut themselves till the blood gushed out, but no one answered, for Baal is not a god at all (1 Kings 18:25-29). When Elijah prayed, the fire of the Lord fell, the people confessed that the Lord is God, and the prophets of Baal were taken down to the brook Kishon and slain (1 Kings 18:36-40).
offenseFull: Elijah told Ahab to gather all Israel to Carmel with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of the groves which ate at Jezebel’s table (1 Kings 18:19). Jezebel was the one feeding these eight hundred and fifty false prophets and encouraging them, and Ahab never checked her. She was a heathen, brought in from Zidon, whose father’s god was Baal, and she multiplied Baal worship throughout Samaria (1 Kings 16:31-33). She established these prophets, men under the authority of an evil woman, taking orders from her and eating at her table, while she killed the real prophets of God. Baal is the devil, and the four hundred and fifty were prophets of the devil. The symbol of Baal is the bull, the same as the calf the children of Israel made in the wilderness, so that our people began to worship Baal back then (Exodus 32:8).

Elijah asked the people how long they would halt between two opinions: if the Lord be God, follow him; if Baal, follow him; and the people answered not a word (1 Kings 18:20-21). It was a demonstration between the righteous and the wicked, to see who was the true God, the god of the Hamites or the God of Israel; our people were wholeheartedly into idolatry back then, the same way they are today.

Elijah proposed the test: each side would lay a bullock on wood with no fire under it, and the God that answered by fire, let him be God (1 Kings 18:22-24). The other nations also sacrificed, but they sacrificed unto devils, for God never made a covenant with them: God never chose the Hamites or the Ishmaelites; he chose only the Israelites, the so-called Negroes, Hispanics and Native Americans of today.

The prophets of Baal called on Baal from morning until noon, and there was no voice nor any that answered, and they leaped upon the altar (1 Kings 18:25-26). Picture the scene: eight hundred and fifty men running wild, while Elijah sat back watching the madness. At noon Elijah mocked them (1 Kings 18:27). They cried aloud and cut themselves with knives and lancets till the blood gushed out, for cutting themselves was part of their false worship whenever they called on Baal (1 Kings 18:28). That is why the law says no cuttings in the flesh (Leviticus 19:28): it was a Hamitic practice which still goes on today, for many of the tribes in Africa still make cuttings of the flesh as tradition.

From midday past the time of the evening sacrifice there was neither voice nor any to answer nor any that regarded (1 Kings 18:29). No one answered because the Most High will not give his glory to another, and the gods of the nations are idols that are not real; they are made up by people who have no God, so when they call on them the idols cannot answer (Isaiah 42:8; Psalms 96:4-5).
judgmentFull: Elijah repaired the altar of the Lord with twelve stones according to the twelve tribes of the sons of Jacob, for the whole book is about the twelve tribes of Israel; he had the sacrifice drenched three times until the water filled the trench, and at the time of the evening sacrifice he prayed that the people might know that the Lord is God in Israel and that he had turned their heart back again (1 Kings 18:30-37). The fire of the Lord fell and consumed the burnt sacrifice, the wood, the stones and the dust, and licked up the water in the trench, and the people fell on their faces and confessed that the Lord, he is the God (1 Kings 18:38-39).

Elijah commanded them to take the prophets of Baal and let not one of them escape, and they were brought down to the brook Kishon and slain there (1 Kings 18:40). The prophet that shall speak in the name of other gods shall die (Deuteronomy 18:20). In the last days it will be the same: when the Most High rains down fire again by the hands of Christ, no false prophet of Baal will escape, for they that feed the sheep of God lies will not be able to flee. Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of his pasture; the Lord will visit upon them the evil of their doings for feeding his people lies, and the same judgment that fell on the prophets of Baal will fall on the false shepherds today (Jeremiah 23:1-2). The prophets of Baal prophesy lies of peace, motivational speeches of money and financial tranquility; the prophets of God preach war, evil and pestilence against great kingdoms (Jeremiah 28:8-9).

There are seven thousand who have not bowed the knee to Baal and have not worshipped the devil, a remnant according to the election of grace, faithful to the true black Messiah, not to Baal, the white one (1 Kings 19:18; Romans 11:4-5). When Jezebel heard that all her prophets had been slain with the sword, she swore to take Elijah’s life; the power of God on Mount Carmel did not bring her to repentance but increased her fury (1 Kings 19:1-2).

cases.name: Elisha
cases.charge: Leaving the oxen and following; asking a double portion of the spirit; and refusing Naaman’s reward, as the Lord liveth, before whom I stand
cases.summary: Elijah found Elisha plowing with twelve yoke of oxen and cast his mantle upon him; Elisha slew the oxen, fed the people, and followed and ministered unto him, not turning back (1 Kings 19:19-21). He would not leave his master, asked for a double portion of his spirit, saw him taken up, and parted the Jordan with his mantle (2 Kings 2:1-15). Because of his obedience, diligence and faith, God put the double spirit of Elijah on him, and he did more miracles than his teacher; he refused Naaman’s gifts, and after his death a dead man who touched his bones revived (2 Kings 5:15-16; 2 Kings 13:20-21).
offenseFull: Elijah found Elisha the son of Shaphat plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and cast his mantle upon him (1 Kings 19:19). Elijah never spoke to him and never said follow me, but the spirit within Elisha told him this was a special calling and no regular person. He left the oxen without any question or doubt, ran after Elijah, and asked to kiss his father and mother first (1 Kings 19:20). Then he slew a yoke of oxen, boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen, gave unto the people, and arose and went after Elijah and ministered unto him (1 Kings 19:21). He fed the people before he left, and then he was gone on his mission, not turning back.

Elisha had faith. Husbandry was his occupation, and the oxen were his money maker, his prime source of resources, yet he destroyed the oxen and the instruments that drove them. No man who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62). A straight furrow takes tunnel vision, a keen eye looking forward on the narrow path; look back, and the furrow is crooked. Twelve oxen are the twelve tribes of Israel, with one goad and one shepherd to keep them in order, guiding all twelve back to repentance, and that is a major responsibility for the shepherds of Christ. The true profession is not the ploughman’s but the minister of God’s, and Elisha ministered unto Elijah: he was a servant, for in order to become a great leader one must first serve.

When the Lord was about to take up Elijah by a whirlwind, Elijah told Elisha to tarry at Gilgal, Bethel and Jericho, and each time Elisha refused to leave him (2 Kings 2:1-6). The sons of the prophets are a prophetic order or company, not the literal blood sons of the prophets. Elijah smote the Jordan with his mantle and they went over on dry ground, and Elisha asked for a double portion of his spirit. It was a hard thing, for it was the Most High, not Elijah, who would bestow that spirit, and it was granted if Elisha saw him taken (2 Kings 2:7-10). He saw him go up, took up the mantle that fell from him, meaning he took on the role of the prophet and teacher willingly, smote the waters, and they parted; the sons of the prophets said the spirit of Elijah rested on Elisha and bowed before him (2 Kings 2:11-15). After Elijah was gone, Elisha placed himself at the head of the prophetic school.
judgmentFull: The spirit that was on Elijah now worked through Elisha: he healed the waters of Jericho with salt (2 Kings 2:19-22). It was not a magical cape; it was the faith that was in him, in that double portion of Elijah’s spirit. For a widow of the sons of the prophets whose sons were to be taken as bondmen for her dead husband’s debt, the oil ran until every borrowed vessel was full, the empty vessels of her people, the children of Israel, filled through the spirit of the Lord (2 Kings 4:1-7). The Shunammite who made him a chamber bore a son at his word, and when the child died Elisha restored him to life (2 Kings 4:8-37). He took the death out of the pot at Gilgal and fed an hundred men with twenty loaves, according to the word of the Lord (2 Kings 4:38-44).

When Naaman was cleansed and confessed that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel, Elisha swore by the Lord before whom he stood that he would receive none, though Naaman urged him (2 Kings 5:15-16). Gehazi ran after the gifts and lied, and because he took in a time that was not the time to receive, the leprosy of Naaman cleaved to him and to his seed forever (2 Kings 5:20-27). There is a season to get and a season to lose (Ecclesiastes 3:6). This shows how Israel thought then and how the nation still thinks now, hasty to grasp things by unjust means.

When Syria sent a great host by night to Dothan for one prophet, Elisha told his servant that those with them were more than those against them, and the Lord opened the young man’s eyes to a mountain full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15-17). When Israel goes out to war there are more with them than with their enemies, for the angels of the Lord are with them (Psalms 34:7). He led the blinded Syrians into Samaria, had them fed and sent home, and the bands of Syria came no more into the land of Israel (2 Kings 6:18-23).

On his deathbed King Joash wept over him as the chariot of Israel, and Elisha put his hands upon the king’s hands for the arrow of the Lord’s deliverance from Syria; the king smote the ground only three times, and Elisha was wroth, for now he would smite Syria but thrice (2 Kings 13:14-19). Elisha died and was buried, and when a dead man was cast into his sepulchre and touched his bones, he revived and stood on his feet: the bones of Elisha were so potent with the spirit of God (2 Kings 13:20-21). Filled with Elijah’s spirit, in his life no prince could move him and none could bring him into subjection, and after his death his body prophesied (Ecclesiasticus 48:12-14).

cases.name: Ben-hadad and the Syrians at Aphek
cases.charge: Saying, the Lord is God of the hills, but he is not God of the valleys, and coming up again against Israel at the return of the year
cases.summary: After the young men of the princes of the provinces routed the Syrians before Samaria while Ben-hadad was drinking himself drunk with the thirty-two kings, his servants told him Israel’s gods were gods of the hills, to be beaten in the plain (1 Kings 20:16-23). He came again in the spring to Aphek, and a man of God told Ahab that because the Syrians had said the Lord was God of the hills and not of the valleys, he would deliver all that multitude into his hand (1 Kings 20:26-28). An hundred thousand fell in a day and a wall fell on twenty-seven thousand; Ahab let go the man the Lord had appointed to utter destruction, and Ben-hadad later died by the hand of Hazael (1 Kings 20:29-42; 2 Kings 8:15).
offenseFull: Ben-hadad the king of Syria gathered all his host, with thirty-two kings, horses and chariots, and besieged Samaria; he demanded Ahab’s silver, gold, wives and children, and then to search his house and take away whatsoever was pleasant in his eyes (1 Kings 20:1-6). This siege was Ahab’s judgment from the Lord for trying to kill Elijah, for serving Baal, and for letting Jezebel run him and kill the prophets. When the elders told Ahab not to consent, Ben-hadad swore by his gods to reduce Samaria to dust for handfuls, and Ahab answered that he who girds on his harness should not boast as he who puts it off; Ahab’s boast provoked him to prepare for battle (1 Kings 20:7-12).

A prophet came to Ahab with the word that the Lord would deliver that great multitude into his hand that day, and he would know that he is the Lord (1 Kings 20:13-14). Two hundred and thirty-two young men of the princes of the provinces went out at noon with seven thousand behind them, while Ben-hadad was drinking himself drunk with the thirty-two kings, taking Israel lightly; every one slew his man, the Syrians fled, and Ben-hadad escaped on a horse (1 Kings 20:15-21). The Most High gave the victory though Israel’s numbers were small.

The prophet warned Ahab to strengthen himself, for at the return of the year the king of Syria would come up again (1 Kings 20:22). The return of the year is the expiration of the year, the springtime, not January the first; in the ancient East the majority of wars were fought at the expiration of the year (2 Chronicles 36:10). Ben-hadad’s servants counselled that Israel’s gods were gods of the hills, so they should fight in the plain, replace the kings with captains, and number a fresh army horse for horse and chariot for chariot, and Ben-hadad hearkened (1 Kings 20:23-25). At the return of the year he came up to Aphek, and the children of Israel pitched before them like two little flocks of kids, while the Syrians filled the country (1 Kings 20:26-27).
judgmentFull: A man of God told Ahab that because the Syrians had said the Lord is God of the hills but not of the valleys, he would deliver all that great multitude into his hand, and they would know that he is the Lord (1 Kings 20:28). Here the Most High was giving Ahab a chance to repent, redeeming him by showing his power with fewer numbers; yet Ahab still did not repent, did not check Jezebel, and did not destroy the idols of Baal, for his sin had blinded him. The armies pitched one against the other seven days, and on the seventh the children of Israel slew an hundred thousand footmen of the Syrians in one day; the rest fled to Aphek, where a wall fell upon twenty-seven thousand of the men that were left (1 Kings 20:29-30). Seven thousand against an hundred thousand, and the numbers did not matter, because the Lord was with Israel.

Ben-hadad fled into an inner chamber, and his servants, having heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings, put sackcloth on their loins and ropes on their heads and went to plead for his life. Ahab called him his brother, brought him up into his chariot, and sent him away with a covenant of restored cities and streets in Damascus (1 Kings 20:31-34). Look at Ahab’s wickedness: this was a Syrian who had just been trying to kill him the year before. Our people have always been like this, showing mercy to a people that has always held us in captivity, for the love of the enemy, while killing their own. The Lord had said he would destroy that nation, and the Lord does not like it when mercy is shown to a people he said should not have mercy.

A prophet, disguised with ashes, brought Ahab a parable and had him judge himself, and then declared that because he had let go a man whom the Lord appointed to utter destruction, his life would go for his life and his people for his people (1 Kings 20:35-42). Ben-hadad was supposed to die at war with Ahab, tied to the word that Hazael would move into the kingship of Syria (1 Kings 19:15). They were to be destroyed; instead Jerusalem was destroyed in 70 AD, and the land is trodden down of the Gentiles, of those now called the Jewish people: Israel’s people went for their people (Luke 21:24). In those days wicked men of Israel persuaded many to make a covenant with the heathen round about (1 Maccabees 1:11). A covenant with the heathen is a covenant with death and an agreement with hell, and our people made it then and do the same today, thinking the overflowing scourge will not reach them (Isaiah 28:15).

Ben-hadad the Second of Aram Damascus and Ahab king of Israel are recorded together on the Assyrian inscription of Shalmaneser III at the battle of Qarqar, in 853 BC, with ten thousand men of Ahab; that Ben-hadad of Damascus is the same Ben-hadad as in the scriptures. When he lay sick and sent Hazael to inquire of Elisha whether he would recover, Elisha wept for the evil Hazael would do to Israel, and on the morrow Hazael took a thick cloth dipped in water and spread it on his face so that he died, and reigned in his stead (2 Kings 8:7-15).

cases.name: The man who refused the prophetic command
cases.charge: Refusing to smite the prophet when commanded in the word of the Lord, and so not obeying the voice of the Lord
cases.summary: A certain man of the sons of the prophets told his neighbour, in the word of the Lord, to smite him, and the man refused. The prophet told him that because he had not obeyed the voice of the Lord, a lion would slay him as soon as he departed, and a lion found him and slew him (1 Kings 20:35-36). Another man smote and wounded the prophet, who then brought Ahab a parable by which the king judged himself for letting go Ben-hadad, whom the Lord had appointed to utter destruction (1 Kings 20:37-42).
offenseFull: The man who gave the command was one of the sons of the prophets (1 Kings 20:35). To know the judgment for the mysteries of God, we have to know who the sons of the prophets are, and it begins with Moses: the Lord took of the spirit that was upon him and gave it unto the seventy elders, and when the spirit rested upon them they prophesied (Numbers 11:16-25). Samuel set up a school called the sons of the prophets, based on what Moses said when he wished that all the Lord’s people were prophets, and Samuel stood as appointed over them (Numbers 11:29; 1 Samuel 19:20).

The sons of the prophets were men upon whom the spirit of prophecy was; they understood that they needed to learn and to study, for the Most High was using them for the spirit of prophecy, and Israel knew them and who they were. Some of them opened schools or houses of instruction, where they taught their disciples the pure religion of Moses: one at Naioth in Ramah where Samuel dwelt, one at Jericho, and a third at Bethel, to which Elijah and Elisha often resorted; thither the people went on Sabbath days and at new moons and received public lessons of piety and morality. The students in these colleges were called the sons of the prophets, and God generally chose the prophets whom he inspired out of these schools.

Ahab had just made a covenant with Ben-hadad and sent him away, though the Lord had appointed him to utter destruction (1 Kings 20:34; 1 Kings 20:42). The son of the prophets said unto his neighbour in the word of the Lord, smite me, and the man refused to smite him (1 Kings 20:35).
judgmentFull: The prophet said that because he had not obeyed the voice of the Lord, a lion would slay him as soon as he departed, and as soon as he departed a lion found him and slew him (1 Kings 20:36).

Another man smote the prophet and wounded him, and the prophet disguised himself with ashes on his face and waited for the king by the way, hiding the certain look that prophets carry, the same way we carry a certain look today (1 Kings 20:37-38). He cried to the king a parable of a soldier charged to keep a prisoner on pain of his own life, who let the man escape, and the king of Israel judged that so his judgment should be; he himself had decided it (1 Kings 20:39-40). Then the prophet took the ashes away, and Ahab discerned that he was one of the prophets (1 Kings 20:41).

The prophet declared that because Ahab had let go a man whom the Lord appointed to utter destruction, his life would go for his life and his people for his people (1 Kings 20:42). Ben-hadad was supposed to die at war with Ahab, tied to the word that Hazael would move into the kingship of Syria, but Ahab made a covenant with him instead of killing him.

The king of Israel went to his house heavy and displeased and came to Samaria, crying again over a just judgment because he would not obey the voice of the Lord (1 Kings 20:43). The lesson for us is the same: as it is written, so shall we do, that we may be justified and our life not be taken from us for rebellion against the Lord.

cases.name: Jezebel and Naboth’s vineyard
cases.charge: Writing letters in the king’s name under his seal, proclaiming a fast, and setting two sons of Belial to bear false witness, so that Naboth was stoned and his inheritance taken for a covetous king
cases.summary: Naboth would not sell Ahab the vineyard beside the palace in Jezreel, because it was the inheritance of his fathers and the land belonged to the Most High (1 Kings 21:1-3; Leviticus 25:23). Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab’s name under his seal, had a fast proclaimed, set two sons of Belial to witness falsely that Naboth blasphemed God and the king, and had him stoned: an evil counsel and a murderous plot (1 Kings 21:8-14). Ahab shares the guilt, for he went down to take the vineyard (1 Kings 21:15-16). Elijah pronounced the sentence on his house and on Jezebel, and the dogs ate her in the portion of Jezreel (1 Kings 21:17-24; 2 Kings 9:30-37).
offenseFull: Ahab asked for Naboth’s vineyard, hard by his palace, as a garden of herbs, offering a better vineyard or its worth in money, and Naboth refused, because it was the inheritance of his fathers (1 Kings 21:1-3). He could not simply hand off an inheritance that was given to him; the land was not to be sold for ever, for it belonged to the Most High and was held as a family inheritance (Leviticus 25:23). If the other vineyard was better, why take this one? A king with all Israel under his control was eyeing what belonged to his neighbour, and the law says thou shalt not covet (Exodus 20:17).

Ahab went home heavy and displeased, laid down on his bed, turned away his face, and would eat no bread (1 Kings 21:4). He threw a fit and sulked because he could not get his way. His attributes were that he was weak, he was emotional, and he had a position of authority.

Jezebel mocked his weakness, asking whether he did not govern the kingdom of Israel, and promised to get him the vineyard (1 Kings 21:5-7). She was mean, controlling and manipulative, and she liked a man with authority. The Jezebel spirit is a controlling spirit: it looks for the mild-mannered brother who has something going on, whom she can control, and it always marries weak men who have some kind of authority, so that she can operate through them. There is a difference between being strong and being mean-spirited.

She wrote letters in Ahab’s name and sealed them with his seal (1 Kings 21:8). The seal was a signet, the official mark of the king’s authority, so the letters carried royal weight as if Ahab himself had written them (Daniel 6:17). She was ruling through his power; to make it plain, Jezebel was the king.

She commanded a fast, to give the illusion that it was done in righteousness, and had Naboth set on high, which was a set up, with two sons of Belial, children of the devil, to witness that he blasphemed God and the king (1 Kings 21:9-13). They were hired to bear false witness, which is exactly what the commandment forbids (Exodus 20:16), the same thing they did to Christ; and the king and Jezebel themselves did not believe in God. There was no judgment and there were no true witnesses, which shows it was an evil and wicked plot. Jezebel, who was not even there, told Ahab to take possession with no remorse, ready to have people killed and to lie with the word of God to make her husband happy (1 Kings 21:14-15).

Ahab rose up to take the vineyard (1 Kings 21:16). This is extortion, seizing what another has by violence and force, and the Most High smites his hand at dishonest gain and shed blood (Ezekiel 22:12-13). Ahab knew exactly what was going on: he let Jezebel commit the crime because he coveted the field, then went to claim the reward, and following a multitude to do evil he became an accomplice to murder and theft (Exodus 23:2). There was none like Ahab, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up (1 Kings 21:25), and the Jezebel spirit will stir a man up.
judgmentFull: The Lord watches everything. Nothing can be hidden from him: he sent Elijah to meet Ahab in the vineyard of Naboth, in possession of stolen property. Elijah was to ask whether he had killed and also taken possession, and tell him the dogs would lick his blood where they licked Naboth’s (1 Kings 21:17-19). Selfishness is the spirit of murder: hatred, murder and theft, all because he wanted somebody else’s possession.

Ahab called Elijah his enemy, as with Christ: tell them the truth and you become their enemy (1 Kings 21:20; John 8:45). Because he sold himself to work evil, every male of his house would be cut off, his house made like those of Jeroboam and Baasha, and the dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel, the curse spoken in the law (1 Kings 21:21-24; Deuteronomy 28:26). He lost everything over one vineyard; one sinner destroys much good (Ecclesiastes 9:18). When a man is wrongly killed for standing firm, the Lord makes sure there will be a restitution for that spirit: it will come back on this earth again, and the Lord will allow it to be prosperous.

Because Ahab humbled himself in sackcloth, the evil was moved to his son’s days (1 Kings 21:27-29). The judgment was not cancelled but delayed and transferred to the next generation; genuine humbling before the Most High moves his hand. Sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, but the Lord is patient, and he will get to them (Ecclesiastes 8:11-13).

Jehu was anointed to avenge the blood of the prophets shed at the hand of Jezebel, whose work was to kill the prophets while weak Ahab let it continue (2 Kings 9:1-10). There is no peace as long as a wicked woman is in power (2 Kings 9:22). Jezebel painted her face, wanting to entice foolish men to her side with a beauty that was superficial; she was thrown down, and they found only the skull, the feet and the palms of her hands, as Elijah had spoken (2 Kings 9:30-37). The Most High does not go by emotions, and it does not matter that she was a woman: whoever puts themselves in the wrong position against his instruction for the nation, he will address it.

cases.name: Micaiah the son of Imlah
cases.charge: Speaking only what the Lord said to him, against four hundred prophets and the king who hated him, and standing by it under a slap and in prison
cases.summary: When four hundred prophets told Ahab to go up to Ramoth-gilead, Jehoshaphat asked for a prophet of the Lord, and Ahab named Micaiah the son of Imlah, whom he hated (1 Kings 22:6-8). Urged to agree with the others, Micaiah answered that whatever the Lord said to him, that he would speak; he saw Israel scattered as sheep having no shepherd and a lying spirit in Ahab’s prophets, and was smitten and imprisoned (1 Kings 22:13-27). His word stood as the test of who truly spoke for the Most High, and Ahab died at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22:28-38).
offenseFull: After three years without war, Jehoshaphat king of Judah came down to Ahab, who wanted Ramoth-gilead back from the king of Syria (1 Kings 22:1-4). Ramoth-gilead, a Levitical city of refuge east of the Jordan, had been lost to Aram-Damascus. Jehoshaphat answered that he was as Ahab was, his people as Ahab’s people, though the kingdom was split by then, and the northern kingdom was no longer considered God’s people. The northern kingdom are the Latino, Hispanic tribes, and Judah is the American Negroes; that is their identity in the Bible. A man cannot join affinity with people just because they are his people, and this was a war not sanctioned by God. Jehoshaphat was making a bad decision in being with the wicked, but he still had the spirit on him, and he asked first to inquire at the word of the Lord (1 Kings 22:5).

Ahab gathered about four hundred prophets, who all said with one mouth, go up, for the Lord would deliver it into the hand of the king (1 Kings 22:6). After the split the northern kingdom fell into idolatry and forsook the Levites, so a prophet of the Most High would want nothing to do with their manner of worship (2 Kings 3:13). They were four hundred state prophets, yes men; and in the same way many Israelite groups today should not be assumed to be connected to God because they have a Bible and a Hebrew name.

Jehoshaphat was not moved by four hundred prophets speaking the same thing; he saw something in the spirit with those men, and asked whether there was not yet a prophet of the Lord (1 Kings 22:7). Ahab said there was one man, Micaiah, but he hated him, because he did not prophesy good concerning him, but evil (1 Kings 22:8). The king already knew where to go for good counsel, but he chose four hundred who would tell him what he wanted to hear, as many do today. They acknowledged that the spirit of the Lord was on Micaiah and hated him anyway, because he prophesied that the Sabbath must be kept, fringes worn on all garments, and one wife kept, not many. Everything that was the counsel of God, Ahab perceived as evil towards him. They hate him that rebuketh in the gate, and they abhor him that speaketh uprightly (Amos 5:10).

The messenger tried to prepare him to agree: all the prophets declared good to the king with one mouth, so let his word be like theirs (1 Kings 22:13). In plain words: lie to him and make it sound good. Micaiah swore by the living Lord that whatever the Lord said to him, that he would speak (1 Kings 22:14). At first he echoed the others, and the king adjured him to tell nothing but the truth, wanting to be told the truth and lied to at the same time (1 Kings 22:15-16).

Then he said he saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep with no shepherd, and the Lord said they had no master and should go home in peace (1 Kings 22:17). Micaiah went against four hundred prophets; numbers mean nothing, you stand by the Bible. It was not evil counsel at all; the counsel was for him to save his life, and it was mercy from God, but Ahab perceived it as evil because he was walking in the flesh and not in the spirit (1 Kings 22:18). Micaiah saw the Lord on his throne with all the host of heaven, and a spirit offered to be a lying spirit in the mouth of all Ahab’s prophets (1 Kings 22:19-23). The decision had already been made in the heavens and was passed down through the prophet. The deceiver as well as the deceived are under the hand of the Most High, who uses the lie to bring the judgment he has already declared (Job 12:16).
judgmentFull: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah smote Micaiah on the cheek, defending his own false prophecy, and the king ordered Micaiah put in prison and fed with the bread and water of affliction until he returned in peace (1 Kings 22:24-27). They put him in prison because they did not like what he spoke, not for adultery, or hitting a brother, or stealing, but for the words of the laws that came out of his mouth. Micaiah’s light shined on their darkness, and roaches are revealed when the light turns on.

Micaiah answered that if Ahab returned at all in peace, the Lord had not spoken by him, and called all the people to hearken (1 Kings 22:28). His word stands as the test of who truly spoke for the Most High. When a man goes against sound counsel from the Lord and the thing works, it was the devil that helped him, not God.

Ahab disguised himself, hoping to escape the word spoken against him, and a certain man drew a bow at a venture and smote Ahab between the joints of the harness (1 Kings 22:29-34). God makes no mistakes: when the counsel is rejected, judgment is coming, and it will fall on the one it was spoken against. Ahab died at even, and the dogs licked his blood according to the word of the Lord (1 Kings 22:35-38). The counsel of the Lord stood, and no one can fight against it (Proverbs 19:21).

Micaiah was not afraid of four hundred men, and that is how we must be. Christ said not to be ashamed of him, or he will be ashamed of us before the Father; and those who stand for the Most High and his laws are hated in the same way today.

cases.name: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah, and the four hundred prophets
cases.charge: Prophesying victory at Ramoth-gilead in the name of the Lord with horns of iron, by a lying spirit, telling the king what he wanted to hear; and smiting Micaiah on the cheek for telling him the truth
cases.summary: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made horns of iron and said in the name of the Lord that with these Ahab would push the Syrians until they were consumed, and all four hundred prophets said the same: they were lying to him (1 Kings 22:10-12). When Micaiah revealed the lying spirit in their mouths, Zedekiah smote him on the cheek and asked which way the spirit of the Lord went from him to speak to Micaiah (1 Kings 22:23-24). Micaiah told him he would see on the day he went into an inner chamber to hide himself, running for his life (1 Kings 22:25), and Ahab died at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22:34-37).
offenseFull: Ahab gathered about four hundred prophets, who all said with one mouth, go up, for the Lord would deliver Ramoth-gilead into the hand of the king (1 Kings 22:6). They came from a kingdom where Jeroboam had cast out the priests of the Lord, the sons of Aaron, and made priests after the manner of the nations, so that any man could consecrate himself to serve gods that are no gods (2 Chronicles 13:9). Jehoshaphat already knew that God was not in that council at all; they were just talking, and they would set the king up for failure.

Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made horns of iron and said in the name of the Lord that with these Ahab would push the Syrians until they were consumed, and all the prophets said go up and prosper (1 Kings 22:10-12). Here again a man claimed to speak for the Most High; everybody repeated what Zedekiah said and hopped on the bandwagon. They were lying to him. There are men set up to lie and to tell you what makes you feel good, and they do not care if you die.

They are the rebellious people and lying children who will not hear the law of the Lord, who tell the seers not to see and the prophets to speak smooth things rather than right things (Isaiah 30:8-10). Rebellion and lies go hand in hand, for to rebel against God a man has to concoct a lie to justify it; They are the false ministers of whom Paul warned: Satan himself takes the form of an angel of light, so it is no surprise that his ministers pass as ministers of righteousness; their end will be according to their works, and that judgment is death (2 Corinthians 11:13-15).

Micaiah saw the Lord on his throne and a spirit that went forth to be a lying spirit in the mouth of all Ahab’s prophets (1 Kings 22:19-23). God despised Ahab so much that he sent a spirit to entice him to his death, and all it took was to convince one wicked leader, and everybody under him would be harmed. There is counsel in the heavens for lying spirits to come to leaders and push lies to the congregation, and it can happen today: God will allow liars to walk this earth to destroy those who do not read, and people who do not read are the ones who bleed.

Then Zedekiah came near and smote Micaiah on the cheek, and asked which way the spirit of the Lord went from him to speak unto Micaiah (1 Kings 22:24). In other words: who do you think you are? God talks to me too. He struck the man of God in the face for telling the truth. That is what is done, spiritually, when the counsel given by the man of the Lord is rejected: he is slapped. The same hatred they had for the prophets then falls on those who tell the truth now.
judgmentFull: Micaiah answered that Zedekiah would see in that day when he went into an inner chamber to hide himself (1 Kings 22:25). He was telling him he was going to die: having struck the man of God in the face, he would be running for his life, looking for a chamber to hide in as they hunted him down to kill him.

Ahab was smitten by a bow drawn at a venture and died at even, and the host was scattered every man to his own country, as Micaiah had seen (1 Kings 22:29-37). God makes no mistakes: when the counsel is rejected, the judgment comes on the one it was spoken against, and the counsel of the Lord stood.

The deceiver as well as the deceived are under the hand of the Most High, who used the lie in their mouths to bring the judgment he had already declared on Ahab (Job 12:16). Religious leaders who deviate from the Bible and make things up still put the people in harm’s way and do not care if they die, in the Christian church and in the Israelite community alike.
