cases.name: Ahaziah of Israel
cases.charge: Sending to inquire of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron, which is Satan, as though there were no God in Israel; and sending captains of fifty to bring down the man of God
cases.summary: Ahaziah fell through a lattice in his upper chamber and sent to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, the lord of the flies, whether he would recover; he turned to an idol rather than to the Most High (2 Kings 1:2). Elijah met the messengers with the word that he would not come down from his bed but would surely die, and fire from heaven consumed two captains and their fifties sent to bring him down (2 Kings 1:3-12). Ahaziah died according to the word of the Lord that Elijah had spoken (2 Kings 1:16-17).
offenseFull: Moab rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab (2 Kings 1:1). Nations that had been subdued under David and brought under tribute began to break away, because Israel no longer walked in the blessing that came from serving the Most High (2 Samuel 8:1-2). If Israel hearkened diligently to do his commandments, the Most High would set them on high above all nations and smite their enemies before them; if not, their carcasses would be meat for the fowls, the same judgment pronounced on the house of Ahab (Deuteronomy 28:1, 7, 15, 25-26).

Joshua set the choice before the people, and before he died told them to serve their God and their God alone (Joshua 24:15-29). So no one can blame God: it is you. Ahaziah fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber and was sick, and he sent messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron whether he would recover (2 Kings 1:2). He reasoned that God was not listening to him. Baal-zebub was a god of the Hamites at Ekron; it means lord of the flies, and it is another name for Satan, the master of devils.

Ahaziah should have known the history that would have kept him from trusting the god of Ekron. When the ark of God came to Ekron, the Ekronites cried out that it had been brought to slay them, for the hand of God was heavy there, so the god of Ekron could not even defend his own people against the God of Israel (1 Samuel 5:10-11).

The angel of the Lord sent Elijah the Tishbite to meet the messengers and ask whether it was because there was no God in Israel that they went to inquire of Baal-zebub: there was a God among his own people, in his own land, so why go to the devil? The word of the Lord was that Ahaziah would not come down from his bed but would surely die (2 Kings 1:3-4). Elijah was quick to the point, and left.

When the messengers described the hairy man girt with a girdle of leather about his loins, the king knew it was Elijah (2 Kings 1:7-8). The hairy man means the clothes he wore, a coat of hair, for Israel was a smooth man, as Jacob had to put on goat’s hair to seem like Esau (Genesis 27:11-16). John the Baptist wore the same clothing, camel’s hair and a girdle of skin, because John the Baptist was Elijah back on the earth (Mark 1:6; Matthew 17:10-13). The king, of Jezebel’s house, already had an inherent vendetta against Elijah, and he sent a captain of fifty with his fifty to command the man of God to come down (2 Kings 1:9).
judgmentFull: Elijah answered that if he was a man of God, fire would come down from heaven and consume the captain and his fifty, and it did; a second captain of fifty spoke the same way, and fire from heaven consumed him and his fifty as well (2 Kings 1:10-12). This is not a lie and not a Marvel movie; it really happened, and it is our history: our forefathers did this. Elijah, who stood up as fire, by the word of the Lord three times brought down fire, one of the times back to back (Ecclesiasticus 48:1-3). God did not let his word fall (1 Samuel 3:19), and the men the Lord sends are not regular men.

The third captain was a wise one. He went up, fell on his knees, and pleaded that his life and the lives of his fifty be precious in Elijah’s sight, for he had heard that the two captains with their fifties were burned up, and he humbled himself quickly (2 Kings 1:13-14). The man who knows he has done wrong is wise to come back and ask the brothers to pray for him.

Elijah went down with the third captain and delivered to the king the same word (2 Kings 1:15-16). Ahaziah died according to the word of the Lord that Elijah had spoken (2 Kings 1:17). By the word of the Most High, Elijah brought kings to destruction and honourable men from their bed (Ecclesiasticus 48:6).

Jehoshaphat king of Judah had joined himself with this Ahaziah, who did very wickedly, to make ships, and the Lord broke his works, so that the ships could not go to Tarshish (2 Chronicles 20:35-37). If we join with those who do wickedness, the Lord will break our works.

cases.name: The young mockers of Bethel
cases.charge: Mocking the prophet of the Lord, an elder to be entreated as a father: go up, thou bald head
cases.summary: As Elisha went up to Bethel, little children came out of the city and mocked him, saying go up, thou bald head (2 Kings 2:19-23). He cursed them in the name of the Lord, and two she bears came out of the wood and tore forty and two of them; the Lord put the spirit on those bears to put the forty-two children to death, because they disrespected the prophet (2 Kings 2:24).
offenseFull: At Jericho Elisha cast salt into the spring and the waters were healed to this day; the sign showed that the spirit that was on Elijah now worked through Elisha (2 Kings 2:19-22). He had that double portion, and he was not a man to be played with.

As he went up to Bethel, little children came out of the city and mocked him, saying go up, thou bald head (2 Kings 2:23). That is how it is known he had some age on him. They were talking trash; they saw a prophet and did not care whether he was a prophet or not. This is the child behaving proudly against the elderly (Isaiah 3:5). A man is not to be dishonoured in his old age (Ecclesiasticus 8:6), and an elder is not to be rebuked but entreated as a father (1 Timothy 5:1). Elisha was not their physical father, but the commandment to honour father and mother is not only for the physical parents (Exodus 20:12): the elders set over the church are to be entreated as fathers. The eye that mocks a father, the ravens of the valley will pick out (Proverbs 30:17), and those children mocked Elisha when they were supposed to treat him as a father.

Children being disrespectful to their elders is a sin. Those children had no home training, the same as the gangs and the evil going on today. A child is known by his doings, so stop making excuses for them (Proverbs 20:11). And do not judge a man by how he looks in the flesh: you might be dealing with an Elisha.
judgmentFull: He turned back, looked on them, and cursed them in the name of the Lord, and two she bears came out of the wood and tore forty and two children of them (2 Kings 2:24). He cursed them in the name of the Lord, so whatever happened next was of the Lord. For two bears to kill forty-two children, it was a spiritual thing. It is the same way Esau was able to conquer us and put us in slavery: the Most High removed the spirit of flight and the strong spirit we had, and put the spirit of fear within us, so that two men, one on a horse and one with a gun, could guard a whole plantation.

There are spirits created for vengeance, which in the time of destruction pour out their force to appease the wrath of their maker, and the teeth of wild beasts are among them (Ecclesiasticus 39:28-30). God created specific spirits to deal with specific matters, and the Lord put the spirit on those bears to kill those children. It might sound very harsh, but that is how the Lord moves. It is a curse of the law that he sends wild beasts among a disobedient people to rob them of their children (Leviticus 26:22). Under the law, the stubborn and rebellious son was stoned, and all Israel heard and feared (Deuteronomy 21:18-21); under the new covenant men do not stone today, and no one may touch the children, but the Lord still can.

God brings every work into judgment, every secret thing, good or evil (Ecclesiastes 12:14). Parents have to take the time to read this to their children and teach them the judgments on disrespectful children, and put the fear of the Lord in them. Why the Lord made those bears kill the forty-two, we do not know; we do not know who those children were. Vengeance belongs to the Lord: a man’s own vengeance is only his self-gratification (Romans 12:19).

cases.name: The prophet’s widow, and the pot of oil
cases.charge: Crying to the man of God in her distress, and in faith borrowing empty vessels of her neighbours, not a few, shutting the door, and pouring, as the prophet said
cases.summary: A woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets cried to Elisha that her husband, who feared the Lord, was dead, and the creditor had come to take her two sons to be bondmen (2 Kings 4:1). She had nothing in the house but a pot of oil; Elisha told her to borrow empty vessels of all her neighbours, not a few, shut the door upon herself and her sons, and pour, and the oil continued until every vessel was full (2 Kings 4:2-6). She sold the oil, paid her debt, and lived with her children on the rest (2 Kings 4:7).
offenseFull: The sons of the prophets were a prophetic order or company, not the literal blood sons of the prophets (2 Kings 2:3-7). Samuel set up a school called the sons of the prophets, and he stood appointed over them as the head instructor (1 Samuel 19:20); they walked in the same footsteps, obedient and learning. Some of the sons of the prophets were married, as this woman’s cry shows (2 Kings 4:1).

Her husband feared the Lord and died in debt, so the creditor came to take her two sons to work off what was owed (2 Kings 4:1). Elisha asked what he should do for her, and what she had in the house, because God already had a plan. This is for the brothers who think their children belong to them: nothing here belongs to us. The man who refuses to stand because he is afraid of who will take care of his wife and his son if something happens to him lacks faith; trust in the Lord, for God already knows the plan, and the map is already there. If a man is put in handcuffs, he should take it cheerfully, as a prophet, and not come with a weak mind.

She said she had nothing in the house but a pot of oil, and he told her to borrow empty vessels of all her neighbours, not a few, then shut the door upon herself and her sons, pour oil into all the vessels, and set aside each that was full (2 Kings 4:2-4). She went and did as the prophet said (2 Kings 4:5). Even this woman showed faith in what Elisha told her.
judgmentFull: Her sons brought the vessels to her, and she poured; when she asked for yet another vessel there was not one more, and the oil stayed (2 Kings 4:5-6). The oil continued until every vessel was full, and only then did it stay. The empty vessels she borrowed from her people, the children of Israel, were filled through the spirit of the Lord. That is the power of God with his prophet.

She told the man of God, and he told her to sell the oil, pay her debt, and live with her children on the rest (2 Kings 4:7). All she had was a little oil, and Elisha multiplied it until she had enough to sell and pay the debt she was distressed about. God is the power.

These were among the miracles the Most High allowed Elisha to do based on his faith and his obedience. When Christ fed the five thousand and twelve baskets were left over, it was not happening for the first time (Luke 9:12-17). By his spirit that was in the prophets, the Lord did marvellous works through the prophets of former times, beyond the aspect of prophesying (1 Peter 1:10-11); in the same chapter Elisha set twenty loaves before a hundred men, and they ate and had some left over, according to the word of the Lord (2 Kings 4:42-44).

cases.name: The Shunammite woman
cases.charge: Constraining the man of God to eat bread, and building him a little chamber on the wall with a bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick
cases.summary: A great woman of Shunem constrained Elisha to eat bread, perceived that he was a holy man of God, and had a little chamber made for him on the wall (2 Kings 4:8-10). Promised a son, like our mother Sarah she did not believe it, yet she bore him at the season set (2 Kings 4:14-17; Genesis 18:11-14). When the child died she laid him on the bed of the man of God, and the Most High restored him through Elisha; when she came home from the famine, the timing was of the Most High, and the king restored all that was hers (2 Kings 4:32-37; 2 Kings 8:1-6).
offenseFull: Elisha passed through Shunem, where a great woman constrained him to eat bread, and as often as he passed by he turned in there to eat (2 Kings 4:8). She perceived that he was a holy man of God and told her husband to make a little chamber on the wall with a bed, a table, a stool and a candlestick, so that he might turn in whenever he came (2 Kings 4:9-10). Elisha wanted to bless her and sent Gehazi to ask whether she would be spoken for to the king or to the captain of the host; she answered that she dwelt among her own people (2 Kings 4:11-13).

Gehazi told Elisha that she had no child and her husband was old, and Elisha told her that about that season she would embrace a son (2 Kings 4:14-16). Like our mother Sarah, she did not believe it and told the man of God not to lie to his handmaid; Sarah laughed within herself because she and Abraham were old, and the Lord asked whether anything was too hard for him (Genesis 18:11-14). Yet she conceived and bore a son at that season (2 Kings 4:17).

When the child was grown he went out to his father to the reapers, cried out for his head, was carried to his mother, sat on her knees till noon, and died, from what seemed only a headache (2 Kings 4:18-20). She laid him on the bed of the man of God, the bed in the chamber she had made for Elisha, shut the door, and asked her husband for a young man and an ass; when he asked why, since it was neither new moon nor sabbath, she answered that it would be well (2 Kings 4:21-23). On the sabbath days and at the new moons the people went to the prophets and received public lessons of piety and morality, for the schools of the prophets taught the pure religion of Moses, God’s laws and commandments; what is done in Israel today in the same way is nothing new.

She rode to Elisha at Carmel and told Gehazi that it was well, and at the hill she caught the prophet by the feet; when Gehazi came to thrust her away, Elisha said to let her alone, for her soul was vexed within her and the Lord had hid it from him (2 Kings 4:24-27). She asked whether she had desired a son, and whether she had not said not to deceive her (2 Kings 4:28). Elisha sent Gehazi ahead with his staff, but she swore that she would not leave him, and he arose and followed her (2 Kings 4:29-30).
judgmentFull: Gehazi laid the staff on the face of the child, but there was neither voice nor hearing (2 Kings 4:31). Elisha found the child dead upon his bed, shut the door upon them both, and prayed unto the Lord first (2 Kings 4:32-33). Prayer is powerful: the prayer of faith shall save the sick, but if a man has doubts, it will not work (James 5:14-15). A prayer out of a poor man’s mouth reaches to the ears of God (Ecclesiasticus 21:5): a man does not have to be rich for the Lord to hear his prayer, for the Most High stretches his ears first to the poor.

He lay upon the child, mouth upon mouth, eyes upon eyes, hands upon hands, and the flesh of the child grew warm, which means life was coming back into the child (2 Kings 4:34). That is what is called CPR today, and the world did not come up with it by its science; it got it from our book, the Bible. He walked in the house to and fro and stretched himself upon him again, and the child sneezed seven times and opened his eyes (2 Kings 4:35). Elijah had done the same for the widow’s son, crying unto the Lord and stretching himself upon the child three times (1 Kings 17:20-22).

Elisha told her to take up her son, and she fell at his feet, bowed herself to the ground, took up her son, and went out (2 Kings 4:36-37). This is another act of the Most High through Elisha, restoring the child to life, one of the miracles the Most High allowed Elisha to do because of his faith and his obedience.

Elisha warned her to arise with her household and sojourn wherever she could, for the Lord had called for a famine of seven years (2 Kings 8:1). The Lord called for a famine in Elisha’s time, and he is calling for a famine upon this country today for a reason; that is why leadership puts out, over and over, the warning to prepare. A famine can purge out evil, and in their affliction the people will seek the Lord early (Hosea 5:15): when the masses realise they need to seek the Lord, they will not find him in a Christian church but will come to the prophets of the Lord, and be told to repent.

She sojourned in the land of the Philistines seven years and returned to appeal to the king for her house and land, at the very moment Gehazi was telling the king how Elisha had restored a dead body to life (2 Kings 8:2-5). The timing was of the Most High, and the king restored all that was hers, and all the fruits of the field from the day she left (2 Kings 8:6).

cases.offense: Elisha passed through Shunem, where a great woman constrained him to eat bread, and as often as he passed by he turned in there to eat (2 Kings 4:8). She perceived that he was a holy man of God and told her husband to make a little chamber on the wall with a bed, a table, a stool and a candlestick, so that he might turn in whenever he came (2 Kings 4:9-10). Elisha wanted to bless her and sent Gehazi to ask whether she would be spoken for to the king or to the captain of the host; she answered that she dwelt among her own people (2 Kings 4:11-13).
cases.judgment: Gehazi laid the staff on the face of the child, but there was neither voice nor hearing (2 Kings 4:31). Elisha found the child dead upon his bed, shut the door upon them both, and prayed unto the Lord first (2 Kings 4:32-33). Prayer is powerful: the prayer of faith shall save the sick, but if a man has doubts, it will not work (James 5:14-15). A prayer out of a poor man’s mouth reaches to the ears of God (Ecclesiasticus 21:5): a man does not have to be rich for the Lord to hear his prayer, for the Most High stretches his ears first to the poor.

cases.name: Naaman the Syrian
cases.charge: Going down and dipping himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God, after his anger
cases.summary: Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, by whom the Lord had given deliverance to Syria, was a leper, and an Israelite sister serving in his house pointed him to the prophet in Samaria (2 Kings 5:1-3). Told to wash in Jordan seven times, he turned away in a rage, full of pride, because this was not the process he expected; his servants humbled him, and when he dipped seven times according to the saying of the man of God his flesh came again like the flesh of a little child (2 Kings 5:10-14). What healed him was his belief and his obedience, and he confessed that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel (2 Kings 5:15).
offenseFull: Naaman was a great man with his master, because by him the Lord had given deliverance to Syria; he was a mighty man of valour, but he was a leper (2 Kings 5:1). A little maid carried captive out of Israel, an Israelite sister serving in a foreign house, told her mistress that her lord would be recovered if he were with the prophet in Samaria (2 Kings 5:2-4). He came with silver, gold and raiment, because a man will give everything for his health (2 Kings 5:5-6).

The king of Israel rent his clothes and asked whether he was God, to kill and to make alive, which he had from the Lord’s own word in the law (2 Kings 5:7; Deuteronomy 32:39). Elisha sent word to let the man come to him, and he would know that there is a prophet in Israel (2 Kings 5:8).

Elisha sent a messenger telling him to wash in Jordan seven times, and he would be clean (2 Kings 5:9-10). Naaman was wroth, for he had thought the prophet would surely come out, call on the name of the Lord, strike his hand over the place and recover the leper; he complained in his pride that this was not the process he expected (2 Kings 5:11). He wanted some big, grandiose miracle; he was a man of repute, sent by the king of Syria, and expected the prophet to come out to him as the pastors do now in Christianity.

He asked whether the rivers of Damascus were not better than all the waters of Israel, and turned away in a rage (2 Kings 5:12). He wanted the clean rivers of Damascus instead of the muddy Jordan and thought it beneath him; he was thinking of a physical cleansing rather than a spiritual one, and his mind was carnal, not thinking as the prophet thinks. That pride almost cost him his healing. When the Lord says do, do; stop wanting God to do it your way. Counsel is often very simple, keep the commandments, and sometimes it will hurt your feelings.

His servants came near and reasoned with him that he would have done some great thing if the prophet had asked it, so how much more should he wash when told only to wash and be clean (2 Kings 5:13). Taking heed, Naaman went down and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God (2 Kings 5:14).
judgmentFull: His flesh came again like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean (2 Kings 5:14). Seven is completion; nothing is accidental with the Most High: the seventh-day rest, Naaman dipped seven times, Jericho compassed seven times. The spirit of Christ did the healing, working through Elisha, and what healed Naaman was his belief and his obedience to the word of the prophet.

That is the true washing: to put away the evil of one’s doings, cease from evil and learn to do well; action, not speech (Isaiah 1:16-20). Washing is not a dip in water; it is keeping the commandments, which is how a man ceases to do evil, since evil is sin. In the same Jordan John preached the baptism of repentance, the people were baptized confessing their sins, and Christ came to be baptized (Luke 3:3; Matthew 3:6, 13).

Naaman returned with all his company, stood before the man of God, and confessed that now he knew there is no God in all the earth but in Israel (2 Kings 5:15). Other non-Israelites came to that same knowledge: Jethro confessed that the Lord is greater than all gods (Exodus 18:11). The heathen understand that the Most High is greater than all other gods; it is our people that want a god that does not look like them.

Elisha refused his blessing, swearing by the Lord before whom he stood (2 Kings 5:16). Naaman asked for two mules’ burden of earth, for he would offer sacrifice to no other god but the Lord, and asked pardon for bowing in the house of Rimmon when his master leaned on his hand (2 Kings 5:17-18). His faith was so strong that he asked pardon even for that: he knew Rimmon was no real god, for all the gods of the nations are idols, but the Lord made the heavens (Psalms 96:4-5). So the image of Caesar Borgia hung up as Christ is an idol; Christ is a black man with woolly hair, not the yellow-haired, blue-eyed image our people were forced to worship. Elisha told him to go in peace (2 Kings 5:19).

Of the many lepers in Israel in Elisha’s time, none was cleansed but Naaman the Syrian: Christ himself reached back and referenced this exact history, and those in the synagogue were filled with wrath and sought to cast him down headlong (Luke 4:27-29).

cases.name: Gehazi
cases.charge: Coveting what his master refused, running after Naaman with a lie to take it, hiding it like a thief, and lying again to the prophet’s face
cases.summary: When Elisha refused Naaman’s gifts, his servant Gehazi ran after the Syrian with a lie, took two talents of silver and two changes of garments, and hid them in the house like a thief (2 Kings 5:20-24). Asked where he had been, he lied again, adding sin to sin because he never controlled his covetousness (2 Kings 5:25). Because he took in a time that was not the time to receive, the leprosy of Naaman was to cleave to him and his seed for ever, and he went out a leper as white as snow (2 Kings 5:26-27).
offenseFull: Elisha had healed Naaman and refused his blessing (2 Kings 5:16). Real men of God know that even when they are lacking, God will find someone to provide; they do not do the Lord’s work for a reward.

Gehazi reasoned that his master had spared this Syrian, and swore that he would run after him and take something of him (2 Kings 5:20). Naaman had come with great treasure, and Gehazi was looking at all that glitter: Elisha did not want anything, but Gehazi meant to get paid. That is covetousness.

He told Naaman that his master had sent him for a talent of silver and two changes of garments for two young men of the sons of the prophets (2 Kings 5:21-22). Covetousness will make a man lie; Elisha had not sent him, and he went of his own accord. Naaman told him to be content and take two talents (2 Kings 5:23); Gehazi should have caught that first word, be content, and woken up then, but he was not content and took both. Elisha himself, when Elijah asked what he wanted, did not ask for money or clothes, but for a double portion of his spirit (2 Kings 2:9).

He hid the goods in the house like a thief and sent the men away, then stood before his master as if Elisha did not know, and said he had gone nowhere (2 Kings 5:24-25). He lied again, adding sin to sin, because he did not control his covetousness; it was a presumptuous sin, for no man accidentally follows after a man for silver and a garment (Psalms 19:13). It shows how Israel thought then and how the nation still thinks now, hasty to grasp things by unjust means.
judgmentFull: Elisha asked whether his heart had not gone with him (2 Kings 5:26): God sees it all, and the spirit of the Lord reveals. Do not try to justify yourself among righteous men; come correct. He asked whether it was a time to receive money, garments and possessions (2 Kings 5:26). There is a time to get and a time to lose, and this was not the time to receive (Ecclesiastes 3:1, 6); the prophet’s word was be content with the little you have.

The leprosy of Naaman was to cleave to him and his seed for ever, and he went out a leper as white as snow (2 Kings 5:27). The same sickness that had just left Naaman came on him because of his covetousness. God does not like covetous people, and Gehazi was judged immediately; many are not judged right away and think they are good, but the money they love will destroy them.

The work of one sinner cost his whole lineage: he destroyed not only himself but his children, and the leprosy is not to depart from that line for ever. These are generational curses, paying for the sins of the fathers, and those who have woken up to the truth must look honestly at their parents and grandparents. We are our forefathers, and so the law says to confess the iniquity of the fathers, and the Lord will remember his covenant (Leviticus 26:40-42).

The leprosy white as snow is the clean leprosy, the whole skin with all its pigment gone and the blood showing under it, as against the unclean that spots all over (Leviticus 13:12-13). That is how Cain looked when he was cursed from the ground and how Esau was born, and the look of the white man is that curse. Gehazi was an Israelite, and the leprosy stripped the melanin from him and his children from their heritage; his children are here today and carry it. The leprosy did not create a race of white people: Edom is the race of that colour, and on Gehazi’s line there may be albinos.

cases.name: The lord on whose hand the king leaned
cases.charge: Doubting the word of the Most High by Elisha in the famine of Samaria: if the Lord would make windows in heaven, might this thing be?
cases.summary: In the siege of Samaria an ass’s head sold for eighty pieces of silver and mothers boiled and ate their sons, the curse of the law fulfilled on a disobedient Israel (2 Kings 6:25-29; Deuteronomy 28:53). Elisha declared the word of the Most High that within a day flour and barley would sell cheaply in the gate, and the lord on whose hand the king leaned doubted the word (2 Kings 7:1-2). The food came as the word said, and the people trod upon him in the gate and he died, just as the man of God had spoken (2 Kings 7:16-20).
offenseFull: Ben-hadad besieged Samaria until an ass’s head, not even a clean animal, sold for four score pieces of silver (2 Kings 6:24-25). A woman cried to the king that she and another had agreed to eat their sons, and they boiled and ate hers (2 Kings 6:26-29). This is historical fact. In the siege a disobedient Israel was to eat the flesh of their sons and daughters, and that curse was fulfilled in this famine (Deuteronomy 28:53). It is what happens to us in the midst of sin when we do not follow the scriptures and prepare: we degrade to our most carnal form.

The king answered that if the Lord did not help her, he could not (2 Kings 6:27). He saw God’s hand in it: the richest man in the province had no power to change those conditions, because they were put on them by God, and the conditions the Lord will put on America and all these nations are put on by him. No one can break that chain; the best a man can do is prepare and keep the commandments with faith in the Son of God. Do not talk about what you would never do; those who have not known that hunger do not know what people will do to survive. The king and his messenger then blamed the Lord for the evil and lost patience waiting for his deliverance (2 Kings 6:31-33).

Elisha declared the word of the Most High that within a day the famine would break, and fine flour and barley would sell cheaply in the gate of Samaria (2 Kings 7:1). The prophet speaks the word of the Most High plainly, without fear and without doubting, whether the message is blessing or judgment. The lord on whose hand the king leaned doubted the word, asking whether the Most High would make windows in heaven (2 Kings 7:2). The windows of heaven are the rain the Lord opens upon the earth, as in the days of Noah, so that the crops grow (Genesis 7:11).
judgmentFull: Elisha told him he would see it with his eyes but not eat of it (2 Kings 7:2). Four leprous men at the gate went over to the camp of the Syrians, for the Most High had made the Syrians hear the noise of chariots and horses, and they fled in the twilight and left everything behind (2 Kings 7:3-7).

The lepers realised that this was a day of good tidings and that they should not hold their peace, and told the king’s household; the people spoiled the tents, and the food was sold cheaply exactly as the word said (2 Kings 7:8-16).

The king set the doubting lord in charge of the gate, and the people trod upon him there and he died, just as the man of God had spoken (2 Kings 7:17). He saw the plenty with his eyes but did not eat of it, and the word of the Most High fell out to the letter (2 Kings 7:18-20). The trampling in the gate stands as a picture of a crowd stampeding after goods, hating one another over things, and here it became the judgment on a man who doubted the word. The thread running through these chapters is the surety of the word of the Most High spoken by his prophets.

cases.name: Hazael king of Syria
cases.charge: Smothering his master with a wet cloth to take the throne of Syria, and doing to Israel the evil Elisha wept over
cases.summary: Sent by the sick Ben-hadad to inquire of Elisha, Hazael saw the man of God weep, because the prophet foresaw the evil he would do to Israel: burning their strongholds, slaying their young men, dashing their children and ripping up the women with child (2 Kings 8:7-12). He went back, smothered his master with a wet cloth, and reigned in his stead, and the Most High used him to cut Israel short (2 Kings 8:15; 2 Kings 10:32). Even though the Lord used him, he would judge him: by Amos he said he would send a fire into the house of Hazael, and the people of Syria would go into captivity unto Kir (Amos 1:3-5).
offenseFull: At Horeb the Lord sent Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Syria, Jehu king over Israel and Elisha prophet in his room, and him that escaped the sword of Hazael Jehu would slay (1 Kings 19:15-17). The Most High was telling Elijah not to worry, for he had things set up: Syria would come against the northern kingdom.

When Elisha came to Damascus, Ben-hadad lay sick and sent Hazael with a present of every good thing of Damascus, forty camels’ burden, to inquire of the Lord by the prophet whether he would recover (2 Kings 8:7-9). The word of a prophet, also called a seer, was precious in those days. The Syrians had their own gods, yet the king sent to the God of Israel; they understood there is only one true and living God, and that did not stop them from fighting against us.

Elisha told Hazael that the king might recover, but the Most High had shown him that he would surely die; then he settled his countenance on Hazael until he was ashamed, and wept, because he knew the evil Hazael would do to the children of Israel (2 Kings 8:10-12). Hazael had done nothing to anybody yet; this was before he was king. The prophet saw into the future that he would be an instrument of terror upon the nation of Israel, and revealed that leadership can discern spirits at work in a man that the man does not see in himself.

Hazael asked whether his servant was a dog to do this great thing, and Elisha answered that the Lord had shown him that Hazael would be king over Syria (2 Kings 8:13). He returned, told his master he would recover, and the next day took a thick cloth, dipped it in water, and spread it on the king’s face so that he died, and reigned in his stead (2 Kings 8:14-15). Hazael murdered the king, Ben-hadad the second, and took his throne.
judgmentFull: When he became king of Syria, that is what he did to us. Jehu did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, and in those days the Most High began to cut Israel short, and Hazael smote them from Jordan eastward through Gilead and Bashan (2 Kings 10:31-33). It says the Lord began, but the Lord used Hazael: when we sin, the Lord brings upon us an adversary, these other nations, to correct us. That is what Elijah and Elisha prophesied coming to pass, and prophecy has no time clock.

The anger of the Most High delivered Israel into the hand of Hazael and Ben-hadad all their days, yet he was gracious because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and would not destroy them, as yet; the northern kingdom was later cast off (2 Kings 13:3, 22-23; 2 Kings 17). The ripping up of the women with child is what was done to our people in slavery on this side, when masters cut open the bellies of pregnant women; no one has suffered what we have suffered (Daniel 9:12). From the Syrians to Edom they have all dealt with us cruelly, and there is going to be a just recompense for that.

Even though the Lord used him, he would judge him. For three transgressions of Damascus and for four the Most High would not turn away the punishment, because they threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron: they thrashed it and took the whole east side of Jordan. He would send a fire into the house of Hazael to devour the palaces of Ben-hadad, break the bar of Damascus, and send the people of Syria into captivity unto Kir (Amos 1:3-5).

The prophecies are carried out in layers. After Hazael died, Jehoash beat Ben-hadad his son three times and recovered the cities of Israel, as Elisha had said (2 Kings 13:24-25). The fire into the house of Hazael means the Lord would put the spirit in the northern kingdom to thrash back, and that is how Jeroboam the second had his success, recovering Damascus and Hamath (2 Kings 14:28). The latter end of the judgment came when the king of Assyria took Damascus, carried its people captive to Kir, and slew Rezin, who held the sceptre (2 Kings 16:9).

The secrets of wisdom are double, and this verse has its future prophecy as well as its history (Job 11:6). The Lord will use the nations, and once they have done what they were to do in correcting us he will cast them off, for Christ will not rule jointly with any of them; God’s judgment is like a ring, and the Lord will take vengeance on his adversaries (2 Esdras 5:42; Nahum 1:2).

cases.name: Jehu
cases.charge: Executing the house of Ahab and destroying Baal out of Israel, and then not departing from the golden calves at Bethel and Dan; taking no heed to walk in the law of the Lord with all his heart
cases.summary: Anointed at Ramoth-gilead by one of the children of the prophets, Jehu was charged to smite the house of Ahab and avenge the blood of the prophets shed at the hand of Jezebel; he did it to the last man and destroyed Baal out of Israel (2 Kings 9:1-10; 2 Kings 10:11, 28). The Most High promised his children the throne to the fourth generation, but Jehu kept the golden calves of Bethel and Dan and took no heed to walk in the law with all his heart, and in those days the Most High began to cut Israel short (2 Kings 10:29-32).
offenseFull: Elisha sent one of the children of the prophets to anoint Jehu king over Israel and flee (2 Kings 9:1-3); he was to anoint him quickly and run because the people would be against the anointing, for the Most High was righting a wrong in the Israelite community. Jehu was charged to smite the house of Ahab to avenge the blood of the prophets shed at the hand of Jezebel, whose work was to kill the prophets while weak Ahab let it continue (2 Kings 9:6-10).

Omri had built Samaria into a northern Jerusalem through his alliance with the Zidonians and married his son Ahab to their daughter Jezebel, so that with the images and priests of Baal it was a little Zidon in northern Israel. The only way to get Ahab’s family out was to raise up men with heart: the Most High needed a man who would take no prisoners and execute judgment, because evil had gone on too long. The captains asked why the mad fellow had come, then put their garments under Jehu and proclaimed him king (2 Kings 9:11-13).

Jehoram asked whether it was peace, and Jehu answered that there could be no peace while the whoredoms and witchcrafts of Jezebel were so many (2 Kings 9:22): there is no peace as long as a wicked woman holds power, and that is what America likes to do, set up wicked women and empower women who go against God. Jehu smote Jehoram through the heart and cast him into the portion of Naboth, the field Jezebel and Ahab had taken after turning the people against an innocent man (2 Kings 9:24-26). Ahaziah of Judah, complicit in it, was smitten as he fled (2 Kings 9:27).

Jezebel painted her face and tired her head, returning to her seductive ways; she wanted to entice foolish men to her side with her beauty, but her beauty was superficial, and that is the Jezebel spirit (2 Kings 9:30). At Jehu’s word she was thrown down, and the dogs left only her skull, feet and palms, exactly as the Most High had spoken by Elijah (2 Kings 9:33-37). This is history, and it is also prophecy concerning the rebellious now: whoever puts himself in the wrong position against God’s instruction for the nation, man or woman, God will address it.

Ahab’s seventy sons were beheaded, and Jehu slew all that remained of the house of Ahab, and forty-two brethren of Ahaziah, guilty by association (2 Kings 10:1-14). Then in subtilty he gathered all the worshippers of Baal, brought out vestments for every worshipper, made sure no servant of the Most High was among them, and slew them all, and made the house of Baal a draught house (2 Kings 10:18-27); the images were to be burned as a cursed thing (Deuteronomy 7:25-26). Idols come with clothing: the vestments of false clergy then, and the pastor’s robe, the Pope’s garments, and the dress of Easter, Christmas and Halloween now. So Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel (2 Kings 10:28).
judgmentFull: Yet he did not depart from the golden calves that Jeroboam set up in Bethel and in Dan (2 Kings 10:29). He did what was right in one thing and kept the sin in another. Baal came from the Zidonians, but the golden calves were stamped into the northern kingdom’s own heritage, the idols their own forefathers made, and so a man who went so hard for the Lord in destroying idols turned around and kept idols.

The Most High commended Jehu for executing what was right against the house of Ahab, and promised that his children to the fourth generation would sit on the throne (2 Kings 10:30). Yet Jehu took no heed to walk in the law with all his heart, showing that a man may do great things and still turn away and stay in sin (2 Kings 10:31). All the kings except David, Hezekiah and Josiah were defective, and there were no good kings in Israel (Ecclesiasticus 49:4). Whoever thinks he is standing must watch that he does not fall, and not everyone who calls Christ Lord will enter, but whoever does the will of the Father (1 Corinthians 10:12-13; Matthew 7:21-23). Jehu was righteous in the beginning, but then he went wicked: the Lord used him to eradicate the house of Ahab, but later on he became wicked himself.

In those days the Most High began to cut Israel short, and Hazael smote them from Jordan eastward (2 Kings 10:32-33), as the word to Elijah had set the sword of Hazael beside the sword of Jehu (1 Kings 19:17); prophecy has no time clock. Jehu reigned twenty-eight years (2 Kings 10:36). The four generations were Jehoahaz, Joash, Jeroboam the second and Zachariah; then Shallum executed Zachariah publicly, and that was the end of the dynasty (2 Kings 15:8-12). By Hosea the Most High said he would avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu and cause the kingdom of Israel to cease (Hosea 1:4).
Jehu’s life is a warning that the walk is a marathon, not a sprint, and the difference is whether a man gets back up and repents or stays down and departs from the law.

cases.name: Athaliah
cases.charge: Counselling her son Ahaziah to do wickedly; destroying all the seed royal of the house of Judah to reign over the land herself; crying treason when the rightful king was crowned
cases.summary: Athaliah the daughter of Omri, of the house of Ahab, was her son Ahaziah’s counsellor to do wickedly, and when he was slain she arose and destroyed all the seed royal, a mother giving orders to kill anybody next in line because her power came through her son (2 Chronicles 22:2-3, 10; 2 Kings 11:1). Jehosheba hid the child Joash in the house of the Lord six years while Athaliah reigned (2 Kings 11:2-3). In the seventh year Jehoiada the priest crowned the rightful king, and when Athaliah cried treason she was taken out of the ranges and slain (2 Kings 11:4-16).
offenseFull: Ahaziah reigned one year in Jerusalem, and his mother was Athaliah the daughter of Omri; he walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counsellor to do wickedly (2 Chronicles 22:2-3; 2 Kings 8:26-27). Instead of going to the priests and the judges, he went to his mother, and she counselled him into ruin; a woman with a grudge can rule a kingdom through her son. Ahaziah was a mama’s boy, and that is why the Most High put him to death: his destruction was of God, by the hand of Jehu, whom the Lord had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab (2 Chronicles 22:7-9).

When Athaliah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal of the house of Judah (2 Kings 11:1; 2 Chronicles 22:10). A mother gave orders to kill anybody next in line, because her power came through her son; then a woman was empowered only through the man. To stay in power, wicked women will destroy the men. She did not do it alone; she had weak men behind her to do her bidding and help her run over everything. She was a black woman of the house of Ahab, and as is the mother, so is her daughter: Jezebel wanted the prophets dead, and her daughter wanted the king’s seed dead so that she could rule through her son (2 Kings 8:18; Ezekiel 16:44).

Jehosheba, the daughter of king Joram, sister of Ahaziah and wife of Jehoiada the priest, stole Joash from among the king’s sons that were slain and hid him and his nurse in a bedchamber, and he was hid in the house of the Lord six years while Athaliah reigned over the land (2 Kings 11:2-3; 2 Chronicles 22:11-12). The rightful king was concealed the entire time the usurper sat on the throne. Her sons broke up the house of God and bestowed all its dedicated things upon Baalim (2 Chronicles 24:7).
judgmentFull: In the seventh year Jehoiada brought the rulers over hundreds, the captains and the guard into the house of the Lord, made a covenant with them, and showed them the king’s son, and set every man with his weapon round about the king, with king David’s spears and shields (2 Kings 11:4-11). This was order; this was strategy. He brought forth the king’s son, put the crown upon him, gave him the testimony, and they anointed him, clapped their hands and cried, God save the king (2 Kings 11:12). That saying is from our forefathers, not from Europe: they had to deal with a wicked woman interfering with the rulership of men, and the priest had to establish a king. Athaliah had no place ruling Israel; being the king’s mother did not make her the ruler.

Athaliah heard the noise, came into the temple, saw the king standing by a pillar as the manner was, rent her clothes and cried treason (2 Kings 11:13-14). She had just killed all the royal seed, and when the rightful king was anointed she screamed treason. When one tries to restore order, that is how some look at it, as treason against them; they do not see that they are out of order. Her cry came too late, for the covenant was already made and the true king was crowned.

Jehoiada commanded the captains to have her forth without the ranges and to kill with the sword him that followed her, but not to slay her in the house of the Lord; they laid hands on her, and by the way the horses came into the king’s house she was slain (2 Kings 11:15-16). The Most High cannot use a man following behind a woman, and the Lord does not deal with men who follow women. It is the same spirit in the church of Thyatira: not the same Jezebel, but the same seducing, manipulating spirit, given space to repent and repenting not, and the children the Lord would kill with death are the weak men following the woman (Revelation 2:20-23). Twice in the history, when wicked women rose up in power to devour, Jezebel and Athaliah, God sent men of the Lord to remove them for not listening to what God had to say.

Jehoiada made a covenant between the Lord, the king and the people, that they should be the Lord’s people; the people broke down the house of Baal and slew Mattan its priest before the altars, and the city was quiet (2 Kings 11:17-21). This same covenant is what happens today: as a person wakes up, repents, keeps the commandments and comes out of idolatry, they again become the Lord’s people. The weapons they carried then were physical; today the weapon of Israel is the scriptures.

cases.name: Jehoahaz of Israel
cases.charge: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord and following the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, worshipping the golden calves; beseeching the Lord under the oppression of Syria, while Israel departed not from the sins of the house of Jeroboam
cases.summary: Jehoahaz the son of Jehu reigned seventeen years in Samaria, about 814 to 798 BC, and followed the sins of Jeroboam, and the Lord delivered Israel into the hand of Hazael and Ben-hadad all their days (2 Kings 13:1-3). He besought the Lord, and the Lord hearkened unto him, for He hears the prayer of the oppressed, and gave Israel a saviour; yet they departed not from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, and Syria left him but fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand footmen (2 Kings 13:4-7). The saviour came not in his lifetime but after his death, in the days of his son and his grandson.
offenseFull: In the three and twentieth year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned seventeen years, from about 814 to 798 BC (2 Kings 13:1). He did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin (2 Kings 13:2). His father Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel but did not depart from the golden calves in Bethel and in Dan, and in those days the Lord began to cut Israel short (2 Kings 10:28-32). Jehoahaz walked in the sins of his forefather Jeroboam: he was an idolater, worshipping the golden calves.

The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and He delivered them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria and of Ben-hadad his son all their days (2 Kings 13:3). Because of our sins, when we sin, the Lord brings upon us an adversary, other nations, to correct us. Jehoahaz besought the Lord, and the Lord hearkened unto him, for He saw the oppression of Israel (2 Kings 13:4). Even though he was wicked and in sin, the Lord hears the prayer of the oppressed (Ecclesiasticus 35:13). Yet they departed not from the sins of the house of Jeroboam but walked therein (2 Kings 13:6).
judgmentFull: Neither did the Lord leave of the people to Jehoahaz but fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand footmen, for the king of Syria had destroyed them and made them like the dust by threshing (2 Kings 13:7). An army does not go to war with fifty horsemen; that is what remains after a nation has taken a major loss in war. Jehoahaz was disobedient, and when we disobey, this is what we get, the judgments of God: to be smitten before our enemies, going out one way against them and fleeing seven ways before them (Deuteronomy 28:25). Threshing here is both analogy and literal: to thresh is also to thrash, and that is what the king of Syria did to the northern kingdom, for Hazael oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz (2 Kings 13:22).

The saviour is written ahead of time: what is read there is not what was happening but what was going to happen. The writer jumps in time to show that when it did happen, it was because Jehoahaz prayed for it (2 Kings 13:5). Israel did not go out from under the hand of the Syrians in his lifetime: the Lord heard his prayer when he was alive and answered it in the time of his son and his grandson, when Jehoash took again the cities his father had lost and Jeroboam restored the former boundaries of Israel (2 Kings 13:24-25; 2 Kings 14:25-27). In the time of their trouble, when they cried unto Him as Jehoahaz did, He heard them from heaven and gave them saviours (Nehemiah 9:27). The saviour was not a Clark Kent; the Lord put in place a plan of salvation to recover what Syria had taken.

The Lord was gracious unto them and had compassion and respect unto them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and would not destroy them, neither cast He them from His presence as yet (2 Kings 13:23). His grace and mercy is with His saints, the Israelites, and He has respect unto His chosen (Wisdom of Solomon 4:15). He has a chosen people and respects His chosen; but when it comes to judgment amongst His chosen He is no respecter of persons, and being a king or of the tribe of Judah does not mean He will not judge. It says as yet, because the northern kingdom was later cast off (2 Kings 17:18-23). Jehoahaz slept with his fathers, was buried in Samaria, and Joash his son reigned in his stead (2 Kings 13:8-9).

cases.name: Jehoash of Israel and the arrows
cases.charge: Doing evil and departing not from the sins of Jeroboam; smiting the ground thrice with the arrows of the Lord’s deliverance and stopping on his own, when the man of God had put his hands on the king’s hands
cases.summary: Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz did evil and departed not from the sins of Jeroboam, yet he came down and wept over the dying Elisha, who put his hands on the king’s hands to shoot the arrow of the Lord’s deliverance from Syria (2 Kings 13:10-17). Told to smite the ground with the arrows, he smote thrice and stayed on his own, and the man of God was wroth: five or six times would have consumed Syria, and now he would smite Syria but three times (2 Kings 13:18-19). He beat Ben-hadad three times and recovered cities of Israel, but not all of them; it would take another generation (2 Kings 13:25).
offenseFull: In the thirty and seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz began to reign over Israel in Samaria sixteen years, from about 798 to 782 BC, not to be confused with Joash of Judah (2 Kings 13:10). He did evil in the sight of the Lord and departed not from the sins of Jeroboam (2 Kings 13:11). When Elisha fell sick of the sickness whereof he died, the king came down and wept over his face and cried, My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof (2 Kings 13:14), the same cry Elisha made when Elijah went up (2 Kings 2:12).

Elisha had him take bow and arrows, laid his own hands upon the king’s hands, and had him open the window eastward and shoot, and he called it the arrow of the Lord’s deliverance, the arrow of deliverance from Syria, for he would smite the Syrians in Aphek till he had consumed them (2 Kings 13:15-17). As prophets do, Elisha had him do this to signify something; the arrows represent the Lord’s deliverance of Israel from Syria. This proves what was read of his father’s reign, that the Lord gave Israel a saviour: they had not yet gone out from under the hand of the Syrians, and now the deliverance was shown to the son (2 Kings 13:5). Syria is synonymous with Aram, the Arameans: Aram was one of the sons of Shem, brother to our forefather Arphaxad, the son of Shem we came from (Genesis 10:22).

Then Elisha told him to take the arrows and smite upon the ground, and he smote thrice and stayed (2 Kings 13:18). Elisha did not tell him how many times; the king shot three arrows and stopped on his own.
judgmentFull: The man of God was wroth with him and said he should have smitten five or six times; then he would have smitten Syria till he had consumed it, whereas now he would smite Syria but thrice (2 Kings 13:19). A few more arrows would have been enough to take back all of Syria in his lifetime. Smiting the ground three times was symbolic of the wars he was going to fight and win against Ben-hadad the son of Hazael. A man is only going to do so much in his time.

Elisha died and was buried, and the bands of the Moabites invaded the land; a dead man cast into the sepulchre touched the bones of Elisha, revived and stood up on his feet (2 Kings 13:20-21). After his death his body prophesied (Ecclesiasticus 48:12-14). Even in death he was still prophesying, because of faith. But he was not taken up in the chariot like Elijah; he had to die a regular death, and that is what separated him from his teacher: though Elisha did more miracles, Elijah, who did not see death, was still greater.

Hazael died, and Jehoash took again out of the hand of Ben-hadad his son the cities Hazael had taken from Jehoahaz by war; three times he beat him and recovered the cities of Israel (2 Kings 13:24-25). He only shot three arrows, and Elisha knew that was not enough: Jehoash beat him three times but did not get all the cities back, and it would take another generation to do that.

The men of Israel whom Amaziah king of Judah hired and sent home at the word of the man of God fell upon the cities of Judah in great anger (2 Chronicles 25:6-13), and after he smote the children of Seir, Amaziah challenged Jehoash, who answered with the thistle and the cedar and told him to tarry at home (2 Chronicles 25:11, 17-19; 2 Kings 14:8-10). It came of God, that He might deliver them into the hand of their enemies, because they sought after the gods of Edom, the gods of the white man (2 Chronicles 25:20). Judah was put to the worse before Israel at Beth-shemesh; Jehoash broke down the wall of Jerusalem and took the gold, silver, vessels and hostages to Samaria (2 Kings 14:11-14). There was civil war between us, the northern and southern kingdoms, at that time.

cases.name: Jeroboam the son of Joash
cases.charge: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord forty-one years; departing not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, while the land he restored grew rich, oppressed the poor and lived at ease
cases.summary: Jeroboam the son of Joash reigned forty-one years in Samaria and departed not from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, yet the Lord restored by him the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, as Jonah had prophesied, not because he was righteous but because the Lord saw the oppression of Israel (2 Kings 14:23-27). The prosperity made the rich richer and the land at ease, and Amos prophesied that the Lord would rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword and that Israel would go into captivity (Amos 7:9-11). The word fell on his son Zachariah, slain after six months, the fourth generation of Jehu (2 Kings 15:8-12).
offenseFull: In the fifteenth year of Amaziah king of Judah, Jeroboam the son of Joash began to reign in Samaria and reigned forty-one years, one year longer than the reign of David and of Solomon, from about 793 to 753 BC (2 Kings 14:23). He did evil and departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat (2 Kings 14:24). Like Omri, he has major accolades in other nations’ history books and only five or six verses in scripture; the Lord does not care about carnal accolades.

In the days of Jeroboam there was a lot of prosperity in the northern kingdom, and more money brings more problems. He made the rich richer and the northern kingdom a place of luxury for the highborn, and Amos railed against the luxury and selfishness of the well-to-do and their lack of concern for the poor: they sold the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of shoes, and woe to them that are at ease in Zion (Amos 2:6; Amos 6:1). They were worried about the new moon and the sabbath being over so they could go back to making money; it was about making their bread (Amos 8:5). He that oppresses the poor to increase his riches shall surely come to want (Proverbs 22:16). Hosea called out the land in those days: no truth, no mercy, no knowledge of God, but swearing, lying, killing and stealing, and blood touching blood, for they were killing each other (Hosea 4:1-2).

The Lord eased the pressure from outside because of the prayer of Jehoahaz and the northern kingdom decided to be at ease too, when they should have feared for the nation, for they were transgressing against God, and the land they got back they could lose right back. Amos prophesied that the sanctuaries of Israel would be laid waste and the Lord would rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword; Amaziah the priest of Bethel tried to report treason on Amos to the king and told him to flee into Judah and prophesy there (Amos 7:9-13). He twisted the words: Amos never said Jeroboam would die by the sword, but he did prophesy that if the northern kingdom did not repent they would go into captivity. The prophet’s job is to carry out the word of the Lord, no more, no less, and Amos was telling the northern kingdom they were going into slavery soon.
judgmentFull: He restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the Lord by His servant Jonah the son of Amittai of Gath-hepher, of the tribe of Zebulun (2 Kings 14:25). The entering of Hamath is the far north at the border of Syria, the border Moses declared and David and Solomon held, and the sea of the plain is the salt sea, the Dead Sea (Numbers 34:8; Deuteronomy 3:17; 1 Kings 8:65). The Lord saw the bitter affliction of Israel and would not blot out their name, and saved them by the hand of Jeroboam (2 Kings 14:26-27). It was the Lord answering the prayer of Jehoahaz, not because they were righteous but because He saw their oppression. Jeroboam recovered Damascus and Hamath because the Lord ordained it, not because he was righteous or mighty (2 Kings 14:28).

Hosea’s first son was named Jezreel, for in a little while the Lord would avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu and cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel (Hosea 1:1, 4). Jeroboam slept with his fathers, and Zachariah his son reigned six months and did evil, until Shallum conspired against him and slew him before the people; the end of Zachariah fulfilled the word spoken to Jehu, that his sons would sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation (2 Kings 14:29; 2 Kings 15:8-12). This was the beginning of the end for the northern kingdom, and Amos’ prediction came true a generation later, when Samaria was taken by the Assyrian army. An unwise king destroys his people, and when the king is wicked and oppressive the people will be the same way (Ecclesiasticus 10:2-3). If the Lord did that to His chosen people, destruction is coming to this land; captivity is headed Edom’s way, and the white man will not avoid this judgment.

cases.name: Hosea the prophet
cases.charge: Taking a wife of whoredoms and naming her children at the Lord’s command as a sign against the northern kingdom; loving again an adulteress as the Lord loves Israel; prophesying the scattering and the return
cases.summary: In the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, the Lord told Hosea to take a wife of whoredoms, for the land had committed great whoredom, departing from the Lord, and he took Gomer and the children were named Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi, a sign of what the Lord would do to the northern kingdom for breaking the covenant (Hosea 1:1-9). Told again to love an adulteress, he bought her and told her to abide for him many days, a sign that Israel would abide many days without a king or sacrifice and afterward return to the Lord and David their king (Hosea 3:1-5).
offenseFull: The word of the Lord came to Hosea the son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah kings of Judah, and of Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel (Hosea 1:1); Hosea and Isaiah were in the same time frame, overlapping, under the same kings (Isaiah 1:1). The Lord told him to take a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms, for the land had committed great whoredom, departing from the Lord, and he took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim (Hosea 1:2-3). He took a whore because it was symbolic of how the people committed spiritual fornication against the Most High: the marriage is a picture of what Israel did to Him, joining to the gods of the other nations.

The first son was Jezreel, which means seed of Israel, for in a little while the Lord would avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu and cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to cease, destroyed and carried into captivity (Hosea 1:4-5). The daughter was Lo-ruhamah, no mercy, for He would no more have mercy upon the house of Israel but would utterly take them away, while He would have mercy upon the house of Judah, which had the temple and the priests, and save them not by bow nor sword (Hosea 1:6-7). The second son was Lo-ammi, not my people, and He would not be their God (Hosea 1:8-9). Three times He said it, and the northern kingdom was carried away into Assyria (2 Kings 17:6). When you are no longer God’s people you become a stranger, a heathen, a Gentile, a foreigner. The Gentiles all throughout Paul’s letters are this chapter.

Then the Lord told him to go yet love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the Lord toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods; he bought her for fifteen pieces of silver and an homer and a half of barley, and told her to abide for him many days, not to play the harlot nor be for another man (Hosea 3:1-3). By the law a man who put away his wife could not return unto her after she had been another man’s, for she was defiled (Jeremiah 3:1; Deuteronomy 24:4). Israel played the harlot with many lovers, many nations, yet the Lord is willing to let us return. It is all mercy: by that law the nation of Israel should have been cut off, let alone the slavery; though we committed spiritual fornication against Him, He still allows us to return.
judgmentFull: Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered, and in the place where it was said unto them, ye are not my people, it shall be said unto them, ye are the sons of the living God (Hosea 1:10). Paul applies it to those He called, not of the Jews only but also of the Gentiles, the children of Israel; Ephraim was cast down but not cast away (Romans 9:24-26). The blacks, Hispanics and Native Americans are the ones whose number is as the sand of the sea, not the so-called white man that calls himself a Jew, and the multitude is a sign of who the people of God are. That place is America and the lands we were carried into, where they call us African-Americans, Puerto Ricans, Jamaicans and Haitians.

Then the children of Judah and the children of Israel, both the northern and southern kingdoms, shall be gathered together and appoint themselves one head (Hosea 1:11). We come together under God’s laws and appoint ourselves one head, which is Christ, and we do not need any other nation to put a stamp on it, because we already know we are the children of God.

The children of Israel shall abide many days without a king, without a prince, without a sacrifice, without an image, without an ephod and without teraphim (Hosea 3:4). Those many days are the roughly 350 years; and Israel went many days without a king for thousands of years, for the southern kingdom last had a king leading into the Babylonian captivity and the northern kingdom in 2 Kings 17. The king is political sovereignty, and we were without it when Europe colonized us in Africa and the transatlantic slave trade took us. Without a sacrifice is no religious establishment teaching us our God; in slavery the white man taught us his god. Without an image, our image was destroyed in slavery and colonialism: when you worship the God of your oppressor, a God who does not look like you, it destroys the way you look at yourself. Without the ephod there was no priest to guide us and tell us what God needs us to do.

Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king in the latter days (Hosea 3:5). That is these days: we were out a long time without the understanding of who we were as a people, and in the last days the Lord raised up the prophets on the earth again to teach the word of God, so we could be delivered. David their king is the one the Lord will raise up when He breaks the yoke from off our neck, serving the Lord and Christ (Jeremiah 30:8-9). In these latter days David is going to be here; who he is is not yet known.

cases.name: Menahem king of Israel
cases.charge: Getting the kingdom by blood; ripping up all the women with child in Tiphsah to make an example of those who would not open to him; paying off Pul king of Assyria with a thousand talents of silver exacted from Israel’s men of wealth, instead of calling on God
cases.summary: Menahem the son of Gadi went up from Tirzah, slew Shallum, and reigned in his stead, and when Tiphsah would not open to him he smote it and ripped up all the women therein that were with child, making an example of them to instil fear (2 Kings 15:14-16). He did evil ten years, and when Pul king of Assyria came against the land he paid him a thousand talents of silver, exacted at fifty shekels a man from the mighty men of wealth, to confirm the kingdom in his hand (2 Kings 15:17-20). It held Assyria off for now; it was the beginning of the end for the northern kingdom (2 Kings 15:29).
offenseFull: Shallum had slain Zachariah and reigned a full month in Samaria, and Menahem went up from Tirzah, smote Shallum and reigned in his stead (2 Kings 15:13-14). Shallum got the kingdom by treason, and Menahem got it by blood.

Menahem smote Tiphsah and all that were therein and the coasts thereof from Tirzah, because they opened not to him, and all the women therein that were with child he ripped up (2 Kings 15:16). This is not the Tiphsah of Solomon’s time by the Euphrates; on his way from Tirzah to Samaria he faced resistance from the surrounding towns, and he made examples of those people, instilling fear in them by killing their pregnant women. He did the same thing Hazael the Syrian king did, the evil Elisha wept to foresee, and worse than a heathen, he did it against his own people (2 Kings 8:12). It is the transgression for which the Lord would not turn away the punishment of Ammon, who ripped up the women with child of Gilead to enlarge their border (Amos 1:13).

He reigned ten years in Samaria and did evil, departing not all his days from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat; he was a wicked idolater too (2 Kings 15:17-18). Pul king of Assyria, who is Tiglath-pileser the third, came against the land to take it over, and Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver that his hand might be with him to confirm the kingdom in his hand (2 Kings 15:19). Instead of calling on his God to defend him, he paid him off: Israel never would come to God for its problems. He exacted the money from all the mighty men of wealth, fifty shekels of silver of each man (2 Kings 15:20). Under Jeroboam the second the northern kingdom had waxed rich, and the rich waxed richer by oppressing the poor and falsifying the balances (Amos 8:4-6); wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished, and the Lord has His way of getting it back (Proverbs 13:11).
judgmentFull: So the king of Assyria turned back and stayed not in the land (2 Kings 15:20). Menahem held him off for now, but it was a major hit financially, and Israel became a vassal nation, servants to Assyria in a tributary state. That was the first time; the kings of Assyria were coming again. This is the beginning of the end for the northern kingdom: the northern kingdom did not render back to the Lord for the blessing of the land restored under Jeroboam the second, but increased the wickedness in the land.

When Ephraim saw his sickness, Ephraim went to the Assyrian, yet he could not heal him nor cure his wound (Hosea 5:13). The wound was the sins they were in; paying him off could not stop what was coming from the Most High God, and those they went to for healing were physicians of no value (Job 13:4). Assyria was the rod of the Lord’s anger, sent against an hypocritical nation, the northern kingdom, which the Lord blessed to overcome their enemies only for them to wax worse in idolatry and oppress the people (Isaiah 10:5-6). Because of unrighteous dealings and riches gotten by deceit, the kingdom is translated from one people to another, from the hand of Israel into the hand of the Assyrians (Ecclesiasticus 10:8).

Menahem slept with his fathers, and Pekahiah his son reigned two years and did evil, until Pekah, a captain of his, conspired against him and smote him in the palace with fifty men of the Gileadites, more backstabbing and conspiracy in the northern kingdom (2 Kings 15:22-25). In the days of Pekah, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came and took Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and carried them captive to Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). When we sin, the Lord brings an enemy upon us: it was the Lord who sent the enemy against us, to put a yoke of iron upon our neck (Deuteronomy 28:48).

cases.name: Hoshea, last king of Israel
cases.charge: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord; reigning as a puppet king under Assyria, then conspiring with So king of Egypt and withholding the tribute, trusting in the strength of Pharaoh instead of the Lord
cases.summary: Hoshea the son of Elah, the last king of the northern kingdom, reigned in Samaria from about 732 to 722 BC and did evil, though not as the kings before him (2 Kings 17:1-2). A puppet king and tributary to Assyria, he turned to So king of Egypt to help him rebel, and the king of Assyria bound him in prison, took Samaria after three years, and carried Israel away, because they obeyed not the voice of the Lord their God (2 Kings 17:3-6; 2 Kings 18:12). In 722 BC the northern kingdom was cut off and became Gentiles.
offenseFull: Pekah had slain Pekahiah and lost half the northern kingdom to Assyria, and Hoshea made a conspiracy against Pekah and slew him the same way (2 Kings 15:25-30). He reaped what he sowed (Galatians 6:7), and history kept repeating itself with the northern kingdom, because they did not care about the laws of God. Hoshea became the servant of Shalmaneser and gave him presents (2 Kings 17:3): a puppet king subservient to his Assyrian master, paying tribute to keep a kingdom shrunk to little more than Samaria and the hill country of Ephraim. When Ephraim saw his sickness he went to the Assyrian and sent to king Jareb, yet he could not heal them (Hosea 5:13). Jareb is no Assyrian name; it means the great king, and it refers to Shalmaneser, to whom Hoshea gave presents (Hosea 10:6).

Then he sent messengers to So king of Egypt and brought no present to the king of Assyria (2 Kings 17:4). Egypt was the ancient enemy, the first nation that held Israel in captivity; the Lord said repent and turn to me, and Israel would rather see what the people who enslaved them had to say. Ephraim was like a silly dove without heart, calling to Egypt for help and going to Assyria into captivity (Hosea 7:11). They thought they were fleeing Assyria and its tribute, when they were fleeing repentance, and they returned, but not to the Most High (Hosea 7:13-16). Woe to the rebellious children that take counsel but not of the Lord, that go down into Egypt to strengthen themselves in the strength of Pharaoh (Isaiah 30:1-3; Isaiah 31:1). That is what Hoshea was trying to do, adding to idolatry the sin of a covenant with the heathen. Trusting in oppression is iniquity (Isaiah 30:12-13); trusting in America and its politics is the same iniquity, and it will get Israel in trouble again. Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, did the same thing, a puppet king for Babylon who rebelled.
judgmentFull: The king of Assyria shut Hoshea up in prison and besieged Samaria three years (2 Kings 17:4-5; 2 Kings 18:9). The purpose of a siege is to break a city down, until the curse of the law is fulfilled and they eat the fruit of their own body (Deuteronomy 28:52-53). The Lord did not want this; that is why he sent the prophets, and they still preferred oppression. He had said he would bring thee and thy king unto a nation thou hast not known (Deuteronomy 28:36), and Hoshea was brought to Assyria and locked up. This Shalmaneser is the Enemessar of Tobit (Tobit 1:2).

Israel was not taken to one place but on a long journey through Damascus and Hamath, across the Euphrates to Habor and Gozan and on to Media, and dropped off all along the way (2 Kings 17:6). The Assyrian kings thrust hooks into the nostrils of their captives, as the Lord had sworn by his holiness through Amos (Amos 4:2). That is why northern kingdom Israelites are found in Corinth, Galatia and Macedonia in the New Testament (Jeremiah 50:17). The captivity came in waves, the first under Tiglath-pileser (2 Kings 15:29), and a remnant of Ephraim stayed faithful to the temple (2 Chronicles 30:6).

That is what Amos was telling them was going to happen; they did not want to hear it, but it happened (2 Kings 17:23). Lo-ammi, for ye are not my people (Hosea 1:9): people who are not God’s people are Gentiles, and Hosea prophesied that the northern kingdom would become Gentiles. The east wind made Samaria desolate (Hosea 13:15-16), and the same thing happened again to the same people, the so-called Native Americans and Hispanics, by way of the conquistadors. Yet he would sift the house of Israel among all nations, and not the least grain would fall (Amos 9:9); because of the promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob he was always going to bring them back, for there cannot be twelve tribes if ten of them are not there.
