cases.name: The captivity of Israel (the northern kingdom)
cases.charge: Fearing other gods and walking in the statutes of the heathen; two calves, a grove, the host of heaven and Baal; sons and daughters through the fire; divination and enchantments; hardening their necks against the prophets
cases.summary: Israel was carried into Assyria because the children of Israel sinned against the Most High who brought them out of Egypt and feared other gods; they walked in the statutes of the heathen, made two calves, worshipped the host of heaven, served Baal, passed their children through the fire and sold themselves to do evil, though he testified against them by all the prophets (2 Kings 17:7-17). The Most High rejected all the seed of Israel and cast them out of his sight, and this rejection is why the seed of Israel are later called heathens and Gentiles in the New Testament (2 Kings 17:18-20). Ephraim was cast down, but not cast away (Leviticus 26:44; Romans 11:2).
offenseFull: They walked in the statutes of the heathen and of the kings of Israel, did secretly what was not right, built high places in all their cities, and set up images and groves on every high hill and under every green tree (2 Kings 17:7-12). The law had already commanded Israel to destroy such high places, not build them (Deuteronomy 12:2-3). The Lord warned them: when Moses gave these laws and commandments, he gave them to all twelve tribes, not to do after the doings of Egypt and of Canaan (Leviticus 18:3). He testified against Israel and Judah by all the prophets and seers, and they hardened their necks like their fathers who did not believe (2 Kings 17:13-14). To believe in the Most High is to take heed to the commandments, so those who claim belief while breaking the commandments do not truly believe (Ecclesiasticus 32:24).

They followed vanity, made two calves and a grove, worshipped all the host of heaven, and served Baal (2 Kings 17:15-16). Israel was warned not to be driven to worship the sun, the moon and the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19); the error is not the images themselves but being driven to worship and serve them. They caused their sons and daughters to pass through the fire and used divination and enchantments (2 Kings 17:17), the abominations for which the Lord drove out the nations before them (Deuteronomy 18:9-12). An observer of times is birthdays and horoscopes; a consulter with familiar spirits is getting your palm read. The Lord said do not do it, and the judgment for it is being read here; repent of it. The Lord charged them not to do like the nations round about them (2 Kings 17:15): do not follow the other nations and their customs, Christmas, New Year, Thanksgiving, Halloween. There was no truth nor mercy nor knowledge of God in the land (Hosea 4:1); Israel walked contrary to the commandments, and that goes for all twelve tribes.
judgmentFull: The Lord was very angry with Israel and removed them out of his sight; Judah also walked in the statutes Israel made, and the Lord rejected all the seed of Israel: all twelve tribes the Lord was angry with (2 Kings 17:18-20). It was the Lord who gave Jacob for a spoil and Israel to the robbers, the Lord against whom they had sinned (Isaiah 42:22-24); now we know who did this to us. The Lord stretches forth his hand to give warning, so when we are destroyed we have no one to blame but ourselves (Isaiah 1:16). He would move them to jealousy with those which are not a people (Deuteronomy 32:21). Zabulon and Nephthalim were called Galilee of the Gentiles (Matthew 4:15), and when Christ said go not into the way of the Gentiles nor into any city of the Samaritans, those Gentiles are the northern kingdom (Matthew 10:5).

The king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, Cuthah, Ava, Hamath and Sepharvaim and placed them in the cities of Samaria (2 Kings 17:24). That was Assyrian policy: put heathens in our land and put us in a foreign one, so that we would lose all sense of national pride and identity and assimilate into the heathen society. The settlers did not belong there; they were imposters, squatters, and the Lord sent lions among them (2 Kings 17:25-28). They feared the Lord and served their own gods (2 Kings 17:33), but the covenant was charged on the children of Jacob whom he named Israel, and it belongs to Israel and not to all nations (2 Kings 17:34). No nation and no treaty can redeem Israel from their condition, only turning to the Most High can, and as a nation Israel today serves the gods of the nations (2 Kings 17:35-41).

The ten tribes took counsel to leave the multitude of the heathen and go forth into a further country where never mankind dwelt, a journey of a year and a half (2 Esdras 13:40-45); no race was living here before the American Indians. The tribes of the north are Ephraim the Puerto Ricans, Manasseh the Cubans, Simeon the Dominicans, Zebulun Guatemala to Panama, the Mayans, Gad the American Indians, Reuben the Seminole Indians, Asher Colombia to Uruguay, the so-called Incas, Issachar the Mexican Aztecs, and Naphtali Argentina to Chile. They would perish among the heathen, and the land of their enemies would eat them up (Leviticus 26:38-41). The punishment is being in America, in Central and South America, and scattered throughout the islands, with the slave masters’ last names and a language that is not ours, out of our homeland; and what humbles the uncircumcised heart is the Lord bringing in the worst of the heathen to oppress us back to his ways. His people are destroyed for lack of knowledge (Hosea 4:6): the whole northern kingdom forgot all that was established, and knowledge is rejected by not consuming it daily. Yet for all that he will not cast them away (Leviticus 26:44), and in the place where it was said they were not his people, they shall be called the sons of the living God (Hosea 1:10; Romans 9:24-26).

cases.offense: They walked in the statutes of the heathen and of the kings of Israel, did secretly what was not right, built high places in all their cities, and set up images and groves on every high hill and under every green tree (2 Kings 17:7-12). The law had already commanded Israel to destroy such high places, not build them (Deuteronomy 12:2-3). The Lord warned them: when Moses gave these laws and commandments, he gave them to all twelve tribes, not to do after the doings of Egypt and of Canaan (Leviticus 18:3). He testified against Israel and Judah by all the prophets and seers, and they hardened their necks like their fathers who did not believe (2 Kings 17:13-14). To believe in the Most High is to take heed to the commandments, so those who claim belief while breaking the commandments do not truly believe (Ecclesiasticus 32:24).
cases.judgment: The Lord was very angry with Israel and removed them out of his sight; Judah also walked in the statutes Israel made, and the Lord rejected all the seed of Israel: all twelve tribes the Lord was angry with (2 Kings 17:18-20). It was the Lord who gave Jacob for a spoil and Israel to the robbers, the Lord against whom they had sinned (Isaiah 42:22-24); now we know who did this to us. The Lord stretches forth his hand to give warning, so when we are destroyed we have no one to blame but ourselves (Isaiah 1:16). He would move them to jealousy with those which are not a people (Deuteronomy 32:21). Zabulon and Nephthalim were called Galilee of the Gentiles (Matthew 4:15), and when Christ said go not into the way of the Gentiles nor into any city of the Samaritans, those Gentiles are the northern kingdom (Matthew 10:5).

cases.name: Hezekiah
cases.charge: Trusting in the Lord God of Israel, so that after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah; cleaving to the Lord and keeping his commandments; breaking the brasen serpent; opening the doors of the house of the Lord and keeping the passover
cases.summary: Hezekiah son of Ahaz did that which was right according to all that David his father did: he removed the high places, broke the images, cut down the groves, and broke in pieces the brazen serpent the people burned incense to (2 Kings 18:1-4). He trusted in the Most High so that none among the kings of Judah, before or after, was like him; he clave to the Most High and kept the commandments, and the Most High was with him (2 Kings 18:5-7). He is a king of God’s mercy: both kingdoms were going downhill, but according to God’s mercy to David’s lineage the Lord would not allow the kingdom of Judah to be consumed as Ephraim had been consumed (Psalm 18:50).
offenseFull: His father Ahaz had multiplied idolatry in the land, even inside the holy place. Hezekiah, whose name means the strength of God, trusted in the Lord and was very faithful. The brazen serpent that Moses made for the people to look upon and be healed, the people had started to worship as a god, so he had to destroy it, and he called it Nehushtan (2 Kings 18:4; Numbers 21:9). Prospering here does not mean a mansion or luxury but the blessing that comes from keeping and doing the commandments (2 Kings 18:7; Deuteronomy 29:9), and he rebelled against the king of Assyria. All the kings except David, Hezekiah and Josiah were defective (Ecclesiasticus 49:4); even decent kings like Asa, Uzziah and Jotham were defective in some way.

In the first month of his first year he opened the doors of the house of the Lord and repaired them, and charged the priests and Levites to sanctify themselves and carry the filthiness out of the holy place, the idols that Ahaz had multiplied (2 Chronicles 29:3-5). He named the sin plainly: the fathers had shut the doors, put out the lamps, and stopped the incense and burnt offerings, which were commanded continually as an everlasting statute (2 Chronicles 29:6-7; Leviticus 24:2-8). The wrath of the Lord was on Judah, and they could see it with their eyes, the borders of Judah minimized and their brothers carried captive (2 Chronicles 29:8-9). Before the offerings and sacrifices came the broken and contrite heart (Psalm 51:16-17): Hezekiah acknowledged that the forefathers had transgressed, and the spirit of repentance comes first, then the Lord is pleased with the sacrifices. It was in his heart to make a covenant with the Lord God of Israel to turn away his wrath, because Judah was about to go out the way the northern kingdom was going out (2 Chronicles 29:10).

He sent letters to all Israel and Judah, even to Ephraim and Manasseh, to keep the Passover at Jerusalem in the second month, the provision of the law for those defiled or on a far journey (2 Chronicles 30:1-5; Numbers 9:10-11). This was six years before the northern kingdom was completely taken away, after the first wave under Tiglath-pileser, and the Lord was using Hezekiah to give the northern kingdom one last chance: turn again, and your captive brethren shall find compassion (2 Chronicles 30:6-9). The posts were laughed to scorn and mocked, the same mockery Israel meets today when the truth is preached; yet some of Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30:10-11).
judgmentFull: Many ate the Passover otherwise than it was written, and Hezekiah prayed that the good Lord pardon everyone who prepares his heart to seek God, and the Lord hearkened and healed the people (2 Chronicles 30:18-20). Grace and mercy are present here in the Old Testament. They kept the feast fourteen days in one mind and one heart, and there had not been the like in Jerusalem since the days of Solomon (2 Chronicles 30:21-26). In every work he began in the service of the house of God, in the law and in the commandments, he did it with all his heart and prospered (2 Chronicles 31:21). Do the work with everything you have as unto the Lord, or it will not be blessed; you cannot halfway walk in the truth and expect to grow.

The Lord would no more have mercy upon the house of Israel, but he would have mercy upon the house of Judah and save them, not by bow nor by sword nor by battle (Hosea 1:6-7). The king trusts in the Lord, and through the mercy of the Most High he shall not be moved (Psalm 21:7): the Lord would not allow Hezekiah to be moved as he did Hoshea the king of Israel. When Sennacherib took the fenced cities, Hezekiah sent to Lachish acknowledging offense, and to pay the tribute he gave all the silver of the house of the Most High and cut the gold from the temple doors (2 Kings 18:13-16). When the nation was threatened, he went into the house of the Lord and sent to Isaiah: when the nation of Israel is threatened, you get the man of God (2 Kings 19:1-7). He made a pool and a conduit and brought water into the city: vision and planning like no other, nation building (2 Kings 20:20).

Sick to death, he was told to set his house in order, meaning his affairs for after his death, the distribution of his inheritance (Ecclesiasticus 33:23). He did not seek the physicians as Asa did in his bitterness against the Lord (2 Chronicles 16:12); he knew better, and he turned his face to the wall, prayed and wept, and the Lord added fifteen years (2 Kings 20:1-6). The lump of figs on the boil shows that remedies and herbs go together with prayer, for healing is in the hand of the Most High (2 Kings 20:7; Wisdom of Solomon 16:12). For a sign the shadow went back ten degrees on the dial of Ahaz (2 Kings 20:8-11): the Lord can manipulate time, and everything is subject to the Most High. Yet he rendered not according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was lifted up in pride (2 Chronicles 32:25).

cases.name: Shebna the treasurer
cases.charge: Hewing himself a sepulchre on high and graving a habitation for himself in the rock, the treasurer over the house, in a city called to weeping that would not humble itself
cases.summary: The word came against Shebna, the treasurer over the house, who had hewn himself out a sepulchre on high and graved a habitation for himself in a rock, and the Most High would carry him away with a mighty captivity and toss him like a ball into a large country, where he would die (Isaiah 22:15-19). In his place the Most High called his servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah and laid the key of the house of David upon his shoulder (Isaiah 22:20-22). Shebna was an actual man, and he also represents the leadership: what happened to him happened to the people, tossed into a strange country on ships, while Eliakim is symbolic of Christ coming.
offenseFull: The burden of the valley of vision is the burden of Jerusalem as a whole (Isaiah 22:1). Assyria came against the city, and they saw the breaches of the city of David, gathered the waters of the lower pool, broke down houses to fortify the wall, and made a ditch between the two walls, yet they had not looked unto the Maker thereof (Isaiah 22:9-11; 2 Chronicles 32:2-4). They were doing everything else but returning unto the Lord. The Lord called them to weeping, mourning and sackcloth to humble them, and instead they were eating, drinking and feasting, saying tomorrow we shall die, not humbling themselves and turning back to him; so the iniquity would not be purged from them till they died (Isaiah 22:12-14). He would return to his place till they acknowledged their offence and sought his face in their affliction (Hosea 5:15).

Into that city the Lord sent Isaiah to Shebna, the treasurer over the house, to ask what he had there and whom he had there, that he had hewn out a sepulchre on high and graved a habitation for himself in a rock (Isaiah 22:15-16). Shebna was an eighth-century official, scribe to King Hezekiah, who took part in the negotiations with the Assyrians who demanded the surrender of Jerusalem, and who was sent with the delegation to consult Isaiah; he carved himself an elaborate rock tomb, for which Isaiah rebuked him, and an inscription on a rock tomb at Siloam is believed to be the tomb of Shebna the royal steward (2 Kings 18:18, 26, 37; 2 Kings 19:2). The story meant something then, and prophetically it goes into something more, for the secrets of wisdom are double to that which is (Job 11:6). Shebna represents the leadership and rulership, and this would happen to us as a people.
judgmentFull: The Lord would carry him away with a mighty captivity, violently turn and toss him like a ball into a large country, and there he would die, and the chariots of his glory would be the shame of his lord’s house; he would be driven from his station and pulled down from his state (Isaiah 22:17-19). Being tossed like a ball into a large country is us being scattered in slavery. A chariot is not only horses; a chariot can be a ship, a vessel to move things and people. Israel had ships: Solomon made a navy of ships at Ezion-geber (1 Kings 9:26). The vessels Israel had used for itself would be used against it. The Lord said he would bring them into Egypt again with ships (Deuteronomy 28:68): Israel would go into slavery on ships, hundreds and perhaps thousands of cargo slave ships. Among them was the Jesus of Lubeck, called the Good Ship Jesus, bought by Henry VIII, passed to Elizabeth I, and given to John Hawkins for the Atlantic slave trade; the Africans were encouraged to enter it for salvation, and those who entered could not leave. Never trust thine enemy, for like as iron rusteth, so is his wickedness (Ecclesiasticus 12:10); Esau cannot be trusted.

In that day the Lord would call his servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, clothe him with Shebna’s robe and girdle, commit the government into his hand, and make him a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah (Isaiah 22:20-21). Eliakim means God sets up, the resurrection of God, and he is symbolic of Christ coming; a father to Jerusalem and to Judah is both kingdoms reuniting under Christ. He that hath the key of David, that openeth and no man shutteth, is Christ (Isaiah 22:22; Revelation 3:7). Christ unlocked the book and opened the understanding of the scriptures, and when he opens the door to give wisdom and understanding no man can close it, though the scribes and Pharisees tried to shut the door against the northern kingdom (Luke 24:44-45; Matthew 23:13). The Lord would fasten him as a nail in a sure place, for a glorious throne to his father’s house (Isaiah 22:23): Christ is that nail fastened in a sure place, the chief cornerstone, and you cannot shake Christ (Ephesians 2:20). Israel had to go into slavery on ships, tossed into a strange country, and then resurrect itself, repent and acknowledge Christ, as the Israelites are doing in the streets today.

cases.name: Sennacherib and Rabshakeh
cases.charge: Reproaching the living God; setting the Holy One of Israel among the gods of the nations that could not deliver their lands, and boasting that the Lord had sent him to destroy the land
cases.summary: Assyria was a rising empire conquering the nations around Israel; it destroyed the northern kingdom, then came against the southern kingdom in the reign of Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:13). Rabshakeh, sent by Sennacherib, cried in the Jews’ language that Hezekiah should not make them trust in the Lord, for no god of the nations had delivered its land out of the hand of the king of Assyria (2 Kings 18:17-35). That was the blasphemy: your God will not deliver you, and the gods of the nations are nothing (2 Kings 19:3-4). That night the angel of the Lord smote a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians, and Sennacherib was slain by his own sons as he worshipped in the house of Nisroch his god (2 Kings 19:35-37).
offenseFull: Judah tried to join the revolt of Edom, Moab and the Philistines against the tribute, and when Sennacherib took the fenced cities, Hezekiah sent to Lachish saying he had offended, and paid the tribute (2 Kings 18:13-16). Paying the tribute was one thing, but Sennacherib intended to take the land, as Assyria had taken the land of the northern kingdom, and Hezekiah was not in agreement with giving it up (2 Kings 18:17). It was not Assyria itself: it was the Lord operating through them, giving them that power and causing them to be puffed up in their minds, as he did with Pharaoh and as he is doing with the so-called white man today.

Rabshakeh mocked Hezekiah’s confidence and called Egypt a bruised reed that pierces the hand of any who lean on it; he twisted the reform into a weakness, because Hezekiah had removed the high places, and he boasted that Assyria came up against the land by the word of the Most High himself (2 Kings 18:19-25). Asked to speak in the Syrian language, he cried aloud in the Jews’ language so everyone on the wall would hear: make an agreement with me, eat every man of his own vine, until I come and take you away to a land like your own; pay your tribute, and then be deported out of your land while their own people are put in it (2 Kings 18:26-32). It is the same thing they try with us now: they threaten your resources, because they know that once people’s food and water are cut off, most will humble themselves and turn their back on God; that is why food should be put away.

He asked where the gods of Hamath, Arpad and Sepharvaim were, and claimed no god could deliver Jerusalem out of his hand (2 Kings 18:33-35); his letter listed the nations Assyria destroyed whose gods could not deliver them (2 Kings 19:10-13). When the heathen get to the point where they say there is none other but we, the Lord smites the heads of their rulers (Ecclesiasticus 36:10). The Assyrian is the rod of his anger (Isaiah 10:5), and the wicked are his sword (Psalm 17:13); in the process they get puffed up and blaspheme the Lord, when it is only by his power that they can do anything. The people held their peace and answered him not a word, for the king had commanded it (2 Kings 18:36). Let him talk: that is why we do not do interviews with these people; we do not have to answer them.
judgmentFull: Hezekiah rent his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth, went into the house of the Lord, and sent to Isaiah, calling it a day of trouble, rebuke and blasphemy (2 Kings 19:1-4). Blasphemy is speaking against the Lord; cursing your God, reproaching the living God, and blaspheming are the same thing. Isaiah returned the word: fear not the blasphemy, for the Most High would send a blast upon Sennacherib, and he would hear a rumour, return to his own land, and fall by the sword there (2 Kings 19:6-7). While Rabshakeh was boasting, the Assyrians were already at war on another front, for Tirhakah king of Ethiopia came out to fight against him; the Lord had already set the ambushes (2 Kings 19:8-9). Hezekiah spread the letter before the Lord and prayed that all the kingdoms of the earth might know he alone is God (2 Kings 19:14-19). This is a righteous prayer, praying for the downfall of enemies and for righteous judgment to come upon them.

The virgin daughter of Zion laughed him to scorn, for he had lifted up his eyes against the Holy One of Israel; Israel laughs at the enemy, for it is already written that they lose (2 Kings 19:21-22). All Assyria’s victories and conquests were because the Most High allowed it (2 Kings 19:25). Assyria put hooks on conquered people and marched them out of their land, and the Lord would put his hook in Sennacherib’s nose and his bridle in his lips (2 Kings 19:28): what you do to people, God does to you. He would not shoot an arrow there, for the Lord would defend the city for his own sake and for his servant David’s sake (2 Kings 19:32-34). That is why we honor our forefathers: God has a relationship with them before us.

That night the angel of the Lord, a celestial being, part of the army from heaven and not one in earthly flesh, smote a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians, and in the morning they were all dead corpses (2 Kings 19:35). Judah did not have to lift a bow, a sword or a shield. It is not by might but by his spirit, for the battle is his to fight for his people (Zechariah 4:6). Sennacherib lifted up his hand against Zion and boasted proudly, and the Holy One heard them out of heaven and delivered them by the ministry of Isaiah, because Hezekiah had done the thing that pleased the Lord (Ecclesiasticus 48:17-22). Sennacherib returned to Nineveh in anger and took it out on the northern kingdom Israelites he held captive, whom Tobit buried privily, and within fifty-five days his own sons killed him (2 Kings 19:36-37; Tobit 1:18-21). God will send strange punishments to the proud, even from inside their own house.

cases.name: Hezekiah and the ambassadors of Babylon
cases.charge: Rendering not again according to the benefit done unto him, for his heart was lifted up; shewing all his treasures to the men of Babylon
cases.summary: Healed and given a sign, Hezekiah rendered not according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was lifted up in pride, and wrath came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 32:24-25). When the king of Babylon sent letters and a present, Hezekiah showed his envoys all his precious things, holding nothing back, trusting his enemies because of the gift, and Isaiah declared that all of it would be carried into Babylon and his own sons made eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon (2 Kings 20:12-18). Hezekiah humbled himself, he and the people of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in his days (2 Chronicles 32:26).
offenseFull: Sick unto death, Hezekiah turned his face to the wall, prayed and wept sore, and before Isaiah left the middle court the word returned: the Most High had heard his prayer, seen his tears, and would add fifteen years and defend the city for his own sake and for David’s sake (2 Kings 20:1-6). A mighty man is brought low by sickness; sickness is to humble you. The Most High brought the shadow ten degrees backward on the dial of Ahaz, reversing the natural course of the sun as proof of his power (2 Kings 20:8-11).

But Hezekiah rendered not according to the benefit done to him (2 Chronicles 32:25). When things go well, do not get puffed up and make it about yourself. Berodach-baladan king of Babylon sent letters and a present because he had heard Hezekiah had been sick; this is the introduction of Babylon, still only a province under Assyria at that time (2 Kings 20:12). Because of a flattering letter and a few gifts, Hezekiah showed them the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious ointment and all the house of his armour; there was nothing in his house nor in all his dominion that he showed them not (2 Kings 20:13; Isaiah 39:2). This is how his heart was lifted up: he gave the heathen a tour of everything, not knowing they were scoping out all that they planned eventually to take from him. A gift destroyeth the heart, which is why Hezekiah let his enemies in and showed them everything he owned (Ecclesiastes 7:7).

In the business of the ambassadors who came to enquire of the wonder done in the land, God left him to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart (2 Chronicles 32:31). That was a test: the Lord was seeing where Hezekiah’s spirit was. The Lord will do the same thing with us. You have been doing well, in the spirit, and then all of a sudden a strange scenario is before you; you have to stop and recognize that the Lord is trying you right now, apply the scriptures, and not get carried away and caught up in the moment. He tried Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the same way, for the examination of their hearts (Judith 8:25-27).
judgmentFull: Hezekiah told Isaiah that the men had seen everything among his treasures, and Isaiah declared the days would come when all in his house, and what his fathers had stored up, would be carried to Babylon with nothing left, and his own sons that issue from him would be made eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon (2 Kings 20:14-18; Isaiah 39:3-7). It is as if your family left you an inheritance, a number of houses, and someone comes by and you start showing him all your deeds: everything you showed them you are going to lose. Nebuchadnezzar carried the vessels of the house of the Lord to Babylon (2 Chronicles 36:7), and the word about the sons was fulfilled when the children of Judah of the king’s seed, Daniel among them, of the lineage of Hezekiah, were made eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon (Daniel 1:3-6). Some are made eunuchs of men, as Daniel and his companions were after they were grown (Matthew 19:12). They were taught the tongue of the Chaldeans and given new names (Daniel 1:4-7): every time we have been conquered we have been forced to take on a language and customs not our own, and new names (Isaiah 28:11).

Hezekiah answered that the word of the Most High was good, content that peace and truth be in his days, and he took some solace in that (2 Kings 20:19). He took the rebuke. He did not complain that the Lord was angry with him over a small thing; he humbled himself for the pride of his heart, he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the Lord came not upon them in his days (2 Chronicles 32:26). That is how to take correction: when you do something foolish, even if you did not think it was foolish, and your elders and leaders show it to you, say you are right and fix it, without justifying yourself. By humbling himself he appeased the wrath of the Lord; the Lord held it off during his time, but the prophecy Isaiah told him still came to pass. He slept with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigned in his stead (2 Kings 20:21).

cases.name: Isaiah
cases.charge: Offering himself when the Lord asked whom He should send; prophesying to a people whose heart was made fat; walking naked and barefoot three years for a sign; and standing beside Hezekiah when Assyria blasphemed
cases.summary: In the year king Uzziah died Isaiah saw the Lord on His throne, was cleansed of his unclean lips by a coal from the altar, and offered himself to be sent (Isaiah 6:1-8). He was sent not to be liked but to wake up a people who would hear and not understand; he walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign; and when Assyria blasphemed he told Hezekiah not to fear, and the word came to pass (Isaiah 6:9-12; Isaiah 20:2-4; Isaiah 37:5-7, 36-38).
offenseFull: Isaiah the son of Amoz saw his vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, a contemporary of Hosea, who prophesied in Samaria while Isaiah dealt directly with the kings of Judah (Isaiah 1:1).

In the year Uzziah died he saw the Lord upon a throne, high and lifted up, and His train, His garment, so long that it filled the whole temple. Above it stood the seraphims, high ranking angels whose work was to cover the throne, as the images of angels covered the mercy seat (Isaiah 6:1-4). Isaiah cried that he was undone, a man of unclean lips among a people of unclean lips, the Israelites, for his eyes had seen the King, the Lord of hosts, and that King is Christ (Isaiah 6:5). When men see the Most High or the day of the Most High, terror comes upon them. A seraphim laid a live coal from the altar upon his mouth, and his sin was purged (Isaiah 6:6-7).

Then the Lord asked whom He should send, and Isaiah offered himself to carry out the purpose of God, though he was sent to prophesy destruction to come (Isaiah 6:8). That is the mindset of a leader, and all the prophets of God that are sent back as saviours made the same agreement with God. Nowhere does it say he was sent to be liked. That is not the job and not the mission: he was sent to wake up the people, to tell them how evil they are, to repent and come back to Messiah.

The people would hear and not understand; to make their heart fat means it is waxed gross, lest they convert and be healed (Isaiah 6:9-10). Christ spoke in parables to fulfil this prophecy, because it is not meant for everybody to get the understanding of the bible (Matthew 13:13-15). A remnant is allotted not to wake up: some mothers, fathers and children will not wake up to this truth,. The answer to how long was until the land was utterly desolate, with no Israelites remaining there. That is 70 A.D., when they fell by Rome’s sword and were led away captive into all nations, as Christ said (Isaiah 6:11-12; Luke 21:24). Yet a tenth would return (Isaiah 6:13).

When Tartan, a captain of the Assyrian army sent by Sargon, took Ashdod, the Lord told Isaiah to loose the sackcloth from his loins and put off his shoe, and he walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign that Assyria would lead the Egyptians and Ethiopians away captive, young and old, to the shame of Egypt (Isaiah 20:1-4). Everyone kept running to Egypt as though it were greater than what God had ordained, and the sign came to pass. The scripture itself marks an uncovered backside as a disgrace, and young brothers should stop sagging. The sign has a double meaning (Job 11:6): as the prophet was naked, so the people were led naked and barefoot into captivity, and even unto this day their descendants from Africa are led away by a wicked people into slavery.
judgmentFull: When Rabshakeh blasphemed, Hezekiah went into the house of the Lord and sent to Isaiah to pray for the remnant, turning to the Most High and not to Egypt or to fear. Isaiah answered that he should not fear, for the king of Assyria would hear a rumour, return to his own land, and fall by the sword there (Isaiah 37:1-7). Jerusalem was not going to be touched, for the Lord would defend it for His own sake and for David’s sake, and the angel of the Lord smote a hundred and eighty-five thousand in one night (Isaiah 37:33-36). Sennacherib was killed in his own land by his own sons (Isaiah 37:37-38). The word of the Most High through Isaiah came to pass, and no nation can stand against Israel when the Most High has spoken against it.

The Holy One heard them out of heaven and delivered them by the ministry of Isaiah, who was great and faithful in his vision, saw by an excellent spirit what should come to pass at the last, and comforted them that mourned in Sion (Ecclesiasticus 48:20-24). That is what a true prophet does: he comforts the people that mourn and explains to them the secret things.

The answer Here am I is also a prophecy that Isaiah would return. Long after he was dead the Lord said by Esdras that for the help of Jerusalem He would send His servants Isaiah and Jeremiah, and He named the prophets He would give for leaders to the people that come from the east (2 Esdras 2:17-18; 2 Esdras 1:37-40). They are part of the hundred and forty and four thousand (Revelation 7:4), and John, who died on Patmos, was told he must prophesy again before many peoples and nations (Revelation 10:11). No one knows who is who, but those prophets are back in these last days; they grew up in a grimy state and will come to the fulfilment of their spirit. Esau cannot stop it, though billions are spent to hide this awakening, for the Most High Himself is doing it.

cases.name: Manasseh
cases.charge: Building again the high places his father destroyed; altars to all the host of heaven in the two courts of the Lord’s house; his son through the fire; observing times, enchantments, witchcraft, familiar spirits and wizards; a carved image in the house of God; Jerusalem filled with innocent blood from one end to another
cases.summary: Manasseh began to reign at twelve and reigned fifty-five years, undoing his father Hezekiah’s reform and seducing Judah to do worse than the heathen the Lord had cast out and filling Jerusalem with innocent blood (2 Kings 21:1-16). The captains of Assyria carried him in fetters to Babylon, where he humbled himself and prayed, and the Lord restored him (2 Chronicles 33:11-13). The sentence on the nation stood, and Judah later went into captivity for the sins of Manasseh (2 Kings 24:3-4).
offenseFull: Hezekiah was one of the very few righteous kings, so righteous that the Most High extended his life, and Manasseh his son reigned in his stead (2 Kings 20:21). The Lord spoke to Manasseh and the people through the prophets, and they would not hearken, because they assumed the son of so righteous a father must be righteous too (2 Chronicles 33:10). He rebuilt the high places Hezekiah had broken down, reared altars for Baal, made a grove as Ahab did, worshipped the host of heaven, the stars and the zodiac, and built altars for them in the two courts of the house where the Lord had put His name (2 Kings 21:1-5; 2 Chronicles 33:1-5). That is wickedness with zero fear of the Most High: he took the Lord’s house and turned it into Baal’s house. The people did not serve idols for nothing but for the self-gratification in it, the same as men keep pagan feasts today for the gifts, the food and the revelling.

He made his son pass through the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom, observed times, used enchantments and witchcraft, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards (2 Kings 21:6; 2 Chronicles 33:6). Passing a child through the fire is child sacrifice, the same spirit as abortion today. The firstborn of Baal worshippers were usually the ones sacrificed, and Manasseh burned his own firstborn, the heir to the throne. Every one of these things was a commandment he broke (Deuteronomy 18:10-13).

He set a carved image in the house where the Lord had promised David and Solomon to put His name for ever and never again move Israel out of the land, on condition that they keep the whole law (2 Kings 21:7-8), and he seduced Judah to do more evil than the nations the Lord destroyed (2 Kings 21:9). Those nations were hated for witchcraft, wicked sacrifices, merciless murders of children and feasts of blood (Wisdom of Solomon 12:3-6), and Israel was sent to kill them out of the land for the very same works. How do you become more pagan than the pagans? Yet that is what we did, and that is why we had to be judged. He shed innocent blood very much, until Jerusalem was full from one end to another, the children sacrificed under his edict (2 Kings 21:16).
judgmentFull: The Lord spoke by the prophets that He would bring such evil on Jerusalem that both ears of whoever heard of it would tingle: famine and diseases beyond what is written (2 Kings 21:10-12). He would stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria and the plummet of the house of Ahab: since Judah worshipped Baal as Ahab did, it would get the same judgment Assyria brought on Samaria. He would wipe Jerusalem as a man wipes a dish and turns it upside down, removing everyone from the homeland, and give the remnant of His inheritance to their enemies as a prey (2 Kings 21:13-15).

In Manasseh’s own day the Lord brought the captains of Assyria, who took him among the thorns, the wicked leaders under him, bound him with fetters and carried him to Babylon, then a province under Assyria (2 Chronicles 33:11). The king was brought into a nation he had not known, exactly as the curse said (Deuteronomy 28:36). In his affliction, locked up, he besought the Lord and humbled himself greatly, the Lord was entreated of him and brought him again to Jerusalem, and then Manasseh knew that the Lord was God (2 Chronicles 33:12-13). That is the pattern of a people called by His name who humble themselves and are heard (2 Chronicles 7:14), and it is the story of the so-called Negroes, blacks, Hispanics and Native Americans: when the affliction came, he humbled himself. Under the law he was condemned on every count, a king worthy of death, but the Lord shows mercy on whom He will show mercy, and let him live to be an example to us in this time (Exodus 33:19).

His prayer is written among the sayings of the seers, and it is the Prayer of Manasses, a writing of the Apocrypha, which is part of the Bible (2 Chronicles 33:18-19). In it he confesses that repentance is not appointed to the just, to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob who kept God’s laws, but to him, a sinner above the number of the sands of the sea (Prayer of Manasses 1:7-9). The law is not made for a righteous man but for the lawless (1 Timothy 1:9). He showed his repentance in works: he cast the strange gods and the idol out of the house of the Lord, repaired the altar, and commanded Judah to serve the Lord (2 Chronicles 33:15-16). Manasseh is the embodiment of us as a nation: what he did as one man we did as a people and still do, and that is why his history is written. Repentance is always possible; our people are repenting, not repented, so no man should judge before the time.

Yet the sentence on the nation stood. Judah would be removed into all kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh did in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 15:4), and the bands of the Chaldees came in the days of Jehoiakim for his sins and the innocent blood, which the Lord would not pardon (2 Kings 24:2-4). In Manasseh’s lifespan Judah did not go into captivity; the Lord visited his iniquities upon the children three and four generations later, who went into captivity under Babylon (Exodus 20:5).

cases.name: Amon
cases.charge: Sacrificing to all the carved images his father had made; humbling not himself as his father had humbled himself, but trespassing more and more
cases.summary: Amon began to reign at twenty-two, reigned two years, and brought back all the idols his father Manasseh had served, without the humbling his father came to at the end (2 Kings 21:19-22; 2 Chronicles 33:21-23). He trespassed more and more, and his own servants conspired against him and slew him in his house, the fruit of his own work; the people of the land slew the conspirators and made his son Josiah king (2 Kings 21:23-24).
offenseFull: Every time a righteous king tried to remove the idolatry, Israel would always find its way back to folly; the Lord speaks peace to His people, but they are not to turn again to folly (Psalm 85:8). Manasseh repented in prison and tried to right the ship, but out of fifty-five years that was maybe the last five. Amon was twenty-two when he began to reign, so the majority of his life he came up under his father, witnessing the orgies and the rituals; that is what he was raised in, that is all he knew, and when he got on the throne that is what he implemented. As soon as his father passed he brought it right back, as if Manasseh had never tried to undo it. He did evil as his father had done, walked in all his ways, served the idols his father served, and forsook the Lord God of his fathers (2 Kings 21:19-22).

He sacrificed to all the carved images Manasseh had made, and did not humble himself as his father had humbled himself, but trespassed more and more (2 Chronicles 33:22-23). Hezekiah was righteous, Manasseh wicked and then humbled, and Amon followed the bad example. If a just man begets a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood, that eats upon the mountains and lifts up his eyes to the idols, it does not matter that the father was righteous, and it does not matter that the father repented: that son shall surely die, and his blood shall be upon him (Ezekiel 18:10-13).

The idols Amon served are named in Josiah’s cleansing: vessels made for Baal, for the grove and for all the host of heaven, and the idolatrous priests, the Chemarim, who burned incense to Baal, to the sun, the moon and the planets (2 Kings 23:4-5). Behind the host of heaven are real demonic forces, and the same worship is kept today in the daily horoscope and the zodiac sign beside the scripture. At the groves children were sacrificed and strange rites performed to receive things from the idols they called gods, and the houses of the sodomites stood by the house of the Lord (2 Kings 23:6-7); that is what is thriving today under the guise of Christianity and American liberty. They slew their children in sacrifices, which today is abortion, used secret ceremonies, kept neither lives nor marriages undefiled, and slew one another traitorously; the worship of idols is the beginning, the cause and the end of all evil (Wisdom of Solomon 14:23-27). Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, the heart of men is set to do evil, which is why Amon’s evil increased, and his sins abounded to his own destruction (Ecclesiastes 8:11; Ecclesiasticus 23:1-2).
judgmentFull: The servants of Amon, the people he had close to him, conspired against him and slew the king in his own house (2 Kings 21:23). Slaying one another traitorously is the spirit that came with the idolatry he enforced; that is the fruit of his own work, and that is why it happened to him, as the son that does these things shall surely die. The people of the land slew all them that had conspired against the king and made Josiah his son king in his stead (2 Kings 21:24).

The power of the earth is in the hand of the Lord, and in due time He sets over it one that is profitable (Ecclesiasticus 10:4); wicked rulership lasts only so long. Amon’s death was a premature murder, and his heir was not grown: Josiah was eight when he took the throne (2 Chronicles 34:1). For the first eight years of his reign Judah was still wicked; in the eighth year, at sixteen, he began to seek after the God of David his father, and at twenty the purge of the idols began (2 Chronicles 34:3). Every king except David, Hezekiah and Josiah was defective, for they forsook the law of the Most High (Ecclesiasticus 49:4).

cases.name: Josiah
cases.charge: A tender heart at the reading of the book; rending his clothes; turning to the Lord with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses
cases.summary: Josiah began to reign at eight, sought the God of David while still young, and in his eighteenth year, while the temple was being repaired, the book of the law was found (2 Chronicles 34:1-3; 2 Kings 22:8). When it was read to him he rent his clothes, and Huldah answered that the curses written in it would come, but because his heart was tender he would go to his grave in peace (2 Kings 22:11-20). He read the book to all the people, made a covenant, cleansed the land from the temple to Samaria, and kept a passover like none since the judges (2 Kings 23:1-25). He fell at Megiddo, meddling in a matter that did not concern him, yet his righteous legacy stands (2 Chronicles 35:20-25).
offenseFull: Manasseh began to reign at twelve, Amon at twenty-two and Josiah at eight, yet the youngest was the wisest: better is a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king who will no more be admonished (Ecclesiastes 4:13). In the eighth year of his reign, at sixteen, he began to seek the God of David, and in the twelfth, at twenty, to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, groves and images (2 Chronicles 34:3-7). Zephaniah prophesied in his early years against the remnant of Baal and the Chemarim, and Jeremiah, a Levite of the priests’ city of Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, was called in his thirteenth year (Zephaniah 1:1-4; Jeremiah 1:1-2).

In his eighteenth year the silver was given to the carpenters, builders and masons repairing the house, and he made sure the workmen were paid, for the workman is worthy of his hire (2 Kings 22:3-7). Hilkiah the high priest found the book of the law (2 Kings 22:8); Manasseh and Amon had been so wicked that the very book of the law was lost. When it was read the king rent his clothes (2 Kings 22:11), for the king was meant to read the law before all the people, which the wicked kings had not done (Deuteronomy 17:18-19). In eight years of seeking the Lord he had not been familiar with the curses (Deuteronomy 28:15). So it is today: people in seminary and Bible study their whole life know about the Exodus, but never knew that the slave ships and the yoke of iron are in the Bible; they never heard the curses, and so they never connected the dots that we are the Israelites.

Great was the wrath because the fathers had not kept the book (2 Kings 22:13). To enquire of the Lord one must go to a saint, a chosen prophet who has the word (Job 5:1). They went to Huldah the prophetess, who dwelt in Jerusalem in the college, the school where the young prophets were instructed and trained up; we always had schools to train the young men in the scriptures, as the brothers go to the school on the Sabbath now (1 Samuel 10:5; 2 Kings 2:3). She answered that all the curses in the book would come on the place (2 Chronicles 34:22-25). But because Josiah’s heart was tender and he humbled himself and wept, he would be gathered to his grave in peace and not see the evil to come (2 Kings 22:18-20).
judgmentFull: He gathered all the people, small and great, read in their ears the whole book of the covenant, stood by a pillar and made a covenant to keep the commandments with all their heart and soul, and all the people stood to it (2 Kings 23:1-3). Our forefathers had the Bible, and the king read it openly.

Then he cleaned house: the vessels of Baal and the host of heaven burned at the Kidron, the idolatrous priests put down, the grove burned to powder, the houses of the sodomites by the temple broken down, Topheth defiled, the horses given to the sun taken away, and Solomon’s high places for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom defiled (2 Kings 23:4-14). Topheth had to be defiled because Israel would not stop the evil on its own. This is repentance in action: cleaning house of every idol that causes a people to fall under punishment. He burned men’s bones on Jeroboam’s altar at Bethel, fulfilling what a prophet had foretold by name hundreds of years before (2 Kings 23:15-16; 1 Kings 13:2), and slew the priests of the high places upon their altars (2 Kings 23:19-20). Those priests had shed innocent blood in the worship of Baal and Molech, the inexcusable sin of Manasseh, and blood defiles the land (Numbers 35:33). Under the old covenant, setting Israel in order from disarray often took much death and much destruction; it was very bloody. The rebuke given in the streets today is with the scripture: no churches are burned and no one is killed.

He commanded the passover as written in the book of the covenant, on the fourteenth day of the first month, in alignment with what Moses instituted; none like it had been kept since the days of the judges (2 Kings 23:21-23; 1 Esdras 1:1; Exodus 12:6). Reading the law brought the nation back to the appointed feasts in order, as the feast is kept in order today. No king before or after him turned to the Lord with all his heart, soul and might (2 Kings 23:25). His remembrance is like perfume and sweet as honey in all mouths; he behaved uprightly in the conversion of the people from the wickedness under Manasseh and Amon back to the Lord; and every king except David, Hezekiah and Josiah was defective (Ecclesiasticus 49:1-4).

Yet the Lord did not turn from the fierceness of His wrath over Manasseh’s provocations (2 Kings 23:26-27). Josiah went up against Pharaoh Necho at Megiddo, would not hearken to the words of Necho from the mouth of God, disguised himself, and was shot by the archers and died (2 Chronicles 35:20-24). He got involved in a matter that did not concern him and lost his life in it; meddle not with many matters (Ecclesiasticus 11:10). But he never went off and served another god, and Jeremiah and all the singing men and women lamented him (2 Chronicles 35:25). His ending was tragic, but his righteous legacy supersedes it, for the memorial of virtue is immortal (Wisdom of Solomon 4:1).

cases.offense: Manasseh began to reign at twelve, Amon at twenty-two and Josiah at eight, yet the youngest was the wisest: better is a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king who will no more be admonished (Ecclesiastes 4:13). cases.name: Jehoahaz (Shallum) of Judah
cases.charge: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord according to all that his fathers had done
cases.summary: After Josiah fell at Megiddo the people of the land anointed his son Jehoahaz, called Shallum, and in three months he did evil according to all that his fathers had done (2 Kings 23:30-32). Pharaoh Necho put him in bands at Riblah, laid a tribute on the land, set his brother Eliakim on the throne as Jehoiakim, and carried Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died (2 Kings 23:33-34). The word was to weep not for the dead king but for the one who went away, for he would never see his native land again (Jeremiah 22:10-12).
offenseFull: Josiah was carried dead from Megiddo, and the people of the land took Jehoahaz his son, anointed him and made him king in his father’s stead (2 Kings 23:30). The people appointed him themselves, and they put the younger son first: Jehoahaz was twenty-three and his brother Jehoiakim twenty-five, though it is supposed to go down the line from the elder (2 Kings 23:31, 36). His mother was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, the same mother as Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:18). The curse said the Lord would bring them and the king they set over themselves into a nation they had not known (Deuteronomy 28:36), and that curse happened over and over again with these kings.

He reigned three months and did evil according to all that his fathers had done, the wicked kings of Israel (2 Kings 23:31-32). He followed after all the wicked examples. Ezekiel took up a lamentation for the princes of Israel: their mother was a lioness who nourished her whelps among the young lions; one became a young lion, learned to catch the prey and devoured men; the nations heard of him, he was taken in their pit, and they brought him with chains to the land of Egypt (Ezekiel 19:1-4). That is Jehoahaz. As Nimrod was a mighty hunter, catching men to lead them into evil against the Most High (Genesis 10:8-9), so he led the nation into evil.

Jeremiah was sent to the king’s house with the terms on which the house of David would stand: execute judgment and righteousness, deliver the oppressed, and do no violence to the stranger, the fatherless or the widow; if they would not hear, the Most High swore by Himself that the house would become a desolation, and the nations would say it was because they forsook His covenant and worshipped other gods (Jeremiah 22:1-9).
judgmentFull: Pharaoh Necho put him in bands at Riblah in the land of Hamath, which is Syria, north of Israel, that he might not reign in Jerusalem, and put the land to a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. He made Eliakim, Josiah’s other son, king and turned his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away to Egypt, where he died (2 Kings 23:33-34; 2 Chronicles 36:3-4). Jehoiakim paid Pharaoh by taxing the people, exacting the silver and gold of every man according to his taxation (2 Kings 23:35), and he also did evil like his forefathers, not like his father Josiah.

The word concerning Shallum the son of Josiah, who reigned instead of his father, was that the people should not weep for the dead but weep sore for him that goes away: he went forth out of that place and would not return, but would die in the place where they led him captive and see his native country no more (Jeremiah 22:10-12). That land was Egypt. Shallum means retribution, or payback. So the curse on the king the people set over themselves came to pass in him (Deuteronomy 28:36).

cases.name: Jehoiachin (Coniah)
cases.charge: Doing evil as his father Jehoiakim had done; a signet plucked from the Lord’s right hand
cases.summary: Jehoiachin, called Coniah and Jeconiah, reigned three months and did evil as his father Jehoiakim had done (2 Kings 24:8-9). Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, and Jehoiachin went out to him with his mother, servants, princes and officers; he was carried to Babylon in the second wave of the conquest with the temple treasures, the mighty men and the craftsmen (2 Kings 24:10-16). Though Coniah were the signet on the Lord’s right hand he would be plucked off, and written childless as to the throne of David (Jeremiah 22:24-30).
offenseFull: Babylon took Judah in three waves. In the first, in the days of Jehoiakim, about 605 BC, Nebuchadnezzar came up and Jehoiakim served him three years and rebelled, and the Lord sent bands of the Chaldees, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites against Judah, as He had spoken by the prophets, for the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood the Lord would not pardon (2 Kings 24:1-4; Jeremiah 25:1-9); Daniel and the three holy children were taken then (Daniel 1:1-6). Jehoiakim built his house by unrighteousness and used his neighbour’s service without wages, not following the example of his father, so he was buried with the burial of an ass, cast forth beyond the gates (Jeremiah 22:13-19). When Israel will not rule in righteousness, the Most High raises a Nebuchadnezzar; Israel’s purpose was never to be wicked and rule at the same time (Ecclesiasticus 10:4).

Jehoiachin his son was eighteen when he began to reign, reigned three months, and did evil according to all his father had done (2 Kings 24:8-9); Chronicles gives eight years, and three months and ten days (2 Chronicles 36:9). His mother Nehushta is named with him, and all these kings that did evil have their mothers named, for their mothers had a significant influence in wickedness over them: children are their oppressors and women rule over them (Isaiah 3:12). Jeremiah was told to say to the king and the queen to humble themselves and sit down, for the crown of their glory would come down (Jeremiah 13:18). The queen in our custom was the mother of the king, not his wife: the king had many wives, and the wives were not regarded as queens, but he had only one mother, and the king and the queen went into captivity together (Jeremiah 29:2; 2 Kings 24:15). Though Coniah were the signet on the Lord’s right hand, He would pluck him off and give him to Nebuchadnezzar, whose face he feared, and cast him and his mother into a country where they were not born (Jeremiah 22:24-26).
judgmentFull: This was the second wave, about 597 BC. Nebuchadnezzar’s servants besieged Jerusalem, and Jehoiachin went out to the king of Babylon with his mother, his servants, his princes and his officers, and was taken in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign. All the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house were carried out, and the vessels of gold Solomon made were cut in pieces, as the Lord had said (2 Kings 24:10-13), the word to Hezekiah fulfilled (Isaiah 39:6). The emptiers emptied the land and marred its vine branches, the gardens, the crops and the livelihood, and the Lord turned away the excellency of Jacob, the temple of gold and the kingdom (Nahum 2:2). Judah was like Jeremiah’s linen girdle, never washed and hidden by the Euphrates: Israel filthy in its sin, carried beyond the rivers of Babylon and snared in prison houses, marred and profitable for nothing (Jeremiah 13:1-11; Isaiah 42:22).

He carried away the princes and the mighty men of valour, ten thousand captives, seven thousand men of might and a thousand craftsmen and smiths, all strong and apt for war; none remained but the poorest sort (2 Kings 24:14-16). They took the best of the best, wanting them to build for Babylon what they had built in their own land, as conquering nations always used Israel’s skill and industry. America did the same: it did not bring illiterate people to build a country, and it had laws that we could not read or write; there is no need for such laws for people who cannot already read. Among those captives was Ezekiel, whose visions by the river Chebar are dated by the years of king Jehoiachin’s captivity (Ezekiel 1:1-3).

The Lord casts down the thrones of proud princes; many kings have sat down upon the ground, and the honourable were delivered into another man’s hand, as Jeconiah and his mother the queen were delivered into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar (Ecclesiasticus 10:14; Ecclesiasticus 11:5). The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, his father’s brother, king and changed his name to Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:17). The Lord wrote Coniah childless: no man of his seed would prosper sitting upon the throne of David or ruling in Judah any more (Jeremiah 22:28-30). In the thirty-seventh year of his captivity Evil-merodach lifted up his head out of prison, spoke kindly to him, changed his prison garments and gave him a continual allowance all the days of his life (2 Kings 25:27-30), a mercy shown at the very end of the account.

cases.name: Asa in his first years
cases.charge: Taking away the altars of the strange gods, the high places, the images and the groves; commanding Judah to seek the Lord and to do the law; crying to the Lord against a thousand thousand Ethiopians
cases.summary: Asa son of Abijah, one of the better kings to reign in the history of Israel, took away the strange altars, high places, images and groves, and commanded Judah to seek the Lord and do the law (2 Chronicles 14:1-5). When Zerah the Ethiopian came against him with a thousand thousand, he cried to the Lord and the Ethiopians were overthrown (2 Chronicles 14:9-15). At the word of Azariah son of Oded he put away the idols, gathered the strangers out of the northern tribes, led the people into a covenant, and removed his own mother from being queen for her idol (2 Chronicles 15:1-16).
offenseFull: Abijah slept with his fathers and Asa reigned, and the land was quiet ten years; he broke down the images, cut down the groves, and commanded Judah to seek the Lord God of their fathers and to do the law and the commandment (2 Chronicles 14:1-5). The pattern of Rehoboam warns what happens when a strong king forsakes that law: for three years Judah walked in the way of David and Solomon, and when Rehoboam had established the kingdom and strengthened himself, he forsook the law of the Lord, and all Israel with him (2 Chronicles 11:17; 2 Chronicles 12:1).

Because the Lord had given him rest, Asa built fenced cities with walls, towers, gates and bars while the land was yet before them, and raised an army of mighty men of valour out of Judah and Benjamin (2 Chronicles 14:6-8). Rest is not idleness; by much slothfulness the building decays, so the rest from war was spent building up, not idling (Ecclesiastes 10:18).

Zerah the Ethiopian, a Cushite, came out against him with a host of a thousand thousand and three hundred chariots, and Asa cried to the Lord that it was nothing with Him to help, whether with many or with them that have no power, for they rested on Him and went in His name (2 Chronicles 14:9-11). Faith in the Most High, not the numbers of the enemy, wins the battle. The victory of battle stands not in the multitude of an host; strength comes from heaven, and the battle is not ours but God’s, as our forefathers proved when a million Ethiopians fell before Judah and Benjamin. They that be with us are more than they that be with them (2 Kings 6:15-17).

The Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded, who told Asa and all Judah and Benjamin that the Lord is with them while they are with Him; if they seek Him He will be found of them, but if they forsake Him He will forsake them (2 Chronicles 15:1-2). That is discipline: the Lord is with us as long as we walk in His discipline, and as soon as we step out of it and forsake Him, He forsakes us. For a long season Israel had been without the true God, without a teaching priest and without law (2 Chronicles 15:3). This describes the northern kingdom after Jeroboam, which got rid of the priests. Yet when in their trouble they turned to the Most High, He was found of them; so Asa was to be strong, for his work would be rewarded (2 Chronicles 15:4-7).

When Asa heard the prophecy he took courage, put away the abominable idols out of Judah, Benjamin and the cities he had taken from mount Ephraim, and renewed the altar of the Lord (2 Chronicles 15:8). Hearing the word gives courage still, for faith comes by hearing, and we teach our people who they are, that the Israelites and the Christ are black (Romans 10:17).

He gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and the strangers with them out of Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon, who fell to him out of Israel in abundance when they saw that the Lord was with him (2 Chronicles 15:9). These strangers were Israelites whose hearts turned back: the northern kingdom is called strangers in the Old Testament, and whenever Judah was on point they followed. In the fifteenth year of Asa they entered a covenant to seek the Lord with all their heart and soul, that whoever would not seek Him should be put to death, and swore it with a loud voice and trumpets (2 Chronicles 15:10-14). He removed Maachah his own mother from being queen because she had made an idol in a grove, and he cut it down, stamped it and burned it at the brook Kidron (2 Chronicles 15:16).
judgmentFull: The Lord smote the Ethiopians before Asa and Judah; they fled to Gerar and were overthrown so that they could not recover, for they were destroyed before the Lord and His host (2 Chronicles 14:12-13). The fear of the Lord came on all the cities round about Gerar, and Judah carried away exceeding much spoil, sheep and camels in abundance (2 Chronicles 14:14-15).

All Judah rejoiced at the oath, for they had sworn with all their heart and sought Him with their whole desire, and He was found of them and gave them rest round about (2 Chronicles 15:15). Though the high places were not all taken away, the heart of Asa was perfect all his days; he brought the dedicated silver, gold and vessels into the house of God, and there was no more war until the thirty-fifth year of his reign (2 Chronicles 15:17-19).

cases.name: Asa in his latter years
cases.charge: Relying on the king of Syria and not on the Lord; putting the seer in a prison house for the rebuke; in his disease seeking not to the Lord, but to the physicians
cases.summary: When Baasha of Israel built Ramah to cut Judah off, Asa, instead of crying to the Most High as he had against Zerah, took silver and gold out of the house of the Lord and hired Ben-hadad of Syria against his brothers in the north (2 Chronicles 16:1-6). Hanani the seer rebuked him for relying on Syria and not on the Lord, and told him he would have wars from then on; Asa put the seer in prison and oppressed some of the people (2 Chronicles 16:7-10). Diseased in his feet, he sought not to the Lord but to the physicians, and the Most High had him die (2 Chronicles 16:12-13).
offenseFull: In the six and thirtieth year of Asa, Baasha king of Israel came up against Judah and built Ramah, to let none go out or come in to Asa (2 Chronicles 16:1). Baasha was trying to stop the northern kingdom from coming down to Judah, because tribes out of Israel had been turning their hearts back to the Most High and joining Asa. There were internal battles among the nation of Israel, and that is why there are still internal battles today.

Ben-hadad smote the cities of Israel, Baasha left off building, and Asa carried away the stones and timber of Ramah to build Geba and Mizpah (2 Chronicles 16:2-6). He went into his treasury and paid the other nations to fight his brother, and so allowed the heathen to come and destroy his brothers. It is a sick mindset to rejoice when the heathen come against our own people; even if a brother is in sin, the heart should hope that the Most High has mercy on him, and that he learns from it and recovers. Cursed be the man that trusteth in man (Jeremiah 17:5).

Hanani the seer told him that because he had relied on the king of Syria and not on the Lord, the host of Syria had escaped out of his hand, as the huge host of the Ethiopians and Lubims had not when he relied on the Lord (2 Chronicles 16:7-8). The eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth to show Himself strong for them whose heart is perfect toward Him (2 Chronicles 16:9). God is always watching, and God wants the glory: the Most High wants to display His power, and His help comes with conditions, for the heart must be right with the Lord to bring effectual change. Herein he had done foolishly: he emptied his treasury to handle a problem that the Lord would have handled, had he come the right way. Many go to therapists, spiritual healers and lying churches instead of asking what the Bible says to do.

Then Asa was wroth with the seer and put him in a prison house, for he was in a rage, and he oppressed some of the people at the same time (2 Chronicles 16:10). He did not ask how to get back right with God; he locked up the man of God who told him the truth, then abused the people around him because he was angry and would not listen to what God said.

In the thirty and ninth year of his reign he was diseased in his feet until his disease was exceeding great, as with diabetics whose toes are cut off and whose legs swell, yet in his disease he sought not to the Lord but to the physicians (2 Chronicles 16:12). His mind was no longer on God. Whoever is sick must seek the Lord first and foremost, not the physician first. The rebuke is not against physicians but against seeking them in place of the Most High, from whom healing comes: honour the physician, for the Lord created him, and the Lord created medicines out of the earth; in sickness pray to the Most High and leave off from sin, then seek the physician (Ecclesiasticus 38:1-4, 9-12). Ye are all physicians of no value: what they give treats the sickness and does not cure it (Job 13:4). The word of the Most High is the ultimate cure (Wisdom of Solomon 16:12).
judgmentFull: Because he did that foolish thing, from then on he had wars (2 Chronicles 16:9). Some problems never go away because the same wrong decision keeps being made, no one turns to the Lord, and nothing changes in the house.

The Most High was angry with him for going to the physicians before the Lord, for he would not pray and fast and deal with the word of God. Healing is ultimately the decision of the Most High. Asa slept with his fathers in the one and fortieth year of his reign and was buried in his own sepulchre in the city of David, on a bed of sweet odours and spices, with a very great burning (2 Chronicles 16:13-14).

His acts first and last are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel (2 Chronicles 16:11), to keep a record of his offense for the children of Israel, for whatever was written aforetime was written for our learning, that through patience and comfort of the scriptures we might have hope, and not through a therapist or a loan from the bank (Romans 15:4). It shows that we have a history of this bad behaviour. There is a God who watches us and waits for us to call on Him the right way; He will defend us when we are under attack and when we are sick.

cases.name: Jehoshaphat
cases.charge: Walking in the first ways of his father David and seeking not unto Baalim; sending princes and Levites with the book of the law to teach in all the cities of Judah; and setting singers before the army
cases.summary: The Lord was with Jehoshaphat because he walked in the first ways of his father David and sought not unto Baal; he took away the high places and groves, and in his third year sent princes, Levites and priests through all the cities of Judah with the book of the law to teach the people (2 Chronicles 17:3-9). The fear of the Lord fell on the kingdoms round about so that they made no war with him (2 Chronicles 17:10). When Moab, Ammon and mount Seir came against him he fasted and prayed, sent singers before the army, and found the enemy dead (2 Chronicles 20:1-24).
offenseFull: Jehoshaphat reigned in the place of his father Asa and strengthened himself against Israel, setting himself apart from the northern kingdom’s ways, and placed forces and garrisons in the fenced cities of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim that Asa had taken (2 Chronicles 17:1-2). A diligent king secures the land and prepares before trouble comes, for he saw problems in the land and set out to fix them.

The Lord was with him because he walked in the first ways of David and sought the Lord God of his fathers and walked in His commandments, and not after the doings of Israel (2 Chronicles 17:3-4). David was a man after the Most High’s own heart because he kept the commandments and charged Solomon to keep them, and the way we must walk is defined by the ordinances and laws we are taught (Exodus 18:20). His heart was lifted up in the ways of the Lord, not in pride but in devotion: a heart lifted up in itself becomes proud, but a heart lifted up in the ways of the Lord takes pride in the Lord’s work. He took away the high places and groves out of Judah, the false idols and their little churches (2 Chronicles 17:6).

In the third year of his reign he sent his princes, and with them Levites and priests, and they taught in Judah, having the book of the law of the Lord with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah and taught the people (2 Chronicles 17:7-9). Jehoshaphat was a man of action, raising up the consciousness of the people’s minds in the ways of the Lord. What Christ did in sending out the twelve was not new, and what IUIC is doing is not new: in Jehoshaphat’s day our people were worshipping Molech, Chemosh and Baal, and the remedy was to tear down the groves and send teachers through the land with the book. It is the same pattern followed today in the streets: go out into the highways and hedges and compel them to come in (Luke 14:23); wisdom cries at the gates, and her call is a rally cry for men (Proverbs 8:1-4).

He brought the people back to the Lord from Beer-sheba to mount Ephraim and set judges city by city, who judged not for man but for the Lord, with whom there is no iniquity, respect of persons or taking of gifts (2 Chronicles 19:4-7). These judges are soldiers with biblical education. It is very easy to get caught up in popular persuasion, even among our own people, so take heed and do what the Bible says; and because there is no iniquity with the Lord, we cannot join ourselves to iniquity either.

When Moab, Ammon and mount Seir came against him, Jehoshaphat feared, proclaimed a fast and prayed that they knew not what to do, but their eyes were upon the Lord (2 Chronicles 20:1-13). Then the spirit of the Lord came upon Jahaziel, a Levite, in the midst of the congregation (2 Chronicles 20:14). The spirit is not always there: the Most High watches how His people respond, and when they do not know what to do He sends the right spirit. He told them not to fear the multitude, for the battle was not theirs but God’s; they should stand still and see the salvation of the Lord (2 Chronicles 20:15-17). Do not be scared of armies and people; teach and speak the word of God no matter what they say or threaten. The battle belongs to the Lord because He is always there fighting with us, and the horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha were angels waiting for the word (2 Kings 6:15-17). The Lord uses our lives to display His power, His strength and His might, and all of it is a test of faith.

Jehoshaphat and all Judah fell before the Lord, and the Levites praised Him with a loud voice (2 Chronicles 20:18-19). In the morning he told them to believe in the Lord their God and so be established, and to believe His prophets and so prosper: believe what the Bible says, and believe the men of God who have been sent. He appointed singers to praise the beauty of holiness as they went out before the army (2 Chronicles 20:20-21).
judgmentFull: The kingdoms round about made no war against him; some of the Philistines brought presents and tribute silver and the Arabians brought him flocks, and he built castles and cities of store (2 Chronicles 17:10-12). Teaching the law had a real effect on the nations, and wisdom disarmed his enemies, for wisdom is better than weapons of war (Ecclesiastes 9:18) and strengthens the wise more than ten mighty men in the city (Ecclesiastes 7:19). Cities of store are cities of provision, like Joseph’s storehouses in Egypt; in captivity our people had neither building nor closet, but the diligent tend to plenty.

When they began to sing and praise, the Lord set ambushments, and Ammon, Moab and mount Seir destroyed one another until none escaped (2 Chronicles 20:22-24). That is how the Most High fights: He sets traps, letting the wicked believe they have the victory, and then He disrupts them. They blessed the Lord in the valley of Berachah, the fear of God was on all the kingdoms when they heard that the Lord fought against the enemies of Israel, and his realm was quiet (2 Chronicles 20:25-30). Some battles you have to sit back and allow the Lord to display His strength.
