cases.name: Jehoshaphat’s alliances
cases.charge: Joining affinity with Ahab and going up with him to Ramoth-gilead against the word of the prophet; joining himself with Ahaziah to make ships
cases.summary: Jehoshaphat, a southern kingdom king who kept the commandments of the Lord, joined affinity with Ahab and went up with him to Ramoth-gilead after the prophet Micaiah had warned that they would lose (2 Chronicles 18:1-16). Ahab disguised himself and sent Jehoshaphat into the battle in his robes, setting him up for the kill, and only the Lord’s help saved him (2 Chronicles 18:28-31). Jehu the son of Hanani rebuked him for helping the ungodly, and when he later joined with Ahaziah to build ships, the Lord broke his works (2 Chronicles 19:1-3; 2 Chronicles 20:35-37).
offenseFull: Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab, marrying his son Jehoram to Ahab’s daughter (2 Chronicles 18:1). Through that marriage the daughter of Jezebel brought Baal worship into the southern kingdom, and since then, even under the righteous kings who came after, it was very difficult ever to fully purge it out.

After certain years he went down to Samaria, and Ahab, the wicked northern kingdom king and weak husband of Jezebel, killed sheep and oxen for him in abundance, good northern kingdom hospitality, and persuaded him to go up to Ramoth-gilead, to a battle with Syria that the kingdom of Judah had nothing to do with (2 Chronicles 18:2). Jehoshaphat answered that he was as Ahab was and his people as Ahab’s people, and they would be with him in the war (2 Chronicles 18:3). His bond with Ahab was a joining together: what is mine is yours. The kingdom was split, and the northern kingdom was no longer considered God’s people. You cannot join affinity with people just because they are your people; this was a war that was not sanctioned by God.

This is an example of a brother showing himself a friend to another brother for his own occasion. A friend must be proved first and not hastily credited, for some man is a friend for his own occasion and will not abide in the day of thy trouble (Ecclesiasticus 6:7-8); a friend cannot be known in prosperity, for adversity shows whether a person was false all along (Ecclesiasticus 12:8).

He was making a bad decision in being with the wicked, but he still had the spirit on him: he asked to inquire at the word of the Lord, and when four hundred prophets told the king only what he wanted to hear, he asked for a prophet of the Lord besides (2 Chronicles 18:4-6). Ahab said there was one, Micaiah, but he hated him because he never prophesied good concerning him, only evil, meaning he told the truth (2 Chronicles 18:7). A rebellious people say to the seers, prophesy smooth things (Isaiah 30:9-11), and the time comes when men will not endure sound doctrine (2 Timothy 4:2-4). Micaiah would speak only what his God said, and he saw all Israel scattered upon the mountains as sheep that have no shepherd (2 Chronicles 18:12-16); nevertheless Ahab persuaded Jehoshaphat to go with him.

At the point of no return Ahab told him that he would disguise himself, but Jehoshaphat should put on his robes (2 Chronicles 18:28-29). The king of Syria had commanded his captains to fight only with the king of Israel, and Ahab knew it: he did not truly love that brother, and he was setting Jehoshaphat up for the kill, so that they would think they had killed him and he would survive. They rewarded him evil for good (Psalm 35:12): Jehoshaphat did not have to go all the way with that man to fight his battle, and he almost lost his life.
After this he joined himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, who did very wickedly, to make ships at Ezion-geber to go to Tarshish (2 Chronicles 20:35-36).
judgmentFull: When the captains took him for the king of Israel and compassed him about, Jehoshaphat cried out, and the Lord helped him and moved them to depart from him; if it had not been for the Lord he would have been killed (2 Chronicles 18:30-31).

When he returned in peace to Jerusalem, Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and asked whether he should help the ungodly and love them that hate the Lord; therefore was wrath upon him from before the Lord (2 Chronicles 19:1-2). Nevertheless good things were found in him, for he had taken away the groves and prepared his heart to seek God (2 Chronicles 19:3). We have to be careful not to bring wrath upon ourselves or upon the congregation; the Lord does not like that thing. Strive not in a matter that concerneth thee not, and sit not in judgment with sinners, for if thou meddle much thou shalt not be innocent (Ecclesiasticus 11:9-10); as with Jehoshaphat, God will have to deal with us too.

Then Eliezer the son of Dodavah prophesied against him that because he had joined himself with Ahaziah, the Lord had broken his works, and the ships were broken and could not go to Tarshish (2 Chronicles 20:37). Mighty works are being done, and all praise for the good leadership, the bishops and deacons, and those who labour in Christ before us; but if we join with those doing wickedness, the Lord will break our works.

cases.name: Jehoram of Judah
cases.charge: Slaying all his brethren with the sword as soon as he was strengthened; walking in the way of the house of Ahab, for he had the daughter of Ahab to wife; making high places and compelling Judah to fornication
cases.summary: As soon as Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat had the throne he slew all his brethren; married to Ahab’s daughter, he walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, made high places and compelled Judah to fornication (2 Chronicles 21:1-11). Edom and Libnah revolted, Elijah’s writing pronounced a plague on his house, and the Philistines and Arabians carried off his goods, wives and sons (2 Chronicles 21:8-17). The Lord smote him in his bowels, and after two years they fell out, and he departed without being desired (2 Chronicles 21:18-20).
offenseFull: Jehoshaphat gave the kingdom to Jehoram because he was the firstborn, and as soon as Jehoram had strengthened himself, he slew all his brethren with the sword, and divers also of the princes of Israel (2 Chronicles 21:1-4). This is a pattern to watch: as soon as some among Israel get power, they turn and hurt everyone around them. He reigned eight years and walked in the way of the kings of Israel as did the house of Ahab, for he had the daughter of Ahab to wife (2 Chronicles 21:5-6). A wicked man is given a wicked woman: Ahab was a wicked, weak king who let his wife do wickedness, her mother was the one who had Naboth killed for his vineyard, and his son married Ahab’s wicked daughter.

He made high places in the mountains of Judah, caused the inhabitants of Jerusalem to commit fornication and compelled Judah thereto (2 Chronicles 21:11). High places are places of worship that have nothing to do with the God of Israel. Dealing with other gods is spiritual fornication, but physical fornication is built into these false worships; the pagan holidays passed down to our people, whatever the season, are built on fornication, and that is what draws the people to follow them.

A writing came to him from Elijah: because he had made Judah go a whoring like the house of Ahab and had slain his brethren who were better than himself, the Lord would smite his people, children, wives and goods with a great plague, and his bowels would fall out by disease day by day (2 Chronicles 21:12-15). When the Most High brings judgment on an evil man it reaches the house, the children and the wives of those who follow him, and all the goods, whatever sustains a man. This is what it looks like to mess with the Most High: every sickness not written in the book of the law He brings upon a disobedient people until they be destroyed (Deuteronomy 28:61), and because of disobedience many are weak and sickly, and many sleep (1 Corinthians 11:30).
judgmentFull: In his days Edom revolted from under the dominion of Judah and made themselves a king, and Libnah revolted at the same time, because he had forsaken the Lord God of his fathers (2 Chronicles 21:8-10). When we obey the Most High the nations are subject to us; when we come out from under the commandments, the other nations rise up and revolt against us and keep us in sin. God controls war and all the kings of the earth; nations do not just attack, and when His people sin He strengthens those they had power over and gives them the upper hand. We had Esau on lockdown, confined around Petra, and this revolt fulfilled the word to Esau, that when he had the dominion he would break his brother’s yoke from off his neck (Genesis 27:40). From then Esau was moving: the descendants of Esau, the sworn enemies of the descendants of Jacob even to the end of the world, increased in numbers and strength, spread their colonies far and wide, subjugated Italy, and founded Rome and the Roman Empire.

The Lord stirred up the Philistines and the Arabians that were near the Ethiopians, and they carried away all the substance of the king’s house, his sons and his wives, save Jehoahaz the youngest (2 Chronicles 21:16-17). When we sin against Him the angels leave, we are not defended, and He allows the enemy to break into the house and take everything. Because of his disobedience his whole family was carried into captivity by the Philistines, the Arabs and the Ethiopians, the same peoples who later held our people in the trans-Saharan slave trade. This was one of the first raids in which Ham and Ishmael worked together against Judah, for they were always confederate against us; the invasion accords with the prophecy of Joel, and it happened to us again in Africa (Joel 3:4-6).

After all this the Lord smote him in his bowels with an incurable disease, and after two years his bowels fell out and he died of sore diseases (2 Chronicles 21:18-19). The Lord let him die a slow death; the sickness started from within, like the cancers of the bowels today. He departed without being desired, and many were glad to see him go; his people made no burning for him, and they buried him in the city of David, but not in the sepulchres of the kings (2 Chronicles 21:19-20). A good name is better than precious ointment (Ecclesiastes 7:1); a man cannot rule wickedly and shame the people and then expect them to stand by him when disease comes.

Yet the Lord would not destroy the house of David, because of the covenant He had made to give a light to him and to his sons for ever (2 Chronicles 21:7). The Most High keeps His promises: just as He did not break His word to David, He did not break His promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; those promises were made to the Israelites and stand to this day. If a man walks in righteousness, the Most High will preserve his lineage; a brother who wakes up to the truth and then goes off destroys his whole line, so secure the legacy and make sure the sons are on point.

cases.name: Ahaziah of Judah
cases.charge: Walking in the ways of the house of Ahab, his mother being his counsellor to do wickedly; going down to Jezreel to see Joram
cases.summary: Ahaziah, Jehoram’s youngest son, reigned one year and walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, was his counsellor to do wickedly (2 Chronicles 22:1-4). He went with Joram son of Ahab to war at Ramoth-gilead and then down to Jezreel to see him, and so came into the path of Jehu, whom the Most High had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab (2 Chronicles 22:5-7). Jehu’s men killed him, and his mother then destroyed the seed royal (2 Chronicles 22:8-10).
offenseFull: The inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah, Jehoram’s youngest son, king in his stead, for the band of Arabians had slain all the elder sons; he reigned one year, and his mother’s name was Athaliah the daughter of Omri (2 Chronicles 22:1-2). Omri was the father of Ahab, and scripture often refers to a grandparent as father or mother; other versions make it plain that she was Omri’s granddaughter, the daughter of Ahab and so of Jezebel. As is the mother, so is her daughter (Ezekiel 16:44): Jezebel was a heathen, but her daughter was an Israelite with the same evil, wicked spirit. The Jezebel spirit manipulates and exercises her authority through weak men.

He walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counsellor to do wickedly, and the house of Ahab were his counsellors after his father died, to his destruction (2 Chronicles 22:3-4). The same way Jezebel stirred up Ahab to do wickedness, Athaliah stirred up Ahaziah. This is a warning against being ruled by the wrong counsel: instead of going to the priests and the judges, as the law sets for a matter too hard in judgment (Deuteronomy 17:8-11), he went to his mother, and she counselled him into ruin. A woman with a grudge can rule a kingdom through her son, and that is what Athaliah did, another wicked woman who used the men around her to manipulate the people of Israel. He was the son-in-law of the house of Ahab (2 Kings 8:27), a picture of the generational curse passed from father to son.

He walked after their counsel and went with Jehoram son of Ahab to war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead, where the Syrians wounded Jehoram; when Jehoram returned to Jezreel to be healed, Ahaziah went down to see him, setting the stage for both kings to meet Jehu’s judgment (2 Chronicles 22:5-6; 2 Kings 8:28-29).
judgmentFull: The destruction of Ahaziah was of the Most High, for by going to Joram he came into the path of Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom the Most High had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab (2 Chronicles 22:7), to avenge the blood of the prophets shed by Jezebel, whose work was to kill the prophets while weak Ahab let it continue (2 Kings 9:7). Joram asked Jehu whether it was peace, and Jehu answered that there could be no peace while the whoredoms and witchcrafts of his mother Jezebel were so many (2 Kings 9:22). There is no peace as long as a wicked woman is in power. Joram turned and fled, crying treachery to Ahaziah, and Jehu drew his bow with his full strength and smote him through the heart (2 Kings 9:23-24). Ahaziah fled by the way of the garden house, was smitten in his chariot at the going up to Gur, and fled to Megiddo and died there (2 Kings 9:27).

The same Jehu who killed the seventy sons of Ahab found the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah’s brethren and slew them, then sought Ahaziah, who was hid in Samaria, and slew him (2 Chronicles 22:8-9). They buried him for the sake of Jehoshaphat his forefather, who sought the Most High with all his heart, but the house of Ahaziah had no power to keep the kingdom, so the wicked king was cut off by the same hand the Most High anointed to avenge Israel.

When Athaliah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal of the house of Judah (2 Chronicles 22:10), killing all her grandsons, or so she thought: a mother giving orders to kill anybody next in line, because her power came through her son. Back then a woman was only empowered through the man. She did not carry out this slaughter alone; she had weak men helping her, which is how she seized and held the throne. But Jehoshabeath, wife of Jehoiada the priest, stole Joash from among the king’s sons and hid him in the house of God six years, while Athaliah reigned in the position of the son she had lost (2 Chronicles 22:11-12).

cases.name: Jehoiada the priest
cases.charge: Hiding the king’s son in the house of God six years; crowning and anointing him by the proper custom; removing the usurper Athaliah; making a covenant that they should be the Lord’s people; doing good in Israel, both toward God and toward his house
cases.summary: When Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, destroyed the seed royal, Jehoshabeath the wife of Jehoiada the priest stole the infant Joash and hid him in the house of God six years (2 Chronicles 22:10-12). In the seventh year Jehoiada made a covenant with the captains and Levites, armed them with king David’s spears and shields, crowned and anointed the boy, and had Athaliah put to death outside the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 23:1-15). He made a covenant that the people should be the Lord’s, the house of Baal was broken down, and at a hundred and thirty he was buried among the kings (2 Chronicles 23:16-21; 2 Chronicles 24:15-16).
offenseFull: Athaliah was the granddaughter of Omri and the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel; as Jezebel stirred up Ahab to do wickedness, Athaliah was her son’s counsellor to do wickedly (2 Chronicles 22:2-3). When she saw her son was dead she arose to destroy all the seed royal, a mother giving orders to kill anyone next in line, because her power had come through her son (2 Chronicles 22:10). She did not do it alone; weak men helped her seize and hold the throne.

But Jehoshabeath, the daughter of king Jehoram, the sister of Ahaziah and the wife of Jehoiada the priest, stole Joash from among the king’s sons who were being slain and hid him and his nurse in a bedchamber, and he was hidden in the house of God six years while Athaliah reigned (2 Chronicles 22:11-12). Jehoiada was righteous, and his wife, one flesh with him, did the righteous thing and preserved the child; the high priest was of Levi and was married to Judah. They had to hide that little boy, because a wicked woman, to stay in power, will destroy the men.

In the seventh year Jehoiada strengthened himself and took the captains of hundreds into covenant; they gathered the Levites and the chief of the fathers out of all Judah, and the congregation made a covenant with the king in the house of God, for the king’s son would reign as the Lord had said of the sons of David (2 Chronicles 23:1-3). He set the priests and Levites in thirds at the doors, the king’s house and the gate of the foundation, and had the Levites surround the king with weapons in hand (2 Chronicles 23:4-7). He did not dismiss the courses of the Levites but kept them at their work with security added for the king. These men stood armed in the house of God on the sabbath day, ready for war. The Levites and all Judah did all that Jehoiada commanded, for Levi does not rule on its own; Levi rules with Judah (2 Chronicles 23:8).

He gave the captains king David’s spears and shields from the house of God, set the people round the king from one side of the temple to the other, brought out the king’s son, put the crown on him, gave him the testimony, and he and his sons anointed him and cried, God save the king (2 Chronicles 23:9-11). This was the proper custom, a priest anointing the king as Samuel anointed Saul and then David, and that saying is from our forefathers, not first made up in Europe. The weapons they carried then were physical; today the weapon of Israel is the scriptures.

Athaliah heard the noise, came into the house of the Lord, tore her clothes and cried treason (2 Chronicles 23:12-13). She had just killed the royal seed, and when the rightful king is anointed she calls it treason; when you try to restore order, some look at it as treason against them and do not see that they are out of order. Jehoiada commanded that she be taken out between the ranks and whoever followed her be slain, but not in the house of the Lord, and she was slain at the entrance of the horse gate (2 Chronicles 23:14-15). The Most High cannot use a man following behind a wicked woman; the children of Jezebel whom the Lord kills with death are the men who follow her (Revelation 2:20-23). Twice in the history, when wicked women rose up in power to devour, God sent men of the Lord to remove them.
judgmentFull: Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, the people and the king that they should be the Lord’s people, and they broke down the house of Baal, smashed its altars and images and killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars (2 Chronicles 23:16-17). Just as Jezebel had prophets at her table, Athaliah had a priest of Baal who answered to her; they had to wipe that clean and purge out the feminist woman and the feminist men who followed her. This same covenant is made today: as a person wakes up, repents, keeps the commandments and comes out of idolatry, he again becomes the Lord’s.

He appointed the offices of the house of the Lord by the priests and Levites as David had distributed them, and set porters so that none unclean should enter; then they brought the king down and set him on the throne, and the city was quiet (2 Chronicles 23:18-21). Before a king takes his position he is under tutors and governors (Galatians 4:1-2); young Joash was king in rank and still a learner under Jehoiada. Athaliah had no place ruling Israel; being the king’s mother did not make her the ruler, and even Deborah, a mother in Israel, set her heart toward the governors and worked with the men of Israel rather than ruling over them (Judges 5:7-9).

Joash did right all the days of Jehoiada, because that is what he was taught; no one comes to the truth alone, for the Most High set up a structure of instruction (2 Chronicles 24:2; 2 Kings 12:2). The sons of Athaliah had broken up the house of God and bestowed its dedicated things upon Baalim, and under Jehoiada the house was repaired and the burnt offerings offered continually (2 Chronicles 24:7, 14). Jehoiada grew old and full of days and died at a hundred and thirty, and they buried him in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel toward God and toward his house (2 Chronicles 24:15-16). That a priest was buried among the kings shows the respect and diligence this man had earned.

cases.name: Joash of Judah
cases.charge: Hearkening to the princes after Jehoiada’s death; leaving the house of the Lord to serve groves and idols; commanding the stoning of Zechariah the son of Jehoiada for warning him, in the court of the house of the Lord
cases.summary: Joash did right all the days of Jehoiada the priest and repaired the house of the Lord, but after Jehoiada died he hearkened to the princes of Judah, who left the house of the Lord to serve groves and idols (2 Chronicles 24:1-18). When the spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada and he asked the people why they transgressed the commandments so that they could not prosper, they stoned him at the king’s commandment in the court of the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 24:20-22). A small company of Syrians destroyed the princes, and Joash’s own servants slew him on his bed for the blood of the priest’s sons (2 Chronicles 24:23-25).
offenseFull: Joash was seven when he began to reign and reigned forty years, and he did right all the days of Jehoiada, because that is what he was taught; he had seen the wicked men try to kill him, and he followed the man who showed him the ropes (2 Chronicles 24:1-2). He did well under the tutelage of the priest, and after that he dropped the ball. He set out to repair the house of God, which the sons of Athaliah had broken up and whose dedicated things they had given to Baalim; a chest was set at the gate, the collection Moses laid on Israel was brought in with rejoicing, and the money paid the masons, carpenters and workers in iron and brass, for the workman is worthy of his hire and we dealt righteously with our people (2 Chronicles 24:4-13).

Then Jehoiada died, and the princes of Judah came and made obeisance to the king, and he hearkened to them (2 Chronicles 24:17). Once Jehoiada passed away Joash started to go off, and he feared the people. They left the house of the Lord and served groves and idols, idols like the cross, the Christmas tree and the Easter bunny, none of which is biblical, and wrath came on Judah and Jerusalem; the Lord sent prophets to turn them back to the laws and commandments, and they would not hear (2 Chronicles 24:18-19). As soon as Jehoiada died Israel went off again, because the king was weak and listened to those who served other gods. Lust drives Israel to idolatry, and the Most High always sends prophets to warn.

The spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, who stood above the people and asked why they transgressed the commandments of the Lord, that they could not prosper; because they had forsaken the Lord, he had also forsaken them (2 Chronicles 24:20). He was not condemning anyone or harassing anyone; he asked a question. We could have had Black Wall Street again and been out from under the hand of the white man; all we had to do was keep the commandments of the Lord and we would have prospered and our captivity would have been turned. As soon as one of us is shot down in the street or some atrocity happens at the hands of the oppressor, we march and ask God why; we forsook him, so he forsook us. If you seek him he will be found, but if you forsake him he will forsake you (2 Chronicles 15:2).

They conspired against him and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of the house of the Lord, for Zechariah was telling Israel they were wicked and God would judge them; the people wanted him dead, and Joash said kill him (2 Chronicles 24:21). You cannot get more evil than that. So Joash remembered not the kindness Jehoiada had done him but slew his son, and as Zechariah died he asked the Lord to look upon it and require it (2 Chronicles 24:22). When the prophet came to correct the king, the king killed him for telling the truth, the same spirit our people show when a labourer brings the medicine and is met with violence. Zechariah prayed for vengeance on his murderer, and this is scripture; it is right to pray for the downfall of enemies who do much wickedness, even while we pray for the recovery and repentance of our own people.
judgmentFull: At the end of the year the host of Syria came against Judah and Jerusalem with a small company, destroyed all the princes of the people, and sent the spoil to the king of Damascus; the Lord delivered a very great host of Judah into their hand because they had forsaken the Lord God of their fathers, and so judgment was executed on Joash for killing Zechariah (2 Chronicles 24:23-24). They left him in great diseases, and his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada and slew him on his bed; he was buried in the city of David, but not in the sepulchres of the kings (2 Chronicles 24:25).

Joash began by doing right under Jehoiada’s guidance, repairing the house and clearing out the idols, but none of that was remembered because of the wickedness he turned to after he was warned: when the righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, his righteousness shall not be remembered, and he shall die in his sin (Ezekiel 3:20; Ezekiel 18:24). The Lord sends the prophet to turn the hearts of the fathers and the children lest he come and smite the earth with a curse, and our people are destroyed for lack of knowledge (Malachi 4:6). The Lord smote their children and they received no correction, and their own sword devoured their prophets like a destroying lion (Jeremiah 2:30).

Christ counted that blood when he said that upon that generation would come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias, slain between the temple and the altar (Matthew 23:34-35). In Babylon the great, which is the United States of America, spiritually Jerusalem, where they killed his prophets, scribes and wise men, is found the blood of prophets and of saints (Revelation 18:24; Revelation 11:8). The same wicked souls who killed Abel and all the prophets are back, come again to do to the prophets what was done to them then.

cases.name: Amaziah
cases.charge: Bringing home the gods of the children of Seir, whom he had just defeated, setting them up to be his gods and bowing down before them; threatening the prophet sent to counsel him; provoking Israel to his hurt
cases.summary: Amaziah did right in the sight of the Lord, but not with a perfect heart; he slew his father’s murderers but spared their children as the law commands, and at the word of a man of God sent home the hundred thousand men he had hired out of Ephraim (2 Chronicles 25:1-10). After the Lord gave him victory over Edom he brought home the gods of the children of Seir and worshipped them, and threatened the prophet sent to rebuke him (2 Chronicles 25:11-16). He then provoked Joash of Israel, was defeated and taken, saw the wall of Jerusalem broken and the house of God plundered, and was slain by conspirators at Lachish (2 Chronicles 25:17-27).
offenseFull: Amaziah was twenty-five when he began to reign, and he did right in the sight of the Lord, but not with a perfect heart (2 Chronicles 25:1-2). Kings says he did right, yet not like David his father, but according to all his father Joash did, and Joash did right only while Jehoiada the priest instructed him (2 Kings 14:3; 2 Kings 12:2). David praised the Lord with his whole heart (Psalm 111:1), while Solomon went not fully after the Lord and his heart was not perfect (1 Kings 11:4-6). Amaziah had a double heart (Ecclesiasticus 1:28): when circumstances change, a double heart changes on the Lord.

When the kingdom was established he took vengeance on the servants who had killed his father, but did not kill their children, as written in the law of Moses that every man shall die for his own sin (2 Chronicles 25:3-4; Deuteronomy 24:16). That is a foundational law: a man answers for his own sin, not for another man’s. It does not contradict the judgments where the Lord cuts off a whole house, as he cut off Ahab’s posterity for the prophets slain and had Achan’s household put to death for the lives lost by his trespass; where the judgment written is on the father alone, his son has nothing to do with it.

He mustered three hundred thousand of Judah and Benjamin to go to war with Edom, with Esau, and hired a hundred thousand mighty men out of Israel for a hundred talents of silver, like mercenaries. A man of God told him not to take them, for the Lord was not with Israel, with all the children of Ephraim, who had not departed from the sins of Jeroboam, and their help would only bring defeat. When he asked about the hundred talents, the man of God answered that the Lord was able to give him much more than that, and he hearkened and sent them home (2 Chronicles 25:5-10). Moses had warned Israel the same way not to go up when the Lord was not among them (Numbers 14:41-43). The hired men went home in great anger and fell on the cities of Judah while he was fighting Esau; a brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city (2 Chronicles 25:13; Proverbs 18:19).

He went to the valley of salt and smote ten thousand of the children of Seir, the Edomites, the so-called white man, and cast another ten thousand down from the top of the rock (2 Chronicles 25:11-12). Then he brought home the gods of the children of Seir, the gods of the white man, set them up to be his gods, bowed down to them and burned incense to them (2 Chronicles 25:14). It makes no sense: the Lord was with him and gave him the victory, and he took the gods of the people who had just lost while praying to them. The law said to consume those nations and not to serve their gods, for that would be a snare (Deuteronomy 7:16).

In mercy the Lord sent a prophet, when he could have sent one to take his head off, to ask why he sought gods that could not deliver their own people out of his hand (2 Chronicles 25:15). The prophet came to counsel him to destroy the idols, and the king asked who had made him of the king’s counsel and told him to forbear before he was smitten. The prophet forbore, and said he knew God had determined to destroy him because he had done this and had not hearkened to counsel (2 Chronicles 25:16). Pride goes before destruction (Proverbs 16:18); better is a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king who will no more be admonished (Ecclesiastes 4:13); and there is more hope of a fool than of a man wise in his own conceit (Proverbs 26:12).
judgmentFull: Somebody boosted his head, since the northern kingdom had fallen on Judah while he was fighting Esau, and he sent to Joash king of Israel to meet him face to face. Joash answered with the riddle of the thistle in Lebanon that asked the cedar for his daughter and was trodden down by a wild beast: Amaziah had smitten the Edomites and his heart was lifted up to boast; why meddle to his own hurt? Amaziah would not hear, for it came of God, that he might deliver them into the hand of their enemies because they had sought the gods of Edom, the gods of the white man (2 Chronicles 25:17-20).

Judah was put to the worse at Beth-shemesh, Amaziah was taken, four hundred cubits of the wall of Jerusalem were broken down, and the gold, silver and vessels of the house of God and the king’s treasures were carried to Samaria with hostages (2 Chronicles 25:21-24). All the spoil they had taken from Edom, Joash snatched away. The two kingdoms had real animosity, calling each other another nation, brother stealing the vessels out of his own brother’s temple.

He lived fifteen years after Joash, and from the time he turned away from following the Lord they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem; he fled to Lachish, and they sent after him and slew him there (2 Chronicles 25:25-27). Like father, like son: he did right for a time without his whole heart, then went off, and his own people conspired against him as they had against his father. Power is given by the Lord, who will try the works and search out the counsels of kings who do not walk after the counsel of God, and a sharp judgment shall be to them that be in high places (Wisdom of Solomon 6:1-5). When a man departs from the Most High, the protection departs with him.

cases.judgment: Somebody boosted his head, since the northern kingdom had fallen on Judah while he was fighting Esau, and he sent to Joash king of Israel to meet him face to face. Joash answered with the riddle of the thistle in Lebanon that asked the cedar for his daughter and was trodden down by a wild beast: Amaziah had smitten the Edomites and his heart was lifted up to boast; why meddle to his own hurt? Amaziah would not hear, for it came of God, that he might deliver them into the hand of their enemies because they had sought the gods of Edom, the gods of the white man (2 Chronicles 25:17-20).

cases.name: Uzziah
cases.charge: His heart lifted up when he was strong, going into the temple of the Lord to burn incense upon the altar of incense, which appertained not to the king but to the priests the sons of Aaron; and raging at the priests who withstood him
cases.summary: Uzziah was made king at sixteen and reigned fifty-two years; as long as he sought God in the days of Zechariah, God made him prosper against the Philistines, the Arabians and the Mehunims, in towers, wells, husbandry and a great army with engines of war (2 Chronicles 26:1-15). When he was strong his heart was lifted up, and he went into the temple to burn incense, which belonged only to the priests (2 Chronicles 26:16). When Azariah and eighty priests withstood him he was wroth with the censer in his hand, and leprosy rose up in his forehead; he was a leper, cut off from the house of the Lord, until the day of his death (2 Chronicles 26:17-21).
offenseFull: All the people of Judah made Uzziah king at sixteen in place of Amaziah; he was of Judah, and he did right and sought God in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the visions of God; as long as he sought the Lord, God made him prosper (2 Chronicles 26:1-5). Uzziah is like Joash, who did well while he had the guidance of Jehoiada and then dropped the ball. All the wise kings consulted with wise and spiritual men; David consulted with every leader (1 Chronicles 13:1), and by wise counsel you make your war (Proverbs 24:5-6). Prosperity comes from the Most High, and it lasts only as long as a man keeps seeking him.

He broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod and built cities among the Philistines (2 Chronicles 26:6). He was not conquering other people’s land: the borders of the Philistines were the land that yet remained, which the Lord gave to our forefathers from the time of leaving Egypt (Joshua 13:2-3). Edom and Libnah had revolted under Jehoram because he forsook the Lord, and that is why Uzziah had to build Elath and restore it to Judah (2 Chronicles 21:10; 2 Chronicles 26:2). Under Jehoram the Most High stirred up the Arabians against us because he was not keeping the laws; Uzziah kept God’s laws, and the Most High helped him against the Philistines, the Arabians and the Mehunims, and the Ammonites, the so-called Japanese, gave him gifts, and his name spread to the entering in of Egypt (2 Chronicles 26:7-8).

He built towers, dug wells for his much cattle and loved husbandry, a picture of the blessings of Deuteronomy 28 as the Lord made the land fruitful. His army numbered three hundred and seven thousand five hundred, with shields, spears, helmets and slings, and engines invented by cunning men to shoot arrows and great stones; he was marvellously helped till he was strong (2 Chronicles 26:9-15). The strength, the army, the wealth and even the ingenuity of his engineers were a gift. Together with Jeroboam II in the north, the two kingdoms held borders close to those of David and Solomon; the Lord was giving his people another chance to get it right before he began to unleash judgments.

But when he was strong his heart was lifted up to his destruction, and he went into the temple to burn incense on the altar of incense (2 Chronicles 26:16). He was not thinking that the Most High was doing this thing; he thought he himself was doing it, and he got big-headed, a Judahite acting like a Levite. The beginning of pride is when one departs from God (Ecclesiasticus 10:12), and success can test your character as much as hardship. The king was to write a copy of the law and read it all the days of his life, so that his heart would not be lifted up above his brethren (Deuteronomy 17:18-20); the greater you are, the more you should humble yourself (Ecclesiasticus 3:18). Only the seed of Aaron could offer incense, lest a man end like Korah (Numbers 16:40); the priesthood was given to Aaron and his sons as a gift, and the stranger who came near was to be put to death, so the office was never the king’s to seize (Numbers 18:7).

Azariah the priest and eighty valiant priests withstood him and told him it did not belong to him, to go out of the sanctuary, for he had trespassed and it would not be for his honour. Then Uzziah was wroth, with a censer in his hand (2 Chronicles 26:17-19). He had beaten nation after nation, and he would not be corrected by men he counted of lower degree than himself; with the censer in his hand he was ready to set fire to the priests of God. Nobody could tell him anything, and he that hateth reproof is brutish (Proverbs 12:1).
judgmentFull: While he was wroth with the priests, the leprosy rose up in his forehead before them beside the incense altar, instant judgment in the midst of the correction. The priests saw it and thrust him out, and he hasted to go out himself, because the Lord had smitten him (2 Chronicles 26:19-20). He that is soon angry deals foolishly, and he that is hasty of spirit exalts folly (Proverbs 14:17, 29); one act out of a quick temper cost him a lifetime. The fear of the Lord goes before the obtaining of authority, but roughness and pride is the losing thereof, and the Lord brought strange calamities on the proud and overthrew them (Ecclesiasticus 10:13, 21).

He was a leper to the day of his death and dwelt in a several house, cut off from the house of the Lord, and Jotham his son was over the king’s house, judging the people (2 Chronicles 26:21). The law said the leper must dwell alone outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46); he was still king in name but could no longer sit on the throne, deposed because of his pride, and leprosy is not merely white skin but a slow deterioration of the whole body. The Lord puts down the mighty from their seats (Luke 1:52). Isaiah wrote the rest of his acts, and they buried him in the field of burial belonging to the kings, for they said he was a leper (2 Chronicles 26:22-23). When Uzziah stayed with the Most High he prospered, and when he departed and went contrary to the laws of God, the Most High made an example of him. Stay in the spirit, stay humble, and never forget who put you in the position you are in.

cases.name: Jotham
cases.charge: Preparing his ways before the Lord his God; doing right according to all that his father Uzziah did, howbeit he entered not into the temple of the Lord
cases.summary: Jotham, son of Uzziah, reigned sixteen years and did right as his father had done, but he did not go into the temple as his father had; the people still did corruptly (2 Chronicles 27:1-2). He built the high gate of the house of the Lord, cities, castles and towers, and put the Ammonites under tribute (2 Chronicles 27:3-5). He became mighty because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God (2 Chronicles 27:6).
offenseFull: Jotham judged the people from the king’s house while his father dwelt as a leper in a separate house, so the last good years counted to Uzziah were really his son reigning in his place; the son’s years are not counted until the father passes (2 Chronicles 26:21; 2 Kings 15:5). He was twenty-five when he began to reign and reigned sixteen years; he did right according to all his father Uzziah did, except that he did not enter the temple of the Lord (2 Chronicles 27:1-2). He was like his father, industrious and a builder, a warrior who served God, but he did not make his father’s mistake of going in to burn incense as though he were a Levitical priest.

Yet the people still did corruptly (2 Chronicles 27:2). Even though Jotham was upright, that does not mean the people also were; the high places were not removed, and the people still sacrificed and burned incense there (2 Kings 15:35). After Solomon’s reign the land was never the same in terms of the pollution of idols, and Uzziah and Jotham, though they kept the commandments, were not able to purge the idolatry completely out of Judah.

Micah began to prophesy in the days of Jotham, and this is the corruption that was taking place: they built up Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity, the heads judged for reward, the priests taught for hire, the prophets divined for money, and still they leaned on the Lord and said no evil could come on them; therefore Zion would be ploughed as a field (Micah 1:1; Micah 3:10-12). Her princes were like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood and get dishonest gain (Ezekiel 22:27). It was a hypocritical nation, as you see today, and Micah, like Hosea and Amos before the Assyrians came, prophesied long before Babylon that Jerusalem would become heaps. Just because the king had it under control in Jerusalem, the corruption still went on in the lower courts, the inner city and the whole realm.

He built the high gate of the house of the Lord and much on the wall of Ophel, and cities in the mountains of Judah, and castles and towers in the forests (2 Chronicles 27:3-4). He cut down the forests and made towns, building and expanding like his father. He fought the king of the Ammonites and prevailed, and they paid him a hundred talents of silver and ten thousand measures each of wheat and barley that year and the next two, so he put Ammon in subjection as his father had done, putting the heathen under tribute (2 Chronicles 27:5).
judgmentFull: So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God (2 Chronicles 27:6). That is what Ezra did when he prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments (Ezra 7:10), and that is how Jotham became mighty and why he had favour during his reign. The Most High was with our forefathers when they followed the commandments. He finished much of what his father started, furthering the campaign of Judah to re-establish its borders and fortifying the land against the enemies who would rise up. In the days of Uzziah and Jotham, Judah for the most part still ruled with God and was faithful with the saints (Hosea 11:12; Isaiah 1:1).

In those days, towards the end of Jotham’s reign, the Lord began to send Rezin king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah against Judah (2 Kings 15:37). Syria had been the northern kingdom’s oppressor, and now the two were teaming up against Judah; it began in the days of Jotham and was accentuated in the days of Ahaz. Jotham slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, and Ahaz his son reigned in his place (2 Chronicles 27:7-9). Uzziah and Jotham were doing good and making progress for Judah in the spiritual aspect, and the Lord was blessing them; then Ahaz came on the scene and took them five steps back.

cases.name: Ahaz
cases.charge: Molten images for Baalim; burning his children in the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom; not believing the Lord by Isaiah but hiring Assyria with the treasure of the Lord’s house; sacrificing to the gods of Damascus that smote him; cutting the vessels in pieces and shutting up the doors of the house of the Lord
cases.summary: Ahaz son of Jotham walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, made molten images for Baalim and burned his children in the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom (2 Chronicles 28:1-4). The Lord gave him into the hands of Syria and of Pekah, and instead of believing Isaiah he sent the Lord’s treasure to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria, who distressed him and did not help him (2 Chronicles 28:5-21). In his distress he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, cut up the vessels of God’s house, shut its doors and set up altars in every corner of Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 28:22-25).
offenseFull: Ahaz was twenty when he began to reign and did not do right like David his father, but walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and made molten images for Baalim (2 Chronicles 28:1-2). The northern kingdom had an influence on the southern; he was enticed by its way of life and went that route instead of serving the Lord. His grandfather and father had Judah making progress, and he came on the scene and set them five steps back. He burned incense in the valley of the son of Hinnom and made his son pass through the fire, after the abominations of the heathen the Lord had cast out (2 Chronicles 28:3; 2 Kings 16:3). This was witchcraft and child sacrifice, the practice called Tophet. Hinnom was a place of burning south of Jerusalem, where children were sacrificed to Molech; its Greek name, Gehenna, became the word for hell. The Lord commanded it not, neither came it into his heart, and it points to the abortions of today (Jeremiah 7:31).

The Canaanites were cast out for their witchcraft, wicked sacrifices and merciless murders of children (Wisdom of Solomon 12:3-6), and Ahaz did the very thing that got them evicted. Israel did not destroy those nations but mingled among them, learned their works and sacrificed their sons and daughters unto devils (Psalm 106:34-38); Baalim means devils. Baal was worshipped as the sun and storm god who gave power, crops and children, with ritual prostitution and the sacrifice of the firstborn: wealth and power for a sacrifice, and it sounds familiar today.

When Rezin of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah came against Jerusalem to set up a pretender, the son of Tabeal, they could not overcome him, for the Lord had his oath with David; within sixty-five years Ephraim would be broken, but if Ahaz would not believe, he would not be established (2 Kings 16:5; Isaiah 7:1-9). He did not believe the Lord; he believed the king of Assyria. He sent to Tiglath-pileser saying he was his servant and his son, and asked him to save him (2 Kings 16:7). That is the same mind as our people today, who want the white man who enslaved them to save them. Isaiah pronounced woe on the rebellious children who take counsel but not of the Lord and cover with a covering but not of his spirit, adding sin to sin (Isaiah 30:1). He took the silver and gold of the house of the Lord and sent it as a present (2 Kings 16:8). At Damascus he saw a heathen altar that captivated him and had Urijah the priest build one on its pattern to supersede the altar the Lord had designed, meddling with the divine pattern according to human taste (2 Kings 16:10-16).

In the time of his distress he trespassed yet more: he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that smote him, reasoning that since the gods of the kings of Syria helped them, they would help him; but they were the ruin of him and of all Israel (2 Chronicles 28:22-23). Why not serve your own God? He cut the vessels of the house of God in pieces, shut up the doors of the house of the Lord, made altars in every corner of Jerusalem and high places in every city of Judah (2 Chronicles 28:24-25). This is the pattern of running to a nation that cannot save, the same spirit that trusts in the systems of the world instead of the Most High.
judgmentFull: The Lord delivered him to the king of Syria, who carried a great multitude captive to Damascus, and to the king of Israel: Pekah slew a hundred and twenty thousand valiant men of Judah in one day because they had forsaken the Lord, and Israel carried away two hundred thousand of their brethren, women and children, to Samaria (2 Chronicles 28:5-8). It was brother against brother, one nation of Israel taking the other captive.

The prophet Oded met the army and told them they had slain their brethren in a rage that reached up to heaven and now meant to keep them as bondmen, adding to their own sins; the heads of Ephraim agreed, and they clothed the naked, fed and anointed the captives, carried the feeble on asses and brought them to Jericho (2 Chronicles 28:9-15). A man who steals his brother and sells him shall die, and the Lord’s servants shall not be sold as bondmen (Deuteronomy 24:7; Leviticus 25:39-42); even in the division these men feared the Most High. Esau is the sword of God, but because of his perpetual hatred he goes beyond the judgment permitted (Ezekiel 35:5); in the transatlantic slave trade the Hamites sold us, and here Israel tried to enslave its own brethren, and the Lord sent the prophet to stop it.

The Edomites smote Judah and the Philistines took the cities of the low country, for the Lord brought Judah low because of Ahaz, who made Judah naked; that nakedness is sin, as Jerusalem grievously sinned and all that honoured her saw her nakedness (2 Chronicles 28:17-19; Lamentations 1:8). Tiglath-pileser took Damascus, carried its people to Kir and slew Rezin, as Amos had foretold (2 Kings 16:9; Amos 1:3-5), but he came to Ahaz and distressed him and strengthened him not, though Ahaz stripped the house of the Lord, the king’s house and the princes to pay him (2 Chronicles 28:20-21). Never trust your enemy: his words are smoother than butter, but war is in his heart (Psalm 55:20-21; Ecclesiasticus 12:10, 16). Running to another nation for deliverance from the curses of God never works, then or now, and Isaiah warned that the Assyrian would overflow Judah up to the neck (Isaiah 8:6-8).

This history shows why we went into captivity: despite every warning of the prophets, we begged the Most High to send us there. Ahaz was buried in Jerusalem but not in the sepulchres of the kings, and Hezekiah his son reigned (2 Chronicles 28:27). The Most High is the only one who can bring the people out of their condition, then and now.

cases.name: Josiah at Megiddo
cases.charge: Meddling in a battle that did not concern him: going out against Necho king of Egypt, hearkening not to the words of Necho from the mouth of God, and disguising himself to fight at Megiddo
cases.summary: After his great passover, Josiah went out against Necho king of Egypt, who was going up to fight at Carchemish by Euphrates and sent word that his war was not with Josiah and that God had commanded him to make haste (2 Chronicles 35:20-21). Josiah would not turn his face, disguised himself to fight, hearkened not to the words of Necho from the mouth of God, and the archers shot him in the valley of Megiddo; he died in Jerusalem, and all Judah mourned him (2 Chronicles 35:22-25). He got involved in a matter that did not concern him and lost his life in it.
offenseFull: Josiah kept the passover on the fourteenth day of the first month, keeping the laws pertaining to the passover, and there was no passover like it from the days of Samuel the prophet (2 Chronicles 35:1, 18); his works were upright before his Lord with a heart full of godliness (1 Esdras 1:23). Once he completed his purge of the evils out of the land, he threw a feast that surpassed Hezekiah’s. It is an example of the beauty of order being established, and that there is nothing impossible with unity and righteousness: even after all the evil we have done and all we have suffered, it is possible to be restored to the standard of our forefathers. The same history gives the other example: you can get too high minded; you can know all the precepts and be righteous, and you still need to mind your God-given business, for if you do not, it is a dangerous game.

In 612 BC the Babylonians and Medes captured Nineveh, and the Assyrians moved their capital to Haran; when Haran fell in 609 BC the remnant of the Assyrian army joined Carchemish, a city under Egyptian rule on the Euphrates, and Pharaoh Necho marched to their aid against the Babylonians, passing through the kingdom of Judah on the way (2 Kings 23:29). Josiah went out against him (2 Chronicles 35:20). Necho sent ambassadors that he had not come against Josiah but against the house he was at war with, for God had commanded him to make haste, and that Josiah should forbear from meddling with God, lest God destroy him (2 Chronicles 35:21).

The Lord is not restricted in whom he deals with: he spoke through a donkey in the book of Numbers and through Balaam, and Pharaoh Necho knew the Lord had come to him and commanded him to go and fight at Carchemish. That does not mean the Lord wanted him to defeat Babylon, for the Lord had foreshadowed in the time of Hezekiah that Babylon would take Judah captive (Isaiah 39:5-7). The battle was already prophesied: the Lord wanted Egypt to go up so that he could destroy Egypt, and Nebuchadnezzar smote Pharaoh Necho at Carchemish in the fourth year of Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 46:2). Pharaoh was letting Josiah know, as an Israelite brother, to fall back, for this had nothing to do with him. In Josiah’s eyes he was standing up against possible Egyptian oppression.

Josiah would not turn his face, but disguised himself to fight, and hearkened not to the words of Necho from the mouth of God (2 Chronicles 35:22); he did not regard the words of the prophet Jeremiah spoken by the mouth of the Lord (1 Esdras 1:28). Strive not in a matter that concerns you not, and meddle not with many matters, for the one who meddles much will not escape being hurt (Ecclesiasticus 11:9-10). That is why it is best to mind your business: when you get caught up in what does not concern you, you will not be able to get yourself out of it. The one who meddles with strife not belonging to him is like one who takes a dog by the ears (Proverbs 26:17): grab a German Shepherd or a pit bull by the ears and you will be torn up. Among the spirits created for vengeance are the teeth of wild beasts, and the one who meddles incurs the wrath of that spirit (Ecclesiasticus 39:28-30).
judgmentFull: Josiah went out to the battle in disguise, and the archers shot at king Josiah, and he told his servants to have him away, for he was sore wounded (2 Chronicles 35:23). Many miscellaneous people get shot in a battle, but the scripture says the archers shot at king Josiah: the Lord put the spirit on the archers to discern which one was the king, spot him, and shoot him, because he was meddling with God. His servants put him in his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem, where he died and was buried in the sepulchres of his fathers; the people of the land took Jehoahaz his son and made him king (2 Chronicles 35:24; 2 Kings 23:30).

Megiddo, from ancient Canaanite roots, is a place of troops, and Armageddon comes from Har Megiddo (Revelation 16:16). It was not Josiah’s fault that Egypt did not reach Carchemish in time to defeat Babylon; the Lord set it up, just as he will set up World War III and gather all nations in that same place, Megiddo, which is Armageddon, the valley of decision. The battle of Carchemish is historically documented; the Bible is real.

All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah, Jeremiah lamented for him, and the singing men and women spoke of him in their lamentations and made them an ordinance in Israel (2 Chronicles 35:24-25). Jeremiah and Josiah were contemporaries: the time of Josiah’s reform matched the time the Lord put the spirit on Jeremiah to prophesy, around 620 BC, and Jeremiah lamented because he knew the evil the Lord had put the spirit on him to prophesy was coming. Because Josiah’s heart was tender and he humbled himself before the Most High, he was gathered to his grave in peace, and his eyes did not see the evil to come (2 Kings 22:19-20).

Josiah meddled in a matter that did not belong to him, but he never went after another god and never took part in evil, and he left a very good example. Virtue leaves a memorial that is immortal: when it is present men take example from it, and when it is gone they desire it (Wisdom of Solomon 4:1-2). Josiah had virtue and accomplished what many kings were never able to accomplish, and when he was gone it was a heartbreak for the entire nation, so that they made it an ordinance to mourn him. He is among the famous men whose bodies are buried in peace and whose name lives for evermore (Ecclesiasticus 44:1-15). His ending was tragic, but his righteous legacy supersedes it, just as with King David, who had great transgressions. His death opened Judah’s last years: the king of Egypt put down Jehoahaz after three months and made Eliakim king, turning his name to Jehoiakim (2 Chronicles 36:2-4).

cases.offense: Josiah kept the passover on the fourteenth day of the first month, keeping the laws pertaining to the passover, and there was no passover like it from the days of Samuel the prophet (2 Chronicles 35:1, 18); his works were upright before his Lord with a heart full of godliness (1 Esdras 1:23). Once he completed his purge of the evils out of the land, he threw a feast that surpassed Hezekiah’s. It is an example of the beauty of order being established, and that there is nothing impossible with unity and righteousness: even after all the evil we have done and all we have suffered, it is possible to be restored to the standard of our forefathers. The same history gives the other example: you can get too high minded; you can know all the precepts and be righteous, and you still need to mind your God-given business, for if you do not, it is a dangerous game.
cases.judgment: Josiah went out to the battle in disguise, and the archers shot at king Josiah, and he told his servants to have him away, for he was sore wounded (2 Chronicles 35:23). Many miscellaneous people get shot in a battle, but the scripture says the archers shot at king Josiah: the Lord put the spirit on the archers to discern which one was the king, spot him, and shoot him, because he was meddling with God. His servants put him in his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem, where he died and was buried in the sepulchres of his fathers; the people of the land took Jehoahaz his son and made him king (2 Chronicles 35:24; 2 Kings 23:30).

cases.name: Zedekiah
cases.charge: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord; humbling not himself before Jeremiah the prophet speaking from the mouth of the Lord; breaking the oath Nebuchadnezzar made him swear by God and rebelling against the king of Babylon, and so against the Lord; stiffening his neck and hardening his heart
cases.summary: The king of Babylon made Mattaniah king, changed his name to Zedekiah, and took an oath of him; Zedekiah did evil, did not humble himself before Jeremiah speaking from the mouth of the Lord, and in his ninth year rebelled, sending ambassadors into Egypt for horses and much people (2 Chronicles 36:11-13; Ezekiel 17:12-15). Jeremiah told him that if he went forth to the king of Babylon’s princes his soul would live and the city would not be burned, but he was afraid of the Jews who had fallen to the Chaldeans (Jeremiah 38:17-19). After a two-year siege he fled by night, was overtaken in the plains of Jericho, saw his sons slain before his eyes, and was blinded and carried in chains to Babylon, where he was in prison till the day of his death (2 Kings 25:1-7; Jeremiah 52:11).
offenseFull: The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s father’s brother, king and changed his name to Zedekiah; he reigned eleven years and did evil according to all Jehoiakim had done, and through the anger of the Lord he rebelled against the king of Babylon (2 Kings 24:17-20). Mattaniah means gift of God, and Zedekiah means righteousness of God. Though a son of Josiah, he was not heir to the throne: Babylon took the mighty men out of the land so that Judah was no threat, and set him up as a puppet king, a weak and cowardly king, to keep Judah in subjection. His rebellion in the ninth year was to fulfil the judgment the Lord had pronounced against us.

Early in his reign false prophets such as Hananiah told the captives in Babylon that the Lord would soon bring Jehoiachin and the captivity back; that was a false hope. Jeremiah said seventy years (Jeremiah 28:1-4; Jeremiah 29:10). Those carried captive with Jehoiachin were the good figs, whom the Lord would put through the seventy years and bring back; those left in the land with Zedekiah were the evil figs, the vile figs that cannot be eaten, on whom the Lord would send the sword, the famine and the pestilence (Jeremiah 24:5-8; Jeremiah 29:17-18).

The king of Babylon took the king’s seed, made a covenant with him and took an oath of him, that the kingdom might be base and not lift itself up, but by keeping the covenant might stand (Ezekiel 17:12-14). If Zedekiah stayed in the covenant, they could stay in the land under the yoke. Jeremiah told him to bring his neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and live: why die by the sword, the famine and the pestilence (Jeremiah 27:12-13)? But he rebelled, sending his ambassadors into Egypt, and because he despised the oath and broke the covenant after giving his hand, he would die in the midst of Babylon, and Pharaoh’s army would not help him (Ezekiel 17:15-18). The covenant was of the Lord, to preserve the remnant; when Zedekiah rebelled he was not really rebelling against Nebuchadnezzar, he was rebelling against the Lord.

Neither he nor his servants nor the people hearkened to the words of the Lord by Jeremiah, yet he sent to the prophet to pray for them (Jeremiah 37:1-3). When Pharaoh’s army came forth and the Chaldeans departed, that emboldened him; Jeremiah told him the Chaldeans would return, take the city and burn it (Jeremiah 37:5-10). The princes smote Jeremiah and put him in prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe, and later demanded his death; Zedekiah said the king could do nothing against them, for he was a weakling and a coward (Jeremiah 37:15; Jeremiah 38:4-5). Secretly he sent for Jeremiah, as though the word might have changed, and got the same word: go forth to the king of Babylon’s princes and your soul shall live; refuse, and you shall cause this city to be burned with fire. He answered that he was afraid of the Jews who had fallen to the Chaldeans, lest they mock him (Jeremiah 38:14-23). He was operating under peer pressure: you give people the solution from the Lord, they act as though they want your help, and there is always a rebuttal. He kept Jeremiah in the court of the prison until the day Jerusalem was taken (Jeremiah 38:28; Jeremiah 32:1-5).
judgmentFull: Ezekiel, dwelling in the midst of a rebellious house, removed his stuff by day and dug through the wall in the twilight as a sign: the burden concerned the prince in Jerusalem, King Zedekiah, who would try to escape and disguise himself; the Lord would spread his net upon him and bring him to Babylon, yet he would not see it, though he would die there (Ezekiel 12:1-13). In the ninth year, the tenth month, the tenth day, the word came to Ezekiel to write the name of the day, the same day the king of Babylon set himself against Jerusalem (Ezekiel 24:1-2; 2 Kings 25:1). The city was besieged two years, until Zedekiah’s eleventh year, and the famine prevailed (2 Kings 25:2-3). The house of Israel had become dross, and the Lord would gather them into the midst of Jerusalem as metal into a furnace and melt them in his fury (Ezekiel 22:17-22).

When the city was broken up, Zedekiah and the men of war fled by night by the way of the king’s garden, through the gate between the two walls; he knew he had brought this destruction on the land, and he ran to leave everyone in Jerusalem to be burned. The Chaldean army overtook him in the plains of Jericho, and at Riblah the king of Babylon slew his sons and all the nobles of Judah before his eyes, then put out his eyes and bound him with chains to carry him to Babylon (Jeremiah 39:4-7). The last thing Zedekiah saw was his own sons being killed, and it was all his own fault; that is how he was brought to Babylon and did not see it, just as Jeremiah had warned him. The king of Babylon put him in prison till the day of his death (Jeremiah 52:11). We cannot play with the Lord.

The Chaldeans burned the king’s house and the houses of the people and broke down the walls of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 39:8). Esau played a very heavy part in it: the Edomites cut off those who escaped, delivered up the remnant to Nebuchadnezzar, cheered Babylon on, and burned the temple when Judea was made desolate, and they took Israelite land when Babylon took Israel captive (Obadiah 1:14; 1 Esdras 4:45, 50).

The crown is fallen from our head: that was the last king, and no more king sat on the throne (Lamentations 5:16). This is the curse of Deuteronomy, that the Lord would bring Israel and the king set over them to a nation they had not known, and it happened again and again (Deuteronomy 28:36). The Most High had set before them the way of life and the way of death: he that stayed in the city died by the sword, famine and pestilence, and he that went out to the Chaldeans lived (Jeremiah 21:8-9). He marred the pride of Judah, an evil people who refused to hear his words, and his soul wept in secret places because the flock was carried away captive (Jeremiah 13:9-10, 17).

cases.name: The captivity of Judah
cases.charge: All the chief of the priests and the people transgressing very much after all the abominations of the heathen and polluting the house of the Lord; mocking the messengers of God, despising his words, and misusing his prophets till there was no remedy; the sabbaths of the land not kept
cases.summary: The chief of the priests and the people followed all the abominations of the heathen and polluted the house of the Lord; the Most High sent his messengers, rising up early, because he had compassion, but they mocked the messengers, despised his words and misused his prophets until the wrath of the Lord arose and there was no remedy (2 Chronicles 36:14-16). The king of the Chaldees slew young and old in the sanctuary, carried the treasures to Babylon, burned the house of God and broke down the walls, exactly the fierce nation the curses warned of (2 Chronicles 36:17-19). Those who escaped the sword served Babylon until Persia, while the land enjoyed her sabbaths seventy years, as Jeremiah said (2 Chronicles 36:20-21).
offenseFull: All the chief of the priests and the people transgressed very much after all the abominations of the heathen and polluted the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 36:14). The Lord God of their fathers sent to them by his messengers, rising up early and sending, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place: because he loved them, he sent them messengers so they could repent. But they mocked the messengers of God, despised his words and misused his prophets until the wrath of the Lord arose against his people, till there was no remedy (2 Chronicles 36:15-16). When judgment comes, then they want help; but there is no help then: you make your bed and you sleep in it.

Christ was mocked, and before him the prophets were mocked; it is nothing new. To minimize the movement because it is being mocked is a self-inflicted wound; it means you never really believed. They cast out your name as evil and call you a cult, but in like manner did their fathers to the prophets: what happens to us today happened to our prophets yesterday (Luke 6:22-23).

For twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of Josiah, the Most High had risen early and spoken by Jeremiah and sent all his servants the prophets, and the people would not hearken nor turn from their evil ways and their other gods (Jeremiah 25:1-7). Ezekiel named every rank. The priests violated his law and profaned his holy things, putting no difference between the holy and the profane, the clean and the unclean, and hid their eyes from his sabbaths, just as today our people put no difference between anything, and it is called Christianity. The princes were like wolves ravening the prey for dishonest gain; the prophets daubed them with untempered mortar, saying the Lord God had spoken when he had not; the people used oppression and robbery and vexed the poor and the stranger; and the Lord sought a man to stand in the gap before him so he would not destroy the land, and found none (Ezekiel 22:26-30).

The land was to rest every seventh year, as Israel rests on the seventh day, a sabbath unto the Lord; letting the land rest is harmony and balance on the earth (Leviticus 25:3-4). The sabbaths were not kept: no keeping of the weekly sabbath, and no rest for the land every seven years, none of it. The Lord had said that if they would not hearken, the land would enjoy her sabbaths as long as it lay desolate and they were in their enemies’ land (Leviticus 26:34-35). The land could not rest while the people dwelt on it doing evil, so he rid the people out of the land, that the land could enjoy her sabbaths while it lay desolate without them.
judgmentFull: The Most High brought upon them the king of the Chaldees, who slew their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary and had no compassion on young man or maiden, old man or him that stooped for age; the vessels of the house of God, great and small, and the treasures of the Lord’s house, of the king and of his princes went to Babylon; and they burned the house of God, broke down the walls of Jerusalem, burned its palaces and destroyed all the goodly vessels (2 Chronicles 36:17-19). That is exactly the fierce nation the curses warned of, which would not regard the old nor show favour to the young (Deuteronomy 28:49-50). The power of the earth is in the hand of the Most High, and in due time he sets over it one that is profitable (Ecclesiasticus 10:4). When Israel will not rule in righteousness, he raises a Nebuchadnezzar; Israel’s purpose was never to be wicked and rule at the same time.

With the temple destroyed, what could no longer take place? Sacrifice. The prophet Jeremiah called Israel a homeborn slave: from captivity to captivity there was no atonement to be had, and that is exactly why we needed a saviour, an ultimate sacrifice (Jeremiah 2:14).

Those who escaped the sword were carried away to Babylon, servants to Nebuchadnezzar and his sons until the reign of the kingdom of Persia, to fulfil the word of the Lord by the mouth of Jeremiah, that the land would enjoy her sabbaths and lie desolate threescore and ten years (2 Chronicles 36:20-21). These nations were to serve the king of Babylon seventy years, and when the seventy years were accomplished the Most High would punish the king of Babylon and that nation for their iniquity (Jeremiah 25:11-12). Even though he may take us down with one kingdom, he then takes that kingdom and punishes it with a new kingdom; the Most High uses people: he used Nebuchadnezzar, he used Cyrus, some of it for our good and some for our punishment.

When the people repent and turn back, confessing the iniquity of their fathers and their own trespass, the Most High remembers his covenant with Jacob, with Isaac and with Abraham, passed down to the children of Israel, and he remembers the land (Leviticus 26:40-42). The Israelites are not done away: he promised not to destroy the seed of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and that promise carries into the future. In the first year of Cyrus the Most High stirred up his spirit to proclaim that any of the Lord’s people could go up, showing again that the Most High sets over the earth one that is profitable for his purpose (2 Chronicles 36:22-23).

Jeremiah was told he would discontinue from his heritage and serve his enemies in a land he knew not (Jeremiah 17:4). Jeremiah never forgot who he was; he stood stiffly for the Lord, and when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem he was let go free and taught the people left in the land; the Babylonians did not take him into Babylon as a slave, and he knew nothing about the United States of America. So it speaks of Jeremiah coming back in the future: Jeremiah is here in the last days, serving his enemies in the land of his captivity, and he will remember who he is, that he is an Israelite, his God and his land.
