cases.name: Nineveh under Jonah
cases.charge: Wickedness come up before the Lord; and turning every one from his evil way, and from the violence that was in their hands
cases.summary: Jonah was sent to cry against Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrians, because its wickedness had come up before the Lord; after fleeing and being brought back out of the belly of the fish, he went in and cried that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown (Jonah 1:1-2; Jonah 3:1-4). The people believed God and fasted in sackcloth, and the king decreed that every one turn from his evil way and from the violence in his hands (Jonah 3:5-9). God saw their works and did not bring the evil he had spoken, for it was not yet time to destroy them, and when Jonah was angry he answered that he would spare that great city (Jonah 3:10; Jonah 4:1-11). The word against the city still stood, and Nineveh fell as Jonah prophesied (Tobit 14:4, 15).
offenseFull: Jonah the son of Amittai is the same Jonah by whose hand the Lord spoke the restoring of the coast of Israel under Jeroboam, and he was around the same time as Hosea and Amos (2 Kings 14:25). The word came to him to arise and go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it, for their wickedness had come up before the Lord (Jonah 1:1-2). Nineveh is the capital of the Assyrians: Sennacherib returned and dwelt there after the angel smote his camp (2 Kings 19:36). The Most High wanted to destroy Nineveh for its wickedness, so he called Jonah to cry against it.

The Ninevites to whom Jonah was a sign were not the Assyrians, as Christians read it (Luke 11:29-30). Tobit, of the tribe of Naphtali, one of the ten tribes of the northern kingdom, was led captive in the time of Enemessar king of the Assyrians and walked in truth among his brethren and his nation who came with him to Nineveh (Tobit 1:1-3). Jonah prophesied against the city of Nineveh in judgment upon that heathen nation, and it fell as he prophesied; but in regard to repentance, so that they would not perish with Nineveh, he preached to the Israelite captives in Nineveh, the northern kingdom, so they could repent before it was too late. Repentance was always for Israel only (2 Esdras 3:32-36).

Jonah rose up to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord; the Lord gave him a strict command, and Jonah chose to flee, refusing to hearken, because he was afraid of the people in Nineveh (Jonah 1:3). When the ship was taking on water and the men were frantically trying to save themselves, Jonah was fast asleep in the sides of the ship (Jonah 1:5). When the lot fell on him he confessed that he was a Hebrew who feared the Lord and told them to cast him into the sea (Jonah 1:7-12). That is accountability and integrity: we can trouble the nation of Israel and our camps when we are in the midst of our secret sins, as Achan troubled the camp with the accursed thing (Joshua 7:1). The fear came upon the mariners when Jonah acknowledged his sin before his God, and they feared the Lord, knowing there is only one true living God, the God of Israel (Jonah 1:14-16).

In the fish’s belly Jonah, who at the beginning was trying to flee from the Lord, was seeking the Lord: in their affliction they will seek him early, and that is true of the Israelites to this day (Jonah 2:1-9; Hosea 5:15). They that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy: our people were in Nineveh observing lying vanities, just as our people observe them today in Babylon, in America (Jonah 2:8). His going down to the bottoms of the mountains and being brought up from corruption goes into Christ (Psalms 16:10), and as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly, so the Son of man would be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matthew 12:39-40).

The word came the second time to preach the preaching the Lord bade him, and now Jonah was simply obedient (Jonah 3:1-2). Nineveh was a city of three days’ journey; he entered a day’s journey and cried that in forty days it would be overthrown (Jonah 3:3-4). The king’s decree named what had to change: the evil way and the violence in their hands (Jonah 3:8). The prophets of that same time named it in Israel: swearing, lying, killing, stealing and committing adultery until blood touched blood, and the same spirit was in Samaria and in Nineveh; wherever Israel was, there was great wickedness, just as it is today (Hosea 4:1-2; Amos 2:6-8).
judgmentFull: The people of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth from the greatest to the least; the king rose from his throne, laid aside his robe, sat in ashes, and decreed that neither man nor beast taste anything nor drink water, but cry mightily to God and turn from their evil way and their violence (Jonah 3:5-8). That is how we know what a true fast is: not restraining oneself from a certain food, nor a water fast, which is a diet; a fast is when you do not eat or drink anything. Jonah’s boldness and courage caused even the king to fear and to fast and pray that the destruction would not come near Nineveh, and that is the courage we must have in teaching this truth.

They did not presume on God: who could tell whether he would turn from his fierce anger (Jonah 3:9)? Judith warned the elders of Bethulia not to bind the counsels of the Lord to their own five days (Judith 8:12-16). We cry to the Lord and make supplication, and in this case they fasted, but we do not tell the Lord what to do. God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way, and he repented of the evil he had said he would do, and did it not, because it was not time to destroy them (Jonah 3:10).

It displeased Jonah exceedingly, for he knew the Lord was gracious, merciful, slow to anger and of great kindness (Jonah 4:1-2). He had gone in on fire, and now he felt the people would see him as a false prophet and a liar, and twice he asked the Lord to take his life (Jonah 4:3, 8). He was vexed and in despair, the one to whom death is acceptable (Ecclesiasticus 41:1-2). The Lord answered with the gourd: Jonah had pity on a plant he did not labour for, and should not the Lord spare Nineveh, with more than sixscore thousand persons that could not discern their right hand from their left, and much cattle (Jonah 4:9-11)? His spirit was not right. We cannot comprehend the Lord’s thoughts or why he does what he does; we must obey and trust in him (Isaiah 55:8-9). The Lord can repent of his thoughts to destroy us; that is his choice (Zechariah 8:14-15). Jonah was angry because of the way it made him look, but when we preach the word, we do not preach it for our own glory; we preach it so that God gets the glory.

The reprieve did not end the word against Nineveh. Tobit told his son to go into Media and depart out of Nineveh, for he surely believed the things which Jonas the prophet spoke of Nineveh, that it would be overthrown; and before he died he heard of the destruction of Nineveh and rejoiced over it (Tobit 14:4, 8, 15). His son followed his advice and was saved: we must always follow the advice of our elders and our fathers who keep God’s laws. The men of Nineveh, the Israelites in Nineveh who repented at the preaching of Jonas, will rise in the judgment and condemn that evil generation which had a greater than Jonas before them and would not hear (Matthew 12:41).

cases.offense: Jonah the son of Amittai is the same Jonah by whose hand the Lord spoke the restoring of the coast of Israel under Jeroboam, and he was around the same time as Hosea and Amos (2 Kings 14:25). The word came to him to arise and go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it, for their wickedness had come up before the Lord (Jonah 1:1-2). Nineveh is the capital of the Assyrians: Sennacherib returned and dwelt there after the angel smote his camp (2 Kings 19:36). The Most High wanted to destroy Nineveh for its wickedness, so he called Jonah to cry against it.
cases.judgment: The people of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth from the greatest to the least; the king rose from his throne, laid aside his robe, sat in ashes, and decreed that neither man nor beast taste anything nor drink water, but cry mightily to God and turn from their evil way and their violence (Jonah 3:5-8). That is how we know what a true fast is: not restraining oneself from a certain food, nor a water fast, which is a diet; a fast is when you do not eat or drink anything. Jonah’s boldness and courage caused even the king to fear and to fast and pray that the destruction would not come near Nineveh, and that is the courage we must have in teaching this truth.

cases.name: Jeremiah
cases.charge: Known and ordained a prophet before he was formed in the belly; not afraid of their faces: speaking all that was commanded, though the word was a burning fire shut up in his bones and his own familiars watched for his halting
cases.summary: Jeremiah, a Levite of the priests in Anathoth, was known and ordained a prophet unto the nations before he was formed in the belly, and he prophesied from the days of Josiah to the carrying away of Jerusalem, about forty years, from about 627 to 586 BC (Jeremiah 1:1-5). Told not to plead his youth nor fear their faces, he spoke against kings, princes, priests and people through the stocks, the burned roll and the miry dungeon (Jeremiah 20:1-2; Jeremiah 36:23; Jeremiah 38:6). The Most High made him a defenced city against the whole land: they fought against him and did not prevail, and when the city fell the enemy looked well to him and set him free (Jeremiah 1:18-19; Jeremiah 39:11-12; Jeremiah 40:1-6).
offenseFull: Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, of the priests in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, a Levite city, and one of the mightiest prophets in the scriptures (Jeremiah 1:1; Joshua 21:17-18). The word came to him in the thirteenth year of Josiah as Josiah began to purge the idols, and Jeremiah and Josiah worked hand in hand, the king enforcing and the prophet prophesying against the idols (Jeremiah 1:2-3; 2 Chronicles 34:3).

Before the Most High formed him in the belly he knew him, sanctified him, and ordained him a prophet unto the nations (Jeremiah 1:4-5). Before the earth was made, we were there, dwelling with the Lord; before he was placed in his mother’s womb, his assignment as one of the sons of God was to be a prophet among the nations (2 Esdras 9:18). The same is happening today: the brothers and sisters waking up were formed in the belly and known from the beginning, raised up to prophesy against the nations.

Jeremiah answered that he could not speak, for he was a child; he was about eighteen, but to be a prophet is whenever the Lord puts the spirit on you (Jeremiah 1:6). He tried to run away from it, and the Lord did not let him. The Most High told him not to say he was a child, which is to say, stop making excuses, but to go wherever he was sent and speak whatever he was commanded, and not to be afraid of their faces, for he was with him to deliver him (Jeremiah 1:7-8). He touched his mouth and put his words there, and this is why we stay within these scriptures and never go wrong; he set him over the nations and the kingdoms to root out, pull down, destroy, throw down, build and plant, which is our job today and is spiritual warfare (Jeremiah 1:9-10). He was to gird up his loins and speak all he was commanded and not be dismayed at their faces, lest he be confounded before them: we cannot go out with a spirit of fear on us (Jeremiah 1:17; 2 Timothy 1:7).

When he stood in the court of the Lord’s house and said the house would be like Shiloh, the priests, the prophets and all the people took him and said he must die (Jeremiah 26:1-11). It was about their feelings getting hurt, as people today say you cannot speak against this country when we are only saying what the Bible says. He put himself in their hand, but warned that they would bring innocent blood upon themselves (Jeremiah 26:12-16). The hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with him (Jeremiah 26:24).

Pashur the priest smote him and put him in the stocks, just for prophesying the truth (Jeremiah 20:1-2). It did not break his spirit; he came out emboldened. Mocked and reproached daily, he said he would not make mention of the Lord nor speak any more in his name, but the word was in his heart as a burning fire shut up in his bones, and he could not hold it (Jeremiah 20:7-9). Shut up in the bones means inescapable, not surface level; it is who you are, and that is how the word of God needs to be for us. His familiars watched for his halting, waiting for him to fall so they could say, gotcha; they plaster it all over social media to defame the whole organization, the same thing that was going on in Jeremiah’s time (Jeremiah 20:10). The princes let him down into the dungeon of Malchiah, where there was no water but mire, and he sank in the mire: that is dung, and it is not far fetched (Jeremiah 38:6).
judgmentFull: The promise of his ordination was kept: they fought against him, but none can prevail against the word of the Most High going out through the prophets (Jeremiah 1:18-19). His own people put him in a pit to die and hated him for forty years, but they could not stop him from what the Lord called him to do. He had the respect of a prophet and the contempt of a prophet, but he never lost his love for his people; that is the plight of all the prophets of the Most High.

Ebed-melech the Ethiopian drew him out of the mire before he died, and he remained in the court of the prison until the day Jerusalem was taken (Jeremiah 38:7-13, 28). Nebuchadnezzar gave charge concerning him to look well to him and do him no harm (Jeremiah 39:11-12). The Lord did not forsake him, but showed him mercy and grace. He had promised to cause the enemy to entreat him well in the time of evil (Jeremiah 15:11): when a man’s ways please the Lord, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him (Proverbs 16:7).

Nebuzaradan, a heathen, told him the Lord had brought this evil on the place because the people sinned and would not obey his voice (Jeremiah 40:1-3). The nations always knew why we went into captivity: sin, the breaking of the Most High’s laws, becomes our weakness and is how we are overcome (Judith 5:17-18). Bound in chains among the captives at Ramah, he was loosed and given his choice, and went to Gedaliah, one of his good friends, at Mizpah and dwelt among the people left in the land (Jeremiah 40:4-6). Jeremiah was never a captive in Babylon; he spent his whole time prophesying to the people in the land of Judah.

He was told that he himself would discontinue from his heritage and serve his enemies in a land he knew not (Jeremiah 17:4). Jeremiah never went to Babylon, so the word was spoken to him for the last days: he would be back on the earth, serving his enemies in a land he did not know, which is called America today, and he will remember who he is, his God and his land.

cases.name: Pashur the son of Immer
cases.charge: Smiting the prophet of the Lord and putting him in the stocks in the high gate of Benjamin for prophesying the truth; prophesying lies
cases.summary: Pashur the son of Immer, the priest and chief governor in the house of the Lord, heard Jeremiah prophesy the evil coming on the city, smote him, and put him in the stocks in the high gate of Benjamin (Jeremiah 19:14-15; Jeremiah 20:1-2). The next day Jeremiah told him the Lord had renamed him Magor-missabib, a terror to himself and all his friends, who would fall by the sword of the king of Babylon; Pashur and his whole household would be carried captive, and he would die in Babylon and be buried there with all the friends to whom he had prophesied lies (Jeremiah 20:3-6).
offenseFull: Jeremiah came from Tophet, where the Lord had sent him to prophesy, stood in the court of the Lord’s house, and told all the people that the Lord would bring upon the city and all her towns all the evil he had pronounced, because they had hardened their necks that they might not hear (Jeremiah 19:14-15). That is what they did not want to hear, that God would bring evil on them as the Bible is written; and it is the same today, hard-necked people, time after time, no change, more evil.

Pashur the son of Immer, the priest, who was also chief governor in the house of the Lord, heard that Jeremiah prophesied the pending judgment from Babylon (Jeremiah 20:1). This is where the opposition to Jeremiah starts. The priests did not want to hear it, because the Lord was not dealing with them on the same level he was dealing with Jeremiah: he revealed his secret to his servant the prophet, and they did not like that. Their stance was that God was not talking to Jeremiah, for they were the priests. Pashur was tired of Jeremiah blasting them for their wickedness and corruption; and Judah did worse than the northern kingdom, because they had its example and knew better, and still did wrong.

Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet and put him in the stocks in the high gate of Benjamin, by the house of the Lord (Jeremiah 20:2). Smote means he laid hands on him and beat him: he punched a prophet of God in the face who was sent to show him how to be delivered. The stocks held a man’s head and hands, twisted up, in a public place, so that everybody could shame him; they are meant to break a man’s spirit. They put him there because he was teaching the truth and they did not want to hear the judgment for the evil they were doing, instead of repenting, changing and submitting. That is how angry he was: rather than hearing what the Bible says and being changed, he put him in prison. It starts with the tongue: they devised devices against Jeremiah and smote him first with the tongue, with accusations and lies, for anger and envy are displayed through speech, and then that speech becomes physical (Jeremiah 18:18). As Amaziah the priest was more concerned with protecting the king’s institution than with hearing the word of the Lord by Amos, so it is today: rather than correct the leaders of these congregations, they prefer we not speak at all (Amos 7:10-17).

Our forefathers in slavery were put in stocks, standing stocks with the hands locked in, and the same was done to Jeremiah: we have lived the same atrocities our forefathers went through (Deuteronomy 28:68).

Pashur was also a prophet of lies: Jeremiah’s sentence names the friends to whom he had prophesied lies (Jeremiah 20:6). During the time of Jeremiah there were a lot of false prophets, saying peace, peace, when there was no peace, and it is the same thing today (Jeremiah 6:14). Both prophet and priest were profane, and the Most High found their wickedness even in his house (Jeremiah 23:11); the prophets spoke a vision of their own heart and not out of the mouth of the Lord, telling those who despised him they would have peace (Jeremiah 23:16-17). This is like the pastor who says, let me tell you what God told me to tell you, when it is a lie. As the husbandmen beat the servants sent to them and sent them away empty, so the leaders of Israel did to the prophets for a very long time (Luke 20:10-11; Jeremiah 25:4). Prophecy is not all loves and kisses: we are supposed to prophesy destruction so our people may wake up, for destruction is headed to America and to Babylon the Great, the same thing Jeremiah did.
judgmentFull: On the morrow Pashur brought Jeremiah out of the stocks, and Jeremiah told him the Lord had not called his name Pashur but Magor-missabib, which means fear round about: the Lord would make him a terror to himself and to all his friends, and they would fall by the sword of their enemies, and his eyes would behold it (Jeremiah 20:3-4). The stocks did not break Jeremiah’s spirit; he was emboldened by it. Jeremiah had no power of his own to give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon; it was the spirit of the Lord speaking through him.

All Judah would be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, to be carried captive and slain with the sword, with all the strength of the city, its labours, its precious things and the treasures of the kings of Judah (Jeremiah 20:4-5). This shows that we had treasures, our own land and wealth; it is the same thing Moses told our people in Deuteronomy 28, and Israel did not believe Moses. Pashur and all that dwelt in his house would go into captivity, and he would die in Babylon and be buried there with all his friends to whom he had prophesied lies (Jeremiah 20:6).

Do what you want to the messenger; it will not stop the judgment God is bringing. It is the same thing taught today: you can do what you want with us, but there is a judgment coming. God is going to destroy Babylon the Great, and all the Israelites who join themselves hand in hand with their enemies, and nothing can stop it.

When the city fell, the king of Babylon slew all the nobles of Judah at Riblah before Zedekiah’s eyes (Jeremiah 39:6). That is the word spoken earlier to Pashur, who had put Jeremiah in the stocks and laid hands on him: they would fall by the sword, and his eyes would behold it, seeing people he would not expect put to death before his eyes (Jeremiah 20:4). When Nebuchadnezzar came, Israel realized Jeremiah was right.

cases.name: Jehoiakim
cases.charge: Reigning as Pharaoh’s vassal and taxing the land to pay him; building his house by unrighteousness and his chambers by wrong with unpaid labour; slaying Urijah the prophet; cutting and burning the roll of the Lord’s words
cases.summary: Jehoiakim, Josiah’s son Eliakim, was set on the throne by Pharaoh-nechoh as a vassal king and taxed the land to pay him; he did evil, built his house with unpaid labour, slew Urijah the prophet, and cut and burned the roll of Jeremiah’s words (2 Kings 23:34-37; Jeremiah 22:13-17; Jeremiah 26:20-23; Jeremiah 36:23). He served Nebuchadnezzar three years and rebelled, and the Lord pronounced that none of his would sit on David’s throne and that he would have the burial of an ass (2 Kings 24:1; Jeremiah 22:18-19; Jeremiah 36:30).
offenseFull: Pharaoh-nechoh bound Jehoahaz at Riblah, put the land to a tribute, and made Eliakim the son of Josiah king, turning his name to Jehoiakim; Jehoiakim taxed the people to pay Pharaoh and did evil like his forefathers, not like his father Josiah (2 Kings 23:31-37). He was set up as a vassal king, a puppet, to do whatever Pharaoh told him, as America today goes into other countries and sets up puppet rulers who are not for the people but serve American policies. He paid his taxes to Pharaoh, but he taxed us to do it. The renaming is a practice among all the nations: when we are taken over, they give us a new name.

Jeremiah pronounced woe on the king who built his house by unrighteousness and his chambers by wrong, who used his neighbour’s service without wages, and made himself a wide house ceiled with cedar and painted with vermilion (Jeremiah 22:13-14). His father did judgment and justice for the poor and needy, and it was well with him, but Jehoiakim’s eyes and heart were set only on covetousness, innocent blood, oppression and violence (Jeremiah 22:15-17). Woe means destruction, and America was built by killing and enslaving us. The White House was built by slaves: those are the chambers by wrong. The slaves who built the Capitol never lived in it and had no proper house of their own. We were never paid for our captivity, and the forty acres and the mule never came. This is against God, and it is why the Lord will come back to avenge our brothers and sisters and all of us: because we were done wickedly.

Urijah the son of Shemaiah prophesied against the city as Jeremiah did; when Jehoiakim sought to kill him he fled to Egypt, but the king sent men who fetched him back, and he slew him with the sword and cast his body into the graves of the common people (Jeremiah 26:20-23). King Jehoiakim killed one of the prophets of the Most High, and he was our own people, our own race. One king, Hezekiah, knew the word came from the Most High and spared the prophet Micah, while this king put his prophet to death (Jeremiah 26:18-19).

The Most High always gives warning first, but the people do not listen. When the roll of Jeremiah’s words was read before him in the winter house, he cut it with the penknife leaf by leaf and cast it into the fire until it was consumed, and neither he nor his servants were afraid or rent their garments, though Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah made intercession with him (Jeremiah 36:21-25). Because he was the king, he did not care about God; he took everything they wrote and burned it. Many have the same regard for God now: they wish we were dead, and they wish they could burn this Bible up. He commanded that Baruch and Jeremiah be seized, but the Lord hid them (Jeremiah 36:26).
judgmentFull: Jeremiah wrote the words again on another roll, with the sentence added: Jehoiakim would have none to sit upon the throne of David, his dead body would be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night, and the Lord would punish him, his seed and his servants for their iniquity (Jeremiah 36:27-31). The king of Babylon would come and kill him and leave his body out night and day in the cold, because he burned the roll. He did not listen; he was rebellious, and he brought it on himself.

No one would lament him; he would be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 22:18-19). He would die outside the land because he was evil, thrown out without an honourable burial. His son Coniah would be plucked off like a signet and written childless, no man of his seed to prosper on the throne of David (Jeremiah 22:24-30).

He served Nebuchadnezzar three years and then rebelled, and the Lord sent bands of the Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites against Judah to destroy it, the evil out of the north (2 Kings 24:1-2; Jeremiah 4:6). This man was so evil that the Lord was sending nations against us. It came at the commandment of the Lord to remove Judah out of his sight for the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood he shed, which the Lord would not pardon (2 Kings 24:3-4).

Nebuchadnezzar bound him in fetters to carry him to Babylon and carried off the vessels of the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 36:6-7). This was the first wave of conquest, about 605 BC, and Daniel and the three holy children were among those taken in it. The Most High set a wicked king over the land because his own people would not do what he said: when Israel will not rule in righteousness, he raises up a Nebuchadnezzar, for Israel’s purpose was never to be wicked and rule at the same time (Ecclesiasticus 10:1-4). All these people and their offspring paid for what this fool did: one man burned up the law, God cursed his seed, and all the nation of Israel paid.

cases.name: Hananiah the son of Azur
cases.charge: Prophesying a lie in the name of the Lord, that the yoke of Babylon was broken and the captives would return within two years, and breaking the yoke from off Jeremiah’s neck; teaching rebellion against the Lord
cases.summary: In the fourth year of Zedekiah, Hananiah the son of Azur, a so-called prophet of Gibeon, told the priests and people in the Lord’s house that the Lord had broken the yoke of Babylon and within two full years would bring back the vessels, Jeconiah and the captives, and he broke the yoke off Jeremiah’s neck (Jeremiah 28:1-4; Jeremiah 28:10-11). Jeremiah told him the Lord had not sent him, that he made the people trust in a lie and taught rebellion against the Lord, and that he would die that year; he died in the seventh month (Jeremiah 28:15-17).
offenseFull: Jeconiah was still alive in Babylon and the people still reverenced him as king, and a false hope was being spread that the Lord would return him to his throne and they would not be carried away into captivity fully. The people knew Zedekiah was a puppet king whom Babylon set up, and it was false prophets giving the people false hope. The Lord had already said that the nations would serve the king of Babylon seventy years, and they understood that the prophecy was seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11-12). Hananiah, a so-called prophet, spoke the things he claimed the Most High was going to do: the yoke broken, and the vessels, Jeconiah and the captives returned within two full years (Jeremiah 28:1-4). That is taking the Lord’s name in vain: false prophets say thus saith the Lord when the Lord has told them nothing, just as the pastors do, prophesying lies in his name (Exodus 20:7).

Jeremiah answered amen, the Lord do so, but told him not to hold on to it: the prophets before them prophesied of war, of evil and of pestilence, nothing of peace, and a prophet who prophesies peace is known to be sent of the Lord only when his word comes to pass (Jeremiah 28:5-9). That is how the prophets of the Lord are known: they come teaching that evil is coming, pestilence is coming, war is coming. Our job is to prophesy against many countries and against great kingdoms, and that is what the leadership is doing today, going to different countries because this gospel cannot be stopped; they will be made manifest when the mission is accomplished.

Hananiah took the yoke from off Jeremiah’s neck, the yoke he wore as the sign of the captivity, and broke it before all the people, saying the Lord would break Nebuchadnezzar’s yoke from the neck of all nations within two full years; and Jeremiah went his way (Jeremiah 28:10-11). Jeremiah rebuked him for teaching peace and safety. There are many false prophets among us today, speaking out of their own heart, prosperity and peace, peace, when there is no peace (Jeremiah 23:16-17; Jeremiah 6:14). The Christian pastor is still telling you to this day that it is your season; they were doing that back then, and it is nothing new under the sun. Hananiah was purposely deceiving the people; the Lord put a lying spirit on him, but he was a false prophet speaking peace, and his sin was presumptuous.
judgmentFull: The word came to Jeremiah: Hananiah had broken the yokes of wood, but he would make for them yokes of iron; the Most High had put a yoke of iron upon the neck of all these nations to serve Nebuchadnezzar, who was the superpower at that time, and gave him the beasts of the field also (Jeremiah 28:12-14). The yoke of Babylon was vassal service, not chattel slavery: to submit under the taxation that Babylon imposed. Israel also had yokes of iron on our necks in the ancient Babylonian captivity, and the prophecy Moses gave from the beginning applied to every captivity, as well as the one we serve in now in Babylon the Great, America (Deuteronomy 28:48).

Jeremiah told Hananiah the Lord had not sent him, but he made the people trust in a lie and was leading his people astray (Jeremiah 28:15). Because he taught rebellion against the Lord, teaching the people to go against the Most High instead of accepting that they had to go through captivity, the Lord would cast him from off the face of the earth, and he would die that year; Hananiah died the same year, in the seventh month (Jeremiah 28:16-17). The law had already set the sentence: the prophet who presumes to speak a word in the name of the Most High which he has not commanded shall die, and the sign is that the thing does not come to pass (Deuteronomy 18:20-22). By this law a lot of these pastors stand condemned: they say things and claim Christ said them, when the Most High never commanded it. These false pastors make our people trust in lies, but everything is not going to be good on this earth, and we are here to tell the truth.

Sin does not affect only the sinner but everybody around him. It takes just one: like Theudas and Judas of Galilee, who drew away much people after them and perished, and all who obeyed them were scattered, such a man is often charismatic, a great speaker able to lead, with a sin in his spirit he is not able to overcome (Acts 5:36-37). That is what Hananiah was doing: corrupting the word of God and speaking a vision out of his own heart (2 Corinthians 2:17). Those sins must not be allowed to have dominion over us; the prayer is to be kept back from presumptuous sins (Psalm 19:13).

cases.name: Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah
cases.charge: Prophesying a lie in the name of the Lord among the captives at Babylon; committing villainy in Israel and adultery with their neighbours’ wives
cases.summary: Jeremiah’s letter to the captives in Babylon told them to build, plant, marry and seek the peace of the city, and not to be deceived by the prophets among them, for the captivity would last seventy years (Jeremiah 29:4-10). He named two of those prophets, Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, who prophesied a lie in the Lord’s name and committed adultery with their neighbours’ wives; the Most High would deliver them to Nebuchadnezzar to be slain before the captives’ eyes, and their names would become a curse, roasted in the fire (Jeremiah 29:20-23).
offenseFull: The letter went to the elders, priests, prophets and people carried away with Jeconiah, among them the carpenters and smiths: just as in this captivity, our people still carried those talents and skills (Jeremiah 29:1-3). They were to build houses and plant gardens, which means to live your life in captivity, just as we do now in America, the daughter of Babylon (Jeremiah 29:4-5). It means get comfortable and do not fight back, because you would be fighting the Most High God: we sinned against our Father by breaking the commandments he gave us as our heritage. They were to marry and increase and not be diminished, and seek the peace of the city where they were carried (Jeremiah 29:6-7; Romans 13:1). Increase is not by marrying into the other nations; marrying the men of the other nations does not increase the seed of Israel but diminishes it. After seventy years the Lord would visit them, thus saith the Lord, not thus saith the lying pastor or the prophet; the seventy years gave the land rest for the sabbaths we did not keep, and it was fulfilled at Cyrus (Jeremiah 29:10; Ezra 1:1; 2 Chronicles 36:21).

They were not to let the false prophets and diviners in their midst deceive them, nor their dreams; today Christianity has so-called prophets and Islam has so-called prophecy, but they deceive people because that is not the right way to serve the right God (Jeremiah 29:8-9). In the reign of Zedekiah false prophets told those in captivity in Babylon that the Lord would cause them to return, and told those in the land that Babylon would not come and destroy them, and both were false. Ahab and Zedekiah were more of these false prophets, taking the Lord’s name in vain along with Hananiah; this Zedekiah was not King Zedekiah but a false prophet.

They committed villainy in Israel and adultery with their neighbours’ wives, and spoke lying words in the Lord’s name which he had not commanded; even he knows, and is a witness (Jeremiah 29:23). They were prophesying in the name of the Lord: that is Christianity, and the same spirits are back again doing the same thing, prophesying strong and sounding good while committing adultery with your wife. That is what the pastors do. Prophet and priest were both profane: the prophets of Jerusalem committed adultery, walked in lies and strengthened the hands of evildoers, and became as Sodom and Gomorrah (Jeremiah 23:11-14). Our people in Jeremiah’s time were like Sodom and Gomorrah, in adultery and all types of filthiness; it is not new to our people, and it is not just one sin. Their way would be slippery ways in the darkness: whatever path they took, they would fall, and the Lord would bring the Babylonians on them (Jeremiah 23:12). They were the prophets who said, I have dreamed, and stole his words; none of them had stood in the counsel of the Most High (Jeremiah 23:22-32).
judgmentFull: The Most High would deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, and he would slay them before the eyes of the captives (Jeremiah 29:21). Their names would become a curse among all the captives of Judah in Babylon, who would wish a man the fate of Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire (Jeremiah 29:22). They were cooked to death. The Lord made an example of these false prophets: when the Lord judges someone, he becomes a proverb, and the false prophets became a proverb and a curse, the Lord will do you as he did Zedekiah.

Wickedness came from Babylon from ancient judges who seemed to govern the people, of whom the Lord had spoken in Jeremiah 29 (Susanna 1:5). These were evil elders in Babylon, and the elders who came out of Babylon and made their way into the Roman captivity started the Talmud: the Babylonian Talmud came from Babylon. The Pharisees came out of that same line of evil elders and did the exact same thing when Rome ruled. That is why, in John 8, they brought only the woman taken in adultery to be stoned, and not the man (John 8:3-11).

Captivity is the chastening and scourging of the Lord, a punishment on a biblical scale (Hebrews 12:6). The prophets understood the time that had to be accomplished in this captivity before we could be free, and in that was our patience and our hope. It was seventy years at that time, and now it is hundreds. When they seek him with all their heart he will be found of them and gather them from all the nations whither he drove them, and that is why the leadership goes out to the four corners of the earth (Jeremiah 29:13-14). No matter where you go on the planet, there are Israelites.

cases.name: Shemaiah the Nehelamite
cases.charge: Sending letters in his own name from Babylon to have Jeremiah put in prison and in the stocks as a madman; prophesying when the Lord sent him not, causing the people to trust in a lie, and teaching rebellion against the Lord
cases.summary: Shemaiah the Nehelamite, among the captives in Babylon, sent letters in his own name to Jerusalem and to Zephaniah the priest, asking why he had not reproved Jeremiah and put him in the stocks for telling the captives that their captivity was long (Jeremiah 29:24-28). Zephaniah read the letter in Jeremiah’s ears, and the word came back that Shemaiah prophesied when the Lord sent him not and caused the people to trust in a lie; he and his seed would have no man among the people nor behold the good the Lord would do, because he taught rebellion against the Lord (Jeremiah 29:29-32).
offenseFull: Jeremiah had written to the captives carried away with Jeconiah that they would be in Babylon seventy years, and must build houses, plant gardens, marry and seek the peace of the city (Jeremiah 29:4-10). Ezekiel was among the captives in Babylon, Jeremiah was with the remnant still in the land with Zedekiah, and messengers were sent back and forth. False prophets told those in captivity that the Lord would cause them to return, which was false; the Lord said they would serve seventy years, and then he would bring them back to the land. Nehelamite means dreamer: Shemaiah was one of the prophets of Jeremiah 23 who prophesied lies, saying I have dreamed, when the Lord had shown them nothing (Jeremiah 23:25-27).

He sent letters in his own name to all the people at Jerusalem, to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests (Jeremiah 29:25). He told Zephaniah the Lord had made him priest in the stead of Jehoiada, to put every man that makes himself a prophet in prison and the stocks, and asked why he had not reproved Jeremiah of Anathoth, who told the captives their captivity was long and to build houses (Jeremiah 29:26-28). The stocks are what they put Jeremiah in, and they put us in the stocks as well: we have lived the same atrocities our forefathers went through (Jeremiah 20:2). Zephaniah read the letter in Jeremiah’s ears, and the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, for the Lord was dealing with Jeremiah: that was the difference (Jeremiah 29:29-30).

The long captivity was what Shemaiah attacked: it was seventy years at that time, and now it is hundreds. The instruction was to build houses within that time, so a doctrine that tells the people today not to do these things, to sit and do nothing when the time is hundreds of years, makes no sense. Build houses means get comfortable and do not fight back, because that would be fighting the Most High God, against whom we sinned.
judgmentFull: Because Shemaiah prophesied when the Lord sent him not and caused the people to trust in a lie, the Most High would punish him and his seed: he would not have a man to dwell among the people, nor behold the good the Lord would do for his people, because he taught rebellion against the Lord (Jeremiah 29:31-32). His sentence reached his seed as well as himself (Jeremiah 29:32). Hananiah was judged for the same offence: he taught rebellion against the Lord, teaching the people to go against the Most High instead of accepting that they had to go through captivity (Jeremiah 28:16).

The good he would not see is the good the letter promised: after seventy years the Most High would visit them and perform his good word to return them, for his thoughts toward them are of peace and not of evil, to give them an expected end (Jeremiah 29:10-11). The same is happening today: knowledge is being increased, we are finding out who we are, and we are coming back to God’s laws to be saved out of this captivity. Everything here is temporary; Jerusalem is our land, and we already know the end (Jeremiah 29:14). The prophets understood the time that had to be accomplished in this captivity before we could be free, and in that was our patience and our hope (Jeremiah 29:12-14).

cases.name: Jonadab and the Rechabites
cases.charge: Obeying the voice of Jonadab their father in all that he charged them: drinking no wine, building no house, sowing no seed, planting no vineyard, but dwelling in tents all their days
cases.summary: In the days of Jehoiakim the Most High sent Jeremiah to bring the house of the Rechabites into the temple chambers and set wine before them, and they refused, because Jonadab the son of Rechab their father had commanded them to drink no wine, build no house, sow no seed and plant no vineyard, but dwell in tents all their days (Jeremiah 35:1-10). The Most High set their obedience against Judah, which would not hearken to him, and promised that Jonadab would not want a man to stand before him for ever (Jeremiah 35:12-19).
offenseFull: Jonadab the son of Rechab was the man whose heart was right with Jehu’s; Jehu took him up into his chariot to see his zeal for the Most High, and he went in with Jehu to the house of Baal when the worshippers of Baal were searched out and destroyed (2 Kings 10:15-23).

In the days of Jehoiakim the word came to Jeremiah to go to the house of the Rechabites, bring them into one of the chambers of the house of the Lord, and give them wine to drink (Jeremiah 35:1-2). He took Jaazaniah, his brethren and all his sons, the whole house of the Rechabites, into the chamber of the sons of Hanan the man of God, set pots full of wine and cups before them, and told them to drink (Jeremiah 35:3-5). They refused: Jonadab the son of Rechab their father had commanded them and their sons to drink no wine for ever, build no house, sow no seed and plant no vineyard nor have any, but dwell in tents all their days, that they might live many days in the land where they were strangers (Jeremiah 35:6-7). They had obeyed his voice in all that he charged them, they, their wives, their sons and their daughters: they drank no wine all their days, built no houses to dwell in, had neither vineyard, field nor seed, and dwelt in tents (Jeremiah 35:8-10). They had come into Jerusalem only for fear of the army of the Chaldeans and of the Syrians, when Nebuchadnezzar came up into the land (Jeremiah 35:11). They obeyed the voice of Jonadab in all things.
judgmentFull: The Most High told Jeremiah to point Judah to the Rechabites: would they not receive instruction to hearken to his words? (Jeremiah 35:12-13). The sons of Jonadab kept their father’s command to drink no wine to that day, but this people would not hearken to the Most High, though he rose early and spoke (Jeremiah 35:14). He sent all his servants the prophets, rising early and sending them, calling every man to return from his evil way, amend his doings and go not after other gods, promising that they would dwell in the land he gave their fathers; yet they would not incline their ear (Jeremiah 35:15). The Lord sends his prophets to tell our people to repent and stop worshipping other idols, gods that are not real: not to serve other gods, not Easter and not Christmas. In our affliction we will seek him early (Hosea 5:15).

The sons of Jonadab performed the commandment of their father, but this people did not hearken to the Lord (Jeremiah 35:16). Because Judah would not hear and would not answer, the Most High would bring upon Judah and upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the evil he had pronounced against them (Jeremiah 35:17). God will bring upon us all the evil because we do not listen. To the house of the Rechabites Jeremiah said that because they obeyed the commandment of Jonadab their father, kept all his precepts and did all that he commanded them, Jonadab the son of Rechab would not want a man to stand before the Lord for ever (Jeremiah 35:18-19).

cases.name: Baruch the scribe
cases.charge: Writing from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the Lord upon a roll, reading it in the house of the Lord and before the princes, and writing it again after the king burned it
cases.summary: Baruch the son of Neriah wrote upon a roll from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words of the Most High and read them in the Lord’s house on the fasting day while Jeremiah was shut up (Jeremiah 36:4-10). The princes told him to hide himself and Jeremiah; Jehoiakim cut the roll and burned it, and Baruch wrote all the words again with many like words added (Jeremiah 36:19-32). When he said the Lord had added grief to his sorrow, he was told not to seek great things for himself, and was promised his life wherever he went (Jeremiah 45:1-5).
offenseFull: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the Most High told Jeremiah to write in a roll all the words he had spoken against Israel, Judah and all the nations, that the house of Judah, hearing all the evil purposed against them, might return every man from his evil way and be forgiven (Jeremiah 36:1-3). The Most High always gives warning first; he sends somebody to tell you that what you are doing is wrong. Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words of the Most High upon the roll (Jeremiah 36:4). God put the spirit on Jeremiah to speak and Baruch documented it, and that is why, when we teach, we have a speaker and a reader, and people make fun of us for that. The scriptures were written by men moved by the spirit of the Lord, commissioned to write down what the Lord gave them, as Moses wrote the journeys at the Lord’s commandment (Numbers 33:2). There is a book of Baruch; Baruch was the scribe of Jeremiah, always with him documenting the words of the Lord, the same way the Lord dealt with Elijah first and then with Elisha.

Because Jeremiah was shut up and could not go into the house of the Most High, he sent Baruch to read the roll in the ears of the people on the fasting day, and Baruch did all that the prophet commanded (Jeremiah 36:5-8). In the fifth year, in the ninth month, he read it in the chamber of Gemariah in the ears of all the people, and Michaiah declared the words to the princes in the scribe’s chamber (Jeremiah 36:9-13). The princes had Baruch read it in their ears and were afraid, and they asked how he wrote all these words; he answered that Jeremiah pronounced them with his mouth and he wrote them with ink in the book (Jeremiah 36:14-18). They did not believe that God put his spirit on these men, and it is the same today: many do not believe that God is putting men in place to warn them. The princes told Baruch to go and hide himself and Jeremiah, and let no man know where they were (Jeremiah 36:19).

The roll was read before Jehoiakim in the winter house, and as it was read he cut it with the penknife and cast it into the fire until it was consumed; neither the king nor his servants were afraid, though Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah made intercession (Jeremiah 36:20-25). Israel does not like the consequences of its sins, and so he burned it. The king commanded that Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet be seized, but the Most High hid them (Jeremiah 36:26). God had to hide them, because evil men did not care about the writings and would destroy them at any time; many purpose to do things to us as their forefathers did, but if God wants it not to happen, it will not happen. Baruch took another roll and wrote from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words of the book the king had burned, and many like words were added (Jeremiah 36:27-32). Just because a book is named in the Bible does not mean we have it now; there are writings of Jeremiah we do not have. But the word is too far out now to be stopped.
judgmentFull: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when he had written these words, Baruch said woe is me, for the Lord had added grief to his sorrow; he fainted in his sighing and found no rest (Jeremiah 45:1-3). That is how we are right now, with that woe is me spirit: we are already in sorrow, and God says he will add grief.

The Most High answered that what he had built he would break down and what he had planted he would pluck up, even this whole land; Baruch was not to seek great things for himself, for he would bring evil upon all flesh, but his life he would give him for a prey wherever he went (Jeremiah 45:4-5). Seeking great things is how the people are, and God already has it documented in this book. The Christian church says to show a tithe and an offering and the Lord will pour out blessings, and that is not what the Bible says. Now you want to seek great things for yourself? Are you clueless? God may never change your situation, but at least you know where you went wrong, and you have hope.

The words of the scribe Baruch are preserved in the Apocrypha (Baruch 1:1). Our forefathers learned through the prophets that in the land of our captivity we would remember ourselves, and this is the understanding the Christian church lacks (Baruch 2:29-33). In our affliction we will seek him early, and so in the land of our captivity he gives us a heart and ears to hear (Hosea 5:15). Baruch was carried into Egypt with Jeremiah and the remnant of Judah (Jeremiah 43:6). He wrote his book in Babylon and read it in the hearing of Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim and of all the people (Baruch 1:1-4). We are captive in Babylon today, and that history is for our learning and our comfort, to escape the philosophy and doctrine of Babylon, America.

cases.name: Ebed-melech the Ethiopian
cases.charge: Going out to the king in the gate of Benjamin and telling him the princes had done evil to Jeremiah, then drawing the prophet up out of the dungeon of mire with old cast clouts and rotten rags under his armholes
cases.summary: When the princes had Jeremiah let down into the miry dungeon, Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch of the king’s house, went to Zedekiah at the gate of Benjamin, told him these men had done evil to the prophet, and with thirty men drew Jeremiah out with old rags under the cords (Jeremiah 38:4-13). Before the city fell the Lord sent him word by Jeremiah that he would be delivered and not fall by the sword, because he had put his trust in the Lord; the Most High dealt with the Ethiopian because he was used to help Jeremiah (Jeremiah 39:15-18).
offenseFull: Shephatiah, Gedaliah the son of Pashur, Jucal and Pashur the son of Malchiah heard Jeremiah tell the people that whoever stayed in the city would die and whoever went forth to the Chaldeans would live, and told the king he must be put to death because he weakened the hands of the men of war and sought not the welfare of the people but their hurt; Zedekiah answered that he was in their hand, for the king could do nothing against them (Jeremiah 38:1-5). Jeremiah was prophesying, and they said he was speaking hate and teaching hate and making the military afraid. It was false accusation from his own brethren, who had already charged him with falling away to the Chaldeans and put him in prison (Jeremiah 37:13-15). They twisted his words to make him seem to be working for Babylon, against Judah and Jerusalem, the same thing that was done to Christ when false witnesses twisted his words about the temple, for the spirit of Christ was in Jeremiah. He was only telling them the word of the Lord, captivity, death and judgment, but they wanted smooth words; they wanted Jeremiah to be like the rest of the false prophets and give the people false hope. Zedekiah was a weakling and a coward, which is why Babylon set him up as a puppet king to keep Judah in subjection; he could not stop them, and told them to do what they would.

They cast Jeremiah into the dungeon of Malchiah in the court of the prison and let him down with cords, and in the dungeon there was no water but mire, and he sank in it (Jeremiah 38:6). The mire was dung; the dungeon was a hole where the dung came up and he could not avoid it. They did not mean to stone him; they meant him to die a slow and agonizing death, sinking in a pit with no water and quicksand at the bottom, and that is what the faithful must be ready to face. Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs in the king’s house, heard of it while the king sat in the gate of Benjamin, went out to the king, and told him these men had done evil in all they had done to Jeremiah, who was likely to die of hunger where he was, for there was no more bread in the city (Jeremiah 38:7-9). The Lord made a way for Jeremiah, because Jeremiah was set: he would not hold back his tongue, the fire was shut up in his bones, and he had to bring the correction and warn the king despite his life, for a messenger who brings unpleasant words before a king may forfeit his life on the spot (Jeremiah 20:9). The king commanded him to take thirty men and lift the prophet out before he died (Jeremiah 38:10). He took old cast clouts and rotten rags, let them down by cords, and told Jeremiah to put them under his armholes beneath the cords; so they drew him up, and Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison (Jeremiah 38:11-13). Jeremiah was malnourished, barely fed in that dungeon, and the rags under his arms let him hold on so he could come up, like a harness.
judgmentFull: While Jeremiah was still shut up in the court of the prison, the word of the Lord came to him for Ebed-melech: the Lord would bring his words upon the city for evil and not for good, and they would be accomplished in that day (Jeremiah 39:15-16). But in that day the Lord would deliver him; he would not be given into the hand of the men he feared, nor fall by the sword, because he had put his trust in the Lord (Jeremiah 39:17-18). The Most High dealt with the Ethiopian because he was used to help Jeremiah, and his deliverance is tied back to the moment the king commanded him to lift the prophet out of the miry dungeon before he perished (Jeremiah 38:10). The Lord looked out for the one who looked out for Jeremiah. The men he feared were Babylon, and the promise was survival: he would not be killed, though he would be subject to Babylon, because he looked out for Jeremiah when he was locked up. The city fell as it was spoken: the king of Babylon slew Zedekiah’s sons and all the nobles of Judah at Riblah before his eyes, put out his eyes, and burned the king’s house and the houses of the people (Jeremiah 39:6-8). Chapters 38 and 39 are to be read together.

cases.name: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah
cases.charge: Smiting with the sword Gedaliah the governor, with whom he had eaten bread at Mizpah, and all the Jews and Chaldeans with him; slaying seventy of the eighty men coming with offerings to the house of the Lord and casting them into the pit; carrying the residue captive toward the Ammonites, who sent him
cases.summary: After Jerusalem fell, the king of Babylon made Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor at Mizpah over the poor left in the land; Johanan warned him that Baalis king of the Ammonites had sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to slay him, and Gedaliah believed it not (Jeremiah 40:7-16). In the seventh month Ishmael, of the royal seed, ate bread with him and then slew him and the Jews and Chaldeans with him, killed seventy of eighty men bringing offerings and filled Asa’s pit with them, and carried off the rest toward the Ammonites; Johanan recovered the captives at Gibeon, and Ishmael escaped with eight men (Jeremiah 41:1-15).
offenseFull: Nebuzaradan, a heathen, told Jeremiah that the Most High had pronounced this evil because the people sinned against him and would not obey his voice (Jeremiah 40:1-3). The nations always knew why we went into captivity: it is sin, the breaking of the Most High’s laws, that becomes our weakness and how we are overcome (Judith 5:17-18). Every other captive was in chains, and Jeremiah was singled out and his chains taken off; he did not go into captivity in Babylon, he was spared (Jeremiah 40:4). He went to Gedaliah at Mizpah, one of his good friends, and dwelt with him among the people left in the land (Jeremiah 40:5-6). Gedaliah swore to the captains of the forces not to fear to serve the Chaldeans, but to dwell in the land, gather wine and summer fruits and oil, and serve the king of Babylon, and it would be well with them; the war was over and they were already conquered (Jeremiah 40:7-10). That is obeying the powers that be, Romans 13 in the Old Testament (Romans 13:1). Gedaliah gave wise counsel (2 Kings 25:24). Israel had run when Nebuchadnezzar came, among Moab, Ammon and Edom, hoping to find sanctuary there, and when word came that Gedaliah was set as governor they returned from those places and gathered wine and summer fruits very much (Jeremiah 40:11-12).

Johanan the son of Kareah and the captains warned Gedaliah that Baalis king of the Ammonites had sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to slay him; Gedaliah believed them not, and when Johanan offered secretly to kill Ishmael so that the remnant would not be scattered, Gedaliah forbade it and said he spoke falsely of Ishmael (Jeremiah 40:13-16). The heathen sent him: Ishmael was sent by the Ammonites to kill Gedaliah, and he worked for the Ammonites. The Babylonians made puppet rulers out of us and set up a governor named Gedaliah; our people hated following those orders, and Ishmael, of the royal seed, rose up and assassinated him. In the seventh month Ishmael, of the royal seed and a prince of the king, came with ten men to Gedaliah at Mizpah, and they ate bread together at a banquet held in Ishmael’s honor (Jeremiah 41:1). Then they rose up and smote Gedaliah with the sword, the governor the king of Babylon had made over the land, and slew all the Jews with him and the Chaldeans and men of war found there (Jeremiah 41:2-3). It was rebellion against Nebuchadnezzar, and against Israel as well. The second day after the murder, before anyone knew of it, eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria with their beards shaven, their clothes rent and their bodies cut, bringing offerings and incense to the house of the Lord (Jeremiah 41:4-5). Ishmael went out from Mizpah weeping as he met them, playing a part, invited them in to Gedaliah, and in the midst of the city he and his men slew them and cast them into a pit (Jeremiah 41:6-7). He killed his own people. Ten of the eighty were spared when they told him they had hidden treasures of wheat, barley, oil and honey in the field: they bribed him (Jeremiah 41:8). The pit he filled with the slain was the one Asa the king had made for fear of Baasha king of Israel, when he built Mizpah with the stones of Ramah (Jeremiah 41:9; 1 Kings 15:22).
judgmentFull: Ishmael carried away captive all the residue of the people at Mizpah, the king’s daughters among them, whom Nebuzaradan had committed to Gedaliah, and departed toward the Ammonites (Jeremiah 41:10). When Johanan and the captains heard of all the evil he had done, not only killing Gedaliah but at least eighty other men, they took their men to fight him and found him by the great waters in Gibeon (Jeremiah 41:11-12). The captives were glad to see Johanan and returned to him, but Ishmael escaped with eight men and went to the Ammonites (Jeremiah 41:13-15). He ran back to the ones who sent him to kill in the first place. No sentence on Ishmael is recorded.

Johanan took the whole remnant he had recovered, the men of war, the women, the children and the eunuchs, and dwelt near Bethlehem on the way toward Egypt (Jeremiah 41:16-17). They set out to seek refuge in Egypt because they were afraid of the Chaldeans, since Ishmael had slain the governor; with Gedaliah dead they felt they had no reason to stay (Jeremiah 41:18). The people fled to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans, and Israel always ran to Egypt for safety (2 Kings 25:26). The killing of Gedaliah forced them to move further into Egypt, and from there they migrated south and westward; from the time of Gedaliah’s murder the Judeans began to settle in Africa.

cases.name: Johanan and the remnant that went down to Egypt
cases.charge: Asking Jeremiah to pray for the way wherein they should walk, swearing to obey the voice of the Lord whether it were good or evil, and then calling the prophet a liar and going into Egypt against the commandment; burning incense to the queen of heaven in the land of Egypt
cases.summary: After Gedaliah’s murder the captains and all the people, from the least to the greatest, begged Jeremiah to pray for the way they should walk and swore to obey the Lord’s voice, good or evil (Jeremiah 42:1-6). When the answer came to abide in the land and not go into Egypt, Azariah, Johanan and all the proud men called Jeremiah a lying prophet and carried the whole remnant, Jeremiah and Baruch with them, to Tahpanhes, because they obeyed not the voice of the Lord (Jeremiah 43:1-7). There they burned incense to the queen of heaven and refused the prophet, and the Lord swore he would watch over them for evil until they were consumed by the sword and famine, and only a small number would escape (Jeremiah 44:15-28).
offenseFull: Johanan, Jezaniah and all the people asked Jeremiah to pray to the Lord for them, and swore that the Lord would be a true and faithful witness against them if they did not obey his voice, whether good or evil (Jeremiah 42:1-6). After ten days the answer came: if they abode in the land he would build them and not pull them down, plant them and not pluck them up, for he repented of the evil he had done to them; they were not to fear the king of Babylon, for he was with them to save them (Jeremiah 42:7-12). He does not desire evil against his people; he only wants his laws kept. But if they went into Egypt to see no war and hunger for no bread, the sword they feared would overtake them there; he set before them life or death and told them to choose life (Jeremiah 42:13-18). They had dissembled in their hearts when they sent him to pray (Jeremiah 42:19-22). Some people speak words they do not believe, and many ask for counsel with their minds already made up, then look for someone who will tell them what they want to hear; we are these same people, quick to say we will not do what the Most High commands. Azariah, Johanan and all the proud men told Jeremiah he spoke falsely and accused Baruch of setting him against them; pride is destruction (Jeremiah 43:1-3). They took the whole remnant, the men, women, children and the king’s daughters, with Jeremiah and Baruch, into Egypt as far as Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:4-7). Jeremiah was always warning us about going into Egypt, for our people always loved Egypt; we sought the Pharaohs instead of the Lord, just as today we look to presidents and not to the Bible (Isaiah 30:1-3).

In Egypt and Pathros the Lord reminded them of Jerusalem’s desolation for burning incense to other gods, though he sent his prophets rising early (Jeremiah 44:1-8). When Babylon came against us we fled into Egypt and kept doing the same thing: we left our own land to do the same thing in another land, and have learned nothing. The men who knew their wives burned incense to other gods, and all the women, answered that they would not hearken but would burn incense to the queen of heaven as they and their fathers, kings and princes had done, for then they had plenty of victuals and saw no evil (Jeremiah 44:15-19). That was madness, for they had been chased out of Jerusalem, and it shows how evil and deluded Israel became: serving the Most High was hard, and serving the queen of heaven was easy. The queen of heaven is Ashtoreth, Isis, Ishtar, a Canaanite goddess. These men did not rule their houses well and had no authority over their households; their wives were in the midst of idolatry, the same disorder seen in the place spiritually called Egypt, in Babylon the great today. The women made cakes and poured out drink offerings without their men; the women were leading the men, and the men knew their wives worshipped other gods and stood back and did nothing, for a woman shall compass a man (Jeremiah 31:22). They were not good stewards of their homes, and those houses were divided; the scripture teaches that a man must set his house in order (2 Esdras 14:13).
judgmentFull: Jeremiah answered the men first, and then the women: the Lord remembered the incense of Judah and could no longer bear it, and therefore the land became a desolation (Jeremiah 44:20-23). He swore by his great name that it would no more be named in the mouth of any man of Judah in Egypt; he would watch over them for evil and not for good until they were consumed by the sword and famine (Jeremiah 44:24-27). The curses pursued even those who went to Egypt for refuge; they would all be consumed, from the least to the greatest (Jeremiah 44:12; Deuteronomy 28:45). Yet a small number escaping the sword would return to Judah, and the remnant would know whose words would stand, his or theirs (Jeremiah 44:28). Not all of them were wicked; some were keeping God’s commandments while they were there. The sign was Pharaoh-hophra given into the hand of his enemies as Zedekiah was given to Nebuchadnezzar, for they had fled there thinking Egypt was a powerhouse (Jeremiah 44:29-30). Nebuchadnezzar, his servant, would set his throne on the stones Jeremiah hid at Pharaoh’s house in Tahpanhes and smite Egypt and deliver such as were for death to death and such as were for the sword to the sword (Jeremiah 43:8-13).

The Lord shall bring thee into Egypt again with ships: Egypt means bondage, and it is not the literal land, for Israel could walk to Egypt; it is the great city spiritually called Egypt, Babylon the great, America (Deuteronomy 28:68; Revelation 11:8). Moses saw the transatlantic slave trade. Ephraim shall return to Egypt, the spiritual Egypt of Revelation 11:8 (Hosea 9:3). America is not literally Egypt but the shadow of Egypt, and to strengthen ourselves in the strength of Pharaoh is to trust in the American economy and political system (Isaiah 30:2-3). The brothers delivered from oppression who talked of going back to Egypt because at least there they had good food are the same as many here today, full and comfortable for now (Numbers 11:4-6); everything learned in Egypt is to be forgotten (Leviticus 18:3).

After ten days the answer came: if they abode in the land he would build them and not pull them down, plant them and not pluck them up, for he repented of the evil he had done to them; they were not to fear the king of Babylon, for he was with them to save them (Jeremiah 42:7-12). He does not desire evil against his people; he only wants his laws kept. But if they went into Egypt to see no war and hunger for no bread, the sword they feared would overtake them there; he set before them life or death and told them to choose life (Jeremiah 42:13-18). They had dissembled in their hearts when they sent him to pray (Jeremiah 42:19-22). Some people speak words they do not believe, and many ask for counsel with their minds already made up, then look for someone who will tell them what they want to hear; we are these same people, quick to say we will not do what the Most High commands. Azariah, Johanan and all the proud men told Jeremiah he spoke falsely and accused Baruch of setting him against them; pride is destruction (Jeremiah 43:1-3). They took the whole remnant, the men, women, children and the king’s daughters, with Jeremiah and Baruch, into Egypt as far as Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:4-7). Jeremiah was always warning us about going into Egypt, for our people always loved Egypt; we sought the Pharaohs instead of the Lord, just as today we look to presidents and not to the Bible (Isaiah 30:1-3).
cases.judgment: Jeremiah answered the men first, and then the women: the Lord remembered the incense of Judah and could no longer bear it, and therefore the land became a desolation (Jeremiah 44:20-23). He swore by his great name that it would no more be named in the mouth of any man of Judah in Egypt; he would watch over them for evil and not for good until they were consumed by the sword and famine (Jeremiah 44:24-27). The curses pursued even those who went to Egypt for refuge; they would all be consumed, from the least to the greatest (Jeremiah 44:12; Deuteronomy 28:45). Yet a small number escaping the sword would return to Judah, and the remnant would know whose words would stand, his or theirs (Jeremiah 44:28). Not all of them were wicked; some were keeping God’s commandments while they were there. The sign was Pharaoh-hophra given into the hand of his enemies as Zedekiah was given to Nebuchadnezzar, for they had fled there thinking Egypt was a powerhouse (Jeremiah 44:29-30). Nebuchadnezzar, his servant, would set his throne on the stones Jeremiah hid at Pharaoh’s house in Tahpanhes and smite Egypt and deliver such as were for death to death and such as were for the sword to the sword (Jeremiah 43:8-13).

cases.name: Moab and Ammon
cases.charge: Moab: magnifying himself against the Lord, trusting in his works and his treasures, and skipping for joy at the derision of Israel. Ammon: saying Aha against the sanctuary when it was profaned, against the land of Israel when it was desolate, and against the house of Judah when they went into captivity
cases.summary: Jeremiah’s burden declared no more praise of Moab: because he trusted in his works and treasures, magnified himself against the Lord and skipped for joy at Israel’s derision, he would be spoiled and Chemosh carried into captivity (Jeremiah 48:1-2; Jeremiah 48:7; Jeremiah 48:26-27). Ammon, which said Aha when the sanctuary was profaned and Judah went into captivity, would be delivered to the men of the east (Ezekiel 25:3-4). Moab is the so-called Chinese and Ammon the so-called Japanese, and the judgment begun under Nebuchadnezzar has a latter-day fulfilment: the Lord will bring again the captivity of Moab in the latter days (Jeremiah 48:47).
offenseFull: Jeremiah 48 to 51 is our redemption, the salvation of Israel by way of the prophesied destruction of our enemies: Moab, the so-called Chinese; Ammon, the so-called Japanese; Edom, the so-called white man; Elam, the ancient and modern Persians and the East Indians; and Babylon, modern-day America. Moab and Ammon began when Lot’s daughters, thinking there was no man left on the earth, made their father drunk and bore Moab and Ben-ammi by him (Genesis 19:30-38). The elders taught in the nineties that Moab is the Chinese and Ammon the Japanese, before the books that confirm it were found; the Koreans are Ammon, and the Vietnamese and Mongolians are Moab. The burden begins with no more praise of Moab, and Madmen cut down (Jeremiah 48:1-2). God calls the so-called Chinese by the name Moab, and calls Moab madmen. Our people praise Moab quickly, and many say the next world superpower is China, but the prophecy says there shall be no more praise of Moab. The history the American Board of Education does not teach is Moab enslaving us during the Tang Dynasty and building whole industries off our people, and all of it will be answered for.

Moab had been at ease from his youth, settled on his lees, never emptied from vessel to vessel nor gone into captivity, so his taste remained in him and his scent was not changed (Jeremiah 48:11). Vessel to vessel is captivity to captivity: it happened to Israel, whose features vary from captivity to captivity, a cake not turned, but not to Moab, and Moab has not changed toward Israel from his beginning until now (Hosea 7:8). Moab would be ashamed of Chemosh as Israel was ashamed of Bethel, where Jeroboam set his calf; the horned gods of Chinese religion are like Baal, the calf god (Jeremiah 48:13; 1 Kings 12:28-33). Moab magnified himself against the Lord; Israel was a derision to him, and he skipped for joy because he helped destroy us and was happy about it (Jeremiah 48:26-27). If the Lord punished his own children, what makes the heathen think their time is not going to come? (Jeremiah 48:27). The Lord knew his pride, his loftiness and his arrogance; whatever Moab boasts of who will be destroyed, his lies shall not so effect it (Jeremiah 48:29-30). Ammon said Aha against the sanctuary when it was profaned, the land when it was desolate, and Judah when it went into captivity, and clapped and rejoiced at our destruction: Ammon laughed when we went into slavery (Ezekiel 25:3-6). Moab and Seir said the house of Judah is like all the heathen, that Judah is no longer the Most High’s chosen people (Ezekiel 25:8); the nations keep hidden the black images on the ancient walls of China, as Rome does in its catacombs.
judgmentFull: Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Moab then (Jeremiah 48:8), and the prophecy carries a duality: Moab is a world superpower today and will be destroyed once again, with Asia, which is partaker of the hope of Babylon (2 Esdras 15:46-49). Because Asia always slew the Most High’s chosen, as she did to them so shall God do to her (2 Esdras 15:53-56). Moab would leave the cities and dwell in the rock, which are China’s bunkers in the mountains (Jeremiah 48:28). The incense of the high places is China’s burning of incense to its gods, and the bald heads and clipped beards are the shaving of Moab, the same as the Mongolians next door (Jeremiah 48:35-37). He that judges shall fly as an eagle over Moab, and the eagle is the symbol of America (Jeremiah 48:40). Fear, the pit and the snare would take whoever fled, and the bunkers beneath the earth will not save them (Jeremiah 48:43-44).

For all that pride Moab will go back to its proper place and serve Israel: Moab is the Lord’s washpot, a pot wherein to wash the feet, a vessel of dishonour set beneath Israel as a servant, and the house of Israel shall possess the nations for servants and handmaids (Psalms 60:8; Isaiah 14:2). The Lord would bring again the captivity of Moab in the latter days; it has not happened yet, but it will come to pass (Jeremiah 48:47). Ammon would be delivered to the men of the east and cut off from the peoples, and Moab opened on its flank, so that Ammon would not be remembered among the nations (Ezekiel 25:4-11). That began with Nebuchadnezzar, followed by Persia and Media; the Lord moved Moab and Ammon from the coasts of Arnon to a further east country, Asia, China on the greater landmass and Japan on the outer coast, where no one calls them Moab and Ammon but Chinese and Japanese. By the time of the Maccabees the Arabs held the land of Ammon and of Moab, which America calls Jordan today (2 Maccabees 5:7-9). The judgment is the Lord’s, like a ring, a steady flow coming upon all nations; the task of Israel is not to harm anybody but to search the scriptures, identify the nations, tell what God says is coming, and come out from among them and be separate (2 Esdras 5:42; 2 Corinthians 6:17).
