cases.name: The priests who despised the Name
cases.charge: Despising the name of the Lord: offering polluted bread upon His altar and the blind, the lame, and the sick for sacrifice, calling His table contemptible; departing out of the way, causing many to stumble at the law, corrupting the covenant of Levi, and being partial in the law
cases.summary: When Nehemiah went back to the king, the Lord raised up Malachi to keep the people in line until he returned, and with Nehemiah gone the priests went back to what they were doing before (Nehemiah 13:6). They despised the name of the Lord, offering polluted bread and the blind, the lame, and the sick on His altar (Malachi 1:6-8). Because they departed out of the way, caused many to stumble at the law, and were partial in the law, He cursed their blessings and made them contemptible and base before all the people (Malachi 2:1-9).
offenseFull: While Nehemiah was with the king, the Lord raised up Malachi to keep them in line until he was able to return (Nehemiah 13:6); once Nehemiah was out, the priests felt free to go back to what they were doing before. During the Persian captivity many of the chief priests and leaders made leagues with the other nations, causing the people to sin, and Eliashib the priest was allied to Tobiah (Nehemiah 13:4-7).

Malachi opens with the Lord’s love: He loved Jacob and hated Esau (Malachi 1:1-3). Edom said it would return and build the desolate places, which is Europe returning to its position of authority in the earth; but they shall build, and the Lord will throw down (Malachi 1:4). Edom is the so-called white people, called the border of wickedness, the people against whom the Lord has indignation for ever (Malachi 1:4). Border means the beginning or end of something: wherever confusion is found in the earth, especially concerning the sexes, the nations of Edom are the common denominator. Esau dwelt in mount Seir, the clefts of the rock, whose pride deceived him (Genesis 36:8; Obadiah 1:3).

The Lord asked the priests that despise His name where His honour was (Malachi 1:6). That is spoken to Levi: the polluted bread on His altar shows it, for Levi were the priests doing the sacrifices (Malachi 1:7). They called His table contemptible; they hated serving the Lord and doing the sacrifices. They offered the blind, the lame, and the sick, and He told them to offer it to their governor (Malachi 1:8); the governor is Nehemiah, who was gone for a time. The priests were finessing the offerings, keeping the best animals for themselves and sacrificing the blind and the broken, and they perverted the teachings of the law for their own benefit.

The priest’s lips should keep knowledge, the laws of God, for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts (Malachi 2:7). Levi once turned the other tribes from iniquity; now Levi caused them to sin and broke the covenant (Malachi 2:6-8). Judah married the daughter of a strange god, for in the time of Persia Israel fell into marrying the other nations and assimilating; the wife of thy youth is their own women, whom Israel put away for the women of other nations (Malachi 2:11-16).
judgmentFull: If the priests would not lay it to heart to give glory to His name, He would curse their blessings, and He had cursed them already (Malachi 2:1-2). Giving glory to His name means the offerings on His altar, going back to the first chapter, not saying a name with some special pronunciation. He would corrupt their seed and spread the dung of their solemn feasts on their faces (Malachi 2:3), and that is literal as well.

Because they had not kept His ways and had been partial in the law, He made them contemptible and base before all the people (Malachi 2:9). Levi ate well through the sacrifices, because the Lord was their provider; all they had to do was teach Israel the commandments of God. But they corrupted the covenant, left off teaching the law, and were partial in it, so the Lord gave them a swift and mighty judgment. That is why Levi, identified in the land of Haiti, has been the poorest in the western hemisphere to this day: their provider was the Lord, and they departed out of the way. Levi is the basest of the twelve tribes, because of sin.

When Nehemiah returned he chased away the high priest’s grandson, son in law to Sanballat, and asked God to remember them, because they had defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites (Nehemiah 13:28-29). That is Malachi: during the Persian captivity Levi was partial in the law.

The only way it can change is for Levi to repent and come back to the law of God, and that is for all twelve tribes. The Lord will purify the sons of Levi as a refiner of silver, that they may offer in righteousness: if Levi repents, he will still receive the kingdom (Malachi 3:3). The high priest today is Christ, and the nation is a whole nation of kings and priests.

cases.name: Judah robbing God in tithes and offerings
cases.charge: Going away from the Lord’s ordinances; robbing God in tithes and offerings by not taking care of Levi, so that there was no meat in His house and the Levites fled every one to his field
cases.summary: From the days of their fathers Judah had gone away from the Lord’s ordinances, and when He called them to return and they asked how, He answered that they had robbed Him in tithes and offerings (Malachi 3:7-8). The other tribes were not taking care of Levi, and the whole nation was cursed with a curse (Malachi 3:9). In Nehemiah’s day the portions of the Levites had not been given, and the Levites had fled every one to his field (Nehemiah 13:10).
offenseFull: The Lord does not change, and the sons of Jacob had gone away from His ordinances; He asked whether a man would rob God, and said they had robbed Him in tithes and offerings (Malachi 3:6-8).

The tithe of the law is the increase of the seed that the field brings forth year by year, the corn, the wine, the oil, and the firstlings of the herds and flocks, not money, eaten before the Lord in the place He chose, which is Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 14:22-23; 2 Chronicles 6:6). If the way was too far, it was turned into money, but the money was taken to Jerusalem and turned back into the tithe (Deuteronomy 14:24-26). The Levite within the gates was not to be forsaken, for he had no part nor inheritance, and the tithe also fed the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow (Deuteronomy 14:27-29).

The robbery was that the other eleven tribes were not taking care of Levi. Levi had no allotment of land, was scattered among the tribes, and did the service of the Lord, atoning for Israel’s sins; the tithes were to take care of him, and Israel was not showing charity, loving their brothers the Levites as themselves. They gave the lame animals, not the best of the flocks, when the Lord required the best.

The people had sworn to bring the tithes of their ground to the Levites (Nehemiah 10:37). The tithes go to the Levites, for the Levite was the one ordained to receive them, and a pastor over a church today is most likely not a Levite. Yet Eliashib the priest gave Tobiah a great chamber where the tithes had been laid, and the Levites’ portions were not given; Nehemiah cast out Tobiah’s stuff, contended with the rulers, set the Levites in their place, and Judah brought the tithe of the corn, the wine, and the oil into the treasuries (Nehemiah 13:4-13).
judgmentFull: They were cursed with a curse, even the whole nation (Malachi 3:9). Not taking care of Levi, who atoned for their sin, brought the curse down on all: no rain, and the crops would not be right; by not taking care of Levi they robbed the whole nation.

The Lord told them to bring all the tithes into the storehouse, that there might be meat in His house, and to prove Him (Malachi 3:10). The storehouse held the increase of corn, wine, and oil (2 Chronicles 32:28): food to eat, not the pastor’s bank account. The tithe was stored so that Levi could survive while he maintained the tabernacle; the forefathers laid it up three years and prepared for famine (Deuteronomy 14:28). The windows of heaven are the rain, as at the flood, the good treasure the Lord opens to give rain in its season (Genesis 7:11; Deuteronomy 28:12), not money raining down or a check in the mail.

The devourer is the locust and the caterpillar, anything that eats the crops or the stores (Psalms 105:34); when the nation is righteous He rebukes it so it destroys not the fruit of the ground, and all nations would call Israel blessed, a delightsome land, as when famine sent the nations down to Egypt (Malachi 3:11-12).

Pastors use this scripture to guilt the congregation into giving money, while keeping no other law; it speaks of food for Levi in Jerusalem. The tithe cannot be kept that way now: Israel is scattered among all people, the Lord Himself will set them in their own land, and the priesthood has been changed out of Levi to Judah (Deuteronomy 28:64; Isaiah 14:1; Hebrews 7:11-14). The tithe was tied to the Levitical priesthood; the duty now is alms.

cases.name: Tobit
cases.charge: Walking in truth and justice all his days; alms, tithes, and burying the dead of his people at the risk of his own life
cases.summary: Tobit was carried into Assyria with the tribe of Nephthali, and while his tribe sacrificed to the calf he alone kept the feasts at Jerusalem and brought the firstfruits and the tenths, giving the third year tithe to the orphans as his grandmother Debora had taught him (Tobit 1:3-8). In Nineveh he clothed the naked and buried the brethren the king had killed and left lying about the walls, and for it he was informed on, hunted, and stripped of everything he owned (Tobit 1:16-20). After one such burial he slept beside his courtyard wall and lost his sight, and the affliction stood until Raphael was sent, who told him that his prayers and his burials had been carried up before the Holy One (Tobit 2:1-10; Tobit 12:12-15).
offenseFull: Tobit says of himself that he walked all the days of his life in the way of truth and justice and did many alms deeds to his brethren (Tobit 1:3). His whole tribe revolted to the calf, and he alone went often to Jerusalem at the feasts with the firstfruits and the tenths, giving the first tenth to the sons of Aaron, spending the second at Jerusalem, and giving the third to those it was owed to, as Debora his father’s mother had commanded him, because he had been left an orphan himself (Tobit 1:4-8). That third year tithe is the provision the law names for the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 14:22-29), and the teaching carries it across: our fathers stopped paying what belonged to them, and the record says we are still in captivity and subject to payments because of it (Baruch 3:8). A man keeping that tithe in a strange land is keeping the nation.

In Nineveh he gave his bread to the hungry and his clothes to the naked, and when he saw any of his nation dead or cast about the walls he buried him, including the men Sennacherib had killed in his wrath and thrown out (Tobit 1:16-18). The nation has a law on this: wherever the dead are found they are to be taken up and buried (2 Esdras 2:23), with tears over the dead, the body covered according to the custom, and the burial not neglected (Ecclesiasticus 38:16). The teaching sets it beside our own captivity, where our dead were left hanging and displayed on purpose. To present the body a living sacrifice is not a private religion, it is a life spent on the nation (Romans 12:1). A Ninevite reported him, he was sought to be put to death, and all his goods were taken by force (Tobit 1:19-20), just as the captivity warns that they will spoil those that fear God and take their goods, and then the chosen are tried as gold in the fire (2 Esdras 16:71-73). At Pentecost he sent his son to bring in a poor man of their brethren who was mindful of the Lord, which is the wisdom of knowing to whom a man does good (Tobit 2:1-2; Ecclesiasticus 12:1-4). Word came instead that one of the nation had been strangled and cast into the marketplace; he left his meal untasted, took up the body, and ate afterward in heaviness because the prophet had said the feasts would be turned into mourning (Tobit 2:3-6). His neighbours mocked him, and that night the sparrows blinded him and the physicians could not help (Tobit 2:7-10).
judgmentFull: Blind, he still kept order in his house, telling his wife to take back a kid she had been given rather than eat what might be stolen. She answered him by naming his alms and his righteous deeds and telling him that all his works were known (Tobit 2:11-14). Blessed is the man that considers the poor, for the Lord will deliver him in the time of trouble (Psalms 41:1), and the righteous considers the cause of the poor while the wicked does not care to know it (Proverbs 29:7). Out of that same mind he charged his son to be mindful of the Lord all his days, to give alms of his substance, and not to turn his face from any poor man, because alms deliver from death (Tobit 4:5-11).

Raphael told them that it is honourable to reveal the works of God, that prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness, and that it is better to give alms than to lay up gold (Tobit 12:6-9). Treasure laid up according to the commandments brings more profit than gold, and alms stored up deliver from affliction and fight

against the enemy better than a mighty shield and a strong spear (Ecclesiasticus 29:11-13). Then he told Tobit why he had come: when Tobit prayed, and when he buried the dead, and when he did not delay to rise up and leave his dinner to go and cover a body, the angel was with him and carried the remembrance of those prayers before the Holy One (Tobit 12:12-15). He charged them to praise God and not to be slack in it, and to write everything in a book, which is why the account is here at all (Romans 15:4). Tobit received his sight and saw his son (Tobit 11:7-15). At the end he told Tobias to keep the law and the commandments, to show himself merciful and just, and to leave Nineveh because what the prophet Jonas spoke would surely come to pass; his son obeyed him, departed, and lived to hear of the destruction of the city (Tobit 14:1-2; Tobit 14:11-15).

cases.offense: Tobit says of himself that he walked all the days of his life in the way of truth and justice and did many alms deeds to his brethren (Tobit 1:3). His whole tribe revolted to the calf, and he alone went often to Jerusalem at the feasts with the firstfruits and the tenths, giving the first tenth to the sons of Aaron, spending the second at Jerusalem, and giving the third to those it was owed to, as Debora his father’s mother had commanded him, because he had been left an orphan himself (Tobit 1:4-8). That third year tithe is the provision the law names for the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 14:22-29), and the teaching carries it across: our fathers stopped paying what belonged to them, and the record says we are still in captivity and subject to payments because of it (Baruch 3:8). A man keeping that tithe in a strange land is keeping the nation.
cases.judgment: Blind, he still kept order in his house, telling his wife to take back a kid she had been given rather than eat what might be stolen. She answered him by naming his alms and his righteous deeds and telling him that all his works were known (Tobit 2:11-14). Blessed is the man that considers the poor, for the Lord will deliver him in the time of trouble (Psalms 41:1), and the righteous considers the cause of the poor while the wicked does not care to know it (Proverbs 29:7). Out of that same mind he charged his son to be mindful of the Lord all his days, to give alms of his substance, and not to turn his face from any poor man, because alms deliver from death (Tobit 4:5-11).

cases.name: Aman, who ensnared Achiacharus
cases.charge: Treachery against the man who brought him up
cases.summary: Achiacharus was Tobit’s brother’s son, cupbearer, keeper of the signet, steward and overseer of the accounts under the king at Nineveh, and it was he who interceded for Tobit and brought him home, and who nourished him while he was blind (Tobit 1:21-22; Tobit 2:10). Tobit’s dying counsel holds up one case against that kindness: remember how Aman handled Achiacharus who brought him up, how out of light he brought him into darkness, and how he was rewarded for it (Tobit 14:10). Achiacharus was saved, and the man who laid the snare fell into it and perished.
offenseFull: The record first shows Achiacharus in office. He was Anael’s son, Tobit’s brother’s son, and the king set him next to himself as cupbearer, keeper of the signet, steward and overseer of the accounts, and he entreated for Tobit so that Tobit could return to Nineveh after his goods had been seized and his life sought for burying the dead (Tobit 1:21-22). When Tobit was blinded, it was Achiacharus who nourished him until he went into Elymais (Tobit 2:10). Everything the man had, Aman had from him. That is the weight of the charge. The teaching on this chapter puts it in one line: you do good and good follows you, you do evil and evil follows you. The injury was not hostility between strangers; it was the return made for the care that had raised him.

Tobit sets the case down at the very end of his life, in the middle of his charge to his son to keep the law and the commandments and to show himself merciful (Tobit 14:9-10). He does not tell the story for its own sake. He tells it as the counterweight to the instruction, because a son who has just been told to be merciful and just needs also to be told what it looks like when a man takes kindness and turns it into an opportunity. The whole book has been arguing that alms and righteousness are what a man is measured by, and here is the man who was fed by another man’s righteousness and used it against him.
judgmentFull: Aman brought his benefactor out of light into darkness, and the reward came back on him: Achiacharus was saved, and the other had his reward, for he went down into darkness (Tobit 14:10). Tobit names the pattern twice over in the same breath, setting Manasses, who gave alms and escaped the snare of death, beside Aman, who fell into the snare and perished (Tobit 14:10). The same two ends are what the wisdom of the fathers teaches about a pit dug for another man and a net laid in secret (Proverbs 26:27; Psalms 35:7-8), and the deliverance of Achiacharus is of a piece with the deliverance of Tobit himself, who was restored and whose nephew came to rejoice with him (Tobit 11:18).

Tobit draws the conclusion himself and gives it to his son as the last thing he says before he dies: consider what alms do, and how righteousness delivers (Tobit 14:11). The teaching on the chapter reads the case exactly that way, as a father’s final advice rather than a story about a villain. The betrayer did not obtain what he intended. The man he wronged lived, the snare took its own maker, and the lesson set beside the charge to keep the law and be merciful is that a man is not saved by his position at the king’s right hand but by what he does with the mercy he has received.

cases.name: Holofernes
cases.charge: Making Nebuchadnezzar a god; blasphemy against the God of Israel; lust and drunkenness
cases.summary: Nabuchodonosor sent his chief captain Holofernes with a great host to bring every nation under him and to destroy all their gods, so that he alone should be called god (Judith 2:4-13; Judith 3:8). When Achior warned him that this people is only overcome when it sins against its own God, he answered that Nabuchodonosor alone is god and gave Achior over to the men of Bethulia (Judith 6:2-4). He besieged the city, and the widow Judith came down to his camp; he drank more wine at her banquet than he had ever drunk in one day, and she took his own sword and struck off his head (Judith 12:16-20; Judith 13:6-10).
offenseFull: The teaching sets this campaign in the Persian period, after the return. The temple was standing and newly sanctified, the people were lately gathered out of the Babylonian captivity, and Joacim, the son of Jeshua the son of Josedec, was high priest and wrote to the men of Bethulia to keep the passages of the hill country (Judith 4:1-8; Nehemiah 12:10; Nehemiah 12:26). The king had just broken Arphaxad in the plain of Ragau, taken Ecbatane, and turned its beauty into shame, and out of that victory he commissioned Holofernes to take vengeance on all the earth (Judith 1:13-15; Judith 2:1-6). The commission was not tribute only. Every place was to destroy its own gods so that all nations should serve Nabuchodonosor and all tongues call on him as a god (Judith 3:8). That is the charge: a man made the instrument of turning worship itself over to a king.

Achior, the captain of the Ammonites, gave him the history of the nation plainly, that as long as they did not sin before their God it went well with them, and that when they departed from the way he had appointed they were destroyed

and carried away, but that if there is no iniquity in them their Lord will defend them (Judith 5:17-21). The teaching lingers on that warning because the nations have always known it. It is the same counsel the enemy’s own records preserve, where men who came against this people were told by their own advisers to leave them alone because their God is the true God and the writing on their tablets is true; the enemy studies to know when we are in sin, because that is the only ground he has. Holofernes would not hear it. He asked who is God but Nabuchodonosor, said the God of Israel would not save his people, and had Achior bound and carried to Bethulia to perish with the people he had defended (Judith 6:2-4; Judith 6:10-13). His confidence was in the numbers of his army, and his answer to a true report was to punish the man who brought it.
judgmentFull: The thing that undid him was not the siege. Judith came down with her maid and was received into his tent, and on the fourth day he made a banquet to his own servants and called for her, saying in his heart that it would be a shame to let such a woman go; and he drank much more wine than he had ever drunk in any one day since he was born (Judith 12:10-20). The captain who had frightened cities into surrender was left alone and helpless in his own tent, filled with wine and lying along on his bed.

Judith stood by his bed and prayed for strength, took down his own sword from the pillar, took him by the hair of his head, and struck twice upon his neck and took away his head (Judith 13:4-8). She gave it to her maid, who put it in the bag of meat, and the two of them went out through the camp by the way they had gone every night to prayer, so that nobody stopped them (Judith 13:9-10). At Bethulia she called the watchmen to open the gate and gave God the praise (Judith 13:11-14), and she had the head hung on the highest place of the wall and told the men to go out at dawn as though they would come down to the plain (Judith 14:1-4). When Bagoas went in to wake his lord and found the body with the head taken away, he cried out, and the whole army was struck with fear and confusion and fled, and Israel pursued and took the spoil (Judith 14:14-19; Judith 15:1-7). Judith’s song puts the whole account in one sentence: the Almighty Lord disappointed them by the hand of a woman (Judith 16:5-6), which is the very thing she had asked for when she prayed that the strength of a woman would smite the man who had purposed cruel things against the sanctuary (Judith 9:7-10).

cases.name: Judith
cases.charge: A widow who feared God greatly, fasting all the days of her widowhood; going out to Holofernes in the name of the Lord
cases.summary: Judith was a widow of Bethulia who had kept sackcloth and fasted every day of her widowhood except the eves of the sabbaths and feasts, and who had refused every man since her husband died (Judith 8:4-8). When the governors promised to surrender the city in five days if God did not help, she told them they were tempting God and putting his counsel to a term of their own making (Judith 8:11-17). She prayed, went down to the Assyrian camp with her maid, kept her own food and her own hours of prayer, and came back with the head of Holofernes (Judith 9:1-14; Judith 12:1-9; Judith 13:4-10). She gave his goods to the sanctuary, and nobody made Israel afraid in her days or for a long time after her death.
offenseFull: The account is careful to say what she was before the crisis came. Her husband Manasses had died in the barley harvest and left her gold and silver, menservants and maidservants, cattle and lands, and she remained upon them, a woman of goodly countenance and very beautiful to look upon (Judith 8:2-8). She made a tent on the roof of her house, put sackcloth on her loins, wore her widow’s apparel, and fasted all the days of her widowhood except the eves of the sabbaths and the sabbaths, the eves of the new moons and the new moons, and the feasts and solemn days of the house of Israel, and none gave her an ill word, for she feared God greatly (Judith 8:5-8). The teaching reads that as loyalty, and reads it both ways: her husband had been loyal to her in leaving the house in order, and she answered it by refusing to give another man what he had provided, and by giving that time to God and to the people instead.

When Ozias and the governors had sworn to deliver the city in five days unless God sent rain, she sent for them and told them that they had no right to bind the counsel of God to a term, that God is not as a man to be threatened, and that they should call on him and remember how the fathers were tried; she set before them what the loss of the city and the sanctuary would mean, and asked them to look to her instead (Judith 8:11-27). Then she prayed, rehearsing what God had done by the hand of Simeon, and asked for the power of a widow’s

hand against the man who had purposed to defile the sanctuary and to cast down the horn of the altar with a sword (Judith 9:1-14). She put off the sackcloth and the garments of her widowhood only for this, washed and anointed herself, braided her hair and put on the garments of gladness she had worn while her husband lived, and decked herself to draw the eyes of every man who should see her (Judith 10:3-4). In the camp she kept the distinction she had made. She would not eat the king’s meat but ate what her maid carried, and she asked leave to go out every night into the valley to wash and pray, which is how she walked out of the camp at the end with nobody stopping her (Judith 12:1-9).
judgmentFull: On the fourth night the captain was left alone with her, full of wine, and she prayed for strength, took his own sword from the pillar of the bed, and struck off his head; her maid carried it out in the bag of meat and the two of them walked out as they had walked out every other night (Judith 13:4-10). She would take no credit for it; she told the men at the gate that God had not taken away his mercy from the house of Israel, and Ozias blessed her above all the women upon the earth, and all the people said amen (Judith 13:14-20). When the host was broken, the people of every coast fell on it, and the men of Israel returned from the slaughter and gave her the tent of Holofernes and all his plate and beds and vessels and furniture (Judith 15:8-11).

The last chapter is where the teaching puts the weight. Judith dedicated all the stuff of Holofernes that the people had given her, and gave the canopy she had taken out of his bedchamber for a gift to the Lord (Judith 16:19). She gave the spoil back. Then she returned to Bethulia and remained in her own possession, honourable in all the country; many desired her and no man knew her all the days of her life after Manasses died, and she set her maid at liberty and distributed her goods to her husband’s kindred before she died at a hundred and five years old (Judith 16:21-24). Israel lamented her seven days, and there was none that made the children of Israel afraid in the days of Judith, nor a long time after her death (Judith 16:24-25). Deliverance did not end in a monument to herself. It ended in the sanctuary being paid, her house set in order, and the nation left unafraid.

cases.name: Susanna
cases.charge: Choosing to fall into the hands of the elders rather than sin in the sight of the Lord
cases.summary: Susanna was the daughter of Chelcias and the wife of Joacim in Babylon, a woman that feared the Lord, whose righteous parents had taught her according to the law of Moses (Susanna 1:1-4). Two elders appointed judges that year hid in her husband’s garden and demanded that she lie with them, threatening to swear that they had caught her with a young man if she refused (Susanna 1:19-21). She answered that if she did it, it was death, and if she did not, she could not escape their hands, and that it was better for her to fall into their hands than to sin in the sight of the Lord; she cried out with a loud voice, and they cried out against her (Susanna 1:22-24).
offenseFull: The account begins with how she was raised. Her parents were righteous and taught their daughter according to the law of Moses, and she feared the Lord (Susanna 1:2-3). The teaching stops there to say what that is worth, that a woman trained from a youth in the law is a different woman under pressure, and that the training is the whole reason the next scene goes the way it does. The two elders appointed judges that year kept much at her husband’s house, where every suit at law came before them (Susanna 1:4-6). They saw her walking in the garden every day and their lust was inflamed, and they perverted their own mind and turned away their eyes so as not to look toward heaven or remember just judgments (Susanna 1:7-9). The sin is named in the teaching before it is acted: it begins as coveting a neighbour’s possession, and it is already adultery in the heart before any hand is laid on anybody (Matthew 5:27-28).

When she had sent the maids for oil and washing balls and shut the garden doors, the two ran to her and said that nobody could see them, and that if she would not consent they would bear witness that a young man had been with her (Susanna 1:15-21). She sighed and said that she was straitened on every side, that to do this thing was death, and that not to do it would not save her from their hands, and then said the sentence the charge is drawn from, that it was better for her to fall into their hands and not do it than to sin in the sight of the Lord (Susanna 1:22-23). She made the calculation deliberately, and chose the death she could see over the guilt she could not undo. Then she cried with a loud voice, and the elders cried out against her, and one ran and opened the garden door so that the servants rushed in and heard their version first (Susanna 1:24-27).
judgmentFull: The next day the assembly gathered at her husband’s house and the two elders came full of mischievous imagination to put her to death (Susanna 1:28-29). She came with her father and mother, her children and all her kindred, and the wicked men commanded that her face be uncovered, for she was covered, so that they might be filled with her beauty (Susanna 1:30-32). Her friends wept, the elders laid their hands on her head, and she, weeping, looked up toward heaven, for her heart trusted in the Lord (Susanna 1:33-35). That is the exact contrast the teaching draws with the two men who had turned their eyes away so as not to look toward heaven. They told the assembly that they had seen her with a young man too strong for them to hold, and the assembly believed them because they were the elders and judges of the people, and condemned her to death (Susanna 1:36-41). Trust no brother and put no confidence in a friend is not cynicism but the warning of the prophets for exactly such a day (Jeremiah 9:4-6; Micah 7:5).

Then Susanna cried out with a loud voice to the everlasting God that knows the secrets and knows all things before they be, saying that they had borne false witness against her and that she must die having never done the things they had maliciously invented, and the Lord heard her voice (Susanna 1:42-44). The teaching makes the practical point here for anyone accused where there is no evidence either way and it is one word against another: the matter has to be taken to God and left with him until he reveals it, and he did. As she was led out to die, God raised up the holy spirit of a young youth whose name was Daniel, who cried out that he was clear from the blood of this woman and rebuked the assembly for condemning a daughter of Israel without examination (Susanna 1:45-49). He had the two put apart, asked each under what tree he saw them, and got a mastick tree from one and a holm tree from the other, and told each that he had lied against his own head (Susanna 1:50-59). The assembly praised God that saves them that trust in him, and did to the two men what they had maliciously intended to do to their neighbour, according to the law of Moses (Susanna 1:60-62). Innocent blood was saved that day, her parents and her husband and all her kindred praised God because there was no dishonesty found in her, and from that day Daniel was held in great reputation in the sight of the people (Susanna 1:63-64).

cases.offense: The account begins with how she was raised. Her parents were righteous and taught their daughter according to the law of Moses, and she feared the Lord (Susanna 1:2-3). The teaching stops there to say what that is worth, that a woman trained from a youth in the law is a different woman under pressure, and that the training is the whole reason the next scene goes the way it does. The two elders appointed judges that year kept much at her husband’s house, where every suit at law came before them (Susanna 1:4-6). They saw her walking in the garden every day and their lust was inflamed, and they perverted their own mind and turned away their eyes so as not to look toward heaven or remember just judgments (Susanna 1:7-9). The sin is named in the teaching before it is acted: it begins as coveting a neighbour’s possession, and it is already adultery in the heart before any hand is laid on anybody (Matthew 5:27-28).
cases.judgment: The next day the assembly gathered at her husband’s house and the two elders came full of mischievous imagination to put her to death (Susanna 1:28-29). She came with her father and mother, her children and all her kindred, and the wicked men commanded that her face be uncovered, for she was covered, so that they might be filled with her beauty (Susanna 1:30-32). Her friends wept, the elders laid their hands on her head, and she, weeping, looked up toward heaven, for her heart trusted in the Lord (Susanna 1:33-35). That is the exact contrast the teaching draws with the two men who had turned their eyes away so as not to look toward heaven. They told the assembly that they had seen her with a young man too strong for them to hold, and the assembly believed them because they were the elders and judges of the people, and condemned her to death (Susanna 1:36-41). Trust no brother and put no confidence in a friend is not cynicism but the warning of the prophets for exactly such a day (Jeremiah 9:4-6; Micah 7:5).

cases.name: The two elders who accused Susanna
cases.charge: Attempted adultery by extortion; false witness against an innocent woman
cases.summary: Two ancients of the people were appointed judges that year, of whom the Lord had said that wickedness came from Babylon from ancient judges who seemed to govern the people (Susanna 1:5). They saw Susanna walking daily in her husband’s garden, perverted their own mind, and turned away their eyes so as not to look toward heaven nor remember just judgments (Susanna 1:6-9). They hid themselves, demanded that she lie with them, and when she refused they swore before the assembly that they had taken her with a young man (Susanna 1:19-21; Susanna 1:36-41). Daniel examined them apart, their answers did not agree, and the assembly did to them what they had intended for her.
offenseFull: The record marks them as judges before adulterers, and the teaching sets the case among leaders bound in their own sin: Eli’s sons, who lay with the women at the door of the tabernacle and made the Lord’s people to transgress (1 Samuel 2:22-25), and the man who says a man should not commit adultery and commits it, through whom the name of God is blasphemed (Romans 2:21-24). These two kept much at Joacim’s house, where every suit at law came, and used the standing it gave them (Susanna 1:6). Their lust was inflamed by watching her, and the teaching traces the order of it: coveting comes first and is already adultery in the heart, and the watching day after day carries a man from the thought to the act (Matthew 5:27-28; Susanna 1:7-12). They were ashamed to declare it even to each other until they were caught in the same place, and then appointed a time together (Susanna 1:10-14). A man who goes on until he is bound with his sins is past the reach of a scripture (2 Esdras 16:77).

They hid in the garden, and when she sent the maids away they rose up and ran to her, saying that nobody could see them, and that if she would not consent they would bear witness that a young man had been with her (Susanna 1:15-21). When she cried out, they cried out against her, and one of them opened the garden door so that the servants would come in on their account of it (Susanna 1:24-27). The next day they came to the assembly full of mischievous imagination to put her to death, and commanded that her face be uncovered, that they might be filled with her beauty even while they were killing her (Susanna 1:28-32). Then they laid their hands upon her head and testified that a young man had come to her and been too strong for them to hold, and the assembly believed them as the elders and judges of the people and condemned her to death (Susanna 1:34-41). It is what the law forbids in one line, not to raise a false report nor put the hand with the wicked (Exodus 23:1).
judgmentFull: The Lord heard her voice and raised up the spirit of a young youth named Daniel, who cried that he was clear from the blood of this woman and rebuked the assembly for condemning a daughter of Israel without examination, and he had the two put apart, one far from another (Susanna 1:44-52). To the first he said that he was waxen old in wickedness, that the sins he had committed before were come to

light, and that he had pronounced false judgment, condemning the innocent and letting the guilty go free; then he asked under what tree he had seen them, got a mastick tree, and told him he had lied against his own head and that the angel of God had the sentence to cut him in two (Susanna 1:52-55). To the second he said that beauty had deceived him and lust had perverted his heart, that this was how the two had dealt with the daughters of Israel, who for fear kept company with them, but that the daughter of Juda would not abide their wickedness; he asked the same question, got a holm tree, and gave the same answer (Susanna 1:56-59). The teaching notes the name Daniel uses for him, seed of Chanaan and not of Juda, read the way Ezekiel reads it, that a man of the nation who goes on in this becomes another nation in his conduct (Ezekiel 16:3).

The whole assembly praised God that saves them that trust in him and rose up against the two elders, because Daniel had convicted them of false witness by their own mouth; then, according to the law of Moses, they did to them as they had maliciously intended to do to their neighbour and put them to death, and innocent blood was saved that day (Susanna 1:60-62). That is the statute exactly: when a witness testifies falsely against his brother, what he thought to have done to his brother is done to him, and the evil is put away (Deuteronomy 19:16-19). The teaching closes on what a lying tongue can do, that a backbiting tongue has disquieted many, pulled down strong cities and cast out virtuous women (Ecclesiasticus 28:14-15), and on the company such a charge puts a man in, since false witnesses rose against David, against Christ, and against the apostles (Psalms 27:12; Psalms 35:11; Matthew 26:59-60; Acts 6:13). It adds one warning to everyone else in the room: the man who sees an unrighteous judgment and stays quiet will answer for it with the one who began it (Proverbs 24:10-12).

cases.name: The priests of Bel
cases.charge: Deceiving the king and the people with an idol that seemed to eat
cases.summary: When Astyages was gathered to his fathers and Cyrus of Persia received his kingdom, Daniel was the king’s companion and honoured above all his friends, and the Babylonians had an idol called Bel on which twelve great measures of fine flour, forty sheep and six vessels of wine were spent every day (Bel and the Dragon 1:1-3). The king worshipped it and went daily to adore it, and asked Daniel why he did not, since Bel ate and drank so much every day; Daniel answered that it was clay within and brass without and had never eaten or drunk anything (Bel and the Dragon 1:4-7). The seventy priests had made a privy entrance under the table, by which they and their wives and children came in continually and consumed the provision (Bel and the Dragon 1:10-13).
offenseFull: The history of the destruction of Bel and the Dragon was cut off from the end of Daniel, and it opens where Astyages, Cyrus’s grandfather on his mother’s side, died and Cyrus received the kingdom, with Darius the Mede reigning under him, the same Darius who set Daniel first of the three presidents (Bel and the Dragon 1:1-2; Daniel 6:1-3). Bel is Baal, the same name shortened, and when the Medes and Persians took Babylon they kept the gods of the city they had conquered; one landlord replaced another and the tenants went on with the same worship. The expense is the point of the record: twelve great measures of fine flour, forty sheep and six vessels of wine, every day, out of the king’s own revenue, for a thing that could not move (Bel and the Dragon 1:3). The prophets say what such a thing is: the idols of the heathen are upright as a palm tree and cannot speak, and must be carried (Jeremiah 10:3-5); they cannot hear a prayer or move a foot (Epistle of Jeremy 1:26-28); and they that make a graven image are all of them vanity (Isaiah 44:9-11).

The king asked why Daniel did not worship, and he answered that he worshipped no idols made with hands but the living God who created heaven and earth (Bel and the Dragon 1:4-6), which is the second commandment kept in front of a king (Exodus 20:4-5). When the king insisted that Bel was living because of how much he ate and drank, Daniel smiled and said it was clay within and brass without (Bel and

the Dragon 1:7). The king then called his priests and told them that if they did not say who devoured the expenses they would die, and that if they could certify him that Bel devoured them, Daniel would die for blasphemy against Bel; and Daniel agreed to those terms (Bel and the Dragon 1:8-9). The seventy priests set the trap themselves. They told the king to go out, to set on the meat and the wine himself, and to shut the door and seal it with his own signet, and promised to suffer death if the food were not eaten (Bel and the Dragon 1:10-12). They regarded it little, because under the table they had made a privy entrance by which they entered in continually and consumed those things (Bel and the Dragon 1:13).
judgmentFull: Daniel had his servants bring ashes and strew them throughout the temple in the presence of the king alone, and then they went out, shut the door and sealed it (Bel and the Dragon 1:14). In the night the priests came with their wives and children, as they were accustomed, and ate and drank up all (Bel and the Dragon 1:15). The king rose early, was told that the seals were whole, opened the doors, saw the table empty and cried out that Bel was great and that there was no deceit at all in him (Bel and the Dragon 1:16-18). Then Daniel laughed, held him back from going in, and told him to mark the footsteps on the pavement; and the king said that he saw the footsteps of men, women and children (Bel and the Dragon 1:19-20). The witness against them was the floor.

The king was angry and took the priests with their wives and children, and they showed him the privy doors by which they came in and consumed the things upon the table, and he slew them (Bel and the Dragon 1:21-22). The teaching does not soften the sentence on the households, and explains what it turns on: they were all of one consent, the whole family in the enterprise together night after night, which is how a charge falls on everyone who kept it running and not only on the man at the head of it. The law gives the same sentence for a man who turns people away from the living God, that the evil be put away from among them (Deuteronomy 13:5). Bel himself was delivered into Daniel’s power, and he destroyed the idol and its temple (Bel and the Dragon 1:22). Then the king pressed him with the great dragon the Babylonians worshipped, saying that this one at least was alive; Daniel asked leave to kill it without sword or staff, made lumps of pitch, fat and hair, put them in its mouth, and it burst asunder (Bel and the Dragon 1:23-27). The men of Babylon then came against Daniel and had him cast into the lions’ den, and he was fed there by Habbacuc, taken up unhurt on the seventh day, and his accusers were cast in and devoured before him (Bel and the Dragon 1:28-32; Bel and the Dragon 1:40-42).

cases.name: The Hellenizers who forsook the holy covenant
cases.charge: Covenanting with the heathen; removing circumcision; profaning the Sabbath; sacrificing to idols
cases.summary: In the days of Antiochus Epiphanes wicked men went out of Israel and persuaded many, saying that they should make a covenant with the heathen round about, because since they had departed from them they had had much sorrow (1 Maccabees 1:11-12). They got the king’s licence to live after the ordinances of the heathen, built a place of exercise at Jerusalem after the custom of the heathen, made themselves uncircumcised and forsook the holy covenant (1 Maccabees 1:13-15). When the king wrote that all should be one people and every man leave his own laws, many of Israel consented to his religion, sacrificed to idols and profaned the sabbath (1 Maccabees 1:41-43; 1 Maccabees 1:52).
offenseFull: The complaint that started it is the oldest one we have, the same reasoning our fathers used in the wilderness about Egypt: the mind that measures the nation by how comfortable it is among the nations will always argue for the covenant that ends the discomfort. The device pleased them, certain of the people were forward in it, and they went to the king, who gave them licence (1 Maccabees 1:11-13). What they built with the licence was a place of exercise at Jerusalem according to the custom of the heathen, the gymnasium, the word itself meaning to exercise naked (1 Maccabees 1:14). Jason bought the office of high priest and paid extra for leave to set up that place, to train up the youth in the fashions of the heathen, and to have the men of Jerusalem written by the name of Antiochians, so that we could be entered on the register as Greeks (2 Maccabees 4:7-10). He brought his own nation to the Greekish fashion, put down the governments that were according to the law, brought the chief young men under his subjection and made them wear the hat, so

that the priests had no courage to serve any more at the altar but despised the temple, neglected the sacrifices and hurried out after the game of the discus, not setting by the honours of their fathers but liking the glory of the Grecians best of all (2 Maccabees 4:11-15). The teaching says that sentence is still describing our people: the glory of another society preferred to our own fathers, and men who will fight you for saying so.

Then they made themselves uncircumcised and forsook the holy covenant and joined themselves to the heathen, and were sold to do mischief (1 Maccabees 1:15). The law makes that a cutting off from the people (Genesis 17:14), as profaning the sabbath is a capital matter (Exodus 31:14), and the prophet had already said what the real condition was, that the house of Israel is uncircumcised in the heart (Jeremiah 9:25-26). When the king’s decree came that all should be one people and every man should leave his own laws, the heathen agreed, and many also of Israel consented to his religion, sacrificed to idols and profaned the sabbath (1 Maccabees 1:41-43), and many of the people resorted to the men who forsook the law and joined them (1 Maccabees 1:52). They also rent in pieces the books of the law that they found, and burnt them (1 Maccabees 1:56), which the teaching reads as the whole object of the campaign: cut the connection and the heritage goes, as the prophet said we would discontinue from the heritage given to us (Jeremiah 17:4), the law of life being that heritage (Ecclesiasticus 17:11). Paul is writing about this very history when he reminds the congregation that they were once carried away to dumb idols (1 Corinthians 12:2).
judgmentFull: Sore calamity came upon them, and the writer names the form of it exactly: they had those to be their enemies and avengers whose custom they had followed so earnestly and whom they had desired to be like in all things (2 Maccabees 4:16-17). The men who had asked for the covenant got the covenant and everything in it. Apollonius came with a pretence of peace and slew them on the sabbath, the temple they had traded away was called by the name of Jupiter Olympius and filled with riot, and the citizens they had made Greeks were sold as slaves like everybody else (2 Maccabees 5:24-26; 2 Maccabees 6:1-6).

Against them Mattathias and his company went about and pulled down the altars, circumcised by force the children that they found uncircumcised, pursued after the proud men, and recovered the law out of the hand of the Gentiles and of the kings (1 Maccabees 2:44-48); and Judas went through the cities of Juda destroying the ungodly out of them and turning away wrath from Israel (1 Maccabees 3:5-8). The end of the men who had led it is set down one by one. Jason, who had undermined his own brother, was undermined by Menelaus and fled to the Ammonites; he obtained not the principality but at the last received shame for the reward of his treason, fled from city to city, pursued of all men, hated as a forsaker of the laws and abhorred as an open enemy of his country, was cast out into Egypt, and he that had driven many out of their country perished in a strange land, and he that had cast out many unburied had none to mourn for him (2 Maccabees 5:5-10). The teaching draws the plain moral: nobody honours a traitor, not even the people he sold his own to.

cases.name: Apollonius
cases.charge: Falling upon Jerusalem on the Sabbath under a pretence of peace; slaying a great multitude; taking women and children captive
cases.summary: Two years after Antiochus had spoiled the sanctuary, the king sent his chief collector of tribute to the cities of Juda, and he came to Jerusalem with a great multitude and spoke peaceable words to them, but all was deceit (1 Maccabees 1:29-30). He was Apollonius, sent with twenty and two thousand men and commanded to slay all those that were in their best age and to sell the women and the younger sort; coming to Jerusalem and pretending peace, he waited for the sabbath, and when he took the Jews keeping the holy day he commanded his men to arm themselves and slew a great multitude (2 Maccabees 5:24-26). Judas met him in the field and killed him, and carried his sword all his life long (1 Maccabees 3:10-12).
offenseFull: The office he came in is part of the charge. He came as the chief collector of tribute, and the teaching stops on that word: tribute is the mark of a people in subjection, which is why Christ answered that the kings of the earth take custom of strangers and not of their own children (Matthew 17:24-27), why the question about the penny with Caesar’s image on it settled who the money belonged to (Mark 12:14-17), and why the record of the captivity says that we are scattered for a reproach and a curse and subject to payments (Baruch 3:8), the curse itself standing for a sign upon us and upon our seed (Deuteronomy 28:46). The Greeks who sent him were themselves vassals paying Rome, and they paid it with us, selling our people to make up what they owed.

He spoke peaceable words, but all was deceit (1 Maccabees 1:30). The psalm the teaching sets beside this describes the man exactly: he put forth his hands against such as be at peace with him and broke his covenant, the words of his mouth were smoother than butter but war was in his heart, his words were softer than oil, and they were drawn swords (Psalms 55:20-21). The teaching says this is not a single bad ambassador but a settled habit, and names the modern form of it, the smooth words spoken to our preachers and our neighbourhoods by men who deliver nothing afterward, and help that arrives carrying sickness. He timed the attack for the day he knew we would not fight, and killed men who had gone up to keep the sabbath (2 Maccabees 5:25-26; Exodus 31:14). When they had given him credence he fell suddenly upon the city, smote it very sore, destroyed much people of Israel, took the spoils, set it on fire, pulled down the houses and the walls on every side, took the women and children captive, and possessed the cattle (1 Maccabees 1:30-32). Then he fortified the city of David with a great wall and mighty towers and put there a sinful nation, wicked men, so that it became a sore snare and a place to lie in wait against the sanctuary, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fled because of them (1 Maccabees 1:33-38). The teaching reads the garrison as the thing we still live with, an armed presence quartered in our own streets whose work is to make the place unlivable. Her sanctuary was laid waste, her feasts were turned into mourning, her sabbaths into reproach, and her honour into contempt (1 Maccabees 1:39-40).
judgmentFull: Judas Maccabeus rose up in his father’s place, and his brethren helped him, and they fought the battle of Israel with cheerfulness (1 Maccabees 3:1-2). The reason the account gives for what followed is not numbers. Salvation prospered in his hand because he had taken to himself those that observed the law, as his father had charged him, and the workers of iniquity were troubled (1 Maccabees 2:67; 1 Maccabees 3:6). He received to himself such as were ready to perish, men who had already given up their own lives for the nation (1 Maccabees 3:9).

Then Apollonius gathered the Gentiles together and a great host out of Samaria to fight against Israel, and Judas, when he perceived it, went forth to meet him and smote him and slew him; many also fell down slain and the rest fled (1 Maccabees 3:10-11). Judas took their spoils, and he took the sword of Apollonius and fought with it all his life long (1 Maccabees 3:12). The man who had come in under a pretence of peace and struck on the holy day was met in the open field and killed, and his own weapon was carried afterward by the man who had kept the law he came to destroy.

cases.offense: The office he came in is part of the charge. He came as the chief collector of tribute, and the teaching stops on that word: tribute is the mark of a people in subjection, which is why Christ answered that the kings of the earth take custom of strangers and not of their own children (Matthew 17:24-27), why the question about the penny with Caesar’s image on it settled who the money belonged to (Mark 12:14-17), and why the record of the captivity says that we are scattered for a reproach and a curse and subject to payments (Baruch 3:8), the curse itself standing for a sign upon us and upon our seed (Deuteronomy 28:46). The Greeks who sent him were themselves vassals paying Rome, and they paid it with us, selling our people to make up what they owed.
cases.judgment: Judas Maccabeus rose up in his father’s place, and his brethren helped him, and they fought the battle of Israel with cheerfulness (1 Maccabees 3:1-2). The reason the account gives for what followed is not numbers. Salvation prospered in his hand because he had taken to himself those that observed the law, as his father had charged him, and the workers of iniquity were troubled (1 Maccabees 2:67; 1 Maccabees 3:6). He received to himself such as were ready to perish, men who had already given up their own lives for the nation (1 Maccabees 3:9).

cases.name: Antiochus Epiphanes
cases.charge: Defiling the temple; forbidding the law; murdering the faithful
cases.summary: Antiochus Epiphanes came out of the Seleucid line as a wicked root, a hostage at Rome who took the kingdom after his brother died, entered proudly into the sanctuary, carried off the golden altar, the candlestick and the hidden treasures, and made a great massacre and spoke very proudly (1 Maccabees 1:10; 1 Maccabees 1:20-24). He wrote to his whole kingdom that all should be one people and that every man should leave his own laws, forbade the burnt offering, the sabbath and the festivals, set the abomination of desolation upon the altar, and put to death the women who had circumcised their children (1 Maccabees 1:41-50; 1 Maccabees 1:54-64; 2 Maccabees 6:1-2). He died in a strange country of an incurable plague, eaten with worms and unbearable to his own army (2 Maccabees 9:5-12).
offenseFull: He called himself God manifest, and his own people renamed him Epimanes, the madman. The prophet had already drawn him: a little horn out of one of the four, waxing exceeding great toward the pleasant land, casting down some of the host and of the stars, magnifying himself even to the prince of the host, and taking away the daily sacrifice (Daniel 8:9-12; Daniel 11:31). After he had taken Egypt he turned on Jerusalem, went into the sanctuary and stripped it of the golden altar, the candlestick, the vessels, the table of the shewbread, the censers of gold, the veil, the crowns and the golden ornaments, and the hidden treasures he found (1 Maccabees 1:20-23). The teaching notes that he did not do this in Egypt: he went for the altar because he knew what our hearts were fixed on. Great mourning came on Israel in every place, and the house of Jacob was covered with confusion (1 Maccabees 1:25-28).

Then he made it law. He wrote that all should be one people and every man leave his own laws, forbade the offerings in the temple, commanded that the sabbaths and festival days be profaned, that altars of idols be set up, that swine’s flesh be offered, and that whoever would not do according to the word of the king should die (1 Maccabees 1:41-50). An old man of Athens was sent to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers; the temple was called by the name of Jupiter Olympius and filled with riot, the altar with profane things, and it was not lawful to keep the sabbath days or the ancient feasts or to profess oneself a Jew (2 Maccabees 6:1-6). On the king’s birthday they were compelled to eat of the sacrifices, and at the feast of Bacchus to go in procession with ivy (2 Maccabees 6:7). The teaching names the object: suppress the identity and the people forget who they are and who their God is, which is why the books of the law were rent in pieces and burnt (1 Maccabees 1:56-57). On the fifteenth day of Casleu the abomination of desolation was set upon the altar; they put to death the women who had caused their children to be circumcised and hanged the infants about their necks, and many in Israel chose rather to die than to be defiled with unclean meats (1 Maccabees 1:54-64).
judgmentFull: He went into Persia for money, the war in Judea having drained him, tried to rob the temple at Persepolis, was driven out and returned with shame; at Ecbatane he was told that Nicanor and Timotheus had been beaten (2 Maccabees 9:1-3). Swelling with anger, he drove without stopping and spoke proudly that he would make Jerusalem a common burying place of the Jews (2 Maccabees 9:4). As soon as he had said it, the Lord Almighty smote him with an incurable and invisible plague, a pain of the bowels that was remediless, and the writer says it was most just, since he had tormented other men’s bowels (2 Maccabees 9:5-6). He fell out of his chariot, so that every member of his body was in pain; worms rose up out of him, his flesh fell away while he lived, and the filthiness of his smell was so intolerable that no man could carry him (2 Maccabees 9:7-10). The man who thought he could weigh the mountains in a balance was carried in a horse litter.
Plagued, he began to leave off his great pride and to come to the knowledge of himself by the scourge of God, saying that it is fitting to be subject to God and that a mortal man should

not proudly think of himself as if he were God (2 Maccabees 9:11-12). He vowed to set the holy city at liberty, to make the Jews equal with the citizens of Athens, to garnish the temple out of his own revenue, and even to become a Jew himself; but for all this his pains would not cease, for the just judgment of God was come upon him (2 Maccabees 9:13-18). So the murderer and blasphemer, having suffered as he had made other men suffer, died a miserable death in a strange country in the mountains (2 Maccabees 9:28). The first book tells the same end from inside his own mind: he fell sick for grief, said that he remembered the evils he did at Jerusalem and that he sent to destroy the inhabitants of Judea without a cause, and perceived that for this cause these troubles were come upon him (1 Maccabees 6:8-13). The teaching precepts that confession with the rule that he that leads into captivity goes into captivity (Revelation 13:10), and observes how late such men come to it.

cases.name: Mattathias
cases.charge: Zealous for the law: refusing the king’s commandment at Modin, and executing the apostate on the altar as Phinehas did Zambri
cases.summary: Mattathias, a priest of the sons of Joarib, left Jerusalem and dwelt at Modin with his five sons, and when he saw the blasphemies committed in Juda and Jerusalem he said that it would have been better not to have been born than to see the misery of his people (1 Maccabees 2:1-7). The king’s officers came to Modin to make them sacrifice and offered him rank, gifts and the friendship of the king, and he answered that though all the nations under the king obeyed him, he and his sons and his brethren would walk in the covenant of their fathers (1 Maccabees 2:15-22). When a Jew came in the sight of all to sacrifice on the altar at Modin, he ran and slew him on the altar, killed the king’s commissioner, and pulled the altar down (1 Maccabees 2:23-25).
offenseFull: He saw the temple made as a man without glory, the vessels carried into captivity, the infants slain in the streets, and asked what nation had not had a part in her kingdom; he and his sons rent their clothes and mourned very sore (1 Maccabees 2:7-14). Every nation confederate against us is the psalm exactly (Psalms 83:1-8). The teaching holds this up as the qualification: oppression makes a wise man mad (Ecclesiastes 7:7), the mark is set on the men that sigh and cry for the abominations done in the city (Ezekiel 9:4), and men who see their people so and are not moved are the men Christ compared to children in the marketplace (Luke 7:31-32). Against that, the Lord has always raised up deliverers when the people cried (Judges 3:9; 2 Kings 13:5; Nehemiah 9:27).

The officers came to Modin with flattery and with a price. They told him that he was a ruler, honourable and great, strengthened with sons and brethren, that the men of Juda and those left at Jerusalem had already done it, and that if he came first he and his house would be numbered among the king’s friends and honoured with silver and gold (1 Maccabees 2:17-18). A gift destroys the heart (Ecclesiastes 7:7), and the apostle’s rule is not to be partaker of other men’s sins (1 Timothy 5:22). Mattathias answered with a loud voice that though all the nations under the king obeyed him and fell away from the religion of their fathers, he and his sons and his brethren would walk in the covenant of their fathers, and would not go from their religion on the right hand or the left (1 Maccabees 2:19-22). It is the answer the three children gave in Babylon (Daniel 3:16-18), and the answer of the apostles, that we ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

Then one of the Jews came in the sight of all to sacrifice on the altar at Modin according to the king’s commandment. Mattathias was inflamed with zeal, his reins trembled, and he ran and slew him upon the altar, killed the king’s commissioner who compelled men to sacrifice, and pulled down the altar (1 Maccabees 2:23-25). The writer measures him by the statute, that he dealt zealously for the law of God as Phinees did to Zambri (1 Maccabees 2:26; Numbers 25:7-13), the sentence the law gives for the man who entices the people to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 13:6-11). He cried through the city that whoever was zealous of the law and maintained the covenant should follow him, and he and his sons fled into the mountains (1 Maccabees 2:27-28). When a thousand in the wilderness let themselves be killed on the sabbath rather than defend themselves, he and his friends decided to fight any man who came against them on that day (1 Maccabees 2:29-41).
judgmentFull: The Assideans and all who fled from the evils joined him, and they went about pulling down the altars, circumcising the children they found uncircumcised, and recovered the law out of the hand of the Gentiles and the kings (1 Maccabees 2:42-48). When his time came to die he charged them to be zealous for the law, to give their lives for the covenant, and to call to remembrance what acts the fathers did in their time (1 Maccabees 2:49-51). He named them one by one, Abraham, Joseph, Phinees, Josue, Caleb, David, Elias, the three saved out of the flame, and Daniel delivered from the lions, and drew the conclusion, that none that put their trust in him shall be overcome, and that the words of a sinful man are not to be feared (1 Maccabees 2:52-62).

Then he told them who each was. Simon is a man of counsel, and shall be a father to them; Judas Maccabeus has been mighty and strong from his youth, let him be their captain and fight the battle of the people; take to you all those that observe the law, avenge the wrong of your people, recompense fully the heathen, and take heed to the commandments of the law (1 Maccabees 2:65-68). The teaching calls that what a father is for, to tell his children who to follow and what to hold on to. So he blessed them and was gathered to his fathers, died in the hundred forty and sixth year, was buried at Modin, and all Israel made great lamentation for him (1 Maccabees 2:69-70). The blessing of a father establishes the houses of the children (Ecclesiasticus 3:9), and the wisdom says of such a man that though he die, he is as though he were not dead, for he has left one behind him like himself, an avenger against his enemies (Ecclesiasticus 30:4-6).

cases.name: The Jew who sacrificed at Modin
cases.charge: Sacrificing on the heathen altar at the king’s command
cases.summary: The king’s officers came to Modin to compel the people to revolt and to make them sacrifice, and offered Mattathias rank and rewards if he would be the first to fulfil the king’s commandment (1 Maccabees 2:15-18). Mattathias refused for himself, his sons and his brethren, and while he was still speaking one of the Jews came in the sight of all to sacrifice on the altar which was at Modin, according to the king’s commandment (1 Maccabees 2:19-23). Mattathias was inflamed with zeal, ran, and slew him upon the altar, and pulled the altar down (1 Maccabees 2:24-25).
offenseFull: What makes this case is the timing and the audience. The refusal had just been made publicly, in front of the officers and in front of the men of the city; Mattathias had said out loud that though every nation under the king obeyed him and fell away from the religion of their fathers, he and his house would walk in the covenant of their fathers and would not go from their religion on the right hand or the left (1 Maccabees 2:19-22). The offer that had been refused was the flattery and the price together, that he was an honourable and great man with sons and brethren, that the men of Juda and those left at Jerusalem had already done it, and that silver and gold and many rewards and the friendship of the king were waiting (1 Maccabees 2:17-18). Then this man stepped out in the sight of all and took the terms that had just been turned down (1 Maccabees 2:23). The teaching says a gift destroys the heart (Ecclesiastes 7:7), and that a man is not to lay his hand with another man’s sin but to keep himself pure (1 Timothy 5:22); this man did in public the very thing the nation had just been told not to do, and gave the officers the example they had come for.

The law does not treat that as a private failure. The man who is found doing wickedly in the sight of the Lord in transgressing his covenant, who has gone and served other gods and worshipped them, is to be brought out and stoned, on the word of two or three witnesses, and the hands of the witnesses are to be first upon him to put him away (Deuteronomy 17:2-7). Where the enticement comes from a brother, a son, a daughter, a wife or a friend, saying let us go and serve other gods, the sentence is the same and the hand of the man who heard it is to be first upon him, so that all Israel hears and fears (Deuteronomy 13:6-10). The altar at Modin was the test case set up in the town precisely so that the rest would follow.
judgmentFull: Mattathias saw it, was inflamed with zeal, and his reins trembled; he could not forbear to show his anger according to judgment, and he ran and slew the man upon the altar, and the king’s commissioner who compelled men to sacrifice he killed at that time also, and the altar he pulled down (1 Maccabees 2:24-25). The writer gives the precedent in the same breath: thus he dealt zealously for the law of God, as Phinees did to Zambri the son of Salom (1 Maccabees 2:26). Phinees rose up from among the congregation, took a javelin in his hand, and thrust both of them through, and the plague was stayed, and he was given the covenant of an everlasting priesthood because he was zealous for his God and made an atonement for the children of Israel (Numbers 25:7-8; Numbers 25:11-13).

The execution was not the end of the day but the beginning of the revolt. Mattathias cried through the city with a loud voice that whoever was zealous of the law and maintained the covenant should follow him, and he and his sons left everything they had in the city and fled into the mountains (1 Maccabees 2:27-28). The teaching reads the whole scene as one lesson about company: the father’s last charge to his sons was to take to themselves all those that observe the law, because the men around you are what decides whether the work stands, and the man on the altar at Modin is the other kind. One man taking the reward in front of everybody was what the king’s policy needed, and the answer to it set the nation in motion.

cases.name: Judas Maccabeus
cases.charge: Going to battle with prayer and the law, keeping the ordinances of war, and cleansing the sanctuary
cases.summary: Judas rose up in his father’s place, and his brethren helped him, and they fought the battle of Israel with cheerfulness; salvation prospered in his hand because he took to himself those that observed the law (1 Maccabees 3:1-6; 1 Maccabees 2:67). Facing Seron with a small company he told them that the victory of battle does not stand in the multitude of a host but that strength comes from heaven, and that they fight for their lives and their laws (1 Maccabees 3:18-22). He set captains over thousands and hundreds and fifties and tens and sent home the men the law excuses from war (1 Maccabees 3:55-60), and after the victories he cleansed the sanctuary and dedicated the new altar with eight days of gladness (1 Maccabees 4:36-59).
offenseFull: The account says why he prospered before saying what he won. All his brethren helped him, and so did all that held with his father; the wicked shrank for fear of him, because salvation prospered in his hand (1 Maccabees 3:2-6). That goes back to the charge his father gave him, to take to himself all those that observe the law (1 Maccabees 2:67), and the teaching will not let the point go: he had no sinners in his company, and the men he received were such as were ready to perish, men who had given up their own lives for the nation (1 Maccabees 3:9). Before the battle at Maspha the congregation gathered where they had prayed of old, fasted, put on sackcloth, cast ashes on their heads, brought out the priests’ garments and the firstfruits and the tithes, and cried toward heaven (1 Maccabees 3:44-53), the assembly the prophet commands when the land is in that condition (Joel 2:16-17).

To men who asked how so few could fight so great a multitude, he answered that with the God of heaven it is all one to deliver with a great multitude or a small company, that the victory of battle stands not in the multitude of a host but that strength comes from heaven, and that they come in pride to destroy us and our children, but we fight for our lives and our laws (1 Maccabees 3:17-22). Then he kept the ordinances of war as they are written, ordaining captains over thousands and hundreds and fifties and tens, and sending home the men building houses, betrothing wives, or planting vineyards, and the fearful, according to the law (1 Maccabees 3:55-56; Deuteronomy 20:5-9). At Emmaus he armed them with good words and said that as the will of God is in heaven, so let him do (1 Maccabees 3:58-60). The second book shows the same discipline: he told them that the enemy trusted in weapons and boldness but that our confidence is in Almighty God, recounted the deliverances under Sennacherib and among the Galatians, divided the army into four parts with his brothers over the bands, appointed Eleazar to read the holy book, and gave the watchword, the help of God (2 Maccabees 8:16-23). After the victory they broke off the pursuit because it was the day before the sabbath, and kept the sabbath giving thanks (2 Maccabees 8:24-28).
judgmentFull: He also kept the army clean. After a battle at Odollam they purified themselves and kept the sabbath, and when they came the next day to bury their own slain, they found under the coats of every one of the dead things consecrated to the idols of the Jamnites, which the law forbids, and every man saw why they had been slain (2 Maccabees 12:38-40). Judas turned it into an exhortation to the living to keep themselves from sin, and sent two thousand drachms of silver to Jerusalem for a sin offering, being mindful of the resurrection (2 Maccabees 12:41-45). The teaching is careful here: it was a good thought made in hope, and does not put in a man’s hand what only Christ can give; what it shows is a captain who reckoned sin in the camp as the reason for the losses.

When the enemies were discomfited, he told his brethren to go up and cleanse and dedicate the sanctuary, and they found it desolate, the altar profaned, the gates burnt, shrubs growing in the courts as in a forest, and the priests’ chambers pulled down (1 Maccabees 4:36-38). He chose priests of blameless conversation, such as had pleasure in the law, to cleanse it; they pulled down the profaned altar and laid up its stones

in the mountain of the temple until there should come a prophet to show what to do with them, and built a new altar of whole stones according to the law (1 Maccabees 4:42-47). On the twenty and fifth day of Casleu, the same day the heathen had profaned it, they rose early and offered sacrifice on the new altar, dedicated it with songs and citherns and harps, and kept the dedication eight days with gladness (1 Maccabees 4:52-59). They kept it as the feast of tabernacles, bearing branches and palms, and ordained by a common statute that the nation should keep those days every year (2 Maccabees 10:6-8). It is the feast Christ is found at in Jerusalem in winter (John 10:22). The second book gives him the vision that goes with the charge: Onias the former high priest praying for the whole body of the Jews, and Jeremias, a lover of the brethren, giving Judas a sword of gold to wound the adversaries (2 Maccabees 15:11-16), after which Nicanor’s host was broken and the day kept yearly (2 Maccabees 15:25-29).
