cases.name: Alcimus
cases.charge: Slandering Judas to the king; slaying sixty Asideans under a sworn peace; pulling down the wall of the inner court
cases.summary: When Demetrius was set on the throne, all the wicked and ungodly men of Israel came to him, having Alcimus, who desired to be high priest, for their captain, and they accused the people, saying that Judas and his brethren had slain the king’s friends and driven them out of their own land (1 Maccabees 7:5-7). The king sent Bacchides with Alcimus, whom he made high priest, commanding him to take vengeance on the children of Israel (1 Maccabees 7:8-9). Under a sworn peace Alcimus took sixty of the Assideans and slew them in one day, and afterward, when he commanded the wall of the inner court of the sanctuary to be pulled down, he was struck with a palsy and died in great torment (1 Maccabees 7:12-18; 1 Maccabees 9:54-56).
offenseFull: The teaching keeps a list running through this period and puts him at the end of it: Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, Jason, Menelaus, Rhodocus, and now Alcimus. The wicked among our own always seek position. The men who came with him to Demetrius had been driven out of the land, because they were of no use to their own people and of no use to the king they sold them to; their complaint was that Judas had slain the king’s friends (1 Maccabees 7:5-7). The king made him high priest and sent Bacchides with him and a great power into the land of Judea, with a commandment to take vengeance on the children of Israel (1 Maccabees 7:8-9). They sent to Judas and his brethren with peaceable words deceitfully, but he gave no heed, seeing that they had come with a great power (1 Maccabees 7:10-11).

The Assideans were the first among the children of Israel to seek peace of them, saying that one that is a priest of the seed of Aaron had come with the army and would do them no wrong (1 Maccabees 7:12-14). The teaching stops on that reasoning, because it is the mistake: he was in the line, but he had defiled himself willingly in the times of their mingling with the Gentiles, and a man in the line who has done that is not what the line says he is. He spoke to them peaceably and swore that he would not seek harm to them or to their friends, and they believed him, and he took sixty of them and slew them in one day (1 Maccabees 7:15-16). The writer reaches for the psalm to say what it looked like, that the flesh of the saints was cast out and their blood shed round about Jerusalem with none to bury them (1 Maccabees 7:17; Psalms 79:2-3). Then the fear and dread of them fell on all the people, who said that there was neither truth nor righteousness in them, for they had broken the covenant and the oath they had made (1 Maccabees 7:18). Bacchides slew many and cast them into the great pit, committed the country to Alcimus, and left him a power to aid him (1 Maccabees 7:19-20).

Alcimus contended for the high priesthood, and all such as troubled the people resorted to him, and when they had gotten the land of Juda into their power they did much hurt in Israel, so that Judas saw that Alcimus and his company had done among the Israelites even above the heathen (1 Maccabees 7:21-23). The teaching does not flinch from that verse: a man of the nation can do us worse than the nations. When Judas took vengeance on the men who had revolted, and Alcimus saw that he had the upper hand and could not abide his force, he went again to the king and said all the worst of them that he could (1 Maccabees 7:24-25). The second book shows the same speech. He came to Demetrius with a crown of gold and a palm and boughs used solemnly in the temple, and in council he said that those called Assideans, whose captain is Judas Maccabeus, nourish war and will not let the realm be in peace, that he himself had been deprived of his ancestors’ honour, meaning the high priesthood, and that as long as Judas lives it is not possible that the state should be quiet (2 Maccabees 14:3-10; 2 Maccabees 14:26-27).
judgmentFull: In the hundred fifty and third year, in the second month, Alcimus commanded that the wall of the inner court of the sanctuary should be pulled down, and he pulled down also the works of the prophets (1 Maccabees 9:54). That is where it ended. As he began to pull down, at that very time he was plagued and his enterprises hindered, for his mouth was stopped and he was taken with a palsy, so that he could no more speak nor give order concerning his house (1 Maccabees 9:55). So Alcimus died at that time with great torment (1 Maccabees 9:56).

The mouth that had slandered his own nation to two kings was stopped first, and the man who had sworn a peace and killed sixty men under it was left unable to give an order about his own house. When Bacchides saw that Alcimus was dead he returned to the king, and the land of Juda was in rest two years (1 Maccabees 9:57). The teaching reads the case as a warning to men who want the office more than the work: he had the pedigree, took the title from a foreign king, held the country with a foreign garrison, and the record of it is four verses about how he died.

cases.name: Nicanor
cases.charge: Blasphemy against the temple; breaking covenant with Judas; resolving to attack on the Sabbath
cases.summary: The king sent Nicanor, one of his honourable princes, a man that bare deadly hate to Israel, with a commandment to destroy the people (1 Maccabees 7:26). He sent to Judas with friendly words asking for a meeting in peace, while his men were prepared to take Judas away by violence (1 Maccabees 7:27-30). When the priests came out of the sanctuary to salute him, he mocked them, abused them shamefully and swore that unless Judas were delivered into his hands he would burn up the house (1 Maccabees 7:33-35). He purposed to fall on the Jews on the sabbath day, and on the thirteenth of Adar his host was broken and he himself was the first man slain in the battle (2 Maccabees 15:1-5; 1 Maccabees 7:39-43).
offenseFull: The teaching notes that the hatred was not there from the first day. Nicanor had first appeared with friendly words, and the relationship between him and Judas ran from good to bad; the second book shows him made governor, bearing Judas good will and loving the man from his heart, advising him to marry and live quietly, until Alcimus accused him to the king of appointing Judas as his successor (2 Maccabees 14:23-27). Forced by the king’s letter to send Judas prisoner, he was troubled and loath to break with a man who had done him no wrong; but he went through with it, and from that point he set himself against the people (2 Maccabees 14:28-30). He sent to Judas and his brethren deceitfully with friendly words, saying that there should be no battle between them and that he would come with a few men to see him in peace, and they saluted one another peaceably, while his enemies were prepared to take Judas away by violence; Judas learned of the deceit and would not see his face again (1 Maccabees 7:27-30).

What the charge turns on is what he said in front of the temple. When he came up to mount Sion and certain of the priests and of the elders came out of the sanctuary to salute him peaceably and to show him the burnt sacrifice that was offered for the king, he mocked them, laughed at them, abused them shamefully and spoke proudly, and swore in his wrath that unless Judas and his host were delivered into his hands he would burn up this house; and he went out in a great rage (1 Maccabees 7:33-35). The second book has him stretching out his right hand toward the temple and swearing that if they did not deliver Judas he would break down the house of God, cast down the altar and set up a temple to Bacchus there (2 Maccabees 14:31-33). The priests went in and stood before the altar weeping, and asked God to remember this man’s blasphemies and to suffer him not to continue (1 Maccabees 7:36-38), which is the psalm’s own plea, that God arise and plead his own cause, and remember the reproach of the foolish man and the tumult of those that rise up against him continually (Psalms 74:22-23). Then he resolved to set upon Judas on the sabbath day, and when the Jews compelled to follow him asked him to honour the day which he that sees all things had honoured with holiness above other days, he asked whether there were a mighty one in heaven that had commanded the sabbath to be kept, and when they answered that there is a living Lord in heaven that commanded the seventh day, he replied that he was mighty upon earth and commanded them to take weapons (2 Maccabees 15:1-5).
judgmentFull: Judas pitched at Adasa with three thousand men and prayed that, as the angel had gone out against the messengers of the king of the Assyrians and smitten a hundred fourscore and five thousand of them, so this host might be destroyed, and that the rest might know that this man had spoken blasphemy against the sanctuary (1 Maccabees 7:39-42). So on the thirteenth day of the month Adar the hosts joined battle, and Nicanor’s host was discomfited, and he himself was the first man slain in the battle (1 Maccabees 7:43). When his host saw that he was slain they cast away their weapons and fled, and the Jews pursued them a day’s journey from Adasa to Gazara, sounding an alarm with trumpets, so that the people came out of all the towns of Judea round about and closed them in, and they were all slain with the sword, and not one of them was left (1 Maccabees 7:44-46).

Then they took the spoils and the prey, and smote off Nicanor’s head and his right hand, which he had stretched out so proudly, and brought them away and hanged them up toward Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 7:47). The second book adds that they hanged the head from the tower as a manifest token of the help of God, and cut out the tongue that had spoken against the holy place and gave it to the fowls (2 Maccabees 15:28-35). For this cause the people rejoiced greatly and kept that day as a day of great gladness, and they ordained to keep it yearly, the thirteenth day of Adar (1 Maccabees 7:48-49; 2 Maccabees 15:36). The teaching reads that ordinance without embarrassment: our forefathers kept a feast over it, told their children what was done to the man who threatened the house, and would do the same again. Thus the land of Juda was in rest a little while (1 Maccabees 7:50).

cases.name: Tryphon
cases.charge: Taking Jonathan the high priest by treachery under a covenant of friendship; slaying him and the young king Antiochus
cases.summary: Tryphon went about to get the kingdom of Asia and to kill the young king Antiochus, whom he himself had set up, but he was afraid that Jonathan would not suffer him, so he sought a way to take Jonathan and kill him (1 Maccabees 12:39-40). At Bethsan he received Jonathan honourably, gave him gifts, persuaded him to send his forty thousand men home, and then shut the gates of Ptolemais on him, took him, and slew the thousand that had come with him (1 Maccabees 12:41-48). He took a hundred talents of silver and Jonathan’s two sons from Simon on a promise of release, kept them, and killed Jonathan at Bascama; then he slew the young king and crowned himself (1 Maccabees 13:12-24; 1 Maccabees 13:31-32).
offenseFull: The teaching sets out who he was. Diodotus was an official under Alexander Balas who revolted against Demetrius, took Alexander’s infant son out of Arabia, proclaimed him king as Antiochus, and acted as his regent while he gathered most of Syria to himself. The boy he was protecting was the obstacle to his own crown, and Jonathan, in league with the boy king, was the obstacle to removing him; so he went about to get the kingdom and kill the king, and because he feared that Jonathan would fight him, he sought a way to take Jonathan first (1 Maccabees 12:39-40).

Jonathan came out to meet him at Bethsan with forty thousand chosen men (1 Maccabees 12:41). When Tryphon saw the size of the force he did not stretch out his hand against him, but received him honourably, gave him gifts, and commanded his men of war to obey him as himself (1 Maccabees 12:42-43). Then he asked why he had put all these people to so great trouble, seeing there was no war between them, and told him to send them home and come to Ptolemais with a few men, promising to give him the city and the rest of the strongholds and forces (1 Maccabees 12:44-45). Jonathan believed him, sent away his hosts, kept three thousand, sent two thousand into Galilee, and went with a thousand (1 Maccabees 12:46-47). As soon as he entered Ptolemais they shut the gates, took him, and slew all that came in with him (1 Maccabees 12:48). The teaching precepts the whole scene with the psalm: he put forth his hands against such as be at peace with him and broke his covenant, the words of his mouth were smoother than butter but war was in his heart, and his words, softer than oil, were drawn swords (Psalms 55:20-21). It reads this as the settled nature of the enemy rather than the character of one man, and the reason we are told to cast our burden on the Lord (Psalms 55:22-23).

Simon rose up in his brother’s place, told the people that he would not spare his own life in a time of trouble, and they answered that he should be their leader (1 Maccabees 13:1-9). Tryphon sent to him saying that he held Jonathan for money owing to the king’s treasury, and that if Simon would send a hundred talents of silver and Jonathan’s two sons for hostages he would let him go (1 Maccabees 13:12-16). Simon perceived that they spoke deceitfully, but sent the money and the children, so that the people could not say that Jonathan had died because he would not send them (1

Maccabees 13:17-18). Tryphon took both and would not let him go, marched into the country, was turned back by a great snow, went into Galilee, and at Bascama slew Jonathan, who was buried there (1 Maccabees 13:19-23). Simon took the bones of his brother to Modin and built the monument with seven pyramids for his father, his mother and his four brethren, with pillars and armour for a perpetual memory (1 Maccabees 13:25-29). Then Tryphon dealt deceitfully with the young king Antiochus and slew him, reigned in his stead, crowned himself king of Asia, and brought a great calamity upon the land (1 Maccabees 13:31-32).
judgmentFull: The book does not record a sentence executed on him. It records the kingdom turning against him. Antiochus the son of Demetrius came into the land of his fathers, and the forces gathered to him, so that few were left with Tryphon (1 Maccabees 15:1-10). He pursued him, and Tryphon fled to Dora by the sea, knowing that troubles were come on him all at once and that his forces had forsaken him (1 Maccabees 15:10-11). The king besieged Dora with a hundred and twenty thousand men of war and eight thousand horsemen, joined his ships to the town, and pressed it by sea and land, so that no man could go out or in (1 Maccabees 15:13-14).

From there Tryphon got away, took ship and fled to Orthosias, and the account leaves him there (1 Maccabees 15:37). What the record shows is the end of everything he killed for. The treachery at Ptolemais and the murder at Bascama were meant to clear his way to the crown of Asia, and what he held at the last was a divided kingdom and a coast he could not defend, while the house he had tried to destroy went on: the yoke of the heathen was taken away from Israel, and the people began to write in their instruments and contracts in the first year of Simon the high priest (1 Maccabees 13:41-42). The sentence on the man is deferred; the judgment on the purpose is on the page.

cases.name: Ptolemy the son of Abubus
cases.charge: Murdering Simon the high priest and two of his sons at a banquet in his own castle
cases.summary: Ptolemeus the son of Abubus was made captain in the plain of Jericho and had abundance of silver and gold, for he was the high priest’s son in law; his heart was lifted up, he thought to get the country to himself, and he consulted deceitfully against Simon and his sons to destroy them (1 Maccabees 16:11-13). When Simon came down to Jericho with his sons Mattathias and Judas, Ptolemeus received them deceitfully into a little hold called Docus which he had built, made them a great banquet, and hid men there; and when they had drunk largely he and his men rose up, took their weapons, came upon Simon in the banqueting place, and slew him and his two sons and certain of his servants (1 Maccabees 16:14-16).
offenseFull: The teaching gives this case a name from the street, the back door, and defines it exactly: being taken down by somebody close to you, a family member or a friend, because that is the one direction you are not watching. The reason it names for it is the same one the record gives, which is that the man has watched you get something and cannot stand it: his heart being lifted up, he thought to get the country to himself (1 Maccabees 16:13). He had the position, the money and the marriage, and he had all three from the man he killed.

The setting was ordinary and the victim was at work. Simon was visiting the cities that were in the country and taking care for the good ordering of them, and came down himself to Jericho with his sons Mattathias and Judas, in the hundred threescore and seventeenth year, in the eleventh month, called Sabat (1 Maccabees 16:14). Ptolemeus received them deceitfully into a little hold called Docus which he had built, made them a great banquet, and hid men there; and when Simon and his sons had drunk largely, he and his men rose up and took their weapons and came upon Simon in the banqueting place and slew him and his two sons and certain of his servants (1 Maccabees 16:15-16). The writer says plainly what was done: in doing this he committed a great treachery and recompensed evil for good (1 Maccabees 16:17). The law curses the man that smites his neighbour secretly and the man that takes a reward to slay an innocent person (Deuteronomy 27:24-25), and the wisdom says that whoever rewards evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house (Proverbs 17:13); and the psalm had already described the shape of it, a familiar friend, trusted, who ate bread with him (Psalms 41:9).

The teaching sets the wise man’s rule against the whole scene, that an enemy is never to be trusted, that though he humble himself and go crouching a man should take good heed and beware of him, that he is not to be set beside you nor allowed to sit at your right hand, because when he has overthrown you he will stand up in your place and seek your seat; that he will speak sweetly with his lips while in his heart he imagines how to throw you into a pit, and that he will weep with his eyes but if he finds opportunity he will not be satisfied with blood (Ecclesiasticus 12:10-16). The banquet hall was built for it, and the men were already in the room.
judgmentFull: The book records no sentence executed on him. It records the rest of the plot failing. He wrote to the king to send him a host to aid him, promising to deliver him the country and the cities; he sent others to Gazara to kill John, and letters to the captains to come to him for silver and gold and rewards, and others to take Jerusalem and the mountain of the temple (1 Maccabees 16:18-20). But one ran before to Gazara and told John that his father and his brethren were slain, and that Ptolemeus had sent to slay him also (1 Maccabees 16:21). Hearing it, John was sore astonished, and he laid hands on the men that had come to destroy him and slew them, for he knew that they sought to make him away (1 Maccabees 16:22).

So the country the man had reached for was not his, and the son he had sent men to kill took his father’s place and his father’s work, and the acts of John and his wars are written in the chronicles of his priesthood from the day he was made high priest after his father (1 Maccabees 16:23-24). The teaching uses the case as a warning about who is allowed near the seat: the treachery was possible only because Ptolemeus had been given rank, wealth and a place in the family, and the record leaves his own end unwritten while it keeps writing about the house he tried to destroy.

cases.name: Onias the high priest
cases.charge: Godliness and hatred of wickedness, so that the laws were kept very well and the city lived in peace
cases.summary: While Onias was high priest the holy city was inhabited with all peace and the laws were kept very well, because of his godliness and his hatred of wickedness, so that even the kings honoured the place and magnified the temple with their best gifts (2 Maccabees 3:1-3). When Simon the governor of the temple could not overcome him he betrayed the treasury to the Greeks, and Onias told Heliodorus plainly that the money was laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children (2 Maccabees 3:4-12). After Heliodorus was struck down, Onias prayed and offered a sacrifice for the life of the man who had come to rob him (2 Maccabees 3:31-35). He was murdered in the end by Andronicus at the persuasion of Menelaus, and the Jews and many of other nations were grieved for the unjust murder of the man (2 Maccabees 4:33-38).
offenseFull: The verse the case turns on makes one man the reason for a city’s obedience: the laws were kept very well because of the godliness of Onias the high priest and his hatred of wickedness (2 Maccabees 3:1). The teaching will not let that pass as a compliment. One man’s faith holds up other people’s faith, and the second half of the sentence is the working part: loving the Lord means hating evil (Psalms 97:10), setting no wicked thing before the eyes (Psalms 101:3), and not putting a hand to the plough to look back (Luke 9:62). The result was that even the kings honoured the place and magnified the temple with their best gifts, and Seleucus of his own revenues bore all the cost of the sacrifices (2 Maccabees 3:2-3).

The trouble came from inside. Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city, and when he could not overcome Onias he told Apollonius the governor of Celosyria that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money and that it could all be brought into the king’s hand (2 Maccabees 3:4-6). The teaching calls that what it is, a friend which is only a friend in name, a companion that rejoices in the prosperity of a friend but in the time of trouble will be against him (Ecclesiasticus 37:1-4); and it is an offence against the multitude of a city, which the wisdom warns a man not to commit (Ecclesiasticus 7:7). What Simon offered to hand over was not a king’s revenue. It was the third year tithe, laid up for the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 14:28-29), the same provision Tobit kept in Assyria (Tobit 1:6-8), and the teaching adds the reckoning we are still under, that we are subject to payments because our fathers stopped paying it (Baruch 3:8).

When Heliodorus came and asked whether the report was true, the high priest did not hide it: there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, and it was wrong to injure those who had committed it to the holy place (2 Maccabees 3:9-12).
judgmentFull: The first thing the record shows him doing after Heliodorus was struck down is praying for him. When the man lay speechless and his friends asked Onias to call on the Most High, the high priest offered a sacrifice for his health; and the messengers who had scourged him appeared again and told him to give Onias great thanks, since for his sake the Lord had granted him life (2 Maccabees 3:31-36). Simon answered that by slandering Onias as if he had terrified Heliodorus, and was bold to call him a traitor, a man who had deserved well of the city and was zealous of the laws (2 Maccabees 4:1-2). When the hatred went so far that murders were committed by Simon’s faction, Onias went to the king, not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both public and private (2 Maccabees 4:3-6). The teaching marks the restraint: he had every cause to accuse, and went to seek the good of all.

His brother Jason bought the priesthood from under him and turned the nation to the Greekish fashion; Menelaus bought it from under Jason and began to steal the vessels of gold out of the temple (2 Maccabees 4:7-10; 2 Maccabees 4:23-32). When Onias knew of it he reproved him and withdrew into a sanctuary at Daphne by Antioch; and Menelaus persuaded

Andronicus to get him into his hands; Andronicus came in deceit, gave him his right hand with an oath, persuaded him out of the sanctuary, and killed him without regard of justice (2 Maccabees 4:33-34). What follows is the blessing on the man’s name. Not only the Jews but many of other nations took great indignation and were much grieved for the unjust murder; the king himself was heartily sorry and wept because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead, took away Andronicus his purple, led him through the city to the very place where he had committed the impiety, and there slew the cursed murderer, the Lord rewarding him as he had deserved (2 Maccabees 4:35-38). The teaching reads that as the report a man ought to have of them that are without (1 Timothy 3:7; 1 Thessalonians 4:12; Colossians 4:5; 1 Peter 2:12): he would not join the nations, and they still could say nothing against him. Long afterward Judas is given a dream of him, a virtuous and good man, reverend in conversation and gentle in condition, holding up his hands and praying for the whole body of the Jews (2 Maccabees 15:12-14).

cases.name: Heliodorus
cases.charge: Attempting to plunder the temple treasury
cases.summary: While Onias was high priest the holy city was inhabited with all peace and the laws were kept very well, so that even the heathen kings honoured the temple. Simon the governor of the temple fell out with him, could not overcome him, and reported the treasury to Apollonius, so the king sent Heliodorus his treasurer to bring the money away. Onias told him it was laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children and for property left in trust, and the whole city lay in sackcloth, but he went in anyway. A horse with a terrible rider and two young men struck him down at the treasury; he lived only because Onias sacrificed for him, and he went back to tell the king that anyone sent to that place as an enemy would return well scourged.
offenseFull: The class makes a city at peace the starting point. The holy city was inhabited with all peace and the laws were kept very well because of the godliness of Onias the high priest and his hatred of wickedness, so that even the kings honoured the place and magnified the temple with their best gifts, and Seleucus king of Asia bore the charges of the sacrifices out of his own revenues (2 Maccabees 3:1-3). Because of the faith of one man, his strength and his love for the laws of God, everybody around him was lifted, and the nations themselves respected what he guarded. That king is the one Daniel called a raiser of taxes, who would be destroyed neither in anger nor in battle (Daniel 11:20).

Then Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about the disorder of the city, and when he could not overcome him he got him to Apollonius and told him the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money; Apollonius told the king, and the king chose Heliodorus his treasurer and sent him to bring it away (2 Maccabees 3:4-7). Heliodorus took his journey under a colour of visiting the cities of Coelosyria and Phenice, but in truth to fulfil the king’s purpose, which is what everybody was told while he surveyed the temple.

The class settles what that money was before it weighs the crime. Every third year the tithe of the increase was brought in so that the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow within the gates might eat and be satisfied (Deuteronomy 14:28-29), and Tobit gave the third part of his increase to those to whom it was meet, having been left an orphan himself (Tobit 1:6-8). That fund was our own relief for our own poor, and the prophet names the failure to keep it up as part of why we are this day in captivity, subject to payments (Baruch 3:8). Onias told Heliodorus that the money was laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, that part of it belonged to Hircanus the son of Tobias, four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold in all, and that such a wrong could not be done to them that had committed it to the holiness of the place; Heliodorus answered that in any wise it must be brought into the king’s treasury (2 Maccabees 3:10-13). The measure the class applies is the saying that the bread of the needy is their life, and he that takes away his neighbour’s living slays him (Ecclesiasticus 34:21-22). Taking that money was murder.
judgmentFull: The priests prostrated themselves before the altar in their vestments and called to heaven, the women girt with sackcloth abounded in the streets, and the virgins ran to the gates and walls; whoever looked the high priest in the face would have been wounded in heart, because Onias was in agony knowing what the loss of that money meant for the widows and orphans of Jerusalem (2 Maccabees 3:15-21). Heliodorus executed what was decreed anyway. As he stood with his guard about the treasury, the Lord of spirits caused a great apparition: a horse with a terrible rider smote at him with his forefeet, and two young men scourged him continually, so that he fell compassed with great darkness and was carried out, unable to help himself with his weapons, and they that were with him acknowledged the power of God (2 Maccabees 3:24-28).

His friends begged Onias to call on the Most High to grant him his life. The high priest, suspecting that the king might think some treachery had been done by the Jews, offered a sacrifice for the health of the man, and while he was making the atonement the same young men appeared again and told Heliodorus to give Onias great thanks, since for his sake his life was granted him, and, having been scourged from heaven, to declare the mighty power of God to all men (2 Maccabees 3:31-34). When the king asked whom he might send to Jerusalem once more, he answered that an enemy or a traitor should be sent, for he would come back well scourged if he escaped with his life, because he that dwells in heaven has his eye on that place and destroys them that come to hurt it (2 Maccabees 3:35-39). The reprieve came through the prayer of the man he had been sent to rob. The history class follows him afterward: it was Heliodorus who killed the king who had sent him, exactly as Daniel had written of that king, and he was then put out of the way himself.

cases.name: Simon the governor of the temple
cases.charge: Betraying the temple treasury to the king out of a private quarrel; slandering Onias the high priest
cases.summary: Simon of the tribe of Benjamin was made governor of the temple, and when he could not prevail against Onias in a quarrel over the disorder of the city he went to the nations and reported the treasury as money lying there for the king. After Heliodorus was driven off, he slandered Onias as the worker of those evils and called a traitor the man who had deserved well of the city, and murders were committed by men of his faction. Onias went to the king seeking the good of all rather than to accuse his countrymen, and the record gives no sentence upon Simon.
offenseFull: Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about the disorder of the city (2 Maccabees 3:4). The class read out what that office carried: management of the temple resources, maintenance of the temple, administration of the worship, the handling of disputes, coordination with the other authorities, and security. Whatever the dispute was, Onias as high priest had the last say. When Simon could not overcome him he got him to Apollonius, the governor of Coelosyria and Phenice, and told him the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money (2 Maccabees 3:5-6). He ran to the other nations. They were working together on that temple, and because of one argument he carried the nations against the man set over him. One man had a problem with one man, and because he could not have his way he thought to tear down the whole nation.

The class measures the offense by the proverbs read with it. Every friend says he is a friend, but there is a friend which is only a friend in name, and it is a grief to death when a companion and friend is turned to an enemy (Ecclesiasticus 37:1-4). Offend not against the multitude of a city; bind not one sin upon another, for in one you shall not go unpunished; and say not that God will look upon the multitude of your offerings, as though a man may sin on purpose and be forgiven anyway (Ecclesiasticus 7:7-9). The money he exposed was for the widows, the orphans, the strangers and the Levites, and the bread of the needy is their life, so that he who takes away his neighbour’s living slays him (Ecclesiasticus 34:21-22). Three things the wise man said his heart feared are the slander of a city, the gathering together of an unruly multitude, and a false accusation, all of them worse than death (Ecclesiasticus 26:5-7). Simon did all three: he slandered the city, he gathered the Greeks to get the money out of Jerusalem, and he falsely accused Onias.
judgmentFull: When the seizure failed, Simon, having been a betrayer of the money and of his country, slandered Onias as if he had terrified Heliodorus and been the worker of these evils, and was so bold as to call a traitor the man who had deserved well of the city, tendered his own nation and was zealous of the laws; and their hatred went so far that murders were committed by one of his faction (2 Maccabees 4:1-3). The class reading this in another year puts the killing plainly: men under Simon took it upon themselves to go and kill men who were with Onias, and they had that spirit because it was the spirit on the man over them. That is the pattern traced through the whole lesson: he coveted the upper hand, from there it turned to anger, from there to slander, and from there to murder, one sin knocking over the next. Wars and fightings come out of lusts that war in a man, who kills and desires to have and cannot obtain, and asks amiss (James 4:1-3); a man angry with his brother without a cause is in danger of the judgment, and the name calling carries the sin further (Matthew 5:21-22); and a man who hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15). The men who saw it and said nothing were not clear either, since a witness who hears and does not utter it bears the iniquity (Leviticus 5:1), and he that is partner with a thief hates his own soul (Proverbs 29:24).

Onias, seeing the danger of this contention, and that Apollonius as governor did rage and increase Simon’s malice, went to the king, not as an accuser of his countrymen but seeking the good of all, both publicly and privately, because he saw it was impossible for the state to continue quiet or for Simon to leave his folly unless the king looked to it (2 Maccabees 4:4-6). Blessed are the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9), and a man is to live peaceably with all men as much as lies in him (Romans 12:18), but the qualifier is there for a reason; some spirits do not want peace, and some men cannot be reasoned with, because all men have not faith (2 Thessalonians 3:1-2). No sentence upon Simon is written. Three years afterward his brother Menelaus bought the priesthood, so that the high priest of Israel was now of the tribe of Benjamin (2 Maccabees 4:23-24), and what Simon set in motion went on working after him.

cases.name: Jason the high priest
cases.charge: Buying the priesthood; setting up a Greek gymnasium; drawing his countrymen to heathen customs
cases.summary: When Antiochus called Epiphanes took the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias worked underhand for the priesthood, promising the king three hundred and threescore talents of silver and more besides for licence to set up a place of exercise and train the youth in the fashions of the heathen. Having the rule, he put down the governments which were according to the law, built the gymnasium under the tower, brought the chief young men under the Greek hat, and the priests left the altar for the games. Menelaus outbid him and drove him out; he died in a strange land with no mourning and no burial with his fathers.
offenseFull: After the death of Seleucus, when Antiochus called Epiphanes took the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias laboured underhand to be high priest, promising the king three hundred and threescore talents of silver and fourscore talents of another revenue (2 Maccabees 4:7-8). The class calls that what it is: bribery, and the priesthood goes by bloodline, so the lot had already fallen to Onias. Sometimes it is not good enough for a man to be the support brother; Jason reckoned he could do better, and would have the money besides. Look at a man’s motives. Seek not of the Lord preeminence, neither of the king the seat of honour (Ecclesiasticus 7:4-5); a man who strives for masteries is not crowned except he strive lawfully (2 Timothy 2:5); the prophet numbered bribe taking among the mighty sins of the nation (Amos 5:12), and all bribery is blotted out (Ecclesiasticus 40:12). Onias already had his friend Simon turned against him. Now it was his own blood brother.

He promised a hundred and fifty talents more for licence to set up a place of exercise and train the youth in the fashions of the heathen, and to write them of Jerusalem by the name of Antiochians (2 Maccabees 4:9). The history class puts the offer plainly: he could bring Israel into the Greek games and make them Greek, which Onias would never have done. Having got the rule, he brought his own nation to the Greek fashion, put down the governments which were according to the law, brought up new customs against the law, built a place of exercise under the tower itself, brought the chief young men under his subjection, and made them wear a hat (2 Maccabees 4:10-12). The hat was shown in class beside the statue of the discus thrower: the hat of Hermes, and gymnasium means a place to be naked. The wicked men of that time did the same, building a place of exercise at Jerusalem after the customs of the heathen, making themselves uncircumcised and forsaking the holy covenant (1 Maccabees 1:11-15); to make yourself uncircumcised is to forsake the covenant, because circumcision is the sign that a man will keep the law (Deuteronomy 10:16).

Through Jason, that ungodly wretch and no high priest, the priests lost the courage to serve at the altar; despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices they hurried to the place of exercise when the game of discus called them, liking the glory of the Grecians better than the honours of their fathers (2 Maccabees 4:13-15). The class applies it without softening: our people love that society more than their own forefathers, and in the colleges they love Greek society best of anything. Sore calamity came of it, for they had those to be their enemies and avengers whose custom they followed and whom they desired to be like in all things; it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God (2 Maccabees 4:16-17). That is the history Paul pointed back to when he told his readers they had been carried away to dumb idols even as they were led (1 Corinthians 12:1-2). At the games at Tyre he sent silver to the sacrifice of Hercules (2 Maccabees 4:18-20).
judgmentFull: Three years afterward Jason sent Menelaus to bear the money to the king, and Menelaus got the priesthood by offering three hundred talents of silver more; so Jason, who had undermined his brother, was undermined by another and fled to the Ammonites (2 Maccabees 4:23-26). On a false rumour that Antiochus was dead he came back with a thousand men and assaulted the city; Menelaus fled into the castle, and Jason slew his own citizens without mercy, thinking them enemies and not countrymen, because he despised his own people (2 Maccabees 5:5-6). The king thought Judea had revolted, and the bidder for an office became the occasion of the slaughter that followed.

For all this he obtained not the principality, but received shame for his treason and fled again to the Ammonites. Accused before Aretas king of the Arabians, fleeing from city to city, pursued of all men, hated as a forsaker of the laws and an open enemy of his own country, he was cast out into Egypt; he that had driven many out of their country perished in a strange land, and he that had cast out many unburied had none to mourn for him, nor sepulchre with his fathers (2 Maccabees 5:7-10). The history class marks where he ran at the end: he retired to the Lacedemonians, hoping for safety by reason of kindred, since the Spartans were of the stock of Abraham (1 Maccabees 12:20-21). Even there he found nothing. Nobody likes a traitor, and all the evil he did came back on him.

cases.name: Menelaus
cases.charge: Buying the priesthood over Jason; stealing the temple vessels; procuring the murder of Onias; bribing his way past the king’s judgment
cases.summary: Sent by Jason to carry money to the king, Menelaus offered three hundred talents more and took the priesthood for himself, bringing nothing worthy of the office but the fury of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast. He stole vessels of gold out of the temple, gave some to Andronicus, and got Onias drawn out of sanctuary and killed; when accused he bought the king’s favour, and the three men who pleaded for the city were condemned instead. He guided Antiochus into the most holy temple, and was later brought to Berea and thrust into the tower of ashes, with no burial in the earth.
offenseFull: Three years afterward Jason sent Menelaus, the brother of that same Simon, to bear the money to the king; being brought before him he magnified the king for the glorious appearance of his power and got the priesthood to himself, offering more than Jason by three hundred talents of silver. He came bringing nothing worthy of the high priesthood, but having the fury of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast (2 Maccabees 4:23-25). The class marks what has now happened to the office: the high priest of Israel is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, put there by a bid, and his own brother Simon is the man who first carried the temple to the nations. He took no good order for the money he had promised, and being called to account he left his brother Lysimachus as his deputy (2 Maccabees 4:27-29).

Supposing that he had a convenient time, he stole certain vessels of gold out of the temple, gave some of them to Andronicus, and sold others into Tyre and the cities round about; and when Onias knew it of a surety he reproved him and withdrew himself into a sanctuary at Daphne beside Antioch, whereupon Menelaus took Andronicus apart and prayed him to get Onias into his hands (2 Maccabees 4:32-34). After his brother’s sacrilege was answered by the people (2 Maccabees 4:39-42), an accusation was laid against Menelaus, and when the king came to Tyre three men sent from the senate pleaded the cause; but Menelaus promised Ptolemy the son of Dorymenes much money to pacify the king toward him and was discharged, while the men who followed the matter for the city, for the people and for the holy vessels were condemned to death, and even they of Tyre, moved with hatred of that wicked deed, buried them honourably. So through the covetousness of them that were in power he remained still in authority, increasing in malice and a great traitor to the citizens (2 Maccabees 4:43-50). The history class names it without softening: this is a man of Israel killing his own people for greed.
judgmentFull: When Antiochus was not content with the slaughter of the city but presumed to go into the most holy temple of all the world, Menelaus, that traitor to the laws and to his own country, was his guide (2 Maccabees 5:15). The class names that plainly: one of our own showed the other nation what to take, and the governors left behind afterward were worse than all the rest, bearing a heavy hand over his own countrymen and having a malicious mind against them (2 Maccabees 5:22-23). That is why to this day they look for the ones who will be harder on us than Esau, because they have something to prove. Even in the letters of peace that came later, when the king wrote that the nation should be at rest and have their temple restored and use their own kind of meats and laws, it was Menelaus who was named as the man declaring the people’s mind and sent to comfort them (2 Maccabees 11:29-32). The traitor was still the go-between.

What became of him is not told until the thirteenth chapter. He joined himself with Antiochus Eupator and with great dissimulation encouraged him, not for the safeguard of the country but because he thought to be made ruler; but the King of kings moved the king’s mind against this wicked wretch, and when Lysias informed him that this man was the cause of all the mischief the king commanded to bring him to Berea and to put him to death there, where a tower of fifty cubits high stands full of ashes, into which whoever is condemned of sacrilege is thrust. So he died, not having so much as burial in the earth, and most justly, because he had committed many sins about the altar whose fire and ashes were holy, and he received his death in ashes (2 Maccabees 13:3-8). If he could not be high priest again he meant to be governor, and one day you are the king’s friend and the Most High says that is not your friend. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap (Galatians 6:7).

cases.name: Andronicus
cases.charge: Murder of Onias the high priest under a sworn assurance
cases.summary: Andronicus was left in authority as the king’s deputy, and Menelaus had given him some of the gold vessels stolen out of the temple. When Onias reproved the theft and took sanctuary at Daphne, Menelaus took Andronicus apart and prayed him to get the high priest into his hands; he came in deceit, gave him his right hand with oaths, drew him out of the sanctuary though he was suspected, and shut him up without regard of justice. The king stripped him of his purple, led him through the whole city to the place of the murder, and slew him there.
offenseFull: Antiochus went in haste to settle a rising in Tarsus and Mallos and left Andronicus, a man in authority, for his deputy (2 Maccabees 4:30-31). Menelaus, having stolen certain vessels of gold out of the temple, gave some of them to Andronicus and sold others into Tyre and the cities round about; and when Onias knew the theft of a surety he reproved him and withdrew himself into a sanctuary at Daphne beside Antioch (2 Maccabees 4:32-33). The class showed on the map how far the high priest of Israel had to flee to be safe, out of Jerusalem and up into Syria, which is exactly what the wise man said a backbiting tongue does: it has disquieted many and driven them from nation to nation, pulled down strong cities and overthrown the houses of great men (Ecclesiasticus 28:13-15).

Menelaus then took Andronicus apart and prayed him to get Onias into his hands. He came to Onias in deceit, gave him his right hand with oaths, and though he was suspected by him, persuaded him to come forth of the sanctuary, and shut him up immediately without regard of justice (2 Maccabees 4:34). He killed the true high priest, the man whose godliness had kept the city in peace (2 Maccabees 3:1), the man seen afterward in the vision holding up his hands and praying for the whole body of the Jews, virtuous and good, reverend in conversation, gentle in condition, well spoken, and exercised from a child in all points of virtue (2 Maccabees 15:12-14). Not only the Jews but many also of other nations took great indignation and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man (2 Maccabees 4:35), because Onias had a good report even among the nations. The class draws the standard for office out of that: a man must have a good report of them which are without (1 Timothy 3:7), walk honestly toward them that are without (1 Thessalonians 4:12), walk in wisdom toward them (Colossians 4:5), and keep his conversation honest among the Gentiles, so that they who speak against him as an evildoer may see his good works (1 Peter 2:12). Onias had that report without ever joining himself to them.
judgmentFull: When the king came back and heard the complaint he was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead; and being kindled with anger he took away the purple from Andronicus, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city to that very place where he had committed the impiety against Onias, and there slew the cursed murderer (2 Maccabees 4:37-38).

The record calls that the Lord rewarding him his punishment as he had deserved. The class set the plain sayings beside it. For the work of a man shall he render to him, and cause every man to find according to his ways (Job 34:11). He that does wrong shall receive for the wrong which he has done, and there is no respect of persons (Colossians 3:25). God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap; it might not be this year, and it might be next year, but it is coming (Galatians 6:7). The oath and the offered right hand were what drew the victim out of safety, and they did not cover the man who gave them. The king who had been served by the murder was the one who carried out the sentence, and he carried it out on the spot where the murder was done.

cases.name: Lysimachus
cases.charge: Sacrilege: robbing the temple with Menelaus’ consent
cases.summary: Left as his brother’s deputy, Lysimachus committed many sacrileges in the city by the consent of Menelaus, and much gold was already carried away when the report of it spread. The multitude gathered against him, and he armed about three thousand men and began the violence himself, with an old man named Auranus leading them. The people answered with stones, clubs and handfuls of dust, wounded and scattered the force, and killed the temple robber beside the treasury.
offenseFull: Menelaus, called to account for the money he had promised the king, left his brother Lysimachus in his place as his deputy (2 Maccabees 4:29). The temple was handed to the same house that had already sold it, and the brother of the man who first betrayed the treasury was now guarding the door of it. Many sacrileges were committed in the city by Lysimachus with the consent of Menelaus, and the report of it was spread abroad, many vessels of gold being already carried away (2 Maccabees 4:39). The history class puts it bluntly: this man was robbing the place openly, and the gold was gone before anyone moved.

When the multitude gathered themselves together against him, the common people rose filled with rage, and Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and began first to offer violence, Auranus being the leader of them, a man far gone in years and no less in folly (2 Maccabees 4:40). An old man, the class said, and evil with it; age had taught him nothing. Rather than restore what was taken, the plunderer answered the protest of his own countrymen with an army of three thousand.
judgmentFull: They that saw the attempt of Lysimachus caught up stones, and others clubs, and some took handfuls of dust that was next at hand and cast them all together upon Lysimachus and those that set upon them; many of them they wounded, some they struck to the ground, and all of them they forced to flee. As for the temple robber himself, him they killed beside the treasury (2 Maccabees 4:41-42). The people had no weapons and used what was under their feet. The place he had plundered was the place where his hired force could no longer keep him.

The corruption did not die with him. Of these matters an accusation was laid against Menelaus, and when the king came to Tyre three men sent from the senate pleaded the cause before him; but Menelaus, being convicted, promised Ptolemy the son of Dorymenes much money to pacify the king toward him and was discharged, while they that followed the matter for the city, for the people and for the holy vessels were condemned to death, and they of Tyre, moved with hatred of that wicked deed, buried them honourably (2 Maccabees 4:43-49). So through the covetousness of them that were in power Menelaus remained still in authority (2 Maccabees 4:50). The man who guarded the sacrilege with soldiers fell at the treasury; the man who bought the king kept the office. The history class reads the whole run of it as one covetousness working its way through a single family until every man in it was dead in disgrace.

cases.name: Eleazar the scribe
cases.charge: Choosing to die gloriously rather than eat swine’s flesh, or pretend to, at ninety years old
cases.summary: When the king sent to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers, Eleazar, one of the principal scribes and an aged man, was forced to open his mouth to eat swine’s flesh and spat it out, choosing to die gloriously rather than live stained. His old acquaintance offered him a way out: bring his own lawful meat and only appear to eat the king’s. He refused, so that no young person should think that Eleazar at ninety years old had gone over to a strange religion, and he went to the torment and died, leaving his death as an example to the nation.
offenseFull: The king sent an old man of Athens to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers, and to pollute the temple at Jerusalem and call it the temple of Jupiter Olympius (2 Maccabees 6:1-2). It was no longer lawful for a man to keep the sabbath days or the ancient feasts, or to profess himself at all to be a Jew, and on the day of the king’s birth every month they were brought by bitter constraint to eat of the sacrifices (2 Maccabees 6:6-7). The class marks what that programme really was: suppression of identity. Do not keep the feast days, do not circumcise your children, do not say what you are, to the end that we might forget the law; and if a man could not profess himself a Jew, what was he called instead.

Eleazar, one of the principal scribes, an aged man and of a well favoured countenance, was constrained to open his mouth and eat swine’s flesh; he spat it out and came of his own accord to the torment, choosing rather to die gloriously than to live stained with such an abomination (2 Maccabees 6:18-19). The class explains why they picked him: he was one of the main men of that time, and the people looked to him for strength and guidance, so corrupting him in front of everybody would corrupt the whole nation at once. His stand is the same answer Mattathias gave, that though all the nations under the king fell away every one from the religion of their fathers, he and his sons would walk in the covenant of their fathers and not go from their religion, to the right hand or the left (1 Maccabees 2:19-22). Our religion is keeping the commandments.

They that had the charge of that wicked feast, being his old acquaintance, took him aside and urged him to bring flesh of his own provision, such as was lawful for him to use, and make as if he did eat of the king’s meat, that in so doing he might be delivered from death (2 Maccabees 6:21-22). The meat would have been clean; only the appearance would have been a lie, and the appearance was the whole point of the exercise. He began to consider discreetly, as became his age and the excellency of his ancient years, the honour of his gray head, and his most honest education from a child in the holy law made and given by God, and told them straightway to send him to the grave (2 Maccabees 6:23-24). It did not become his age in any wise to dissemble, so that many young persons should think that Eleazar, being fourscore years old and ten, was now gone to a strange religion. Ninety years old, and he would not so much as pretend, because the old are the example the younger generation copies. The class sets his answer beside the charge to Timothy, that a man continuing in the doctrine saves himself and them that hear him (1 Timothy 4:15-16), and beside the proverb that the just man walks in his integrity and his children are blessed after him (Proverbs 20:7). He added that if he were delivered for the present from the punishment of men, he could not escape the hand of the Almighty, alive or dead (2 Maccabees 6:26).
judgmentFull: They that led him changed the good will they bore him into hatred, because the words he spoke proceeded, as they thought, from a desperate mind. Ready to die with stripes he groaned and said that he suffered grievous pains in body from the beating, but in soul was well content to suffer these things because he feared God (2 Maccabees 6:29-30).

So he died, leaving his death for an example of noble courage and a memorial of virtue, not only to young men but to all his nation (2 Maccabees 6:31). The class set that end beside what Esdras saw: a great multitude upon mount Sion praising the Lord with songs, and in the midst of them a young man of high stature, taller than all the rest, setting crowns upon their heads, because it is the Son of God whom they confessed in the world; these are they that have put off the mortal clothing and put on the immortal, and the commendation is for those who stood so stiffly for the name of the Lord (2 Esdras 2:42-47). That is what Eleazar was doing. He was not going to go against the commandments of God, and the record keeps his name for it. Not long after, Judas Maccabeus gathered about six thousand men and called upon the Lord, and the persecution this old man refused to bow to began to break (2 Maccabees 8:1-5).

cases.offense: The king sent an old man of Athens to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers, and to pollute the temple at Jerusalem and call it the temple of Jupiter Olympius (2 Maccabees 6:1-2). It was no longer lawful for a man to keep the sabbath days or the ancient feasts, or to profess himself at all to be a Jew, and on the day of the king’s birth every month they were brought by bitter constraint to eat of the sacrifices (2 Maccabees 6:6-7). The class marks what that programme really was: suppression of identity. Do not keep the feast days, do not circumcise your children, do not say what you are, to the end that we might forget the law; and if a man could not profess himself a Jew, what was he called instead.
cases.judgment: They that led him changed the good will they bore him into hatred, because the words he spoke proceeded, as they thought, from a desperate mind. Ready to die with stripes he groaned and said that he suffered grievous pains in body from the beating, but in soul was well content to suffer these things because he feared God (2 Maccabees 6:29-30).

cases.name: The seven brethren and their mother
cases.charge: Refusing to taste swine’s flesh under torture, seven times over, in hope of the resurrection
cases.summary: Seven brothers and their mother were taken and compelled by the king, against the law, to taste swine’s flesh, and were tormented with scourges and whips when they refused. Each chose death rather than transgress the laws of the fathers, and each spoke to the king before he died, of the correction of their own people, of the resurrection, and of the punishment waiting for the persecutor. Their mother saw all seven slain within the space of one day and bore it with good courage, exhorting every one of them in her own language, and she died last of all.
offenseFull: Seven brethren with their mother were taken and compelled by the king, against the law, to taste swine’s flesh, and were tormented with scourges and whips when they would not (2 Maccabees 7:1-2). One of them spoke for the rest: they were ready to die rather than transgress the laws of their fathers. The class asked the question the record puts to us now, why swine’s flesh is all through the church today, when these are the ones who stood stiffly for the law and died for it. It also weighed what that answer costs: you truly cannot desire anything left in this world. We are already captives, with the bills and the fourteen hour days; what is it you are leaving behind? There has to be something better.

The king and they that were with him marvelled at the young man’s courage (2 Maccabees 7:12). They marvel, the class said, because they understand there is a certain spirit in these people, something they know. The brothers answered in turn while they watched what was done to the ones before them. The fourth told the king it is good, being put to death by men, to look for hope from God to be raised up again by him, and that for the persecutor there would be no resurrection to life (2 Maccabees 7:14). The sixth told him not to be deceived without cause, for they suffered these things for themselves, having sinned against their God, but that he who strives against God should not think to escape unpunished (2 Maccabees 7:18-19).

The mother was marvellous above all, and worthy of honourable memory, for she saw her seven sons slain within the space of one day and bore it with good courage because of the hope that she had in the Lord. She exhorted every one of them in her own language, filled with a courageous spirit, and took no credit for them: she neither gave them breath nor life, neither was it she that formed the members of every one of them, but the Creator of the world, who formed the generation of man and found out the beginning of all things, would also of his own mercy give them breath and life again (2 Maccabees 7:20-23). The class reads her as the pattern for a house. Children are to be nurtured in the law (2 Esdras 8:12), and fathers are charged not to provoke them to wrath but to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4). What she had put in them from childhood is what stood up under the whips.
judgmentFull: The hope is written plainly in their own answers. The King of the world would raise up those who die for his laws to everlasting life (2 Maccabees 7:9). That is the hope Daniel wrote of, that they who sleep in the dust of the earth awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt, and that they who turn many to righteousness shine as the stars (Daniel 12:2-3), and the reason a man is told to fear the one able to destroy both soul and body rather than them that kill the body (Matthew 10:28). The class drew the mercy of God out of the other half of the fourth brother’s answer: what kind of mercy would it be if the same people who tormented us received an equal reward in the kingdom? That is not a merciful God, if he allows them to do that to us and then gives them the same portion.

The youngest was offered riches, happiness and the friendship of the king, and the mother was called to counsel him; she bowed herself toward the tyrant, laughed him to scorn, and spoke to her son in her own country language instead, telling him not to fear the tormentor but to take his death as his brethren had (2 Maccabees 7:24-29). Last of all, after the sons, the mother died (2 Maccabees 7:41). Nothing in the account promises that the torments would stop short of death. What it promises is that the One who formed them will form them again, and the record keeps the whole household as one witness to it (Hebrews 11:35-38).

cases.name: Timotheus
cases.charge: Gathering the heathen to root out the Jews; a second campaign after being once spared
cases.summary: Timotheus was captain of the heathen forces gathered to root out the Jews, and he was beaten in the field more than once, gathering another host each time, hiring the Arabians, and at last bringing foreign forces and horses out of Asia to take Judea by arms. Judas and his company answered him with prayer, sackcloth and earth upon their heads before they took up their weapons. His army was destroyed, he fled to the stronghold at Gazara, and when it was taken he was found hidden in a pit and killed with his brother.
offenseFull: The campaign begins with the temple. When the nations round about heard that the altar was built and the sanctuary renewed as before, it displeased them very much, so they thought to destroy the generation of Jacob that was among them and began to slay and destroy the people (1 Maccabees 5:1-2). The history class sets that beside the same thing in the Persian captivity: when the walls of Jerusalem were made up and the breaches began to be stopped, Sanballat and Tobiah and the Arabians and the Ammonites were very wroth and conspired together to come and fight against Jerusalem (Nehemiah 4:7-9). The temple was the sign of our connection to our God, and its renewal is exactly what angered them.

Judas passed over to the children of Ammon, where he found a mighty power and much people with Timotheus their captain, and fought many battles with them (1 Maccabees 5:6-8). Then the heathen at Galaad assembled themselves together against the Israelites that were in their quarters, to destroy them, with Timotheus as captain of their host, and those who fled to the fortress at Dathema sent letters to Judas and his brethren saying that many of them were already slain and that the enemy was coming to take the stronghold (1 Maccabees 5:9-13). Simon was sent into Galilee and Judas and Jonathan into Gilead. When the battle was begun and the cry of the city went up to heaven, Judas told his host to fight that day for their brethren, and the host of Timotheus, knowing that it was Maccabeus, fled from him, and about eight thousand men were killed of them that day (1 Maccabees 5:30-34).

Being beaten, he gathered another host, hired the Arabians to help him, and pitched beyond the brook, ready to come and fight (1 Maccabees 5:37-39). Beaten again, he gathered a great multitude of foreign forces and horses out of Asia not a few, and came as though he would take Jewry by force of arms. When he drew near, they that were with Maccabeus turned themselves to pray, sprinkled earth upon their heads, girded their loins with sackcloth, fell down at the foot of the altar, and besought God to be an enemy to their enemies and an adversary to their adversaries, as the law declares (2 Maccabees 10:24-26). The history class sets the two sides against each other: the one part had their courage and their refuge in the Lord, and the other side made their own rage the leader of their battle.
judgmentFull: There were slain of the footmen twenty thousand and five hundred, and six hundred horsemen; and Timotheus himself fled into a strong hold called Gazara, where Chereas was governor. They that were with Maccabeus laid siege to the fortress four days, and they that were within, trusting to the strength of the place, blasphemed exceedingly and uttered wicked words. Upon the fifth day early, twenty young men of Maccabeus’ company, inflamed with anger because of the blasphemies, assaulted the wall manfully, and others likewise ascending after them burnt the towers and kindled fires and burnt the blasphemers alive, while others broke open the gates. They killed Timotheus, who was hid in a certain pit, and Chereas his brother, with Apollophanes; and when this was done they praised the Lord with psalms and thanksgiving, who had done so great things for Israel and given them the victory (2 Maccabees 10:28-38).

The governors named afterward, who would not suffer the people to be quiet and live in peace, include a man of the same name (2 Maccabees 12:2). The history class settles it at that point: the Timotheus of the tenth chapter is dead, and this is a different man. That second commander fell into the hands of Dositheus and Sosipater, and talked his way out with much craft, because he held many of the parents and brethren of the Jews and could tell them that if he were put to death they would never be found again; so on his undertaking to restore them without hurt they let him go for the saving of their brethren (2 Maccabees 12:24-25). The class calls that his trump card. Two captains of the same name, two outcomes; and in both, what was gathered against Judah failed of its purpose, and the pit a man digs for others is the net his own foot is taken in (Psalms 9:15-16).

cases.name: The men of Joppa
cases.charge: Drowning two hundred of the Jews that dwelt among them, under a pretence of peace
cases.summary: The men of Joppa asked the Jews who dwelt among them to go with their wives and children into boats they had prepared, as though they meant them no hurt. The Jews accepted according to the common decree of the city, desiring to live in peace and suspecting nothing, and when they were out in the deep no less than two hundred of them were drowned. Judas called upon God the righteous Judge, burned the haven and the boats by night, and dealt with Jamnia the same way when he learned they intended the like.
offenseFull: The case stands at a moment of settled peace. The covenants had been made, Lysias had gone up to the king, and the Jews were about their husbandry (2 Maccabees 12:1). But the governors of the several places would not suffer them to be quiet and live in peace (2 Maccabees 12:2). The history class reads that verse as the standing history of our people among the nations: they do not want us living peaceably among them, and when we are left to ourselves and begin to prosper they are angered. It named Black Wall Street and Rosewood in the same breath as Joppa.

The men of Joppa did an ungodly deed: they prayed the Jews that dwelt among them to go with their wives and children into the boats which they had prepared, as though they had meant them no hurt (2 Maccabees 12:3). The class gives the setting that made it work. Joppa was a port, and the sailing went by a common decree of the city, so there was nothing in the request that looked out of the ordinary. They accepted it according to the common decree of the city, being desirous to live in peace and suspecting nothing. When they were gone forth into the deep, the men of Joppa drowned no less than two hundred of them (2 Maccabees 12:4). The boats that carried them were the murder, and the wives and the children went out in them.
judgmentFull: When Judas heard of the cruelty done to his countrymen, he had his men make ready, called on God the righteous Judge, and came against the murderers of his brethren: he burned the harbour by night, set the boats on fire and killed those who had fled there, and because the town was shut against him he withdrew, meaning to return and root out the whole city of Joppa (2 Maccabees 12:5-7). The prayer came before the weapons did, and the class marks that order as the whole difference between this campaign and a reprisal.

He heard also that they of Jamnia were minded to do the like to the Jews that dwelt among them, so he came upon the Jamnites by night and set fire on the haven and the navy, so that the light of the fire was seen at Jerusalem two hundred and forty furlongs off (2 Maccabees 12:8-9). He went through the places where our people were living among the nations and were being set upon, and he did not wait for the second city to carry out what it had planned.

Nine furlongs further on their journey, no fewer than five thousand men on foot and five hundred horsemen of the Arabians set upon them; there was a very sore battle, and the side of Judas got the victory by the help of God, so that the Arabians, being overcome, besought him for peace and promised to give him cattle, and Judas, thinking they would be profitable in many things, granted them peace, and they shook hands and departed (2 Maccabees 12:10-12). The appeal to the righteous Judge reached the deed already done, the plan to repeat it, and the ambush laid on the road afterward; and where the nation that met them asked for peace instead of pretending it, peace was given.

cases.name: Judas’ soldiers with idol tokens under their coats
cases.charge: Carrying things consecrated to idols into battle
cases.summary: After the fight with Gorgias, Judas and his company kept the sabbath at Odollam and came the day following to take up their dead and bury them with their kinsmen. Under the coat of every slain man they found things consecrated to the idols of the Jamnites, which the law forbids the Jews, and every man then saw why they had been slain. They praised the righteous Judge who had opened the things that were hid, prayed that the sin might be put out of remembrance, and Judas sent two thousand drachms of silver to Jerusalem for a sin offering.
offenseFull: When they that were with Gorgias had fought long and were weary, Judas called upon the Lord to show himself their helper and leader of the battle, began in his own language and sang songs with a loud voice, and rushing unawares upon the men of Gorgias put them to flight (2 Maccabees 12:36-37). He gathered his host and came into the city of Odollam, and when the seventh day came they purified themselves as the custom was and kept the sabbath in that place (2 Maccabees 12:38). Wherever they were, and whatever had happened the day before, they kept the sabbath.

Upon the day following, as the use had been, Judas and his company came to take up the bodies of them that were slain and to bury them with their kinsmen in their fathers’ graves; and under the coats of every one that was slain they found things consecrated to the idols of the Jamnites, which is forbidden the Jews by the law. Then every man saw that this was the reason they had been killed (2 Maccabees 12:39-40). Men inside the army of Israel were carrying idols under their clothes. The class draws the plain reason for the losses out of it: he was losing men because some of the men he lost were in the midst of that evil. The law had said the graven images of the gods of the nations were to be burnt with fire, and that a man was not to desire the silver or gold on them nor take it, lest he be snared by it and become a cursed thing (Deuteronomy 7:25-26); Israel had already lost a battle at Ai over one accursed thing taken at Jericho, and was told that they could not stand before their enemies until it was taken away (Joshua 6:18; Joshua 7:11-13).
judgmentFull: All men therefore praised the Lord, the righteous Judge, who had opened the things that were hid, and betook themselves to prayer, beseeching him that the sin committed might wholly be put out of remembrance (2 Maccabees 12:41-42). The class reads that as mercy asked for men who had been caught in idolatry and yet had died fighting for their people. Judas also exhorted the people to keep themselves from sin, for so much as they saw before their eyes the things that came to pass for the sins of those that were slain.

He made a gathering throughout the company to the sum of two thousand drachms of silver and sent it to Jerusalem to offer a sin offering, doing therein very well and honestly in that he was mindful of the resurrection; for if he had not hoped that they that were slain should have risen again, it had been superfluous and vain to pray for the dead. He perceived that there was great favour laid up for those that died godly, and it was a holy and good thought, and he made a reconciliation for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:43-45). The class weighs that wording carefully. The record calls it a good thought, and a good thought is not a guarantee; Judas could not promise the kingdom to a man who died in the middle of that sin, and no man can. He prayed and hoped, the way David fasted and prayed for the child while there was still hope (2 Samuel 12:22), because he knew out of the prophet that they who sleep in the dust of the earth awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt (Daniel 12:2).

The class also answers the use that is made of this passage against the apocrypha, that praying for the dead proves the writer was a pagan. The offering went to Jerusalem for the living as much as for the dead, and the exhortation bound up with it is that the men still standing keep themselves from the same sin. The exposure brought warning to the living and intercession for the dead in one act.
