cases.name: Joseph, the husband of Mary
cases.charge: A just man; doing as the angel of the Lord bade him, four times, without a word recorded
cases.summary: Joseph stands in the record as the husband of Mary and the last name in the king’s line that runs through Zerubbabel, the heir to a throne he could not sit on because the nation was in captivity. Betrothed to a woman found with child, and a just man, he meant to put her away privately rather than make her a public example, and when the angel told him in a dream whose the child was he took her. He was told to flee into Egypt and went by night, told to return and returned, warned again and turned aside into Galilee, and he kept the circumcision, the purification and the yearly passover for the child according to the law. Scripture records nothing he said, only what he did.
offenseFull: Matthew runs the line from the captivity down, from Jechonias to Salathiel to Zorobabel, and on through the generations to Jacob, the father of Joseph the husband of Mary (Matthew 1:12-16). The class works that line carefully, because it settles who Joseph was: it is Solomon’s line, the king’s line, and Zerubbabel stands in the middle of it. God said he would bring forth his servant the Branch, and that Zerubbabel would bring forth the headstone (Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 4:7); Zerubbabel laid the foundation of the second temple, and through his loins brought forth the stone the builders refused, the head of the corner (Psalms 118:22; Ephesians 2:20-22). Joseph was therefore heir to the throne of David and could not sit on it, because Rome ruled and had set an Edomite over Judea instead.

Luke reckons the same man through Heli (Luke 3:23), and the class settles why there are two lines: Luke comes down through Nathan and not through Solomon, and no man has two fathers’ fathers. Heli was Mary’s father and had no sons, so his son in law was written in the record as his son, as Tobias inherited the substance of Raguel, who had only a daughter (Tobit 14:13). That marriage had been arranged by her father long before.

Betrothed to a woman found with child, and being a just man, he would not make her a public example but was minded to put her away privately; and when the angel of the Lord appeared in a dream and told him not to fear taking Mary as his wife, he did as he was bidden, and took her (Matthew 1:18-25). Then a decree from Caesar Augustus sent every man to his own city to be taxed, and he went from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David (Luke 2:1-5). The verse by verse class marks two things in that journey. Paying tribute to a foreign king is the proof of captivity, which is why the prophet wrote that we are yet this day in our captivity, subject to payments, and why Christ said the children are free and the strangers pay the tribute (Baruch 3:8; Matthew 17:24-26). And it explains how a man of Judah came to live in Galilee: that was Naphtali’s portion, emptied in the Assyrian captivity and joined to Judea again in the days of the Maccabees (Tobit 1:1-2; 1 Maccabees 10:30).

The angel told him to take the young child and his mother into Egypt, because Herod would seek the child to destroy him, and he arose and took them by night (Matthew 2:13-14). The study notes make the point about that hiding: they hid among the Egyptians, and a family that did not look like the people of that land would have been no more hidden there than anywhere. Told to return, he came into the land of Israel; hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judea in his father’s room he was afraid to go there, and being warned of God in a dream he turned aside into Galilee and dwelt in Nazareth, a town with no reputation (Matthew 2:19-23; John 1:45-46).
judgmentFull: The prophet’s word, that God called his son out of Egypt, was written long before that flight, and the return fulfilled it (Matthew 2:15; Hosea 11:1). The study notes call it twofold: Israel came out of Egypt, and the son came out after. Protection came to that household as instructions Joseph had to carry out, by night, with a ruler hunting the child.
The house kept the law for the child it was

given. On the eighth day he was circumcised and named as the angel had said, as the law appoints for a man child (Luke 2:21; Leviticus 12:2-3). When the days of purifying were fulfilled, seven days and thirty and three more, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord and to offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, forty days in all (Luke 2:22-24; Leviticus 12:4-6); he was born under the law, and everything done for him was done after it (Galatians 4:4-5). They returned into Galilee to Nazareth (Luke 2:39), and went up every year at the passover, as the law required of the men three times in the year (Luke 2:41; Deuteronomy 16:16). The class marks that he was twelve at a passover, and that the custom of the feast was the feast, not a birthday. He was subject to them, and increased in wisdom and in favour with God and man (Luke 2:51-52). By the time of the cross Joseph was gone, and Christ committed his mother to the disciple he loved (John 19:25-27). The promise concerning the child was never treated in that house as leave to let the commandments go undone.

cases.name: Herod the Great and the children of Bethlehem
cases.charge: Slaying all the male children of Bethlehem from two years old and under
cases.summary: Herod was set over Judea by Rome and was an Edomite, not of Israel, and when the wise men asked after the one born King of the Jews he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. He got the birthplace out of the chief priests, enquired privately after the time of the star, and sent the wise men to search under a pretence that he also wished to worship. When they did not come back he was exceeding wroth and slew all the children in Bethlehem and its coasts from two years old and under. Matthew reports his death and no sentence explaining it, and joins the mourning to Jeremiah’s word about Rachel.
offenseFull: Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, and wise men came from the east to Jerusalem asking where he was that is born King of the Jews, and when Herod heard it he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him (Matthew 2:1-3). The study notes press the reason: Herod was set up as king over Judea by Rome, and he was an Edomite, not of Israel. If the messiah were coming to save all nations, there would be nothing in his birth to trouble a ruler of the nations. He is troubled because the messiah coming to Israel means judgment on those who hold Israel down.

The class traces the house behind the name. Antipater, a native of Idumea, founded the Herodian dynasty and was the father of Herod; he rose under the later Hasmonean kings, became a client of Pompey, was made chief minister of Judea by Julius Caesar, and set his sons over Jerusalem and Galilee. That family had converted to Judaism, so they were schooled in the customs and prophecies of Israel without being of Israel, and the Herodians of the gospels were that same stock, the ones spoken of as saying they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan (Revelation 2:9). Herod married a Hasmonean princess to give himself a claim and then killed her, and destroyed the old priestly line and the men who might have been rivals. The history class puts it sharply: this is the man who now says he also wishes to worship the child.

He gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people and demanded of them where Christ should be born, and they answered at once out of the prophet, Bethlehem of Judea (Matthew 2:4-6; Micah 5:2). They knew the scriptures concerning the messiah, and the same men who could quote where he would be born were blinded when he walked among them; Israel obtained not that which he sought for, and the rest were blinded (Romans 11:7-10). Then Herod called the wise men privily, enquired what time the star appeared, and sent them to Bethlehem to search for the young child and bring him word, saying that he would come and worship also (Matthew 2:7-8). What he did next showed what he had in mind.

Being warned of God in a dream, they departed into their own country another way (Matthew 2:12); and when Herod saw that he was mocked of the wise men, he was exceeding wroth, and sent forth and slew all the children in Bethlehem and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently enquired (Matthew 2:16). The history class explains the age he chose: the star had been standing out about two years, so he killed every child of two years and under in hope that the messiah was among them; that is why Luke shows an infant and Matthew a child already walking. The study notes set the pattern beside Egypt, where the ruler charged that every son born be cast into the river, the same attempt to cut off a deliverer before he could rise (Exodus 1:22), and beside the great red dragon standing before the woman ready to be delivered, to devour her child as soon as it was born (Revelation 12:3-4), that dragon being the old serpent, the Devil and Satan (Revelation 12:9), and red the colour Esau was born (Genesis 25:25).
judgmentFull: The design failed. The angel had already told Joseph to take the young child and his mother into Egypt, and he departed by night and remained there until the death of Herod, so that the prophet’s word, that God called his son out of Egypt, was fulfilled (Matthew 2:13-15; Hosea 11:1). When Herod was dead the angel told Joseph to return to the land of Israel, because they were dead which sought the young child’s life (Matthew 2:19-20). Matthew reports the death of the king and nothing of the manner of it, and he pronounces no separate sentence upon him.

What Matthew does set down is the mourning, written beforehand by Jeremiah: a voice heard in Ramah, lamentation and weeping, Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they were not (Matthew 2:17-18; Jeremiah 31:15). The ruler died and the promised child lived. The children of Bethlehem were still murdered, and neither the failure of the plot nor the fulfilling of the prophecy touches the guilt of the hand that shed their blood; hands that shed innocent blood are among the things the Lord hates (Proverbs 6:16-17), and the man that takes reward to slay an innocent person is under the curse pronounced before all the people (Deuteronomy 27:25).

cases.name: John the Baptist
cases.charge: Telling a king it is not lawful for thee to have thy brother’s wife
cases.summary: John came preaching repentance in the wilderness of Judea, in the raiment and the spirit of Elijah, and demanded the works that go with repentance from the crowds, the publicans, the soldiers and the rulers alike. He took no title for himself, confessing that he was not the Christ but the voice sent before him. He told Herod the tetrarch that it was not lawful for him to have his brother’s wife and was imprisoned for it, and at a birthday feast the king, for his oath’s sake, sent the executioner. Christ called him more than a prophet, and named him the Elias that was to come.
offenseFull: John the Baptist preached in the wilderness of Judea, saying repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand; he is the messenger the prophets said would go before the Lord in the spirit of Elijah (Matthew 3:1-2; Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4:5-6). His raiment of camel’s hair and the leathern girdle about his loins were Elijah’s manner, marking him as of the same spirit (2 Kings 1:8). The voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord is Isaiah’s word spoken of him (Isaiah 40:3-5). They were baptized of him in Jordan confessing their sins, which the study notes mark as more than a dipping in water; a man must be taught the law to know what he is confessing (Matthew 3:5-6).

To the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism he said to bring forth fruits meet for repentance, and not to say within themselves that they had Abraham to their father, since God can raise up his children of stones (Matthew 3:7-9). The study notes settle what those fruits are: works, the same works Paul preached (Acts 26:20). Descent from Abraham without the works of Abraham counts for nothing, and those works are to believe God and keep his commandments, his charge, his statutes and his laws (Genesis 26:5; John 8:39). The works he named were practical: a man with two coats to give to the man with none, the publicans to exact no more than was appointed, the soldiers to do violence to none, accuse none falsely, and be content with their wages (Luke 3:10-14).

He took no title, confessing that he was not the Christ, nor Elias, nor that prophet, but the voice in the wilderness (John 1:19-23). His own baptism with water was not the baptism of the one coming after him, who would baptize with the Holy Ghost and with fire, gathering the wheat and burning the chaff (Luke 3:16-17; Psalms 1:4). The class ties that promise to the commandments: the Comforter is given to them that obey him and brings the words of Christ to remembrance (John 14:15-16; John 14:26; Acts 5:32).

He reproved the ruler as plainly as the crowds, telling Herod the tetrarch that it was not lawful for him to have his brother Philip’s wife, and reproving him for all the evils he had done (Mark 6:17-18; Luke 3:19; Leviticus 18:16; Leviticus 20:21). The class marks who that ruler was: an Idumean, a convert raised in the customs of the Jews and set over Judea, who knew the law well enough to be accused by it (Acts 26:3). John rebuked him anyway, and Herod added this above all, that he shut him up in prison (Luke 3:20).
judgmentFull: Herod feared John, knowing him a just man and holy, and heard him gladly; Herodias had a quarrel against him and would have killed him, but could not (Mark 6:19-20). At the birthday feast the oath was made before the guests, the girl asked her mother what to ask and was told to ask the head of John the Baptist, and the king, exceeding sorry, sent the executioner for his oath’s sake (Mark 6:21-29). The killing was no sentence of God upon John. A ruler who knew him righteous valued his own word above a righteous man’s blood.

From the prison John sent two disciples to ask whether Jesus was he that should come, and Christ answered by the works, quoting Isaiah: the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have the gospel preached to them (Matthew 11:2-6; Isaiah 35:5-6). He then asked the multitude what they went out into the wilderness to see: not a reed shaken with the wind nor a man in soft clothing, but a prophet, and more than a prophet, the messenger sent before the face of the Lord (Matthew 11:7-10). Among them born of women none greater had risen, and yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater; the law and the prophets prophesied until John, and he is the Elias that was to come (Matthew 11:11-14).

The class carries that word past the grave. The disciples were told that Elias had come already, and that men knew him not but did to him whatever they wished, and they understood he spoke of John the Baptist (Matthew 17:10-13). A short time later, on the mount, two men talked with Christ in glory, and they were Moses and Elias (Luke 9:28-31). The man beheaded in a prison was standing there, comforting the one he had been sent before, which is the promise Christ made to the living, that a man believing in him shall never die (John 11:25-26). The executioner ended the ministry and did not end the man.

cases.name: The centurion of Capernaum
cases.charge: Loving the nation and building the synagogue; not counting himself worthy that the Lord should come under his roof: speak the word only
cases.summary: A centurion at Capernaum had a servant who was dear to him and ready to die, and he sent elders of the Jews to plead for him; they said of him that he loved their nation and had built them their synagogue. He himself sent word that he was not worthy to have Jesus come under his roof, and asked him to say the word only, reasoning from the authority he himself exercised over soldiers and servants. Christ marvelled and said he had not found so great faith, no, not in Israel, and the servant was found whole.
offenseFull: When Christ had ended all his sayings in the audience of the people he entered into Capernaum (Luke 7:1). The verse by verse class begins with where that is, because it settles who the man in this case is. Capernaum lies upon the sea coast in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim, the country the prophet calls Galilee of the Gentiles, which is the northern kingdom of Israel and not another nation (Matthew 4:13-16; Isaiah 9:1-2). Christ came there when Nazareth thrust him out (Luke 4:28-31), and he said plainly in that same gospel that he was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24).

A certain centurion’s servant, who was dear to him, was sick and ready to die, and when he heard of Jesus he sent elders of the Jews to plead for him; and they besought him instantly, saying that the man was worthy for whom he should do this, for he loved their nation and had built them a synagogue (Luke 7:2-5). A centurion is a man set over a hundred soldiers, which is how two of them could be told to make ready two hundred men (Acts 23:23), and this one had the standing and the means to build the people a sanctuary. The class reads him as one of our own, a commandment keeping man of the scattered northern kingdom, and sets him beside Cornelius the centurion of the Italian band, a devout man who feared God with all his house, gave much alms to the people, and whose prayers and alms came up for a memorial before God (Acts 10:1-4). That is the test the class applies: God hears not sinners, but if a man be a worshipper of God and does his will, him he hears (John 9:31). And what both men did with what they had is exactly what the rich are charged to do, not to be highminded nor to trust in uncertain riches, but to be rich in good works, ready to distribute (1 Timothy 6:17-18).

He did not rest the petition on that commendation. When Jesus was not far from the house he sent friends to say that he was not worthy that he should enter under his roof, and that he had not thought himself worthy even to come out to him, but to say in a word, and his servant would be healed. He gave his reason out of the thing he knew: he was himself a man set under authority, having soldiers under him, and he said to one to go and he went, and to another to come and he came, and to his servant to do this and he did it (Luke 7:6-8). The class marks the humility in a man who could move a hundred soldiers and would not walk up to Christ himself: the fear of the Lord is the instruction of wisdom, and before honour is humility (Proverbs 15:33), and all are to be subject one to another and clothed with humility, because God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (1 Peter 5:5-6).
judgmentFull: When Jesus heard these things he marvelled at him, and turned about and said to the people that followed him that he had not found so great faith, no, not in Israel (Luke 7:9). They that were sent returned to the house and found the servant whole that had been sick (Luke 7:10), and Matthew sets down that he was healed in the selfsame hour (Matthew 8:13). The class answers the reading that makes this a heathen praised above Israel: the town is in Zabulon and Nephthalim, the elders of the Jews carried his petition, and he had built the synagogue the nation worshipped in.

Matthew tells the same account with the centurion himself speaking to Christ (Matthew 8:5-10), and the class settles the apparent contradiction with a rule taken out of the record itself. What one man does by another, he does by himself. The friends and the servants who carried the words were the very men he commanded to go and to come, so the words are his words whoever carried them; and the Lord said he would save his people Israel out of the hand of the Philistines by the hand of his servant David, though David did it with an army under him (2 Samuel 3:18).
What is praised here is the faith, and what answered it was a word spoken at a distance, to a house Christ never entered.

cases.name: Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum
cases.charge: Not repenting after the mighty works done in them
cases.summary: Most of Christ’s mighty works were done in Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, and those cities did not repent. He upbraided them and measured them against Tyre, Sidon and Sodom, saying those cities would have repented at what these had seen, and that it would be more tolerable for them in the day of judgment. Capernaum, which had been exalted to heaven, was to be brought down to hell. Luke sets the same woes beside the sending of the seventy and the rule that to despise the messenger is to despise the one who sent him.
offenseFull: When John was cast into prison Christ departed into Galilee, left Nazareth, and came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the sea coast in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim, and from that time he began to preach the same word John had preached, that men should repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand (Matthew 4:13-17). The study notes mark what the prophet calls that country: Galilee of the Gentiles (Isaiah 9:1-2). Zabulon and Nephthalim are tribes of the northern kingdom, and that is the key to who the gentiles are that the gospel goes to after the southern kingdom rejects it. These towns were not outsiders looking on. They were where the ministry lived.

Then he began to upbraid the cities wherein most of his mighty works were done, because they repented not. Woe to Chorazin and woe to Bethsaida, for if the mighty works done in them had been done in Tyre and Sidon, those cities would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. And Capernaum, which was exalted to heaven, would be brought down to hell, for if the mighty works done in her had been done in Sodom, it would have remained to that day (Matthew 11:20-24). The study notes put the charge in plain terms: men watched works no ordinary man could do and still would not turn, and other nations would have turned at what Israel watched and did not turn at. That is what a stiffnecked people looks like. Christ said the same thing another way, that if he had not come and spoken to them they had not had sin, but now they have no cloke for their sin (John 15:22-24).
judgmentFull: It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment than for Chorazin and Bethsaida, and more tolerable for the land of Sodom than for Capernaum (Matthew 11:20-24). The comparison takes away the comfort of measuring yourself against a city with a worse name; the greater the light given, the greater the reckoning for it. The class is careful about the timing: the judgment spoken of here is the one at the return of Christ, not a report that every part of the sentence had already fallen. And that is why the epistle asks how a man shall escape if he neglects so great salvation, spoken first by the Lord and confirmed by them that heard him (Hebrews 2:1-3).

Luke sets the same woes beside the sending out of the seventy, whom the Lord appointed and sent two and two before his face into every city and place where he himself would come (Luke 10:1-2). The class explains the pairing out of the law: no matter is established except at the mouth of two or three witnesses, so the men were sent in twos because they were being sent to bear witness, and to bear witness against a city is to bring judgment on it. Where they were received they said that the kingdom of God is come nigh; where they were not received they were to go out into the streets of that city and wipe off the very dust of it against them, and it would be more tolerable in that day for Sodom than for that city (Luke 10:8-12). The teaching class puts the working edge on that: the same word is carried into the cities now, and a man who walks past it cannot say afterward that he was never told.

What is done to the messenger is done to the one who sent him. He that hears them hears Christ, and he that despises them despises Christ, and he that despises Christ despises the one that sent him (Luke 10:13-16). That has been the standing answer of the nation to the men sent to gather it; the Lord said he had sent his servants the prophets, and they had been taken and slain and their bodies torn in pieces, and the house was left desolate (2 Esdras 1:32-33; Matthew 23:37-38). To be exalted to heaven and thrust down to hell is the prophet’s own language for Zion cast down from heaven to the earth in the day of his anger (Lamentations 2:1). And when the seventy came back with joy, Christ answered that he beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven (Luke 10:17-18): the going out of the witnesses was the beginning of the fall of the kingdom that held them.

cases.name: The Canaanite woman
cases.charge: Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table
cases.summary: A woman of Canaan came out of the coasts of Tyre and Sidon crying after him for a daughter grievously vexed with a devil, and he answered her not a word. The disciples asked him to send her away, and he said he was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; she came and worshipped and asked for help, and he told her it was not meet to take the children’s bread and cast it to dogs. She agreed with him and asked only for the crumbs, and he called her faith great and healed the daughter from that hour.
offenseFull: Jesus departed into the coasts of Tyre and Sidon, and a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts and cried after him, asking mercy of the son of David for a daughter grievously vexed with a devil (Matthew 15:21-22). The history class takes the name Canaan for the land and not for her nation: Tyre and Sidon stand in the land of Canaan, so calling her a woman of Canaan tells you where she lived. Mark gives her nation plainly: she was a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation, whose young daughter had an unclean spirit, and she heard of him and came and fell at his feet (Mark 7:25-26). The class also marks what she called him. She said son of David, because everyone in that country knew he was born of a man out of a known line.

He answered her not a word. The disciples came and asked him to send her away because she cried after them, and he said that he was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:23-24). The class presses the question that a reading of a messiah for all nations cannot answer: he was going through that country healing and teaching, so why would he not so much as speak to this woman, and why would his own disciples ask him to send her off. Then she came and worshipped him and said, Lord, help me (Matthew 15:25), and he told her to let the children first be filled, for it is not meet to take the children’s bread and cast it to the dogs (Matthew 15:26; Mark 7:27). The study notes mark the point exactly there: the order is stated plainly, and he does not soften it for her.
judgmentFull: She did not argue with the order; she asked inside it, saying that the dogs under the table eat of the children’s crumbs (Matthew 15:27; Mark 7:28). The class weighs what that admission was. Israel was told they were a holy people, chosen to be a special people above all people on the face of the earth (Deuteronomy 7:6), and the nations were counted as a drop of a bucket and the small dust of the balance, as nothing before him (Isaiah 40:15-17). You never find an Israelite in the scriptures calling himself a dog. This woman did, and what she asked for was the dust of the balance, a crumb off the table.

Jesus answered that her faith was great and told her it would be to her as she would, and her daughter was made whole from that very hour (Matthew 15:28). Mark records that he sent her away on the strength of that saying, and that when she came to her house she found the devil gone out and her daughter laid upon the bed (Mark 7:29-30). The class marks both what she was commended for and what she was not given. She was not told to go and sin no more, and nothing was said to her about everlasting life. Set beside the woman of Samaria, who claimed Jacob as her father and was offered water springing up into everlasting life without even asking for it (John 4:12-14), the difference between the two answers is the difference between the two nations.

The class closes without malice in it. The crumb was still given; Christ showed her no hate, and the rule that follows for us is to live peaceably with all men as much as lies in us (Romans 12:18). The blessing did not come by overturning what he had said about the order of the house; it came to a woman who accepted the order and still believed mercy could reach her child. Matthew has already set down the only other faith commended in those words, and that was the centurion of Capernaum (Matthew 8:10).

cases.name: The wicked husbandmen
cases.charge: Beating and killing the servants sent for the fruit, and killing the heir to seize the inheritance
cases.summary: A certain man planted a vineyard, let it out to husbandmen and went into a far country, and at the season sent a servant for the fruit; the husbandmen beat him and sent him away empty, and beat and wounded the servants who followed (Luke 20:9-12). Last of all the owner sent his beloved son, and the husbandmen reasoned among themselves that this was the heir and killed him to seize the inheritance (Luke 20:13-15). Asked what the lord of the vineyard would do, the chief priests and elders passed the sentence out of their own mouths, and then perceived that the parable had been spoken against them (Matthew 21:40-41; Luke 20:19-20).
offenseFull: A parable is opened by precept upon precept, which is the only way the dark sayings are understood (Isaiah 28:9-10; Psalms 78:1-2). The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel and the men of Judah his pleasant plant (Isaiah 5:7). The husbandmen are the leaders set over that vineyard, the shepherds who were to feed the flock and instead fed themselves, eating the fat and clothing themselves with the wool (Ezekiel 34:1-3). The servants sent at the season are the prophets, sent rising early and often because God had compassion on his people (Jeremiah 25:4-5; 2 Chronicles 36:15-16). What was done to them is on record: Pashur the priest smote Jeremiah and put him in the stocks for prophesying the judgment, and Jeremiah told him the beating would not turn the judgment aside (Jeremiah 20:1-4). The same office did the same thing after Christ was gone, laying hands on the apostles and putting them in hold for teaching the people and preaching the resurrection (Acts 4:1-3). The parable describes a pattern the leaders of the nation had kept for centuries.

Then the owner said he would send his beloved son, which is the word spoken over Christ at the Jordan and again in the mount (Matthew 3:16-17; Matthew 17:5). When the husbandmen saw him they said among themselves that this was the heir, and that killing him would make the inheritance theirs (Luke 20:13-15). That saying carries the weight of the case, because to call him the heir they had to know who he was. The council said as much: if they let him alone all men would believe on him and the Romans would take away their place and nation, and Caiaphas, being high priest that year, said it was expedient that one man die for the people, which was itself a prophecy of the thing they were plotting (John 11:47-53). Even among the chief rulers many believed on him and would not confess him, for fear of being put out of the synagogue (John 12:42). The killing was not done in ignorance of the son. It was done because of who he was, to keep a place and a position.
judgmentFull: Asked what the lord of the vineyard would do, they answered that he would miserably destroy those wicked men and let the vineyard to other husbandmen who would render him the fruits in their seasons, and in Luke the hearers recoiled from the sentence as soon as it was spoken (Matthew 21:40-41; Luke 20:16). They had judged themselves. He answered out of the scriptures that the stone the builders rejected is become the head of the corner, that the kingdom of God would be taken from them and given to a nation bringing forth its fruits, and that the stone would break some and grind others to powder (Matthew 21:42-44; Luke 20:17-18). Peter afterward named the builders to their faces, telling the rulers and elders of Israel that this was the stone set at nought of them which is become the head of the corner (Acts 4:5-11). That stone is Christ, the chief corner stone, the only foundation any man may build on (Ephesians 2:20; 1 Corinthians 3:11), and the stone cut out without hands that breaks every kingdom in pieces and stands for ever (Daniel 2:44-45).

The account against that generation was reckoned from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zacharias, slain between the temple and the altar, and their house was left desolate (Matthew 23:35-38). Pilate was told he could have no power at all except it were given from above, and that the men who delivered Christ to him had the greater sin (John 19:10-11). The chief priests and scribes sought to lay hands on him that same hour, feared the people, and then sent spies who pretended to be just men, so they might deliver him to the power of the governor (Luke 20:19-20). Notice what the sentence does not say. The vineyard is not destroyed. It is let out again to husbandmen who will render the fruit, which is why Paul described his own work and that of Apollos in the same figure, one planting and another watering while God gives the increase, and called the people God’s husbandry (1 Corinthians 3:6-9). The office was not abolished. It was taken from men who would not render the fruit and given to men who would.

cases.name: The marriage of the king’s son
cases.charge: Making light of the call, and killing the servants who brought it
cases.summary: A king made a marriage for his son and sent his servants to call those who were bidden, and they would not come; at the second sending they made light of it, one going to his farm and another to his merchandise, while the rest took the servants, treated them spitefully and killed them (Matthew 22:1-6). The king sent his armies, destroyed those murderers and burned their city, then filled the wedding from the highways with guests both bad and good (Matthew 22:7-10). One guest was found without a wedding garment, had nothing to answer, and was bound and cast into outer darkness: many are called, but few are chosen (Matthew 22:11-14).
offenseFull: The servants in this parable are not any man who says he loves God. The law names them: the children of Israel are the servants of the Most High, the people he brought out of the land of Egypt (Leviticus 25:55). So both the refusal and the killing fall on a nation called by name, and on the messengers sent to that nation. Luke carries the same parable as a great supper and sets down the excuses one by one, a piece of ground just bought, five yoke of oxen to prove, a wife just married (Luke 14:16-24). Those three are lifted straight out of the law of war, where the man who had built a house and not dedicated it, planted a vineyard and not eaten of it, or betrothed a wife and not taken her was sent home from the battle (Deuteronomy 20:5-7). But the weapons of this warfare are not carnal (2 Corinthians 10:4-5), and Paul told the brethren the time is short, so that those who have wives should be as though they had none (1 Corinthians 7:29). What was once a lawful release from a physical battle is here called what it now is. A sinful man will not be reproved, but finds an excuse according to his own will (Sirach 32:17).

The second offense is inside the wedding. When the king came in to see the guests he found a man with no wedding garment on, and the man was speechless (Matthew 22:11-14). The garment is not cloth. It is righteousness, the keeping of the laws of the Most High, the clothing the psalm asks for when it prays that the priests be clothed with righteousness (Psalms 132:9). A man can be gathered in off the highway and still be missing the one thing the king came in to look for.
judgmentFull: The king was wroth, sent his armies, destroyed those murderers and burned their city, and said that those who were bidden were not worthy (Matthew 22:7-10). The honour of the invitation did not shield them; it measured them. Then the servants went out into the highways and gathered as many as they found, both bad and good, and the wedding was furnished with guests. Luke names who is gathered in: the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind, and the poor of his people are Zion (Isaiah 14:32). The order of that gathering is set down in Acts, where Paul said it was necessary that the word be spoken to them first, and since they judged themselves unworthy of everlasting life he turned to the Gentiles (Acts 13:44-46), who are named in the same gospel as Zebulun and Naphtali, Galilee of the Gentiles, the northern kingdom (Matthew 4:15). The last servant is sent into the highways and hedges to compel them to come in, and to compel is to press and to force, which is what the preaching in the street is for.

The man without the garment was bound hand and foot, taken away and cast into outer darkness where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, and the parable closes with its own reason: many are called, but few are chosen (Matthew 22:11-14). Luke closes the same teaching by saying that none of the men who were bidden would taste of that supper. Not every man of the nation will answer, for they are not all Israel which are of Israel (Romans 9:6). The refusal has an answer written long before: the Lord called and they refused, he stretched out his hand and no man regarded, and he will laugh at their calamity when their fear comes as desolation, and they will seek him early and not find him (Proverbs 1:24-28). Both halves of the sentence stand together. Refusing the call brought the armies on the city, and coming in without righteousness brought the binding at the table.

cases.name: The scribes and Pharisees
cases.charge: Shutting up the kingdom against men; devouring widows’ houses; tithing mint and omitting judgment, mercy and faith; whited sepulchres
cases.summary: Christ told the multitude and his disciples that the scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat, so whatever they bid the people observe they should observe and do, but they were not to follow their works, for they say and do not (Matthew 23:1-4). The woes that follow name the crimes: shutting up the kingdom of heaven against men, devouring widows’ houses and making long prayer for a pretence, tithing mint and anise and cummin while omitting judgment, mercy and faith, and appearing as whited sepulchres, beautiful outside and full of dead men’s bones within (Matthew 23:13-15; Matthew 23:23-24; Matthew 23:25-28). This is the plainest speaking in the gospel, and Christ was no soft man with these teachers of the law who did not believe it.
offenseFull: They sat in Moses’ seat, and that seat is the law; they were the judges of the people, which is why the instruction was to observe what they taught and not to do after their works. They bound heavy burdens grievous to be borne and laid them on men’s shoulders, and would not move them with one of their fingers (Matthew 23:1-4). All their works they did to be seen of men, loving the uppermost rooms at feasts, the chief seats in the synagogues and the greetings in the markets, when the greatest among them was to be the servant (Matthew 23:5-12). Luke keeps the same charge and adds the lawyers, who took away the key of knowledge, entered not in themselves, and hindered those who were entering (Luke 11:45-52). That key is understanding, and Christ is the one who opens and no man shuts (Revelation 3:7). Taking it away is teaching a man he need not keep what was commanded, when the answer given to the man who asked how to enter into life was plain: keep the commandments (Matthew 19:16-17).

The cup was clean outside and full of extortion and excess within, and the order given was to cleanse first that which is within (Matthew 23:25-28). Washing does not reach it. Though a man wash with nitre and take much soap, his iniquity is still marked before the Lord (Jeremiah 2:22); a man cleanses his way by taking heed to the word (Psalms 119:9), and Christ told the disciples they were clean through the word he had spoken (John 15:3). They paid tithe of mint and rue and all manner of herbs and passed over judgment and the love of God, and both were to be done (Matthew 23:23-24; Luke 11:42). The love of God is walking after his commandments (2 John 1:6), and to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22); what the Lord desires is mercy and the knowledge of God, and the priest’s lips should keep that knowledge and seek the law at his mouth (Hosea 6:6; Malachi 2:7). They were told instead to give alms of such things as they had, which is the counsel Tobit gave his son, that alms delivers from death (Luke 11:41; Tobit 4:7-11).
judgmentFull: The sentence in this chapter is a curse pronounced in the open, woe after woe, on men who held the office and would not keep the law they taught. Those who shut up the kingdom and devoured widows’ houses under a pretence of long prayer were told they would receive the greater damnation (Matthew 23:13-15). They compassed sea and land to make one proselyte and made him twofold more the child of hell than themselves, and their rules about swearing by the gold rather than the temple are called blindness, because the temple sanctifies the gold (Matthew 23:15-22). Christ called them serpents and a generation of vipers and asked how they could escape the damnation of hell (Matthew 23:33). Their leaven was named beside the leaven of Herod, which shows whose manner they were following, and leaven is an influence that spreads, which is why the warning was given to the multitude and the disciples before it was said to the men themselves (Mark 8:15).

Luke records the same men as graves which appear not, so that the men who walk over them are not aware of them (Luke 11:44). The outside is handsome and the people walking among them do not know what they are standing on. That is the mark of the perilous times, when men are lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, having a form of godliness and denying the power of it (2 Timothy 3:1-5). The blood of all the prophets, from Abel to Zacharias who perished between the altar and the temple, was required of that generation (Luke 11:50-51; Matthew 23:35-36). When the teaching ended, the scribes and Pharisees began to urge him vehemently and to lay wait for him, seeking to catch something out of his mouth that they might accuse him (Luke 11:53-54). The office did not shield the conduct. It raised the account against them.

Luke keeps the same charge and adds the lawyers, who took away the key of knowledge, entered not in themselves, and hindered those who were entering (Luke 11:45-52). That key is understanding, and Christ is the one who opens and no man shuts (Revelation 3:7). cases.name: Jerusalem, that killeth the prophets
cases.charge: Killing the prophets and stoning them that are sent; not knowing the time of her visitation
cases.summary: Christ named the city by what it did: it killed the prophets and stoned those sent to it, and he said how often he would have gathered her children together as a hen gathers her brood, and they would not (Luke 13:34-35). The sentence follows in the same breath, that her house is left desolate (Matthew 23:37-38). He told the disciples that of all the buildings of the temple there would not be left one stone upon another (Matthew 24:1-2), and Luke gives the cause: she knew not the time of her visitation (Luke 19:41-44).
offenseFull: They built the tombs of the prophets and garnished the sepulchres of the righteous and said that if they had lived in the days of their fathers they would not have been partakers in the blood of the prophets, and by saying it they witnessed against themselves that they were the children of those who killed the prophets (Matthew 23:29-32). The record of the kings says the messengers were sent early and often because God had compassion on his people, and they mocked them and despised his words until there was no remedy (2 Chronicles 36:15-16); Nehemiah says the same, that they cast the law behind their backs and slew the prophets that testified against them (Nehemiah 9:26). The account was reckoned from righteous Abel to Zacharias, whom they slew between the temple and the altar, and it was required of that generation (Matthew 23:33-36). They followed that man into the temple to kill him, which is what hatred does when it is let run; it does not stop at the door of a holy place. Of the prophets and wise men and scribes he would send, some they would kill and crucify and some they would scourge in their synagogues and persecute from city to city. That spirit comes back on the earth in every generation, and it is the reason a man can be laid hands on today for opening a Bible in the street.

Coming near the city he wept over it, because the things belonging to her peace were hidden from her eyes (Luke 19:41-44). He had just been told by some of the Pharisees to rebuke his disciples for calling him the king that comes in the name of the Lord, and he answered that if these held their peace the stones would immediately cry out (Luke 19:37-40; Habakkuk 2:11). Then he said the stones of the city would be thrown down. The weeping was not sentiment over buildings. It was over a people who had the visitation standing in front of them and did not know the day of it.
judgmentFull: The disciples came to show him the buildings of the temple, and he told them not to be taken with what they were looking at, because there would not be left one stone upon another that would not be thrown down (Matthew 24:1-2). Luke gives the sign to watch for: when Jerusalem is seen compassed with armies, then the desolation of it is near, and those in Judaea are to flee to the mountains and those in the midst of it to depart out (Luke 21:20-21). Those who took the word left. Those who came up to the passover anyway were shut inside it. These are the days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled (Luke 21:22), and what was written is the curse in the law: a nation brought from far, swift as the eagle flies, of fierce countenance, which would besiege them in all their gates until their high and fenced walls came down, and they would eat the flesh of their own sons and daughters in the siege (Deuteronomy 28:49-53). The eagle was the standard of Rome. Christ had already said woe to those who give suck in those days, and told the daughters of Jerusalem to weep for themselves and for their children (Luke 23:28-31).

The people would fall by the edge of the sword and be led away captive into all nations, and the city would be trodden down of the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (Luke 21:24). That is the same word given in the law, that the Lord would scatter them among the nations and leave them few in number (Deuteronomy 4:27; Deuteronomy 28:64), and it is the reason the great multitude that no man could number is gathered out of all nations and kindreds and people and tongues (Revelation 7:9). The siege of 70 AD did not end the nation; it

scattered it, first into Africa and from there into the hands of every empire that followed, which is how a people came to be mingled among the heathen and to learn their works (Psalms 106:35). Perpetual hatred stood behind the armies, the hatred of Esau who shed the blood of the children of Israel in the time of their calamity (Ezekiel 35:5). The house was pulled down and the nation was not. The word left standing is the one Christ gave with the sentence: they would not see him again until they said he was blessed who came in the name of the Lord, and they would look on the one they had pierced and mourn for him (Luke 13:35; Zechariah 12:10).

cases.name: Peter’s denial
cases.charge: Denying Christ three times with cursing and swearing
cases.summary: Peter said that though all men should be offended because of him he would never be offended, and that though he should die with him he would not deny him (Matthew 26:33-35). In the high priest’s hall he denied it to a damsel, then with an oath, and then with cursing and swearing that he did not know the man, and the cock crew (Matthew 26:69-75). The Lord turned and looked on Peter, and he remembered the word that had been spoken to him, and went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:60-62).
offenseFull: Before the denial he was warned and he was prayed for. Satan had desired to have them, to sift them as wheat, and Christ told Peter he had prayed for him that his faith fail not, and that when he was converted he should strengthen his brethren (Luke 22:31-32). Peter had walked with him and was not yet converted. What converts a man is named in the psalm: the law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul (Psalms 19:7), and that is also what he was to strengthen his brethren with. Peter answered out of his own confidence that he was ready to go both into prison and to death, and was told what he would do before the cock crew (Luke 22:33-34). A man does not know tomorrow, for his life is a vapour that appears for a little time and then vanishes away (James 4:14-15).

He denied three times. The third time he was picked out by his speech, because he was a Galilaean; the way he talked gave him away, so that he sounded like the man he was denying (Luke 22:54-60). Matthew records the oath, and then the cursing and swearing that he did not know the man (Matthew 26:69-75). The warning about that stands in the same gospel: whoever confesses him before men, him will he confess before his Father, and whoever denies him before men will be denied (Matthew 10:32-33). It was the hour given to the other side, as Christ told the chief priests and the captains of the temple when they came out against him with swords and staves, that this was their hour and the power of darkness (Luke 22:52-53). Isaiah had written it plainly of the servant: he was despised and rejected of men, and we hid as it were our faces from him, and we esteemed him not (Isaiah 53:3). That verse is Peter in the courtyard.
judgmentFull: The look and the tears are the first part of the answer. The Lord turned and looked on Peter, and Peter remembered the word and went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:60-62). The difference between this case and the traitor in the same chapter is what came after the weeping. When Judas saw what he had done he did not go back and reconcile; he went and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3-5). Peter reconciled. Godly sorrow works repentance to salvation, but the sorrow of the world works death (2 Corinthians 7:10).

The reconciliation is recorded. After the resurrection Christ asked Peter three times whether he loved him and three times charged him to feed his lambs and his sheep, once for each denial, and Peter was grieved at the third asking (John 21:15-17). Then he was told by what death he should glorify God, that when he was old another would gird him and carry him where he would not (John 21:18-19), which answers what he had been told in the upper room, that where Christ was going he could not follow then but should follow afterwards (John 13:36). The history says he was held nine months in prison at Rome, converted the keepers and others while he was in there, and was scourged and crucified with his head downward, a position he asked for because he did not count himself worthy to die as his master died. The man who bounced back from that courtyard is the same man who stood at the gate called Beautiful and told a lame beggar that he had no silver and gold, but gave him what he had (Acts 3:1-8). The charge given with the warning stood: once converted, he was to strengthen his brethren. The fall did not cancel the man, and it did not cancel what he was sent to teach.

cases.name: The chief priests, and the watch at the sepulchre
cases.charge: Paying the soldiers large money to report a lie about the resurrection
cases.summary: The day after the preparation the chief priests and Pharisees came to Pilate, called Christ a deceiver, and asked that the sepulchre be made sure until the third day, because they remembered his saying that after three days he would rise; Pilate gave them a watch, and they sealed the stone and set it (Matthew 27:62-66). When some of the watch came into the city and told the chief priests all the things that were done, the priests assembled with the elders, took counsel, and gave large money to the soldiers to say that the disciples came by night and stole him away while they slept (Matthew 28:11-13).
offenseFull: They remembered the saying better than the disciples did. That is the weight of the request: the men who had him put to death were the men who took his words about the third day seriously enough to post a guard against them. There was an earthquake, and the angel of the Lord came down and rolled back the stone and sat on it, and the keepers shook and became as dead men, and the angel told the women he was not there, for he was risen as he said (Matthew 28:1-6). At that point the matter was settled in front of witnesses, and the men who had asked for the guard could have conceded it. They did not. They assembled, took counsel, and bought the report they had set the watch to prevent (Matthew 28:11-13). Men love darkness rather than light, because their deeds are evil (John 3:19).

The money had a reason behind it. A soldier who lost a prisoner under his watch answered for it with his own life, which is why the priests added that if it came to the governor’s ears they would persuade him and secure them (Matthew 28:14). So the soldiers were bought with money and with a promise of protection from the same men who had just been shown that the promise was worth nothing, since they had made a covenant with death and an agreement with hell, saying the overflowing scourge would not come to them (Isaiah 28:15). Never trust an enemy, whatever the terms (Sirach 12:10). The bargain itself broke the law twice over, against raising a false report and against bearing false witness (Exodus 23:1; Exodus 20:16).
judgmentFull: The soldiers took the money and did as they were taught, and that saying was commonly reported among the Jews until the day the account was written (Matthew 28:15). No sentence on the chief priests, on the elders, or on the soldiers is recorded in the passage. What is recorded is the bargain, with their names attached to it, in a book that has outlived every copy of the story they bought.

The report also could not hold, because of how the resurrection was shown. God raised him the third day and showed him openly, not to all the people, but to witnesses chosen before, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead (Acts 10:40-41). He was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve, and after that of above five hundred brethren at once, most of whom were still alive when Paul wrote it down (1 Corinthians 15:5-6). He showed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs over forty days (Acts 1:3). A crucifixion was a public thing in that city, and so was the darkness and the earthquake that went with this one, so the men who were paid to say they had slept through the one event everyone was talking about were given a story that could not survive the witnesses. The standing rule on such a report is written: a false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaks lies shall not escape (Proverbs 19:5).

cases.name: The woman with the issue of blood
cases.charge: Believing that if she might but touch his clothes she should be whole
cases.summary: A woman had an issue of blood twelve years, had suffered many things of many physicians and spent all her living on them, and was nothing bettered but rather grew worse (Mark 5:25-26). She came behind him in the press and touched the border of his garment, and straightway the fountain of her blood was dried up (Luke 8:43-44). He would not let the touch pass, and when she came trembling and told all the truth before the people he called her daughter, told her that her faith had made her whole, and sent her away in peace, whole of her plague (Mark 5:30-34).
offenseFull: The law puts a woman apart seven days for her issue, and anyone who touches her or what she sits on is unclean until the evening; if the issue runs beyond the time of her separation, all those days are counted as the days of her separation and she remains unclean (Leviticus 15:19-25). Twelve years of that is what this woman had carried. The gospel calls it a plague, and a sickness of long continuance that is not written in the book of the law is one of the things named in the curses that would cleave to the nation (Deuteronomy 28:59-61; Mark 5:29). She was not a woman with an inconvenience. She was a woman under a curse, cut off from the congregation, out of money, and worse than when she started.

What she reached for was not his sleeve or his hand. It was the border of the garment (Luke 8:43-44; Matthew 9:20-21), and of all the things on a man walking through a crowd it is the hardest to take hold of, which means she went down for it on purpose. The fringe on the border with the ribband of blue is commanded in the law, to be looked on so that the people remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them (Numbers 15:38-39). She knew what was in those fringes. The people of that country knew the same thing, and wherever he entered they laid the sick in the streets and asked that they might touch if it were but the border of his garment, and as many as touched were made whole (Mark 6:56).
judgmentFull: The issue stopped straightway, and she felt in her body that she was healed of that plague (Mark 5:29). He would not let it pass as one more press of the crowd. When Peter said the multitude thronged him and pressed him, he answered that somebody had touched him, for he perceived that virtue had gone out of him (Luke 8:45-46). The distinction matters, because a whole crowd was touching him and one woman was healed. The chapter is one work of power after another and every one of them turns on faith; healing came by faith and by the works that go with it, and not by the touching of a hand.

She came trembling, fell down before him, and declared before all the people why she had touched him and how she was healed immediately (Luke 8:47). He did not let her keep it quiet, and the reason is in what she was given. A woman who had been put apart for twelve years was named daughter in front of the congregation, told that her faith had made her whole, and sent away in peace, whole of her plague (Luke 8:48; Mark 5:34). The verdict was public because the uncleanness had been public. What years of physicians and all her living could not buy was given for nothing, and the one thing she brought was the thing the Lord named.

cases.offense: The law puts a woman apart seven days for her issue, and anyone who touches her or what she sits on is unclean until the evening; if the issue runs beyond the time of her separation, all those days are counted as the days of her separation and she remains unclean (Leviticus 15:19-25). Twelve years of that is what this woman had carried. The gospel calls it a plague, and a sickness of long continuance that is not written in the book of the law is one of the things named in the curses that would cleave to the nation (Deuteronomy 28:59-61; Mark 5:29). She was not a woman with an inconvenience. She was a woman under a curse, cut off from the congregation, out of money, and worse than when she started.
cases.judgment: The issue stopped straightway, and she felt in her body that she was healed of that plague (Mark 5:29). He would not let it pass as one more press of the crowd. When Peter said the multitude thronged him and pressed him, he answered that somebody had touched him, for he perceived that virtue had gone out of him (Luke 8:45-46). The distinction matters, because a whole crowd was touching him and one woman was healed. The chapter is one work of power after another and every one of them turns on faith; healing came by faith and by the works that go with it, and not by the touching of a hand.

cases.name: Herod Antipas and Herodias
cases.charge: Taking his brother’s wife; beheading John for saying so
cases.summary: Herod the tetrarch had married Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, and John told him plainly that it was not lawful for him to have his brother’s wife (Mark 6:17-18). For that word Herod shut John up in prison, adding it above all the other evils he had done (Luke 3:19-20). Herodias held a quarrel against John and would have killed him but could not, because Herod feared him, knowing that he was a just man and holy; at the birthday feast an oath sworn before the guests put the prophet’s head on a charger and into her hands (Mark 6:19-28).
offenseFull: When Herod the Great died his kingdom was split among three sons, and Herod Antipas was made tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea (Luke 3:1). That house was Idumaean, of the stock of Esau, put in place by Rome to rule over Israel, and its head had already killed the children of Bethlehem trying to reach the child (Matthew 2:16). They were not strangers to the law. They were raised and groomed in the customs of Israel, which is exactly why Rome used them, and Paul said as much to Agrippa, that he knew him to be expert in all customs and questions among the Jews (Acts 26:3). Herod knew the law well enough to be accused by it. The statute is written plainly: the nakedness of a brother’s wife is not to be uncovered (Leviticus 18:16), and a man who takes his brother’s wife has done an unclean thing (Leviticus 20:21).

John reproved him for Herodias and for all the evils he had done, and Herod added this above all, that he shut John up in prison (Luke 3:19-20). Mark records that Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just man and holy, observed him, heard him gladly and did many things at his word (Mark 6:19-20). Hearing him gladly never turned into obeying him, and the whole case turns on that gap. On his birthday he made a supper for his lords, his high captains and the chief estates of Galilee; the daughter of Herodias danced and pleased him and those who sat with him, and he swore to give her whatever she asked, to the half of his kingdom. She asked her mother what to ask and was told, the head of John the Baptist. The king was exceeding sorry, and for his oath’s sake and for the sake of the company at the table he would not reject her, and sent an executioner (Mark 6:21-28). A rash oath sworn in front of guests did not make the killing lawful. The fear of looking small in front of his own table outweighed everything he knew about the man in his prison.
judgmentFull: No sentence on Herod or on Herodias is recorded in these accounts. What is recorded is a conscience that would not settle. When Herod heard of the fame of Jesus he said that this was John the Baptist, whom he had beheaded, risen from the dead (Mark 6:14-16). When certain of the Pharisees came telling Christ to depart because Herod would kill him, he told them to go and tell that fox that he cast out devils and did cures that day and the next, and the third day he would be perfected, and that it could not be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem (Luke 13:31-33). To call a man a fox in that day was to call him a crafty and cruel enemy of God’s servants, not to flatter him. A threat from that house did not move Christ off his work by a single day.

At the trial Herod was exceeding glad to see him, because he had heard many things of him and hoped to see some miracle done. He questioned him in many words, and Christ answered him nothing; then Herod with his men of war set him at nought, mocked him, arrayed him in a gorgeous robe and sent him back to Pilate (Luke 23:8-12). He had nothing to say to that house at all. Its head had sought his life as a child, and this one had beheaded John. The man who would not lose face in front of his dinner guests got no word out of the Son of God in front of a whole court. The charge in this case is proved and the sentence is not executed in the record.

cases.name: The rich young ruler
cases.charge: Going away sorrowful, because he had great possessions
cases.summary: A ruler came running and kneeled to him and asked what he should do to inherit eternal life, and was answered that if he would enter into life he should keep the commandments, which were then named to him (Mark 10:17-19; Luke 18:18-20). He said he had observed all these from his youth. Christ, looking on him, loved him, and named the one thing he lacked: sell what he had, give to the poor, take up the cross and follow him. He was sad at that saying and went away grieved, for he had great possessions (Mark 10:20-22).
offenseFull: Luke sets the case immediately after the word that a man must receive the kingdom of God as a little child or he will not enter it (Luke 18:16-17). That is the measure the ruler is laid against. Coming into this truth means putting down what a man thought he knew, and a man who says he is grown and nobody can teach him is a man who will not make it. The answer to his question came out of the law: keep the commandments, and the ones named to him were the commandments of loving a neighbour, do not commit adultery, do not kill, do not steal, do not bear false witness, defraud not, honour his father and his mother (Mark 10:19). Money buys nothing here, and what is paid week by week to a preacher washes away no sin. Matthew adds the one that the list was building toward, to love a neighbour as himself (Matthew 19:19).

He answered that he had observed all these from his youth. That is the arrogancy the scripture warns about: talk no more so exceedingly proudly, for the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed (1 Samuel 2:3). He was wise in his own conceit (Romans 12:16). So the one thing lacking was named, and it was drawn straight out of the commandment he had just claimed to keep: sell what he had, give to the poor, and come and follow (Mark 10:21). He had kept the letter of what was named to him and had not loved his neighbour as himself, or he would already have given to the poor of his own people. What that looked like when men did it is written in Acts, where those who were possessors of lands and houses sold them and laid the price at the apostles’ feet, and distribution was made to every man according as he had need, and none of them lacked (Acts 4:32-35). He was sad at that saying and went away grieved, for he had great possessions (Mark 10:22).
judgmentFull: Nothing further is recorded of the man and no sentence is passed on him. What follows is the warning drawn out of his case. Christ looked round about and said how hardly those who have riches shall enter into the kingdom of God, and that it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter in (Mark 10:23-25). The eye of a needle is the low gate a camel has to stoop and unload to get through, and the point of the picture is that a rich man will not stoop. He that trusts in his riches shall fall, but the righteous shall flourish as a branch (Proverbs 11:28), and riches profit not in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death (Proverbs 11:4). The prayer in Proverbs asks for neither poverty nor riches, lest a man be full and deny the Lord, or be poor and steal (Proverbs 30:8-9). The danger is named again in Revelation, where a man says he is rich and increased with goods and has need of nothing, and does not know that he is wretched and miserable and poor and blind and naked (Revelation 3:17).

The disciples were astonished out of measure and asked who then could be saved, and he answered that with men it is impossible, but not with God, for with God all things are possible (Mark 10:26-27). Wealth is not the charge in itself; blessed is the rich that is found without blemish and has not gone after gold (Sirach 31:8), and rich men in the body are charged not to be high minded nor to trust in uncertain riches, but to be rich in good works, ready to distribute and willing to communicate (1 Timothy 6:17-18). Peter said they had left all and followed him, and the answer names what

the exchange is worth: no man who has left house or brethren or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or lands for his sake and the gospel’s shall fail to receive a hundredfold now in this time, with persecutions, and in the world to come eternal life (Mark 10:28-30). What is forsaken coming into this truth is repaid in the nation. A man may lose one parent and gain a congregation, and beyond that a whole people. That exchange was set in front of the ruler, and he kept what he had instead.

cases.name: The widow and her two mites
cases.charge: Casting in all that she had, even all her living
cases.summary: Jesus sat over against the treasury and watched how the people cast money into it, and many that were rich cast in much; a certain poor widow came and threw in two mites, which make a farthing (Mark 12:41-42). He called his disciples and said that this poor widow had cast in more than all those who had cast into the treasury, because they all cast in of their abundance, but she of her want cast in all that she had, even all her living (Mark 12:43-44; Luke 21:1-4).
offenseFull: The treasury was not a collection plate. It was the store in the temple, and what was laid up in it is stated in the history: when a governor came to seize the money, the high priest told him it was laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, with some of it the private deposit of a man of great dignity, and that it was impossible such a wrong should be done to those who had committed it to the holiness of the place (2 Maccabees 3:4-12). The custom carried down to the day in this chapter, when the giving was done in the open and everyone could see what went in. So this is a widow putting her last coin into the fund that existed to relieve widows.

The two mites together make a farthing, the smallest coins in circulation in that country, worth a fraction of a penny. Measured against the sums going in around her it was nothing. Measured against what she held it was everything, because it was not a portion of her living, it was all her living (Mark 12:44). The law measures a gift that way: every man is to give as he is able, according to the blessing of the Lord his God given to him (Deuteronomy 16:17), and a willing mind is accepted according to that a man has, and not according to that he has not (2 Corinthians 8:12). Tobit told his son to give alms of his substance, and if he had but little, not to be afraid to give according to that little, because alms delivers from death (Tobit 4:7-11).
judgmentFull: The blessing recorded here is the verdict he spoke over her in front of the disciples. He called them to him and said that this poor widow had cast in more than all those who had cast into the treasury (Mark 12:43; Luke 21:3). The rich cast in much. She cast in more than all of them together, and the reason is given with the verdict: they all cast in of their abundance, but she of her want cast in all the living that she had.

Nothing is said against the rich men in the passage. They were doing what they were supposed to do with an abundance, and the charge laid on such men is not to be high minded nor to trust in uncertain riches but to be rich in good works, ready to distribute (1 Timothy 6:17-18). The comparison is not between a good giver and bad ones. It is between what a gift costs and what it counts, and by that measure the smallest sum that went into the treasury that day was the largest gift given in it. He which sows sparingly shall reap also sparingly, and he which sows bountifully shall reap also bountifully (2 Corinthians 9:6). The verdict is also the warning, because it stands in the same chapter as the scribes who devoured widows’ houses and for a pretence made long prayers (Mark 12:40). Christ had just named the men who eat widows like her, and then pointed at her and called her the greatest giver in the room.

cases.name: Barabbas
cases.charge: Insurrection and murder
cases.summary: At the feast the governor released one prisoner to the people, and there was a notable prisoner named Barabbas, who lay bound with those who had made insurrection with him and had committed murder in the insurrection (Matthew 27:15-16; Mark 15:6-7). Luke states the charge plainly: he had been cast into prison for a certain sedition made in the city, and for murder (Luke 23:18-19). The chief priests moved the people to ask for Barabbas, and Pilate released him and delivered Jesus to their will (Mark 15:11; Luke 23:25).
offenseFull: Barabbas was not an unknown man. He was a notable prisoner, taken with a band that had risen against the government and killed in the rising (Mark 15:6-7; Luke 23:18-19). John calls him a robber (John 18:40). He was not brought out because his cause had been heard and he was found innocent; he was brought out because the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude to ask for him and to destroy Jesus (Matthew 27:20).

Peter afterward set the exchange before the people in plain words: they denied the Holy One and the Just, desired a murderer to be granted to them, and killed the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead, of which the apostles were witnesses (Acts 3:14-15). That is the offense of this case as the apostles preached it. Peter said in the same breath that through ignorance they did it, as did also their rulers, and then called them to repent and be converted so that their sins might be blotted out (Acts 3:17-19). The crowd that shouted for a murderer was not written off. It was preached to.
judgmentFull: Pilate said a third time that he found no cause of death in him, and asked what evil the man had done (Luke 23:22). He knew the man was innocent and gave sentence anyway. Matthew records how the choice was put, whether he should release Barabbas or Jesus which is called Christ, and gives the governor’s own reading of the court: he knew that for envy they had delivered him (Matthew 27:17-18). His own wife sent word to him while he sat on the judgment seat, telling him to have nothing to do with that just man (Matthew 27:19). The envy was written on their faces and in their spirit and they could not hide it, and a heathen governor could see it from the bench.

So the guilty man went free and the innocent man was delivered to their will (Mark 15:15; Luke 23:25). No further history of Barabbas is given, and no penalty on him is recorded anywhere in the gospels. He stands in the book as a man spared, and spared in the very proceeding that laid the sentence he had earned on another. The rule the court broke is written: he that justifies the wicked, and he that condemns the just, are both an abomination to the Lord (Proverbs 17:15). And the release is not the end of the reckoning, because the same word that named the exchange also named the day when he whom they pierced will be looked on and mourned for (Zechariah 12:10).

cases.name: Joseph of Arimathaea
cases.charge: Going in boldly unto Pilate and craving the body; and not having consented to the counsel and deed of them
cases.summary: Joseph of Arimathaea was an honourable counsellor who waited for the kingdom of God, a good man and a just, and he had not consented to the counsel and deed of the council he sat in (Mark 15:43; Luke 23:50-51). When the evening was come, because it was the preparation, he went in boldly to Pilate and craved the body. He took it down, wrapped it in clean linen, and laid it in his own new tomb hewn out of a rock, where no man had been laid before (Matthew 27:57-60).
offenseFull: He sat in the council that condemned Christ and did not consent to their counsel and deed (Luke 23:50-51). Not every man was let into that room, so the record is telling you he had standing among the Pharisees and was a follower of Christ at the same time. John says he was a disciple, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38). That fear has a definition in the gospel: Christ had sent them out as sheep among wolves and told them to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves, and warned that men would deliver them up to the councils and scourge them in their synagogues (Matthew 10:16-18). Joseph was inside one of those councils. He is named with Nicodemus, who came to Christ by night and told him plainly that they knew he was a teacher come from God (John 3:1-2), and the two of them together are the proof that the rejection of Christ was the work of the elders, the chief priests and the scribes, and not of every man in the nation (Mark 8:31; John 8:31).

When the evening was come he went in boldly to Pilate and craved the body, which was the dangerous part of it (Mark 15:43). It takes position and standing to walk into that hall and ask a Roman governor for the corpse of a man his own court had just executed as a rebel, and to be heard. He used what he had, the way Esther used her place for the nation and Daniel used his. He bought fine linen, took the body down, wrapped it, laid it in a sepulchre hewn out of a rock, and rolled a stone to the door; Nicodemus came with him bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pound weight (Mark 15:46; John 19:39-40). The burial was made the same day, which is the custom written in the law: the body of a man hanged on a tree shall not remain all night, but shall be buried that day, that the land be not defiled (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). There is no waiting days over a body.
judgmentFull: The prophet had written that he would make his grave with the wicked and with the rich in his death (Isaiah 53:9). He was crucified between two malefactors, and then a rich man buried him in his own new sepulchre (Matthew 27:57-60). Joseph is how that word came to pass, and the passage names him as rich in the same sentence that names what he did with it.

The women who came with him out of Galilee followed after and beheld the sepulchre and how the body was laid, then returned and prepared spices and ointments, and rested the sabbath day according to the commandment (Luke 23:55-56). Their witness of the place is what makes the report bought from the watch worthless, because they knew exactly where the body had been put. Nothing is promised to Joseph in the text beyond the record itself. A counsellor who did not consent, who spent his standing, his linen and his own tomb on a body nobody else would claim, is named in all four gospels and set beside Nicodemus as proof that some of those men did change. The honour is in what he did, and in the word it fulfilled.
