cases.offense: He sat in the council that condemned Christ and did not consent to their counsel and deed (Luke 23:50-51). Not every man was let into that room, so the record is telling you he had standing among the Pharisees and was a follower of Christ at the same time. John says he was a disciple, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38). That fear has a definition in the gospel: Christ had sent them out as sheep among wolves and told them to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves, and warned that men would deliver them up to the councils and scourge them in their synagogues (Matthew 10:16-18). Joseph was inside one of those councils. He is named with Nicodemus, who came to Christ by night and told him plainly that they knew he was a teacher come from God (John 3:1-2), and the two of them together are the proof that the rejection of Christ was the work of the elders, the chief priests and the scribes, and not of every man in the nation (Mark 8:31; John 8:31).
cases.judgment: The prophet had written that he would make his grave with the wicked and with the rich in his death (Isaiah 53:9). He was crucified between two malefactors, and then a rich man buried him in his own new sepulchre (Matthew 27:57-60). Joseph is how that word came to pass, and the passage names him as rich in the same sentence that names what he did with it.

cases.name: Zacharias
cases.charge: Not believing the words of the angel Gabriel, and asking for a sign
cases.summary: While Zacharias executed the priest’s office before God in the order of his course, his lot was to burn incense, and the angel Gabriel stood on the right side of the altar and told him his prayer was heard, that Elisabeth would bear him a son, and that he should call his name John (Luke 1:8-13). Zacharias asked how he should know this, since he was an old man and his wife well stricken in years (Luke 1:18). Gabriel answered that because he did not believe the words, which would be fulfilled in their season, he would be dumb and unable to speak until the day these things were performed (Luke 1:19-20).
offenseFull: Everything about his position argued against the question. He was of the course of Abia, the eighth of the twenty-four courses of the sons of Aaron that David set in order when he was preparing the house, by a pattern the Lord gave him in writing (Luke 1:5; 1 Chronicles 24:7-10; 1 Chronicles 28:11-19). His wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and among the priests a man who could not be reckoned by genealogy was put from the priesthood as polluted (Ezra 2:61-63). He was standing at the altar of incense at the hour the law appointed, with the whole multitude praying outside (Exodus 30:7-8; Luke 1:9-10). He was in the exact place the Most High had built for that conversation, and the answer to his own prayer was handed to him there.

The question had been asked and answered before, in the same circumstances. Abraham and Sarah were old and well stricken in age when they were told she would have a son, and the answer given then was that nothing is too hard for the Lord (Genesis 18:11-14). Here the promise came with the name of the messenger attached to it: Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God, sent to speak and to show him these glad tidings (Luke 1:19). The fault named in the sentence is not the asking of a question. It is the not believing. The words would be fulfilled in their season whatever he made of them (Luke 1:20). He was a righteous man, blameless in the commandments and ordinances, serving in his appointed course, and he doubted the one thing he had been praying for (Luke 1:6-7).
judgmentFull: He was struck dumb and unable to speak until the day the things spoken were performed (Luke 1:20). The people outside waited and marvelled that he tarried so long in the temple; when he came out he could not speak to them, and they perceived that he had seen a vision, for he beckoned to them and remained speechless. As soon as the days of his ministration were accomplished he departed to his own house, and after those days his wife Elisabeth conceived (Luke 1:21-24). The performance the angel spoke of took place in its order, and the sentence had a stated cause and a stated limit. His unbelief cost him his speech; it did not cost Elisabeth the child, and it did not delay the promise by a day.

The judgment ended exactly where the angel said it would. At the circumcision on the eighth day the neighbours and cousins would have called the child Zacharias after his father, and Elisabeth said he should be called John. They made signs to his father, and he asked for a writing table and wrote that his name is John, and they all marvelled. At once his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke and praised God (Luke 1:57-64). The tongue that was stopped for unbelief was given back to prophesy: blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people and raised up a horn of salvation in the house of his servant David, to perform the mercy promised to the fathers and the oath sworn to Abraham, that being delivered out of the hand of their enemies they might serve him without fear (Luke 1:67-75). The child would go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death (Luke 1:76-79), and that shadow is the affliction and the iron of captivity (Psalms 107:10). The first words out of his mouth were about the deliverance of the nation, not about the year he had spent silent.

cases.name: Zacharias and Elisabeth
cases.charge: Both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless
cases.summary: Zacharias was a priest of the course of Abia and Elisabeth was of the daughters of Aaron, and they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless; they had no child, because Elisabeth was barren, and they were both now well stricken in years (Luke 1:5-7). The answer came at the altar of incense: a son named John, great in the sight of the Lord, filled with the Holy Ghost from his mother’s womb, who would turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God and go before him in the spirit and power of Elias (Luke 1:13-17).
offenseFull: Luke states the verdict on this household before he states its trouble. Both were righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless; and they had no child, because Elisabeth was barren, and they were both well stricken in years (Luke 1:5-7). The childlessness is set down beside the blamelessness, not against it. It is the commandments that make a man righteous (Deuteronomy 6:25), and a house without children was not therefore a house under judgment.

Both of them were found in their place. Zacharias was executing the priest’s office in the order of his course when the answer came, at the hour of incense that the law fixed, with the whole multitude of the people praying outside (Luke 1:8-10; Exodus 30:7-8). That course was one of the twenty-four David had set in order by the pattern the Lord gave him (1 Chronicles 24:7-10). Elisabeth held the same line at the other end of it. When the neighbours and kinsfolk would have named the child after his father, she said he should be called John and would not be moved from it, though none of her kindred was called by that name (Luke 1:59-61). Neither of them took an unanswered prayer as a licence to leave off what they had been keeping all their lives.
judgmentFull: What was promised was more than a child in the house. There would be joy and gladness and many would rejoice at his birth; he would be great in the sight of the Lord, drink neither wine nor strong drink, be filled with the Holy Ghost from his mother’s womb, turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and go before him in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and make ready a people prepared for the Lord (Luke 1:13-17). That is the word Malachi had left standing at the end of the prophets (Malachi 4:5-6), and it is the child of whom Christ said that among those born of women there had not risen a greater (Matthew 11:11). A man filled with the Spirit from the womb is spoken of the same way Jeremiah was, known before he was formed in the belly and ordained a prophet to the nations (Jeremiah 1:5). The answer to one household’s prayer was sent for the whole nation.

Elisabeth conceived and hid herself five months, saying that the Lord had dealt with her so in the days wherein he looked on her, to take away her reproach among men (Luke 1:24-25). Her reproach was that she was called barren, and what was done for her is what was done for Sarah, which is what the angel meant in telling Mary that with God nothing shall be impossible: an old woman past the age was carrying a child and was already in her sixth month (Luke 1:36-37; Genesis 18:11-14). When Mary came into the house and greeted her, the child leaped in her womb, and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost and cried out with a loud voice (Luke 1:41-42). Her neighbours and kin heard how greatly the Lord had shown her mercy, and they rejoiced with her (Luke 1:57-58). Her husband’s silence did not withdraw any of it, and when his mouth was opened the house that had been childless was filled with prophecy of the covenant sworn to Abraham and of salvation from the hand of their enemies (Luke 1:67-75).

cases.name: Mary, the mother of Jesus
cases.charge: Be it unto me according to thy word; blessed is she that believed
cases.summary: The angel Gabriel was sent to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin espoused to a man named Joseph, of the house of David, and the virgin’s name was Mary. She was told she would bring forth a son and call his name Jesus, that he would be great and be called the Son of the Highest, and that with God nothing shall be impossible; she asked how it should be, and then answered as the handmaid of the Lord, that it be to her according to his word (Luke 1:26-38). Elisabeth gave the verdict on that answer: blessed is she that believed, for there shall be a performance of the things told her from the Lord (Luke 1:39-45).
offenseFull: Her answer was the answer of a servant. She called herself the handmaid of the Lord and said, let it be to me according to your word (Luke 1:38). The same messenger had stood in the temple six months earlier and told Zacharias that his wife would bear a son, and the promise was performed in its season, in the order the Most High set, and the same order holds here (Luke 1:13; Luke 1:23-24). Mary went from there into the hill country with haste, into a city of Judah, and saluted Elisabeth, who was then six months with child (Luke 1:39-40).

Everything done for the child was done after the law. He was circumcised when eight days were accomplished and his name was called Jesus, as the law of circumcision requires on the eighth day, a covenant older than the Levitical priesthood and given to Abraham (Luke 2:21; Leviticus 12:3; Genesis 17:9-12; John 7:22). When the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord and to offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, which is the offering the law appoints for a woman who cannot bring a lamb (Luke 2:22-24; Leviticus 12:6-8). He was made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those that were under the law (Galatians 4:4-5), and his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover (Luke 2:41). She kept the sayings spoken of him and pondered them in her heart (Luke 2:19). At the marriage in Cana she told him they had no wine, and when he answered that his hour was not yet come she turned to the servants and told them to do whatever he said (John 2:1-5). After the ascension she is named in the upper room with the eleven and the women and his brethren, continuing with one accord in prayer and supplication (Acts 1:14).
judgmentFull: Elisabeth, filled with the Holy Ghost, called her blessed among women and blessed for believing, because there should be a performance of the things told her from the Lord (Luke 1:41-45). Mary answered with the song that magnifies the Lord for regarding the low estate of his handmaiden, and said that from that time all generations would call her blessed (Luke 1:46-48). The song does not stop with her. Her song says that God had shown the strength of his arm against the proud, brought the mighty down from their thrones and lifted the lowly, fed the hungry and sent the rich away empty, and helped Israel his servant in remembrance of his mercy, as he had promised the fathers, Abraham and his seed for ever (Luke 1:51-55). The mercy she was given is the mercy promised to the nation she belonged to.

Christ himself fixed where the honour goes. When a woman in the crowd blessed the womb that bare him, he answered that rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God and keep it (Luke 11:27-28), and when he was told his mother and his brethren stood outside, he said that his mother and his brethren are those who hear the word of God and do it (Luke 8:21). He turned the honour off the mother and onto the keeping of the word, which is the same thing his mother had done at Cana when she pointed the servants at him. And the blessing came with a sword in it. Simeon told her that this child was set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be spoken against, and that a sword should pierce through her own soul also (Luke 2:34-35). John places her standing by the cross, and records the care of her committed to the disciple whom he loved (John 19:25-27). She was called blessed, and she was not spared the grief that came with it.

cases.name: Simeon and Anna
cases.charge: Just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel; a widow who departed not from the temple, serving God with fastings and prayers night and day
cases.summary: Simeon was a man in Jerusalem, just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and it was revealed to him by the Holy Ghost that he should not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ (Luke 2:25-26). He came by the Spirit into the temple when the parents brought in the child to do for him after the custom of the law, took him up in his arms and blessed God (Luke 2:27-28). Anna, a prophetess of the tribe of Aser who never left the temple but served God with fasting and prayer night and day, came in at that moment and spoke of him to all who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem (Luke 2:36-38).
offenseFull: Simeon is described before he is heard, and the two words used of him have definitions in the scriptures. A just man is a man made perfect in his generations, the way Noah is called just and perfect (Genesis 6:9), and the perfecting is the law of the Lord, which is perfect, converting the soul (Psalms 19:7). A devout man is a man who feared God with all his house, the way Cornelius is described, giving much alms and praying always (Acts 10:1-2). So the man waiting in the temple was a keeper of the law and a man in the fear of God, and what he was waiting on was not a private comfort. It was the consolation of a nation, at a time when there was no New Testament and everything anyone knew about the Messiah came out of the prophets they read every sabbath.

He came into the temple by the Spirit at the hour the parents brought the child in to do for him after the custom of the law, which is the same hour they came to present him to the Lord and to offer the pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons written in the law (Luke 2:22-24; Leviticus 12:6-8). Anna is named by her tribe: a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser. Asher was still there in that day, and the proof of it is set down in this chapter. She was of a great age, had lived with a husband seven years from her virginity, and was a widow of about fourscore and four years, who departed not from the temple but served God with fastings and prayers night and day (Luke 2:36-37). That is how the two of them were found ready: one waiting on a promise, and one in the house fasting and praying.
judgmentFull: Simeon took the child up in his arms and blessed God, saying that his servant could now depart in peace according to the word, for his eyes had seen the salvation prepared before the face of all people, a light to lighten the Gentiles and the glory of his people Israel (Luke 2:28-32). The light is Christ, the light that is come and the glory of the Lord risen on the people (Isaiah 60:1), given for a covenant of the people and for a light of the Gentiles (Isaiah 42:6-7). Who those Gentiles are is named in the prophecy itself and in the gospel that quotes it: the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles, the people that walked in darkness and sat in the region and shadow of death (Isaiah 9:1-2; Matthew 4:15-16). The consolation of Israel and the light of the Gentiles are not two errands. They are the gathering of one nation that had been split in two.

Joseph and his mother marvelled at the things spoken of him, and Simeon blessed them, and then said the harder part to the mother: this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be spoken against, and a sword shall pierce through her own soul also, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed (Luke 2:33-35). Set that beside the sign the angel gave the shepherds, which was a babe wrapped in swaddling clothes lying in a manger (Luke 2:12). The child is the sign, not the woman. Anna came in at that moment, gave thanks to the Lord as well, and spoke of him to all who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem (Luke 2:38). She did not keep what she had seen to herself. Both of them received the thing they had waited on, and both of them turned it straight into testimony to people who were waiting for the same thing.

cases.name: Nazareth, his own country
cases.charge: Being offended at him; seeking to cast him down the hill
cases.summary: As his custom was, he went into the synagogue of his own country on the sabbath day and stood up to read, and after reading from Esaias he told them that the scripture was fulfilled that day in their hearing (Luke 4:16-21). They wondered at the gracious words and then asked whether this was not Joseph’s son, and when he named the widow of Sarepta and Naaman the Syrian they were filled with wrath, thrust him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the hill to cast him down headlong; he passed through the midst of them and went his way (Luke 4:22-30). Mark records that he could there do no mighty work, save that he laid his hands on a few sick folk and healed them, and that he marvelled because of their unbelief (Mark 6:1-6).
offenseFull: What he read to them was the commission itself: the Spirit of the Lord was on him, because he had anointed him to preach the gospel to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, and to set at liberty them that are bruised (Luke 4:18-19; Isaiah 61:1-2). Every clause of it is about a people in bondage; the bruising is the hard bondage a nation was made to serve under, and the same prophet promises rest from that sorrow and fear and a proverb taken up against the king that ruled them (Isaiah 14:3-6). He closed the book, sat down, and said that this day the scripture was fulfilled in their ears, and the eyes of all in the synagogue were fastened on him (Luke 4:20-21).

It began with astonishment. They wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth, which is the grace poured into the lips of the king in the psalm (Psalms 45:1-2), and then they went through his family: is not this Joseph’s son, the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joses and Simon and Judas, and are not his sisters here with us (Luke 4:22; Mark 6:2-3). They knew the whole household. They had seen him small, and that was the whole of their argument. A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house (Mark 6:4). That happens to the men teaching today; the people who knew you before you repented are the ones who ask who you think you are.

In Luke the offense goes past words. He reminded them that many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias when the heaven was shut up three years and six months, and none of them was he sent to but the widow of Sarepta, and many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus, and none was cleansed but Naaman the Syrian (Luke 4:25-27). Both prophets had to go outside to be received. At that the whole synagogue was filled with wrath, and they rose up, thrust him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, to cast him down headlong (Luke 4:28-29). That is still how it goes when the word is carried into a man’s own neighbourhood.
judgmentFull: He passed through the midst of them and went his way (Luke 4:30). The judgment on that town is in what they lost by their own hand. He could there do no mighty work, save that he laid his hands on a few sick folk and healed them, and Matthew says he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief (Mark 6:5; Matthew 13:58). The record does not say the town got nothing. It says the works stopped where the believing stopped.

He marvelled because of their unbelief (Mark 6:6). Consider what that means: the unbelief of his own people was such that it made the Son of the Most High marvel. In the very next town the contrast is set down for you. He went down to Capernaum and taught on the sabbath days, and they were astonished at his doctrine, for his word was with power; and a man with the spirit of an unclean devil cried out that he knew him, the Holy One of God (Luke 4:31-34). The demon in the synagogue knew who he was while his own town was walking him to a cliff. When it was day he departed and the people sought him and would have kept him from leaving, and he told them he must preach the kingdom of God to other cities also, for that was what he was sent to do (Luke 4:42-43). It is written of him more widely than one town, that he came

to his own and his own received him not (John 1:11), and that word is defined by the gospels themselves, which say he was rejected of the elders and the chief priests and the scribes (Mark 8:31; Luke 9:22), while other men of the nation believed on him and were told to continue in his word (John 8:31). Nazareth had the first hearing and the closest knowledge of him, and came away with the least.

cases.name: The Samaritan village, and the sons of thunder
cases.charge: Refusing to receive him because his face was toward Jerusalem; James and John asking for fire from heaven
cases.summary: A village of Samaria would not take him in because he was travelling toward Jerusalem, and James and John asked leave to call fire out of heaven and consume it as Elias had done (Luke 9:51-54). The village was of the northern kingdom, and the refusal was the old grudge between the two houses. He rebuked the two disciples rather than the village, told them they did not know what manner of spirit was on them, and said the Son of man came to save lives and not to destroy them, and they went on to another village (Luke 9:55-56).
offenseFull: When the time came that he should be received up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem and sent messengers ahead into a village of the Samaritans to make ready, and they would not receive him because of where he was going (Luke 9:51-53). That village was of the northern kingdom. Samaria was the head of Ephraim (Isaiah 7:9), and the Samaritans were Israelites, which is why the woman at the well appealed to their father Jacob and why the record notes that the Jews had no dealings with them (John 4:9; John 4:12). This was the beef between the two houses, not a stranger turning away a stranger. James and John, the sons of Zebedee, whom he had surnamed the sons of thunder, asked leave to command fire out of heaven and consume the village, as Elias had done to the captains sent against him (Luke 9:54; 2 Kings 1:9-12). In plain terms they wanted to burn their own brothers over a slight.

Their anger came dressed as loyalty. Just before this, John had reported that they forbade a man casting out devils in Christ’s name because he did not walk with them, and was told to forbid him not, since the man who is not against us is on our side (Luke 9:49-50). The same spirit was still running. Men teaching the same identity who do not speak against Christ are not to be hindered merely because they do not stand with us, and a brother who will not receive a labourer is not thereby marked for destruction. Rejection is real, and it falls back on the one who rejects: the man who despises the labourer despises the one who sent him, and despises not man but God (Luke 10:16; 1 Thessalonians 4:8). It was not theirs to avenge.
judgmentFull: He turned and rebuked the two, not the village, telling them they did not know what manner of spirit was on them, for the Son of man came to save men’s lives and not to destroy them, and they went to another village (Luke 9:55-56). John records the same purpose in other words, that the Son was sent to save the world and not to condemn it (John 3:17). The correction fell on the disciples who proposed the fire. The work is to win the soul, not to end it: a true witness delivers souls (Proverbs 14:25), and the man who wins souls is wise (Proverbs 11:30). The servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle toward all men, able to teach, patient, instructing in meekness those who oppose themselves, so that God may give them repentance and they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil (2 Timothy 2:24-26). Those two brothers had no patience, and that is exactly what the name they carried meant.

The rebuke prepared them. The same two had been taken up into the mountain with Peter (Luke 9:28), and they became an integral part of building up the believers and teaching them, which they could not have done carrying the temper they had on that road. John afterward went with Peter into Samaria when its people received the word of God, and prayed for them (Acts 8:14-17), serving the very people he had once asked to burn. Where a house or a city will not receive the labourer, the instruction was to shake off the dust from the feet for a testimony and go on, and the account is left with God, who will settle it in the day of judgment (Luke 9:5; Matthew 10:14-15). No fire fell on that village. The only sentence in the record is the one spoken to the men who asked for it.

cases.name: Mary of Bethany
cases.charge: Sitting at his feet to hear his word; anointing his body aforehand to the burying
cases.summary: While Martha was taken up with much serving, Mary sat at Christ’s feet and heard his word, and was told she had chosen the good part that would not be taken from her (Luke 10:38-42). At Bethany she anointed his feet with costly spikenard and wiped them with her hair, and Judas objected in the name of the poor, being a thief who carried the bag (John 12:1-6). Christ defended the act and said she had kept the ointment against the day of his burying, and the promise given her was a memorial wherever the gospel is preached (John 12:7-8; Mark 14:3-9).
offenseFull: Martha received him into her house and was cumbered about much serving, while her sister Mary sat at his feet and heard his word; when Martha asked that Mary be told to help, she was answered that she was careful and troubled about many things, that one thing was needful, and that Mary had chosen that good part which would not be taken away from her (Luke 10:38-42). The serving was not wrong. People have to eat, and the body needs it. But man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God (Luke 4:4), and Job said he esteemed the words of God’s mouth more than his necessary food (Job 23:12). A man can be so taken up with the business of the day that the word never gets in him. Mary put the word first, and that is what was commended.

At Bethany she took a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, anointed his feet and wiped them with her hair, and the house was filled with the smell of it (John 12:1-3). Judas Iscariot objected that the ointment could have been sold for three hundred pence and given to the poor; John says plainly that he did not say it because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and had the bag and took what was put in it (John 12:4-6). The bag is where the money was kept. Concern spoken in another man’s name covered his own appetite. Mary answered nothing; Christ answered for her.
judgmentFull: He told them to let her alone, that she had kept the ointment against the day of his burying, and that they had the poor always with them but would not always have him (John 12:7-8; Matthew 26:6-13). She had poured it on his body for his burial. Burying a man decently is an old custom among our people and it runs through the scriptures: Jacob made Joseph swear to carry him out of Egypt and bury him with his fathers, and Joseph went up and did it (Genesis 47:29-31; Genesis 50:4-5), and Tobit charged his son to bury him decently and to lay his mother by him in one grave (Tobit 4:3-4; Tobit 14:9). Mary honoured that custom beforehand and at her own cost, while men at the table were counting the price of it.

Defending her gift did not cancel the duty to the poor. Mark preserves the whole of it: the anointing at Bethany, the indignation over the waste, the word that they could do the poor good whenever they would, that she had done what she could, and the promise that what this woman had done would be told for a memorial wherever the gospel is preached in the whole world (Mark 14:3-9). What was exposed was the wrong of condemning an honourable act by invoking another duty insincerely. The law asks the whole heart and soul and might (Deuteronomy 6:5), and both of the acts recorded of her, the sitting and the anointing, were that. Neither was taken from her.

cases.name: The barren fig tree
cases.charge: Cumbering the ground three years without fruit
cases.summary: Answering the news of Galilaeans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices, Christ refused to rank the dead as worse sinners than the rest, and warned twice that without repentance they would all likewise perish (Luke 13:1-5). He then gave the parable of a fig tree in a vineyard that had been sought for fruit three years and found barren, and the order to cut it down (Luke 13:6-7). The dresser asked for one more year to dig about it and dung it, and if it still bore nothing, then it would be cut down (Luke 13:8-9).
offenseFull: Word was brought of Galilaeans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices, and he refused to let the hearers rank those men as sinners above all other Galilaeans, and said the same of the eighteen killed when the tower in Siloam fell; twice, in the same words, he answered that without repentance they would all likewise perish (Luke 13:1-5). He was not speaking of dying in the body, because every man dies. Ezekiel makes the same demand and names what is at stake: repent and turn from all transgressions, so that iniquity is not your ruin, and make a new heart and a new spirit, for why will a house of Israel die (Ezekiel 18:30-32). The perishing in view is of the soul. Comparing themselves favourably with men who died suddenly took nothing off their own account.

Then the parable. A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, came three years seeking fruit on it and found none, and told the dresser to cut it down, since it was only taking up the ground (Luke 13:6-7). The vineyard is named in the prophets: the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant, and what he looked for in it was judgment and righteousness (Isaiah 5:1-7). The three years is the length of his own ministry among the people, who began to be about thirty years of age (Luke 3:23). The fruit sought is what John required of those coming to his baptism, fruits meet for repentance (Matthew 3:7-8), and what is named as the fruit of the spirit: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness and temperance (Galatians 5:22-23). A tree standing in the vineyard, tended and watered, and returning nothing, is the charge.
judgmentFull: The dresser asked that it be let alone one more year, until he should dig about it and dung it, and if it bore fruit, well; and if not, then it would be cut down (Luke 13:8-9). Digging and dunging is cultivation: feeding the tree, working the ground, giving it time. That added year is the longsuffering of God, the same longsuffering that waited in the days of Noah while the ark was preparing (1 Peter 3:20). The extra time came with labour spent on the tree and with an expectation attached to it, not with a ruling that barrenness no longer mattered.

The parable stops on that condition. It never reports that this tree bore, and it never reports the axe. The history reports what the parable leaves open: three years was the length of the ministry, and the city was cut down after it, the house left desolate as he said standing over it (Luke 13:34-35). Time given is time to turn. Men grow bold in evil because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, and yet it shall be well with them that fear God (Ecclesiastes 8:11-13). The reprieve here was real, it was worked for, and it was measured.

cases.name: The Samaritan leper who returned
cases.charge: One of ten: turning back to glorify God with a loud voice, and giving thanks at his feet
cases.summary: Ten lepers stood far off and cried for mercy, and were sent to show themselves to the priests as the law requires, and were cleansed as they went (Luke 17:11-14). Nine kept going. One turned back, glorified God with a loud voice and fell on his face at Christ’s feet giving thanks, and Luke names him a Samaritan, that is, an Israelite of the northern kingdom (Luke 17:15-16). He alone was asked after and told that his faith had made him whole (Luke 17:17-19).
offenseFull: Passing through the midst of Samaria and Galilee, he entered a village and ten men that were lepers met him, standing far off, and lifted up their voices for mercy; he told them to go and show themselves to the priests, and as they went they were cleansed (Luke 17:11-14). The order was the law. When he cleansed a leper earlier he charged the man to tell no one, but to go and show himself to the priest and offer for his cleansing according as Moses commanded, for a testimony (Luke 5:12-14), and that offering is set out in the law of the leper (Leviticus 14:2-4). Christ did not set the statute aside; he sent men to keep it. They moved on his word before the record says a thing about them being healed.

One of them, seeing that he was healed, turned back and glorified God with a loud voice, and fell down on his face at his feet giving thanks; and Luke adds that he was a Samaritan (Luke 17:15-16). That does not mean another nation. Samaria held Israelites: the woman at the well asked whether he was greater than their father Jacob, and the record notes that the Jews had no dealings with the Samaritans (John 4:9; John 4:12). The man Christ goes on to call a stranger is an Israelite of the northern kingdom, and the scriptures use the word that way. The sons of the stranger who join themselves to the Lord, keep the sabbath and take hold of his covenant are brought to the holy mountain and their sacrifices accepted (Isaiah 56:6-7), and the strangers gathered with Judah and Benjamin came out of Ephraim and Manasseh and Simeon, and entered into a covenant to seek the Lord with all their heart (2 Chronicles 15:9; 2 Chronicles 15:12).
judgmentFull: He asked whether there were not ten cleansed, where the other nine were, and why none was found returning to give glory to God except this stranger, and then told the man to arise and go his way, for his faith had made him whole (Luke 17:17-19). All ten were cleansed; one was commended. The thing named is faith, and faith is what marks the children of Abraham, for they which are of faith are the children of Abraham (Galatians 3:7). Israel did not obtain that which it sought, but the election obtained it and the rest were blinded (Romans 11:7). The nine were of the blood. The one who came back had the faith with it.

The account does not announce the end of the nine or take back what was given them. It makes their absence a question that has to be answered. Thanksgiving belongs together with the mercy received: the man who offers praise glorifies God (Psalms 50:23), and the charge is to bless the Lord and forget none of his benefits, who forgives all iniquities and heals all diseases (Psalms 103:1-3). This man did not forget once the trouble was lifted off him. He turned around and went back to the one who lifted it.

cases.offense: Passing through the midst of Samaria and Galilee, he entered a village and ten men that were lepers met him, standing far off, and lifted up their voices for mercy; he told them to go and show themselves to the priests, and as they went they were cleansed (Luke 17:11-14). The order was the law. When he cleansed a leper earlier he charged the man to tell no one, but to go and show himself to the priest and offer for his cleansing according as Moses commanded, for a testimony (Luke 5:12-14), and that offering is set out in the law of the leper (Leviticus 14:2-4). Christ did not set the statute aside; he sent men to keep it. They moved on his word before the record says a thing about them being healed.
cases.judgment: He asked whether there were not ten cleansed, where the other nine were, and why none was found returning to give glory to God except this stranger, and then told the man to arise and go his way, for his faith had made him whole (Luke 17:17-19). All ten were cleansed; one was commended. The thing named is faith, and faith is what marks the children of Abraham, for they which are of faith are the children of Abraham (Galatians 3:7). Israel did not obtain that which it sought, but the election obtained it and the rest were blinded (Romans 11:7). The nine were of the blood. The one who came back had the faith with it.

cases.name: Zacchaeus
cases.charge: Extortion as chief of the publicans
cases.summary: Zacchaeus, chief among the publicans at Jericho and rich, could not see Christ for the crowd, so he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree, and was called down by name and received him joyfully while the people murmured (Luke 19:1-7). Standing before him he said he gave half of his goods to the poor, and that if he had taken anything from any man by false accusation he restored it fourfold, which is the rate the law names (Luke 19:8; Exodus 22:1). Salvation came to his house, and he was named a son of Abraham, since the Son of man came to seek and to save that which was lost (Luke 19:9-10).
offenseFull: Jesus entered and passed through Jericho, and a man named Zacchaeus, who was chief among the publicans and rich, sought to see who he was and could not for the press, because he was little of stature; so he ran before and climbed up into a sycamore tree on the road he would take (Luke 19:1-4). He had been hearing the reports. A cleansed leper had published the matter and blazed it abroad until Christ could no more openly enter a city (Mark 1:40-45), and this man wanted to see for himself who everybody was talking about. The office and the money are the setting of the case; the interest that put him up that tree was already faith.

Christ came to the place, looked up, called him by his name and told him to make haste and come down, for he must abide at his house that day; he made haste and came down and received him joyfully, while the onlookers murmured that he had gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner (Luke 19:5-7). Receiving a man carries a promise with it: he that receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward, and even a cup of cold water given in the name of a disciple does not lose its reward (Matthew 10:40-42). That cold water is good news from a far country to a thirsty soul (Proverbs 25:25). The murmurers had already been answered once: the whole need no physician, but they that are sick, and they were sent to go and learn what it means that God will have mercy and not sacrifice (Matthew 9:11-13; Hosea 6:6).
judgmentFull: Zacchaeus stood and said that half of his goods he gave to the poor, and that if he had taken anything from any man by false accusation he restored him fourfold (Luke 19:8). That is a man applying the law to himself. Fourfold is the rate the statute names for a stolen sheep, where an ox requires five (Exodus 22:1); the law of the trespass requires the principal restored with a fifth part added, paid to the man who was wronged (Leviticus 6:1-5; Numbers 5:6-7); and David passed the same fourfold sentence on himself when Nathan set the parable before him (2 Samuel 12:5-6). John had already told publicans coming to his baptism to exact no more than was appointed them, and to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance (Luke 3:8; Luke 3:12-13). A sacrifice cannot stand in the place of dealing justly with the man a person has robbed.

Salvation came to that house that day, and he was called a son of Abraham, because the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost (Luke 19:9-10). Sonship there is by faith, not by the sacrifice: Abraham believed God and it was counted to him for righteousness, and circumcision was afterward the seal of a righteousness of faith he already had (Romans 4:1-3; Romans 4:11). A rich young ruler heard a like word about selling and giving to the poor and went away sorrowful because he had great possessions (Matthew 19:16-22); a rich man hardly enters the kingdom, and yet this rich man did, because his hand was already open. And the salvation spoken over the house is the one Zacharias named, to be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all that hate us (Luke 1:68-74), for the lost that the Son of man came after are the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24).

cases.name: Pontius Pilate
cases.charge: Condemning a man he had three times pronounced innocent
cases.summary: The council brought Christ to Pilate on charges they had made up, that he perverted the nation, forbade tribute to Caesar and called himself a king, every one of which the record refutes (Luke 23:1-3; Matthew 22:15-22; John 18:33-34). Pilate examined him, said he found no fault in the man, said it again, and a third time asked what evil he had done, finding no cause of death in him (Luke 23:4; Luke 23:13-16; Luke 23:20-25). Knowing that they had delivered him for envy, and warned by his wife’s dream, he still gave sentence when releasing the prisoner was turned into disloyalty to Caesar (Matthew 27:18-19; John 19:12-16).
offenseFull: The whole multitude led him to Pilate and began to accuse him, saying they had found this fellow perverting the nation, forbidding to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ a king (Luke 23:1-2). Every count was a slander. He had been asked plainly whether it was lawful to give tribute to Caesar, had called the men who asked it hypocrites, and had told them to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, so that they marvelled and left him (Matthew 22:15-22). And when Pilate asked whether he was the King of the Jews, his answer was to ask whether Pilate said that of himself, or whether others had told it to him (John 18:33-34; Luke 23:3). He never claimed the title they charged him with.

Pilate examined him and told the chief priests and the people that he found no fault in this man; when they grew the more fierce he said it again, and a third time asked what evil the man had done, finding no cause of death in him (Luke 23:4; Luke 23:13-16; Luke 23:20-25; John 18:38; John 19:4). Matthew gives the reason he could see it: he knew that for envy they had delivered him, and his wife sent word of what she had suffered in a dream (Matthew 27:18-19). He tried to move the case out of his hands to Herod’s jurisdiction, and Herod, whose house had sought the child’s life and who had beheaded John, got no answer at all (Luke 23:6-11). The governor who said three times that the prisoner was innocent is the governor who handed him over, and he handed him over when releasing him was cast as disloyalty to Caesar (John 19:12-16). Washing his hands before the multitude did not undo the sentence he gave (Matthew 27:22-26). The law forbids following a multitude to do evil, and forbids slaying the innocent and righteous (Exodus 23:2; Exodus 23:7).
judgmentFull: No divine sentence upon Pilate is recorded in the Gospels. What is recorded is the company he was put in: against the holy child Jesus, Herod and Pontius Pilate were gathered together with the Gentiles and the people of Israel (Acts 4:27-28). That their gathering fulfilled what God’s counsel had determined before did not turn a false judgment into a just one. And the weight of the record does not fall on the Roman. Even he said he found no fault in the man; it was his own nation that grew the more fierce and pressed the case (Luke 23:5).

The apostles kept his name in the testimony: Christ witnessed a good confession before Pontius Pilate (1 Timothy 6:13). The contrast stands there, between a prisoner bearing witness to the truth and a judge who announced innocence and then yielded to pressure. To justify the wicked and to condemn the just are both an abomination to the Lord (Proverbs 17:15). What was done to the Master sets the pattern for the servants: the followers of Christ are brought before governors on invented charges and have all manner of evil said against them falsely, and are told to rejoice and be exceeding glad, for so were the prophets persecuted before them (Matthew 5:10-12).

cases.name: The penitent thief
cases.charge: Robbery, under sentence of crucifixion
cases.summary: Two malefactors were crucified with Christ, one on either side, and one of them railed on him while the other rebuked his fellow, owned that they received the due reward of their deeds, and said that this man had done nothing amiss (Luke 23:32-33; Luke 23:39-41). He then asked to be remembered when Christ came into his kingdom, which is not the speech of a man who thought him a common prisoner (Luke 23:42). He was answered with the promise of paradise that same day (Luke 23:43).
offenseFull: Two other malefactors were led with him to be put to death, and they crucified him at the place called Calvary, one criminal on the right hand and one on the left (Luke 23:32-33). The soldiers mocked him and offered him vinegar, the superscription over him was written in letters of Greek and Latin and Hebrew, and one of the two railed on him, telling him to save himself and them if he was the Christ (Luke 23:36-39). The other rebuked his companion, asked whether he did not fear God seeing he was under the same condemnation, said that they were there justly and received the due reward of their deeds, and that this man had done nothing amiss (Luke 23:40-41). He did not use his own suffering as an argument for his innocence. He judged himself first, and he judged his fellow for railing.

Then he asked to be remembered when Christ came into his kingdom (Luke 23:42). That petition tells what the man already knew. A prisoner who thought this was just another condemned man would not have spoken of a kingdom that was coming. The rulers of his nation had said they had no king but Caesar (John 19:15), having settled into their place under Rome and their share of its comfort; this man, with nothing left and hours to live, was still looking for the kingdom the scriptures promised. He had broken Rome’s law and Rome was killing him for it. His repentance showed itself in the rebuke he gave, the guilt he owned and the mercy he asked for.
judgmentFull: The answer was that he would be with him that day in paradise (Luke 23:43). The promise did not take him off the cross and did not declare his former deeds harmless. Nor is it a general rule that every man goes somewhere at death. Esdras was told he would be taken away from all and would remain with the Son and with such as were like him until the times were ended (2 Esdras 14:9), and Christ said that where he is, there also shall his servant be (John 12:26). John saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, speaking, asking how long until their blood was avenged, receiving white robes and told to rest yet for a little season (Revelation 6:9-11), while the rest of the dead lived not again until the thousand years were finished (Revelation 20:5). The righteous is taken away from the evil to come, and enters into peace (Isaiah 57:1-2). The promise is particular, and it was spoken over a man who had just acknowledged that his punishment was just.

Isaiah had written that the servant would be numbered with the transgressors and make intercession for the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12), and here is the scene in the flesh: the innocent man between two guilty ones, the one railing and the other receiving mercy. There was darkness over all the earth from the sixth hour to the ninth, the sun was darkened and the veil of the temple was rent, and when it was over the centurion glorified God and said that certainly this was a righteous man, and all the people that had come to the sight beat their breasts and went home (Luke 23:44-48). The last hour was not out of reach of repentance. It is no warrant for counting on a last hour that has not been promised to anybody.

cases.name: The traders in the temple
cases.charge: Making the house of prayer a den of thieves
cases.summary: At the passover Christ found in the temple those selling oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting, made a scourge of small cords and drove them all out, poured out the money and overthrew the tables (John 2:13-16). The other account names what the place had become, a house of prayer turned into a den of thieves, in the words of Isaiah and Jeremiah (Matthew 21:12-13; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11). The trade was put out, the disciples remembered the writing about the zeal of God’s house, and the scribes and chief priests answered the correction by seeking how to destroy him (John 2:17; Mark 11:18).
offenseFull: The passover was at hand and he went up to Jerusalem, and found in the temple those that sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting (John 2:13-14). This was during the feast, in the court of the house, and no man had business trading in there at the passover. What they had made of the place is named in the later account: the house of prayer turned into a den of thieves (Matthew 21:12-13; Mark 11:15-17), the words taken out of the prophets (Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11). A den is where robbers go to divide what they have taken and to plan the next one. That is what the house of the Lord had been turned into.

Jeremiah had already described the leadership that let it get that way. They were waxen fat, they shone, they overpassed the deeds of the wicked, they judged not the cause of the fatherless, and they judged not the right of the needy, and still they prospered (Jeremiah 5:27-28). Men who live off the people will overlook the wickedness of whoever pays them. And the warning that stands next to the den of thieves is the place God had already destroyed for the wickedness of his people (Jeremiah 7:12): the house itself protects nobody who steals, murders, commits adultery and swears falsely and then comes and stands in it (Jeremiah 7:8-11). Zechariah said the day would come when there would be no more the trader in the house of the Lord of hosts (Zechariah 14:21).
judgmentFull: He made a scourge of small cords and drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and the oxen, poured out the changers’ money and overthrew the tables, and told those that sold doves to take those things away and not make his Father’s house a house of merchandise (John 2:15-16). He drove grown men out of the temple with a whip. The Christ who did that was not the soft and mealy mouthed figure of the films; Mark adds that he would not allow a vessel to be carried through the temple, and that the scribes and chief priests heard it and sought how they might destroy him, because they feared him, since all the people were astonished at his doctrine (Mark 11:16-18). The men whose trade was overturned answered the correction with a plot.

His disciples remembered that it was written, that the zeal of God’s house had eaten him up (John 2:17; Psalms 69:9). When they demanded a sign for what he had done he spoke of the temple of his body raised up in three days, which went over their heads at the time and which false witnesses carried into his trial later on (John 2:18-22; Matthew 26:59-61). The judgment in this record is temporal and immediate: the trade driven out, the money on the floor, the tables turned over, the house cleared. The same trade goes on wherever money is extracted from our people in the name of the house, and the seat is defended instead of the flock, and the same correction stands written against it.

cases.name: Nicodemus
cases.charge: Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth?; and bringing a hundred pound weight of myrrh and aloes
cases.summary: A Pharisee and ruler of the Jews came to Christ by night, acknowledged that his works showed God was with him, and was told that a man must be born again to see the kingdom of God (John 3:1-3). He was asked whether he was a master of Israel and did not know these things (John 3:9-10). When the council raged that no ruler had believed, he put their own law to them about hearing a man before judging him, and at the burial he came with a hundred pound weight of myrrh and aloes and wound the body with Joseph (John 7:45-52; John 19:38-42).
offenseFull: There was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews, who came to Christ by night and said they knew he was a teacher come from God, because no man could do those miracles unless God were with him

(John 3:1-2). Those men taught the synagogues, and coming openly would have cost him his standing, so he came in the dark; he was a secret disciple. The answer he got was not a welcome but a requirement: except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God (John 3:3). He took it in the flesh and asked how a man can be born when he is old, and enter the second time into his mother’s womb, and was told that a man must be born of water and of the Spirit (John 3:4-5). Being born again is by the word of God, an incorruptible seed that lives and abides for ever (1 Peter 1:23); what is born of the flesh is flesh, and they that are in the flesh cannot please God (John 3:6-8; Romans 8:8). Esdras puts the same demand plainly: subdue your own understanding and reform your hearts (2 Esdras 14:34). That is a hard word to a man who already believes he is right, which is why sinners and publicans received Christ sooner than a ruler did.

He was asked whether he was a master of Israel and did not know these things (John 3:9-10). Men depended on him for the understanding of the law. Later, when the council sent officers to take Christ and raged that none of the rulers had believed on him, Nicodemus asked them whether their law judges a man before it hears him, and was answered with a sneer about Galilee (John 7:45-52). The law he invoked is written: hear the causes between brethren and judge righteously, and make diligent inquisition (Deuteronomy 1:16-17; Deuteronomy 19:18). At the burial he came bringing about a hundred pound weight of myrrh and aloes, and wound the body with Joseph in the linen clothes with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury (John 19:38-42). His appearances move from a night visit, to a demand for a lawful hearing, to costly service in the daylight.
judgmentFull: The teaching he was given is the heart of that chapter. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up (John 3:14-15). The history behind it is plain and so is who it was for: it was Israel in the wilderness that spoke against God and against Moses, Israel that was bitten, and Israel that looked and lived (Numbers 21:5-9). The serpent of brass was a sign of salvation, given to put them in remembrance of the commandment of the law (Wisdom of Solomon 16:5-6), so the looking was never apart from repentance. The verse that follows, that God so loved the world (John 3:16), comes straight off the serpent and has the same people in view: the world John names elsewhere is the one Christ was made manifest to (John 1:29-31), the one the Pharisees said was gone after him (John 12:19), and the one he taught openly in the synagogue and the temple (John 18:20).

Then the condemnation: light is come into the world and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil, while the man who does truth comes to the light so that his deeds may be made manifest (John 3:19-21). A man can be comfortable and even do well in the darkness he was raised in, and coming into the light costs him change. Christ did not condemn the rulers; they condemned themselves by not humbling down to repent. Nicodemus is the one of them who did come to the light, and the record of it is his deeds, not a sentence pronounced over him. The man first identified as coming by night is named again at the tomb (John 19:39). What he lacked at the first meeting he was still being called out of, and in the end he answered, at his own risk and his own cost.

cases.offense: There was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews, who came to Christ by night and said they knew he was a teacher come from God, because no man could do those miracles unless God were with him
cases.judgment: The teaching he was given is the heart of that chapter. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up (John 3:14-15). The history behind it is plain and so is who it was for: it was Israel in the wilderness that spoke against God and against Moses, Israel that was bitten, and Israel that looked and lived (Numbers 21:5-9). The serpent of brass was a sign of salvation, given to put them in remembrance of the commandment of the law (Wisdom of Solomon 16:5-6), so the looking was never apart from repentance. The verse that follows, that God so loved the world (John 3:16), comes straight off the serpent and has the same people in view: the world John names elsewhere is the one Christ was made manifest to (John 1:29-31), the one the Pharisees said was gone after him (John 12:19), and the one he taught openly in the synagogue and the temple (John 18:20).

cases.name: The woman taken in adultery
cases.charge: Adultery, in the very act
cases.summary: While Christ was teaching in the temple early in the morning, the scribes and Pharisees brought in a woman taken in adultery, set her in the middle, cited Moses on stoning and asked what he said, tempting him so they might have something to accuse him of (John 8:1-6). Their own words condemned them, because adultery takes two and the law puts both to death, and they brought only the woman (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22-24). He told them that the man among them without sin should cast the first stone, and they went out one by one beginning at the eldest, and he told her that neither did he condemn her, and to sin no more (John 8:7-11).
offenseFull: Early in the morning he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them, as he did daily, lodging at the mount of Olives at night (John 8:1-2; Luke 21:37). Into that teaching the scribes and Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery and set her in the midst, saying that Moses in the law commanded that such should be stoned, and asking what he said; John states their purpose outright, that they said it tempting him, so that they might have something of which to accuse him (John 8:3-6).

Their own mouths condemned them (Job 15:6). Adultery takes two. The law they were quoting forbids the man to lie carnally with his neighbour’s wife (Leviticus 18:20), puts both the adulterer and the adulteress to death (Leviticus 20:10), and orders that both of them die, and that both be brought out to the gate of the city and stoned (Deuteronomy 22:22-24). If she was taken in the very act, then a man was taken with her, and they brought the woman only. These were the men who sat in Moses’ seat (Matthew 23:2-3), the judges and officers the law requires in every gate, charged to judge the people with just judgment and not to wrest judgment (Deuteronomy 16:18-19), and evil men understand not judgment (Proverbs 28:5). They were willing to have a woman killed in order to catch a man in his speech and charge him with speaking against the law, which is the one accusation they believed would not be forgiven (Matthew 12:31).
judgmentFull: He stooped down and with his finger wrote on the ground as though he did not hear them, and the record never says what he wrote; there is no room in it to invent the words. When they continued asking, he lifted himself up and said that the man among them that is without sin should first cast a stone at her (John 8:7-8). Sin is the transgression of the law (1 John 3:4), and the law he was pointing them back to is their own procedure: at the mouth of two or three witnesses a man is put to death, and the hands of the witnesses are to be first upon him, and afterward the hands of all the people (Deuteronomy 17:6-7). They had come with witnesses. They were being told to throw.

Convicted by their own conscience, they went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, until he was left alone with the woman standing in the midst (John 8:9). The eldest knew what the next statute says: if a false witness rises up, both parties stand before the priests and the judges, diligent inquisition is made, and what the false witness thought to do to his brother is done to him, so that the rest hear and fear (Deuteronomy 19:16-21). The law also forbids going up and down as a talebearer among the people and standing against the blood of a neighbour (Leviticus 19:16). Blessed is the man whose conscience has not condemned him (Ecclesiasticus 14:2); theirs had. He asked her where her accusers were and whether no man had condemned her, and she said no man, and he told her that neither did he condemn her, and to go and sin no more (John 8:10-11). That is the mercy those men had omitted, one of the weightier matters of the law along with judgment and faith (Matthew 23:23). She was spared; adultery was not made lawful. The Son of man came to save men’s lives and not to destroy them (Luke 9:56), and the last word spoken to her was an order to stop.

cases.name: Caiaphas and the council
cases.charge: Seeking false witness against Christ; condemning him by night; delivering him to the Gentiles; forbidding the apostles; stoning Stephen
cases.summary: The chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council and said that if they let this man alone all would believe on him and the Romans would take away their place and nation, and Caiaphas told them it was expedient that one man die for the people (John 11:47-53). From that day they took counsel to put him to death, sought false witness and found none that agreed, condemned him and carried him to Pilate with invented charges (Matthew 26:59-61; Luke 23:1-2). Afterward they threatened and beat the apostles, forbade them to speak in that name, and killed Stephen (Acts 4:13-21; Acts 5:40; Acts 7:57-60).
offenseFull: The chief priests and the Pharisees gathered a council and asked what they were doing, since this man did many miracles; if they let him alone all men would believe on him, and the Romans would come and take away both their place and their nation (John 11:47-48). The motive is stated there in their own words. Rome kept them in their seat of authority; without Rome they had nothing. Caiaphas, being the high priest that year, told them they knew nothing at all, and that it was expedient that one man should die for the people, and from that day they took counsel together to put him to death (John 11:49-53). The verdict was settled before there was any hearing.

Annas had held the office and kept the title after the Romans put him out, and Caiaphas his son in law was the high priest the year Christ was killed; both are named with John and Alexander and the kindred of the high priest (Acts 4:5-6). These were the very men who procured the death. The council sought false witness to put him to death and found none that agreed together, two coming at the last with the saying about destroying the temple (Matthew 26:59-62; Mark 14:55-59). They condemned him on his own answer and then carried accusations to Pilate that contradicted what he had taught, that he perverted the nation and forbade tribute to Caesar (Matthew 26:63-66; Luke 23:1-2). The law they administered forbids raising a false report and joining hands with the wicked as an unrighteous witness, forbids following a multitude to do evil, and forbids slaying the innocent (Exodus 23:1-2; Exodus 23:7), and it requires diligent inquisition, with the false witness punished as he intended (Deuteronomy 19:15-19).
judgmentFull: Peter set it before their faces in their own chamber: the stone which was set at nought of the builders had become the head of the corner, and there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:7-12). It was the builders’ own office to build and bind the nation, to feed the flock and bind up the brokenhearted; when the stone came, envy and vainglory put it out. They could say nothing against the healed man standing there with the apostles, and they still conferred and threatened, because it was never about the miracle but about their position and their following (Acts 4:13-18). Told to judge for themselves whether it is right to hearken to men rather than to God, they let the apostles go for fear of the people (Acts 4:19-21), and afterward beat them and commanded them again not to speak in that name (Acts 5:27-28; Acts 5:40).

Stephen named them the betrayers and murderers of the Just One, men who received the law by the disposition of angels and did not keep it, and they answered by killing him also (Acts 7:51-53; Acts 7:54-60). Their allegiance was to Rome and to a kingdom here; Paul writes of those who both killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, who please not God and are contrary to all men (1 Thessalonians 2:14-16). Christ had said the kingdom would be taken from them and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits of it, and that their house was left to them desolate (Matthew 21:43; Matthew 23:38). Office did not cover them, and the whole council was not of one mind: Joseph of Arimathaea had not consented to their counsel and deed (Luke 23:50-51), and Nicodemus had called for a lawful hearing (John 7:51).

cases.name: Judas Iscariot
cases.charge: Theft from the common purse; betraying innocent blood for thirty pieces of silver
cases.summary: One of the twelve, he carried the bag and took what was put in it, and his objection to the ointment at Bethany was made in the name of the poor although he cared nothing for them (John 12:4-6). Satan entered into him, he asked the chief priests what they would give him, they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver as the prophet had written, and he delivered Christ with a kiss (Luke 22:3-6; Zechariah 11:12-13; Luke 22:47-48). When he saw that Christ was condemned he brought the money back, confessed that he had betrayed innocent blood, threw the silver into the temple and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3-5).
offenseFull: He was one of the twelve and he kept the bag, which is where the money was, and he took what was put in it (John 12:4-6; John 13:29). His objection to Mary’s ointment at Bethany was spoken in the name of the poor, and John says plainly that it was not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief. He walked with Christ, saw the healing, was around the commandment keeping, and never repented of what he was. The commandment on it is one line: do not steal (Exodus 20:15). Riches are not comely for a niggard, and what should an envious man do with money (Ecclesiasticus 14:3)? They that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts which drown men in destruction and perdition, for the love of money is the root of all evil, and some coveting after it have erred from the faith and pierced themselves through with many sorrows (1 Timothy 6:9-10).

Then Satan entered into him, and he went to the chief priests and captains and asked what they would give him, and they were glad and covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver, and from that time he sought opportunity to betray him away from the multitude (Luke 22:3-6; Matthew 26:14-16). Men are not in their right mind when they can be glad over a thing like that. The price was written beforehand: thirty pieces of silver, cast to the potter in the house of the Lord (Zechariah 11:12-13), which Matthew credits to Jeremy because Zechariah was repeating what the earlier prophet had said in a writing that did not survive. Judas delivered him with a kiss, and was asked whether he betrayed the Son of man with a kiss (Luke 22:47-48). The statute names the act without disguise: cursed is the man that takes reward to slay an innocent person (Deuteronomy 27:25), and the psalm had said it would be the familiar friend who lifted up his heel (Psalms 41:9).
judgmentFull: When he saw that Christ was condemned, he repented himself, brought the thirty pieces of silver back to the chief priests and elders and said he had sinned in that he had betrayed innocent blood; they told him to see to it himself, and he cast the silver down in the temple, departed, and went and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3-5). Giving the money back did not give back the life he had sold. The priests would not put it into the treasury because it was the price of blood, and bought the potter’s field with it to bury strangers in, so that the field is called the field of blood to this day (Matthew 27:6-10). Acts records the fearful end there and the office given to another man, as the psalm had said (Acts 1:16-20; Acts 1:25; Psalms 109:8).

The warning had been spoken at the table: the Son of man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed, and it had been good for that man if he had never been born (Mark 14:21; Matthew 26:24). He was sorry afterward, and sorrow by itself is not repentance: godly sorrow works repentance to salvation not to be repented of, but the sorrow of the world works death (2 Corinthians 7:10). He that loves gold shall not be justified, and gold has been the ruin of many, their destruction being present with them (Ecclesiasticus 31:5-6). A place among the twelve, three years in the company of Christ and the trust of the bag did not make a hidden covetousness safe. Money was his demise, and men will still give a brother up for it.

cases.name: Barnabas
cases.charge: Selling his land and laying the money at the apostles’ feet; a good man, full of the Holy Ghost and of faith
cases.summary: Joses, whom the apostles surnamed Barnabas, a Levite of Cyprus, sold his land and laid the money at the apostles’ feet, in a congregation where none lacked because distribution was made to every man according to his need (Acts 4:32-37). When the disciples feared Saul, Barnabas brought him to the apostles and told them what had happened on the road and at Damascus, and afterward sought him at Tarsus to share a year of teaching at Antioch (Acts 9:26-28; Acts 11:22-26). Luke calls him a good man, full of the Holy Ghost and of faith, and the church commended him and Paul as men that had hazarded their lives for the name of the Lord (Acts 15:25-26).
offenseFull: The multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul, and no man said that anything he possessed was his own, but they had all things common; none among them lacked, because those who owned lands or houses sold them and laid the money down at the apostles’ feet, and distribution was made to every man according as he had need (Acts 4:32-35). Joses, whom the apostles surnamed Barnabas, which is the son of consolation, a Levite of the country of Cyprus, sold his land and brought the money and laid it at their feet (Acts 4:36-37). This was never a prosperity arrangement where a man gives in order to get rich. The congregation was the centre of the community, and the alms circulated through it, so that when one lacked, the rest supplied him, whether the need was food, a rent or a proper burial. The law had long required the open hand toward a poor brother (Deuteronomy 15:7-8). Barnabas was a ranked man and he still gave, and his gift stands in the record immediately before the deceit of Ananias and Sapphira; giving and the appearance of giving are not the same thing.

His consolation reached further than his purse. When Saul came to Jerusalem and tried to join the disciples, they were all afraid of him and did not believe that he was a disciple, until Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared how he had seen the Lord in the way, and how he had preached boldly at Damascus in that name (Acts 9:26-28). He did not ask them to forget what Saul had done; he brought them the witness of what had happened since. Sent out from Jerusalem to Antioch when a great number there turned to the Lord, he saw the grace of God and was glad, and exhorted them all that with purpose of heart they would cleave to the Lord; then he departed to Tarsus to seek Saul, brought him to Antioch, and for a whole year they assembled with the congregation and taught much people (Acts 11:22-26).
judgmentFull: Luke describes him there as a good man, full of the Holy Ghost and of faith, and adds that much people was added to the Lord. To be full of the Holy Ghost is first and foremost to be keeping the laws; the wisdom and understanding come after that, and then the power. The name the apostles gave him, the son of consolation, matches both his giving and his care for the brethren. When the prophet Agabus signified by the spirit that a great dearth was coming, which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar, the disciples at Antioch determined, every man according to his ability, to send relief to the brethren in Judaea, and they sent it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul (Acts 11:27-30). The same care for need bound congregations together across distance.

The Holy Ghost afterward separated Barnabas and Saul for the work to which they were called, and the congregation sent them away with fasting and prayer and the laying on of hands (Acts 13:1-3). The work cost them. At Antioch in Pisidia they told the rulers that the word of God had to be spoken to them first, and turned to the scattered when it was put from them, and the two were raised persecution against and expelled out of the coasts by their own countrymen (Acts 13:46-50). When certain men came down from Judaea teaching that no man could be saved without circumcision after the manner of Moses, Barnabas and Paul had no small dissension with them and carried the matter up to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem, and the letter that came back out of that council named them men that had hazarded their lives for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 15:1-2; Acts 15:25-26). Money, reputation, teaching and life itself were all put into the work.
