cases.name: The Bereans
cases.charge: Receiving the word with all readiness of mind, and searching the scriptures daily, whether those things were so
cases.summary: Driven out of Thessalonica by an uproar, the brethren immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and they went into the synagogue of the Jews. These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so. Many of them believed, also of honourable women which were Greeks, and of men not a few. Then the Jews of Thessalonica came there also and stirred up the people.
offenseFull: At Thessalonica there was a synagogue of the Jews, and Paul, as his manner was, went in to them, and three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures, opening and alleging that Christ must needs have suffered and risen again from the dead (Acts 17:1-3). His method was to reason out of the writings they already held. What broke it up was not the argument but the men of the city: certain lewd fellows of the baser sort gathered a company, set the city in an uproar, assaulted the house of Jason, and when they could not find the apostles they dragged Jason before the rulers and told on him, saying these men do contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying there is another king, one Jesus (Acts 17:5-7). That is where their allegiance lay, and it is the same allegiance the chief priests showed when they feared the Romans would come and take away their place and nation (John 11:47-48). Brothers of our own nation, filled with envy, on the payroll of Esau. So the brethren immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, who coming there went into the synagogue of the Jews (Acts 17:10).

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so (Acts 17:11). There were believers in Thessalonica too; what Berea did not have was the riffraff stirring up the multitude against the word. Readiness and examination stood together in the same men, and the daily search was made against the same scriptures the preacher was arguing from. Christ had given the same charge in Jerusalem: search the scriptures, for in them men think they have eternal life, and they are they which testify of him (John 5:39-40). The men he said it to could not match the prophecies to the life being lived in front of them; he had to open the scriptures himself, beginning at Moses and all the prophets, and expound the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). The Bereans did with the writings what those men would not do.
judgmentFull: Therefore many of them believed, also of honourable women which were Greeks, and of men not a few (Acts 17:12). Do not get caught up at that verse. The Greeks there are our own people scattered in Greece, the same Jews of Thessalonica and Berea spoken of from verse one, following the Hellenistic culture that is read about in Maccabees; the audience never changed. The searching produced conviction in the very people the letters were afterward written to.

But when the Jews of Thessalonica had knowledge that the word of God was preached of Paul at Berea, they came there also and stirred up the people, and then immediately the brethren sent Paul away to go as it were to the sea, but Silas and Timotheus abode there still (Acts 17:13-14). Sound hearing did not keep the opposition out of the city; it produced brethren who moved to protect the teacher and kept the work going. Paul went on to Athens, where he found the city wholly given to idolatry, and sent an urgent request for Silas and Timotheus, still at Berea, to come to him with all speed, while he disputed in the synagogue of the Jews and in the market daily with the philosophers of the Epicureans and of the Stoics (Acts 17:15-18). Afterward he wrote to the Thessalonians that they had suffered the same things of their own countrymen that the churches in Judaea suffered of the Jews who killed the Lord and their own prophets (1 Thessalonians 2:14-15). The
noble mind and the murderous mind were in the same nation in the same season, and the difference between the two cities was whether men went to the book.

So the brethren immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, who coming there went into the synagogue of the Jews (Acts 17:10).

The Greeks there are our own people scattered in Greece, the same Jews of Thessalonica and Berea spoken of from verse one, following the Hellenistic culture that is read about in Maccabees; the audience never changed. The searching produced conviction in the very people the letters were afterward written to.

cases.name: Priscilla and Aquila
cases.charge: Laying down their own necks for Paul’s life; and expounding unto Apollos the way of God more perfectly
cases.summary: Paul found at Corinth a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome, and because he was of the same craft he abode with them and wrought. They sailed with him to Ephesus and stayed there, and when Apollos came speaking only of the baptism of John, they took him and expounded the way of God more perfectly. Paul afterward called them his helpers in Christ Jesus, who had laid down their own necks for his life, and said that all the churches of the Gentiles gave them thanks.
offenseFull: After Athens, Paul came to Corinth and found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome (Acts 18:1-2). Claudius was the Roman emperor from the year forty-one to fifty-four, and the histories date that expulsion around the year forty-nine, which is why the two of them had just arrived. Aquila was born in Pontus, which is in Asia Minor, in what is Turkey today, and he had been living in Italy, which is nothing strange, because our people were scattered through Cappadocia, Pontus, and Asia, and into Rome itself, as the list of dwellers at Jerusalem shows (Acts 2:9-10). Scholars cannot tell a Roman Jew from a Roman by his name alone for the same reason.

Because Paul was of the same craft he abode with them and wrought, for by their occupation they were tentmakers (Acts 18:3). They were already believers, holding the same thing he held, which is why he lodged with them and not merely near them. The household and the trade became part of the ministry; he lived and worked in their house while he reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath and persuaded the Jews and the Greeks, the southern kingdom and the northern (Acts 18:4). When he departed he took them with him and sailed to Syria, and left them at Ephesus while he went into the synagogue there and reasoned with the Jews (Acts 18:18-19). They stayed where they had been set.

At Ephesus a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man and mighty in the scriptures, began to speak boldly in the synagogue, knowing only the baptism of John; and when Aquila and Priscilla had heard him, they took him to themselves and expounded the way of God to him more perfectly (Acts 18:24-26). They did not contend with him publicly and they did not leave him where he was. A tentmaker and his wife carried what he lacked to him privately.
judgmentFull: When Apollos was disposed to pass into Achaia, the brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him, and when he was come he helped them much which had believed through grace, for he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publicly, showing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ (Acts 18:27-28). What they gave him in a house at Ephesus went on working in another province.

Paul afterward greeted Priscilla and Aquila as his helpers in Christ Jesus, who had for his life laid down their own necks, to whom not only he gave thanks but also all the churches of the Gentiles, and greeted the church that was in their house (Romans 16:3-5). He sent their salutation again from Ephesus with the church that was in their house (1 Corinthians 16:19), and named them once more at the very end of his last letter (2 Timothy 4:19). Their work, their lodging, their teaching, and their risk are all in the record, and the thanks the churches owed them was not a private friendship but a debt many congregations owed.

cases.name: Apollos
cases.charge: Being instructed in the way of the Lord, and receiving correction from a tentmaker and his wife
cases.summary: A certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus; he was instructed in the way of the Lord and being fervent in the spirit he spoke and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John. Aquila and Priscilla heard him speak boldly in the synagogue, took him to themselves, and expounded the way of God more perfectly. He then passed into Achaia and helped them much which had believed. Paul afterward refused to be set against him, saying he had planted and Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.
offenseFull: A certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus (Acts 18:24). Note where he was born. We always had settlements in Egypt, which is why the angel told Joseph to take the young child and his mother and flee into Egypt rather than into a strange people (Matthew 2:13); a man of our nation born and raised at Alexandria is another witness of that settlement, and he came out of it mighty in the scriptures. Eloquent means articulate, well spoken, a man who can hold a room with his speech; and mighty in the scriptures means he knew the law.

He was instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in the spirit he spoke and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John; and when Aquila and Priscilla had heard him speak boldly in the synagogue they took him to themselves and expounded the way of God to him more perfectly (Acts 18:25-26). Fervent means he had a passionate intensity about it, and bold means he did not care what it cost him to say what the Lord said; some brothers cannot even confront their own household, and this one stood up in a synagogue. John’s teaching had spread and men were carrying it and talking it among themselves, so what he held was real as far as it went;

the water baptism he knew was the whole of what he knew. That is the same condition Paul had been in, a man taught the law by the best teacher in Israel who had not yet been shown that the law was speaking of Christ. What was missing was supplied by a tentmaker and his wife without a public contest. He did not refuse it, and the diligence he already had was joined to the fuller word.
judgmentFull: When he was disposed to pass into Achaia, the brethren wrote exhorting the disciples to receive him, and when he was come he helped them much which had believed through grace, for he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publicly, showing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ (Acts 18:27-28). His strength was in what he could establish out of the writings, not in eloquence by itself.

At Corinth the people took his name and made a party out of it, every one saying, I am of Paul, and I of Apollos, and I of Cephas, and I of Christ (1 Corinthians 1:12). Paul refused the comparison and answered it with the order of the work: who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom they believed; he had planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase, so neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth, and every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour (1 Corinthians 3:5-8). That is the same order seen at Samaria, where Philip the deacon planted and the apostles came and watered (Acts 8:14-17). Paul kept him as a brother and afterward greatly desired him to come to Corinth with the brethren, though his will was not at all to come at that time (1 Corinthians 16:12).

cases.name: The Ephesians who burned their books
cases.charge: Confessing and shewing their deeds, and burning fifty thousand pieces of silver worth of curious arts before all men
cases.summary: After the seven sons of Sceva were overcome by the man they tried to exorcise, this was known to all the Jews and Greeks dwelling at Ephesus, and fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified. Many that believed came and confessed and showed their deeds, and many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together and burned them before all men. They counted the price and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver. So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed.
offenseFull: Paul had come to Ephesus and gone into the synagogue and spoken boldly for three months, and then separated the disciples and disputed daily in the school of one Tyrannus, and this continued by the space of two years, so that all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks (Acts 19:8-10). The Jews are the southern kingdom and the Greeks are the Greek-speaking of our nation, the northern; that is who the Ephesians are, Israelites dwelling at Ephesus. That is also how Colosse heard it, though there is no verse saying Paul ever went to Colosse; look at the map and see how close it sits to Ephesus, and there is the precept for it. And what they were being turned from is named in the same chapter: not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul had persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods which are made with hands, and the temple of the great goddess Diana was in danger of being despised, whom all Asia and the world worshipped (Acts 19:26-27). Ephesus was a city given to the worship of a female deity, the fertility goddess whose small images were sold in every street and whose trade fed the silversmiths; that is why Demetrius could raise the craftsmen, and why the city cried out about the space of two hours in the theatre, Great is Diana of the Ephesians (Acts 19:24-25, Acts 19:34). Our brothers have stood in those ruins and seen what the place was.

Then came the defeat of the vagabond exorcists, and it was known to all the Jews and Greeks also dwelling at Ephesus, and fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified (Acts 19:17). Many that believed came and confessed and showed their deeds; and many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together and burned them before all men, and they counted the price of them and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:18-19). Curious arts are the magical arts and jugglery practised by the conjurers of that city, and that is witchcraft by another name, the very thing the law forbids: no diviner, no observer of times, no enchanter, no witch, no charmer, no consulter with familiar spirits, no wizard, no necromancer, and no witch suffered to live (Deuteronomy 18:10-12, Exodus 22:18). Witchcraft is still named among the works of the flesh in the letters, so it did not stop being real in the New Testament (Galatians 5:19-20). Notice also that they came and confessed and showed their deeds, which no man does unless the law still stands and he knows what he has broken. The confession was made in the open, and the instruments of the old practice went into the fire in front of the same people. They burned their own books, and they did not sell them first.
judgmentFull: So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed (Acts 19:20). The gain counted in the record is not the money given up but the growth of the word in that city, and from that city into all Asia. The spirit was so heavy in Ephesus that places Paul never physically walked into were touched by it, and a congregation rose at Colosse that had never seen his face (Colossians 1:1-6, Colossians 2:1). Some of the instruction written back to that region reads differently once the goddess is known: the charge that the women keep silence in the congregation went to a people repenting out of a religion built on female power and woman worship, which is the same doctrine under new names today (1 Corinthians 14:34-35).

The turning did not end the watch. Paul later called the elders of that same church and warned them that after his departing grievous wolves would enter in among them, not sparing the flock, and that of their own selves men would arise speaking perverse things to draw away disciples after them, and told them to watch and remember that by the space of three years he ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears (Acts 20:29-31). What is burned can be replaced by another corruption under a better name, and the men who had made the fire were the ones told to watch.

cases.name: The seven sons of Sceva
cases.charge: Exorcising in the name of Jesus whom Paul preacheth
cases.summary: God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul at Ephesus, so that handkerchiefs and aprons brought from his body healed the sick and the evil spirits went out. Then certain vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying that they adjured them by Jesus whom Paul preached; and there were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jew and chief of the priests, which did so. The evil spirit answered that it knew Jesus and Paul, and asked who they were, and the man in whom it was leaped on them and overcame them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.
offenseFull: God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul at Ephesus, so that from his body were brought to the sick handkerchiefs and aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them (Acts 19:11-12). There is nothing deep in the cloth. All Asia was coming out to hear him and the crowds could not reach him, so he blessed handkerchiefs and sent them out, the same way the multitudes pressed to touch the hem of the garment and were made whole, and the same way four men tore open a roof because the press was too thick to get to the door (Matthew 14:35-36, Mark 2:1-5). The cloth was not healing them; their belief was. And notice what Paul was not doing: he was not selling holy water or blessed cloths the way the modern pastor hucksters sell them.

Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying that they adjured them by Jesus whom Paul preached; and there were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jew, and chief of the priests, which did so (Acts 19:13-14). Take the words one at a time. They were vagabonds, men who travel from place to place causing trouble with no camp and no congregation behind them. They were of the priestly house, the very men at whose mouth the people were supposed to seek the law (Malachi 2:7), and they were not teaching it. And they took it upon themselves, which is to say they were not sent and the spirit of Christ was not leading them. What moved them is the spirit of emulation, wanting the results another man was getting, and the words they used prove it, because they named the authority of another man’s preaching and handled the name as a formula to be spoken over a case rather than as the authority of one who had sent them. That is handling the word of God deceitfully, which Paul afterward said he had renounced (2 Corinthians 4:2).
judgmentFull: The evil spirit answered and said that Jesus it knew and Paul it knew, but asked who they were; and the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them and overcame them and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded (Acts 19:15-16). Seven men were driven out of one house by the one man they had come to deliver, and the thing beat the clothes off their backs. The spirit named Christ and Paul in the same breath and put them on the same side, so let no man tell you Paul taught against what Christ taught; only an unlearned man reads Paul as though he superseded the Messiah. The spirits know who was sealed and who was sent, and they knew these men were neither. They did not know how to use the scriptures against an unclean spirit, and they had no business in that room. The same thing still happens: men with no camp and no congregation stand up and run their mouths about doctrine they were never taught, and the spirit they provoke prevails against them and they flee.

This was known to all the Jews and Greeks also dwelling at Ephesus, and fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified (Acts 19:17). The account records no sentence pronounced by the apostles on these men; the judgment came out of the house on its own feet. Many that believed came and confessed and showed their deeds, and many of them which used curious arts brought their books together and burned them before all men, at a price counted at fifty thousand pieces of silver; so mightily grew the word of God and prevailed (Acts 19:18-20). A city given over to witchcraft was shaken by the public humiliation of seven priests’ sons who tried to work it in the name of a man they did not follow. The name is not a charm, and the law that forbids the enchanter and the consulter with familiar spirits was never repealed (Deuteronomy 18:10-11, Leviticus 19:31). Christ said plainly that many would tell him in that day that they had cast out devils in his name, and would be told he never knew them, because they worked iniquity (Matthew 7:22-23).

cases.name: Demetrius and the silversmiths of Ephesus
cases.charge: Raising an uproar over lost trade under the colour of zeal for Diana
cases.summary: Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines for Diana, called the craftsmen of like occupation together and told them plainly that their wealth and their goddess were both at stake because Paul had persuaded much of Asia that gods made with hands are no gods (Acts 19:24-27). The city filled with confusion, Paul’s travelling companions were dragged into the theatre, and the crowd cried up Diana for about two hours (Acts 19:28-34). The townclerk quieted them, sent the craftsmen to the courts and the deputies, and dismissed the assembly; no sentence on Demetrius is recorded (Acts 19:35-41).
offenseFull: Demetrius made silver shrines for Diana and brought no small gain to the craftsmen, and when he gathered the workmen he said the quiet part first: by this craft we have our wealth (Acts 19:24-25). Only after that did he mention the goddess, whose temple was in danger of being despised because Paul was teaching throughout Asia that gods made with hands are no gods (Acts 19:26-27). Diana is the Roman name; the Greeks called her Artemis, and she is the same mother goddess our people have met under other names, the queen of heaven, Ishtar, Easter, the many breasted image of Asia Minor, worshipped in the same city where our people were set to pick cotton and tobacco. Her image was said to have fallen down from Jupiter (Acts 19:35), which is stone worship, the same practice the heathen still keep over a stone today. Paul was teaching the first commandments, that there is no other god and no image to bow to (Exodus 20:4), and the prophets had already priced the trade: they that make a graven image are all of them vanity, and their own witnesses see nothing (Isaiah 44:9-11). The parallel is not ancient. The pictures and statues sold as the Messiah bring no small gain today, and every year the stores panic when the presents are not moving. Take the idolatry out of the people’s minds and you have taken somebody’s money.

When they heard it they were full of wrath and cried that Diana was great, and the whole city was filled with confusion (Acts 19:28-29). Gaius and Aristarchus were caught and the crowd rushed into the theatre. Paul would have gone in to them and the disciples would not let him, and certain of the chief of Asia who were his friends sent word that he should not venture himself there (Acts 19:30-31): he kept friends with standing in these cities and they were worth something that day. The assembly itself was confused and the greater part did not know why they had come together (Acts 19:32), which is why the law says not to follow a multitude to do evil. When the Jews put Alexander forward to make a defence, the crowd would not hear a word once they knew what he was, and screamed for their goddess for about two hours (Acts 19:33-34). Two hours of a crowd shouting a name with no understanding in it is the same spirit that fills the so called Christian church.
judgmentFull: The townclerk appeased the people, but he did not correct them. He told them every man knew the city of the Ephesians was a worshipper of the great goddess Diana and of the image which fell down from Jupiter, and that these things could not be spoken against (Acts 19:35-36). He was of the same chief men of the city who had just sent Paul a warning as friends, and in the pinch he stood with the goddess. He then did the one useful thing: he said the men brought in were neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers, and that if Demetrius and his craftsmen had a matter against any man, the law was open and there were deputies, and other questions belonged in a lawful assembly (Acts 19:37-39).

He warned that the city itself could be called in question for that day’s uproar, since there was no cause they could give for it, and he dismissed the assembly (Acts 19:40-41). Nothing is recorded against Demetrius. What the record leaves standing is the trade and the goddess behind it. Ephesus was the seat of that worship, and it is the reason Paul afterwards charged that congregation that the women keep silence and learn in subjection, not usurping authority over the man (1 Corinthians 14:34; 1 Timothy 2:11-12): the sisters repenting there were coming out of a city built on woman worship, and they had to be converted out of it. Brothers who have walked the ruins report that the same little images are still sold on the spot.

cases.offense: Demetrius made silver shrines for Diana and brought no small gain to the craftsmen, and when he gathered the workmen he said the quiet part first: by this craft we have our wealth (Acts 19:24-25). Only after that did he mention the goddess, whose temple was in danger of being despised because Paul was teaching throughout Asia that gods made with hands are no gods (Acts 19:26-27). Diana is the Roman name; the Greeks called her Artemis, and she is the same mother goddess our people have met under other names, the queen of heaven, Ishtar, Easter, the many breasted image of Asia Minor, worshipped in the same city where our people were set to pick cotton and tobacco. The parallel is not ancient. The pictures and statues sold as the Messiah bring no small gain today, and every year the stores panic when the presents are not moving. Take the idolatry out of the people’s minds and you have taken somebody’s money.

cases.name: Ananias the high priest
cases.charge: Commanding Paul to be smitten on the mouth, contrary to the law, while sitting to judge him by the law
cases.summary: When Paul began his answer before the council, Ananias the high priest ordered those standing by to strike him on the mouth. Paul told him God would smite him, calling him a whited wall, because he sat to judge by the law and commanded a blow against the law; rebuked for speaking so to the high priest, he answered that he had not known him and cited the command against speaking evil of a ruler of the people (Acts 23:1-5). More than forty men afterwards bound themselves under a curse to kill Paul, the plot was broken, and Ananias came down to Caesarea with an orator to accuse him before Felix (Acts 23:12-24; Acts 24:1).
offenseFull: Paul said he had lived in all good conscience before God to that day, and the high priest commanded those beside him to strike him on the mouth before any finding had been stated (Acts 23:1-2). The law puts the judgment of guilt before any ordered beating (Deuteronomy 25:1-2), and the law judges no man before it hears him (John 7:51). Paul named the contradiction to his face and called him a whited wall, which is the prophets’ figure for a wall daubed with untempered morter that will not stand when the storm comes (Ezekiel 13:10-15). When those standing by asked whether he reviled God’s high priest, he answered that he had not known him to be the high priest, and cited the commandment against speaking evil of the ruler of the people (Acts 23:3-5; Exodus 22:28). Both halves stay in the record: the wrong of the judge, and the restraint required of the man on trial.

Ananias was no stranger to that seat. He had sat with Caiaphas and the kindred of the high priest when Peter and John were examined over the healing of the lame man, and heard them answer that they ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 4:5-7; Acts 5:29). He belongs with the leadership Stephen charged with resisting the Holy Ghost, asking which of the prophets their fathers had not persecuted (Acts 7:51-52), and the treatment of the true prophets is on record: cruel mockings, scourgings, bonds, imprisonment, stoning, the sword (Hebrews 11:36-37). Paul, perceiving the council was split, declared himself a Pharisee and the son of a Pharisee, called in question over the hope and resurrection of the dead, and the Sadducees who say there is no resurrection, angel, nor spirit fell out with the Pharisees who confess both (Acts 23:6-9). He was raised in that school and brought up under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), so he knew exactly where the seam was. The point the teaching presses is that these parties did not believe the same things and united anyway against the man preaching Christ, the same way the Pharisees took counsel with the Herodians to destroy him (Mark 3:6).
judgmentFull: When it was day, more than forty men banded together and bound themselves under a curse that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul, and they brought the chief priests and elders into the plan (Acts 23:12-15). Paul’s sister’s son heard of the ambush. Paul did not tell the young man to hold his peace and wait on the Lord; he sent him to the chief captain to repeat exactly what he had heard (Acts 23:16-21). The captain called out two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen and moved Paul out by night to Caesarea (Acts 23:23-24). Forty men under an oath had nothing left to do against four hundred and seventy under arms, and the street code that says a man should have kept his mouth shut would have buried the apostle.

Ananias came down five days later with the elders and an orator named Tertullus to inform the governor against Paul (Acts 24:1). Acts does not narrate the smiting Paul had foretold. The warning was left with God and not executed by any hand of Paul’s, who in the same breath had acknowledged the law governing his own speech. He had the office, the escort, and the hired speaker. In the one act the record charges against him, he did not have the law.

cases.name: Felix the governor
cases.charge: Trembling at the judgment to come, hoping for a bribe, and leaving a man he knew to be innocent bound
cases.summary: Felix already had a more perfect knowledge of that way when he deferred the hearing (Acts 24:22). He sent for Paul with his wife Drusilla, and as Paul reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, the governor trembled and put him off to a convenient season (Acts 24:24-25). He sent for him often afterwards, hoping money would be given him, and after two years he left Paul bound to do the Jews a pleasure (Acts 24:26-27). No repentance and no sentence upon Felix is recorded.
offenseFull: The record says Felix had more perfect knowledge of that way before he deferred the case (Acts 24:22). That is the key to the man. The liar knows the lie he told: he knew exactly what Paul was teaching, which is why the preaching reached him. He came with his wife Drusilla, called a Jewess; she was the daughter of Herod Agrippa, of the stock of Edom, converted in generations earlier, and she is the living example of what Christ afterwards named, the blasphemy of them which say they are Jews and are not (Acts 24:24; Revelation 2:9). Paul reasoned of righteousness, which is the commandments, of temperance, and of judgment to come, and Felix trembled (Acts 24:25). Trembling is not faith. The devils also believe, and tremble (James 2:19). And if what Paul preached had been nonsense, a Roman governor would have laughed at him instead of shaking.

He put the preacher off to a convenient season, then sent for him the oftener, hoping that money would be given him to loose Paul (Acts 24:25-26). The law forbids the gift outright, because the gift blinds the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19), and he that justifies the wicked and condemns the just is an abomination to the Lord (Proverbs 17:15). The histories place him exactly. Judea had been annexed and put under procurators who tampered with the high priesthood, beheaded the men they called false prophets, and crucified the sons of Judas the Galilean. Felix was the newest of them and was guilty of fanning the hatred of the growing zealot camp by his harsh handling of every discontent, until the daggermen stepped up their own resistance and began assassinating the sympathizers of Rome, the corrupt high priest Jonathan among them. A governor who tried both to frighten a nation and to sell its prisoners was hurrying his province toward 70 AD.
judgmentFull: After two years Porcius Festus came into his room, and Felix, willing to show the Jews a pleasure, left Paul bound (Acts 24:27). There is no divine sentence carried out on him in the book and no repentance either. There is only the list of his acts: postponement, the hope of a payment, and a last concession to political favour at the prisoner’s expense. The convenient season never came, and the accepted time and the day of salvation are now (2 Corinthians 6:2).

The warning in the case is for the hearer. A man can hear this gospel repeatedly, know in himself that it is true, shake while he hears it, and still hand the preacher back to the men who want him dead. Fear of judgment is not obedience. And the same evidence that convicted Felix convicts the men who spend money and airtime fighting the teaching now: if the work were of men it would come to nothing on its own, and Gamaliel’s counsel was to leave it alone, lest they be found fighting against God (Acts 5:38-39). Nobody goes to that expense over something they believe is nothing.

cases.name: The Corinthian who had his father’s wife
cases.charge: Fornication not so much as named among the Gentiles: a man with his father’s wife
cases.summary: It was reported commonly that there was fornication in the congregation at Corinth, of a kind not so much as named among the other nations, that a man should have his father’s wife (1 Corinthians 5:1). The congregation was puffed up instead of mourning and putting him away. Paul judged the case in absence and directed the gathered assembly to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 5:3-5).
offenseFull: Reported commonly means it was going on a lot, the way a particular spirit will settle in a particular congregation. The woman was not his mother; she was a woman promised or married to his father, and under the law a betrothed woman is already that man’s wife, as Mary was called the wife of Joseph while they were still espoused. The law forbids uncovering the nakedness of a father’s wife, and uncovering nakedness means the act itself, not a look (Leviticus 18:8). Under Moses both parties in such a case were put to death (Leviticus 20:10-11), and the congregation pronounced the curse on it aloud (Deuteronomy 27:20). It had happened before in our own family: Reuben lay with Bilhah his father’s concubine, Israel heard it, and he lost the birthright over it (Genesis 35:22).

Paul’s heavier charge is against the assembly. They were puffed up and had not rather mourned, that the man who did the deed might be taken away from among them (1 Corinthians 5:2). He had already written that some among them were puffed up as though he would not come, and asked them whether they wanted him with a rod or in love and the spirit of meekness (1 Corinthians 4:18-21): young men who had learned a few scriptures and thought themselves on the apostle’s level. The figure he uses is bread. A little leaven leavens the whole lump, and sin left sitting rises and spreads through the whole house (1 Corinthians 5:6); a little fornication allowed in one school starts spreading. Israel came out of Egypt in such haste that the dough went unleavened (Exodus 12:33-39), and Christ our passover is the lamb without blemish of that same night (Exodus 12:3-5; John 1:29), so the feast is to be kept with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, not with malice and wickedness (1 Corinthians 5:7-8).
judgmentFull: Paul judged the case though absent in body, and directed the assembly, gathered together with his spirit and the power of the Lord Jesus, to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord (1 Corinthians 5:3-5). Delivering a man to Satan means putting him out of the school: he cannot be among us any more, and it is only for the man who will not repent or change. That is congregational discipline, not an order to execute him. Paul had done far worse himself before mercy found him and was not trying to destroy anybody; he was keeping order. The instruction is to put away from among themselves that wicked person and not to keep company with a man called a brother who goes on in such things (1 Corinthians 5:11-13). Under the law he would have been stoned. In Christ the body cuts him off, and the shame is meant to work on him, which is why a man who obeys not the word is noted and avoided, that he may be ashamed (2 Thessalonians 3:14).

The second letter supplies the other half, and it is the half congregations forget. Paul wrote out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears, not to grieve them but that they might know his love, and he said the punishment inflicted of the majority was sufficient for such a man, so that they ought rather to forgive him and comfort him, lest he be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow, and lest Satan get an advantage where the body will not forgive (2 Corinthians 2:4-11). Paul did not take back the correction; he said he did not repent of the letter, though he was sorry for the pain it cost the good brothers and sisters who had to hear it read out. He rejoiced not that they were made sorry, but that they sorrowed to repentance, because godly sorrow works repentance to salvation, while the sorrow of the world works death (2 Corinthians 7:8-10). Cutting off is the beginning of a healing, and when the man repents he comes back into the body.

cases.name: The Corinthians at the Lord’s supper
cases.charge: Eating and drinking unworthily; shaming them that have not
cases.summary: When the Corinthians came together it was not for the better but for the worse: there were divisions among them, every one took his own supper before another, one was hungry and another drunken, and those who had nothing were shamed (1 Corinthians 11:17-22). Paul asked whether they had no houses to eat and drink in, and told them they despised the congregation of God. For that cause many among them were weak and sickly, and many slept; being judged, they were chastened of the Lord, that they should not be condemned with the world (1 Corinthians 11:30-32).
offenseFull: The supper was given for unification. The cup of blessing is the communion of the blood of Christ and the bread the communion of his body, and being many we are one bread and one body, all partakers of that one bread (1 Corinthians 10:16-17). The northern and southern kingdoms were divided and he brought us under one head; the table is where that is shown. So a man does not come into the assembly and eat all the food, drink all the drink, and get drunk with no moderation while a brother sits there with nothing. That is not the Lord’s supper, however often it is called that (1 Corinthians 11:17-22). Paul also told them there must be heresies among them, so that they which are approved may be made manifest (1 Corinthians 11:19); the breaking of bread is exactly where it shows, because a man can sit and break bread with a body whose faith he does not share.

Paul returned them to what he had received and delivered: the bread given in remembrance, and the cup as the new testament in his blood, and as often as they eat and drink they show the Lord’s death till he come (1 Corinthians 11:23-26). To eat and drink unworthily is to do it out of that mind, not discerning the Lord’s body, and it makes a man guilty of the body and blood of the Lord and brings damnation on himself (1 Corinthians 11:27-29). What a man sows is what he reaps: sowing to the flesh reaps corruption, sowing to the spirit reaps life everlasting (Galatians 6:7-8). And the assembling is not to be forsaken, as the manner of some is, but so much the more as the day is seen approaching (Hebrews 10:25).
judgmentFull: For this cause many were weak and sickly among them, and many slept (1 Corinthians 11:30). The teaching turns the verse into an inventory. Examine whether you actually have a charitable spirit, whether you are looking out for the people sitting around you or serving your own belly, and you will find how much of the body is sick and how much of it is still asleep to the understanding of Christ. When we say Israel is sick, this is what is meant. If we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged (1 Corinthians 11:31).

The sentence on that congregation was correction and not destruction. When we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world (1 Corinthians 11:32), and the instruction that follows is plain and domestic: when they come together to eat, tarry one for another, and let the man who is hungry eat at home, so that they do not come together to condemnation (1 Corinthians 11:33-34). The Lord chastens the son he loves and scourges every son he receives, and the chastening is neither to be despised nor fainted under, because it is proof of sonship (Hebrews 12:5-8; Proverbs 3:11-12).

cases.name: Epaphroditus
cases.charge: For the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me
cases.summary: Paul, writing from confinement in Rome, called Epaphroditus his brother, companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, and the congregation’s messenger who ministered to his wants (Philippians 2:25). The brother fell sick near to death carrying that service, and grieved because the congregation had heard of it (Philippians 2:26-27). Paul sent him back with the charge that they receive him with all gladness and hold such in reputation, because for the work of Christ he came near to death, not regarding his life, to supply what their own service to Paul had lacked (Philippians 2:28-30).
offenseFull: Paul could not travel. He was held in Rome, and the work of the congregations had to be carried by men he could trust with letters and with money. Epaphroditus is the man he names, and the titles are stacked: brother, companion in labour, fellowsoldier, your messenger, and he that ministered to my wants (Philippians 2:25). The teaching makes the practical point that Paul had no fear this brother would run off with the collection or edit the doctrine on the road, which is more than can be said for the men calling themselves messengers and pastors now. He is not a famous name. He served a great man and was faithful with the churches’ business. The word fellowsoldier is not ornament either; Paul used it of Archippus too (Philemon 1:2), and it states our actual condition. This is a war. Every man in it is a soldier whatever his rank, told to endure hardness and not to entangle himself with the affairs of this life, so that he may please him who chose him to be a soldier (2 Timothy 2:3-4). Some fall in it, some are taken, some go absent.

He longed after the whole congregation and was full of heaviness because they had heard that he had been sick (Philippians 2:26). Read that again slowly: he was the one lying sick, and his distress was over their distress. Indeed he was sick, near to death, and God had mercy on him, and on Paul also, lest Paul should have sorrow upon sorrow (Philippians 2:27). The Lord does not try a man above what he can bear. Paul was already in chains and downtrodden; taking that brother out of the earth would have been more than the load. And the reason he was in that condition is stated without flattery: for the work of Christ he was near to death, not for his own work and not for a job, and he did not regard his life, to supply what was lacking in their service toward Paul (Philippians 2:30). The Philippians had given before, when no other congregation communicated with him in the matter of giving and receiving, sending to his necessity more than once (Philippians 4:15-16), and Paul called the fresh supply this brother carried an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable and wellpleasing to God (Philippians 4:18).
judgmentFull: Paul sent him back the more carefully, so that they might rejoice at the sight of him and Paul be the less sorrowful, and told them to receive him in the Lord with all gladness and to hold such in reputation (Philippians 2:28-29). That is the blessing pronounced over him, and the teaching insists on what it is worth. A good name is better than precious ointment (Ecclesiastes 7:1). A man is told to have regard to his name, because it continues with him above a thousand great treasures of gold (Ecclesiasticus 41:12). Daniel came out of the matter of Susanna in great reputation in the sight of the people (Susanna 1:64), and when Paul went up to Jerusalem he communicated privately with them which were of reputation (Galatians 2:2). Every brother and sister who comes into this truth is building a name, either as a labourer or as a murmurer and a busybody, and the name follows the man and follows his children after him. Epaphroditus is the pattern of the right kind. He was not famous, which is why the congregation had to be told to honour him. What he was known for was work that almost killed him, done for somebody else’s sake.

cases.name: Timothy, with Lois and Eunice
cases.charge: Unfeigned faith that dwelt first in his grandmother and his mother; knowing the holy scriptures from a child
cases.summary: Paul came to Derbe and Lystra and found a disciple named Timotheus, son of a believing Jewess, whose father was a Greek; the brethren there spoke well of him, and Paul circumcised him and took him along (Acts 16:1-3). Paul called to remembrance the unfeigned faith that dwelt first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and was persuaded it was in Timothy also (2 Timothy 1:5), and reminded him that from a child he had known the holy scriptures, which are able to make a man wise to salvation (2 Timothy 3:14-15).
offenseFull: Greek in this account does not mean another nation. His father was a hellenized Jew, a man of the northern kingdom living in the Greek customs, which is why the boy had never been circumcised; his mother and grandmother were Israelite women raised under the law of Moses, and they raised him in it (Acts 16:1). Paul circumcised him because of the Jews in those quarters and took him on the journey (Acts 16:2-3). The teaching of children in the law at home is the commandment itself, to be taught diligently to the children and talked of in the house and by the way (Deuteronomy 6:6-7), with the promise that a child trained in the way he should go does not depart from it when he is old (Proverbs 22:6). Two women in one household kept a boy in the scriptures while the man of the house did not, and by the time the apostle arrived the work was already done.

Paul called to remembrance the unfeigned faith that dwelt first in Lois and then in Eunice, and said he was persuaded it was in Timothy too (2 Timothy 1:5). Unfeigned means not put on, not a false appearance; the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart and of a good conscience and of faith unfeigned (1 Timothy 1:5). That family was sincere through three generations, and Paul saw it. He told the young man that from a child he had known the holy scriptures, which are able to make a man wise to salvation through faith in Christ, and that all scripture given by inspiration is profitable for doctrine, reproof, correction, and instruction in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:14-17). He told him to stir up the gift of God that was in him by the putting on of his hands (2 Timothy 1:6), which is what Moses did to Joshua, so that Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom and the children of Israel hearkened to him (Deuteronomy 34:9). Paul knew he was about to be beheaded in Rome. The letters were written to get the young man ready to stand where he had stood.
judgmentFull: Paul called him his own son in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2), committed the charge to him that he might war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18), and told him to let no man despise his youth but to be an example of the believers in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity (1 Timothy 4:12). The teaching applies that to every young man the Lord sets over a congregation: you may be young, but you are not a novice, and the first thing the men creeping in will try is to hem you up on your age. Show the example because the hearts of the brethren depend on it (Judith 8:24). Paul told him to give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine, and not to neglect the gift in him, given by prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery (1 Timothy 4:13-14), and warned him that all who will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution, as Paul himself had at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra (2 Timothy 3:11-12). And of all the men around him Paul said he had none likeminded who would naturally care for the state of the congregation; the proof of this one was that, as a son with the father, he had served with him in the gospel (Philippians 2:19-22). Paul greatly desired to see him, being mindful of his tears, that he might be filled with joy (2 Timothy 1:3-4). That is what a family that kept a child in the scriptures produced.

cases.name: Onesiphorus
cases.charge: Oft refreshing Paul, and not ashamed of his chain; seeking him out very diligently in Rome
cases.summary: Writing from Rome while he waited on execution, Paul said that all they which are in Asia had turned away from him, and then named one house that had not: the house of Onesiphorus, who often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chain, sought him out very diligently in Rome until he found him, and had ministered to him in many things at Ephesus (2 Timothy 1:15-18). Paul’s prayer over him is that the Lord give mercy to his house and that he find mercy of the Lord in that day, and at the close of the same letter he salutes that household again (2 Timothy 4:19).
offenseFull: Paul had already told Timothy not to be ashamed of the testimony of the Lord nor of him, his prisoner, but to be partaker of the afflictions of the gospel (2 Timothy 1:8). Then he stated the plain case: all they which are in Asia be turned away from me, Phygellus and Hermogenes among them (2 Timothy 1:15). These were not strangers. Men who had stood strong in this gospel and warred alongside him had left him. The teaching refuses to soften it and applies it directly, because we have watched it happen: brothers and sisters we called friends, who broke bread with us, stayed in our homes, and knew our families, offended at the word and turned to tearing the work down. Christ had already said that many would be offended, and would betray one another and hate one another (Matthew 24:10).

Against all of Asia, one house. Paul asked the Lord to give mercy to the house of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chain (2 Timothy 1:16). When he was in Rome he sought Paul out very diligently, and found him (2 Timothy 1:17). There were no phones and no addresses to call; a man looking for a prisoner in Rome had to go on foot and keep asking until somebody told him, and he did it knowing what the chain meant and knowing who would see him doing it. This was not a single gesture either, because Timothy knew very well in how many things the same man had ministered to Paul at Ephesus (2 Timothy 1:18). Christ counts a visit to a man in prison as done to himself, and sets it among the works that divide the sheep from the goats (Matthew 25:36-40). The command is to remember them that are in bonds as bound with them (Hebrews 13:3), and the Hebrews had already done it, becoming companions of them that were so used and taking the spoiling of their goods joyfully (Hebrews 10:33-34).
judgmentFull: Paul had nothing left to give him but a prayer, and he prayed it twice: mercy on his house, and that the man himself might find mercy of the Lord in that day (2 Timothy 1:16-18). That day is the day Paul had been reasoning about all through the letter. In that day the song is sung in the land of Judah, and the gates are opened that the righteous nation which keeps the truth may enter in (Isaiah 26:1-2). The truth there is the law, since his righteousness is an everlasting righteousness and his law is the truth (Psalms 119:142), and it is the keeping of the commandments that gives right to the tree of life

and entrance through the gates into the city (Revelation 22:14), the city with twelve gates and the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel written on them (Revelation 21:12). A man who was not ashamed of a prisoner’s chain in Rome is asking for mercy at the only bar that matters. At the end of the same letter, when almost everyone else had gone, Paul saluted the household of Onesiphorus by name (2 Timothy 4:19). That is the whole reward on record, and it is the one he asked for.

cases.name: Hymenaeus, Alexander, and Philetus
cases.charge: Making shipwreck of the faith; blasphemy; teaching that the resurrection is past already
cases.summary: Paul charged Timothy to hold faith and a good conscience, which some had put away and so made shipwreck concerning the faith, naming Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom he delivered to Satan that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:19-20). The error is named in the second letter: the word of Hymenaeus and Philetus ate as a canker, and they erred concerning the truth, saying that the resurrection was past already, and overthrew the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:16-18).
offenseFull: Paul set two words beside each other on purpose. Some had swerved and turned aside to vain jangling (1 Timothy 1:6), and some had put away faith and a good conscience and made shipwreck (1 Timothy 1:19). Swerving and putting away are the same motion: men walking away from a truth they once had. The charge does not come from a man who had never been wrong. Paul had just finished telling Timothy that he was before a blasphemer, a persecutor, and injurious, who shut up the saints in prison, gave his voice against them when they were put to death, punished them often in every synagogue and compelled them to blaspheme, and obtained mercy because he did it ignorantly in unbelief (1 Timothy 1:13; Acts 26:10-11).

The doctrine itself is identified: their word would eat as a canker, and Hymenaeus and Philetus, concerning the truth, had erred, saying that the resurrection was past already, and overthrew the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:17-18). These men had rolled with Paul. The obvious question is how a man goes from strong in the gospel to speaking heresy, and the answer is that somebody got into his ears. Paul never taught it, and he had to spend a whole chapter with the Corinthians proving from what he himself had received and delivered that Christ died, was buried, rose the third day, and was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve, then of above five hundred brethren at once (1 Corinthians 15:3-8,12). That is why Timothy is told to shun profane and vain babblings, which increase to more ungodliness, and to charge men not to strive about words to no profit, because such talk subverts the hearers (2 Timothy 2:14-16). Shut it down immediately and give it no place, not for an hour, which is exactly what Paul did with the false brethren brought in privily at Jerusalem (Galatians 2:4-5).
judgmentFull: Paul delivered Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan, that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:20). It is the same sentence passed on the man at Corinth and it means the same thing: put out of the assembly (1 Corinthians 5:5). A man who will not be corrected is cut off so that what he carries stops spreading, and a man that is a heretick, after a first and second admonition, is to be rejected, being subverted and condemned of himself (Titus 3:10-11). Mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine, and avoid them (Romans 16:17).

The remedy Paul gives the rest of the congregation is a house with vessels in it. In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and of earth, some to honour and some to dishonour, and the man who purges himself from these is a vessel to honour, sanctified and fit for the master’s use and prepared to every good work (2 Timothy 2:20-21). Hymenaeus and Philetus are the examples of what to purge yourself from, because God cannot use a man tangled up with them. What Timothy heard was to be committed to faithful men, which is to say loyal ones (2 Timothy 2:2). And the foundation of God stands sure with its seal, that the Lord knows them that are his, and that every one that names the name of Christ is to depart from iniquity (2 Timothy 2:19). Alexander does not disappear from the record here; Paul warns of him again in the last chapter he ever wrote (2 Timothy 4:14-15).

cases.name: Paul, at the end of his course
cases.charge: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith
cases.summary: Paul wrote his last letter knowing he was ready to be offered and that the time of his departure was at hand (2 Timothy 4:6). He said he had fought a good fight, finished his course, and kept the faith, and that a crown of righteousness was laid up for him, which the Lord the righteous judge would give him at that day, and not to him only but to all them also that love his appearing (2 Timothy 4:7-8). At his first answer no man stood with him, yet the Lord stood with him and strengthened him (2 Timothy 4:16-17).
offenseFull: Paul was not guessing about the ending. Christ had said of him at the very beginning that he was a chosen vessel to bear his name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel, and that he would be shown how great things he must suffer for that name (Acts 9:15-16), and Peter likewise knew he must shortly put off his tabernacle because Christ had showed him (2 Peter 1:14). So when Paul told the elders at Miletus that bonds and afflictions awaited him in every city, he could add that none of these things moved him, neither counted he his life dear to himself, so that he might finish his course with joy and the ministry he had received (Acts 20:22-24). He was not out to preserve his life; he was out to finish the work, because the man who saves his life loses it.

The course is itemised: stripes above measure, prisons more frequent, deaths often, five times forty stripes save one, three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three shipwrecks, a night and a day in the deep, perils of waters, of robbers, of his own countrymen, of the heathen, in the city, in the wilderness, in the sea, among false brethren, and on top of all of it the care of all the churches daily (2 Corinthians 11:23-28). The stoning at Lystra was the worst of it: they drew him out of the city supposing he was dead, and he rose up and went back in (Acts 14:19-20). The teaching sets that hour beside the man caught up to the third heaven, into paradise, who heard unspeakable words not lawful for a man to utter (2 Corinthians 12:2-4). Paul counted himself the least of the apostles, not fit to be called one because he persecuted the congregation of God, and said he laboured more abundantly than they all, yet not he but the grace of God with him (1 Corinthians 15:9-10): he did more work because he had done more damage. He forgot the things behind and reached toward the mark for the prize of the high calling (Philippians 3:13-14), and kept his own body under, lest after preaching to others he himself should be a castaway (1 Corinthians 9:24-27).
judgmentFull: He had fought a good fight, finished his course, and kept the faith, and there was laid up for him a crown of righteousness which the Lord the righteous judge would give him at that day (2 Timothy 4:7-8). The crown is not his alone. It is promised to all them also that love his appearing, which puts it in front of everybody who actually wants that day to come.

The ending itself was lonely. At his first answer no man stood with him and all men forsook him, and he prayed that it would not be laid to their charge (2 Timothy 4:16). Demas had gone, Crescens was in Galatia, Titus in Dalmatia, and only Luke was with him (2 Timothy 4:10-11). Notwithstanding, the Lord stood with him and strengthened him, so that by him the preaching might be fully known and all the Gentiles hear, and he was delivered out of the mouth of the lion (2 Timothy 4:17). He said the Lord would deliver him from every evil work and preserve him to his heavenly kingdom (2 Timothy 4:18). He had also left the elders at Ephesus a clean account of how he had lived among them: he coveted no man’s silver, gold, or apparel, his own hands ministered to his necessities and to them that were with him, and he taught them that it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:33-35). He was beheaded at Rome under Nero soon after the letter was sent.

cases.offense: Paul was not guessing about the ending. Christ had said of him at the very beginning that he was a chosen vessel to bear his name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel, and that he would be shown how great things he must suffer for that name (Acts 9:15-16), and Peter likewise knew he must shortly put off his tabernacle because Christ had showed him (2 Peter 1:14). So when Paul told the elders at Miletus that bonds and afflictions awaited him in every city, he could add that none of these things moved him, neither counted he his life dear to himself, so that he might finish his course with joy and the ministry he had received (Acts 20:22-24). He was not out to preserve his life; he was out to finish the work, because the man who saves his life loses it.
cases.judgment: He had fought a good fight, finished his course, and kept the faith, and there was laid up for him a crown of righteousness which the Lord the righteous judge would give him at that day (2 Timothy 4:7-8). The crown is not his alone. It is promised to all them also that love his appearing, which puts it in front of everybody who actually wants that day to come.

cases.name: Demas
cases.charge: Forsaking Paul, having loved this present world
cases.summary: Demas is greeted with Luke in the letter to Colossae (Colossians 4:14) and counted among Paul’s fellowlabourers in the letter to Philemon (Philemon 1:23-24). In the last letter Paul wrote, Demas had forsaken him, having loved this present world, and departed to Thessalonica (2 Timothy 4:9-10). No sentence upon him and no repentance is recorded.
offenseFull: Three mentions tell the whole story. First he is a name in the greetings beside Luke the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14). Then he is listed among the fellowlabourers, with Marcus, Aristarchus, and Lucas (Philemon 1:23-24). Then he is gone (2 Timothy 4:9-10). He was not a bystander; he travelled with Paul and warred with Paul, and Paul was in chains under Nero when he left.

The reason is given with no excuse attached: having loved this present world. The teaching reads it as a man who looked around at what the world was offering, decided he had needs the apostle’s company could not meet, and let it overcome him. All that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, and it is not of the Father; the world passes away and the lust of it, and the man that does the will of God abides for ever (1 John 2:15-17). Friendship with the world is enmity with God (James 4:4). And the seed on stony ground is this man exactly: he hears the word and immediately receives it with gladness, has no root in himself, endures for a time, and when affliction or persecution arises for the word’s sake he is offended at once (Mark 4:16-17). The cares of this world, the deceitfulness of riches, and the lust of other things entering in choke the word so that it becomes unfruitful (Mark 4:19). The affliction around Paul at that moment was real, and it sorted out who had root.
judgmentFull: No sentence is recorded against Demas. What the scripture supplies instead is the standing rule that answers him. No man having put his hand to the plough and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62). Whoever will save his life shall lose it, and what is a man advantaged if he gain the whole world and lose himself (Luke 9:24-25). The thing he went back for was the thing that passes away.

He was not alone in that season, which is the sober part of the case. All they which are in Asia had turned away, Phygellus and Hermogenes among them (2 Timothy 1:15); Crescens went to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia, and only Luke stayed with Paul (2 Timothy 4:11). Christ had already prophesied that many would be offended, would betray one another, and would hate one another (Matthew 24:10), which is why Paul was not undone by it. The application made in class is not comfortable: we have watched brothers and sisters who were called friends, who ate in our homes and knew our families, turn and try to pull the work down, and some who left to start their own assemblies saw them fall overnight, because God does not bless a hand that did that much evil to its own brethren. The sentence on Demas is deferred. Paul left the name in the book, and that by itself is a record.

cases.name: Alexander the coppersmith
cases.charge: Doing Paul much evil; greatly withstanding his words
cases.summary: In the uproar at Ephesus the Jews put Alexander forward out of the multitude to make a defence, and the crowd shouted him down for about two hours once they knew what he was (Acts 19:33-34). Paul later names Alexander with Hymenaeus among those who made shipwreck of the faith and were delivered to Satan that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:19-20), and at the end writes that Alexander the coppersmith did him much evil and greatly withstood their words, and that the Lord would reward him according to his works (2 Timothy 4:14-15).
offenseFull: Alexander first appears in the city of the silversmiths. Demetrius had stirred the craftsmen over the shrines of Diana, the town was in confusion, and the Jews pushed Alexander forward; he beckoned with his hand and would have made his defence to the people, but when they knew he was a Jew they cried up their goddess for about two hours instead (Acts 19:24-27; Acts 19:33-34). The teaching reads him plainly: he was a coppersmith in the city where the trade was making idols, which is where Paul met him, and for a moment he stood between Paul’s companions and a mob. One teacher takes it further and says that once the crowd turned he went along with the foolishness.

Whatever he was then, he did not stay. Paul names him with Hymenaeus among those who put away faith and a good conscience and made shipwreck concerning the faith, and delivered them to Satan that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:19-20), after charging Timothy with the same commission that he might war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18). In the last chapter Paul ever wrote he returns to him: Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil, and Timothy is told to beware of him also, for he greatly withstood our words (2 Timothy 4:14-15). Put the weight where it belongs. Imagine being in the ministry and then turning against the ministry. That was this man, and Paul writes it in the same breath as the line that at his first answer no man stood with him and all men forsook him (2 Timothy 4:16).
judgmentFull: Paul did not lift a hand and did not ask anybody else to. He said, the Lord reward him according to his works (2 Timothy 4:14). That is the law he taught: avenge not yourselves, for vengeance belongs to God, who will repay (Romans 12:19), and mercy belongs to the Lord, for he renders to every man according to his work (Psalms 62:12). Paul had been the chief of persecutors himself and obtained mercy, so he was not looking to destroy this man. He was keeping order and leaving the account where accounts are settled.

What Paul does command is separation. Mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which you have learned, and avoid them (Romans 16:17). Under Moses a man who drew the people after another doctrine was to be stoned and the hand of the witness first upon him (Deuteronomy 13:6-10); in Christ the body cuts him off and nothing more, and the words passed to Timothy are a warning to a young leader, not an execution. In the same passage where he asks the Lord to repay Alexander, Paul prays that the forsaking of the others be not laid to their charge, and records that notwithstanding, the Lord stood with him and strengthened him, so that the preaching might be fully known and he was delivered out of the mouth of the lion (2 Timothy 4:16-17). The case stands as cursed on the word Paul spoke over him. The carrying out of it is not in the book.

cases.name: Gaius, the wellbeloved
cases.charge: Walking in the truth; doing faithfully to the brethren and to strangers; bringing them forward on their journey after a godly sort
cases.summary: John wrote his third epistle to the wellbeloved Gaius, whom he loved in the truth, and rejoiced greatly when the brethren came and testified of the truth that was in him, because he walked in the truth (3 John 1:1-4). He did faithfully whatever he did to the brethren and to strangers, who bore witness of his charity before the congregation, and John told him he would do well to bring them forward on their journey after a godly sort (3 John 1:5-6).
offenseFull: A whole doctrine turns on how John words the greeting. He does not merely say the truth was in the man; he says he loved him in the truth, then says the brethren testified of the truth that was in him, even as he walked in the truth (3 John 1:1,3-4). A man is in the truth because he walks in it, and the truth is in him because he learned it from somewhere and from somebody. The teaching raises this against a doctrine going around that a man only needs the truth to be in him and does not need to be in the body: that is the subtle way of telling people they do not need a congregation and do not need the elders who taught them, and the very verse they lean on answers them. John also prayed that he would prosper and be in health even as his soul prospered (3 John 1:2), which puts the state of the soul first and makes the rest follow it.

What he actually did is set down without decoration. He did faithfully whatever he did to the brethren and to strangers, and they bore witness of his charity before the whole congregation (3 John 1:5-6). Those men had gone out for the Name’s sake, taking nothing of the Gentiles, so we ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth (3 John 1:7-8). Bringing them forward on their journey after a godly sort means paying the road, feeding them, and sending them on able to keep working. This is the plain law of the body: given to hospitality, distributing to the necessity of the saints (Romans 12:13), continuing in brotherly love and not forgetful to entertain strangers (Hebrews 13:1-2). Christ himself set the price on it: he that receives you receives me, and he that receives me receives him that sent me, and even a cup of cold water given in the name of a disciple does not lose its reward (Matthew 10:40-42).
judgmentFull: John’s word over him is beloved, and the charge attached is the standard he is to keep: follow not that which is evil, but that which is good, because he that does good is of God, and he that does evil has not seen God (3 John 1:11). In the same short letter Demetrius is given a good report of all men and of the truth itself (3 John 1:12), so the commendation is not flattery, it is testimony the congregation could verify. The setting matters. John, the apostle who walked with Christ, is writing as a father to a household, the way Paul called Timothy his own son in the faith and Titus his own son after the common faith, and told the Corinthians that though they had ten thousand instructors they had not many fathers, for he had begotten them through the gospel (1 Timothy 1:2; Titus 1:4; 1 Corinthians 4:15). Gaius is not praised for rank; there is no office named for him. He kept the brethren moving, paid their way forward, and had the whole congregation testify to it. The reward Christ named for that work is the one that is never lost.

cases.name: Diotrephes
cases.charge: Loving the preeminence; prating against the apostle with malicious words; casting the brethren out of the church
cases.summary: John wrote to the congregation, but Diotrephes, who loved to have the preeminence among them, received them not (3 John 1:9). John said that if he came he would remember the deeds: prating against them with malicious words, refusing to receive the brethren, forbidding those who would, and casting them out of the congregation (3 John 1:10). No sentence is pronounced; John gives the rule instead, to follow not that which is evil but that which is good (3 John 1:11).
offenseFull: The teaching will not let the verse pass lightly. This was a man the apostles themselves had set up, an overseer over a congregation, and the men he would not receive had walked with Christ, eaten with him, and been taught by him. The sin is named as covetousness, and not of money or a garment: he coveted power. He wanted to be the top teacher in Israel and to be known as number one, and he could not work with anybody who might be greater or know more than he did. Zimri had the same spirit and killed a drunken king to sit on the throne, and then destroyed the whole house of Baasha (1 Kings 16:8-12). Diotrephes did not receive the apostles because he thought he was over them.

John lists the deeds. Prating against the apostles with malicious words is verbal abuse and name calling, the same evil that fills the internet now, men who learned a few scriptures running their mouths at the men who taught them. Refusing the brethren, forbidding them that would, and casting people out of the congregation is what it looks like on the ground (3 John 1:10). A man like this builds a clique out of the brothers who will not question him, raises them up, and pushes away the ones who come asking from the scriptures; the clique keeps evil quiet in the midst and the whole thing turns into partiality. Then, when brothers are sent to check on a school, he tells them today is not a good day, come back another time, and any member who goes over his head is put out. Paul warned the overseers of it at Miletus: after his departing grievous wolves would enter in, not sparing the flock, and of their own selves men would arise speaking perverse things to draw away disciples after them (Acts 20:28-30).
judgmentFull: John pronounces no sentence on him. He gives the congregation the rule instead: follow not that which is evil, but that which is good; he that does good is of God, but he that does evil has not seen God (3 John 1:11). The standard for a leader is the one Christ set. The princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion and the great ones authority, but it shall not be so among us; whoever will be great shall be the minister, and whoever will be chief shall be the servant (Matthew 20:25-27). He that is greatest among you shall be your servant, and the man who exalts himself shall be abased while the man who humbles himself shall be exalted (Matthew 23:11-12). Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall (Proverbs 16:18).

The answer the teaching keeps returning to is that there is only one preeminent. Christ is the head of the body, the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence (Colossians 1:18). Not the bishop, not the captain, not Diotrephes. Gamaliel’s test applies to every man who rises up boasting himself to be somebody: Theudas drew four hundred after him and was slain, Judas of Galilee drew much people and perished, and all that obeyed them were scattered and brought to nothing, because if the work is of men it comes to nothing, and if it is of God it cannot be overthrown (Acts 5:34-39). Cursed is the man that trusts in man and makes flesh his arm (Jeremiah 17:5), so the men who followed such a leader away from the scriptures carry their own judgment. And the class sets him among the hirelings: the hireling is not the shepherd, the sheep are not his own, so he sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, because he cares not for the sheep (John 10:12-13). The brethren he shut out were the very strangers the body is commanded to entertain (Hebrews 13:2).
